     Acknowledgements.
     This work started off when the author was nearing the end of his first year as a Graduate Student at
Stanford under Brian Conrad. It took nearly 12 years to assemble. Brian Conrad and Ravi Vakil were in the
process of making arrangements for me to return to Stanford for a year to finish the polishing of the paper.
     In light of the current climate I am being advised to release the current version as it is. The math is
complete, and only filling in some writing remains on several parts across this long paper. The plan was to
take a year of doing just this, with Brian Conrad helping me completing the task of polishing and improving
the exposition.
     The introduction itself is unfinished and will be soon replaced by a proper one, and the plan will continue
as stated above.
     I have included excerpts from a letter to Peter Sarnak that was sent to him mid October 2026, containing
an overview of all the methods. Brian Conrad and I went visiting him at IAS last Sunday, for a four and a
half hour long blackboard discussion with him.
     Brian Conrad and I are aware of several glitches here and there that I was in the process of addressing on
the way to completing the typewriting. The ideas are however all here, and many of the chapters are already
fairly stable. The excerpts from the letter to Sarnak explain the overall strategy (generality: all number fields,
all unitary Hecke characters).
     If any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace
and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.

    Alessandro

       Notation and terminology.
       We denote by Π the set of all prime numbers. We denote by Q the field of rational numbers.
       We reserve the letter F for finite field extensions of Q, and denote by [F : Q] the degree of the extension.
We refer to finite field extensions of Q as number fields. We denote by OF the ring of integers of F , i.e. the
normalization of Z in F , a finitely generated free (or “finite free”, for brevity) Z-module of rank [F : Q].
       We adopt the lexicon customarily used within Number Theory and refer to equivalence classes of absolute
values (in the sense of [CF, Ch.II,§2]) on F as “places”. We denote by ΣF the set of all non-trivial places F .
       To a prime ideal p of the ring of integers of F , we will associate the p-adic absolute value on F , denoted
| · |p . In particular, to a prime number p we will associate the p-adic absolute value.
       For a non-trivial place of F , written “v”, we denote by | · |v the corresponding normalized absolute value on
F (in the sense of [CF, Ch.II,p.51] if v is finite, and induced by the Euclidean absolute value on R, respectively
the square of the Euclidean absolute value on C, if v is infinite).
       We refer to the absolute values on F corresponding to the prime ideals of OF as the finite places of F ,
and denote by ΣF,f the set of all finite places of F .
       We refer to the Archimedean absolute values as the infinite places of F , and denote by S∞ the (finite) set
of all infinite places of F .
       We reserve the letter v to denote the arbitrary place of F , and write Fv for the v-adic completion of F ,
by which we mean the completion of the field F with respect to the topology induced by any absolute value
corresponding to v: if v corresponds to the prime ideal p, this is, up to isomorphism of topological fields, the
p-adic field Fp , a finite extension of the field of p-adic rationals Qp , where p is the residue characteristic of Fp .
We write v | p to mean that Fv is an extension of Qp .
       If v is Archimedean, then Fv is, up to isomorphism of topological fields, either the field R of real numbers
or the field C of complex numbers. We call v “real” or “complex”, accordingly.
       For v a finite place of F , we denote by OFv the subset defined by the condition {x ∈ Fv : |x|v ≤ 1}, i.e.
the unit ball within the metric space Fv . We denote by O×      Fv the “unit circle” within Fv , i.e. the subset defined
by the condition {x ∈ Fv : |x|v = 1}. This is the unit group of OFv .
       We denote by AF the adele ring of the number field F . We recall that AF is the topological ring obtained
as the restricted product
                                                          Y
                                                    AF =     (Fv , Rv )
                                                          c
                                                          v
topologized with the restricted product topology, where v varies over all the places of F , including the
Archimedean places, and with Rv = OFv for every finite place v, and Rv = {0} for every infinite place v.
     We denote by GL1 (AF ) the group of units of AF topologized with the idelic topology, i.e. the topology
induced by the anti-diagonal map GL1 (AF ) → AF × AF given by x 7→ (x, x−1 ). We refer to GL1 (AF ) as the
idele group of the number field F .
     We denote by
                                           | · |F : GL1 (AF ) → R>0
                                          Q
the idelic norm, defined on GL1 (AF ) as v | · |v , where the product is indexed by all the places of F .
     For a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, we denote by Gb the Pontryagin dual group, the Hausdorff
locally compact abelian group of all continuous characters χ : G → U(1) endowed with the compact-open
topology. We refer to Gb as the “dual group”.

        • S(G) the space of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G.

          space of I-exponentially decaying Schwartz-Bruhat functions, i.e. ϕ ∈ C ∞ (G) such that | · |aG ϕ ∈ S(G)
          for all a ∈ I. We topologize SI (G) with the locally convex inductive limit topology of the nuclear
          Fréchet topologies on SI (k, G) for k ⊂ G varying over the compact subgroups of G whose orthogonal
          k⊥ ⊂ G  b is compactly generated. The topology on SI (k, G) is the subspace topology induced by the

       • For I = R, we denote SI (G) by SE (G), and call this the space of exponentially decaying Schwartz-
         Bruhat functions on G.
       • Under the above assumptions on G, SI (G) is a strict LF-space. Nuclear (this is used to get good
         properties of topological tensor products and to get a handle on continuous duals of quotient linear
         maps, such that they are linear topological embeddings; nuclearity often ensures that quotient maps
         lift bounded sets, which is the crux of the matter behind the good behavior of the continuous duals
         of quotient maps), complete (used for vector valued integration), Montel (used for the Heine-Borel
         property: to get constants in some estimates that are uniform on bounded sets of functions).

    Even with s = 0, these Hilbert spaces were never considered in the literature. In particular, they were
never considered by Connes nor Meyer, in any instance.

     We refer to WIs,2 (G) as the Hardy-Sobolev space of G with base I.
     If I = {0}, then WIs,2 (G) agrees with the Sobolev space W s,2 (G) introduced in the paper.
     The topology on WIs,2 (G) is also generated by the finitely many semi-norms:
                                   ||ϕ||α,k := ||∂zk M (ϕ)(z)||L2 (α+iR,dx) , α = a, b
for all 0 ≤ k ≤ s/2 (assume that s is an even integer), i.e. by integration of the Mellin transform M (ϕ) and
some of its holomorphic derivatives along the edge of the vertical strip CI of bounded width.

                              1.2. Into the method: orbital Schauder bases
    Let L(s, χ) be the completed Hecke L-function of χ ∈ CcF . We denote by Lf (s, χ) the finite Hecke
L-function, i.e. for s ∈ C>1 :                   Y

where ΣF,f is the set of all finite places of F .
   The solution amounts to the following:

    1.2.1. Fundamental Divisor Exact Sequence. Consider the following situation initially envisioned
by Connes, but, contrary to what Connes does (who works, instead, with L2 -completions throughout) working
with the Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces:
                                        1/2
                             0 → | · |F H0,cont (F × , S0 (AF )) → SE (CF ) → HF → 0
and each of their CF1 -isotypes, i.e.
                             1/2
                     0 → | · |F H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S0 (AF )) → SE (CF )(χ|CF1 ) → HF (χ|CF1 ) → 0
these latter being nuclear Fréchet spaces.
    The Mellin transform turns the second exact sequence into (forgetting about the uniformly Schwartz
condition defining Schwartz-Bergman spaces):
                                                                            Y
           0 → L(s + 1/2, χ)((s + 1/2)(s − 1/2))δ O(C) ∩ AS(C) → AS(C) →          CN (z) → 0
                                                                                     z:L(z,χ)=0

where N (ρ) is the multiplicity of ρ as a zero of L(s, χ). Here δ = 0 if χ|CF1 ̸= 1, and δ = 1 otherwise. This
connection to the L-function requires all the Structure Theorems, and use of known analytic properties of the
L-function (convexity bound, existence of a sequence of horizontal segments across the critical strip on which
the reciprocal of Lf (s, χ) is defined and grows at most polynomially in the absolute ordinate).
    This is the reason why I called this the “divisor exact sequence”: it mirrors the global sections of
                                              0 → OX (−D) → OX → OD → 0
for the Stein space X = C, and D = div(L(s + 1/2, χ)((s + 1/2)(s − 1/2))δ ).

    Considering these spaces systematically is already new. Only Meyer did so to some limited extent.

    The following is completely new and was, instead, never done before.

    Reducing to the S-local calculation of CF kS,φ (x, x) dµ(x) is what this work is all about. Once the

    The ingredients in the S-local calculation (as present already in the papers of Connes and Meyer) are:
      (1) The S-adelic Fourier transform: we need to transform kS,φ (x, y) in the y-variable. The construction
          will give that kS,φ factors through a kernel on GL1 (AF,S )×CF with the same diagonal mass (skewered

          the diagonal, into |x|2a
                                F,S . If a = 1/2 exactly, then this is |x|F,S , which will multiply the multiplicative
          Tamagawa measure µS on GL1 (AF,S ) to give the additive measure νS , up to a positive multiplicative
          constant.
              This forces the 1/2 in the very statement of GRH. Connes’ expectation on the S-adelic Fourier
          transform playing this role and being related to the necessity of the 1/2 in the very statement of
          GRH, is therefore correct.
      (2) A version of known calculations of Connes from his paper from 19981.

     1.2.4. Poles of the S-idelic Zeta functions.

     1.2.6. Periodic orbits and fixed points.

    1.2.7. Orbital bases and orbital traces. From this moment onwards, all techniques, ideas and results,
are original and never even partially present in prior work (as was the case in §2, apart from §2.3).

    We explain where the Schauder bases are found, and how to think of them. We will make a brief analogy
with Sarnak’s paper on long horocycles to highlight periodic orbits and fixed points and their role. This leads
to the identification of those elements of Deninger’s Program that are correct, and why there is no 3-manifold,
nor foliation, nor foliated cohomology theory.

1.3. Orbital decomposition of the lifted convolution kernel, and the orbital pieces of the kernel
    In this section we explain the main ingredients that enter the method to reduce the calculation of the
diagonal mass of the global geometric kernel, to the calculation of the diagonal mass of an “S-local piece” of it.
By “S-local” we will always be referring to the property of the kernel being supported over
                                                               b×
                                                 GL1 (AF,S ) × OΣF −S

and factoring through GL1 (AF,S ).
    We are, for the moment, giving for granted that the kernel being referred to is a scalar-valued function,
measurable, enjoying certain additional integrability properties inherited from the spectral kernel, of two
variables on
                                             GL1 (AF ) × CF
even though the global geometric kernel is given to us as a scalar-valued function on CF × CF .
    This is one of the aspects we will be discussing: how to lift such kernel with respect to the first of the two
variables, from a scalar-valued function on CF × CF to a scalar-valued function on GL1 (AF ) × CF .

   1.3.1. Indentations and skewered diagonal mass. In this subsection we illustrate how to “lift” a
measurable kernel function
                                    k(x, y) : X × X → C
when X is a topological quotient space Y /H equipped with a regular Radon measure µ, and H is a group of
measure-preserving transformations acting freely and properly by homeomorphisms.
     We will be immediately specializing to the case X = G, for G a second countable Hausdorff locally compact
abelian group, H a closed subgroup. For the purposes of this work, G will be GL1 (AF ) or GL1 (AF,S ), and H
will be either F × , O×                 1             1
                      F,S , or GL1 (AF ) , GL1 (AF,S ) .
     One key structure that the situation will come equipped with is that of fundamental domains. We start
off with a brief review of the general recipe to lift functions from the quotient G/H to G preserving certain
support conditions.
     Let G be a second countable Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, µG a choice of Haar measure on
G, H ⊂ G a closed subgroup, µH a choice of Haar measure on H. We call µG/H the quotient Haar measure
on G/H. We denote by π : G → G/H the continuous quotient homomorphism. There exists a function
u0 : G → C satisfying the following properties:
      (1) u0 is real-valued, nonnegative, continuous.
      (2) Let K be an arbitrary compact subset of G. Then the intersection of the support of u0 with
          π −1 (π(K)) is compact.

     We need the following “two-variable” complements around H-indentations on G. It is useful to discuss it

     Let G be a second countable Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, µG a choice of Haar measure on G,

     Assume H is discrete, and µH is the counting measure.
     Let µG/H be the unique quotient measure on G/H.
     We denote by π : G → G/H the continuous quotient homomorphism. Assume there exists a fundamental
domain D for the continuous left-translation action by H on G.
     Now recall that a general version of Lebesgue’s Differentiation Theorem exists for Hausdorff locally
compact abelian groups G. It rests upon an analog of the Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Theorem and the
statement are directly analogous to those of the classical Theorems in the case of the real line and Euclidean
spaces, so long as an analog of the closed balls that we find in Euclidean spaces can be found in G.
     We call a sequence of Borel subsets Uk ⊂ G that axiomatize properties satisfied by the closed balls in
Euclidean spaces, a D′ -sequence. Terminology borrowed from Hewitt-Ross4. The axioms defining D′ -sequences
are recalled in the main text. In our cases of interest, G will always carry such sequences by direct construction
(using continuous sections to the idelic and S-idelic norms).
     Say D is a fundamental domain for the H-action on G.
     Assume that {Uk }k≥0 is a D′ -sequence for G such that Uk ⊂ D, and Uk is a relatively compact open
symmetric unit-neighborhood for all integers k ≥ 0. Then, upon defining U k := π(Uk ) for each integer k ≥ 0,
{U k }k≥0 is a D′ -sequence for G/H.
     We define smoothenings over G × G and G/H × G/H using the D′ -sequences {Uk × Uk }k≥0 for G × G
and {U k × U k }k≥0 for G/H × G/H. Namely, for u : G → C a locally µG -integrable function on G, we define

     This implies that Lf (s, χ), and hence L(s, χ), has no zeros over C>1/2 , and likewise for L(s, χ), so by the
functional equation the same holds for L(s, χ) over C<1/2 .
     This completes the overview of how to deduce the main results on the location of the zeros of L(s, χ),
from the Trace Formula.

    1.4.6. Weil’s Positivity Criterion is not used. This is reminiscent of the avoidance in Deligne’s
proof of the Weil Conjectures of the positivity aspect of the intersection pairing.

    Positivity of the Weil functional from Weil’s Explicit Formulas is not addressed: rather, the trace formula
holds on a large enough class of test functions enabling us to approximate the holomorphic family of piece-wise
smooth functions φs (t) := ts for t > 1, φs (t) := 0 for t ∈ (0, 1), and φ(1/2) := 1/2, to obtain information
about
                                                     L′f (s, χ)
                                                                .
                                                     Lf (s, χ)
    Indeed, the trace formula can only be proved for test functions φ on CF (i.e. elements φ of D(CF )) such
that φ(CF1 ) = 0. In fact, the trace calculation is performed for test functions supported over [1 + ε, +∞) for
some ε > 0 fixed, arbitrary. The Trace Formula is then extended to the test functions supported over (0, 1 − ε]
for 0 < ε < 1 fixed, arbitrary, and then further extended to the test functions such that φ(CF1 ) = 0 by a
continuity argument.

    The condition φ(CF1 ) = 0 cannot be removed before GRH is proved. The Trace Formula indeed is valid
on any test function (even without this vanishing condition) but this can only be proved a posteriori, once
novel information on the zeros, deduced from the Trace Formula when φ(CF1 ) = 0, is incorporated into Weil’s
Explicit Formulas.


    1.4.7. Non-vanishing of the finite Hecke L-function Lf (s, χ) on the line 1 + iR is used.
This is analogous to when Deligne, in the process of proving the Riemann Hypothesis for the L-functions of
smooth proper varieties over finite fields, had to prove the non-vanishing on the boundary of their critical strips.

    For example, assume S is a finite set of places containing all the Archimedean places. Then the transition

       • There exists a sequence of ordinates {Tk }k∈Z such that lim→±∞ Tk = ± + ∞, such that the reciprocal

         seen by means of analogs of arguments of Titchmarsh on the Riemann Zeta function.
       • 1/Lf (s, χ) grows at most polynomially over 1 + iR.

     1.4.9. The Orbital Bases are the crux of the matter. They allow to bridge the spectral side to the
S-local piece of the Trace Calculation.
     Because they enable us to write down “on the basis”, much as one does in linear algebra, the orbital pieces
of the kernel (after one splits the global convolution kernel into a sum of pieces dictated by the stratification
of the ideles by non-Archimedean local “units-versus-balls”, as in §4, i.e. write their truncations down as
32                                         CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION


trace-class limits of explicit finite rank operators).

     As the cutoff tends to +∞, the limit value of the trace is computed by summing diagonal elements on
Jordan blocks, and the Poisson Summation Formula gives the epxlict answer. For all but finitely many prime
residue characteristics, the orbital traces associated to those primes are all zero!

    The Trace Calculation then reduces to Connes’ “S-local Trace Formula” from his paper from 1998 (some-
thing very similar).

                                   s,2
     This can all be done within W[−a,a] (CF ) for any fixed real number a > 0, and so we can compute the
                                  s,2
spectral side by staying within W[−a,a] (CF ) too.


    1.4.10. The orbital bases are the principal tool to bridge the spectral side to the S-local
piece of the geometric side. They reveal a massive cancellation phenomenon of the mass of the global
kernel along the diagonal, concentrating all of the geometric side into the S-local piece, for S large enough
and fixed (the calculation is done “character by character”, and S depends on the test function φ and the
character, and it is always assumed to satisfy Pic(OF,S ) = 1).


    1.4.11. A version of this deconstruction method of mine resting on the bases. This went under
the name of “infinite excision” approximately a decade ago, when we were about to visit Princeton. The ideas
back then were immature in my head and it became clear that it would take much more time and work to
bring all of it into focus.


                             1.5. On the programs of Connes and Deninger
     1.5.1. Relation to Connes’ and Meyer’s work. The calculations in Connes’ S-local trace formula
are used in the end to compute the diagonal mass of kS,φ . Observations from Connes’ paper are also reviewed
and much expanded. His “spectral interpretation” is recovered as the special case I = {0} as discussed in the
section on Notation (with our Sobolev degree s being Connes’ δ in his paper).
     Connes never tried to use the locally convex spaces of Schwartz-Bruhat functions and θ-functions that are
the backbone of this work. In his paper, they are never considered.
     Meyer considered SI (G) and the spaces of S-local and global θ-functions, but only through their bornology
(an axiomatization of bounded sets in a locally convex topological vector space). He never established anything
on their isotypes, let alone defining and studying Schauder bases on the various S-local and global orbital
subquotients.
     Meyer’s method of trace calculation rests upon operator-theoretic Euler products which only converge
when the function spaces are given the bornologies associated to the locally convex topology on SE (CF ) and
H0,cont (F × , S(AF )), rather than coarser topologies associated to Sobolev or Hardy-Sobolev norms. It follows
that in Meyer’s work all the zeros, irrespective of their location, contribute to the spectral side of his trace
formula the same way as they already do in Weil’s own Explicit Formulas, i.e. through point-evaluation of the
Mellin transform at the zero, shifted by 1/2 to the left.
     My method of trace calculation instead rests on leveraging the bases to compute the orbital kernels and
get their traces, while identifying the effect each such kernel has by means of an approximate, weaker version of
the Euler product convergence Meyer used (which for us comes down to a much simpler convergence assertion
on relatively compact subsets of CF , caused by the rapid decay condition on Schwartz-Bruhat functions on the
                               1.7. EXCERPTS FROM A LETTER TO PETER SARNAK                                       33


adeles). We get compensation from the bases, and the method works within WIs,2 (CF ) (isotype by isotype)
instead of requiring to work with respect to the topology of SE (CF ).
    The idea of bases to write down pieces of a deconstructed global kernel, reducing the calculation of its
diagonal mass to the calculation of the diagonal mass of an S-local piece of the kernel, which is the computed
using a version of Connes’ S-local trace formula, is novel and was never considered in any form nor part,
before.
     1.5.2. Relation to Deninger’s work. Periodic orbits and fixed points are confirmed to exist, their role
clarified through the role of the Mellin transform: it is similar to that of the periodic cylinders featuring in
Sarnak’s paper on long horocycles.
     The local traces that Deninger contemplated in his paper on Lefschetz trace formulas and the Explicit
Formulas are indeed all realized as actual trace formulas using the orbital subquotients of the spaces of local
and global θ-functions and the Schauder bases on each.
     The visualization resting on the orbits helps to organize the trace calculation. Logically, it is not needed.

                               1.7. Excerpts from a letter to Peter Sarnak
    1.7.1. Why “yes” for number fields, and “no” for function fields. The short answer is: because
of the presence of Archimedean places (and, ultimately, the Q-linear independence of the logarithms of the
prime numbers, which plays a pervasive role sometimes explicitly and sometimes behind the scenes in many of
the turns throughout my paper).
       • They make all the function spaces involved far more interesting. At a basic level, as is well-known,
         they make the connected components of the Riemann surface of idelic quasi-characters be simply
         connected, contrary to the case of global function fields of positive characteristic where “vertical
         strips” are instead annuli of finite area.
              By far the most important difference directly affects the calculation in Caveat ??: let f ∈ S(AF )
         be any Schwartz-Bruhat function, with F a number field. Assume f (0) = fb(0) = 0 (so as to remove
         the poles of its idelic zeta integral in the sense of Tate’s thesis, extended analytically using the
         functional equation [CF, Ch.XV,Thm.4.4.1]). Then the function
                                                    X
                                                       f (ξg)
                                                   ξ∈F ×

         of g ∈ CF obtained by periodizing f over the F × -orbits on the ideles GL1 (AF ) turns out to be
         Schwartz-Bruhat on CF (this holds also for F a global function field of positive characteristic) but if
         this function of g is not identically zero then it is never compactly supported.
             This is ultimately caused by the Γ-factors of the idelic zeta function associated to f (use Stirling’s
         asymptotics combined with the convexity bound, and pass them through the lens of the Paley-Wiener
         Theorem).
       • One instrument that is pervasive in the first seven chapters of my paper, and occurs frequently, is
         the use of diagonal quotients of the form:
(1.7.1.1)                                        (RN × A)/Γ0
            for A an open subgroup of a locally profinite second-countable topological group and Γ0 ⊂ RN × A
            a discrete subgroup.
34                                          CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION


             These quotients (termed “solenoids” sometimes in the literature) have the advantage that one
         can use the diagonal action of Γ0 (which can be either F × , or a discrete group of S-units, or
         subgroups of these, for example) to transfer displacements in the “A-variable” under group actions,
         to displacements in the Euclidean variables.
             This is used all the time to make explicit constructions of functions with certain properties,
         to prove statements such as “the subquotient of the following topological vector space carries a
         topological basis satisfying the following conditions”.
             Quotients as in (1.7.1.1) are unavailable in the case F is a global function field, and the great
         advantages of having them throughout are lost.
       • I would like to offer an analogy, to guide intuition as to why in the number field case the methods in
         my paper carry much more information than their positive characteristic analogs.
             For F = k(X) with X a smooth projective geometrically irreducible curve over a finite field k,
         and G a connected reductive group over k, mere double coset spaces such as
(1.7.1.2)                                         G(F )\G(AF )/K
            are certainly useful for some purposes (such as in the function field analogue of Tate’s thesis, and the
            work of Godement-Jacquet on automorphic L-functions of unit groups of simple algebras that can be
            done uniformly over all global fields), but usually these spaces require richer geometric structure
            such as identifications of the form
                                            BunG (k) ≃ G(F )\G(AF )/K
         (giving access to the moduli stack BunG of G-bundles on the curve X, and then function spaces as
         sections of ℓ-adic sheaves) to get deeper results on global L-functions (e.g., the works of Laurent
         and Vincent Lafforgue). Consider, specifically, L. Lafforgue’s proof of Global Langlands for GLn .
         Intersection cohomology and Deligne’s methods from Weil II are used as an input in an essential
         manner. Weil II gives estimates on the Frobenius eigenvalues on the intersection cohomology of the
         moduli stack of Shtukas, in the process of accessing the Converse Theorem. The point that I am
         making is that deeper insight into automorphic L-functions and representations in the function field
         case, necessitates techniques from Algebraic Geometry, aimed at compensating for the much-too-poor
         geometric structure of the topological double quotients in (1.7.1.2).
              However, for F a number field, the double coset spaces in (1.7.1.2) are perfectly good! There is
         no need to imbue them with more structure.
              This is thanks to the Archimedean places. In the presence of Archimedean places, the double
         coset spaces from (1.7.1.2) already carry rich function spaces of smooth functions. Functional analysis
         and harmonic analysis are much less trivial and lead to flavorful results, all enabled by accessing
         differential geometry and Riemannian geometry through the Archimedean components of these spaces.
         With the non-Archimedean places serving the role of “transversals”, much as in the book by Moore
         and Schochet [MS] on global analysis on foliated spaces and in the book Geometric Asymptotics by
         Guillemin and Sternberg [GS].
              A similar phenomenon is at play here: for F a global function field of positive characteristic,
         the function spaces that are directly analogous to those arising in my paper do not carry enough
         information to lead to anything more than an analog of the Lefschetz trace formula, which, as you
         know, even for curves is insufficient to establish the Weil bound. For F a number field, they are
         much more interesting and intricate, and several phenomena specific to number fields spring into
         action. One of them is the subject of the next bullet point.
       • The Q-linear independence of the logarithms of the prime numbers (a phenomenon that has no analog
         in positive characteristic, with comparable strength) pervades the choices of normed-topologies,
                                 1.7. EXCERPTS FROM A LETTER TO PETER SARNAK                                       35


            defining the completions in which the trace calculation that proves the main Theorem of the paper
            is carried out.
                 How? The following phenomenon gives you an example of how. It is a simple consequence of a
            result from my paper, and the Q-linear independence of the logarithms of the prime numbers is used
            in an essential manner throughout:

                 Theorem 1.7.1.1 (On polar multiplicities - a consequence of a Theorem from Chapter 7). Let F
            be a number field, χ ∈ C     cF a continuous (unitary) character. Denote by L(s, χ) the Hecke L-function,
            and by Lv (χv | · |sv ) its local Euler factor at v, for any place v of F .
             (1) For v1 , v2 two finite places of F with distinct residue characteristics, the local Euler factors
                 Lv1 (χv1 | · |sv1 ) and Lv2 (χv2 | · |sv2 ) have at most one pole in common.
             (2) If χ = χ0 | · |sF0 for s0 ∈ C and χ0 algebraic then assuming Schanuel’s Conjecture, there exists
                 at most one point s1 of the complex s-plane (namely, s1 = −i Im(s0 )) such that s1 is a pole of
                 Lv (χv | · |sv ) for infinitely many finite places v of F .
             (3) If χ is of finite order then the assertion in (2) holds unconditionally and s1 = 0.

                 This Theorem has nothing to do with the zeros of the Hecke L-function, and is used to select
            normed-topologies on the function spaces of interest (such as Sobolev topologies of Sobolev degree
            at least 2[F : Q]) to ensure that certain “coefficient functionals” are continuous, thanks to results
            surrounding Theorem 1.7.1.1. These comprise the (dual bases of the) Schauder bases that Brian
            mentioned over the phone, and that enable the trace calculation that leads to the main Theorem of
            the paper.
                 Theorem 1.7.1.1 has no useful analog for F a function field of positive characteristic.

   1.7.2. Highlights. The main highlights that I would like to convey, for then stating and outlining the
main results face to face, are:
       • Weil’s Positivity Criterion is not used. The Trace Formula can only be proved under an
         additional assumption on the test function φ ∈ D(CF ):
(1.7.2.1)                                            φ(CF1 ) = 0.
         This assumption cannot be removed. It stays there until after GRH is deduced from the Trace
         Formula. It is forced on us by two divergence phenomena that can only be resolved by assuming
         that (1.7.2.1) holds.
             Weil’s Positivity Criterion uses test functions of the form φ = ψ1 ∗ ψ2 , where ψ2 (g) = ψ1 (g −1 ),
         and the only φ of this form that satisfies (1.7.2.1) is identically zero.
             The fact that GRH does not follow from positivity of the Weil functional feels analogous to how
         Deligne through the use of families avoided having to address positivity of the intersection pairing.
       • Properties of the Hecke L-function on the 1-line (including the non-vanishing) are used
         as an input throughout. Mostly to propagate Theorems from “S-local” (where we have access to
                                                                                         Q
         additional flexibility; e.g., smooth compactly supported functions on GL1 ( v∈S Fv ) extend by zero
         to elements of S( v∈S Fv ), which fails globally) to “global”.
                           Q

             This feels analogous to how Deligne too had to prove that the L-functions of a smooth projective
         geometrically irreducible variety over a finite field have no zeros at the edge of the critical strip, before
         employing the “tensor power trick” to enlarge the zero-free region and asymptotically maximize it.
       • The Geometric Side of the Trace Formula drives everything. The Spectral Side is only
         computed at the very end, once the choice of normed-topology has been made, pinned down by the
         ingredients that are necessary to compute the Geometric Side. In other words, the zeros play no
         role in selecting the linear topological environment in which the Trace Formula is proved. They
36                                         CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION


          are never used as an input anywhere, nor to make any construction. They remain “passive”, so to
          speak. They are “victims” of the topology of the normed environment. In other words, we endow
          certain locally convex spaces arising from Tate’s thesis with normed topologies chosen by looking
          at what ingredients are truly necessary to perform the calculation of the Geometric
          Side of the Trace Formula. The zeros play no role here.
              The relevant topologies turn out to be the subspace topologies induced by each of the norms

                 The entire paper itself is about the Geometric Side of the Trace Formula only. It is about
         spelling out all the ingredients for the Geometric Side at the locally convex level first (the first seven
         chapters of the paper) and then passing them through the lens of coarser normed topologies. Only
         at the very end, once the calculation of the Geometric Side of the Trace Formula is performed by
         working intrinsically within the || · ||a,b -completions and closures, we observe that, therefore, we can
         keep going and compute the Spectral Side too while remaining within the || · ||a,b -completion. The
         normed topology of the environment now prevents some zeros from expressing themselves because
         their point-evaluation functionals and derivatives of those will not be continuous with respect to the
         || · ||a,b -normed topology, depending on whether such functionals are supported on C(−a,a) , on the
         edges of C(−a,a) (in which case they are not counted with their full multiplicity; only multiplicity up
         to the smallest integer less than or equal to |b − 1|/2), or outside C[−a,a] altogether.
                 The takeaway is a collection of analogs of the Explicit Formulas of Weil in which the side
         involving the places of F (finite and Archimedean) and the poles (the Geometric Side) is identical to
         that from the Explicit Formulas, and the side involving the zeros (the Spectral Side) is not.
                 The degenerate case a = 0 does not lead to a Trace Formula anymore, but it does appear to lead
         to some information on the multiplicities of the zeros as outlined in the next section (so long as we
         choose b ≥ 2mχ , where mχ is the supremum over all prime numbers p of the highest pole-order of
         the poles of the product of all the local Euler factors at the finite places of residue characteristic p; in
         particular, b ≥ 2[F : Q] qualifies). As Brian mentioned over the phone, conclusions on multiplicities
         cannot be obtained through the trace formula. In the next section, however, I do mention that from
         the extremal case a = 0 and b ≥ 2mχ , we can extrapolate conclusions on the multiplicities at least in
         the form of expectations (which I had yet to discuss with Brian, and only briefly touched upon them
         with him about a year ago). These have yet to be fully worked out in writing, and are reserved for
                                 1.7. EXCERPTS FROM A LETTER TO PETER SARNAK                                    37


            sequel work (it takes time, it is unnecessary right now, and it is not a low-hanging fruit). I plan to
            return on this only after all is said and done. No need now.


    1.7.3. Outline of a sanity check: the multiplicities of the zeros. As mentioned in the last bullet
point of the previous section, the extremal case of the methods (the case a = 0 in (1.8.2.2)) leads to information
on the multiplicities of the zeros.

     This will not be a part of my paper, and it is reserved for a sequel. I worked out enough of
it for myself to arrive at the conclusions below, aiming to get to conclusions that I could test against the
existing literature. What follows therefore constitutes an example taken from a class of sanity checks that I
put the methods through. Once again, allow me to be as clear as I can be: I have not fully worked out all
details for this part, but only enough to arrive at a conclusion in the form of expectations, so
that I could test it against the literature. I can sketch what I have in mind for this, in person.
The takeaways are as follows:
       • For a = 0, no trace formula can be proved for any b ≥ 0 (see (1.8.2.2) for this notation). The
         obstruction is already contained in Theorem 1.7.1.1, as we now explain.
             Let F be a number field, χ ∈ C cF a continuous (unitary) character. We define, for each prime
         number p:

         grows unboundedly at at most one point of the connected component of the Riemann surface of idelic

         repeated pole” exists. As it happens, in such examples the central zero of L(s, χ0 | · |F    ), for w the

       • If a trace formula was provable for a = 0 and b ≥ 2mχ then it would also lead to a bound on the
         multiplicities of all zeros: their multiplicities would turn out to be bounded above by mχ . In light of
         the previous bullet point, this is false by means of examples. In particular, we must expect to find
         an obstruction to the method of trace calculation!
              And indeed, we find it: the infinitely repeated pole to the finite Euler products turns out to be
         the obstruction. How, I will explain face to face. In other words, the fact that the trace formula
         cannot be proved in this extremal version of the methods is itself a sanity check.
       • However, even without a full trace formula, we can still draw some conclusions about the multiplicities.

             Although a full trace formula cannot be proved in the extremal situation a = 0 (not even if

             The outcome that profiles itself is the following:

             Expectation 1.7.1 (On the multiplicities of the zeros). Let F be a number field, χ0 an algebraic
         Hecke character of weight w. Then:
                                                                             w/2
         (1) Conditionally on Schanuel’s Conjecture, all zeros of L(s, χ| · |F ) except at most the central
             zero s = 1/2 have multiplicity bounded above by mχ .
         (2) If χ0 is of finite order (and hence w = 0) then, unconditionally, all zeros of L(s, χ0 ) except at
             most the central zero s = 1/2 have multiplicity bounded above by [F : Q].

             I looked into this extremal case of the methods precisely with the aim of challenging them. The
         outcome is:
           – We expect an obstruction to the trace formula for a = 0 and any b ≥ 0, even for b ≥ 2mχ or
              b ≥ 2[F : Q], due to central zeros with high multiplicities (examples using CM abelian varieties
              through theory of Néron models. Numerical examples usually conditional on BSD), and we find
              one.
           – Nonetheless, we are led to expectations on the multiplicities (the tentative argument will be
              outlined verbally to you face to face). I do not know that Expectation 1.7.1 was ever formulated
              before.
              The question becomes: does Expectation 1.7.1 hold against the existing literature? Close
              inspection (using work of Langlands and Deligne on Weil’s generalization of Artin L-functions,
              to deal with point (1) of Expectation 1.7.1; point (2) is simpler, and relies on invariance of
              formation of the non-abelian L-function of F under induction down to Q, up to inflating the finite
              order Hecke character to the Galois closure F ′ of F ) shows that indeed Expectation 1.7.1 would
              follow from the Grand Simplicity Hypothesis, and it is therefore compatible with it (assuming
              that the L-functions of irreducible continuous finite dimensional complex representations of the
              Weil group of Q are automorphic, as is expected and is known to hold in special cases).
         Note that part (2) of Expectation 1.7.1 for F = Q leads to mχ = [F : Q] = 1.

                      1.8. A view from the sky: from a letter to Peter Sarnak
     1.8.1. The missed trip to Princeton from a decade ago. Towards the end of my first year and
the beginning of my second year as a Graduate Student at Stanford, inspired by p-adic Hodge Theory, the
possibility occurred to me that one could use “Koszul complexes” of entire functions (a modern way to
paraphrase what I was thinking) to make a trace calculation in a vein that would be hybrid between Connes’
dream and Deninger’s.
     It all stemmed from the observation that if F is a number field (with idele class group CF ), χ : CF → C×
is a quasi-character, and S is a finite set of places of F containing all Archimedean places, all places ramified
over Q, and all places at which χ is ramified then for a generic Schwartz-Bruhat function of the form
                                                           O

with fS ∈ S( v∈S Fv ), if we replace 1OFv with 1O× one finite place outside S at a time we would slowly
             Q

“degenerate” f into fS in the sense that on the connected component Ω(χ) of χ in the space of idelic quasi-
characters the local contributions of 1O× ’s (for v ̸∈ S) to the Mellin transform on Ω(χ) are equal to 1 (when
                                        Fv
using the standard Haar measures).
                         1.8. A VIEW FROM THE SKY: FROM A LETTER TO PETER SARNAK                                  39


     At the S-local level, Connes already had a perfectly good technique to compute the relevant trace. His
calculation is a reformulation of a calculation of Weil’s from his papers on the Explicit Formulas, resting on
the observation that a certain additive local Fourier transform of a logarithm function would be expressed
as a principal value arising out of the Residue Theorem applied to the logarithmic derivative of the Hecke
L-function.
     In my eyes, a version of Connes’ S-local calculation is definitive, i.e. at the “S-local level”, it is the right
scenario to hope for indeed. I have come to view parts of the calculations in Connes’ S-local “trace formula”
as his most important contribution (I have a feeling he would get annoyed, if told).
     And so the strategy “degenerate something global into something S-local” seems a good rule of thumb
to follow. This is exactly what Ralf Meyer does in his paper [Me1]: he uses operators which, under Mellin
transform, turn into multiplication operators by finite reciprocal Euler factors. For his method to succeed, he
needs them to converge to infinite reciprocal Euler products (with a few finitely many Euler factors removed).
     This is possible only by working with very fine locally convex strict-LF topologies (or ensuing bornologies,
as he does) and indeed his method of degeneration from global to S-local pans out, and leads to a trace
formula in the vein that Connes was partly hoping for.
     Such topologies, however, render all point-masses (and their derivatives) at all zeros of the Hecke L-
function, continuous, and so the resulting trace formula is just a copy of Weil’s own Explicit Formulas. This
continuity aspect concerning the point-masses and their derivatives at all zeros, is what makes all the zeros
(whatever their location and multiplicity may be) contribute to the spectral side of the trace formula on equal
footing.
     Now look at the situation with our chosen Schwartz-Bruhat function. We choose an enumeration {vk }k≥0
of all the places of F outside S.
     Assume we have fixed a continuous (unitary) character χ ∈ C    cF , and that S contains all the Archimedean
places, all the primes at which χ is ramified, and all the ramified places of F over Q (for other technical
reasons it is also important in the main work to make S big enough to ensure Pic(OF,S ) = 1, but the need for
this isn’t addressed here). Going from f = fS ⊗ (⊗v∈S   / 1OFv ) restricted to the idele group to
                                                           O
(1.8.1.1)                                    f ′ := fS ⊗ ⊗     1O×
                                                                      Fv

                                                            k≥0

as a function on the idele group can either be done one step at a time, or infinitely many steps at a time. This
latter is what Meyer does, roughly speaking.
     Each time we replace 1OFv with 1O× for some k, the effect on the zeta integral of the Schwartz-Bruhat

and so an infinite iteration of this process will converge as an operator (on the quotient of all χ|CF1 -homogeneous

transform by a topology at least as fine as the topology of uniform convergence on all vertical strips of bounded
width of C>1 = {σ > 1} for Z(f, χ| · |sF ), and of C<0 = {σ < 0} for Z(fb, χ| · |1−sF ).
     This is, loosely, what Meyer does: he degenerates a global convolution operator using infinite Euler
products, makes a trace calculation following Connes at the S-local level, and observes that by enlarging S by
a finite amount the “part of the kernel” that he has left behind in the degeneration process contributes zero to
the global trace. Convergence of infinite Euler products is crucial for him to prove this last fact.
     The obstruction to repeating what Meyer does, but by working in normed completions such as the L2 -norm
topology on S(CF ), is that infinite Euler products do not converge absolutely within the critical strip, by
Mertens’ Theorem.
40                                        CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION


    The advantage of proving a global trace formula while working with respect to much coarser normed
topologies as my work does, as opposed to the very fine limit-Fréchet topologies or bornologies that Meyer
has to work with to make infinite Euler product operators converge, is enormous because the spectral side of
such a global trace formula is affected by the choice of topology: not all zeros support point-masses (and their
derivatives) that extend by continuity!
    Mertens’ Theorem is, in my eyes, a herald for GRH. If you clash against it, it means that you are entering
forbidden territory: it means you have to come up with something new.
    What occurred to me is the following: what if instead of doing this wished-for degeneration process from
global to S-local by using an infinite iteration of 1OFv 7→ 1O× to reach (1.8.1.1) (equivalently, to infinitely
                                                       k         Fv
                                                                      k
iterate multiplication by terms as in (1.8.1.2)), which is what Meyer does (I am paraphrasing a lot for him),
we did it one step at a time only?
     What if there is a way to keep track of the loss of information, step by step, instead of going all the way
down straight away? And what if we could compute pieces of the trace step by step, until all that is left is at
the “S-local level”? Imagine that f varies across all Schwartz-Bruhat functions on the global adeles (remove
global poles by assuming f (0) = fb(0) = 0) and follow me into the following toy example.

     This is the key idea: follow the rough strategy of “degenerating a global convolution kernel from global to
S-local”, but instead of doing it using infinite Euler product operators, as Meyer instead does (paraphrasing),
doing it step by step using Schauder bases of point-masses at the zeros of reciprocal local non-Archimedean
Euler factors.
     Shift the burden of the degeneration process a little onto the function space, as opposed to the Euler
product operators of Meyer’s, thus replacing this step in Meyer’s trace formula with something that can work
in coarser topologies too.
     At this point the question is: can we make the calculation of the geometric side of the Trace Formula,
while working solely inside a norm completion, such as those alluded to coming out of the Hardy-Sobolev
norms from (1.8.2.2)?
                                                The answer is “yes”.
    Long story short, the Hardy-Sobolev norms give us all we need to find, after completion, “enough” of the
Schauder bases to pull off the step-wise deconstruction I have alluded to above (and specifically to write down
42                                          CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION


explicitly “pieces” of a global convolution kernel as trace-norm limits of finite rank kernels constructed by
acting on basis elements), and reduce the calculation of the geometric side of the trace formula to an analog of
the S-local trace calculation put forth by Connes, Meyer and, before them, Weil (in a way).
    A version of the idea of the bases of point-masses at the zeros of reciprocal non-Archimedean Euler factors
to compute a “piece” of the total trace is what came to me very early on.
    Upon recognizing its value, the writing of the paper got started, and became all-consuming. A full-time
endeavor taking 12 years to put it all together through efforts to find the right context (spanning functional
analysis, harmonic analysis, and analytic number theory) and run various sanity checks. Back then, I became
concerned that you might view it as a pipe-dream, one of many, had I shared a form of the ideas before such
time as a paper would be fully or almost fully written up, so we stayed at Stanford.
    We will now take a closer look.

    1.8.2. Notation. We briefly summarize here notation for certain function spaces whose study is under-
taken in the paper, both in the main text and in some of the appendices.
    Throughout this subsection only, we will use the notation k(x, y) to mean that k is a function of the two
variables x and y (perhaps only defined almost everywhere, with x, y varying over some appropriate measure
space). This notation does not refer to the value of k at (x, y). It is adopted only through this subsection, for
simplicity (it is not employed anywhere in the paper).
    We will be using the following terminology: the backward side of the Mellin transform, to mean its source
function space (according to the situation). The forward side of the Mellin transform, to mean its target space,
according to the situation.

promote the Mellin transform into a linear topological isomorphism, are discussed in one of the appendices to
my paper, and never appeared in prior work).
     The first to ever introduce an incarnation of these “weighted” spaces, was Tate, who, without every
initiating a systematic study, introduces an “L1 -version” in [CF, Ch.XV,§4.4,p.338]. Meyer’s is a “smooth
version” of Tate’s definition, with no topology but only retaining a good theory of bounded sets, and in my
paper its topology is defined and studied, both directly and through the lens of the Mellin transform.

the point-masses at the zeros of L(s + 1/2, χ) and their derivatives.
    This connection to the L-function requires all the Structure Theorems, and use of known analytic properties
of the L-function (convexity bound, existence of a sequence of horizontal segments across the critical strip
on which the reciprocal of Lf (s, χ) is defined and grows at most polynomially in the absolute ordinate. In
the process of describing the image of H0,cont (F × , S0 (AF )) under the Mellin transform, we must also draw
from Bohr’s theory of almost periodic functions, taken to a fuller expression in Bagchi’s Ph.D. thesis, to prove
that finite Euler products of non-Archimedean local factors admit a sequence of horizontal segments whose
ordinates tend to ±∞ respectively, and on which they are bounded, in order to perform asymptotic contour
integration. This can also be done using the Kronecker-Weyl Theorem).
    The sequence (1.8.3.2) is the reason why I titled this subsection the “divisor exact sequence”: (1.8.3.2)
mirrors the global sections of
                                       0 → OX (−D) → OX → OD → 0
for the Stein space X = C, and D = div(L(s + 1/2, χ)((s + 1/2)(s − 1/2))δ ).

     1.8.3.2. Normed completions. One of the key steps on the way to the Trace Formula, is to pass the sequences
(7.2.0.1) and (1.8.3.2) (linearly and topologically exact) through the lens of coarser normed completions.
     Why Hardy-Sobolev completions, specifically? They do something for us: they make point-mass functionals
supported on the imaginary line, together with their derivatives of arbitrary order, continuous. To this end,
giving ourself a little bit of interior around the imaginary line (which is what the Hardy-Sobolev norms do, if
46                                         CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION


you rethink them through the Mellin transform, i.e. you re-interpret the topology they, each, define, as also
obtained by a finite family of seminorms defined by integration along the edges of the strip CI as in (1.8.2.3)).
This feature of the Hardy-Sobolev normed topologies (promoting point-masses supported on the imaginary
line along with their derivatives, to continuous functionals with respect to such normed topologies) provides
us with one of the ingredients that we necessitate, in order to make the calculation of the Geometric Side of
the Trace Formula (note that the zeros are playing no role in how we select such topologies. It will be the
Geometric Side of the Trace Formula, to dictate what such normed topologies must do for us, in order for the
calculations to work within such normed environments too).
     We will briefly return to these points later. Ultimately, we will be doing the following:

                                         Adelic θ-functions

    We fix a number field F , writing OF for its ring of integers.
    In [CF, Ch.XV,§4,Def.4.4.1], idelic zeta integrals, i.e. integrals over GL1 (AF ) of the form
                                           Z
                                                     f (g)c(g) dµ(g)
                                             GL1 (AF )

for f a suitable measurable function on the Hausdorff locally compact abelian topological group GL1 (AF ),
µ a fixed choice of Haar measure on GL1 (AF ), and as c varies over a suitable subset of all continuous
quasi-characters of GL1 (AF ) satisfying c(F × ) = 1, are defined and shown to be well behaved for test functions
f from the complex vector space z introduced in [CF, Ch.XV,§4.4, z1 -z3 ].
     The set of continuous quasi-characters of GL1 (AF ) satisfying c(F × ) = 1 is equipped with the structure
of a Riemann surface Ω. Such functions are designed to ensure convergence of the integrals from [CF,
Ch.XV,Def.4.4.1] over GL1 (AF ) over large domains within Ω, and the validity of the adelic “Riemann-Roch
Theorem” from [CF, Ch.XV,Thm.4.2.1].
     In this Chapter we study properties of the Hausdorff locally convex topological complex vector space
S(AF ) of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on the adele ring AF .
     A consequence of the results recorded here is the well known fact that Schwartz-Bruhat functions on AF
are examples of functions from z.
     The topological properties of S(AF ) and its strong dual S(AF )′β will enable us to study the continuous
representation of GL1 (AF ) on S(AF ) and its homological and co-homological invariants, leading to precise
information on Hecke L-functions and their divisor of zeros and poles.
     The main goals of this Chapter are as follows:
(1) Analyze the decay properties of functions on the idele class group CF of F constructed by averaging under
    the continuous left-translation action by F × , Schwartz-Bruhat functions on AF (restricted to GL1 (AF )
    under composition with the continuous map GL1 (AF ) → AF ).
(2) Discussing S-local analogs of the constructions and results from (1), for S a finite set of places of F
    containing all the Archimedean places.
(3) Revisiting [CF, Ch.XV,§4.4] of Tate’s dissertation, with the specific purpose of rewriting Tate’s idelic zeta
    integrals as Mellin transforms of smooth functions on R>0 with rapid decay at infinity, such functions
    being linearly associated to the Schwartz-Bruhat functions on AF , respectively AF,S .
(4) Studying continuity properties of the formation of the functions constructed in (2), together with the
    interaction with directional derivation along continuous 1-parameter subgroups of GL1 (AF ), respectively
    GL1 (AF,S ).

                                      2.1. Schwartz-Bruhat functions
    Distribution theory rests upon the construction of Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces of test
functions, usually satisfying favorable topological properties, such as completeness, nuclearity, barrelledness
and the Heine-Borel property (these latter two properties defining the class of Montel Hausdorff locally convex
topological vector spaces; see [Jar, Part II,Ch.11,§11.5]).
    Distributions are ordinarily defined as the strong dual of a Hausdorff locally convex topological complex
vector space of suitable test functions. Such spaces of distributions often receive a linear topological embedding
from the space of test functions itself, enabling us to think of distributions as generalized functions.
    For the concept of strong dual we refer the reader to Definition C.2.1.5(3): for a Hausdorff locally convex
topological C-vector space E, its strong dual is the continuous dual endowed with the topology of uniform
convergence on bounded subsets, and denoted as Eβ′ .
    In this section we recall the notion of tempered distribution on the real line, briefly reviewing its
generalization to tempered distributions on Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups, specializing to the case
of the Hausdorff locally compact abelian group AF of the adeles of a number field.
    The general theory of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups G is
reworked in Appendix D, with the aim at providing proofs of the main structural results on S(G), relying on
Appendix C, where we discuss complements and background material from functional analysis.
    For the purposes of this Chapter, we will be recalling basic facts on Schwartz-Bruhat functions as the
need arises, and in the specific cases of interest only.


    2.1.1. Schwartz-Bruhat functions. We begin by reviewing the example of the space of Schwartz
functions on the real line.

     2.1.1.1. Schwartz functions on the real line. Let f1 , f2 be smooth complex valued functions on the real
line. Deciding how “near” f1 and f2 are is a task to be addressed depending on the behavior of f1 (x), f2 (x) as
|x| → +∞, since R is not compact.
     The uniform norm provides one notion of nearness among smooth complex valued functions on R, so
long as the functions are bounded over R. The resulting topology on the C-vector space of bounded smooth
complex valued functions is too coarse to allow a rich strong dual. Even on smooth functions with compact
support, the resulting linear topology is uninteresting.

    Example 2.1.1.1. The space of distributions on the real line is built as the strong dual (see [Sch-a,
Ch.III,§3,p.71]) of the Hausdorff locally convex topological complex vector space of smooth compactly supported
functions Cc∞ (R), endowed with the locally convex (strict) inductive limit topology (see [Scha, Ch.II,§6,p.57]
                                                                                             ∞
and [Jar, Part I,Ch.4,§4.6], [Sch-a, Ch.III,§1,Thm.II]) promoting the linear inclusions CK     (R) ⊂ Cc∞ (R) to
continuous linear operators (in fact, linear topological embeddings).
            ∞
    Here CK   (R) denotes the complex vector space of smooth functions on R with support contained within
the compact subset K ⊂ R (see [Sch-a, p.24]), endowed with the topology of uniform convergence of functions
and their derivatives of any order. We refer the reader to [Sch-a, Ch.III,§1].

    Before continuing, we caution the reader on the difference between inductive limit topologies and locally
convex inductive limit topologies.

    Remark 2.1.1.2 (Cautionary remark on the difference of inductive limit and locally convex inductive limit
topology). The locally convex inductive limit topology on Cc∞ (R) differs from the inductive limit topology,
which is generally not locally convex. A counterexample can be constructed from [Shi, Lemme 4] and its
proof.
60                                       CHAPTER 2. ADELIC θ-FUNCTIONS


     The inductive limit topology of a sequence of topological spaces equipped with continuous transition maps
(satisfying good properties, such as being topological embeddings with closed image) may be unwieldy. It is
difficult to write down examples of open neighborhoods.
     For locally convex inductive limits of filtered families of Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
spaces, instead, we can write down a 0-neighborhood base as follows. Let I be a filtered set (i.e. equipped
with a partial ordering) and {Ei }i∈I an I-indexed collection of Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
spaces.
     Assume given injective transition maps uij : Ei → Ej for every j ≥ i in I, and let E be the filtered colimit
linear space. We call ui : Ei → E the induced linear inclusion. A 0-neighborhood base for the locally convex
inductive limit topology on E is given by the convex hulls
                                                     [
                                                  ch( ui (Vi ))
                                                        i∈I

for Vi varying through a given fundamental system of 0-neighborhoods in Ei . We refer the reader to [Gro-f,
Ch.4,§1,Prop.1(2),p.136].
    Locally convex inductive limits have a tendency to be large and do not satisfy the second-countability
condition (in particular, they are usually non-metrizable).
                                              L
    For example the N-indexed direct sum N C is non-metrizable because it does not have a countable
0-neighborhood base.

    The space of tempered distributions on the real line is, instead, built as the strong dual of the Hausdorff
locally convex topological complex vector space of Schwartz functions on R.

    Example 2.1.1.3. The complex vector space S(R) of Schwartz functions on R is comprised of the smooth
functions f ∈ C ∞ (R) such that
                                   ||f ||m,N := sup (1 + |x|N ) |∂xm f (x)| < +∞

where ∂xm f is the order-m derivative of f , for all integers N, m ≥ 0, topologized with the locally convex
topology generated by the family {|| · ||m,N }m,N ≥0 of seminorms.
    The space of tempered distributions on R is defined to be the Hausdorff locally convex topological vector
space S(R)′β : the strong dual of S(R). This is the continuous dual of S(R) endowed with the topology of
uniform convergence (for continuous linear functionals) on the bounded subsets of S(R).

with complex coefficients. We refer the reader to [KG, Part I,Ch.III,(3)].

    We shall next record a result on properties of the linear topology on S(Rm ), but first we must clarify
the role of boundedness in the definition of strong duals. The β-topology, or strong topology, on the
continuous dual E ′ of a Hausdorff locally convex topological complex vector space E is defined in [Jar,
Part II,Ch.8,§8.4,Example 3.A,p.153] as the topology of uniform convergence on all subsets of E that are
σ(E, E ′ )-bounded, i.e. bounded for the weakened topology on E. However, the subsets of E that are bounded
with respect to the weakened topology are exactly the subsets of E that are bounded for the intrinsic topology
on E by [Jar, Part II,Ch.8,§8.3,Thm.4,p.151] (see also [NB, Thm.8.8.7]). Definition C.2.1.5 is therefore
equivalent to the definition in [Jar, Part II,Ch.8,§8.4,Example 3.A,p.153], and it is [Scha, Ch.III,§3,Example
4(d),p.81].

    Proposition 2.1.1.6. Let m ≥ 0 be an integer. The locally convex topological C-vector space S(Rm ) is
nuclear, Fréchet and reflexive. The strong dual S(Rm )′β is complete, nuclear and Montel.

     Remark 2.1.1.7. We recall that a Hausdorff locally convex topological complex vector space E is semi-
Montel if and only if it satisfies the Heine-Borel property: if B ⊂ E is a bounded subset, then B is relatively
compact in E; see [Jar, Part II,§11]. By [Jar, Part II,§11,Prop.1], if E is semi-Montel, then it is barrelled
(see [Jar, Part II,§11.1]) if and only if it is reflexive, and semi-Montel spaces satisfying any of these additional
properties are, by definition, Montel spaces.

     Proof of Proposition 2.1.1.6. Nuclearity of S(Rm ) is [Tre, Part III,Ch.51,Corollary,p.530]. The
family of seminorms || · ||α,β from (2.1.1.4) is separating. The locally convex topology on S(Rm ) is therefore
Hausdorff.
     The seminorms from (2.1.1.4) are countably many, and hence S(Rm )is, by [Kothe-I, Ch.4,§18,(2),p.205],
metrizable. It is Fréchet so long as it is complete. Since it is metrizable (because (2.1.1.3) is a countable
fundamental family of seminorms), it is enough to show convergence of any Cauchy sequence {fk }k≥0 in S(Rm )
with respect to the topology generated by the given seminorms.
     We first observe that {fk }k≥0 converges with respect to the uniform norm topology, since C0 (Rm ) is
Banach (see [Fol, Prop.4.35]). We call its limit f .
     The functions gα,k := Dxα fk (x) also define a Cauchy sequence {gα,k }k≥0 for each α ∈ Nm with respect to
the uniform norm topology on C0 (Rm ), converging to some fα , which is seen to be Dxα f since the convergence
is, in particular, uniform on compact subsets for {Dxα fk }k≥0 for each α ∈ Nm , and fα is therefore of the
desired form on every compact subset of Rm .
62                                     CHAPTER 2. ADELIC θ-FUNCTIONS


     The function f is therefore smooth and rapidly decaying at infinity. We need to show that the convergence
of {fk }k≥0 to f is in the sense of the Hausdorff locally convex topology on S(Rm ).
     For each β ∈ Nm , {xβ gα,k }k≥0 is a Cauchy sequence for the uniform topology on C0 (Rm ), and its limit
fα,β is, by uniqueness, xβ Dxα f , since this can be checked locally. It follows that xβ Dxα fk → xβ Dxα f with
respect to the uniform topology on C0 (Rm ), and since this holds for every α, β ∈ Nm , we deduce that fk → f
in S(Rm ).
     Since S(Rm ) is nuclear, then every bounded subset in S(Rm ) is relatively compact by [Tre, Part
III,Ch.50,Prop.50.2(5.12)]. By completeness, S(Rm ) has the Heine-Borel property, i.e. it is semi-Montel as per
[Jar, Part II,Ch.11,§11.5,p.230].
     By [NB, Thm.13.2.13], its strong dual S(Rm )′β , the space of tempered distributions on Rm , is complete,
and it is nuclear by [Tre, Part III,Ch.50,Prop.50.6]. Both S(Rm ) and S(Rm )′β are reflexive (the latter by
[Tre, Part II,Prop.36.10]). We further refer the reader to [Sch-a, Ch.VII,§3].
     By reflexivity and [Jar, Part II,Ch.11,§11.5,Prop.1], S(Rm ) is Montel, and hence so is S(Rm )′β by [Jar,
Part II,Ch.11,§11.5,Prop.4(f)].                                                                              □




     2.1.1.3. Schwartz-Bruhat functions on Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups. Definition 2.1.1.4 boot-
straps to the case of elementary abelian Lie groups, i.e. Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups isomorphic
to Rm × (R/Z)n × Zk × F for integers m, n, k ≥ 0, and a finite abelian group F , and, from this case, to the
case of arbitrary Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups through their classification theory. This is done in
Bruhat’s paper [Bru], and specifically in [Bru, §9]. Such functions are termed Schwartz-Bruhat throughout
this work.
     By Lemma D.1.3.7(2), the Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space of Schwartz-Bruhat functions
on elementary Lie groups (i.e. Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups of the form Rm × (R/Z)n × Zk × F )
is linearly and topologically isomorphic to S(Rm ) ⊗                 b π sk ⊗π CF , where S(Rm ) was studied in
                                                   b π C ∞ ((R/Z)n ) ⊗
Proposition 2.1.1.6, C ∞ ((R/Z)n ) is endowed with the topology of uniform convergence on functions and their
derivatives of arbitrary order, and s = S(Z) is the space of rapidly decaying Z-indexed sequences ({ak }k∈Z
such that ak = O(|k|−N ) for every integer N ≥ 0 as |k| → +∞), with sk the k-th projective tensor power of s.
     Recall that an arbitrary Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G is the direct limit, as a topological
abelian group, of its open compactly generated subgroups (i.e. generated as a group by a compact neighborhood
of 1).
     Any compact subgroup k ⊂ G is called good (following [Bru, §1]) if and only if its open annihilator k ⊥
is ompactly generated as a subgroup of the dual group G.    b Any open compactly generated subgroup Γ ⊂ G
containing k is such that Γ/k is an elementary Lie group (seen upon combining, for instance, [DE, Cor.4.2.5]
and [DE, Cor.4.2.6] with [DE, Prop.3.6.1(c)]).
     We now briefly recall how to define and topologize S(G) (we refer the reader to [Bru, §9]). To construct
S(G), we will work with pairs (k, Γ) where k ⊂ G is a good subgroup and Γ ⊂ G is an open compactly
generated subgroup containing k. Since Γ/k is an abelian Lie group, we have already discussed the space
S(Γ/k) of Schwartz-Bruhat functions. These can be viewed as special k-invariant functions on Γ, and we
topologize this space as discussed above. The collection of all such pairs (k, Γ) is filtered and S(G) is defined
to be the filtered colimit of the S(Γ/k)’s as a C-linear space, linearly topologized with the locally convex
inductive limit topology.
     The topological vector space S(G) is Hausdorff for general G (see Theorem D.1.5.7, resting, as far as the
Hausdorff property is concerned, on Lemma D.1.5.6). If G is separable, S(G) is complete, nuclear and Montel,
and so is its strong dual S(G)′β . We refer the reader to Theorem D.1.5.7 for a proof.
                                      2.1. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT FUNCTIONS                                          63


    As a special case, for G = R the classical Schwartz space S(R) is recovered, and it is complete, nuclear
and Montel, with strong dual S(R)′β sharing the same properties. Throughout this work, we will be referring
to S(G) as the Schwartz-Bruhat space of G, and to its topology as the Schwartz-Bruhat topology.

    2.1.2.1. Smooth functions on non-Archimedean fields. We recall that for G a Hausdorff locally compact
abelian group, a function f : G → C is called smooth if and only if it is k-invariant for some compact subgroup
k ⊂ G whose open annihilator k ⊥ is compactly generated as a subgroup of the dual group G    b and for every open
compactly generated subgroup Γ ⊂ G containing k the induced function on the quotient Γ/k (an elementary
Lie group!) is smooth in the sense of differential geometry.
    We denote by C ∞ (G) the C-algebra of smooth complex-valued functions on G, and denote by Cc∞ (G) the
subspace of those elements of C ∞ (G) that are also compactly supported. When G is locally profinite, Cc∞ (G)
coincides with the C-linear space of complex-valued locally constant functions with compact support.
    Let F be a number field, v a finite place of F . We have, as C-linear spaces,
                                               Cc∞ (Fv ) = S(Fv ).

    2.1.2.2. The locally convex topological complex vector spaces S(Fv ) for v ∈ ΣF,f . In this subsection we
recall how to explicitly describe the elements of the Schwartz-Bruhat space of the local fields Fv for v
non-Archimedean.
    As a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, we recall that Fv is the filtered union of compact open
subgroups Kv ⊂ Fv , and for two compact open subgroups Kv,1 ⊂ Kv,2 , by openness of Kv,1 in Kv,2 and
compactness of Kv,2 the quotient Kv,2 /Kv,1 is a finite abelian group.
    As per the very construction of S(G) for G a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, the basic Hausdorff
locally convex topological vector spaces S(k, Γ) (see [Bru, §1]) arising in the construction are all of the form
S(Kv,2 /Kv,1 ), which is a finite dimensional complex vector space. As such, it carries a unique Hausdorff
locally convex topology (i.e. the Euclidean topology) compatible with the Euclidean topology on the complex
numbers, and S(Fv ) is a locally convex inductive limit of finite dimensional complex vector spaces, each
endowed with its natural Euclidean topology.

    Remark 2.1.2.2. We inform the reader concerned about the possibility of uncountably-indexed locally
convex inductive limits arising, that the locally convex inductive systems of interest throughout this work will
always be equivalent to countable ones. They will often arise from topological vector spaces related through
formation of quotients of spaces of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on second-countable Hausdorff locally compact
64                                     CHAPTER 2. ADELIC θ-FUNCTIONS


abelian groups. For example, S(Fv ) is countably generated, since Fv has a countable 0-neighborhood base of
compact open subgroups.

     Remark 2.1.2.3 (On the necessity of topologizing S(Fv )). Let F be a number field. The aim of the
next few Chapters of this work is to collect certain averages over F × -orbits on GL1 (AF ) of Schwartz-Bruhat
functions on AF , into topological vector spaces, for then studying them through the lens of the Mellin
transform. Several subquotients of such topological vector spaces will be essential in performing the trace
calculation that is the main subject of study of this work.
     Their topology will be of great importance, because it will be one of the purposes of the first half of this
work to identify Schauder bases on such subquotients, and Schauder bases are sensitive to the topology of
their linear environment. The defining conditions of a Schauder basis is that every element of the ambient
Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space, should be expressible as a convergent countably infinite
linear combination of basis elements in a unique way, with continuous coefficient functionals.
     To build such topological vector spaces, we will be starting off from the Schwartz-Bruhat topology on
S(AF ) and S(AF,S ). It renders itself necessary to topologize S(Fv ) for every non-Archimedean place as well,
as simple as such topology is: it is the finest locally convex topology, equivalently the topology rendering any
linear form continuous.

     Proposition 2.1.2.4. Let F be a number field, v a finite place.
(1) S(Fv ) is countably C-linearly generated, and it carries the finest locally convex topology. In particular, it
    is a strict LF-space.
(2) S(Fv ) is Hausdorff locally convex, complete, nuclear, Montel, and its strong dual is a nuclear Fréchet
    space.
(3) Every C-linear subspace of S(Fv ) is linearly and topologically complemented.

    Recall that a subspace V of a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E is called linearly
and topologically complemented if and only if there exists a subspace W ⊂ E such that V ⊕ W → E is a
homeomorphism. In particular, V and W are closed, since E is Hausdorff.

    Proof. A cofinal sequence of compact open subgroups of Fv is given by {πvm OFv }m∈Z , for πv any choice
of generator of the maximal ideal of the complete discrete valuation ring of OFv .
    As a C-linear space, S(Fv ) is therefore the countable inductive limit of the countably many finite
dimensional vector spaces S(πvN OFv /πvm OFv ) for N ≤ m, where the finite group πvN OFv /πvm OFv is endowed
with the discrete topology since πvm OFv is open in πvN OFv . As such, it is countably linearly generated. By
Proposition C.2.5.1(6), the rest of the assertions hold.                                                    □
