     Remark 2.1.3.3 (Cautionary remark on inductive and projective tensor topologies). We refer to [Scha,
Ch.II,§5] for a discussion of projective topologies. For E, F two locally convex complex vector spaces, there
exists on the algebraic tensor product E ⊗ F a unique locally convex topology such that for any locally
convex complex vector space G, continuous linear maps E ⊗ F → G correspond bijectively to continuous (i.e.
not merely separately continuous) bi-linear maps E × F → G under the canonical correspondence given by
composing a continuous linear map E ⊗ F → G with the canonical continuous linear map E × F → E ⊗ F .
     This topology is referred to as the projective tensor product topology on E ⊗ F , due to its projective
nature, and also termed π-topology. A fundamental system of neighborhoods of 0 for this topology on E ⊗ F
is given by the convex circled hulls of the sets of the form
                                      Ui ⊗ Vj := {u ⊗ v : u ∈ Ui , v ∈ Vj }
where Ui and Vj are fundamental systems of neighborhoods of 0 in E, respectively F .
   In this work, the projective topology is often used in combination with the inductive tensor topology. The
completed inductive tensor product is denoted by E ⊗ F , and it is most suitable to inductive constructions
                                       2.1. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT FUNCTIONS                                            69


and “kernel theorems” (results expressing a class of functions on a product space as a suitable completed
tensor product of function spaces on the factors). Lemma D.1.8.1 gives examples of kernel theorems with
Schwartz spaces and their strong duals in the setting of locally compact abelian groups.
    We refer the reader to §C.2.3 of Appendix C, to [Gro-c, Thm.1] (and the discussion preceding the
Theorem), [Scha, Ch.II,§5] and [Jar, Part III,§15.1] for a discussion of the projective (or π-)topology on an
algebraic tensor product of two Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces, and to (C.2.3.23) and
particularly to Proposition C.2.3.13 for a discussion and basic properties of inductive tensor products.
    We observe here that the canonical continuous linear map:
                                  S(AF,S∞ ) ⊗ι S(AfF ) → S(AF,S∞ ) ⊗π S(AfF )
is a continuous linear bijection. It is not, however, a linear topological isomorphism, because S(AfF ) is a strict
locally convex inductive limit of finite dimensional Euclidean spaces (in particular, a strict locally convex
inductive limit of Fréchet spaces) and the transition maps are strict inclusions. Moreover, S(AF,S∞ ) is a
non-normable Fréchet space. Under such circumstances, the continuous linear bijection from the inductive to
the projective tensor product is not a linear topological embedding, hence not a linear topological isomorphism.
This is a consequence of [Gro-b, Ch.I,§1,No.3,Rem.1,p.47].
     We further refer the reader to Remark 4.5.1.3 where a similar situation is discussed.
     We further refer the reader to Remark 2.1.3.4 below, where the three main tensor topologies occurring
throughout this work, are compared on S(AF,S∞ ) ⊗ S(AfF ).

    Proof of Proposition 2.1.3.2. Both AF and AfF are Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups, and
both are separable, being second-countable (see Lemma ??). As such, [Bru, §9,Prop.11] applies and gives
that S(AF ) and S(AfF ) are Hausdorff, complete, nuclear and Montel with their strong duals satisfying the
same properties.
    We now provide a direct argument.
    The locally convex complex topological vector space S(AfF ) is a strict inductive limit of finite dimensional
C-vector spaces (each endowed with its unique linear topology compatible with the Euclidean topology on the
complex numbers).
    Indeed, since AfF is the filtered union compact open subgroups of the form Kv = v∈ΣF,f Hv , with

inductive limit of the finite dimensional complex vector spaces S(Kv′ /Kv ), as (Kv , Kv′ ) varies across pairs of
compact open subgroups in AfF with Kv ⊂ Kv′ . The set of such pairs contains a cofinal filtered subset that is
countable, since AfF is second-countable.
     It follows that S(AfF ) carries the finest locally convex topology, and Proposition C.2.5.1(6) describes its
properties. Alternatively, see Proposition 2.1.2.8 applied to G2 = AfF .
     By Proposition 2.1.2.8(6), S(AfF )′β is a nuclear Fréchet space, hence Montel: by [Tre, Part III,Ch.50,Prop.50.2(5.12)],
it is semi-Montel, as per [Jar, Part II,Ch.11,§11.5,p.230], and since it is barrelled, it is Montel (see [Tre, Part
III,Ch.50,Cor.3,p.520]). This finishes the proof of (1) for S(AfF ).

every place v of F , and fv = 1OFv for all but finitely many finite places of F , linearly generate a dense (and

quadratic fields.

    For E a Hausdorff locally convex C-vector space, we denote by L (E) := L (E, E) the C-linear space of

Schwartz-Bruhat spaces S(AF,S ) encompass large pieces of the global Schwartz-Bruhat space S(AF ), up to a
closed subspace (“smaller and smaller” as S grows large) that splits off linearly and topologically. This will
be a general pattern to follow throughout the later Chapters of this work, where we will be analyzing large
subquotients of S(AF ) by studying their S-local analogs for all large enough S: the fact that such analysis is
possible rests on properties of Hecke L-functions, to be harnessed through the systematic use of the Mellin
transform (idelic, in the spirit of Tate’s dissertation from [CF, Ch.XV], and S-idelic).

    Proof. To see this, we let B ⊂ S(AF ) be a bounded subset. By Proposition 2.1.4.1(4), and by [Scha,

contains I(S0 ) as a filtered subset.

                                        2.2. Global adelic θ-functions
    Let F be a number field. In this section we will be defining and studying the linear map associating to a
Schwartz-Bruhat function f : AF → C its restriction to GL1 (AF ) averaged over the continuous translation
action by the discrete subgroup F × . We will show that such averages are themselves continuous as functions
on the idele class group CF of F , and decaying rapidly at infinity in a precise sense that can be controlled
using the idelic norm.
                                       2.2. GLOBAL ADELIC θ-FUNCTIONS                                         75


    Such F × -averaged Schwartz-Bruhat functions are called global adelic θ-functions. We will study them
systematically throughout the rest of Chapter 2, and then collect them into a topological vector space in the
next Chapter.
     2.2.1. Averaging over a full lattice. In this subsection we record a convergence result concerning
averages of norm functions on Euclidean spaces under the translation action by a full lattice.
     Let N ≥ 1 be an integer and consider Γ ⊂ RN a discrete subgroup. If Γ is co-compact, then Γ is a finite
free abelian group of rank N , i.e. a full lattice.
     We denote by || · ||∞ : RN → R≥0 the norm ||x||∞ := max{|xi |R , 1 ≤ i ≤ N }.
    Lemma 2.2.1.1. Let N ≥ 1. Let Γ ⊂ RN be a full lattice. For every real number r ≥ 1, the set
(2.2.1.1)                         Xr := {x ∈ RN : ||ξ||∞ ∈ [r, r + 1)} ⊂ RN
is bounded, Lebesgue measurable, and it satisfies:
(2.2.1.2)                                  |Γ ∩ Xr | = OΓ,N (rN −1 )
as r → +∞, the implied constant depending N and on Γ.
     Remark 2.2.1.2. We note that the implied constant in (2.2.1.2) depends on N on itself, and also on N
through Γ, through its successive minima: for a full lattice Γ ⊂ RN , the successive minima r1 , . . . , rN are
defined as, for each integer 1 ≤ k ≤ N , the infimum over all real numbers r ≥ 0 such that B0 (r) ∩ Γ contains k
vectors which are R-linearly independent (the closed ball B0 (r) of radius r > 0 and center the origin 0 ∈ RN
being defined using the standard Euclidean norm); see [Schm, §2,p.347].
                                                             vol(Xr )                                    N
     The method to estimate the error term for |Γ ∩ Xr | − vol(R N /Γ) , where volumes are computed in R    with
                                                                                    N

Lemma 1,p.347] and springs from the proof of [Davenport-1, §2,Thm.p.180].
      Proof. We denote, for every real number r ≥ 1, by Xr ⊂ RN the subset Xr := {x ∈ RN : ||x||∞ ∈
[r, r + 1)}. Since || · ||∞ : RN → R≥0 is continuous, surjective and proper, and Xr is the pre-image of the
bounded interval [r, r + 1), we deduce that Xr is measurable and relatively compact, and so is its image under
the orthogonal projection onto any linear subspace of RN . Indeed, such image is a convex polyhedron within
such subspace.
      Let L ⊂ RN be a line. Then L ∩ Xr is either empty or the union of at most two segments. Indeed, for
x, y ∈ RN and such that L = x + R · y, we have
                                                 x + ty ∈ Xr
if and only if
                                     f (t) := sup |xk + tyk | ∈ [r, r + 1).
                                             1≤k≤N
     Note that y is necessarily nonzero.
    The function f : R → R≥0 is continuous, surjective and proper. Moreover, its fibre over r ∈ R≥0 is the
pre-image under the map t 7→ x + ty, of the intersection of the closed surface Sr := {||x||∞ = r}, the boundary
of the N -dimensional hypercube in RN with edge-length r, with L. The fibres of f are therefore finite of size
at most 2, since the interior of Sr is convex.
    The subset Xr is obtained from the interior of Sr+1 by removing the interior of Sr , and so the intersection
of L with the interior of Sr+1 , which, by the foregoing, is either a point of a segment, intersects Xr in the
complement of the intersection of L with the interior of Sr , again a point of a segment. This shows that
L ∩ Xr is either empty, a segment or two segments.
     It follows that [Schm, Lemma 1,p.347] (see also [Gao, p.15]) applies. Indeed, Xr is of class 2, following
the terminology of loc.cit., and for λ1 , . . . , λN the successive minima of Γ (for each k ≥ 1, each λk is the

infimum among all positive real numbers λ such that Γ contains k linearly independent vectors in RN of

    2.2.3. The θ-function operator ΦF : S(AF ) → C(CF ). In this section we study the linear operator
                                              ΦF : S(AF ) → C(CF )
defined by sending a Schwartz-Bruhat function on AF to its restriction to the idele group GL1 (AF ), averaged
over the orbits under the action of the discrete subgroup F × .
     The operator ΦF is a special case of ΨF defined in Lemma 2.2.2.1. The Riemann-Roch Theorem in [CF,
Thm.4.2.1] will enable sharp estimates for the resulting functions over the idele class group CF , over both loci
CF≫1 and CF≪1 , i.e. the subsets of those idele classes whose idelic norm is very large, respectively very small.
     By Lemma 2.2.2.1(2), for any f ∈ S(AF ) the continuous function ΨF (g, 0) of g ∈ GL1 (AF ) is invariant
under the left translation action by the discrete subgroup F × ⊂ GL1 (AF ).

     Definition 2.2.3.1 (Global adelic θ-functions). Let F be a number field, f ∈ S(AF ) a Schwartz-Bruhat
function.
     We denote by
                                                                   X
(2.2.3.1)                         ΦF (f )(g) := ΨF (f )(g ′ , 0) =   f (ξg ′ )
                                                                      ξ∈F ×
82                                      CHAPTER 2. ADELIC θ-FUNCTIONS


the continuous function of g ∈ CF obtained from f by averaging the restriction of f to GL1 (AF ) over the
F × -orbits, where g ′ is any choice of lift of g under the continuous surjective homomorphism GL1 (AF ) → CF .
     We refer to the function ΦF (f ) on CF as the global adelic θ-function of f .
    The definition of ΦF in (2.2.3.1) is independent of such choice by F × -invariance of ΨF (g, 0).
    The assignment ΦF on S(AF ) is valued in C(CF ) and its formation is C-linear. We will now proceed to
study the function ΦF (f )(g) of g ∈ CF , and its asymptotic behavior as |g|F → 0+ and as |g|F → +∞.
    We refer to ΦF (f ) as “θ-function”, with a non-capitalized θ, because the true direct analog of the Jacobi
Θ-function from Riemann’s paper on the number of prime numbers below a given magnitude, is the function
defined by the full sum                                    X
                                             ΘF (f )(g) :=    f (ξg)
                                                            ξ∈F
i.e. not merely the sum over the translates by nonzero elements of F . The construction under consideration is
indeed the one in use throughout this work, i.e. we will be using ΦF (f ) throughout this work, as opposed to
ΘF (f ).
     We have taken a habit of using the letter Φ to denote the adelic θ-functions thus defined, because we will
be showing that the operator ΦF is valued in the Schwartz-Bruhat space S(CF ) of the idele class group, and
we will be denoting with the letter ϕ the generic element of S(CF ).

    2.2.4. Compatibility with directional derivatives: global adelic θ-functions. We fix a choice
τ : R>0 → GL1 (AF ) of continuous homomorphic section to the idelic norm. This is a continuous 1-parameter
subgroup, which, we thought of as such, we denote by γτ : R>0 → GL1 (AF ). It makes sense to form derivatives
along γτ of smooth functions on GL1 (AF ) and CF .
    Before we state and prove the main results of this subsection, we classify the images of the continuous
1-parameter subgroups of GL1 (AF ), i.e. continuous homomorphisms γ : R>0 → GL1 (AF ) of Hausdorff locally
compact abelian groups.

     Lemma 2.2.4.1. Let F be a number field. Let γ : R>0 → GL1 (AF ) be a continuous 1-parameter subgroup.
                                        2.2. GLOBAL ADELIC θ-FUNCTIONS                                           87


    Then γ(R>0 ) is contained in the closed subgroup:
(2.2.4.1)                GL1 (AF,S∞ ) × {1} ⊂ GL1 (AF,S∞ ) × GL1 (AfF ) = GL1 (AF ).
    Then γ satisfies exactly one of the following two conditions:
(1) The composition | · |F ◦ γ is a smooth automorphism of the abelian Lie group R>0 , and there exists a
    unique nonzero real number α such that |γ(t)|F = tα for all t ∈ R>0 .
(2) The image of γ is contained in the closed subgroup GL1 (AF,S∞ )1 × {1} of GL1 (AF ).
    Proof. Since GL1 (AF ) = GL1 (AF,S∞ ) × GL1 (AfF ) as Hausdorff locally compact topological abelian
groups, and GL1 (AfF ) is totally disconnected, then, as R>0 is connected, γ(R>0 ) is connected and hence
contained in the identity component of GL1 (AF ), which is indeed contained within the closed subgroup
GL1 (AF,S∞ ) × {1} from (2.2.4.1).
    The composition | · |F ◦ γ is a continuous group endomorphism of R>0 , and it is therefore smooth (by the
Closed Subgroup Theorem: a closed subgroup of a Lie group is an embedded Lie group), being R>0 a Lie
group. Its tangent map is multiplication by a real number α. If α ̸= 0, then it is smoothly invertible and
hence a Lie group automorphism. Since R>0 is simply connected, it is of the form t 7→ tα .
    If α = 0, then γ(R>0 ) ⊂ GL1 (AF )1 ∩ (GL1 (AF,S∞ ) × {1}) = GL1 (AF,S∞ )1 × {1}.                      □

    Let F be a number field. Throughout this section, we fix a finite set S of places containing all of the

            1

      Recall that we denote by AF,S the product v∈S Fv , where Fv is the additive topological group of the

      The Hausdorff locally compact abelian group GL1 (AF,S ) is therefore isomorphic to the product v∈S Fv× ,

| · |F,S : JF,S → R>0 , in particular, its kernel JF,S  is compact.
      In the previous sections we studied the “global averaging” of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on the adeles AF
over the orbits in GL1 (AF ) of the F × -action, leading to the global adelic θ-functions of Definition 2.2.3.1.
In this section, we define S-local analogs of the θ-function operators ΦF and ΦF,ω , for ω now a continuous
                 1
character of JF,S  .
      The reason we seek S-local analogues is as follows. Eventually we will collect the global adelic θ-functions
discussed so far into a topological vector space, and study several large quotients of that space (for example,
proving that such quotients admit Schauder bases with certain good properties for later use, to compute
traces). The study of the topological vector spaces of global θ-functions rests on the following principle: we
“exhaust” them by more manageable S-local analogs, where explicit constructions are possible and several
additional tools available. One illustration of this is that smooth compactly supported functions on GL1 (AF )
do not extend by zero to global Schwartz-Bruhat functions on AF (the ideles have additive measure zero
within the adeles), but they do at the S-local level.
      We further note that there is a relation between continuous characters of CF1 and of JF,S           1

     Remark 2.3.2.3. For fS ∈ S(AF,S ) we can build the global Schwartz-Bruhat function f := πS (fS ) ∈
S(AF ), and pass to its global adelic θ-function ΦF (f ). We can also associate to fS its S-local adelic θ-function
ΦF,S (fS ). The two θ-functions are indeed related. How this goes will be explained throughout the next
Chapters up to Chapter 6. Relating ΦF,S (fS ) and ΦF (f ) will require use of the Mellin transform, so it is not
elementary. In particular, Proposition 2.3.2.2 cannot be deduced from its global analog (see Lemma 2.2.4.3) at
this time, so it requires its own argument which is however very similar to the global argument already seen.

                 2.4. Asymptotic behavior as |g|F,S → 0+ by lattice point-counting
    Let F be a number field, S a finite set of places of F containing all the Archimedean places. In this
section we estimate ΦF,S (f )(g), for f ∈ S(AF,S ), as a function of g ∈ JF,S and in the regime |g|F,S → 0+ .
    For every Schwartz-Bruhat function f ∈ S(AF,S ), the function ΦF,S (f ) on JF,S is smooth along every con-
tinuous 1-parameter subgroup (by Proposition 2.3.2.2. In this section we will be quantifying the unboundedness
of ΦF,S (f ) on JF,S as |g|F,S → 0+ , proving an estimate of the following form:
                                          ΦF,S (f ) = O(|log|g|F,S ||S|−1 )
as |g|F,S → 0+ , and discussing the dependencies of the implied constant.
     Lattice-point counting methods and Dirichlet’s S-unit Theorem are the main ingredients in the calculations
that lead to such estimate.
    2.4.1. Warm-up: the case of the rational number field. As a warmup, we begin with the special
case F = Q to provide indications as to the origin of the O(|log|g|F,S ||S|−1 ) bound. The general case is
discussed in §2.4.2 (see Theorem 2.4.2.1).
                        2.4. ASYMPTOTIC BEHAVIOR AS |g|F,S → 0+ BY LATTICE POINT-COUNTING                                 107


    We refer the reader to the discussion preceding [Co, §VII,(4),p.29], where reference to a special case of
the result in Proposition 2.4.1.1 below is made.

C>0 ).
     The poles on the imaginary line all have multiplicity bounded above by |S|, and this is a direct consequence
of Mellin Inversion applied to the estimate from (2.4.1.1).
     We will be classifying and studying the poles of the meromorphic functions ZS (f, χ| · |sF,S ) throughout
Chapter 5, and their relation to the Schauder bases that have a fundamental role to play in performing the
trace calculation that is the main subject of this work.
     It is important to be aware of the relation between such poles, and the action of O×        F,S on AF,S and
especially on the “boundary hyperplanes” Hv of which the complement of GL1 (AF,S ) is comprised.

    2.4.2. The general case. In the special case of F = Q, direct arguments sufficed to establish the desired
estimate on ΦF,S (f )(g) in the regime as |g|F,S → 0+ .
    In the Theorem below, we treat the general case, and show that the implied constants can be arranged to
be uniform on bounded subsets within S(AF,S ).
    Theorem 2.4.2.1 below will serve the later purpose of showing the operators arising as S-idelic Zeta
functions LS on S(AF,S ) (see (5.1.1.2)) valued in meromorphic functions on the Riemann surface Ω(JF,S ), are
continuous with respect to finer topologies than that of uniform convergence on the compact subsets away
from the poles.
    We refer the reader to [Co, §VII,(6),p.30], where a similar estimate based on lattice-point counting and a
volume calculation, is referred to.

                                                 CHAPTER 3


                                       Idelic Zeta Functions

     In this Chapter we collect results on how to recover the global idelic Zeta integrals in [CF, Ch.XV,§4]
as transforms of functions on the idele class group and on the positive reals, as opposed to integrals of
Schwartz-Bruhat functions on the adeles restricted to the idele group.
     We will further discuss the S-idelic analog of the global idelic Zeta functions from [CF, Ch.XV,§4].
Equivalently, we will be discussing in general, the paradigm envisioned by Riemann in his paper “On the
Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude” (for which we refer the reader to [Riemann]) where he
used the Jacobi θ-function to prove the functional equation and existence of the analytic continuation to the
Riemann Zeta function.
     We will be using the global and S-local adelic θ-functions constructed in the previous Chapter and whose
study we initiated therein, to a similar effect. This Chapter will therefore consist in a reformulation of several
of the results contained in Tate’s dissertation from [CF, Ch.XV], with a few complements being discussed.
     Subsequently, we will be viewing global and S-local adelic θ-functions as their own function space, i.e.
we will be topologizing the C-linear space of all global adelic θ-functions, and all S-local adelic θ-functions,
respectively.
     The reason for doing this is that certain operators on the spaces of global and S-local adelic θ-functions
will enable us to read off non-trivial information about the zeros of Hecke L-functions through trace formulas.
The reader familiar with Selberg’s classical trace formula and subsequent refinements will know how powerful
trace formulas are. They are a pivotal instrument throughout the literature on automorphic representations
and the Langlands program.
     Trace calculations will be made accessible to us by promoting each of the spaces of adelic θ-functions
to Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces. The trace calculation that is the subject of this
work takes place on Sobolev spaces (hence normed) but, leading to the main calculation, finer locally convex
topologies are also necessary for reasons that will become clear by Chapter 7. They will give us Schauder
bases, which will enable us to compute “large pieces” of the trace that interests us.
     This is a good time to anticipate for the reader what “local convexity” does for us: it is a condition on
bases of 0-neighborhoods in topological vector spaces leading to robust control on several conditions through
the machinery of “duality”. There is, in other words, good reason to appeal to this side of functional analysis,
on which profound and expressive literature is available. Those elements that are relevant to us are discussed
in Appendix C.
     Topologizing the spaces of S-local and global adelic θ-functions will be the job that the next two Chapters
(Chapters 4 and 5 of this work) are tasked with. The linear topologies arising throughout this work will all
originate from spaces of Schwartz-Bruhat functions (such as S(AF ) and S(AF,S )) and normed completions.
     The topological vector spaces of adelic θ-functions will be identified via Mellin transforms with topological
vector spaces of meromorphic and holomorphic functions on the Riemann surfaces of continuous quasi-
characters of JF,S , respectively CF . The Mellin transform will recover Tate’s idelic Zeta integrals in much
the same way as the classical Mellin transform of the Jacobi θ-function recovers the Riemann Zeta function,
completed with its own Γ-factor.


                                                       117
118                                     CHAPTER 3. IDELIC ZETA FUNCTIONS


    One of the purposes of Chapter 4 of this work is to describe the image of the Mellin transform as an
operator between two Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces (a space of θ-functions, on the
source, and a space of Z-functions, on the target), promoting it to a linear topological isomorphism between a
space of θ-functions and a space of meromorphic functions satisfying growth conditions over vertical strips of
bounded width and a functional equation, in a similar vein as the Converse Theorems from [CPS, Thm.1,p.165]
for GLn .
    So far we have only defined the adelic θ-functions, both S-local and global. This is what we have done in
Chapter 2. We will be calling the θ-functions the “backward side” of the Mellin transform.
    This Chapter, instead, defines the Z-functions. It provides the terminology and basic results to define
and study the “forward side” of the Mellin transform, i.e. spaces of meromorphic functions on the Riemann
surfaces of idelic and S-idelic quasi-characters.

    3.1.1. Generalities. For G a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, we denote by Ω(G) the set of all
continuous homomorphisms G → C× . These are called quasi-characters. We make Ω(G) into a topological
space via the compact-open topology.
    If G is modulated, meaning (as in Definition D.2.1.1) that it is equipped with a continuous proper
non-trivial homomorphism | · |G : G → R>0 (often called a “module”) then the kernel G1 of the module is
compact. There are only two cases:
          • | · |G is surjective, in which case we say that G is R>0 -modulated.
                         3.1. RIEMANN SURFACES OF CONTINUOUS QUASI-CHARACTERS                                 119


       • Γ := |G|G ⊂ R>0 is a non-trivial discrete subgroup, hence of the form γ Z for a unique γ ∈ R>0 with
         γ > 1, in which case we say that G is discretely modulated.

many connected components). Indeed, the natural continuous map

                                     3.2. Global Idelic Zeta Functions
    The correspondence between θ-functions and Zeta functions goes back to Riemann’s paper [Riemann] on
the distribution of prime numbers, where he established the functional equation and existence of the analytic
continuation for the Riemann Zeta function by exhibiting it as the Mellin transform of the Jacobi θ-function.
    Tate’s dissertation from [CF, Ch.XV] mirrored Riemann’s θ-function approach to the study of the analytic
properties of abelian L-functions. Therein, however, the focus is mostly on the global Zeta integrals arising as
the Fourier-Mellin transforms of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on the adeles.
    Chapter 2 of this work initiated the systematic study of their θ-functions. This will be continued throughout
the next three Chapters, by studying the linear spaces comprising of those θ-functions, both global and S-local,
as topological vector spaces.
    The Mellin transform will produce idelic Z-functions from adelic θ-functions, and these too are going to
be studied by packaging them into a topological vector space, with the Mellin transform promoted to a linear
topological isomorphism.
    While the previous Chapter was tasked with defining and studying the first properties of the adelic
θ-functions, short of collecting them into a topological vector space, this Chapter is tasked with doing the
same for the resulting idelic Z-functions, to be defined and studied herein.
    We will be referring to the spaces of adelic θ-functions as the “backward side” of the Mellin transform,
and to the spaces of Idelic Z-fuctions as the “forward side” of the Mellin transform.
    To paraphrase further, while the previous Chapter was tasked with introducing the main elements
comprising the backward side of the Mellin transform, this Chapter is tasked with doing the same for the
forward side of the Mellin transform, so that in the subsequent Chapters we can study both sides systematically
through the lens of functional and harmonic analysis.

is also bornological (see [Scha, Ch.II, Cor. 2 to 8.2]).

    The reader will recognize a phenomenon of resolution of the singularity at s = 0 for π −s/2 Γ(s/2)ζ(s)
similar to that for the Dirichlet η-function, which, recall, is the “alternating zeta function” defined as
                                                      X (−1)m−1

                                                              ms

which, over the half-plane of absolute convergence Re(s) > 1, agrees with (1 − 2s−1 )ζ(s). The Dirichlet series
defining η(s) converges conditionally over the half-plane C>0 , and absolutely over the half-plane C>1 .
    See, for example, [T1, Ch.IX,§9.13]; see also [H], where a proof of the functional equation for ξ(s) is
provided using the Dirichlet η-function.
    The local Mellin transform of the Fourier transform of 1Z× resolves the singularity at s = 1 of
                                                                      2
π −s/2 Γ(s/2)ζ(s), in light of the calculation from Example A.3.1.6, in a similar manner as the factor (1 − 2s−1 )
does for η(s).
    We observe that indeed fb(0) = 0, which leads to Z(f, | · |sQ ) having no pole at | · |Q .
    We may think of the idelic Zeta functions Z(f, c) for f ∈ S(AF ) satisfying f (0) = fb(0) = 0, as idelic
analogs of the Dirichlet η-function, and we may think of Theorem 3.2.2.1(2) as the corresponding analog of
the conditional convergence over C>0 of the Dirichlet series defining η(s).

      We introduce the following terminology:

    Definition 3.2.2.5 (Global Idelic Z-functions). Let F be a number field, f ∈ S(AF ) a Schwartz-Bruhat
function.
    We refer to the meromorphic function Z(f, c) of c ∈ Ω(CF ) defined in (3.2.2.2) of Theorem 3.2.2.1, as the
Global Idelic Z-function of f .

    We will often write Z(f, c) even though the arguments under discussion will concern the global adelic
θ-function ΦF (f ) only, i.e. will depend on f only through its θ-function.
    We will start referring to Z as the Mellin transform of f , and of ΦF (f ), alike.


                                    3.3. S-Local Idelic Zeta Functions
    Throughout this subsection, we fix a number field F and a finite set S of places of F containing all of the
Archimedean places.

     3.3.1. S-local Idelic Z-functions. Recall that the local Fourier transforms on each S(Fv ), normalized
using the standard continuous additive character for each v, which we constructed in Example A.3.1.8 and
Example A.3.1.9, induce the S-adelic Fourier transform on S(AF,S ) with respect to a standard additive
                                                                                             N
character of the S-adeles AF,S and the additive Tamagawa measure νS (the Haar measure v∈S νv on AF,S
from Definition A.3.4.1, with νv the local additive Tamagawa measure on the additive topological group of
the local field Fv from Definition A.3.1.2). This is a continuous automorphism with respect to the Hausdorff
locally convex topology on S(AF,S ). We further refer the reader to Remark A.3.4.2 and to Remark A.3.2.5.
     If S is large enough so as to contain all the places of F ramified over Q then νS is also characterized as
the unique Haar measure such that the counting measure on OF,S and the additive Tamagawa measure νS
on AF,S induce the unique Haar measure on the compact Hausdorff quotient AF,S /OF,S (as per Theorem
D.1.2.1) giving it volume 1.
     The additive Tamagawa measure νS on AF,S is self-dual with respect to the standard S-local additive
character (see Example A.3.1.11). Fourier Inversion therefore holds with no normalizing constants and can be
deduced from the local case by [RV, Prop.5.6(iii),p.186], where the index set in [RV, Prop.5.6,(5.2),p.186] is
finite.

     Remark 3.3.1.4 (Tensor decomposition of ZS (·, c) for c ∈ Ω(JF,S )). Let F be a number field, S a finite
set of places containing all the Archimedean places, c ∈ Ω(JF,S )>0 a fixed quasi-character. We call c∞ the
restriction of c to the closed subgroup GL1 (AF,S∞ ), and for each place v of F we call cv the restriction of c to
the closed subgroup Fv× .
     We have built the linear functional ZS (·, c) on S(AF,S ), and want to express the sense in which this
is a (completed) tensor product of the functionals Zv (·, cv ) : S(Fv ) → C for v ∈ S. Note that these latter
functionals are continuous by inspection of their definition as an integral when cv ∈ Ω(Fv× )>0 (using for
Archimedean v that the topology on S(Fv ) can be described using L1 seminorms) and via the local functional
equation when cv ∈ Ω(Fv× )<1 (using also continuity of the local Fourier transform on S(Fv )). Here we recall
that the spaces S(Fv ) for v ∈ Sf are equipped with their finest locally convex topology (see Proposition 2.1.2.4
and Proposition C.2.5.1).
     On the Archimedean factor AF,S∞ Schwartz-Bruhat functions f∞ are not generally built as a product
of functions arising from the spaces S(Fv ) for Archimedean v, so the purely algebraic tensorial aspects
for handling the finite places don’t apply at the Archimedean places. Instead, we recall that naturally
   v∈S S(Fv ) ≃ S(AF,S ) (using the completion of the inductive tensor product, where completion is relevant

this Chapter and the next Chapters on this work.
     The theory of vector-valued holomorphic and meromorphic functions (which is discussed in Appendix C
and specifically in §C.5.2 and §C.5.3) will be used occasionally throughout this work when we want to think
about certain residue operators and coefficients of principal parts, as themselves operators on a space of vector
valued meromorphic functions. This perspective has indeed appeared in relevant literature before: we have in
mind Sarnak’s paper on the equidistribution of long horocycles (see [Sarnak]) where certain residue operators
arise of meromorphic vector-valued Eisenstein series. We will return to Sarnak’s paper in Chapters 7 and 8 of
this work when we explain the connection of our work with a number of elements of Deninger’s program.

      3.3.2.1. Poles and residues of the local Z-functions at the Archimedean places. Recall from §3.1.1 on
generalities concerning quasi-characters of modulated groups, that for G a modulated group (i.e. a Hausdorff
locally compact abelian group equipped with a continuous proper homomorphism | · |G : G → R>0 , which we
assume to be non-trivial and call module) the set of continuous quasi-characters (i.e. continuous homomorphisms
G → C× ), denoted Ω(G), is a Riemann surface whose connected components are cylinders, if the image of
| · |G is a discrete subgroup of R>0 , complex planes, if | · |G is surjective.
      We have denoted in §3.1.1 by Ω(G)(c) the connected component of Ω(G) that contains the quasi-character
c. If ω ∈ G  c1 , with G1 the compact kernel of | · |G , then we denote by Ω(G)(ω) the connected component
parametrized by ω (when we view Ω(G) as fibred over G       c1 by restricting quasi-characters of G to characters
      1
of G ). In the former case we call G discretely modulated and in the latter we term it R>0 -modulated. The
local fields Fv for v a non-Archimedean place of the number field F are all discretely modulated by the v-adic
absolute value | · |v . The Archimedean local fields Fv are R>0 -modulated.

                                   3.4. Eigendistributions and Weil’s Identity
    In this section we discuss what we refer to, throughout this work, as Weil’s Identity. It is a formula to
compute the meromorphic function Z(f, χ| · |sF ) from Theorem 3.2.2.1 in terms of the finite Hecke L-function
Lf (s, χ), for any Schwartz-Bruhat function f on AF .
142                                  CHAPTER 3. IDELIC ZETA FUNCTIONS


     This was observed by Weil in his paper on eigendistributions (see [Weil-a, §3]). The study of the global
Idelic Z-functions defined in Definition 3.2.2.5 through the lens of functional analysis, was initiated by Weil in
his paper [Weil-a] on adelic eigendistributions.
     Therein, Weil gave a direct construction and a characterization (proving their uniqueness up to normaliza-
tion, in a similar vein as for uniqueness of the Haar measure on a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group)
of those adelic tempered distributions, i.e. elements of the strong dual S(AF )′β , satisfying a homogeneity
condition with weight a continuous idelic quasi-character, under the adjoint of the continuous left-translation
action of GL1 (AF ) on S(AF ).
     They turn out to be equal to the continuous functionals:
                                                     Z(·, c)
                                                      L(c)
on S(AF ) for each c ∈ Ω(CF ), and they vary holomorphically with respect to the continuous quasi-character
c ∈ Ω(CF ). They define a holomorphic family of eigendistributions, equivalently an S(AF )′β -valued holomorphic
function on Ω(CF ): its value at each c ∈ Ω(CF ) is homogeneous of weight c under the adjoint of the continuous
left-translation action of GL1 (AF ) on S(AF ).
     The Theory of holomorphic and meromorphic functions valued in a quasi-complete Hausdorff topological
C-vector space, is developed in §C.5. The reader is referred to §C.5 (and specifically to Theorem C.5.2.6), and
the references contained therein.
     Eigendistributions will be reprised throughout the next Chapter, where we will be studying the Hausdorff
locally convex topological C-vector spaces of Adelic (both global and S-local) θ-functions, as well as the
resulting Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces of meromorphic functions on Ω(CF ) under the
Mellin transform Z. We refer the reader to §5.5 of Chapter 4.
     In this section, we record Weil’s main results from [Weil-a, §1,3], and provide a few complements, for
later reference.

      3.4.1. Weil’s Identity: the unramified case. We begin by recalling the following:

    Notation 3.4.1.1. We recall that for c ∈ Ω(CF ), i.e. for c a continuous quasi-character of CF , we denote
by cv the restriction of c to Fv× ⊂ CF , where Fv× is embedded as a closed subgroup under the insertion into
the v-adic “coordinate” Fv× → GL1 (AF ) followed by the quotient homomorphism GL1 (AF ) → CF . By [CF,
                                            N
Ch.XV,§3.2,Lemma 3.2.1,p.324] we have v∈ΣF cv = c.

    3.4.2.2. Estimates on adelic θ-functions, uniformly on Schwartz-Bruhat-bounded subsets. We record here

146                                    CHAPTER 3. IDELIC ZETA FUNCTIONS


of the estimates from Theorem 2.2.5.4 on the decay properties of the functions ΦF (f )(g) over CF as |g|F → 0+
and as |g|F → +∞, for f a Schwartz-Bruhat function on AF .
     The Theorem below was already established in Theorem 2.2.5.4. The proof we provide has one important
advantage though. It gives a concrete interpretation to the constants CN that appear in the estimates stated
in Theorem 2.2.5.4, revealing why they can be maximized over bounded subsets in S(AF ). The existence of
maxima comes down to S(AF ) satisfying the Heine-Borel property. Already through the proof of the existence
of uniform versions of the constants CN from Theorem 2.2.5.4 (uniform as f varies over a fixed bounded subset
B ⊂ S(AF )) the Heine-Borel property was used to the same effect: maximizing certain auxiliary continuous
functions (seminorms) arising in the process of building the uniform constants CB,N from parts (5) and (6) of
Theorem 2.2.5.4.
     The idelic Mellin transform in the proof below reveals the nature of those constants, and why they can be
rendered uniform on bounded subsets of S(AF ).

    Therein, we used the following important fact about S(AF ): it satisfies the Heine-Borel property, i.e.
closed bounded subsets are compact. It is a Montel space by Lemma 2.1.3.2, and hence it satisfies this
property, just as the Schwartz space of any Euclidean space (in the special case of Euclidean spaces, this is a
consequence of Ascoli-Arzelà). We used the Heine-Borel property to maximize certain continuous functions on
bounded subsets in S(AF ) on our way to build the uniform constants CB,N . Upon exhibiting such constants
CN in the statement of Theorem 2.2.5.4 as L1 -norms of Z(f, c) on vertical lines of Ω(CF )>1 , then the fact that
one can render them uniform on bounded subsets is not only reproved, but explained: such L1 -norms induce
continuous seminorms on S(AF ) and by the Heine-Borel property they attain maxima on bounded subsets.

over a slightly larger open vertical strip CJ of bounded width containing CI , with Φ holomorphic over CJ

vertical strip of bounded width contained within CJ .
     Indeed, v∈Sf (1 − qv−s ) is bounded uniformly on vertical strips of bounded width, together with all of

its derivatives, and its zeros resolve the singularities of ZS (fS , | · |sF,S ) located on the imaginary line of the

Proposition B.1.1.3), and it has simple poles at s = 0 and s = 1. The functions Zev (1Kv , | · |sv ) are, for each
v ∈ Sf , entire (by (3.4.1.3) combined with the local functional equation, see [CF, Ch.XV,Thm.2.4.1] and

derivatives.
     Finally, ZS (fS , | · |sF,S ) is Schwartz uniformly over the vertical strips of bounded width of the complex half-
plane C>0 by the Uniform Riemann-Lebesgue Lemma of Proposition B.2.2.3, which applies as a consequence of

complex half-plane C>−N for each fixed N > 0, and u meromorphic with slow growth near its poles therein.

to Theorem 2.2.3.4 and Theorem 2.2.5.4), which will lead to a proof of continuity of the S-idelic Zeta
                                3.4. EIGENDISTRIBUTIONS AND WEIL’S IDENTITY                                    151


function operators ZS taking values in S(0,+∞) (JF,S ) (the nuclear strict LF-space of I-exponentially decaying
Schwartz-Bruhat functions on JF,S , with I = (0, +∞), see Definition D.3.3.3 in Appendix D).
     The remaining ingredient is then the Convexity Bound on the finite Hecke L-function (see Proposition
B.1.1.3), combined with Weil’s Identity in the unramified case (Theorem 3.4.1.1) and in the general case, to
be proved in Theorem 3.4.3.3 by the end of this Chapter (using eigendistributions).
     This Remark wants to point out to the reader how the uniform constants CB,N from the estimates from
Theorem 2.2.3.4 come to life, i.e. where they come from and how they can be thought of. They arise as
maxima over bounded subsets in S(AF ), of continuous seminorms on S(AF ). This is the punchline of this
Remark. The fact that such maxima exist is due to an important structural property of S(AF ): it is a Montel
space. This means, concretely, that a version of Ascoli-Arzelà holds within it. Specifically, bounded subsets
are relatively compact (equivalently precompact, since S(AF ) is complete). This is why continuous functions
                                                             ′
(hence in particular the continuous functions CN (f ) and CN   (f )), can be maximized over the bounded subsets
of S(AF ). Ultimately, however, some work with concrete estimates and lattice point-counting techniques has
to be done: indeed, Theorem 2.4.2.1 and Proposition 2.3.1.2 are, for all practical purposes, unavoidable.
     Proving the continuity aspects of the formation of ZS (f, c), even for c ∈ Ω(JF,S )>0 , requires the bounds
proved therein as inputs. Throughout the arguments in the proofs of Theorem 2.4.2.1 and Proposition 2.3.1.2
and those bounds, we find that once again the Montel property of the S-local Schwartz-Bruhat spaces S(AF,S )
is used therein, to maximize certain continuous seminorms on bounded subsets in the process of maximizing
constants dependent on the Schwartz-Bruhat function, and obtain the CB,1 and CB,2 in Theorem 2.4.2.1, and
the CB,N in Proposition 2.3.1.2.
     This gives a big-picture idea to the reader of how the elements of this work fit together: a detailed study
of the S-local θ-functions and Zeta functions is required, because proving assertions on their global analogs is
then done by reduction to the S-local case, where more flexibility is available and arguments are concrete and
manageable. This is what the first nine Chapters of this work are for.
     “Global-to-S-local” is the motto to keep in mind, entering the next Chapter and up to the very main trace
calculation. The “global-to-S-local” general rule of thumb will underlie the trace calculation itself.
    3.4.3. Eigendistributions and Weil’s Identity: the general case. We will need an extension of the
identity in (3.4.1.6) to the case χ is not unramified outside S. To this end we will be using the completed
Hecke L-function L(s, χ) as opposed to the finite Hecke L-function Lf (s, χ) with finitely many Euler factors
removed, i.e. LΣF −S (χ, s), and we will be using results of Weil on local and global eigendistributions from
[Weil-a, §1,3], whose main elements we briefly recall below, to be reprised in the next Chapter.
    Definition 3.4.3.1. Let F be a number field, v a place of F , Fv the completion of F at v.
(1) Let c ∈ Ω(Fv× ) be a quasi-character. We say T ∈ S(Fv )′β is an eigendistribution of weight c if and only if:
(3.4.3.1)                                       ρ′v (g, T ) = c(g)T
    for all g ∈ Fv× , where ρ′v is the dual of the continuous right-translation action ρv : Fv× × S(Fv ) → S(Fv );
    i.e., (ρ′v (g, T ))(f ) = T (f ◦ mg ) where mg is g-multiplication on Fv . We denote by S(Fv )′β (c) the closed
    subspace of S(Fv )′β of eigendistributions on Fv of weight c.
(2) For c ∈ Ω(CF ) an idelic quasi-character, say T ∈ S(AF )′β is a global eigendistribution of weight c if
(3.4.3.2)                                       ρ′F (g, T ) = c(g)T
    for all g ∈ GL1 (AF ), where ρ′F is the dual of the continuous right-translation action ρF : GL1 (AF ) ×

                                           4.1. Schauder bases
   In this section we briefly discuss basic facts about Schauder bases in Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector spaces, providing references to the literature and recording some foundational results for later use.
                                                     155
156                    CHAPTER 4. PERIODIC SCHAUDER BASES ON MODULATED GROUPS


      4.1.1. Basic concepts and properties. Finite dimensional C-vector spaces admit finite basic frames
(i.e. C-linear bases), and several invariants of linear endomorphisms of a finite dimensional C-vector spaces,
while intrinsic, can be computed upon making a choice of basic coordinate frame, i.e. a C-linear isomorphism
to CN for some integer N ≥ 0.
      The theory of complex Hilbert spaces is another source of example where bases provide a robust tool to
make calculations. If the Hilbert space E is infinite dimensional, not all linear endomorphsms of E can be
understood in terms of their effect on a basis of E, and not all types of bases of E offer robust control over
meaningful classes of linear endomorphisms of E.
      The Hilbertian normed topology on E makes orthonormal frames particularly well suited to understand
important classes of continuous C-linear endomorphsims of E.
      We refer the reader to §C.3, and particularly to §C.3.6, for a discussion of Hilbert-Schmidt and nuclear
(equivalently, by [Kub, Thm.6.1], trace class) operators, and more generally on the Schatten-von Neumann
classes Sp (E) for every real number p ≥ 1 (nuclear operators being the class S1 (E), and Hilbert-Schmidt
operators being the class S2 (E)).
      See also Lemma C.3.4.1, for more on how these classes of operators can be understood from their effects
on an orthonormal frame for E (i.e. an orthonormal basis).
      Even in Hilbert spaces, orthonormal frames are not the only type of bases available, and capable of
offering control over classes of continuous operators. Riesz bases are images of orthonormal frames under
linear topological automorphisms. In particular, they are not necessarily orthonormal. Orthonormal bases
and more generally Riesz bases are examples of Schauder bases in Hilbert spaces.
      Weaker types of bases are also available on Hilbert, and, more generally, Banach spaces: Markushevich
bases. We will be discussing a few in the later Chapters of this work, and solely in the special cases of interest.
They are often obtained as images of a Schauder basis under a continuous injective linear operator with dense
range, whose target is a Banach space originating as the normed completion of a locally convex source. These
conditions are not sufficient for such image to be a Markushevich basis, but often times such is the origin of
Markushevich bases in Banach spaces. We refer the reader to [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.1,p.289].
      We further refer to [BJL, Ch.IV,§7] for criteria to detect “completeness” of a basic system of holomorphic
functions on non-empty domains of the complex plane with respect to the topology of uniform convergence on
compact subsets, criteria to which we shall return throughout this Chapter.
      An example to bear in mind is that of the exponential system on C ∞ (T), where T := R/Z is the
1-dimensional real torus, which we equip with the volume-1 Haar measure, and C ∞ (T) is topologized with
the Fréchet topology on uniform convergence on functions and their derivatives of arbitrary order.
      Thus topologized, C ∞ (T) is a nuclear Fréchet space (see [Tre, Part III,Ch.51,Thm.51.3,p.528] combined
with [Tre, Part III,Ch.51,Thm.51.5,p.529]).
      We refer to the complete metrizable topology on C ∞ (T) as the smooth topology.
      The 1-periodic smooth functions:
                                        em (x) := e2πimx , x ∈ R, m ∈ Z
uniquely determine smooth functions on T, which we also denote by em , and the countable collection {em }m∈Z
is an orthonormal basis for the L2 -norm completion of C ∞ (T), i.e. L2 (T).
     The continuous dual C ∞ (T)′ contains the continuous functionals am : C ∞ (T) → C obtained by sending
a smooth 1-periodic function on R, equivalently a smooth function on T, to its mth Fourier coefficient, for
m ∈ Z.
     Every element ϕ ∈ C ∞ (T) has a unique Fourier series expansion:
                                                  X
(4.1.1.1)                                 ϕ(x) =      am (ϕ)e2πimx
                                                    m∈Z
                                             4.1. SCHAUDER BASES                                            157


where the series converges with respect to the smooth topology on C ∞ (T) (a consequence of [Fol-2,
Ch.2,§2.3,Thm.2.6,p.41]).
    For any ϕ ∈ L2 (T), the Fourier series expansion ϕ(x) = m∈Z am (ϕ)e2πimx still converges, pointwise
                                                            P

almost everywhere over T, and with respect to the L2 -norm topology (this latter is a consequence of [Fol-2,
Ch.3,§3.3,Thm.3.5,p.78]. The convergence almost everywhere is a Theorem of Carlson, for which we refer the
reader to [Carleson, Thm.(c)]).
    Both in C ∞ (T) and in L2 (T), the datum
                                           {(em , am )}m∈Z ∈ E × E ′
with E = C ∞ (T), L2 (T), is an example of a Schauder basis.
    The defining property of a Schauder basis is extrapolated from this example: it is the existence of a series
expansion as in (4.1.1.1), convergent with respect to the intrinsic Hausdorff locally convex topology on E,
together with continuity of the coefficient functionals (without this latter condition, the resulting basis is
termed a topological basis. We refer the reader to [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.2,p.292]).
    We further refer the reader to [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.2,p.292], for the definition of Schauder basis in a
Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E, which we record here below for ease of access:

    Definition 4.1.1.1. Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space, {(xm , fm )}m≥0 a
bi-orthogonal sequence in E × E ∗ , i.e. fm (xn ) = δm,n for all m, n ≥ 0.
(1) {xm }m≥0 is a topological basis for E, if and only if for every u ∈ E, the series:
                                                 X
(4.1.1.2)                                            fm (u)xm
                                                 m≥0

    converges in E, and its limit is u.
(2) Assume {xm }m≥0 is a topological basis for E. We say {xm }m≥0 is a Schauder basis, if and only if we
    have {fm }m≥0 ⊂ E ′ .
We refer to the sequence {fm }m≥0 ⊂ E ∗ as the sequence of coefficient functionals of {xm }m≥0 .

    The Schauder basis {(em , am )}m∈Z in C ∞ (T) is termed the exponential system, and it is the aim of this
Chapter to generalize it to the case of R>0 -modulated abelian groups G (see Definition D.2.1.1), recording the
growth properties of the basis elements with respect to the generic continuous seminorm on the Schwartz-Bruhat
space of certain compact quotients of G by closed monogenic discrete subgroups.
    To clarify what is meant by “growth properties” of the basis elements, we consider the continuous seminorm:
                                           pN (ϕ) := sup |∂xN ϕ(x)|
                                                       x∈[0,1)
          ∞
for ϕ ∈ C (T), composed with the quotient homomorphism R → T, and N ≥ 0 an integer.
    Then
                                         pN (em ) = (2π|m|)N
which, as a function of m ∈ Z, grows polynomially.
    Examples of normed completion E of C ∞ (T) such that the exponential system maps to a sequence in E
which is not a Schauder basis, even though the coefficient functionals {am }m≥0 remain continuous functionals
on E, are E = C(T), equipped with the uniform norm, and E = L1 (T), both Banach spaces.
    The exponential system remains a Schauder basis in Lp (T) for all real numbers 1 < p < ∞ (see [Katzn,
Ch.II,§1.5,Theorem,p.59]), and the convergence of (4.1.1.1) is not only with respect to the normed topology,
but almost everywhere (a generalization of Carleson’s result; see [Hunt]).
    These examples amount to the well known phenomenon that continuous, respectively absolutely integrable,
functions on T do not generally have a uniformly convergent Fourier series, respectively convergent with
158                    CHAPTER 4. PERIODIC SCHAUDER BASES ON MODULATED GROUPS


respect to the L1 -norm; see [Katzn, Ch.II,§1.3,p.57], resting on the Uniform Boundedness Principle, for the
former, and Kolmogorov’s famous example (for which we refer the reader to [Kol]), for the latter.
    Much as finite basic frames on finite dimensional C-linear spaces, and orthonormal or Riesz frames on
complex Hilbert spaces, are useful to understand classes of operators and compute some of their invariants, to
Schauder bases goes the same role, on more general Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces E.
    Depending on robustness of properties of the topology on E, Schauder bases in E will enjoy stronger
stability properties, such as absolute summability of their basic series expansions (as for (4.1.1.1) with respect
to the smooth topology on C ∞ (T), which promotes the exponential system to an absolute Schauder basis).
    These will be recalled throughout this Chapter and the subsequent ones, as the need arises.
    We will be using Schauder bases on countable strict inductive limits of nuclear Fréchet spaces, and with
the specific aim of recognizing certain nuclear operators, and computing their nuclear traces.
    It is the content of [Lit-II, §4,Cor.2], that Schauder bases can be used to compute nuclear traces of
nuclear operators, under reasonable assumptions on the Hausdorff locally convex topology on E (i.e. E has
the approximation property and admits a Schauder basis; see [Lit-I]).

    4.1.2. On Absolute Schauder Bases and duality. With a view towards the following discussion, we
refer the reader to [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.6,p.305] for the concept of unconditionally summable sequences
within Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces.
    For a sequence {xm }m≥0 ⊂ E in a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E, {xm }m≥0 is
unconditionally summable if and only if for any countable collection of mutually disjoint finite subsets {Σk }k≥0
                                  S                                                                  P
with Σk ⊂ N for all k ≥ 0, and k≥0 Σk = N, we have that the sequence {sk }k≥0 , with sk := m∈Σk xm ,
converges in E.
                                                                P
    Equivalently, for any bijection σ : N → N, the sequence { 0≤m≤N xσ(m) }N ≥0 converges in E.
    We further refer the reader to [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.7,p.314] for the concept of absolute Schauder
basis, which will be the most discussed throughout this Chapter, and for the following properties of Schauder
bases: equicontinuous (see [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.2,p.296]), unconditional (see [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.7,p.309],
boundedly complete, respectively shrinking (see [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.5,p.302]), regular (see [Kal, §1,Def.1.1])
and normalized (see [Kal, §1,Def.1.2]), all of which we recall below for ease of access.

     Definition 4.1.2.1 (Properties of Schauder bases). Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector space, {xm }m≥0 ⊂ E a Schauder basis, {fm }m≥0 ⊂ E ′ its sequence of coefficient functionals. We
say {xm }m≥0 is:
                                                                   P

     {Pk }k≥0 ⊂ L (E) is equicontinuous.
(2) unconditional, if and only if for every u ∈ E, the sequence {fm (u)xm }m≥0 is unconditionally summable.
(3) absolute, if and only if for any continuous seminorm q on E, there exists a continuous seminorm q ′ on E
     satisfying:
                                            X
(4.1.2.1)                                       q(fm (u)xm ) ≤ q ′ (u).
                                           m≥0
                                                                                               P
(4) boundedly complete, if and only if for every sequence {αm }m≥0 ⊂ C such that the sequence { 0≤m≤k αm xm }k≥0 ⊂
                         P
    E is bounded, then m≥0 αm xm converges in E.
(5) shrinking, if and only if {fm }m≥0 ⊂ E ′ is a Schauder basis for Eβ′ .
(6) regular, if and only if there exists a 0-neighborhood U such that xm ∈   / U for all integers m ≥ 0. It is
    normalized, if and only if it is regular and bounded.

    Remark 4.1.2.2. Note that in (4.1.2.1), we have m≥0 q(fm (u)xm ) = m≥0 |fm (u)|q(xm ) by absolute
homogeneity of q. We further note that even if the Schauder basis {xm }m≥0 ⊂ E is equicontinuous, this
                                              4.1. SCHAUDER BASES                                               159


does not make the sequence of coefficient functionals {fm }m≥0 ⊂ E ′ an equicontinuous subset; see [Jar, Part
II,Ch.14,§14.3,No.7,Remarks,p.299]. We further refer the reader to [Kal, §2,Prop.2.1,p.92], where it is shown
that if {fm }m≥0 is equicontinuous (as a subset of E ′ , i.e. without necessarily being itself a Schauder basis for
E ′ with respect to any polar topology), then {xm }m≥0 is regular. The converse also holds if E carries the
Mackey topology and τ (E ′ , E) is sequentially complete.

    Remark 4.1.2.3 (On regular Schauder bases and continuous norms). Let E be a Fréchet space. Then
by [Kal, §2,Thm.2.3,p.93], if E has a regular Schauder basis, then E has a continuous norm, and admits no
                                                                        Q
complemented closed subspace linearly and topologically isomorphic to m∈N C.
    We will be using this observation to run a few sanity checks, as we construct Schauder bases on certain
nuclear Fréchet spaces arising as subquotients of the strict LF-spaces SI (G) of I-exponentially decaying
Schwartz-Bruhat functions on a second-countable Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G.


     4.1.2.1. Schauder bases in the presence of nuclearity. Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector space. We let {xm }m≥0 be an absolute Schauder basis, and write {fm }m≥0 ⊂ Eβ′ for its sequence
coefficient functionals. In particular, {(xm , fm )}m≥0 is a bi-orthogonal sequence in E × E ′ .
     Under assumptions on E, {fm }m≥0 ⊂ Eβ′ is itself a Schauder basis, i.e. {xm }m≥0 is shrinking.
     Let ιE : E → E ′′ = (Eβ′ )′ be the evaluation map sending u to the continuous functional ιE (u) := ⟨u, ·⟩E,E ′
(see (C.4.1.1) and Lemma C.4.1.1(1)).

Schauder basis.

Then {xm }m≥0 is shrinking and boundedly complete, and {fm }m≥0 is an unconditional, boundedly complete
Schauder basis for Eβ′ .
    If E is, in addition, nuclear, then {fm }m≥0 too is shrinking.

    We record here below the following Theorem of Dynin-Mityagin, providing a criterion to detect absolute
Schauder bases. Often times, we will be showing the absoluteness of the Schauder basis under consideration
directly, to describe finer information, such as growth conditions on its elements with respect to the generic
continuous seminorm.
    We refer the reader to [Jar, Part III,Ch.21,§21.10,Thm.1,p.510], and to [McAr, §9,Thm.9.1,p.900] and
[DyM].

     Remark 4.1.2.5 (Cautionary remark on the concept of absolute Schauder basis). In [McAr, §9,p.900], a
Schauder basis {(xm , fm )}m≥0 in a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E, is termed absolute
if and only if for every continuous seminorm p on E, the following series:
                                               X
                                                   p(fm (u)xm )
                                                    m≥0

converges for every u ∈ E.
     If E is a Fréchet space, this concept of absolute basis, which, a priori, differs from that defined in [Jar, Part
II,Ch.14,§14.7,(*),p.314], which is the one we adopt throughout this work, agrees with it, by the Closed Graph
Theorem (see [Jar, Part I,Ch.5,Cor.3,p.94]), since absolute summability of the sequence {fm (u)xm }m≥0 ⊂ E
for each u ∈ E implies closedness of the induced linear operator E → ℓ1 {E}, and since E is Fréchet, so is
ℓ1 {E}, the space of absolute Cauchy sequences in E (see [Jar, Part II,Ch.15,§15.6]. Note that for E = C, we
obtain ℓ1 {E} = ℓ1 , the Banach space of absolutely summable sequences of complex numbers).
     Similarly, if E is a strict LF-space, it is strictly webbed (see [Jar, Part I,Ch.5,§5.6,Thm.2,p.97]), and so
[Jar, Part I,Ch.5,§5.4,Thm.1,p.92] applies, so long as we show that ℓ1 {E} is webbed.
     This is indeed the case, if E is a strict inductive limit of a sequence of nuclear Fréchet spaces. To see this,
we proceed as follows. Let {Em }m≥0 be a defining sequence of Fréchet spaces.
     By [Jar, Part II,Ch.15,§15.8,Cor.6,p.341], we have a linear topological isomorphism ℓ1 ⊗         b π E → ℓ1 {E}.
         1
Since ℓ is a Banach space, then by [Jar, Part II,Ch.15,§15.5,Cor.4(a),p.334], the continuous linear map
limm≥0 ℓ1 ⊗π Em → ℓ1 ⊗π E is a linear topological isomorphism.
−→
     Corollary C.2.3.12 applies to ℓ1 ⊗ι Em → ℓ1 ⊗π Em , and hence the continuous linear operator ℓ1 ⊗ι Em →
ℓ1 ⊗π Em is a linear topological isomorphism for each integer m ≥ 0.
     We refer the reader to the discussion following (C.2.3.22) and to Proposition C.2.3.13 of §C.2.3, for more
on inductive tensor products.
         4.2. BASES OF EXPONENTIALLY DECAYING SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT FUNCTIONS: THE CASE G = R>0                     161


     By Proposition C.2.3.13(2), ℓ1 ⊗ E is therefore the strict inductive limit of a countable sequence of Fréchet
spaces (using nuclearity of the members of the defining sequence for E, to deduce strictness from [Jar, Part
III,Ch.16,§16.2,Cor.3,p.348]). In particular, ℓ1 ⊗ E is webbed and strictly webbed.
     The foregoing further shows that ℓ1 ⊗ E → ℓ1 ⊗   b π E is a linear topological isomorphism, and we deduce
       1
that ℓ {E} is webbed and strictly webbed.
     In particular, if E is either a nuclear Fréchet space, or a strict inductive limit of nuclear Fréchet spaces,
the concept of absolute Schauder basis in E is unambiguous: the one implicitly used in [McAr, §9] is, in these
special cases, equivalent to the one defined in [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.7,(*),p.314].

    Theorem 4.1.2.6 (Dynin-Mityagin). Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space.
(1) If E is nuclear, then every equicontinuous Schauder basis in E is absolute.
(2) Assume E is a nuclear Fréchet space. Then every Schauder basis is absolute.
(3) Assume E is a strict inductive limit of a sequence of nuclear Fréchet spaces. Then every Schauder basis is
    absolute.

    Proof. (1) : This is [Jar, Part III,Ch.21,§21.10,Thm.1,p.510].
    (2) : By [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.3,Thm.4,p.296], every Schauder basis in E is equicontinuous, and hence
by (1), it is absolute.
    (3) : By [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.3,Thm.4,p.296], since strict countable inductive limits of Fréchet
spaces are complete, bornological and ultrabornological (see [Jar, Part II,Ch.13,§13.1,Cor.4,p.273] and
[Jar, Part II,Ch.13,§13.1,Cor.5,p.273]) and strictly webbed (see [Jar, Part I,Ch.5,§5.6,Prop.1,p.96] and [Jar,
Part I,Ch.5,§5.6,Thm.2,p.97]), every Schauder basis (noting that every Schauder basis is, in particular, a
weak Schauder basis), is also an equicontinuous basis. By (1), it is an absolute basis; see also [Jar, Part
II,Ch.14,§14.3,Cor.3,p.296], noting that strict LF-spaces are barrelled (see [Scha, Ch.II,§7.2,Cor.2,p.61]), and
hence the Corollary applies.                                                                                   □

    A consequence of Theorem 4.1.2.6 is that every nuclear Fréchet space E with a Schauder basis is linearly
and topologically isomorphic to a Köthe sequence space (see [Jar, Part III,Ch.21,§21.6,p.496]). It does not
however describe the corresponding Köthe set, which depends specifically on growth conditions satisfied by
the basis elements with respect to the generic continuous seminorm on E.
    In the special cases of interest to this work, which we discuss in this Chapter for the later purpose of
identifying copies of the Schauder bases constructed herein, into subquotients of spaces of S-local and global
adelic θ-functions, it is these growth conditions that we are required to describe, which happen to exhibit the
resulting sequence spaces as being linearly and topologically isomorphic to s, the nuclear Fréchet space of
rapidly decreasing sequences (see [Tre, Part III,Ch.51,p.527]).

       4.2. Bases of exponentially decaying Schwartz-Bruhat functions: the case G = R>0
    In this section we exhibit the existence of absolute Schauder bases on subquotients of the Hausdorff locally
convex space SE (G) of exponentially decaying Schwartz-Bruhat functions on an R>0 -modulated group G (see
Definition D.2.1.1, Proposition D.3.2.5 and Theorem D.3.3.7) related from averaging operators over the action
of a discrete subgroup of the form γ Z ⊂ G.
    In the final subsection of this Chapter, §4.6.3, we will be propagating the existence of these Schauder
bases, to subquotients of the Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces SI (G) of I-exponentially
decaying Schwartz-Bruhat functions, with I an arbitrary non-empty open interval of the real line, with a view
towards applications in the later Chapters of this work.

    4.2.1. The exponential system on SE (R>0 /γ Z ). We begin with a first construction: a special case of
the periodization operator from (D.1.7.2), associated to a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G, and

these assumptions, we prove the main properties of the periodization operator over γ Z -translates in R>0 , for

k = γ Z , for γ ∈ G with |γ|G > 1.

    4.2.1.1. Recollections on the two strong topologies on orthogonals and the bounded lifting property. We
recall the following:

    Lemma 4.2.1.3 (Homomorphic weak and strong adjoints to quotient maps). Let E be a Hausdorff locally
convex topological C-vector space, and M ⊂ E a closed subspace.
    The linear bijection:
(4.2.1.8)                                       (E/M )′ → M ⊥
where the orthogonal M ⊥ is formed with respect to the duality ⟨E, E ′ ⟩, is a linear topological isomorphism,
upon endowing the source with the weak topology, and the target with the subspace topology of the weak topology
inherited from Eσ′ .
(1) If E is a nuclear Fréchet space, then (4.2.1.8) is a linear topological isomorphism, upon endowing the
    source with the strong topology, and the target with the subspace topology of the strong topology inherited
    from Eβ′ .
164                     CHAPTER 4. PERIODIC SCHAUDER BASES ON MODULATED GROUPS


(2) If E is a Hilbert space, then (4.2.1.8) is a linear topological isomorphism, upon endowing the source with
    the strong topology, and the target with the subspace topology of the strong topology inherited from Eβ′ .

     Proof. The linear operator (E/M )′ → M ⊥ is defined by sending a continuous functional T to the
composition of T by the quotient E → E/M . By [NB, Thm.8.12.1(a)], it is a linear bijection.
     By [NB, Thm.8.13.2], which applies by [NB, Thm.8.11.3(c)], the linear operator (E/M )′ → E ′ is a linear
topological embedding with respect to the weak topology on source and target. By [NB, Thm.8.12.1(a)], its
range is M ⊥ , and hence the linear operator from (4.2.1.8) is a linear topological isomorphism upon endowing
source and target with the weak topologies.
    (1) : By [Apiola, §4,Thm.4.3], nuclear Fréchet spaces are separated quotients of Köthe Schwartz spaces,
and by [MV-2, Thm.7], they are quasi-normable.
     By [Jar, Part II,Ch.10,§10.7,Cor.3,p.215] and [Tre, Part III,Ch.50,Prop.50.2(50.12),p.519], nuclear Fréchet
spaces are therefore Fréchet-Schwartz spaces, and by [Val-b, Thm.2.4(2)], for any closed subspace M ⊂ E of
the nuclear Fréchet space E, the quotient map E → E/M lifts bounded subsets.
     Let H ⊂ (E/M )′′ be an equicontinuous subset. Since E/M is reflexive, being nuclear Fréchet (by [Scha,
Ch.III,§7,Thm.7.4,p.103]), hence Montel by [Tre, Part III,Ch.50,Cor.3,p.520], hence reflexive, then by [Scha,
Ch.III,§4.1,Corollary,p.83] H is bounded with respect to the strong topology, and hence its pre-image under
the evaluation linear topological isomorphism ιE/M : E/M → (E/M )′′ is bounded. There therefore exists
a bounded subset B ⊂ M whose image under the quotient map E → E/M is ι−1              E/M (H). Under the linear
                                       ′′                                            ′′
topological isomorphism ιE : E → E , ιE (B) is therefore a bounded subset of E , hence equicontinuous by
[Scha, Ch.III,Thm.4.2,p.83] combined with [Scha, Ch.III,§3.4,Corollary,p.82]. Its image under the continuous
linear operator E ′′ → (E/M )′′ , which is the continuous adjoint of the continuous adjoint (E/M )′β → Eβ′ , is H.
     By [NB, Thm.8.13.4], applied to X = (E/M )′β , Y = Eβ′ , A : X → Y the continuous adjoint of the
quotient map E → E/M , by weak relative openness of A, which was shown in the foregoing, and since we
have shown that every equicontinuous subset of X ′ is the image under A′ of some equicontinuous subset of Y ′ ,
we deduce that A is relatively open. Its range is M ⊥ , and hence (4.2.1.8) is a linear topological isomorphism,
upon topologizing the source with the strong topology, and the target with the subspace topology of the
strong topology.
    (2) : By [Val-b, Thm.2.4(1)] (or by direct construction), for any closed subspace M ⊂ E of the Hilbert
space E, the quotient map E → E/M lifts bounded subsets. By total reflexivity of Hilbert spaces (i.e. E
and all of its separated quotients are reflexive) and again applying [Scha, Ch.III,§4.1,Corollary,p.83], [Scha,
Ch.III,Thm.4.2,p.83] and [Scha, Ch.III,§3.4,Corollary,p.82], the same argument provided for (1) shows that
[NB, Thm.8.13.4] applies, and (4.2.1.8) is a linear topological isomorphism, upon topologizing the source with
the strong topology, and the target with the subspace topology of the strong topology.                          □

    Remark 4.2.1.4. We note that the same assertion as in the Lemma does not hold for the weak topology
replaced by the strong topology, unless additional assumptions on E and the quotient E/M are in force.
    Assume E is a totally reflexive Fréchet space (i.e. every separated quotient of E is also reflexive; see
[Gro-e, §II.3,Def.2,p.99]), and M ⊂ E is a closed subspace.
    The continuous adjoint (E/M )′σ → Eσ′ is relatively open by Lemma 4.2.1.3.
    Assume that (E/M )′β → Eβ′ is a linear topological embedding. Then by reflexivity, [NB, Thm.8.13.4]
applies to A the continuous adjoint of the linear operator from (4.2.1.8), and to X = (E/M )′β and Y = M ⊥
equipped with the subspace topology of the strong topology.
    It follows that the quotient map E → E/M lifts equicontinuous subsets (with respect to the β(E ′′ , E ′ )-
topology, using reflexivity of E).
    By [Scha, Ch.III,§4,4.1,Corollary,p.83], any equicontinuous subset of E/M and E is strongly bounded
(each identified with the strong dual of (E/M )′β , respectively Eβ′ , by reflexivity; see also [NB, Thm.11.3.5] and
         4.2. BASES OF EXPONENTIALLY DECAYING SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT FUNCTIONS: THE CASE G = R>0                      165


[NB, Thm.11.3.6]), and since E is barrelled by [NB, Thm.11.7.2] (see also [Scha, Ch.II,§7,Thm.7.1,p.60]),
the converse also holds by [Scha, Ch.III,§4,Thm.4.2,p.83].
    It follows that the quotient map E → E/M would have to lift bounded subsets.
    By [Val-b, Thm.2.4(2)], E is either a Fréchet-Schwartz space, a Banach space, or a product of a Banach
space by ω.
    Nuclear Fréchet spaces are totally reflexive and Fréchet-Schwartz. We further refer the reader to [FlM,
§5.5,Corollary,p.110], for several sufficient conditions for a homomorphism between Hausdorff locally convex
topological C-vector spaces, to have homomorphic strong adjoint.
    We refer the reader to Definition C.1.5.9 and subsequent discussion for information on the bounded lifting
property for continuous linear maps between Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces.

     Remark 4.2.1.6. Note that for M ⊂ SE (R>0 ) a closed subspace, the orthogonal M ⊥ of M with respect

subspace M ⊂ SE (R>0 ), every bounded subset of SE (R>0 )/M is contained in the image of a bounded subset
of SE (R>0 ) under the quotient map SE (R>0 ) → SE (R>0 )/M .
     We refer the reader to Lemma 4.2.1.3 and to [FlM, §5.5,Corollary,part (1),p.110].
     The key to this fact is quasi-normability of Fréchet-Schwartz spaces, of which nuclear Fréchet spaces are
an example. We further refer the reader to Valdivia’s characterization of those Fréchet spaces that possess the
bounded lifting property (see [Val-b, Thm.2.4(2)]).

     Proof of Lemma 4.2.1.5. (1) and (2) : The exponential decay of f ensures that formation of the
derivative (t∂t )k f and of the ∂αk Φγ (f ), where α : R>0 → R>0 /γ Z is the continuous 1-parameter group defined
by the quotient homomorphism, commute, i.e. ∂αk Φγ (f ) = Φγ ((t∂t )k f ) as continuous functions on R>0 /γ Z .
We will be showing this towards the end of the argument.

   Remark 4.2.1.8 (On the unboundedness of the exponential system). Note that throughout the proof of
Lemma 4.2.1.5, we have shown that the canonical continuous linear map:
                                                  SE (R>0 /γ Z ) → S(R>0 /γ Z )
is a linear topological isomorphism. We will be reprising this in general in Corollary 4.5.3.1.
     We have shown that the absolute Schauder basis {em }m∈Z given by the exponential system on E :=
S(R>0 /γ Z ), SE (R>0 /γ Z ) respectively, is shrinking, i.e. its sequence of continuous coefficient functionals
{am (·)}m∈Z ⊂ E ′ is itself a Schauder basis. It is also strongly bounded and an equicontinuous subset of E ′ .
     By [Kal, §2,Prop.2.1,p.92], {em }m∈Z is a regular Schauder basis (see Definition 4.1.2.1(6)), and by [Kal,
§5,Thm.5.6,p.103], it cannot be bounded, otherwise it would be normalized (see Definition 4.1.2.1(6)), and
hence normal, in the sense of [Kal, §1,Def.1.3,p.91]. However, since E is a nuclear Fréchet space, hence Montel,
this cannot be the case, given [Kal, §5,Thm.5.6,p.103].
     Indeed, let N ≥ 0 be an integer, and consider the continuous seminorm pN on S(R>0 ) defined as
                                                 pN (ϕ) := sup |(t∂t )N ϕ(t)|.

hence in SE (R>0 /γ Z ).

     4.2.2. Schauder bases on SE (R>0 /γ Z ) with a support condition. Recall that for any compact
subset K ⊂ R>0 with non-empty interior, we denote by DK (R>0 ) ⊂ D(R>0 ) the linear subspace of those
smooth compactly supported functions on R>0 whose support is contained in K.
     By [Sch-a, Thm.II,p.66] and [Scha, Ch.II,§6,6.4,p.58], the topology induced on DK (R>0 ) by the locally
convex inductive limit topology on D(R>0 ) is the topology of uniform convergence on functions and their
derivatives of any order, i.e. the continuous linear inclusion DK (R>0 ) ⊂ D(R>0 ) is a linear topological
embedding.
     We let γ ∈ R>0 be a real number satisfying γ > 1.
     We will now show that the exponential system in S(R>0 /γ Z ), which, so far, we have shown can be lifted
to a sequence in SE (R>0 ), can in fact be lifted to a sequence of smooth compactly supported functions all
contained in DK (R>0 ), for a large enough compact subset K ⊂ R>0 with non-empty interior, depending only
on γ.
     This means, in particular, that all basis elements comprising the exponential system in S(R>0 /γ Z ) can be
lifted to smooth compactly supported functions on R>0 whose support is contained within the same compact
subset K ⊂ R>0 with non-empty interior, so long as K satisfies a largeness condition dependent on γ.
     The argument rests on one of the forms of the Paley-Wiener Theorem, and specifically on [Ru-2,
Ch.19,Thm.19.3,p.375].
     In this form, recall that the Paley-Wiener asserts the following:

     Theorem 4.2.2.1 (Paley-Wiener Theorem on compactly supported Fourier transforms). Let A > 0 be a

(1) There exists F ∈ L2 ((−A, A), λ), for λ the normalized Lebesgue measure, such that:
