    Remark 4.2.2.3. Note that the largeness condition on K from (1) is satisfied, for instance, if K contains
an interval of the form γ N [1 − ε, γ + ε] for some integer N ≥ 1 and a real number 0 < ε < 1.

    We begin with the following:

    Lemma 4.2.2.4. For any compact subset K ⊂ R>0 with non-empty interior, the linear subspace DK (R>0 ) ⊂
SE (R>0 ) is closed, and the subspace topology agrees with the topology on DK (R>0 ) of uniform convergence of
functions and their derivatives of arbitrary order.

    Proof. The subspace topology on DK (R>0 ) is stronger than the Fréchet topology of uniform convergence
on functions and their derivatives of arbitrary order (because it is defined by a larger fundamental family of
seminorms; see Definition D.3.3.1).
    With respect to the subspace topology, DK (R>0 ) is a closed subspace, since such topology preserves the
support condition upon formation of limits in SE (R>0 ) of Cauchy sequences of elements in DK (R>0 ), and
hence DK (R>0 ) is sequentially closed in SE (R>0 ), hence closed, being SE (R>0 ) a Fréchet space by Lemma
D.3.1.2.
    Since DK (R>0 ) is a Fréchet space with respect to the topology of uniform convergence on functions and
their derivatives of arbitrary order, the two topologies are equivalent by the Open Mapping Theorem (see
[NB, Thm.14.4.5(b)]).                                                                                       □

     Proof of Proposition 4.2.2.2. (1) : Under the given assumptions on K, the continuous linear operator
DK (R>0 ) → S(R>0 /γ Z ) is surjective, hence open by the Open Mapping Theorem (see [NB, Thm.14.4.5(b)]),
being source and target Fréchet spaces. Since it induces an injective linear operator from the Hausdorff
quotient DK (R>0 )/(ker(Φγ ) ∩ DK (R>0 )), itself a Fréchet space, to S(R>0 /γ Z ), the linear operator Φγ from
(4.2.2.2) is therefore a linear topological isomorphism.
172                     CHAPTER 4. PERIODIC SCHAUDER BASES ON MODULATED GROUPS


     We show that if K = b · [1/a, a] for a, b ∈ R>0 , with a > 1, then K satisfies the surjectivity condition in
(2), i.e. Φγ from (4.2.2.2) is surjective in this case.
     Indeed, let u0 ∈ DK (R>0 ) be a real valued nonnegative function whose support contains b′ · [1, γ] in its
interior for some b′ > 0. u0 exists because 2 log(a) > log(γ), and so [1, γ] ⊂ ab · (1/a, a), and it is enough to
choose b′ := 1/a.
     The compact subset b′ · [1, γ] maps surjectively onto R>0 /γ Z under the quotient homomorphism π :
R>0 → R>0 /γ Z , since γ Z · (b′ · [1, γ]) = b′ · ( m∈Z γ m · [1, γ]) = b′ · R>0 = R>0 . Then u1 := Φγ (u0 ) is real
                                                   S

                                4.3. Preparations on isotypic projectors
    In this section, we study the continuous action of a compact Hausdorff abelian group k on a Hausdorff
locally convex topological C-vector space E, and discuss assumptions on E and on the action of k on E, so
that E splits, linearly and topologically as a continuous C-linear representation of k, into a (completed, under
suitable completeness conditions on E) topological direct sum of generalized eigenspaces for the continuous
action of k on E.
    We will be first discussing the special case of E a separable Hilbert space and k := G1 the compact
Hausdorff closed subgroup of elements of module-1 in an R>0 -modulated group G. We recall from Definition
D.2.1.1 that we term R>0 -modulated those Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups G equipped with a
continuous proper surjective homomorphism | · |G to R>0 , i.e. G1 := ker(| · |G ).
    We further refer the reader to §D.3.3 for more on modulated groups, and to Theorem D.3.3.7 for the
structure of their Schwartz-Bruhat spaces (of I-exponential decaying Schwartz-Bruhat functions).

    Situation 4.3.0.1 (Isotypic projectors - preparatory notation). Let F be a number field, S a finite set of
places of F containing all the Archimedean places.
      (1) We denote by G either the Hausdorff locally compact abelian group CF , or JF,S .
      (2) We denote ν the Haar measure µ on CF , respectively µS on JF,S .
      (3) We write G1 for the closed subgroups CF1 of CF , respectively JF,S 1
                                                                                 of JF,S , and we denote by
                                       1                          1
          ν1 the Haar measure µ1 on CF , respectively µS,1 on JF,S , obtained upon choosing a continuous
          homomorphic section τ to the idelic norm, respectively to the S-idelic norm.

    In practice, G will be often assumed to satisfy the conditions from Situation 4.3.0.1.
    Throughout this section and this Chapter, unless otherwise stated, it will be assumed to be a second-
countable R>0 -modulated group with closed subgroup of module-1 elements G1 . We will denote by | · |G the
module of G, i.e. the continuous proper surjective homomorphism to R>0 promoting G to an R>0 -modulated
group.

   4.3.1. Strong continuity and unitarity. We let G be a second-countable R>0 -modulated group with
module | · |G . We denote by G1 the kernel of | · |G . We let ν a choice of Haar measure on G. We further choose
a Haar measure ν1 on the compact Hausdorff abelian group G1 .
   In this subsection we record some results on G1 -isotypes within the left-regular representation
                                              R(G) := L2 (G, ν)
of G.
    By this we mean, for each continuous character ω of G1 , the closed subspace
                          R(G)(ω) := {ϕ ∈ R(G) : ρG (g, ϕ) = ω(g)ϕ for all g ∈ G1 }
where we denote by ρG the left-translation action by G1 on R(G) induced by that of G.
    The closed subspaces R(G)ω) are simpler to study since they are separable Hilbert spaces, being R(G) a
separable (since G is second-countable; see [Fol, Prop.6.7]) Hilbert space. We will be recalling some important
facts about them, for later use in the early arguments of this Chapter, throughout this subsection.
    We will later introduce a locally convex analog of the spaces R(G)(ω), which will require more work to
describe.

     Recall that the idelic “norm” |·|F : GL1 (AF ) → R>0 is defined as the product v |·|v of all v-adic absolute
values on each Fv ; see (A.1.3.2). | · |F is not a norm and it is only referred to as such, by convention. Rather,
it is only a continuous homomorphism of Hausdorff locally compact abelian topological groups. Moreoever,
recall that by Artin’s product formula, we have |F × |F = 1. We will denote by GL1 (AF )1 the closed subgroup
of “norm-one” elements in GL1 (AF ), i.e. the kernel of | · |F . Its topology is the subspace topology. Similar
assertions hold for the S-idelic norm | · |F,S on GL1 (AF,S ) and its class group JF,S := GL1 (AF,S )/O×  F,S .

i.e. it is either CF or JF,S .
     As for G = CF , JF,S , a general R>0 -modulated group admits continuous homomorphic sections to the
module | · |G ; see Remark D.2.1.2.

    We recall the following facts about the Haar measure ν on G.

    Lemma 4.3.1.3. The measure ν on G is regular, Radon and σ-finite.

    Proof. Since ν is Radon as a Borel measure on G, as any Haar measure on a locally compact Hausdorff
abelian group, ν is finite on compact subsets (see [DE, Thm.1.3.5]). It is therefore regular Radon by [Fol,
Thm.7.8]. Since G is second-countable, then it is σ-compact, and hence ν is σ-finite.                   □

    Remark 4.3.1.4. One important consequence of Lemma 4.3.1.3 is that Cc (G), the complex vector space
of complex valued continuous compactly supported functions on G, is contained in L2 (G, ν) = R(G) and it is
dense in the L2 -norm topology. This is [Fol, Prop.7.9] or [DE, Prop.1.3.3], applied to X = G, µ in either
Theorem is the Haar measure ν, and p = 2.

    We note that R(G) carries an action of G by left-translation on functions through its continuous left-
translation action on itself.
    It is defined as follows: on continuous compactly supported functions, we define
(4.3.1.3)                                   ρG : G × Cc (G) → Cc (G)
by the assignment, for any ϕ ∈ Cc (G), and any (g, x) ∈ G × G
(4.3.1.4)                                    ρG (g, ϕ)(x) := ϕ(g −1 x)
    We will recall below that ρG extends uniquely to R(G) as a continuous representation of G.
176                     CHAPTER 4. PERIODIC SCHAUDER BASES ON MODULATED GROUPS


    Lemma 4.3.1.5 (Basic properties of the left-regular representation R(G)). Let G be a second-countable
R>0 -modulated group. Let τ be a choice of continuous homomorphic section to the module | · |G . The Hilbert
space R(G) satisfies the following conditions:

(1) R(G) is separable.
(2) ρG from (4.3.1.4) uniquely extends to a continuous unitary representation of G on R(G). For every
    ϕ1 , ϕ2 ∈ R(G) and every g ∈ G, we have
(4.3.1.5)                           ⟨ρG (g, ϕ1 ), ρG (g, ϕ2 )⟩R(G) = ⟨ϕ1 , ϕ2 ⟩R(G) .
(3) Upon defining the assignment
(4.3.1.6)                                  UG,τ : R>0 × R(G) → R(G)
      as UG,τ (t)(ϕ) := ρG (τ (t), ϕ) for every ϕ ∈ R(G), then UG,τ is a strongly continuous one-parameter group
      of unitary operators on R(G).

      On the concept of continuity for ρG being used, we devote a few words.

    Remark 4.3.1.6 (Strong continuity of the left-translation action of G on R(G)). We note that continuity
of ρG from (4.3.1.4) is often referred to as strong continuity, usually in the context of one-parameter groups or
semi-groups of unitary operators. It means that the map
(4.3.1.7)                                       ρG : G → GL(R(G))
sending g to ρG (g, ·) is a continuous map with respect to the topology on the Hausdorff locally compact
abelian group G on the source, and the subspace topology of the strong operator topology on the target,
GL(R(G)) being the group of invertible continuous C-linear endomorphisms of the Hilbert space R(G).
     That GL(R(G)) is indeed a group, is a consequence of the Open Mapping Theorem (see [Cnw-a,
Ch.III,Thm.12.1]).
     The strong operator topology on B(R(G)), the C-vector space of bounded C-linear endomorphisms of
R(G), is the Hausdorff locally convex topology defined by the separating family of seminorms {qϕ }ϕ∈R(G)
with qϕ (T ) := ||T (ϕ)||R(G) .
     The group GL(R(G)) is not a topological group with respect to the strong operator topology, if R(G) is
infinite dimensional (equivalently, if G is not a finite abelian group).
     The Lemma however says that ρG factors through U(R(G)), the unitary group of R(G). The subgroup
U(R(G)) of GL(R(G)) is a topological group with respect to the strong operator topology (because all subsets
of U(R(G)) are strongly bounded, hence equicontinuous by the Uniform Boundedness Principle (see [Scha,
Ch.III,§4,Thm.4.2,p.83]; see also [Cnw-a, Ch.IX,§1,Prop.1.3(d),p.256]). It is Hausdorff, complete (by another
application of the Uniform Boundedness Principle) but not locally compact, unless R(G) is finite dimensional,
equivalently if G is a finite abelian group. It is second-countable, metrizable (see [EU, Lemma 1.6]) and hence
paracompact.
     We further note that by the Spectral Theorem for normal operators (see [Cnw-a, Ch.IX,§2,Thm.2.2,p.263]),
U(R(G)) is connected and path-connected, since for each A ∈ U(R(G)), there exists a bounded, self-adjoint
endomorphism ϕ(A) ∈ B(R(G)), for ϕ(z) := θ, z = eiθ for θ ∈ [0, 2π), a bounded Borel-measurable function ϕ :
U(1) → [0, 2π) ⊂ R, and since the spectrum σ(A) is contained in U(1) (see [Cnw-a, Ch.IX,§2,Thm.2.3,p.264]),
and the strongly continuous (by [Cnw-a, Ch.X,§5,Thm.5.1,p.327]) path γ(t) := exp(itϕ(A)) connects A = γ(1)
to the identity Id = γ(0).
     Note that indeed ϕ(A) is self-adjoint, since the image of ϕ is contained in [0, +∞), and hence, by [Cnw-a,
Ch.IX,§2,(2.4),p.264] and [Cnw-a, Ch.IX,§1,Lemma 1.9,p.257] (noting that orthogonal projectors are positive
operators), [Cnw-a, Ch.II,§2,Prop.2.12,p.33] applies.
                                  4.3. PREPARATIONS ON ISOTYPIC PROJECTORS                                      177


    Strong continuity of ρG amounts to the homomorphism:
(4.3.1.8)                                      ρG : G → U(R(G))
being a continuous homomorphism of Hausdorff topological groups.
     We refer the reader to [Cnw-a, Ch.IX,Def.1.2], and to [Cnw-a, Ch.X,Def.5.3]. In Lemma 4.3.1.5(3),
continuous unitary actions of R>0 on R(G) are studied, induced by the action ρG of G. Continuity of R>0 is
intended with respect to the strong operator topology.
     We refer to [HP, Ch.II,§2.16,p.51] for more on the strong operator topology, and to [Cnw-a, Ch.X,Thm.5.4]
and to [HP, Ch.X] for comparisons among various notions of topologies on linear operators, for one-parameter
unitary groups. Note that the strong operator topology on U(R(G)) is equivalent to the weak operator topology
(see [EU, Lemma 1.5]), while the norm-topology is generally strictly finer (see [EU, pp.50-51]). We further
note that the strong operator topology on U(R(G)) is equivalent to the topology of pre-compact convergence,
by Uniform Boundedness and [Scha, Ch.III,§4,Thm.4.5,p.85]. In particular, U(R(G)) is contractible, by [AS,
Appendix 2,Prop.A2.1].
     We further refer the reader to §C.3.3 and §C.3.4 in Appendix C, for more on the strong operator topology

    Terminology 4.3.2.1 (G1 -isotypes on the regular representation R(G) of an R>0 -modulated group).
Let G be a second-countable R>0 -modulated group, with module | · |G . Let ν a choice of Haar measure on G,

to G1 of the continuous left-translation action of G on R(G):
                      R(G)(ω) := {ϕ ∈ R(G) : ρG (g, ϕ) = ω(g)ϕ, for all g ∈ G1 } ⊂ R(G).
    We refer to R(G)(ω) as the ω-isotype of R(G), and to the orthogonal projector ν1 (G1 )−1 ΠG1 ,ω as the

and the kernel of ΠG,ω,τ is linearly and topologically generated within R(G) by the elements of the form
ϕ − ω(g)ρG (g, ϕ) as (ϕ, g) varies over R(G) × G1 .

     4.3.3. G-invariants in a quasi-complete Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space.
Using the results on integration in the sense of Pettis from §C.4), the following Lemma 4.3.3.1 studies formation
of continuous invariants and co-invariants under the continuous action of a compact Hausdorff abelian group
G, on a quasi-complete Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E.
     The Lemma will be used systematically throughout this Chapter in the presence of a continuous left-
translation action by a compact Hausdorff abelian group, and we record it here for convenience.
     Throughout the remainder of this subsection, G will denote a compact Hausdorff abelian group, as opposed
to a Hausdorff locally compact R>0 -modulated group.
     We recall that a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E is quasi-complete if and only if
every bounded Cauchy net in E converges in E (see also Remark C.4.3.4).
     Quasi-completeness is also termed, in light of the definition, bounded completeness, and a quasi-complete
E is also termed boundedly complete. We further refer the reader to §C.4.3 for more on quasi-completeness, a
condition that, combined with the Bipolar Theorem (see [Bou-TVS, Ch.II,§6,No.3,Thm.1,TVS II.44]), ensures
that the closed convex circled hull of a precompact subset of E is contained in E (see Lemma C.4.1.2(1)).
This leads to E-valued integration, for E quasi-complete, to exist and be well behaved, as discussed in §C.4.3
(see Theorem C.4.3.5).
     We refer the reader to §C.2, §C.5.1 and §C.3.3 for classes of examples of quasi-complete Hausdorff locally
convex topological C-vector spaces.

    Lemma 4.3.3.1 (Norm isomorphism of continuous representations of compact Hausdorff abelian groups).
Let G be a compact Hausdorff abelian group, E a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space equipped
with a continuous C-linear action ρG of G by linear topological automorphisms. Let µG be a choice of Haar
measure on G. Assume that E is quasi-complete and that either one of the following two conditions is satisfied:
(a) the action ρG is uniformly continuous, i.e. for every u ∈ E and for every net {ui }i∈I ⊂ E converging to
    u, we have ρG (g, ui ) → ρG (g, u) uniformly as g ∈ G.
                                 4.3. PREPARATIONS ON ISOTYPIC PROJECTORS                                      181


(b) E is bornological, and condition (a) is satisfied for every u ∈ E and for every sequence {um }m≥0 ⊂ E
    converging to u ∈ E.
    Then:
(1) For every u ∈ E, the C-linear form on E ′ :
                                                    Z
(4.3.3.1)                           ΦG (u) : φ 7→       ⟨ρG (g, u), φ⟩E,E ′ dµG (g)
                                                    G
    is in the image of the canonical continuous linear operator ιE : E → (E ′ )∗ , i.e. ΦG (u) is the evaluation
    functional on E ′ on a unique element of E. Equivalently, the linear operator ΦG : E → (E ′ )∗ assigned by
    u 7→ ΦG (u), factors through ιE .
         Its formation is continuous with respect to the intrinsic topology on E, i.e. ΦG : E → E is a continuous
    linear operator.
(2) ΦG surjects onto the closed subspace H0 (G, E) of G-invariant elements of E, and µG (G)−1 ΦG is idempo-
    tent.

    linear topological isomorphism:
(4.3.3.2)                               NG : H0,cont (G, E) → H0 (G, E)

    {u − ρG (g, u), u ∈ E, g ∈ G} as u varies over E.
    Remark 4.3.3.2 (On E-valued integration). The reader may think of the operator ΦG as an E-valued
integral:                                   Z
                                            ΦG =            ρG (g, ·) dµG (g)
                                                        G
in the sense of Pettis, for which we refer to Appendix C, and specifically to §C.4.
     We highlight for the reader that the theory of E-valued integration is indeed needed for the purposes of
this work beyond the case of Banach spaces, for multiple reasons, all related to the following fact.
     Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, assume G is compactly generated, and let k ⊂ G be a
compact subgroup with compactly generated orthogonal k ⊥ . Then S(k, G), the closed subspace of k-invariant
Schwartz-Bruhat functions on G, is a nuclear Fréchet space, and hence it is, in particular, never a Banach
space, unless G/k is finite.
     Vector-valued integrals will often be, throughout this work, valued in S(G) or quotients of S(G), or in
closed subspaces of S(k, G) and their quotients. This leads us to the necessity of vector-valued integration
beyond the case of the Banach-valued integral of Bochner. We will be using continuity properties of the
integral in the sense of Pettis, and the reader familiar with the Banach-valued theory of integration will
recognize extensions of the known results on the Bochner integral, which is recovered as a spacial case, in §C.4.
     Terminology 4.3.3.1 (Norm isomorphisms). We refer to the linear topological isomorphism NG from

     Proof of Lemma 4.3.3.1. (1) : By Theorem C.4.3.5, applied to X = G, µ = µG , f : X → E defined as

     Terminology 4.3.3.2 (Locally convex isotypes). Let G be a compact Hausdorff abelian group, E a
Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space equipped with a continuous C-linear action ρG of G on E
by linear topological automorphisms.
     Assume (ρG , E) satisfy either of the assumptions (a) and (b) of Corollary 4.3.3.3.
     Let ω ∈ Gb be a continuous character.
     We refer to both H0,cont (ω, E) and H0 (ω, E) as the ω-isotype of E. As the need arises, we will refer to
the former, equipped with the quotient topology, as the space of continuous ω-co-invariants of E, and to the
latter, equipped with the subspace topology, as the space of ω-homogeneous elements of E.

     Proof of Corollary 4.3.3.3. We define the continuous C-linear action ηG,ω := ωρG of G on E, i.e.
for every g ∈ G and u ∈ E, ηG,ω (g, u) := ω(g)ρG (g, u).
     Since ω, and hence ω = ω −1 , is a continuous character of the compact Hausdorff abelian group G, then
ηG,ω is a continuous C-linear action of G on E, since ρG is. For each g ∈ G, ηG,ω (g, ·) is a linear topological
automorphism whose continuous inverse is ηG,ω (g −1 , ·).
    (1), (2) and (3) follow from (1), (2) and (3) of Lemma 4.3.3.1 applied to ηG,ω in place of ρG of the Lemma,
upon observing the following on the continuous action ηG,ω of G on E.
     Since ρG is assumed to be sequentially uniformly continuous, and since the image of ω, and hence of ω, is
the unit circle in the complex plane, then, by absolute homogeneity of any continuous seminorm on E, ηG,ω is
also uniformly sequentially continuous. Indeed, for any continuous seminorm p on E, and any u ∈ E, and for
any sequence {um }m≥0 ⊂ E converging to u in E, we have
              sup p(ηG,ω (g, um − u)) = sup |ω(g)| p(ρG (g, um − u)) = sup p(ρG (g, um − u)) → 0.
              g∈G                        g∈G                             g∈G

    Since E is bornological, (1.b) of Lemma 4.3.3.1 applies.
    We then observe that if G acts on E through ηG,ω , then the resulting H0 (G, E) is the closed subspace of
those elements u ∈ E satisfying, for every g ∈ G:
                                                  u = ηG,ω (g, u)
which reads u = ω(g)ρG (g, u), equivalently ρG (g, u) = ω(g)u. µG (G)−1 ΦG,ω is idempotent by the same
assertion from Lemma 4.3.3.1(2), applied to ηG,ω in place of ρG .
    These observations having been made, Lemma 4.3.3.1 implies all the assertions of the Corollary.  □




    4.3.3.1. Hilbertian and locally convex isotypic projectors. We now show how to recover the orthogonal

    Corollary 4.3.3.4 (Hilbertian and locally convex isotypic projectors). Let G be a second-countable
R>0 -modulated group, with module | · |G and compact Hausdorff closed subgroup of module-1 elements G1 .
Let R(G) be the Hilbert space L2 (G, ν), for µG a choice of Haar measure on G. Let ν1 be a choice of Haar

(4.3.3.10)                                        ΠG1 ,ω = ΦG1 ,ω

linear endomorphism of R(G) defined in (4.3.3.17).
     Moreover, ν1 (G1 )−1 ΠG1 ,ω , equivalently ν1 (G1 )−1 ΦG1 ,ω , are orthogonal projectors, whose ranges are, for
distinct continuous characters ω of G1 , mutually orthogonal.
                                  4.3. PREPARATIONS ON ISOTYPIC PROJECTORS                                        185


     Proof. We note that the Hilbert space E := R(G) is complete, hence quasi-complete. All metrizable
Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces are bornological (see [NB, Example 13.2.8(b)]), and by
(4.3.2.5), ΠG1 ,ω is a continuous linear operator.
     The continuous left-translation action of G on E is unitary (see Lemma 4.3.1.5(2)) and hence uniformly
continuous. Its restriction to the compact Hausdorff abelian subgroup G1 , therefore also is.
     Lemma 4.3.3.1 therefore applies, and gives ΦG1 ,ω through its Corollary 4.3.3.3.
     The composition ιE ◦ ΠG1 ,ω agrees with ιE ◦ ΦG1 ,ω by the Riesz Representation Theorem (see [Fol,
Ch.6,§6.2,Thm.6.15,p.190]). Since ν1 (G1 )−1 ΦG1 ,ω is idempotent by Corollary 4.3.3.3(2), it is an orthogonal
projector by [Cnw-a, Ch.II,§3,Prop.3.3(f)], so long as we show that it is a positive operator. The linear
                        0  ′
             N
direct sum ω′ ∈G   c1 H (ω , E) of mutually orthogonal closed subspaces of E, is dense in E by the Peter-Weyl
Theorem (see [Kn, Thm.1.12]). By continuity of the Hermitian inner product on E, and continuity of ΦG,ω , it
is enough to check that ΦG,ω is positive on H0 (ω, E) (i.e. for ω ′ = ω, since ΦG,ω annihilates H0 (ω ′ , E) for every
continuous character ω ′ of G1 such that ω ′ ̸= ω). ΦG,ω is positive on H0 (ω, E) since it acts as multiplication
by ν1 (G1 ).                                                                                                        □
   Corollary 4.3.3.4 provides an alternative take on Lemma 4.3.2.2, noting that a form of the Peter-Weyl
Theorem is used in the proof of both, respectively, to infer than the linear subspace linearly generated by the
matrix coefficients is dense.
    Example 4.3.3.5 (Finite dimensional representations of compact abelian groups). Let G be a second-
countable compact abelian group, and E a finite dimensional C-vector space, equipped with the Euclidean
topology, i.e. the unique, up to equivalence, linear topology promoting E to a Hausdorff locally convex
topological C-vector space.
    Let ρG : G×E → E be a continuous C-linear action of G by linear topological automorphisms, equivalently
linear automorphisms.
    There exists a compact subgroup k ⊂ G with finitely generated orthogonal k ⊥ ⊂ G,  b such that ρG restricts
to k to the trivial action of k on E, i.e. ρG factors trough G/k, which is a compact abelian Lie group, and the
resulting action of G/k is faithful, i.e. ρG induces an injective continuous homomorphism ρ : G/k → GL(E).
Indeed, the kernel k of the continuous homomorphism ρ : G → GL(E) qualifies, since GL(E) is itself a Lie
group, and hence so is the image of ρ(G) since a closed subgroup of a Lie group is an embedded Lie subgroup,
since ρ(G) is compact, hence closed in GL(E).
    We may replace G with G/k and rename G/k as G.
    Then G is a compact abelian Lie group, and it acts faithfully and semisimply on E. We choose a Haar
measure µG on G.
    The operators µG (G)−1 ΦG,ω , as ω varies over the continuous characters of G, are the projectors onto
the ω-isotypic component E(ω) of E. Since E is finite dimensional, only finitely many continuous characters
ω∈G  b exist such that E(ω) ̸= 0.

    Example 4.3.3.6 (Finite dimensional representations of finite groups). Let G be a finite group. Then
upon choosing µG to be any Haar measure on G, there exists a unique positive real number r > 0 such that
µG is rνG , for νG the counting measure on G (see [DE, Prop.1.4.4(c)]).
    Let E := C[G], the finite dimensional regular representation of G, equipped with the Euclidean topology.
    The linear operator µG (G)−1 ΦG,ω does not depend on the choice of Haar measure µG , and we may therefore
assume r = 1. The linear operator µG (G)−1 ΦG,ω is, therefore, the isotypic projector u 7→ |G|
                                                                                             1

                                                                                                 g∈G ω(g)g.v
where g.v is the effect of the action of G on C[G] by left-translation on itself.


    4.3.3.2. Averaging over relatively compact locally closed subsets of a Hausdorff locally compact abelian
group. We conclude this subsection by recording here below and integrability and continuity criterion for the
186                     CHAPTER 4. PERIODIC SCHAUDER BASES ON MODULATED GROUPS


vector-valued continuous functions obtained from the action of a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G,
acting continuously on a quasi-complete Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E, restricted to
the compact subsets of G.

     Lemma 4.3.3.7 (Integrability and continuity of actions of relatively compact subsets). Let G be a Hausdorff
locally compact abelian group, X ⊂ G a relatively compact locally closed subset with non-empty interior. Let E
be a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space, equipped with a continuous C-linear action ρG by
linear topological automorphisms. Let µG be a choice of Haar measure on G.
     Assume E is quasi-complete, and that either of the following two conditions on ρG and E is satisfied:
(a) the action ρG is continuous, uniformly on the compact subsets of G, i.e. for every u ∈ E and for every net
    {ui }i∈I ⊂ E converging to u, we have, for every compact subset K ⊂ G, ρG (g, ui ) → ρG (g, u) uniformly
    as g ∈ K.
(b) E is bornological, and condition (a) is satisfied for every u ∈ E and for every sequence {um }m≥0 ⊂ E
    converging to u ∈ E.
      Then:
(1) For every u ∈ E, the C-linear form on E ′ :

    is in the image of the canonical continuous linear operator ιE : E → (E ′ )∗ , i.e. ΦX (u) is the evaluation
    functional on E ′ on a unique element of E. Equivalently, the linear operator ΦX : E → (E ′ )∗ assigned by
    u 7→ ΦX (u), factors through ιE .
         Its formation is continuous with respect to the intrinsic topology on E, i.e. ΦX : E → E is a continuous
    linear operator.
(2) ΦX surjects onto the closed subspace H0 (X, E) of elements u of E satisfying the equations ρG (g, u) = u
    for all g ∈ X, and µG (X)−1 ΦX is idempotent.
(3) The σ(E, E ′ )-closure of the closed subspace ker(ΦX ) ⊂ E is the σ(E, E ′ )-closure of the C-linear subspace
    VE generated by the elements {u − ρG (g, u), u ∈ E, g ∈ X} as u varies over E.

     Proof. (1) : By Theorem C.4.3.5, applied to X, µ = µG |X (the restriction of the Radon measure µG to

is ιE (E)-valued and linear, and hence it factors through ιE as a C-linear operator on E → (E ′ )∗ . We denote
by ΦX the resulting unique linear operator ΦX : E → E such that its composition with ιE is ΦX : E → (E ′ )∗ .
     By Lemma C.4.3.12, ΦX : E → E is continuous with respect to the intrinsic topology on E, if condition
(a) is satisfied.
     If condition (b) is satisfied, instead, then we proceed as in the proof of (1) from Lemma 4.3.3.1: by Lemma
C.4.3.12, ΦX is sequentially continuous. By [NB, Thm.13.2.7(a)], which applies to X = Y = E (notation as
in loc.cit.) since E is bornological, then ΦX is continuous.
     (2) : Since H0 (X, E) is the intersection of the linear subspaces ker(IdE − ρG (g, ·)) as g varies over X, each
of which is closed, it is itself a closed subspace of E.
     We have, for every u ∈ E, for every continuous functional φ ∈ E ′ , and for every g ∈ G:

     We refer the reader to Proposition D.1.9.2, which proves that for G a second-countable, compact Hausdorff

we refer the reader to §2.1) is uniformly continuous (hence sequentially uniformly continuous). Since S(G) is

             4.4. Exponential system on monogenic quotients of R>0 -modulated groups
    The reader may use Lemma 4.2.1.5 and Proposition 4.2.2.7 from the previous section, as guidance through
the following more general analogs, which cover the case of an arbitrary R>0 -modulated Hausdorff locally
compact abelian group G equipped with an element γ ∈ G with |γ|G > 1 (therefore) generating a free closed
subgroup γ Z .
    This generality is needed for the intended applications. The arguments for the respective results below,
closely follow those we have just provided for the special case G = R>0 , and are, for the most part, only
notationally more involved.

    4.4.1. Complements on the Mellin transform on SI (G). We make a brief interlude on the Mellin
transform on the Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space SI (G) of I-exponentially decaying
Schwartz-Bruhat functions on G, a Hausdorff locally compact second-countable R>0 -modulated abelian group.
    In this subsection, we show how to reconcile all of the various instances of the Mellin transform arising
throughout this work, comparing them through changes of variables and across linear topological isomorphisms.

   We let G be an R>0 -modulated group.

     Remark 4.5.1.3 (Caveat on tensor products and inductive limits). The phenomenon highlighted in
Remark 4.5.1.2 is caused by a general result observed in [Gro-b, Ch.I,§1,No.3,Rem.1,p.47]: let E be a Fréchet
space, and F a strict LF-space. Assume that E is not normable and that there exists a defining sequence
{Fm }m≥0 for F , presenting F as the Hausdorff locally convex inductive limit of the Fréchet spaces Fm . Further
assume that the sequence is such that Fm ⊂ Fm+1 is a strict containment.
     Then limm≥0 (Fm ⊗    b π E) → F ⊗b π E is not a linear topological isomorphism.
            −→
     In the case of SI (G) for G a general modulated group, by Theorem D.3.3.7(3) any choice of continuous
homomorphic section τ to the module | · |G induces a linear topological isomorphism SI (G) ≃ SI (R>0 ) ⊗ S(G1 ),
with G1 := ker(| · |G ) a compact Hausdorff abelian closed subgroup.
     The Schwartz-Bruhat space S(G1 ) is indeed a strict LF-space, since G is assumed to be second-countable,
which forces G1 to also be second-countable.
     If G1 does not have finitely generated dual group, then a defining sequence {Fm }m≥0 as in the foregoing
can be found, i.e. such that the closed inclusions Fm ⊂ Fm+1 are strict.
     Since SI (R>0 ) is a non-normable Fréchet space, we are led to the conclusion from Remark 4.5.1.2,
i.e. the inductive tensor product topology on SI (R>0 ) ⊗ S(G1 ) and the projective tensor product topology
on SI (R>0 ) ⊗ b π S(G1 ) are not equivalent. The canonical continuous linear operator SI (R>0 ) ⊗ S(G1 ) →
SI (R>0 ) ⊗b π S(G1 ) is, however, a continuous bijection.
     Its linear inverse is sequentially continuous (as an application of Proposition C.2.3.11) and hence source
and target have equivalent von-Neumann bornologies.

     Formation of the series defining Φγ (f )(x) as a function of x ∈ G for any f ∈ SE (G) converges pointwise
over G to a γ Z -invariant function, hence a function on G/γ Z . To see this, we proceed as follows.
     We call γ0 := |γ|G > 1, and, for each g ∈ G1 , ϕg (t) := f (τ (t)g) as a Schwartz-Bruhat function of t ∈ R>0
of exponential decay.
     The function t 7→ ϕ(t) := supg∈G1 ϕg (t) is continuous over R>0 because G1 is compact Hausdorff, and, for
every integer N ≥ 1, there exists TN > 0 and a real number CN > 0, such that ϕ(t) still satisfies the estimate
|ϕ(t)| ≤ CN e−N |log(t)| for all t ∈ R>0 such that |log(t)| > TN .
     The same method from the proof of Lemma 4.2.1.5 then shows that the series defining Φγ (f )(x) converges
for every x ∈ G, since it is dominated from above by the series k∈Z |ϕ(γ0k t)|, for γ0 := |γ|G > 1. Upon
                                                                        P

replacing f with ∂αk f for each integer k ≥ 0 and for α : R>0 → G the arbitrary continuous 1-parameter
subgroup, the same holds for the series defining Φγ (∂αk f ), and the convergence is uniform over the compact
subsets of G: since G1 is compact, the locally uniform mode of convergence is seen by means of the same
method from the proof of Lemma 4.2.1.5, which discusses the case G = R>0 .
     Formation of ∂αk commutes with Φγ for each integer k ≥ 0, and hence Φγ (f ) is a smooth γ Z -invariant
function on G (we refer the reader to the proof of Lemma 2.2.4.3, for a similar argument. Inducting on
the degree k ≥ 1 of ∂α , we may rename ∂αk−1 f as f and assume k = 1. Since G ≃ R>0 × G1 as Hausdorff
locally compact abelian groups, it is enough to treat the case of α with image contained in G1 , respectively
α(R>0 ) ∩ G1 = {e}, the neutral element.
     In the former case, uniform convergence of the series defining Φγ on compact subsets, and uniform
convergence over G of the incremental ratio (u − 1)−1 (f (α(u)−1 x) − f (x)) as u → 1, for any f ∈ SE (G), imply
the desired commutation of Φγ and ∂α .
     We therefore assume α(R>0 ) ∩ G1 = {e}. In this case, the argument is closely analogous to the proof of
Lemma 4.2.1.5.

that Φγ (f ) is Schwartz-Bruhat over S(G/γ Z ).

to [Bou-II, Ch.VII,§2,No.1,Lemma 1,INT VII.28] and to the footnote [Bou-II, Ch.VII,§2,No.1,Remark 1,INT

     4.5.2. Periodic Schauder Bases: support conditions in the monogenic case. The following is an
analog for general R>0 -modulated groups satisfying the assumptions from Situation 4.4.2.3 of Proposition
4.2.2.2.
     We let G be an R>0 -modulated group satisfying the assumptions made in Situation 4.4.2.3.
     For any compact subset K ⊂ R>0 with non-empty interior, and for any compact subgroup k ⊂ G1 whose
orthogonal k ⊥ is compactly generated, we denote by SK (k, G) ⊂ D(G) the linear subspace of those smooth
compactly supported functions on G that are k-invariant, and whose support is contained in τ (K) · G1 ⊂ G.
     By [Sch-a, Thm.II,p.66] and [Scha, Ch.II,§6,6.4,p.58] and the definition of the topology on D(G) in [Bru,
§1], the topology induced on SK (k, G) by the locally convex inductive limit topology on D(G) is the topology
obtained by transport of structure from the Hausdorff locally convex Fréchet topology of uniform convergence
on functions and their derivatives (directional, along arbitrary continuous, equivalently smooth, 1-parameter
subgroups) of any order on DZ (P ) for P := τ (R>0 ) · G1 /k, an abelian elementary Lie group since G1 is
compact, and Z ⊂ P the compact subset τ (K) · G1 /k, i.e. the continuous linear inclusion SK (k, G) ⊂ D(G) is
a linear topological embedding.
     We further note that under the linear topological isomorphism SE (G) ≃ SE (R>0 ) ⊗ b π S(G1 ) from Theorem
D.3.3.7(3), for any compact subgroup k ⊂ G with k compactly generated, we have that SK (k, G) is
                                                  1         ⊥

mapped linearly and topologically isomorphically onto DK (R>0 ) ⊗   b π S(k, G1 ). To see this, we use nuclearity
of DK (R>0 ) (which is [Tre, Part III,Ch.51,Corollary,p.530]) and [Jar, Part III,Ch.16,§16.2,Cor.3,p.348], to
deduce that the linear inclusion DK (R>0 ) ⊗π S(k, G1 ) → SE (R>0 ) ⊗π S(G1 ) is a linear topological embedding
(by Proposition 4.2.2.2(1)), and it remains so upon passage to completions on source and target. The source is
DK (R>0 ) ⊗b π S(k, G1 ) and the target is SE (R>0 ) ⊗
                                                     b π S(G1 ).
     We further denote by DK (G) ⊂ SE (G) the linear subspace of those Schwartz-Bruhat functions on G of
exponential decay, whose support is compact and contained within τ (K) · G1 .

Fréchet space by [Jar, Part III,Ch.15,§15.1,Cor.4,p.26], it is sequential, and hence SK (k, G) is closed, being
sequentially closed within the larger ambient, and since SE (k, G) is itself closed within the larger ambient by
the foregoing.

     Remark 4.5.2.2. Note that in the proof of Proposition 4.5.2.1 we are not claiming that SE (G) is a
sequential space, nor are we claiming that in a strict LF-space, a subspace is closed if and only if its pre-image
in each of the spaces in a defining sequence is closed.
     In the special case at hand, SK (k, G) is already entirely contained within SE (k, G) := SE (R>0 ) ⊗ S(k, G1 ),
which is itself linearly and topologically isomorphic to SE (R>0 ) ⊗b π S(k, G1 ) since the tensor factors are Fréchet
spaces (see Corollary C.2.3.12), and the projective tensor product topology on the latter is equivalent to
the subspace topology inherited by SE (G). We use [Jar, Part III,Ch.16,§16.2,Cor.3,p.348] and nuclearity of
SE (R>0 ), to identify injective and projective tensor topologies; see also Proposition C.2.3.13(2).
     We deduce that SE (k, G) := SE (R>0 ) ⊗ S(k, G1 ) ≃ SE (R>0 ) ⊗   b π S(k, G1 ) is metrizable, hence sequential,
and it therefore suffices to prove sequential closedness of SK (k, G) in SE (R>0 ) ⊗ b π S(k, G1 ) to deduce closedness
of SK (k, G) in SE (k, G), and hence in SE (G), being SE (k, G) a closed subspace of SE (G) (since S(k, G1 ) ⊂ S(G1 )
is).

    By Proposition 4.5.1.1(1), Φγ : SI (G) → S(G/γ Z ) is surjective since Φγ : SE (G) → S(G/γ Z ) is.
    It follows that we have continuous linear bijections:
(4.5.3.4)                   SE (G)/Pγ SE (G) → SI (G)/ ker(Φγ ) → S(G)/ ker(Φγ Z )
where we used Proposition 4.5.1.1(5),(6) to deduce that we have ker(Φγ ) = Pγ SE (G), and hence Pγ SI (G) =
SI (G) ∩ Vγ (where the intersection denotes the pre-image of Vγ along the continuous linear inclusion SI (G) →
S(G)).
                      4.6. PERIODIC SCHAUDER BASES IN THE PRESENCE OF MULTIPLICITY                                   209


    Since we also have continuous linear bijections:
(4.5.3.5)                         SE (G)/Pγ SE (G) → SI (G)/VI,γ → S(G)/Vγ
we deduce that the canonical continuous linear operators:
(4.5.3.6)                SI (G)/VI,γ → SI (G)/ ker(Φγ ), S(G)/Vγ → SI (G)/ ker(Φγ Z )
induced by the inclusions VI,γ ⊂ ker(Φγ ) ⊂ SI (G), and Vγ ⊂ ker(Φγ Z ), are also bijections. This gives
VI,γ = ker(Φγ ) and Vγ = ker(Φγ Z ), as closed subspaces of SI (G), respectively S(G).
    Compatibilty of the formation of VI,γ and Vγ with passage to G1 -isotypes is a consequence of the
commutation of the continuous left-translation actions on G by γ Z and G1 .                           □

    4.6.3. The case of SI (G).


    Corollary 4.6.3.1. Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. Assume G is R>0 -modulated.
Let γ ∈ G be such that |γ|G > 1. Assume the choices and assumptions from Situation 4.6.1.1 are in force.
    Let I ⊂ R be a non-empty open connected interval. Assume 0 ∈ I.
    Upon denoting S = (γ1 , . . . , γN ) for N ≥ 1 an integer and γk ∈ G with |γk |G > 1 for each 1 ≤ k ≤ N as
in Situation 4.6.1.1, we write PS for the composition of the operators Pγk from (4.5.3.3) on SI (G) and S(G).

are linear topological isomorphisms, compatible with passage to G1 -isotypes.


    Proof. We write S = (γ1 ) ∪ S0 with S0 = (γ2 , . . . , γN ).
    Recall from Situation 4.6.1.1 that the notation (γ2 , . . . , γN ) means the set {γ2 , . . . , γN } whose elements
are counted with multiplicity. For example, for N = 2 and γ1 = γ2 = γ, P(γ,γ) = Pγ2 (see Example 4.6.1.6).

Pγ1 SE (G) ⊂ SE (G), Pγ1 SI (G) ⊂ SI (G), and Pγ1 S(G) ⊂ S(G).
     By Corollary 4.5.3.1, the rightmost vertical arrows in (4.6.3.2) are linear topological isomorphisms.
     The operators Pγ1 are continuous and with closed range by Proposition 4.5.1.1(5),(6) and Corollary 4.5.3.1.
     Let E be any of the three Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces SE (G), SI (G) and S(G).
     Let ϕ ∈ E be such that Pγ1 (ϕ) ∈ PS (E). Following the same argument provided in Lemma 4.6.1.3 (applied
upon relabelling γ1 as γN ) shows that we have ϕ ∈ PS (E), from which we deduce that the leftmost, and
hence the middle, vertical arrows are continuous linear bijections, by replacing S with S0 and inducting on
the integer N ≥ 1, and by another application of Corollary 4.5.3.1 to treat the base case of the induction.

     It follows that the continuous linear bijection SE (G)/PS SE (G) → SI (G)/PS SI (G) is also a linear topological
isomorphism.

         5.1. The topological vector spaces of adelic θ-functions and Idelic Z-functions
    Let F be a number field, S a finite set of places of F containing all the Archimedean places.
    In this subsection we define the Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space
                                              H0,cont (F × , S(AF ))
of continuous co-invariants of the left-translation action by F × on the Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector space S(AF ) of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on AF . After defining it, H0,cont (F × , S(AF )) will be
identified with a Hausdorff quotient of the C-linear space of algebraic co-invariants
                                                  Z[F × ]
                          H0 (F × , S(AF )) = Tor0          (Z, S(AF )) = Z ⊗Z[F × ] S(AF )
of S(AF ) under the left-translation action by the discrete subgroup F × ⊂ GL1 (AF ), which promotes S(AF )
to a (continuous Z[F × ]-module. The ring map Z[F × ] → Z is the augmentation map.
    These will be spaces of global, respectively S-local, adelic θ-functions, topologized as quotients of S(AF ),
respectively S(AF,S ).
                                                            221
222                   CHAPTER 5. SPACES OF ADELIC θ-FUNCTIONS AND IDELIC Z-FUNCTIONS


    We will study the topology on H0,cont (F × , S(AF )) and prove several structural results in the spirit of
Proposition 2.1.4.1 for S(AF ), by relating H0,cont (F × , S(AF )) to its S-local analogs H0,cont (O× F,S , S(AF,S )), in
turn a Hausdorff quotient of the C-linear space of algebraic co-invariants H0 (O×      F,S , S(A F,S )) of the Z[O× F,S ]-
module S(AF,S ).
    The main ingredients in the arguments for the main results of this Chapter are the existence of the analytic
continuation to the idelic zeta functions as per Theorem 3.2.2.1, the structural results on S(AF ) and their
S-local analogs, and the Asymptotic Residue Theorem (see Theorem B.3.2.1), applicable by known estimates
on the order of growth of Hecke L-functions and related meromorphic functions uniformly on vertical strips of
bounded width, recalled in Appendix B.
    At least formally, there is some overlap between some of the results discussed throughout this Chapter,
and some of the results from [Me1, §4], insofar as some of the statements from [Me1, §4.6,4.7] are formally
analogous, and at times their proofs share some elements in common (with particular emphasis on the use
of multiplier operators from [Me1, §4.7] in the proof of [Me1, §4.7,Lemma 4.20,p.20]. We will be using
similar operators, constructed and discussed at length in §5.3.1 of this Chapter, to a similar effect throughout
the proof of Theorem 5.4.1.1, even though the statement of Theorem 5.4.2.2 from §5.4.2, a consequence of
Theorem 5.4.1.1, is different, though analogous, to [Me1, §4.7,Lemma 4.20,p.20]).
    We will be referring the reader to the relevant contents from [Me1, §4] whenever appropriate, explaining
the similarities and differences. An important difference that we record here from the outset, is that the
results being discussed in this Chapter concern the Hausdorff locally convex topologies on H0,cont (F × , S(AF )),
H0,cont (O×
          F,S , S(AF,S )), as well as their corresponding spaces of meromorphic functions on the Riemann surfaces
Ω(CF ), respectively Ω(JF,S ), under the Mellin transform, while those results from [Me] that find analogs
throughout this Chapter, are concerned with the von Neumann bornologies underlying the topological vector
spaces which are the subject of our study.
    These are referred to as bornological vector spaces in [Me1] (see also [Me2] and [Me3]), with the caveat
that, therein and in the quoted references, a bornological vector space is meant to be a complex vector space
equipped with a bornology of bounded subsets, rather than a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space
which is bornological (see [NB, Ch.13,§13.2]). The latter class provides examples of the bornological vector
spaces from the former.
    We further refer the reader to Remark 5.2.3.4.



    5.1.1. Definition of the global and S-local spaces of adelic θ-functions and Idelic Z-functions.
For any Schwartz-Bruhat function f ∈ S(AF ), respectively f ∈ S(AF,S ), the resulting idelic zeta integral

located within the subsets {c = 1, c = | · |F }, respectively among the poles of the meromorphic function ρS over
Ω(JF,S ) from (3.3.1.3): they are at most simple, in the former case, and they are counted with multiplicity
bounded above by the polar multiplicity of each pole of ρS (c), in the latter.

(3) For every ω ∈ Jd1

    convex topological C-vector space S(AF,S ).
    The Theorem will enable to study the quotient topologies on H0,cont (F × , S(AF )) and H0,cont (O×F,S , S(AF,S ))
induced by the operators ΦF , respectively ΦF,S , and deduce that such topologies are Hausdorff, locally convex,
and promote each of them to complete LF-spaces that are nuclear and Montel, whose strong duals are complete,
nuclear and Montel.
    We will be recalling these concepts from the theory of Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces
further, as the need arises.

    5.1.2. The kernels of the S-local and global adelic θ-function operators. In this subsection we
establish preparations on the kernels of the global and local adelic θ-function operators, to prove Theorem 5.1.1.3,

    This is the first instance of a structural result on the locally convex topological C-vector spaces
H0,cont (OF,S , S(AF,S )) and H0,cont (F × , S(AF )), whose arguments rest on the idelic (both S-local and global)
Mellin transform.

H0,cont (OF,S , S(AF,S )) and H0,cont (F × , S(AF )) inherited from the S-local and global Schwartz-Bruhat spaces
S(AF,S ) and S(AF ), both locally convex, are also Hausdorff.

     5.1.3. Continuity of the Mellin transform operators. We recall that as a consequence of Theorem
3.2.2.1, the global Idelic Z-function operator Z : S(AF ) → M (Ω(CF )) from (5.1.1.1), which we also termed
global Idelic Mellin transform, is valued in the linear subspace of the C-vector space of meromorphic functions
M (Ω(CF )) on the Riemann surface Ω(CF ), of those meromorphic functions on Ω(CF ) whose divisor is bounded
below by the divisor D := −(1) − (| · |F ) on Ω(CF ).
     We call such linear subspace M (Ω(CF ), D) and topologize it with the topology inherited from H (Ω(CF )),
the space of entire functions on Ω(CF ) topologized with the topology of uniform convergence on the compact
subsets of Ω(CF ), under the linear bijection:
                                          M (Ω(CF ), D) → H (Ω(CF ))
defined by sending each meromorphic function in M (Ω(CF ), D) to the entire function obtained by multiplication
by the entire function which is constant and equal to 1, on each connected component of Ω(CF ) other than
Ω(CF )(1), and, upon parametrizing Ω(CF )(1) as {| · |sF , s ∈ C}, by s(s − 1).
     This linear topology promotes M (Ω(CF ), D) to a separable Fréchet space, by [Jar, Part I,Ch.5,§5.5,p.96]
(separability being a consequence of countability of the dual group of CF1 ).
     Similarly, as a consequence of Theorem 3.3.1.1, the S-Idelic Z-function operator ZS : S(AF,S )) →
M (Ω(JF,S )) from (5.1.1.2), which we also termed S-Idelic Mellin transform, is valued in the linear subspace
of the C-vector space M (Ω(JF,S )) of meromorphic functions on Ω(JF,S ), of those meromorphic functions
                                                                                                    Q
whose divisor is bounded below by the divisor DS of the meromorphic function LS (c) := v∈S Lv (cv ), for
Lv (cv ) the local Euler factor at v ∈ S of the Hecke L-function L(c) of F .
     Recall from (3.3.1.32) that LS (c) is related to the correcting factor ρS (c) in the S-local functional equation
of (3.3.1.2) from Theorem 3.3.1.1, by the identity of meromorphic functions on Ω(JF,S ):

countability of the dual group of JF,S  ).
     The topologies described above on the spaces of meromorphic functions M (Ω(CF ), D) and M (Ω(JF,S ), DS ),
respectively, agree with the topology termed Holdgrün topology in [GE, §3.1,p.290].
     Indeed, the Hausdorff locally convex topologies defined on M (Ω(CF ), D) and M (Ω(JF,S ), DS ), promote
each to a separable Fréchet space as a consequence of the Maximum Modulus Principle (see [Cnw-b,
Ch.VI,§1,Thm.1.2,p.128]) and [Cnw-b, Ch.VII,§2,Thm.2.1,p.151], and the Holdgrün topology also promotes
each of the two linear spaces M (Ω(CF ), D) and M (Ω(JF,S ), DS ) to Fréchet spaces (see [GE, §2.2,p.290]
applied to Ω = Ω(G)(ω) ∪ {∞} for G = CF , G = JF,S , respectively, and for each continuous character of G1 ,
upon choosing a holomorphic parametrization {χ| · |sG , s ∈ C} for each, with δ(∞) = 0 and δ : Ω − {∞} → N
supported on a countable discrete subset of the complex s-plane; see also [Kothe-I, Ch.6,§27,(3),p.373]).
     By [NB, Thm.14.5.1] (noting that Fréchet spaces are Baire), the identity on M (Ω(CF ), D) and M (Ω(JF,S ), DS ),
which is continuous with respect to the Höldgrun topology on the source, and the topology from the foregoing,
on the target, is a linear topological isomorphism.
     We further refer the reader to [GE] for more on Hausdorff locally convex topologies on the space of
meromorphic functions on a complex domain, and how the respective induced topologies on the linear subspaces
of meromorphic functions with prescribed location and order of poles, relate (and to [GE, Appendix,p.301] for
an account on the problem of topologizing the linear space of meromorphic functions on a complex domain,
with unconstrained divisor of poles).

     As such, H0,cont (ωS , S(AF,S )) is Hausdorff, locally convex and complete. It is nuclear (by [Scha,

with [Tre, Part III,Ch.50,Prop.50.2(5.12)], which applies by nuclearity (see also [Scha, Ch.III,§7,Cor.2,p.101]).
     Being these properties stable under passage to locally convex inductive limits, they are inherited by
H0,cont (ω, S(AF )) by (1). By [Scha, Ch.IV,§6,6.1,p.148] (which applies since H0,cont (ωS , S(AF,S )) and
H0,cont (ω, S(AF )) are bornological by [Scha, Ch.II,§8.8.2,Cor.2,p.62], being separated quotients of S(AF,S ),
respectively S(AF )) and [Scha, Ch.IV,§5,5.9,p.147] (see also [Jar, Part II,Ch.11,§11.5,Prop.4(f),p230]), the
strong duals (H0,cont (ωS , S(AF,S )))′β and (H0,cont (ω, S(AF )))′β are complete and Montel.
     The strong duals (H0,cont (ωS , S(AF,S )))′β and (H0,cont (ω, S(AF )))′β are nuclear by [Scha, Ch.III,§7,Thm.7.4,p.103],
because, being ΦF,S,ωS , respectively ΦF,ω , are quotient maps, and hence the adjoints Φ′F,S,ωS and Φ′F,ω are
linear topological embeddings: to see this, we use [NB, Thm.8.11.3(b)] to deduce that ΦF,S,ωS and ΦF,ω are
weakly continuous, and being surjective, by [NB, Thm.8.13.2] their adjoints are weakly relatively open and
injective. By Theorem 5.1.1.3, since ker(ΦF,S,ωS ) and ker(ΦF,ω ) are closed, then by [NB, Thm.8.12.4(b)], the
assumptions of [NB, Thm.8.13.4] are satisfied by A := Φ′F,S,ωS , respectively A := Φ′F,ω , proving that they are
both linear topological embeddings.

                                   5.3. Weil’s Principal Value Operators
     In this section we discuss continuous operators on S(AF,S ) and H0,cont (O×     F,S , S(AF,S )), that have the
effect of removing the poles of the S-idelic Zeta functions ZS (f, c) on Ω(JF,S ) in a controlled manner, enabling
a detailed study of the topology of H0,cont (O×  F,S , S(AF,S )) and its isotypes, which will in turn enable the
remaining of the Structure Theorems in this Chapter to be stated and proved, and upon which several
constructions in sequel Chapters rest.

     5.3.2. Preparations on tempered distributions supported at the origin. We record here results
describing the topology on the space of tempered distributions on a finite product of Archimedean local fields,
whose support is contained in a union of standard hyperplanes.
     We begin with the two cases of interest, R, C.
     We recall here that the bi-dual of a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space is defined to be
the continuous dual of the strong dual; see [Jar, Part II,Ch.11,§11.2]. This convention, adopted throughout
this work, is also in force throughout [Kothe-I, Kothe-II] (see [Kothe-I, Ch.V,§23,p.298]), as is in [Scha,
Ch.IV,p.143], from which we shall be referring on occasion throughout this subsection, concerning topologies
on the bi-dual.
     Recall that the support of a tempered distributions T ∈ S(Rm ) for each integer m ≥ 0, is defined to
be the smallest closed subset supp(T ) of Rm such that for any x ∈ Rm − supp(T ), there exists an open
neighborhood U ⊂ Rm − supp(T ) of x such that for any f ∈ S(Rm ) whose support is entirely contained in U ,
then ⟨T, f ⟩S(Rm )′β ,S(Rm ) = 0.
     We refer the reader to [Horm, Ch.II,§2.2,Def.2.2.2], which applies by definition to elements of S(Rm )′β
too, since S(Rm )′β is a C-linear subspace of D(Rm )′β equipped with a finer topology, and to Definition D.1.8.2,
which shows how to generalize this definition to tempered distributions Hausdorff locally compact abelian
groups.

     This shows that indeed the assignment X k Y k 7→ k!(k1 ′ )! ∂zk ∂zk δ0 is a linear isomorphism C[X, Y ] → S00 (C)⊥ ,
and the degree N of a monomial matches the order of the resulting tempered distribution supported at 0 ∈ C.
     The linear operator C[X, Y ] → S00 (C)⊥ is continuous, upon endowing the source with the finest locally
convex topology, hence a continuous bijection.
     The source is a strict LF-space, and the target is the strong dual of the nuclear Fréchet space S(C)/S00 (C)
(we refer the reader to [NB, Thm.8.12.1(a)] for the linear isomorphism between S(C)/S00 (C) and S00 (C)⊥ ).
     We call F := S(C)/S00 (C) the quotient Fréchet space.
     Since both S(C) and S00 (C) are nuclear Fréchet (the former by Proposition 2.1.1.6, the latter by [Scha,
Ch.III,§7,Thm.7.4,p.103]), so is F (by [Scha, Ch.III,§7,Thm.7.4,p.103], since F is a separated quotient of
a nuclear Fréchet space), and hence F is Montel (see [Tre, Part III,Ch.50,Prop.50.2,(50.12),p.519]), hence
reflexive (see [Jar, Part II,Ch.11,§11.5,Prop.1,p.11] and the subsequent discussion). It is, in fact, totally
reflexive, because every quotient by a closed subspace of F inherits nuclearity and is a Fréchet space, hence
Montel, hence reflexive (alternatively, note that any nuclear Fréchet space is the countable projective limit of
a sequence of separable Hilbert spaces; see [Scha, Ch.III,§7.3,Cor.3,p.103]).
     The same argument as for the rest of (1) from Theorem 5.3.2.3(1), resting on the proof of the “only if”
implication of [Val-a, §5,Thm.3,p.343], then applies, and gives that Fβ′ is an LF-space.

     It follows that the composition of the linear topological isomorphisms C[X, Y ] → Fβ′ ≃ S00 (C)⊥ , which is

     We further refer the reader to Lemma 4.2.1.3 for the equivalence between the strong topology on the

     5.3.3. Smoothness and rapid decay of extensions by zero. We recall that we defined, in Definition
D.3.3.1 of §D.3 from Appendix D, the Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces SI (G) of Schwartz-
Bruhat functions on a Hausdorff locally compact R>0 -modulated abelian group G with I-exponential decay,
for I ⊂ R a non-empty connected interval.
     These are functions f : G → C such that | · |aG f ∈ S(G) for every a ∈ I.

     Example 5.3.3.1. Recall from Definition D.2.1.1 that a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G is
modulated if it is equipped with a continuous proper homomorphism | · |G : G → R>0 whose kernel G1 is
(therefore) a compact Hausdorff abelian subgroup. G is R>0 -modulated if | · |G is surjective.
     To fix ideas, the reader may consider the case G = R>0 , with | · |G the identity homomorphism, in which
case f : G → C has I-exponential decay if and only if ta f (t) ∈ S(R>0 ). Upon performing the change of
variables t = ex , i.e. upon defining the module homomorphism |x|R := ex , then SI (R) is the C-linear space of
smooth functions f : R → C such that eax f (x) decays faster than any positive power of |x|−1 as |x| → +∞
for every a ∈ I, hence the lexicon “I-exponential decay”. Slog(I) (R) is linearly and topologically isomorphic to
SI (R>0 ) with the above module homomorphisms.
     We refer the reader to Theorem D.3.3.7 for the properties of the Hausdorff locally convex topology on
SI (G).

    We will now use only the special cases G = R× , C× , and I = (0, +∞), respectively I = [−m, +∞) for
each integer m ≥ 0.
    We note that we have injective continuous linear inclusions S(R) → S(0,+∞) (R× ) and S(C) → S(0,+∞ )(C× ).

    Proposition 5.3.3.2. Let m ≥ 0 be an integer. Then:
(1) pointwise multiplication by x, respectively z, z, denoted Mx , respectively Mz , Mz , is a bounded linear
    operator on D(R× ), S[a,+∞) (R× ) for any a ∈ R ∪ {−∞}, respectively D(C× ), S[a,+∞) (C× ) for any a ∈

    Proof. (1) : Multiplication by x is bounded and boundedly invertible on D(R× ).
    Indeed, since R× and C× are abelian Lie groups, we topologize D(R× ) and D(C× ) with the strict
locally convex inductive limit topology of the Fréchet space topologies on DK (R× ), respectively DK (C× ) (see

embedding DK (R× ) → D(R× ).
    If φ ∈ DK (R× ), then Mx (φ) is the function xφ(x) on R× , and it is still compactly supported with support
contained in K, i.e. Mx preserves the subspaces DK (R× ). It is therefore enough to show that Mx is bounded
and boundedly invertible on DK (R× ), for K ⊂ R× an arbitrary compact subset with non-empty interior.
    A similar reduction is valid for Mz and Mz on D(C× ), being the Hausdorff locally convex topology on
D(G) for G an abelian Lie group, the strict inductive limit of the topologies on each DK (G), for K ⊂ G a
compact subset with non-empty interior.

     We let ϕ ∈ SI (R× ). We need to show that the extension by zero of ϕ to R is smooth at 0 ∈ R. This will
prove that such extension by zero is Schwartz over R (the reader may compare this step in the argument,
with the proof of Lemma B.2.1.4, where boundedness and convergence to zero of ∂xm ϕ as |x| → 0+ is obtained
by direct calculation).
     We know that, for every integer m ≥ 0, ∂xm ϕ is continuous on R× and tends to 0 as |x| → 0. We have yet
to show that the derivative of ϕ exists at 0 ∈ R and agrees with the limit value of ∂xm ϕ (which is zero).
     This is seen by observing that we have, over (−A, A):
                                            Z A                     Z A
                                ϕ(x)     1                       C
(5.3.3.23)                           ≤          |(∂x ϕ)(y)| dy ≤        |y|M dy
                                 x      2A −A                    2A −A
for some integer M > 1 and a real number C > 0, which gives the desired result, as A → 0+ . To argue that we
have |∂x ϕ(y)| ≤ C|y|M for y ∈ (−A, A), we used boudedness of Mx and continuity of ∂x on SI (R× ), to deduce
that ∂x ϕ is of the form xM u for some u ∈ SI (R× ), and hence xM u tends to 0 as |x| → 0+ , giving boundedness
of u over (−A, A) by some C > 0, and the bound |∂x ϕ(y)| ≤ C|y|M over (−A, −ε) ∪ (ε, A), propagated to
(−A, A) by continuity.
     The middle improper integral in (5.3.3.23) therefore converges and the inequalities in (5.3.3.23) hold.
     Upon replacing ϕ with ∂xm ϕ for any m ≥ 0, which is possible by Proposition 5.3.3.2, we deduce that the
derivative of the extension by zero of ϕ to R exists at 0 and vanishes, therefore showing that such extension
by zero is smooth and Schwartz. This shows surjectivity of the restriction operator S00 (R) → SI (R× ).
     A similar argument shows that the restriction operator S00 (C) → SI (C× ), where the middle integral in
(5.3.3.23) is replaces with the line integral from the origin to an arbitrary point z along an arbitrary smooth
rectifiable curve γ : [0, 1] → C. This proves that the directional derivative along γ ′ of the extension by zero of
ϕ exists at z = 0 and vanishes there, proving smoothness at z = 0.
     To conclude the proof of (3), we observe that, since we have shown that the linear restriction operator

                                         N             N

each 1 ≤ k ≤ p, and c′m a continuous quasi-character of C× for 1 ≤ m ≤ q, then, using the linear topological

it is enough to treat the cases (p, q) = (1, 0), (0, 1), in order to show that pointwise multiplication by

(hence) continuously invertible.
     Continuous unitary characters on R× , respectively C× , are smooth, bounded, with smooth and bounded
(x∂x )m -derivatives, respectively (z∂z )m and (z∂z )m -derivatives, for every integer m ≥ 0. Continuity and

    We will be viewing Mxn and Mzp zq as analogs for Archimedean local fields, of the operators PVv for v
non-Archimedean. The reason is that their application resolves the singularities of the Archimedean local
L-functions, while PVv does so for the non-Archimedean local L-functions.

     5.3.4. Weil’s Principal Value Operators and holomorphic S-idelic Zeta functions. We now
discuss how to produce examples of S-idelic Zeta functions from Schwartz-Bruhat functions on AF,S , with a
prescribed divisor of poles. This theme will be reprised in the subsequent two Chapters, which will discuss
poles and zeros in depth: Schauder bases arising from poles of S-idelic Zeta functions and zeros of global idelic
Zeta functions are one of the principal instruments throughout the trace calculation which is the main subject
of study of this work.
     Specifically, before we learn how to construct Schwartz-Bruhat functions that satisfy prescribed divisorial
conditions, we will now discuss how to resolve the singularities of their L-functions.
     The Definition below exhibits a rich source of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on AF,S whose Mellin transform
LS is entire. We will then use Weil’s Principal Value Operators to modify an arbitrary Schwartz-Bruhat
function on AF,S into one whose only poles arise from its Archimedean component, and these, we will classify
completely at the end of this subsection.
     This completes the preparations for the Second Structrue Theorem (see Theorem 5.4.1.1), which is in
turn the stepping stone for the remaining Structure Theorems throughout this Chapter.

     Definition 5.3.4.1. For F a number field and S a finite set of places of F containing all the Archimedean
places.
     We choose, for each real place v of F , an isomorphism of topological fields Fv ≃ R, and for each complex
place v of F , an isomorphism of topological fields Fv ≃ C.
     We define the closed linear subspace S00 (AF,S∞ ) ⊂ S00 (AF,S∞ ) as the pre-image along the pullback by
the induced isomorphism of Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups AF,S∞ ≃ Rr1 × Cr2 , of the closed
subspace S00 (Rr1 × Cr2 ) ⊂ S(Rr1 × Cr2 ).
     We define the following linear subspace of S(AF,S ):
                                                            O
(5.3.4.1)                    S00 (AF,S ) := S00 (AF,S∞ ) ⊗π     S(Fv× ) ⊂ S(AF,S ).
                                                                    v∈Sf

We refer to S00 (AF,S ) as the subspace of polar-free Schwartz-Bruhat functions on AF,S .

locally convex topology (see Lemma C.2.5.2).
     Stability under the continuous left-translation action of GL1 (AF,S ) on S(AF,S ) is a consequence of the fact
that both S00 (Rp × Cq ) is stable under the continuous left-translation action of (R× )p × (C× )q on S(Rp × Cq ),
and S(Fv× ) is stable under the continuous left-translation action of Fv× on S(Fv ) for any finite place v ∈ S.
     Any isomorphism of topological fields Fv ≃ R, if v is real, and Fv ≃ C, if v is complex, induces an
isomorphism of Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups i : AF,S∞ ≃ Rr1 × Cr2 . We choose, for each
Archimedean place v, two such isomorphisms iv , i′v .
     We call ι : Rr1 × Cr2 → Rr1 × Cr2 the isomorphism of Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups induced
by iv ◦ i−1
          v for each Archimedean place v of F .
     i is therefore smooth, being source and target abelian Lie groups, and preserves the C-algebras of
differential operators on source and target.
     Each is isomorphic to the tensor product of the algebras of differential operators on each of the factors
R and C, and since ι is diagonal, and it is the identity on each real component, and either the identity or
complex conjugation on each complex component, it preserves the subspace S00 (Rr1 × Cr2 ).
     It follows that the vanishing conditions defining S00 (Rr1 × Cr2 ) as a subspace of S(Rr1 × Cr2 ), define
on S(AF,S∞ ) vanishing conditions defining S00 (AF,S∞ ) that do not depend on the choice of isomorphisms
Fv ≃ R and Fv ≃ C.

     Remark 5.4.1.5. We recall from the First Structure Theorem (see Theorem 5.2.1.1), that the Hausdorff
locally convex topological C-vector space H0,cont (F × , S(AF )) is complete, nuclear, Montel, and its strong dual
satisfies the same properties. It is an LF-space. From Theorem 5.4.1.1(4) we have that H0,cont (ω, S(AF,S )) is
a Fréchet space,. In particular, H0,cont (ω, S(AF )) is itself realized as a strict LF-space, improving on Theorem
5.2.1.1. We shall see that the transition operators π S are eventually surjective, and hence, since they are
linear topological embeddings, H0,cont (ω, S(AF )) will be realized as itself a nuclear Fréchet space.

                   5.5. Structure Theorem III: strong duals and Eigendistributions

     Remark 5.5.1.4. We note that Theorem 5.5.1.2(1) partially informs us about the structure of the linear
image of Φ′F,S within S(AF,S )′β . It contains the S-local eigendistributions, and hence the linear subspace they
topologically (being Φ′F,S a linear topological embedding) generate. In fact, a converse is also true: it turns
out that the S-local eigendistributions are linear topological generators of the range of Φ′F,S , and hence of the
strong dual of H0,cont (O×F,S , S(AF,S ))β . This is the content of the Third Structure Theorem (see Theorem
                                         ′

5.5.3.2) and it rests on the Second Structure Theorem, describing the topology on H0,cont (O×   F,S , S(AF,S )) (see
Theorem 5.4.1.1), and on the Spectral Theorem for unbounded densely defined normal operators on Hilbert
spaces (see [Cnw-a, Thm.4.11]). Similar considerations hold for Theorem 5.5.1.3(1), which says that the range
of Φ′F within S(AF )′β contains the global eigendistributions, and hence the linear subspace they topologically
(being Φ′F a linear topological embedding) generate.

    5.5.3. Third Structure Theorem. The Third Structure Theorem (Theorem 5.5.3.2) places Weil’s
eigendistributions into their natural place to work organically, obtaining a precise result on the structure of the
locally convex spaces of co-invariants of S(AF ) and S(AF,S ) under the action of GL1 (AF ) and its subgroups,
respectively GL1 (AF,S ) and its subgroups.
    The following Proposition provides a local converse to Theorem 5.5.1.2(1) (i.e. local at a single place v of
the number field F ), and builds towards Theorem 5.5.3.2.
     Proposition 5.5.3.1. Let F be a number field, v a place of F , ω ∈ Ω(Fv× ) a unitary character. Then
S(Fv )′β is linearly and topologically generated by the functionals {∆′v (c), c ∈ Ω(Fv× )}, and the closed subspace
of S(Fv )′β of the ω-homogeneous tempered distributions is linearly and topologically generated by the functionals
{∆′v (c), c ∈ Ω(Fv× )(ω)}.
    Proof. We show that {∆′v (c), c ∈ Ω(Fv× )} separates the points of S(Fv ). Indeed, let f ∈ S(Fv ) and
assume ∆′v (c)(f ) for every c ∈ Ω(Fv× ). Then Zv (f, c) = ∆′v (c)(f )Lv (c) = 0 as a meromorphic function over
Ω(Fv× ). In particular, f vanishes identically over Fv× , and hence over Fv by continuity. We now call E
the linear subspace of S(Fv )′β generated by {∆′v (c), c ∈ Ω(Fv× )}. Since {∆′v (c), c ∈ Ω(Fv× )} separates the
points of S(Fv ), then by [NB, Thm.7.7.3] E is dense with respect to the σ(S(Fv )′β , S(Fv ))-topology on S(Fv )′ ,
which is the strong topology by [NB, Thm.11.3.6] since S(Fv )′β is barrelled, as S(Fv ) is Montel, and hence
σ(S(Fv )′β , S(Fv )) = σ(S(Fv )′β , (S(Fv )′β )′ ) since S(Fv ) is reflexive (recall that the bi-dual of a Hausdorff locally
convex space is defined to be the dual of the strong dual; see [Jar, Part II,Ch.11,§11.2]).
    Assume now that v is non-Archimedean.
    Since the closed subspace of ω-homogeneous tempered distributions on S(Fv ) is closed in S(Fv )′β , which is
complemented. Indeed, integration over the compact Hausdorff abelian group O×                       Fv with respect to the local
multiplicative Tamagawa measure produces a linear form, for each f ∈ S(Fv ):
                                                   Z

    Remark 6.1.2.3. For the sake of clarity, we recall that by “left-translation action” of a Hausdorff locally
compact abelian group G on a function space F (X) on a Hausdorff topological space X on which G acts
continuously, we mean the assignment ρG : G × F (X) → F (X) defined by ρG (g, f )(x) := f (g −1 x) as functions
of x ∈ X. ρG preserves continuity of functions.

                          6.2. Structure Theorem V: isotypic exhaustiveness
    We conclude this Chapter with the final Structure Theorem on the spaces
                                  H0,cont (F × , S(AF )), H0,cont (O×
                                                                    F,S , S(AF,S ))

and their isotypes.
    It amounts to the statement that so long as the finite set of places S containing all Archimedean places, is
large enough, so as to ensure Pic(OF,S ) = 1 holds and, for each given continuous character ω of CF1 , that ω is
unramified outside S, then the transition operator:
                                 π S : H0,cont (ωS , S(AF,S )) → H0,cont (ω, S(AF ))
is a linear topological isomorphism. Recall from the First Structure Theorem (see Theorem 5.2.3.1) that π S is
a linear topological embedding. The assertion on π S being a linear topological isomorphism therefore amounts
to the surjectivity of π S , and it requires the homology calculations from the previous section.
