    In this Chapter we construct Schauder bases on certain important subquotients of the separable nuclear
Fréchet spaces:
                              H0,cont (χ|JF,S
                                          1   , S(AF,S )), H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S(AF ))
with F a number field, χ a continuous character of JF,S , respectively CF .
    The constructions are made in the S-local case, and then propagated globally using the slow growth of
the reciprocal of the Hecke L-function Lf (s, χ) on the 1-line, and classical zero-free regions.
    For the purposes of applications, the S-local Schauder bases will be the main instrument in use in later
Chapters.
    We recall from [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.2,p.292] that for E a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
space, {xm }m≥0 ⊂ E is a Schauder basis if and only if:
     (1) For every u ∈ E, there exists a unique sequence {cm (u)}m≥0 ⊂ C of complex numbers such that
                                                  X
                                             u=      cm (u)xm
                                                  m≥0

         the convergence of the sum being in E.
     (2) Formation of each cm is continuous on E.
    Condition (1) identifies the concept of topological basis (see [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.2,p.292]) while the
datum {(xm , fm )}m≥0 with {xm }m≥0 ⊂ E, and {fm }m≥0 ⊂ E ′ , such that the linear span of the xm ’s is dense
                                                     311
312                        CHAPTER 7. SCHAUDER BASES OF IDELIC ZETA FUNCTIONS


in E, and the linear span of the fm ’s separates the points of E (equivalently, is weakly dense in E ′ ) is termed
a Markushevich basis; see [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.1,p.289].
    For {xm }m≥0 ⊂ E a Schauder basis, upon denoting fm := cm , then {(xm , fm )}m≥0 is a Markushevich
basis for the duality ⟨E, E ′ ⟩ (see [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.2,Prop.1,p.292]).
    Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces with a Schauder basis satisfy several additional
properties. We refer the reader to [Jar, Part II,Ch.14] for more on Schauder bases, unconditional and absolute
bases, and to [Kal] for more on properties of Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces in the presence
of Schauder basic sequences within their closed subspaces, as well as some terminology.
    We recall from [Kal, §3,p.95] that a Schauder basis {bk }k≥0 in a Hausdorff locally convex topological
                                                                                      P
C-vector space E is simple if and only if the finite rank projection operators PN := 0≤k≤N ⟨φk , ·⟩E ′ ,E bk , for
{φk }k≥0 the dual basic sequence of {bk }k≥0 , are a bounded set in Lβ (E), i.e. they are strongly bounded.
    We further recall from [Kal, §1,Def.1.1,p.91] that a Schauder basis {bk }k≥0 of E is regular if and only if
there exists a 0-neighborhood V such that bk ∈    / V for all k ≥ 0.
    Finally, from [Kal, §1,Def.1.2], a Schauder basis is normalized if and only if it is bounded and regular.
    The example to keep in mind is that of E = S(T), for T the circle group R/Z, with xm = e2πimx , as a
function of x ∈ R descended to R by 1-periodicity, for each m ∈ Z, and with fm the mth Fourier coefficient
functional. Then {xm }m∈Z is an absolute Schauder basis for E, and its dual basis {fm }m∈Z is an unconditional
Schauder basis for Eβ′ (see Lemma 4.2.1.2, with γ = e, below, noting that the exponential isomorphism x 7→ ex
induces a linear topological isomorphism S(T) ≃ S(R>0 /eZ )).


                                          7.1. Polar Multiplicities
     In this section we discuss the poles of the S-idelic Zeta functions.
     This will serve the two-fold purpose of later selecting the Sobolev degree that suffices for a Sobolev space
of the global idele class group to serve as ambient for the Trace Formula which is the main subject of study of
this work, and it will serve the purpose, at the end of this Chapter, of discussing the existence of periodic
orbits and fixed loci of the action of CF on certain sub-loci of the global adeles.
     This section will enable us to sharpen the analogy between our trace formula, and Selberg’s Trace Formula
(see [Iwaniec, Ch.10], by appealing to a paper of P. Sarnak on the uniform distribution of long horocycles on
the space of elements of a Riemann surface, equipped with the Poincaré metric, for which we refer the reader
to [Sarnak, §0,Thm.1,p.719].

     7.1.1. Almost periodic functions. Pioneering work of Harald Bohr from [Bohr1, Bohr2, Bohr3]
investigated self-approximation conditions on a large class of functions directly related to Dirichlet series:
“almost periodic” functions (we do not review its definition since the present discussion is purely for motivation;
what we will really need is “strongly recurrent” (Definition B.5.3.1) . These are functions that are holomorphic
on a vertical strip CI of bounded width of the complex s-plane, and, while not necessarily periodic, recur enough
often over CI to allow the study of their distribution of values. Examples of almost periodic functions are
finite sums and finite products of vertically periodic functions with different, possibly Q-linearly independent,
vertical periods.
     An example of such function is any finite partial sum of a Dirichlet series. Let F be a number field, S a
finite set of places containing all the Archimedean places, and Sf the subset of S of all of the finite places of
F contained in S. Then the function:
                                                 Y
(7.1.1.1)                                           (1 − qv−s−itv )
                                                v∈Sf

is, for qv := N (pv ) for pv the unique prime ideal of OF corresponding to the finite place v, almost periodic.
                                           7.1. POLAR MULTIPLICITIES                                           313


     Each factor is periodic of period 2πi/log(qv ). For finite places v, v ′ contained in S with different residue
characteristics, the real numbers log(qv ) and log(qv′ ) are Q-linearly independent, and the function in (7.1.1.1)
is not periodic.
     However, it recurs enough often for us to find a sequence of vertical segments within the vertical strips
CI (with I an open interval containing 0 ∈ R) the absolute value of whose ordinates tend to +∞, and on
which the function in (7.1.1.1) remains bounded below a positive threshold NS > 0 fixed at the beginning.
For instance, it has zeros at {2πi Z/log(qv ), v ∈ Sf }.
     The reciprocal function
                                                Y
(7.1.1.2)                                          (1 − qv−s−itv )−1
                                                v∈Sf

is, however, not holomorphic and is even unbounded over some CI . The question of whether there exists a
sequence of ordinates whose absolute value tends to +∞, and such that on the corresponding vertical segments
contained in CI , (7.1.1.2) is uniformly bounded, is a non-trivial one.
     We cannot use [Bohr, Ch.2,§46,p.35] applied to the restriction of the function (7.1.1.1) to iR since the
function has zeros within CI on iR. For this reason, we use a weaker notion than almost periodicity: strong
recurrence.
     In §B.5.3.1 we review the notion of (strong) “recurrence” for a holomorphic function on a vertical strip
CI , for I ⊂ R a non-empty open interval, the study of which was initiated in B. Bagchi’s PhD thesis [Ba1,
Ch.1,2]. Strong recurrence is a vertical self-approximation property of holomorphic functions on vertical strips.
We refer the reader to [Ba1, Ch.1, §1.4] (respectively [Ba1, Ch.2, §2.3]) for further background of a general
character (respectively specific to the holomorphic functions of interest to number theory), and to [Ba2, §3] for
applications. It is indeed weaker than almost periodicity (for analytic functions on vertical strips of bounded
width, as defined in [Bohr4, Appendix II,§104,p.101]), in light of [Bohr, Ch.2,§47,Corollary,p.37] and [Ba1,
Ch.2,§2.4,Prop.2.4.2,p.46] (since, by [Bohr4, Appendix II,§106,p.104], an almost periodic analytic function on
CI has uniformly strongly recurrent vertical sections in the sense of [Ba1, Ch.2,§2.4,Def.2.4.1]). It can be
thought of as a “local” analog of almost periodicity.
     The following Lemma also follows from Proposition B.5.3.3, to which the reader is referred, whose proof is
direct and rests upon the Kronecker-Weyl Theorem (see Theorem B.5.2.1).
     Recall that for F a number field, v a finite place of F , we denote by qv the absolute norm of the unique
prime ideal pv ⊂ OF associated to v.

below.
     Throughout this work we refer to “order of pole” at s0 ∈ Ω of a meromorphic complex valued function
f : Ω → C on a domain of the complex s-plane Ω ⊂ C as the nonnegative integer N ≥ 0 such that am (f, s0 ),
the mth coefficient of the Laurent series expansion of f centered at s = s0 for m ∈ Z, vanishes for m < −N ,
minimal (among the nonnegative integers) with respect to this property, i.e. a−N (f, s0 ) ̸= 0. We therefore say
f has a pole of order N at s = s0 .

functions ρv ∈ Ω(Fv× ) are tabulated explicitly on each connected component in [CF, Ch. XV, pp. 316-322].
Inspection shows that on the connected components of ramified quasi-characters for non-Archimedean v the
function ρv is entire and non-vanishing (related to local root numbers of ramified characters), while in all
other cases a zero of any of these never cancels a pole of another (not even the real parts ever coincide).
     Thus, the set of poles of ρS (χ| · |sF,S ) is exactly the union of the sets of poles of the meromorphic functions
ρv (composed with the analytic covering map Ω(JF,S ) → Ω(Fv× )) for v ∈ S − Sχ , and the pole order of ρS
at such a pole agrees with that of the corresponding ρv for a uniquely determined v (depending on the pole
under consideration). Since we have parameterized the connected component of χ in Ω(JF,S ) via χ| · |sF,S , for
such a point to be a pole of ρv with v ∈ S − Sχ we note that its restriction to Fv× is χv | · |sv , so the possibilities
for such s are exactly read off from Tate’s formulas for the ρv ’s in all cases (Archimedean v on each connected
component of Ω(Fv ), and non-Archimedean v on the connected component of unramified quasi-characters in
Ω(Fv )). This yields exactly the list of points (in effect, the values for s) as claimed.                             □



     The following, is the main Theorem of this section. We will be subsequently explain the connection with
Sarnak’s Theorem on the uniform distribution of long horocycles (see [Sarnak, §0,Thm.1]), a connection that
will accompany us all the way through this Chapter until we find and describe the periodic orbits associated
to the non-Archimedean places of the number field F , and show they serve a similar role as the periodic orbits
of the horocycle flow from [Sarnak]. The higher rank version of the methods being presented in this work will
generalize [Sarnak, §0,Thm.1], eventually rendering the analogy discussed at the end of this Chapter, sharper.
     We let F be a number field, S a finite set of places of F containing all the Archimedean places. For a
prime number p, we denote by Sp the subset of those finite places v of F contained in S such that the residue
characteristic of the non-Archimedean local field Fv is p.
     We denote by Π the set of all prime numbers, and by Π(S) ⊂ Π the subset of the prime residue
characteristics of the non-Archimedean local fields Fv for each v ∈ Sf := ΣF,f ∩ S.

    We now look at Theorem 7.1.2.3 through the lens of Sarnak’s paper on the uniform distribution of long
horocycles (see [Sarnak, §0,Thm.1]).
    We let M be a Riemann surface, and T 1 M → M its unit tangent bundle. We equip M with its Poincaré
metric, promoting it to a complete Riemannian manifold with constant negative curvature. We assume M is
non-compact, with finite volume.
    For r ≥ 0 the finite number of inequivalent cusps, there exist r pairwise disjoint immersed submanifolds
Pk ⊂ T 1 M , 1 ≤ k ≤ r, whose union consists of all the periodic points of the horocyclic flow on T 1 M .
                                               7.1. POLAR MULTIPLICITIES                                        319


    For each cusp xk , 1 ≤ k ≤ r, and for each real number t > 0, ν (k) (t) is the probability measure on the
closed orbit of period t−1 of the horocyclic flow on T 1 M assigning uniform mass with respect to arc-length to
such closed orbit.
    ν (k) (t) is constructed in [Sarnak, §2,(2.1)] as an element of the strong dual of D(T 1 M ), by means of the
Uniformization Theorem. Let Γ ⊂ PSL2 (R) be a discrete subgroup acting properly discontinuously on the
upper half-plane H equipped with the Poincaré metric, such that M is isometric to Γ\H.
    Γ acts on T 1 H ≃ PSL2 (R) through tangent maps and we identify T 1 M isometrically to Γ\T 1 H. Since Γ
acts on H and T 1 H by isometries, the horocyclic flow on T 1 H descends to the quotient T 1 M , and in order to
define ν (k) (t) it is enough to do so for k = 1 on T 1 H for then propagating the measure to the cusps other
than the first, i.e. the one at ∞ ∈ H, by push-forward along the Γ-action.
    This is done in [Sarnak, §2,(2.1)] by integrating over a fundamental domain within the standard
fundamental domain for the Γ-action on T 1 H, for the closed orbit of period 1/t on T 1 M of the horocyclic
flow, the generic automorphic function f on T 1 H.
    The JF,S -parametrized families of continuous functionals

     What we are most interested in, however, is the question of whether an analog of the periodic orbits and
periodic loci Pk in [Sarnak, §2] exists in the context of our Theorem 7.1.2.3 too.
     By the end of this Chapter, this question will be answered in the affirmative, exhibiting orbital quotient
stacks arising as topological quotient stacks of certain closed loci within AF,S which are responsible for the
existence of poles of the S-idelic Zeta functions ZS (f, c), and which are in correspondence with divisors on the
Riemann surface Ω(JF,S ) under LS from (5.1.1.2).
     This leads to the finding of periodic orbits and fixed loci that realize the structures predicted by C.
Deninger in his expectations on the existence of a functional approach to the problem of a Trace-Formula
theoretic interpretation to Weil’s Explicit Formulas.
     They will indeed be underlying indirectly the trace calculation which is the main subject of study of this
work.

(see Theorem B.5.2.1), by Proposition B.5.3.3.

    This uniform form of Theorem 7.1.2.3 is closer to Sarnak’s [Sarnak, §0,Thm.1], insofar as it highlights the
functional nature of the result. In other words, it concerns the vector-valued Mellin anti-transform of ZS (·, c),
the S-idelic zeta function as a vector valued meromorphic function, i.e. we think ZS (·, c) as a meromorphic
function over Ω(JF,S ) valued in S(AF,S )′β (i.e. valued in tempered distributions on AF,S ).
    The coefficients am (·, c) are thus obtained as the vector-valued Laurent coefficients provided by the
formulas in Grothendieck’s Theorem C.5.3.2, as contour integrals in the sense of Pettis (see (C.5.3.3)).
    Namely, upon fixing a holomorphic parametrization {χ| · |sF,S } as in §3.1.1 for the connected component of
χ in Ω(JF,S ), for every integer k ≥ 1 the Laurent coefficient operator ak (·, c) satisfies
                                                          ZS (·, χ| · |sF,S )

as continuous operators on S(AF,S ), for sc corresponding to c under the chosen parametrization for any
continuously differentiable simple closed curve Γ ⊂ C enclosing sc .

     Theorem 7.1.3.2 (On Polar Multiplicities). Let F be a number field, S a finite set of places of F containing
all the Archimedean places.
     Let χ ∈ C

     The polar multiplicities of ρS on the connected component of χ in Ω(JF,S ) from Lemma 7.1.2.2 satisfy:
(1) For v1 , v2 ∈ S two finite places with distinct residue characteristics at which χ is unramified, the local
    Euler factors L(χv1 | · |sv1 ) and L(χv2 | · |sv2 ) of the Hecke L-function have at most one pole s in common.
(2) For v Archimedean, mS (cv,0,χ ) ≤ |S|, mS (cv,m,χ ) ≤ r1 +r2 if m is a negative even integer, mS (cv,m,χ ) ≤ r2
    if m is a negative odd integer. (In particular, mS (cv,m,χ ) ≤ [F : Q] for m < 0 and Archimedean v.)
(3) Let S0 = Sf − Sχ be the set of finite places in S at which χ is unramified. If v ∈ S0 then mS (cv,m,χ ) ≤ |S|
    for all m, and as we vary across all such points c = cv,m,χ ∈ Ω(JF,S )(χ) we have mS (c) ≤ [F : Q] with at
    most r1 + r2 + |S0 |(|S0 | − 1)/2 exceptions.
    (a) If χ = χ0 | · |ix
                       F for x ∈ R and χ0 of finite order (i.e., χ is of Galois type) then the only pole with order
        exceeding [F : Q] is s = −ix.
    (b) If χ = χ0 | · |sF0 for s0 ∈ C and χ0 algebraic then assuming Schanuel’s Conjecture the only points in
        Ω(JF,S )(χ) where ρS can have a pole order exceeding [F : Q] are the imaginary axis points on the
        horizontal lines of Archimedean poles and at s = −Im(s0 )i. Unconditionally for such χ, the only point
        on Ω(JF,S )(χ) where the pole order can exceed 2[F : Q] is s = −Im(s0 )i.

     Proof. (1): If s is a common pole then χv1 (πv1 )qv−s1
                                                             = 1 = χv2 (πv2 )qv−s
                                                                                2
                                                                                  , so qvs1 = χ1 (πv1 ) and qvs2 = χ2 (πv2 )
for uniformizers πvk at vk . The condition qvsk = χk (πvk ) determines s up to adding an element of (2πi/log(qvk ))Z.
Since log(qvk ) is a positive integer multiple of log(pk ), so the log(qvk )’s are Q-linearly independent, the two
equations qvsk = χvk (πvk ) determine s uniquely (if it exists at all).
     (2) Since ρS is a product of |S| meromorphic functions whose poles are all simple, it has pole-order at
most |S| at any of its poles. In particular mS (cv,0,χ ) ≤ |S|. The non-Archimedean factors ρv have all poles on
the imaginary axis in Ω(JF,S )(χ) (since if qvs = χv (πv ) ∈ U (1) then Re(s) = 0), whereas the Archimedean
factors ρv have poles in the half-plane to the left of that axis.
     Consider an Archimedean v ∈ S. If m is a negative even integer then cv,m,χ has polar multiplicity at
most multiplicity the number of Archimedean local factors of ρS , which is the number r1 + r2 of Archimedean
places of F . For m odd, cv,m,χ can only occur as a pole of ρv for complex v, so its multiplicity as a pole of ρS
is bounded above by the number r2 of complex places of F .
     (3). Suppose for some cv,m,χ with non-Archimedean v ∈ S0 = Sf − Sχ , the pole-order of ρS exceeds
[F : Q]. Since there are at most [F : Q] places of F with the same residue characteristic p as v, for such excess
pole order to occur it must also be a pole of ρw for some Archimedean w or some non-Archimedean w with
residue characteristic different from p. If there is a common pole with ρw for an Archimedean w then the pole
is the rightmost of the Archimedean poles in Ω(JF,S )(χ). There are at most r1 + r2 horizontal lines on which
                                               7.1. POLAR MULTIPLICITIES                                                  325


the Archimedean local factors have their poles (the number of such distinct lines depends on the infinity-type
of χ). Each such line has only its rightmost polar point on the imaginary axis, so setting aside those points
(which have meaning independently of v), we aim to show at most |S0 |(|S0 | − 1)/2 such points cv,m,χ can arise.
     There are at most |S0 |(|S0 | − 1)/2 pairs of places v, w in S0 with distinct residue characteristics, so it
suffices to show that for any such pair there is at most one common pole for ρv and ρw . The relation of ρv to
L(χv | · |sv ) reduces this “at most one” assertion to (1).
     (3.a): We may and do reparameterize the connected component by a pure-imaginary translation so the
unitary base point is χ = χ0 (i.e., x = 0). Suppose ρS has pole-order exceeding [F : Q], so by (2) it occurs
as a pole of ρv and ρw for some non-Archimedean v and some place w ̸= v that either is Archimedean or is
non-Archimedean with a residue characteristic distinct from v. In the case of Archimedean w, the pole would
have to be at s = 0 (as desired) since this is the only pole of an Archimedean local factor which occurs on the
imaginary axis (where the non-Archimedean local factors have their poles): the infinity type for finite-order
χ0 puts all Archimedean poles on the same horizontal line.
     Thus, we can assume v, w are as in (1), in which case the common pole s satisfies qvs = χ0 (πv ) and

                                 7.2. Poles of the S-idelic Zeta functions
    Let X be a Riemann surface, D ⊂ X a divisor. The following is a short exact sequence of sheaves of
OX -modules, the sheaf of holomorphic functions on X:
(7.2.0.1)                              0 → OX (−D) → OX → OD → 0
and if X is Stein, then H (X, F ) = 0 for all integers m > 0 and for any coherent analytic sheaf of OX -modules
                         m

F , which leads to the exact sequence of global sections:
                                       0 → OX (−D) → OX → OD → 0.
Twisting by OX (D), we further obtain the short exact sequence of sheaves of OX -modules:
(7.2.0.2)                              0 → OX → OX (D) → PX,D → 0
where PX,D is the sheaf of principal parts.
    The C-linear spaces of global sections involved can be topologized so as to render the above short exact
sequences strict exact. We refer to (7.2.0.1) and to (7.2.0.2) as the divisor exact sequence and the principal
parts exact sequence, respectively.
    We refer the reader to work of Grosse-Erdman on topologizing spaces of meromorphic functions, focusing
on the Hausdorff locally convex topologies on spaces of meromorphic functions, and comparing the topology
induced by combining the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets for holomorphic functions,
with the product topology on Euclidean lines generated by principal parts, termed Mittag-Leffler topology,
with other Hausdorff locally convex topologies on spaces of meromorphic functions on complex domains: the
standard topology inherited from the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets for holomorphic
functions on complex domains (an inductive topology by nature), and the Holdgründ topology, a projective
topology obtained by writing spaces of meromorphic functions on complex domains as projective limits of
spaces of holomorphic functions up to rational functions obtained as principal parts.
    We refer the reader to [GE, §3.2], as well as to [Jor-a, §3], for vector-valued analogs, and particularly to
[Jor-a, Thm.3.6].

σ(H0,cont (ω, S(AF,S ))′ , H0,cont (ω, S(AF,S )))-topology by [NB, Thm.8.9.2(d)], and hence it is closed with
respect to the strong topology on H0,cont (ω, S(AF,S ))′ , since the strong topology is finer than the topology of
simple convergence.
    It is therefore enough to show that {ak (·, c)}(c,k)∈I , linearly and topologically generates Hm (ω, S(AF,S ))⊥
with respect to the topology of simple convergence. By (7.2.1.9), this follows from [NB, Thm.8.9.2(a)]. □

                       7.3. Paley-Wiener Levels and Schauder Bases of Principal Parts
    We now discuss an S-local analog of the Theorem 7.1.4.2, describing certain S-local divisor exact sequences
encoding the poles of the S-idelic Zeta functions, and describing orthogonals by means of Schauder bases
comprised of S-local eigendistributions.
    We will also be analyzing principal parts at the poles of the Archimedean local Euler factors, and relate
them to point evaluation functionals on global idelic Zeta functions supported at the trivial zeros.

    7.3.1. Orbital Schauder Bases. The following Theorem describes the orthogonals of the closed
subspaces PVS,S0 H0,cont (χ|JF,S
                             1   , S(AF,S )) as S0 ⊂ S is a fixed subset of finite places.

    Situation 7.3.1.1 (Saturated sets of places). Let F be a number field, S be a finite set of places of F
containing all the Archimedean places. Let S0 be an arbitrary finite set of places of F .
(1) We will term S0 saturated if and only if for every prime number p, if a place v of F whose residue
    characteristic is p is contained in S0 , then all places of F whose residue characteristic is p are also
    contained in S0 .
(2) Let p be a prime number such that at least one place of F whose residue characteristic is p, is contained
    in S. Assume S is saturated.

     Corollary 7.3.1.8. Let F be a number field, S a finite set of places containing all the Archimedean
places, χ ∈ CcF a continuous character, unramified outside S. Let χS be the unique continuous character of
JF,S obtained as the descent of χ|CF,S by O b×
                                             ΣF −S -invariance.
     Then the Orbital Schauder Systems from Theorem 7.3.1.2(3) are such that for any choice of enumeration,
the resulting Schauder bases satisfy the following conditions:
(1) They are equicontinuous, shrinking and boundedly complete bases.
(2) Their dual bases are equicontinuous, shrinking and boundedly complete bases.
     Proof. We observe that [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.3,Cor.3,p.296] applies since, by Theorem 5.4.1.1 and
by Theorem 6.2.1.1 (see also Corollary 6.2.1.2), H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S(AF )), H0,cont (χ|JF,S
                                                                                       1   , S(AF,S )), are barrelled
by [NB, Thm.11.7.2], since they are Fréchet spaces. Their strong duals are Montel by Theorem 5.2.3.1(2).
It follows that said bases and their duals are equicontinuous Schauder bases. Being H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S(AF )),
H0,cont (χ|JF,S
            1   , S(AF,S )) and their strong duals Montel by Theorem 5.2.3.1(2), they are reflexive, and by [Jar,
Part II,Ch.14,§14.5,Thm.1(a)], all said bases are shrinking and boundedly complete.                                 □
    7.3.2. Paley-Wiener Levels. We let F be a number field, S a finite set of places of F containing the
Archimedean places. Let χ ∈ JdF,S be a continuous character.
    In this subsection we construct a one-parameter family of closed subspaces of H0,cont (χ|JF,S

    Their aim is to enable an approximation method to perform the final trace calculation of this work in

in the process of identifying (see Theorem 7.3.1.6).

     7.3.3. Orbital Schauder Bases on the Paley-Wiener Levels. In this subsection, we extend Weil’s
Principal Value operators PVS,S0 , introduced in Definition 5.3.1.4 of §5.3.1, for S0 a finite set of finite places
satisfying certain saturation properties, to the invariant and the asbolute Paley-Wiener spaces introduced in
the previous subsection.
     This will enable us to construct Schauder bases for the orthogonals to their range, even on the Paley-Wiener
spaces, building on the work that was done in §6.3.2 on the Orbital Schauder Bases.
     The Orbital Schauder Bases on the Paley-Wiener levels will then enable us to deconstruct the global
                    geom
geometric kernel kφ,a,s   from 10.4.3.27 of Chapter 6, “lifted” to a kernel on GL1 (AF ) × CF using the methods
from §12.2.1, step by step, into an S-local kernel whose integral along the diagonal can be computed explicitly
with a volume calculation.

numbers depending on (ρ, m) that decays rapidly as |Im(ρ)| → +∞, by N (ρ)!, therefore preserves its rapid
decay condition, providing the coefficients λi satisfying the required decay property.
     The nuclear trace of Aspec,a,χ,N (φ) therefore agrees with its matrix trace by [Lit-II, §4,Cor.2,p.61], which

                                           7.5. Strong Co-Primality
    The Theorems contained within this subsection and the next are not logically necessary for the rest of the
arguments leading to the main trace calculation, which is the subject of this work.
    However, we will be using them to explain the presence and role of certain structures underlying the
nuclear Fréchet spaces
                            H0,cont (χS |JF,S
                                          1   , S(AF,S )), H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S0 (AF ))
for χ ∈ C cF a continuous character, and S a finite set of places of the number field F containing all the
Archimedean places, and such that χ is unramified outside S.
    Specifically, we will be dicussing how predictions of Deninger on the existence of a “space” exhibiting
periodic orbits and fixed points related to the primes, both infinite and finite, of F , are indeed correct, and
the role that such structures play behind the scenes (without directly entering the arguments).
    The next Theorem is an important ingredient leading to the construction of such periodic orbits and fixed
points, and the space hosting them: a topological stack built as a quotient of a sub-locus within the S-adeles
AF,S for all large S, serving as the equivariant support for the eigendistributions and their derivatives, of which
the unconditional Schauder bases we have identified throughout the previous sections on large subquotients of
                                             H0,cont (χS |JF,S
                                                           1   , S(AF,S ))
are comprised.
     In other words, the periodic orbits and fixed points whose existence and role Deninger predicted, serve, in
a precise sense to be explained in the next subsection, as the supports of the Orbital Schauder bases, therefore
justifying the terminology.
     The Mellin transform, both S-local and global, sets up a correspondence between these, and certain
divisors on the Riemann surfaces Ω(JF,S ) and Ω(CF ).
     The following Theorem, uses the existence of classical zero-free regions (through the non-vanishing and
polynomial growth of the reciprocal of the finite Hecke L-function on the 1-line; see Theorem B.6.1.6), together
with the existence and properties of the S-local Orbital Schauder Bases provided by Theorem 7.3.1.6, as an
input.

    We will be collecting the following Corollary, which is a strong form of the non-vanishing of the Hecke
L-function L(s, χ) on the 1-line. By solving the a Second Cousin Problem for the pair of entire functions
(Λ(s, χ), (1 − χ(pv )qv−s )), we know from the non-vanishing of L(s, χ) (see [CF, Ch.VIII,Thm.2,p.212]) that
there exist entire functions u, v ∈ O(C) such that:
                                    Λ(s, χ) · u(s) + (1 − χ(pv )qv−s ) · v(s) = 1
as entire functions over the complex s-plane.
    We have no way to tell anything about the growth behavior of u, v. Using the Schauder Bases identified
throughout this Chapter, and as a consequence of Theorem 7.5.0.1, we have the following:
     Corollary 7.5.0.3 (Strong Co-Primality). Let F be a number field, χ ∈ C        cF a continuous character. Let
S be a finite set of finite places of F at which χ is unramified. We write, for each v ∈ S, qv := N (pv ), with
pv ⊂ OF the unique prime ideal corresponding to the finite place v.
     Let τ be a choice of continuous homomorphic section to the idelic norm.

     Let F be a number field.
     In this section we collect the main results of this Chapter and explain them through the lens of Theorem
7.1.2.3, which was the starting point of the Chapter itself. We also compute the support of the distributions
that comprise the dual Schauder bases of the absolute bases that we found on the subquotients ES,Sp (χ|JF,S      1 ).
     The supports will be loci within the S-adeles, for any finite set of places of F containing all the Archimedean
places, and they will be stable under the continuous left-translation action by O×                          1
                                                                                        F,S and GL1 (AF,S ) .
     Since such distributional basis elements are obtained from an eigendistribution through derivation of
uniformly bounded above order, their supports only enter through their topological quotient stacks, which we
compute explicitly: they are either fat points (equipped with a canonical concept of multiplicity, much like the
closed point of a formal unit disc over a discrete field) or periodic orbits: quotient stacks whose coarse space is
a loop with a natural length inherited form the Haar measure on the S-ideles, of log N (pv )| for each finite
place v ∈ S.
     This shows how exactly predictions of Deninger turn out to feature and play a role within this work.




                                        8.1. On Orbital Supports - I
    The following Theorem uses Theorem 7.5.0.1 as an input, and it should be thought of as a refinement
of Theorem 7.3.1.6: it informs us on the existence of absolute Schauder bases on the p-primary Orbital

below, each of whose subquotients are supported each on a stack-theoretic periodic orbit, respectively on a
stack-theoretic fixed point.

    Proposition 8.2.0.5. Let F be a number field, S a finite set of places of F containing all the Archimedean
places. For every Archimedean place v ∈ S, the action of GL1 (AF,S )1 on DS,v is transitive. For every
Archimedean place v of F , the action of GL1 (AF )1 on Dv is transitive.
(1) If v is real, then every point of DS,v , respectively of Dv , is stabilized by {±1} as a subgroup of GL1 (AF,S ),
    respectively GL1 (AF ), embedded injectively as the subgroup of the units of Fv× .
                                           8.3. ON ORBITAL SUPPORTS - II                                         387


(2) If v is complex, then every point of DS,v , respectively Dv , is stabilized by U(1) as a subgroup of GL1 (AF,S ),
    respectively GL1 (AF ), embedded injectively as the subgroup of the units of Fv× .

     Proof. Since v is Archimedean, we may choose a continuous homomorphic section τv to the S-idelic,
respectively idelic norm, and hence τv (R>0 ) · GL1 (AF,S )1 acts on DS,v only through GL1 (AF,S )1 . Simiarly for
τv (R>0 ) · GL1 (AF )1 acting on Dv only through GL1 (AF )1 . Since DS,v is the orbit of ev under the continuous
action of GL1 (AF,S ) on AF,S , as is Dv of ev under the continuous action of GL1 (AF )1 on AF , we deduce
that GL1 (AF,S )1 , respectively GL1 (AF )1 , acts transitively on DS,v , respectively Dv .
     Such actions factor through the quotients of GL1 (AF,S )1 , respectively GL1 (AF )1 , by the stabilizers of ev ,
which are {±1} ⊂ Fv× if v is real, and U(1) if v is complex.                                                      □

(2) The closure within DF of τv0 (R>0 ) ⊂ D1 is τv0 (R>0 ) ∪ {ev0 }.

    Proof. In either case, τv0 (R>0 ) ∪ {ev0 } is homeomorphic to [0, +∞), a complete metric subspace of the
metrizable spaces DF,S , respectively DF , and, as such, sequentially closed, hence closed, being the ambient
second-countable, hence sequential, by Lemma 8.2.0.3.                                                      □

                                                           F,S
of the PWS,X (χS ′ |J 1 ′ , S(AF,S ′ )) is sequentially dense within H0,cont (χS ′ |J 1 ′ , S(AF,S ′ )).
                     F,S                                                             F,S
    This means that the Paley-Wiener levels retain knowledge of the trace of A(φ) asymptotically as X → +∞,
missing exactly the closed subspace H0,cont (χS ′ |J 1 ′ , S00 (AF,S ′ )) which is the main cause of the non-nuclearity
                                                      F,S
of A(φ) on H0,cont (χS ′ |J 1 ′ , S(AF,S ′ )).
                            F,S
    We are going to use the Paley-Wiener levels, in their invariant form (see Definition 7.3.2.3), in the next
two Chapters, to define and compute the trace of A(φ) rigorously, doing so with respect to coarser normed
topologies on the ambient H0,cont (χS ′ |J 1 ′ , S00 (AF,S ′ )), than its intrinsic nuclear Fréchet space topology.
                                                             F,S

    A choice of test function φ ∈ D(CF ), which we again assume supported over the closed semigroup CF≥1 ,
induces a test function φS ∈ D(JF,S ) for all large enough S. Indeed, for S any finite set of places of F
containing all the Archimedean places, such that χ is unramified outside S, and with Pic(OF,S ) = 1, we have
that φ is k-invariant for k ⊂ CF a compact subgroup with open compactly generated orthogonal k ⊥ ⊂ C    cF .
394                               CHAPTER 8. PERIODIC ORBITS AND FIXED POINTS


     In particular, φ is invariant under the compact subgroup given by the image in CF of O b×
                                                                                              ΣF −S ′ ⊂ GL1 (AF )
                        ′                   ′                  ′
for all large enough S . Upon replacing S with a larger set S if necessary, so as to have that χ is unramified
outside S ′ and Pic(OF,S ′ ) = 1, we may descend φ to a unique φS ′ ∈ D(JF,S ′ ) and A(φS ′ ) acts on
                                              H0,cont (χS ′ |J 1      , S(AF,S ′ ))
                                                              F,S ′

compatibly with the action of A(φ) on the global H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S(AF )) under the transition operator π S ′ ,
which, under the above conditions on S ′ , is a linear topological isomorphism.
    We conclude this Chapter by observing that as S grows to encompass all places of F , the trace of A(φS )
stabilizes in finite time, i.e. for all large enough finite sets of finite places S ′ of F containing all the Archimedean
places, the trace of A(φS ′ ) remains constant with respect to S ′ . The largeness of S ′ depends on the character
χ and on the support of the test function φ ∈ D(CF ).
    We are led to eyeball the following situation: the continuous operator A(φ) on H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S(AF )) is
traceable. Its trace will be defined rigorously in the next two Chapters, for then to be computed in Chapter 7.
    Its trace is concentrated at the S-local level, on the orbital subquotients of H0,cont (χS |JF,S      1 , S(AF,S )), for
S large enough.
    The Paley-Wiener levels approximate the orbital subquotients from within, filling them in asymptotically,
and they inhert the full Orbital Schauder bases on the primary Orbital quotients.
    At the global level, the topologically short exact sequence:
                          0 → H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S0 (AF )) → SE (CF )(χ|CF1 ) → HF (χ|CF1 ) → 0
leads to computing the trace of A(φ) by computing the trace of operators induced by the continuous
left-translation action of CF on the spectral subquotient HF (χ|CF1 ) (see Theorem 7.4.1.1).
     This is a first look into the elements that enter the trace calculation in Chapter 7. The idea is to perform
it not within the nuclear Fréchet spaces from above, but rather within normed completions, whose topology is
much coarser.
     The mere fact that the trace calculation can be performed with respect to such coarser topologies, is
what puts constraints on the zeros that are allowed to contribute to the spectral side of the trace formula:
only some of the point-evaluation functionals from (7.1.4.6) of Theorem 7.1.4.2, will remain continuous with
respect to coarser normed topologies, and only those, will be contributing to the spectral side.
     It turns out that the coarsest possible normed completion of H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S0 (AF )) which enables the
trace calculation, is a Sobolev completion of degree 2 [F : Q]. We will be studying these Sobolev completions
in the next Chapter.
     The Orbital Schauder bases on the Paley-Wiener levels will remain in place after such normed completions,
turning into Markushevich bases. They will enable us to reduce the trace calculation into a calculation to be
done S-locally only, as opposed to globally, and this is where the choice of Sobolev degree 2 [F : Q] is forced
on us: it ensures the orbital Schauder bases on the absolute and invariant Paley-Wiener levels, are inherited
by the normed completions, at least in the weaker sense of Markushevich bases, insofar as all the continuous
dual basis elements remain continuous on the Sobolev completions.

    Let F be a number field, S a finite set of places of F containing all the Archimedean places. Let χ be a
continuous character of CF , respectively of JF,S .
    In this Chapter, we coarsen the nuclear Fréchet topologies on SE (CF ), SI (JF,S ) and their CF1 -, respectively
 1
JF,S -isotypes, for I an appropriate choice of non-empty connected interval of the real line, as well as the nuclear
Fréchet topologies on H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S0 (AF )), respectively H0,cont (χ|JF,S
                                                                           1   , S(AF,S )), to normed topologies arising
by integration along a chosen vertical line within the Riemann surfaces Ω(CF ), respectively Ω(JF,S ), with
continuity requirements on finitely many degrees of holomorphic differentiation.
    In other words, we form completions of the above Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces, to
Sobolev spaces.
    These will serve as the ambients for the trace calculation which is the main subject of study of this work.


                                          9.1. Sobolev spaces W s,2 (G)
    We discuss here general constructions of normed topologies on the Hausdorff locally convex topological
complex vector spaces SE (CF ) and SI (JF,S ) of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on the idele class group CF ,
respectively on the S-idele class group JF,S , with exponential, respectively I-exponential decay, for some
appropriate chocie of non-empty connected interval I ⊂ R.
    Equivalently, this amounts to constructing continuous norms on SE (CF ), respectively SI (JF,S ), and study
the Banach spaces obtained by completion.
                                                          395

u. The entire function as ϕ(s) is now an element of H 2N,2 (C<b ), and hence the Mellin anti-transform
of a−s ϕ(−s), i.e. u(a/t) is such that | · |bR u(a/t) is supported over (0, 1], by another application of the
proof of [Dur, Ch.11,§11.5,Corollary,p.197], which implies that u is supported over [1/a, +∞). This
shows that u ∈ M[1/a,1] Wb2N,2 (R>0 ), where u is uniquely determined almost everywhere, and hence M
maps M[1/a,1] Wb2N,2 (R>0 ) onto PW2N,2        b   (C, a). We further refer the reader to the argument in [Yos,
Ch.VI,§4,Thm.2,p.164].
     We have therefore proved that M is surjective onto PW2N,2        b    (C, a), and since M is isometric, we deduce
that PW2N,2b     (C, a) is closed   in HS 2N,2
                                          b    (C, (1/a, +∞))  (which is also  a consequence of the Asymptotic Residue
Theorem; see Theorem B.3.2.1) and that the bottom leftmost horizontal arrow in (9.2.1.6) is itself an isometric
isomorphism onto its closed range.                                                                                    □

     9.2.2. General base intervals: the Hardy-Sobolev spaces WIs (G). We briefly recall here the
definition of the Hardy-Sobolev space H 2N,2 (C<b ), for b ∈ R a real number, and N ≥ 1 an integer.
     This is the C-linear space of holomorphic functions on the half-plane C<b that are square-integrable with
their holomorphic derivatives of order 0 ≤ k ≤ N on each vertical line of C<b and such that the resulting
L2 -norms are bounded uniformly with respect to the abscissa σ < b, topologized with the metrizable topology
generated by the finitely many norms:
                                                          Z σ+i∞               1/2
                                                                    k      2
(9.2.2.1)                       || · ||HS,2N,k : ϕ 7→ sup         |∂s ϕ(s)| |ds|
                                                       σ<b      σ−i∞
                                2N,2
for 0 ≤ k ≤ N . We refer to H          (C<b ) topologized with this seminormed topology, as the Hardy-Sobolev
space of degree 2N . It is a complex Hilbert space (since the finitely many norms can be reassembled into a
single norm inducing a Hilbert space structure on H 2N,2 (C<b )).
     We note that the norms, for each 0 ≤ k ≤ N and as σ varies over the real numbers σ < b:
                                                        Z σ+i∞               1/2
                                                                  k      2
(9.2.2.2)                       || · ||HS,2N,k,σ : ϕ 7→         |∂s ϕ(s)| |ds|
                                                              σ−i∞
                         2N,2
are all continuous on H     (C<b ), and hence their collection as σ varies over the real numbers σ < b induces
a Hausdorff locally convex topology on H 2N,2 (C<b ) that is coarser than the topology induced by the finitely
many norms from (9.2.2.1).
     By [Dur, Ch.11,Cor.2,p.191] and [Dur, Ch.11,§11.4,Thm.11.8,p.195], the Asymptotic Cauchy Integral
Formula (see Theorem B.2.2.4) applies, and it implies that H 2N,2 (C<b ) topologized with this coarser topology,
is complete, and that a countable subfamily of the seminorms from (9.2.2.2) indexed by a countable subset of
σ < b such that b is an accumulation point, generates an equivalent Hausdorff locally convex topology, which
therefore exhibits H 2N,2 (C<b ), re-topologized in this manner, as a Fréchet space (this can also be seen using
[Dur, Ch.11,§11.2,Thm.11.5,p.192]).
     The identity map on H 2N,2 (C<b ) with the Hardy-Sobolev topology on the source, and the coarser Fréchet
topology defined above on the target, is therefore open by [NB, Thm.14.4.5(b)], and hence a linear topological
isomorphism.
     We will therefore describe the topology on the Hardy-Sobolev space H 2N,2 (C<b ) by either the finite
collection of norms from (9.2.2.1), or by the topology of L2 -convergence of holomorphic functions and their
kth holomorphic derivatives for all 0 ≤ k ≤ N , on all vertical lines strictly contained in C<b (equivalently on
a countable collection of vertical lines strictly contained in C<b whose abscissas are a countable subset of
412                                 CHAPTER 9. HARDY-SOBOLEV TOPOLOGIES


(−∞, b) with b as an accumulation point). We further refer the reader to Lemma D.3.1.2 and its proof, for
a similar equivalence of Hausdorff locally convex topologies, resting upon the Asymptotic Cauchy Integral
Formula from Theorem B.2.2.4).
    Similar assertions hold on the topology of H 2N,2 (C>b ) and are obtained from the foregoing upon acting
on the complex s-plane using the bi-holomorphic involution s 7→ −s (and applying the result to −b).

                      9.3. Module structures over D(G) and approximate units
    In this section we discuss, for G a second-countable R>0 -modulated group, the continuous D(G)-module
structure on WIs (G), with D(G) acting by convolution. We further construct, according to whether I is a single
point or has non-empty interior, approximate units for WIs (G), i.e. a net of continuous linear endomorphisms
converging to the identity with respect to the topology of simple convergence.

    9.3.1. Module structure over D(G). Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. We recall
that we denote by D(G) the convolution C-algebra of smooth compactly supported test functions, equipped
with its locally convex inductive limit topology as in [Bru, §4]. Similarly, S(G) is the convolution C-algebra
of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on G (see [Bru, §8] and Appendix D of this work).
    For any φ ∈ D(G), we may regularize the continuous left-translation action ρG of G on S(G) and its closed
G-invariant subspaces, to obtain an operator A(φ). Such operator may extend by continuity to completions of
S(G) with respect to coarser topologies.
    For G a second-countable R>0 -modulated group, G acts continuously by left-translation on SI (G), for
I ⊂ R any non-empty open interval. We denote by ρG : G × SI (G) → SI (G) such action, i.e. ρG (g, ϕ)(x) :=
ϕ(g −1 x) as functions of x ∈ G. The same construction as in the foregoing defines a module structure of D(G)
on SI (G) which is continuous, giving the convolution operator A(φ) associated to each φ ∈ D(G).
    The operator A(φ) may extend by continuity to completions of SI (G) with respect to coarser topologies.
This is the subject of study of this subsection: we discuss herein the convolution action of G on WIs (G) for
any real number s ≥ 0.

    The truncation operators alluded to in the foregoing are obtained by integration on growing relatively
compact domains of the R>0 -modulated group G of the form {g ∈ G : |g|G ∈ (1/Λ, Λ)} for Λ > 0.
    We refer the reader to Definition D.2.1.1 for more on modulated groups. Recall that an R>0 -modulated
group is a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G equipped with a module homomorphism | · |G : G → R>0
which is assumed to be surjective and proper. Its fibre over 1 ∈ R>0 , i.e. its kernel G1 := ker(| · |G ), is a
closed compact Hausdorff abelian group.
    Let K ⊂ R>0 be a compact subset. We define GK to be the compact subset:
                                        GK := {g ∈ G : |g|G ∈ K} ⊂ G.
     For instance, for any real number Λ > 0:
                                   G[1/Λ,Λ] := {g ∈ G : |g|G ∈ [1/Λ, Λ]} ⊂ G
a compact subset of G with non-empty interior.
    Definition 9.3.3.1 (Smooth cutoffs). Let G be an R>0 -modulated group, with module | · |G . We let µG
be a choice of Haar measure on G. Let I be a closed non-empty interval.
    Let Λ, ε > 0 and s ≥ 0 be real numbers. Assume 0 < 1/Λ − ε < Λ − ε.
    We let ρ : G → C be a function such that:
(1) ρ is bounded with ||ρ||u = 1, real-valued and nonnegative.
(2) ρ is constant on the fibres of the module | · |G : G → R>0 , equivalently ρ is G1 -invariant.
(3) The unique function induced by ρ on R>0 by G1 -invariance and through the module | · |G : G/G1 ≃ R>0 ,
    is smooth away from finitely many points, at each of which its derivatives of any nonnegative integer order
    have at worst jump discontinuities, such that both one-ended limits exist and are finite.
(4) ρ is multiplicatively symmetric, i.e. ρ(g) = ρ(g −1 ).
(5) ρ is supported over G[1/Λ,Λ] .
(6) ρ is identically 1 over G[1/Λ+ε,Λ−ε] .
We refer to ρ as a (Λ, ε)-cutoff. If ρ is smooth, then we refer to ρ as a smooth (Λ, ε)-cutoff.
   For ρ a (Λ, ε)-cutoff, we define the ρ-truncation operator to be the multiplication operator:
(9.3.3.1)                                    Mρ : WIs (G) → WIs (G)
defined as:
(9.3.3.2)                                    Mρ (ϕ)(g) := ρ(g)ϕ(g)
as functions of g ∈ G.
    Remark 9.3.3.2. We note that indeed Mρ is a continuous linear endomorphism of WIs (G), since for any

                                    10.2. Spectral Markushevich Bases
    We recall that for a complete Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E with a Schauder
basis {xm }m≥0 , and {fm }m≥0 the bi-orthogonal sequence in E ′ , then if E is semi-reflexive, {fm }m≥0 is
also a Schauder basis (see [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.5,Thm.1(a),p.302]), and the datum {(xm , fm )}m≥0 is a
Markushevich basis.
    Being a Schauder basis is an unstable property with respect to coarsening of the Hausdorff locally convex
topology. The reader may consider the example of the exponential system on S(T) = C ∞ (T), with T := R/Z
the circle group, which is an absolute Schauder basis with respect to the topology of uniform convergence on
functions and their derivatives of arbitrary order, but is not a Schauder basis on L1 (T) := L1 (T, µ), µ being
the volume-1 Haar measure on T.
    It is, however, a Markushevich basis. The property that is lost under coarsening of the Hausdorff locally
convex topology from S(T) to L1 (T) is that of the simple convergence of the finite rank basis projections.
    We let F be a number field, S a finite set of places of F containing all the Archimedean places. Let χ be
a continuous character of CF , respectively of JF,S .
    In the remaining sections of this Chapter, we analyze to what extent the Schauder bases constructed in the
previous Chapter with respect to the strong topology on the Hausdorff locally convex space H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S(AF ))

5Return here.
                                      10.2. SPECTRAL MARKUSHEVICH BASES                                      439


and its subquotients, and on H0,cont (χ|JF,S
                                         1   , S(AF,S )) and its orbital subquotients, remain bases with respect
to the coarser Sobolev topologies introduced in Definition 10.1.1.1.
    10.2.1. The a-line Spectral Markushevich Basis. In the special case the compact non-empty interval
I ⊂ R from the definition of the Hardy-Sobolev spaces WIs (CF ) is of the form I = {0}, we have
                                                WIs (CF ) = W s,2 (CF )

                                                              s
                                                                  H0,cont (χ|CF1 , S0 (AF )).

     Remark 10.2.1.2 (On Markushevich Bases). Since, by [Jar, Part II,Ch.14,§14.1,Prop.2,p.290], bi-
orthogonal sequences are unique, for a Markushevich basis {(xm , fm )}m≥0 for the duality ⟨E, E ′ ⟩ with
E a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space, we will be omitting either {xm }m≥0 or {fm }m≥0
from the notation, referring to the former as a Markushevich basis for E, and to the latter as a Markushevich
basis for Eσ′ . If E is a Hilbert space, then so is Eβ′ , and then {fm }m≥0 linearly generates a subspace of
E ′ which is dense in the strong topology too, by [Jar, Part II,Ch.8,§8.2,Prop.1,p.149] and reflexivity. The
                                      10.2. SPECTRAL MARKUSHEVICH BASES                                           441


sequence {xm }m≥0 linearly generates a σ(E, E ′ )-dense subspace, which is, by the same token, dense with
respect to the intrinsic topology on E.
     Markushevich bases throughout this work will only be with respect to Hilbert normed topologies, and we
will therefore be making no distinction between strong and weak denseness of the linear spans of the basis
elements.

     Terminology 10.2.1.2 (Normalized Markushevich Bases). As before Corollary 11.2.0.5, we recall the
following terminology from [Kal], which applies to Schauder bases.
     We recall from [Kal, §3,p.95] that a Schauder basis {bk }k≥0 in a Hausdorff locally convex topological
                                                                                       P
C-vector space E is simple if and only if the finite rank projection operators PN := 0≤k≤N ⟨φk , ·⟩E ′ ,E bk , for
{φk }k≥0 the dual basic sequence of {bk }k≥0 , are a bounded set in Lβ (E), i.e. they are strongly bounded.
     We further recall from [Kal, §1,Def.1.1,p.91] that a Schauder basis {bk }k≥0 of E is regular if and only if
there exists a 0-neighborhood V such that bk ∈  / V for all k ≥ 0.
     Finally, from [Kal, §1,Def.1.2], a Schauder basis is normalized if and only if it is bounded and regular.
     We extend the concepts of boundedness, regularities and normalization, to Markushevich bases, as follows.
Let E be Banach space, and {(xm , fm )}m≥0 ⊂ E × Eβ′ a Markushevich basis. We say it is:
(1) Bounded, if and only if {xm }m≥0 ⊂ E is a bounded subset.
(2) Regular, if and only if {xm }m≥0 ⊂ E is strictly bounded away from 0 ∈ E. In particular, {fm }m≥0 ⊂ Eβ′
    is bounded.
(3) Normalized, if and only if it is both bounded and regular.

                                                10.3. Spectral Nuclearity
    A consequence of Theorem 10.2.1.1 is that it enables us to identify certain nuclear operators on HF,a    s

explicitly, and compute their trace.
    The contents of this subsection reprise [Co, §III,Cor.2,pp.13,14] and especially [Co, Appendix II,pp.62,68],
providing only a few complements on the convergence of certain finite rank operators with respect to the
appropriate Schatten-von Neumann norms (see Definition C.3.6.2) so as to enable a discussion on explicit
integral kernels early in the next Chapter.
    We recall from [Kothe-I, Part III,Ch.19,§19.9] that for two Banach spaces E1 , E2 , the C-linear space
S (E1 , E2 ) denotes the C-linear space of those linear operators T : E1 → E2 which can be written as
                                              X
                                         T =       λm ⟨am , ·⟩E1′ ,E2 · ym
                                                     m≥0

with {am }m≥0 ⊂ BE1′ , {ym }m≥0 ⊂ BE2 , where BE denotes the unit ball of the Banach space E, and
{λm }m≥0 ⊂ s, where s is the Köthe sequence space of sequences of complex numbers {λm }m∈Z that are
rapidly decaying, i.e. such that {mk λm }m∈Z ⊂ c0 for every integer k ≥ 0 (equivalently, s = S(Z), the space of
Schwartz-Bruhat functions on the discrete abelian group Z).
    The space s is a Fréchet space when endowed with the countable family of seminorms:
                                                    X
                                  pk ({λm }m≥0 ) :=   (1 + |m|)k |λm |, k ≥ 0.
                                                           m∈Z
448                               CHAPTER 10. TRACE FORMULA: SPECTRAL SIDE


We further refer the reader to [Tre, Part III,Ch.51,Rem.51.1,p.527] for more on s = S(Z).
    The linear space S (E1 , E2 ) can be made into a complete metrizable topological vector space (see [Kothe-I,
Part III,Ch.19,§19.9,Thm.3]).
    S (E1 , E2 ) is a linear subspace of the space S1 (E1 , E2 ) of nuclear operators, and when E1 = E2 is a
separable Hilbert space, S1 (E) := S1 (E1 , E2 ) is the C-linear space of trace class linear endomorphisms on E.
    There is a well-defined trace functional
                                                 Trace : S1 (E) → C
which, for E a closed invariant subspace or quotient of W s,2 (CF ), we shall denote by Trace to record the
dependence on the Sobolev degree s, i.e. the real number s ≥ 0 built into the Sobolev weight defining
W s,2 (CF ).
    We refer the reader to §C.3 and §C.3.4 for more on the trace class and nuclearity.
    We specifically refer the reader to Definition C.3.4.2 for the trace of a nuclear endomorphism of a Hilbert
space.

    Remark 10.4.2.6. We note that the quotient E → E/E0 in Lemma 10.4.2.5 maps the open unit ball
in E surjectively onto the open unit ball in E/E0 . If E is reflexive, then it maps the closed unit ball in E
surjectively onto the closed unit ball in E/E0 (a consequence of [Jar, Part II,Ch.11,§11.4,Cor.2,p.280], to
deduce that continuous linear functionals attain their maximum on the closed unit ball). The requirement that
the lift {um }m≥0 of the subset {xm }m≥0 ⊂ E/E0 contained in the closed collar {x ∈ E/E0 : ||x||E/E0 ∈ [r, r′ ]},
should not only be contained in a similar closed collar in E bounded away from 0 ∈ E, but also be contained
in F , leads to the necessity of enlarging the closed collar in E from {u ∈ E : ||u||E ∈ [r, r′ ]} to its closed
ε-neighborhood for a small enough choice of ε > 0.

    Remark 10.4.2.7. The Lemma says that given a normalized Schauder basis of E/E0 , we can lift it to a
Schauder basic sequence of E contained in a given subspace F ⊂ E such that F ∩ E0 is dense, and the image
of F in E/E0 is dense (hence, in particular, F is itself dense in E), and upon perturbing such lift a little, to
another that satisfies the same properties, the closures of their linear spans are linearly and topologically
isomorphic.
    If E is a Hilbert space, then we can find {um }m≥0 such that its closed linear span is linearly and
topologically isomorphic to the orthogonal complement of E0 , and hence so are the closed linear spans of all
small enough perturbations of {um }m≥0 .

     We note that the concept of “diverging to infinity” for sequences in I is already intrinsically defined,
inherited from N × N × N. It reads as follows: i → +∞ if and only if, writing i = (k(i), j(i), mk(i),j(i) ), we have
(k(i), j(i)) → (+∞, +∞) in N × N. In other words, “infinity” within I is the subset of the closure I of I within
the one-point compactification of the countable discrete set N × N × (N ∩ [0, Cs ]) with Cs := [(s − 1)/2 + 1],
obtained as I − I, which is contained within (+∞, +∞) × (N ∩ [0, Cs ]).

   11.3.1.1. Divisorial stratification of the ideles. The next step now is to split kgeom,I,φ (x, y) into an infinite

     12.1.1. Localization along the global diagonal. In this subsection we discuss how to use the kernel
            geom          spec

     This requires a discussion of how to make sense of each of the above kernel functions along the diagonal
in CF × CF , a null set with respect to the product measure µ ⊗ µ.
     To this end, we will be using the analog for the idele class group CF (and later for its S-local subgroup
CF,S and this latter’s quotient JF,S ) of the Differentiation Theorem of Lebesgue, together with continuity
properties of the Haar integral of µ-absolutely integrable functions over CF .
     This rests on an analog of the Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Theorem on Maximal functions, for which we
refer the reader to Appendix A (see Theorem A.5.3.7 and Theorem A.5.4.1).
     We begin with some results of a general nature, on Hilbert-Schmidt kernels on L2 (G, λ), where G is a
Hausdorff locally compact second countable abelian group, and λ is a Radon measure on G subordinate to a
choice of Haar measure µG , i.e. such that there exists a locally µG -integrable function f : G → R≥0 satisfying
f µG = λ as Radon measures on G.
     Definition 12.1.1.1. Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. Assume G is second countable.
Let {Uk }k≥0 be a D′ -sequence for G in the sense of Definition A.5.2.1.
     Let ϕ ∈ L1loc (G, µG ) be a locally µG -integrable complex-valued function on G. We define the smoothening
of ϕ to be the function defined as:
                                                              Z
                                                         1
(12.1.1.1)                            ϕ(x)
                                       e   := lim                  ϕ(y) dµG (y)
                                               k→+∞ µG (Uk ) xU
                                                                 k

at each point x ∈ G at which the limit in (12.1.1.1) exists and is finite, and zero elsewhere.
    We call a point x ∈ G at which the limit in (12.1.1.1) exists and is finite, a regular point for ϕ.
     We recall that a D-sequence for a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G, with µG a choice of Haar
measure on G, is the datum of a sequence {Uk }k≥0 where for each integer k ≥ 0, Uk ⊂ G is a µG -measurable
subset, Uk+1 ⊂ Uk , the µG -measure of each Uk is finite and nonzero, there exists a real number C > 0 such
that µG (Uk Uk−1 ) < C µG (Uk ) for every k ≥ 0.
     We say {Uk }k≥0 is a Borel D-sequence, respectively an open, symmetric D-sequence, if and only if each
of its members is a Borel set, respectively an open subset, respectively a symmetric subset (i.e. stable under
the inversion homomorphism on G).
     We say {Uk }k≥0 is a D′ -sequence, if it is a Borel D-sequence satisfying the following additional property:
for every unit-neighborhood V of G, there exists a large enough integer k0 ≥ 0 such that Uk0 ⊂ V . In
particular, there exists k0 ≥ 0 such that for every k ≥ k0 , Uk has compact closure.
     For instance, for G = RN , the two sequences {Uk := B(0, rk )}k≥0 and {Uk′ := Qrk }, for {rk }k≥0 a strictly
decreasing sequence of real numbers with r0 > 0, and with B(0, r) the closed ball centered at 0 with radius r,
and Qr the cube in RN of the form [−r, r]N , are both symmetric D′ -sequences.
     The Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups under consideration throughout this work (global ideles,
S-local ideles, their class groups, their closed subgroups of norm-one elements, their class groups of norm-one
elements) are all equipped with symmetric D′ -sequences. These are constructed in Appendix A,§A.5.2; see
Definition A.5.2.1 and Definition A.5.2.18.
     The presence of a D′ -sequence in G enables the definition of a corresponding maximal function analogous
to the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function on Euclidean spaces, and analogs of the Maximal Theorem and of
Lebesgue’s Differentiation Theorem both hold. We refer the reader to [HR-2, Ch.XI,§44], and to Theorem
A.5.3.7 and Theorem A.5.4.1.
                                   12.1. SMOOTHENINGS ALONG THE DIAGONAL                                         499


    In particular, maximal functions, the Maximal Theorem and Lebesgue’s Differentiation Theorem, are
available on the idelic groups and groups of idele classes being considered throughout this Chapter.
    For locally integrable functions on G × G, if {Uk }k≥0 is a D′ -sequence for G, we will be using the
  ′
D -sequence {Uk × Uk }k≥0 for G × G to define smoothenings (see Lemma A.5.2.5(1), which proves that indeed
{Uk × Uk }k≥0 is a D′ -sequence for G × G).

of Hardy-Littlewood, and of the Differentiation Theorem of Lebesgue.

                           12.2. Lebesgue Differentiation along the diagonal
                                                                    geom
     In this section we analyze the Hilbert-Schmidt kernel of PΛ,a       ◦ A(φ) and its trace, as Λ → +∞, with the
aim of reducing the computation of the limit value of the latter to separate simpler tasks, amounting to trace
calculations for component kernels.
     We recall that throughout this Chapter, for (X, A, µ) a measure space, we will be assuming X is a
Hausdorff locally compact second countable topological space, the σ-algebra A contains the Borel σ-algebra
B(X), µ is a complete positive Radon measure on A, and, for simplicity, that A is the initial σ-algebra
containing B(X) and such that µ is complete on A. In particular, for any N ⊂ X such that µ(N ) = 0, N is
measurable.
     Recall that any Radon measure on such X is regular (see [Fol, Thm.7.8]).
     We will be abbreviating Lp (X, µ) for Lp (X, A, µ), for every real number p ≥ 1.
     Under these assumptions, for any element ϕ ∈ Lp (X, µ), there exists a Borel measurable function
ϕ0 : X → C such that ϕ = ϕ0 away from a subset N of X such that µ(N ) = 0.
     Any element in Lp (X, µ) is, recall, an equivalence class of Lebesgue measurable functions on X, the
equivalence relation being equality away from µ-null subsets of X.
     In light of [Fol, Prop.7.9], Lp (X, µ) is also obtained as the norm-completion of Cc (X) with respect to the
                                                                                                                  1/p
seminormed topology induced by the Lp -seminorm (in fact a norm) on Cc (X), i.e. ||f ||p := X |f (x)|p dµ(x)
                                                                                                 R
                                                                                                                       .
                                                p
     Both perspectives on the elements of L (X, µ) will be used below.
     In light of [Fol, Prop.7.1] (see also [Bou-I, Ch.III,§1,n.3,(4),INT III.7]; see also [Bou-I, Ch.III,§1,n.5,Thm.1,INT
III.12]) and [Fol, Thm.7.2], under the assumptions being made on X, the approaches to measure theory and
integration contained in [Bou-I, Bou-II] and from classical measure theory (see [Fol, Ch.1,§1.3] and [Fol,
Ch.7], and the related literature referred to throughout this work) are equivalent.

   Remark 12.2.1.4. We let X be a Hausdorff locally compact topological space, G a Hausdorff locally
compact abelian group. Assume consider a continuous action:
(12.2.1.9)                                     θ :G×X →X
We assume that the action θ of G on X is proper, by which we mean, following [Bou-GT, Ch.III,§4,n.1,Def.1,p.250],
that the continuous map:
                                               G×X →X ×X
sending (g, x) to (x, θ(g, x)), is proper (see [Bou-GT, Ch.I,§10,n.1,Def.1,p.97]).
    By [Bou-GT, Ch.III,§4,n.2,Prop.3,p.253], the quotient space X/G is Hausdorff.
    If the action θ of G on X is, in addition, free, then, by [Bou-GT, Ch.III,§4,n.4,Corollary,p.257] to
[Bou-GT, Ch.III,§4,n.4,Prop.8,256], the quotient map:
(12.2.1.10)                                     π : X → X/G
is open.
     In this case, if X is second countable, so is X/G.
     We assume two Radon measures given, one, µX , on X, another, a choice of Haar measure µG on G. We
assume µX is G-invariant, and denote by µ the unique Radon measure on X/G induced by these choices, so
that the following integral formula holds:
                            Z                 Z     Z                    
(12.2.1.11)                    ϕ(x) dµX (x) =           ϕ(θ(g, x)) dµG (g) dµ(π(x)).
                          X                  X/G     G

     In the special case X is itself a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, and G is a closed subgroup,
with θ the action by continuous left-translation, the existence and uniqueness of µ, upon choosing µX to
be a Haar measure on X, is by Theorem D.1.2.1. For the general case, we refer the reader to [Bou-II,
Ch.VII,§2,n.2,Prop.4,INT VII.31].
     Assume that there exists a non-empty connected subset D ⊂ X with non-empty interior, such that
                                       [
(12.2.1.12)                               θ(g, D) = X, D ∩ θ(g, D) = ∅
                                     g∈G

the last condition being assumed to hold for every g ∈ G with g ̸= 1.
    Assume that for every g ∈ G, with g ̸= 1, the intersection:
(12.2.1.13)                                      D ∩ θ(g, D)
has µ-measure zero.
    We will be referring to such D as a fundamental domain for the continuous G-action on X.
    The above general situation and the respective terminology will be specialized shortly to the cases
X = GL1 (AF ), respectively GL1 (AF,S ), and G = F × , respectively G = O×

    Remark 12.2.2.3. For a complex-valued function f : X → C on a Hausdorff locally compact second
countable topological space X, and a Radon measure µ on X, Lebesgue measurability for f (upon endowing
X with the completion of the Borel σ-algebra, i.e. with the σ-algebra of µ∗ -measurable sets, promoting µ to
a complete measure; see [Fol, Thm.1.11] and [Bou-I, Ch.IV,§5,n.1,Cor.1,INT IV.60]) and µ-measurability
in the sense of [Bou-I, Ch.IV,§5,n.1,Def.2,INT IV.60], are equivalent concepts. µ-measurability of a map
f : X → T for T a Hausdorff locally compact topological space, is defined in [Bou-I, Ch.IV,§5,n.1,Def.1,INT
IV.59], and will be used only for f continuous, surjective and open, in which case it holds by [Bou-I,
Ch.IV,§5,n.2,Cor.4,INT IV.62].

we have K ⊂ K ′ × K ′ .

     Proposition 12.2.2.4. Let G be a second countable Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, H ⊂ G a
discrete subgroup, µH the counting measure on H, µG a choice of Haar measure on G, µG/H the unique Haar

     For each integer k ≥ 0, we define Hk := H ∩ Gk the induced filtration on H.

(2) D ⊂ G0 .

    We denote by αk the indicator function of Gk in G, and by βk the indicator function of the clopen subset
G − Gk .

   Proof. Note that since Gk ⊂ G is an open subgroup, it is closed by [DE, Lemma 1.1.7(c)]. In particular,
G/Gk , and hence Gk+1 /Gk , is a discrete group with respect to the quotient topology.
   We note that the induced group homomorphism:
(12.2.2.28)                                    Hk+1 /Hk → Gk+1 /Gk
is continuous upon endowing Hk+1 /Hk with the quotient topology. Since H ⊂ G is closed, Hk ⊂ Gk is closed,
and hence so is Hk ⊂ Hk+1 . Since Gk ⊂ Gk+1 is open, so is Hk ⊂ Hk+1 , since each Hk is endowed with the
subspace topology inherited from G.
     In particular, Hk+1 /Hk is also discrete, and since Hk+1 ∩ Gk = Hk , then Hk+1 /Hk free, being a subgroup
of a free abelian group of finite rank. It is therefore either trivial or of rank 1, in which case the homomorphism
in (12.2.2.28) is an isomorphism.
     Let g ∈ Gk+1 be of the form h · x for unique x ∈ D and h ∈ Hk+1 . Since D ⊂ Gk , the homomorphism in
(12.2.2.28) is surjective, and hence an isomorphism.
     We now consider the continuous homomorphisms:
(12.2.2.29)                                       Gk /Hk → G/H
for each integer k ≥ 0, all injective since H ∩ Gk = Hk , and open since Gk ⊂ G is an open subgroup, and
hence Gk · H ⊂ G is open by [DE, Lemma 1.1.3(e)].
                            12.2. LEBESGUE DIFFERENTIATION ALONG THE DIAGONAL                                  513


   The cokernel of the injective continuous open group homomorphism from (12.2.2.29) is discrete when

   The quotient group:
(12.2.2.30)                                           G/Gk
is discrete and free. Indeed, it is the direct limit topological group (see [DE, Ch.1,§1.8,p.29]; see also [DE,
Prop.1.8.6]) of the open and closed subgroups Gm /Gk for m ≥ k: open and closed since the pre-image of
Gm /Gk in G is Gm , since Gk ⊂ Gm for every integer m ≥ k, and Gm ⊂ G is open and closed. The transition
maps Gm /Gk → Gm+1 /Gk are injective, their source is free of rank m − k, and their cokernel is free of rank
1, and hence Gm+1 /Gk splits as the product of Gm /Gk by the free group Gm+1 /Gm of rank 1.
     Upon therefore choosing a Z-basis {ξk , . . . , ξm+k } for Gm /Gk , and an element ξm+k+1 of Gm+1 that

  12.3. Putting the pieces together: global to S-local deconstruction of the geometric kernel
      1


                                            12.4. S-local trace calculation
     In this section we compute the part of the trace formula that is delegated to the S-local function spaces
discussed. The calculations are analogous to calculations performed by Connes (see [Co, §VII,Thm.4,p.31])
and reprised by R. Meyer (see [Me1, §3]). The calculation presented below exhibits small variations on the
same theme.
     Most importantly, the role of the S-adelic Fourier transform, whose job is to turn the integral calculation
of interest into a simpler one coming down to a volume calculation on the S-idele class group JF,S , was
identified by Connes in his 1998 paper (see [Co, §VII,Thm.4,p.31]).

                                12.5. Trace formula: the Main Theorem of this work

                                  14.1. On the multiplicities of the zeros
    In this section we record a few complements, and discuss an important sanity check: we explain how the
Multiplicity Bound obtained in Theorem 13.3.1.2, is compatible with expectations from Global Langlands and
the Grand Simplicity Hypothesis.
    We will then explain how the methods discussed throughout this paper, do not adapt to the case of Hecke
L-functions of global function fields of smooth projective geometrically connected curve X over a finite field
Fq of positive characteristic p.
    Specifically, we will be discussing which parts extend to this case, and which, most importantly, do not,
and why this is to be expected: briefly, a phenomenon caused by the existence of maximal curves, leading to
counterexamples to the positive characteristic direct analog of the Simplicity Hypothesis (i.e. that the zeros of
the L-functions L(s, π) attached to cuspidal automorphic representations π of GLm over F = Fq (t) for some
integer m ≥ 0, are simple).



    14.1.1. Artin-Weil L-functions. We let F be a local or global field, and F a fixed choice of separable
closure. We denote by WF any Weil group for F . We recall that a Weil group for F , is a triple
                                                 (WF , φ, {rE }E )
where WF is a topological group
                                              φ : WF → Gal(F /F )
is a continuous group homomorphism with dense image.
     We will be referring to φ as the reciprocity homomorphism.
     For any finite separable sub-extension E/F contained within the chosen F , we define WE := φ−1 (Gal(F /E)),
noting that since φ is continuous, then WE ⊂ WF is an open subgroup of finite index.
     If E/F is Galois, then WE ⊂ WF is normal.
     Denseness of the image of φ ensures that we have a bijection of finite homogeneous spaces:
(14.1.1.1)                              WF /WE → Gal(F /F )/Gal(F /E)
where E/F is a general finite separable extension. In the special case E/F is finite Galois, then this is a group
isomorphism.
    The collection {rE }E , as E varies over the finite separable extensions of F contained in the chosen F , is a
family of isomorphisms of Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups:
(14.1.1.2)                                       rE : CE → WEab
where CE is the idele class group, if F is global, and CE = E × , if F is local. For each finite separable extension
E/F contained within F , WEab is notation for the Hausdorff locally compact abelian quotient of WE obtained
as the quotient of WE by the closure WEc of the commutator subgroup of WE .
    We will be referring to the isomorphisms of topological groups rE from (14.1.1.2) as abelianization
isomorphisms.
    The triple (WF , φ, {rE }E ) is assumed to satisfy a collection of axioms, for which we refer the reader to
[Tate, §1]. Most importantly, the composition of rE followed by the unique continuous group homomorphism
WEab → Gal(F /E)ab induced by φ, is assumed to agree with Artin’s Reciprocity map ArtE from Class Field
Theory.
    We define, for any finite Galois extension E/F contained within the chosen F :
(14.1.1.3)                                      WE/F := WF /WEc
equipped with the quotient topology, where WEc again denotes the closure of the commutator subgroup of WE .
                                  14.1. ON THE MULTIPLICITIES OF THE ZEROS                                    525


     We refer the reader to [Tate, §1,pp.3,4], to Artin and Tate’s treatise on Class Field Theory (see [AT,
Ch.XV,Thm.7,p.179] and [AT, Ch.V,Thm.11,p.186]), and to Weil’s own work on the Explicit Formulas
(see [Weil-e, §1,6] (where Weil groups are termed W -groups) and [Weil-f, §II,V]) where Weil groups are
constructed and introduces a generalization of Artin L-functions associated to continuous finite dimensional
complex representations of WF , for F a global field.
     We further refer the reader to Langlands’ notes on Artin L-functions (see [Langlands, Ch.20]), where
Weil’s generalization of Artin L-functions is defined and their basic properties summarized.
     The construction of the Weil group WF is carried out in [AT, Ch.XV] and rests upon the formalism of
(topological class formations). The group WE/F is a topological extension of Gal(E/F ) by CE , classified by a
class αE/F ∈ H2 (Gal(E/F ), CE ), which turns out to agree (granting the existence of a Weil group for the
topological class formation [AT, Ch.XV,Def.3,p.175]) with the fundamental class of Class Field Theory, or
can be defined to be such fundamental class, for then deducing the existence of a Weil group as a projective
limit topological group of the extensions classified by αE/F , whose properties and functorialities follow from
the cohomological formalism discussed in [AT, Ch.XIII,XIV].
     We collect the most important facts about Weil groups throughout the Proposition below:

    Proposition 14.1.1.1. Let F be either a global field, or a local field. We fix a separable closure F of F .

(14.1.1.5)                                     WF → lim WE/F

(14.1.1.6)                                      θ v : WF v → WF
