    14.1.2. Expected Multiplicity Bound. Let F be a number field, χ ∈ C           cF a continuous character.1
    The Trace Formula (Theorem 13.3.1.1) reveals constraints on the multiplicity of the non-trivial zeros of
the Hecke L-function L(s, χ), although not all of them. Indeed, Theorem 13.3.1.2, a consequence of the Trace
Formula combined with the Positivity Criterion (in its form from Theorem ??), asserts that if ρ ∈ C is a
non-trivial zero of L(s, χ), then ρ ∈ 1/2 + iR, and if, in addition, ρ ∈
                                                                       / R, i.e. ρ ̸= 1/2, then
                                                 N (ρ) ≤ [F : Q]
where N : C → N is the multiplicity function of the divisor of L(s, χ).
    In particular, no information is provided on the value of N (c) when c is the central zero. This is due to
the assumption on the test functions φ ∈ D(CF ) on which the Trace Formula holds, that they should vanish,
together with their holomorphic derivatives of order up to [F : Q] − 1, at all the central zeros.
    Recall that by central zero we mean the unique point of each connected component of the Riemann surface
                                 1/2
Ω(CF ), that is of the form | · |F c0 , where c0 is the unique point of each connected component allowed to

1Correct this subsection.
                                  14.1. ON THE MULTIPLICITIES OF THE ZEROS                                      529


occur as a pole of multiplicity higher than 1 of the partial Euler products v∈S Lv (χv | · |sv ) for any finite set
                                                                           Q

S of places of F containing all the Archimedean places.
    Upon fixing a continuous homomorphic section τ to the idelic norm, and calling x0 ∈ R the unique
real number such that χ(τ (t)) = tix0 as smooth functions on R>0 , then the central zero in the connected
component Ω(CF )(χ|CF1 ) parametrized according to the holomorphic parametrization
                                                  χ| · |sF , s ∈ C
is parametrized by the complex number s = 1/2 − ix0 .
     We could of course renormalize our very definition of Hecke L-function L(s, χ) to ensure that this point is
located at s = 1/2, which we have not done throughout this work (such normalization is a generalization of
the normalization customarily in force in discussions from the literature concerning Dirichlet L-functions and,
more generally, the L-functions associated to cuspidal automorphic representations of GLn (AQ ). It is referred
to as unitary normalization).
     This one point of each connected component of Ω(CF ) therefore remains mysterious: understanding its
multiplicity is beyond the reach of the methods of this work.
     We will show in this subsection by means of examples, that in fact it does not obey the multiplicity bound
of [F : Q] which applies to the other non-trivial zeros. As we do so, we will also show how the multiplicity
bound of [F : Q] on the non-central non-trivial zeros, is compatible with expectations from Global Langlands
and the Grand Simplicity Hypothesis, i.e. it follows as a consequence of a combination of conjectures on
automorphic L-functions for GLn (AQ ) for n ≥ 1.
     The following two conjectures can be found in the existing literature on automorphic L-functions. We
write L(s, π) for the completed and unitarily normalized L-function of a cuspidal automorphic representation
π of GLn (AQ ). In particular, the line of symmetry of the functional equation for L(s, π) is Re(s) = 1/2, and
the central zero of L(s, π) is s = 1/2, with multiplicity N ≥ 0.

    Conjecture 14.1.2.1 (GRH and GSH). Let n ≥ 1 be an integer, and π a cuspidal automorphic
representation of GLn (AQ ).
    Then:
     (1) (GRH - Grand Riemann Hypothesis) All the zeros of the L-function L(s, π) are located on 1/2 + iR.
     (2) (GSH - Grand Simplicity Hypothesis) With the sole possible exception of s = 1/2, all the zeros of
         L(s, π) are simple.

     Our main references on the Grand Simplicity Hypothesis are the papers by Rudnick-Sarnak and Rubinstein-
Sarnak (see [Rud-Sa] and [Ru-Sa, §5,p.195]). The methods contained in the former lead to the observation
that the zeros of pairs of (unitarily normalized) completed L-functions of cuspidal automorphic representations
of GLn (AQ ) (for possibly distinct integers n ≥ 1) are, in a precise sense, uncorrelated, with the possible
exception of central zeros, if any.
     In the latter (see [Ru-Sa, §5,p.195]) expectations on the non existence of relations of algebraic origin
on the ordinates of the zeros of the L-functions of cuspidal automorphic representations of GLn (AQ ) are
discussed, with the exception of those concerning the existence of central zeros.
     To illustrate the phenomenon concerning central zeros, we refer the reader to [Arm], where an example is
constructed of an Artin representation ρ of Gal(Q/Q) whose Artin L-function L(s, ρ) vanishes at s = 1/2,
leading to an example of a number field F whose Dedekind zeta function ζF (s) vanishes at s = 1/2 with
multiplicity higher than 1. The existence of the central zero at s = 1/2 is caused by the sign of the root
number in the functional equation for the Artin L-functions in the Artin-Takagi factorization of ζF (s).
     Serre produced an example of another number field, a quaternionic Galois extension of Q, with ζF (1/2) = 0
(see [Ng, Ch.2,§2.5,p.23]).
530                                       CHAPTER 14. COMPLEMENTS


    Central zeros with high multiplicity are, however, expected to not exceed the multiplicity bound of
Theorem 13.3.1.2, even though the multiplicity bound of Theorem 13.3.1.2 does not apply to them.
    A conjecture of Serre in fact predicts that the Artin L-functions of irreducible representations of the
Galois group of Q have only simple zeros (central zeros being no exception), and expects that a central zero
exist if and only if the character of the Artin representation is real and the root number is −1. We refer the
reader to [Goss, Ch.8,§8.24,Conjecture 8.24.1,p.324] for the statement of Serre’s conjecture.
    Some evidence in support of such conjecture of Serre can be found in [Omar, §6].
    The question of whether Hecke L-functions L(s, χ) with a central zero whose multiplicity is higher than
the degree of the number field, exist, has an affirmative answer. Before exhibiting explicit examples from the
theory of CM elliptic curves, we will be showing that the multiplicity bound obtained in Theorem 13.3.1.2 and
which applies to all other non-trivial zeros of Hecke L-functions apart from central zeros, is compatible with
expectations from the literature, and specifically with Conjecture 14.1.2.1, and the Langlands Program.
    Let now Q be a fixed choice of separable closure of Q. We choose, up to isomorphism, a Weil group WQ
for Q relative to the choice Q, and refer to it as the Weil group of Q.
    We further record here a form of Global Langlands for continuous finite dimensional complex representations
of the Weil group WQ of the field of rational numbers.

    Conjecture 14.1.2.2 (Global Langlands for GLn (AQ ) - Weil representations). Let n ≥ 1 be an integer.
    Let ρ : WQ → GLn (C) be a continuous finite dimensional complex representation of the Weil group WQ .
Assume:
(1) ρ is irreducible.
(2) For each g ∈ WQ , ρ(g) is semisimple.
      Then there exists a cuspidal automorphic representation π of GLn (AQ ) such that:
(14.1.2.1)                                      L(s, ρ) = L(s, π)
where L(s, ρ) is the Artin-Weil L-function of ρ, normalized as in the discussion between [Langlands, Intro-
duction,Thm.A,p.vii] and [Langlands, Introduction,Thm.B,p.vii], and L(s, π) is the completed and unitarily
normalized automorphic L-function of π.

     We recall from the previous subsection that Artin-Weil L-functions are not assumed to be unitarily
normalized throughout this work.
     The L-functions arising from the Hasse-Weil L-functions of elliptic curves will instead have Re(s) = 1
as the line of symmetry of their functional equations, as opposed to Re(s) = 1/2, in order for this work to
adhere with conventions from the literature on Hasse-Weil L-functions of elliptic curves (which will serve as
our source of examples at the end of this subsection).
     We will therefore be mentioning explicitly when such Hasse-Weil L-functions are being unitarily normalized.
     Both Conjecture 14.1.2.1 and Conjecture 14.1.2.2 serve the sole purpose of instructing us on the expectations
from the literature concerning the multiplicity of the zeros of Artin-Weil L-functions, for the purposes of
testing the multiplicity bound obtained in Theorem 13.3.1.2: such multiplicities are unaffected by unitary
normalization.
     We will now perform the desired test on the multiplicity bound obtained in Theorem 13.3.1.2.
     Assuming Conjecture 14.1.2.1 and Conjecture 14.1.2.2, we will be proving that indeed the bound obtained
in Theorem 13.3.1.2 holds as stated, for all non-trivial zeros of Hecke L-functions of the number field F , with
the sole possible exception of the central zero.
     We will then be showing by means of examples, constructed using the theory of CM elliptic curves, that
the central zero indeed does not obey such bound.

                  14.2. The case of global function fields of positive characteristic
     In this subsection, we answer the question of whether the Trace Formula from Theorem 13.3.1.1 holds
when F is a global function field of positive prime characteristic p, and whether it leads to a novel approach
to GRH for the Hecke L-functions of global fields of positive characteristic.
     The short answer is “no” to both parts of the question.
     The trace calculation cannot be performed within the Sobolev ambient that is responsible for the constraints
on the zeros contributing to the spectral side (on their location and multiplicity).
     Let p be a prime number, and q a positive integer power of p, i.e. q = pd for some integer d ≥ 1. Let X
be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over k := Fq , and F its function field, F := k(X).
     We will be referring to F as a global function field.
     While the methods from Chapters 2,3,4 and 5 adapt to the case of such F , as do the main results from
[CF, Ch.XV], instrumental to these Chapters (see [RV, Ch.7,§7.2,p.264]), it is Chapter 6 and Chapter 7 that
are unavailable for such F . It is not possible to perform the necessary trace calculations and within a Sobolev
ambient, as is done for F a number field.
     The reason can be traced directly to the Euler product of the zeta function of X:
                                                       Y         1
(14.2.0.1)                                 ζ(X, s) =
                                                           1 − |k(x)|−s
                                                      x∈|X|

where the product is indexed by the closed points of X, and k(x) is the residue field of X at the closed point
x ∈ X, itself a finite field of size |k(x)|.
     The size |k(x)| of the residue field k(x) is an integer divisible by q for all closed points x ∈ X, and hence
the Euler factors of ζ(X, s) have infinitely many poles in common. This is the key difference with the case of
F a number field: for any closed point x ∈ Spec(OF ), only finitely many closed points y ∈ Spec(OF ) have the
same residue characteristic, i.e. are in the same fibre over xp : Spec(Fp ) → Spec(Z).
     Let f : X → P1Fq be a non constant morphism, hence finite flat surjective.
     This amounts to choosing a structure on F of finite field extension of Fq (t), i.e. a field embedding
ι = f ∗ : Fq (t) ⊂ F .
     Since f is finite, it has finite fibres. However, correcting the superposition of the poles of the Euler factors
of ζ(X, s) as is done for Euler factors over distinct prime numbers in the number field case, by assuming
the vanishing of the test function along with finitely many of its derivatives, cannot be done for F a global
function field, since such vanishing condition would have to hold for the holomorphic derivatives of arbitrarily
high order of the Mellin transform of the test function, an entire function on the Riemann surface Ω(CF )
(whose connected components are, for F a global function field, non simply connected).
     Such correction enables the deconstruction of the global geometric kernel, and it is at this early stage that
the trace calculation cannot be carried out any further: only finitely many of the infinitely many functionals
(obtained as derivatives of point-evaluation functionals supported at points of Ω(CF ), with unbounded order)
required for the method to adapt, remain continuous on W s,2 (CF ), shifting the burden of correcting the
discrepancy between the S1 - and S2 -limits of the analogs of the finite rank operators from Theorem 11.2.2.1,
onto the test function, forcing the necessity of vanishing conditions to hold for its Mellin transform and its
derivatives of unbounded order. A necessity that cannot be fulfilled, since no nonzero holomorphic function
exists on any connected non-empty complex domain, which vanishes at a point, with infinite order of vanishing.
     In short, the Theorem on Polar Multiplicities (see Theorem 7.1.3.2) does not hold, when F is a global
function field.
     What is more, is that not only Euler factors have infinitely many poles in common, but they repeat
themselves as Euler factors infinitely many times. As many as the number of closed points x ∈ X whose
residue field has fixed degree m ≥ 0 over Fq .
                  14.2. THE CASE OF GLOBAL FUNCTION FIELDS OF POSITIVE CHARACTERISTIC                            535


      This number is estimated from the Weil bound and it is:
                                                 qm
                                                    + OX (q m/2 /m)
                                                 m
as m → +∞ (see [TsV, Ch.2.3,(2.3.2),p.177] combined with the inequality mBm ≤ Nm − N1 , with Bm the
number of closed points of X of degree m, and Nm := |X(Fqm )|).
      The implied constant depends on the curve through its genus.
      An analog of the trace calculation underlying Theorem 13.3.1.2 can indeed be made, although the topology
on H0,cont (F × , S0 (AF )) and SE (CF ) that serves the desired purpose is non-normable, rendering the kernels
of the continuous operators on each Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space only generalized
functions, as opposed to measurable functions on the idele classes.
      This in turn leads us to employing topologies that are fine enough to render infinite compositions of the
Principal Value Operators of Weil (see (5.3.1.5)), i.e. indexed by infinitely many places of F , convergent
with respect to the topology of uniform convergence on bounded subsets. These serve as a replacement the
operation of multiplying a measurable kernel function k(x, y) on GL1 (AF ) × CF by an indicator function
                                    / OFv ) × CF to restrict k(x, y) to smaller loci of the product.
                                 Q
supported over GL1 (AF,S × v∈S
      The desired convergence of such countably infinite compositions only holds with respect to topologies
that are fine enough to promote multiplication by | · |aF for a ∈ [0, 1 + ε] to a continuous and continously
invertible endomorphism on the resulting completion of SE (CF ) for all small enough ε > 0, to access the
absolute convergence of the Euler product of Hecke L-functions over the half plane of absolute convergence.
We refer the reader to the proof of [Me, §5,Lemma 5.3,p.39,40], for a similar assertion and connection to
convergence of operator-theoretic Euler products.
      We are lead to a trace formula where the spectral side involves no non-trivial constraints on the non-trivial
zeros of ζ(X, s): if we did not know GRH for ζ(X, s) as an input.
      In other words, the resulting trace formula by itself would not inform us on the location nor on the
multiplicity of such zeros. It would recover Weil’s own Explicit Formulas only.
      This has been accomplished by R. Meyer in [Me, §5], and a trace calculation along the lines being
alluded to in the foregoing would be close to the one performed in [Me, §5,Thm.5.8,p.43], leading to a
representation-theoretic proof of the Explicit Formulas only.
      Not only does the method of trace calculation not adapt, for F a global function field, but the Multiplicity
Bound obtained in Theorem 11.2.2.1 for F a number field, does not hold in its analogous formulation.
      Indeed, if it did, then it would be so for any choice of non-constant morphism f : X → P1Fq , and hence
                                                                              1
it would imply that the multiplicity of the Frobenius eigenvalues on Hét       (Xksep , Qℓ ), the geometric ℓ-adic
                                                  sep
cohomology of X, for ℓ a prime invertible on k , a separable closure of k = Fq would be bounded above by
the gonality of the curve X. This is most definitely not the case, due to additional symmetries of X that may
arise in positive characteristic: maximal curves provide counterexamples to this assertion.
      Maximal curves over k = Fq2 are such that the characteristic polynomial of geometric Frobenius on
  1
Hét (Xksep , Qℓ ) is P1 (X) ∈ Z[X], with:
                                                P1 (X) = (X + q)2g
a consequence of the relative Frobenius acting on the geometric Jacobian
                                               J(X) = Pic0Xksep /ksep
of X as multiplication by −q.
     It follows that while the multiplicity of each Frobenius eigenvalue is 2g, the gonality of the curve is strictly
lower, being equal to g + 1 (for g the genus of X). We refer the reader to [FGT], for more on maximal curves
(including examples and a partial classification in terms of Hermitian curves).
536                                          CHAPTER . COMPLEMENTS


    We further note that already over Fq (t), the analog of Serre’s conjecture from [Goss, Ch.8,§8.24,Conjecture
8.24.1] on simplicity of the zeros of Artin L-functions of irreducible representations of Gal(Q/Q) does not
hold.
    Indeed, for q = p2 , we let E be a supersingular elliptic curve over Fq , a double cover f : E → P1Fq of the
projective line. By Geometric Class Field Theory, the associated quadratic character χf of Fq (t) is such that
L(s, χf ) has a double zero.

                                          14.3. The higher rank case
    For π a cuspidal automorphic representation of GLn (AF ), the bound on generic zeros to which we are led
by the n > 1 version of these methods is:
                                                 n[F : Q].
    In particular, for F = Q, the bound is the rank n itself, which shows how the Grand Simplicity Hypothesis
remains beyond the reach of the methods developed throughout this work, and its version GLn .
    We will now share a few elements of the version of these methods for GLn (AF ), i.e. to analyze the divisor
of the completed, unitarily normalized, L-function of a cuspidal automorphic representation π of GLn (AF ),
to highlight what changes from the case n = 1.

                  Preparations from Algebraic Number Theory

     In this appendix we review some classic results in algebraic number theory, encompassing compactness of
the norm-1 subgroup of the idele class group CF of a number field F , along with the construction of normalized
Haar measures on GL1 (AF ), CF , and their closed subgroups of norm-1 elements, as well as the construction
of fundamental domains for the F -action on AF and the F × -action on GL1 (AF )1 . We also review an adelic
version of the theory of Hardy-Littlewood maximal functions for use in our work with measurable adelic kernel
functions.
     For F a number field, we denote by:

    §13-14]).

(3) SF,f or Sf the set of non-Archimedean places of F . We refer to its elements as the finite places.

            A.1. Topology of AF , AF,S and GL1 (AF ), GL1 (AF,S ), and their class groups
    In this section we review some basic notation and definitions related to the adele ring of a number field F
and the idele group GL1 (AF ). We will henceforth adopt the terminology and conventions from [CF, Ch. II].
In particular, the square of the complex Euclidean norm is an absolute value according to our conventions. Its
equivalence class contains the complex Euclidean norm. We moreover note that a place v of F is required to
be non-trivial. Proofs for assertions below are given in many references (such as [CF] and [RV]), so they are
generally not given here.

    A.1.1. The adeles AF as a topological ring. Let F be a number field. In this subsection we recall
the construction of the adele ring AF and its topological ring structure.

                             A.2. Orbital structures on adeles and ideles
    In this section, we examine adelic and idelic quotients explicitly, constructing relatively compact funda-
mental domains for the additive F -translation action of F on AF , and the multiplicative translation action of
F × on GL1 (AF )1 .
    While the topics are covered in detail within the literature (for which our main references will be [RV,
Ch. 5, §5.1], [CF, Ch. XV, §4.1, §4.3]), we will be highlighting certain structural, measure-theoretic and
topological properties of these domains, to be used later throughout this work.
    A.2.1. Fundamental domain of the additive F -translation action on AF . In light of Lemma
A.1.2.1, the diagonal image of F in AF is discrete and co-compact. We recall how to construct a fundamental
domain for the action by additive translation of F on AF , i.e. a relatively compact subset D ⊂ AF with
non-empty interior, such that F + D = AF , and (ξ + D) ∩ D = ∅ for every ξ ∈ F × .

    A.2.1.1. The adelic fundamental domain F . In this subsection we describe the compact Hausdorff quotient
AF /F by means of a fundamental domain within AF of the continuous left-translation action by F .

                                             A.3. Haar measures
    In this section we normalize Haar measures on AF , GL1 (AF ) and their S-local analogs AF,S , respectively
GL1 (AF,S ), along with certain closed subgroups.
    The following section will assume knowledge of Haar measures and the Fourier transform on a Hausdorff
locally compact abelian group and its basic properties, for which we refer the reader to §D.1.1.

    A.3.1. Tamagawa measure on AF . As an additive abelian topological group, AF is Hausdorff and
locally compact. As such, it carries a left- and right-invariant Haar measure. Since it is commutative, it is
unimodular.

    A.3.1.1. Self-duality of local additive Tamagawa measures. We now discuss calculations that identify the
local Tamagawa measures chosen in Definition A.3.1.2 on each local field Fv , for F a number field, with its
own Plancherel measure with respect to an associated choice of non-trivial additive continuous character of Fv .
    On any Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, there exists a unique Haar measure up to a nonzero
constant multiplier, a positive real number. As recalled in Lemma D.1.1.2, Pontryagin duality determines,
associated to a choice of Haar measure µG on a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G, a unique Plancherel
measure µGb on the dual group G: b the unique Haar measure on G b such that the inversion formula of (D.1.1.11)
holds as stated with no constant correcting factors.

A.3.1.2.

   Remark A.3.2.5 (On the normalizations for additive character and measure). The Tamagawa measures
on AF and GL1 (AF ) constructed in this section are the same choices of Haar measures made on AF and
GL1 (AF ) made in [CF, Ch.XV,p.313,328,334].
                                                 A.3. HAAR MEASURES                                            561


     The former is also the same choice of normalized Haar measure made in [Co, Appendix I,(34),p.57]. Its
purpose is to normalize the adelic Poisson Summation Formula, removing the volume factor (which equals 1,
under this choice of normalization; see Theorem 2.2.3.2 as well as [CF, Ch.XV,§4.2,Thm.4.2.1].
     They are special cases of general Tamagawa measures on the adelic points of algebraic groups over
a number field, for which we refer the reader to [Oes, §3.1,4] (the former corresponding to the invariant
differential on (Ga )F given by dx, and the latter to dx/x on (GL1 )F , x being the standard global parameter
on A1F ).

                A.4. Dirichlet’s S-unit Theorem: estimates by lattice point-counting
     In this section we illustrate two applications of Dirichlet’s S-unit Theorem (see Theorem A.1.5.2(2))
resting on lattice point-counting techniques that go back to Davenport’s paper on a principle of Liouville (see
[Davenport-1]). These techniques will enable us to make estimates on the growth of lattice point-counting
functions counting the number of S-units contained in certain convex polytopes, with the aim of applying
such estimates to the study of the S-local adelic θ-functions through Theorem 2.4.2.1.

            A.5. Idelic Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Theorem and Lebesgue Differentiation
     In this section we collect analogs of the Maximal Theorem on the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function
(see [Fol, Thms.3.17,3.18]) and of Lebesgue’s Differentiation Theorem (see [Fol, Thm.3.21]) for absolutely
integrable functions on idele and S-idele groups and their quotient groups of idele classes. Our main reference
is [HR-2, Ch. XI, pp. 637-672].

    A.5.1. Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Theorem on the real line. We begin by recalling the elementary
fact that for f : R → R a continuous function and every x ∈ R, we have

Theorem of Lebesgue, for which we refer the reader to [Fol, Thm.3.18] and [Fol, Thm.3.21].
    In this section we discuss a generalization of the Differentiation Theorem, to locally integrable functions
over a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group equipped with some additional structure, and with respect to
a regular Radon measure.
    A key tool to proving such analog of the Differentiation Theorem is an analog for Hausdorff locally compact
abelian groups of the Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Theorem, which will be of interest itself and used throughout

    A.5.2. D-sequences, D′ -sequences, D′′ -sequences in Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups.
We will be recording, throughout this subsection and the next, analogs of both Theorem A.5.1.1 and Theorem
A.5.1.3, when R is replaced by a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G equipped with a decreasing
sequence of Borel measurable subsets satisfying certain axioms.
    This is discussed in detail in [HR-2, Ch.XI,§44,44.50], the proofs are close in structure and technique to
those presented above for Theorem A.5.1.1 and Theorem A.5.1.3, and we will be only providing complementary
details to the arguments in loc.cit..
    We will then show that the structural assumptions on G are all satisfied by all the Hausdorff locally
compact abelian groups of interest to this work, i.e. GL1 (AF ), GL1 (AF,S ), CF , CF,S and JF,S , and closed
subgroups of norm-1 elements, for F a number field, S a finite set of places of F containing all the Archimedean
places.
    The ability to use analogs of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function for these choices of G, and the
analog of both the Maximal Theorem and Lebesgue’s Differentiation Theorem, will be instrumental for us to
make sense of certain measurable kernel functions over self-products of the above groups, along their diagonal,
and compute their integrals on such diagonals (used to compute some nuclear operator traces).
    We refer the reader to [Bris-a, Bris-b] for related techniques, aimed at computing traces of trace-class
integral operators on L2 -spaces of a large class of metric measure spaces.

    A.5.2.1. D-sequences and D′ -sequences in Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups. We begin with a
definition, introducing the additional structure on a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group for an analog of
the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function to be available, and for analogs of the Hardy-Littlewood Maximal
Theorem and Lebesgue’s Differentiation Theorem to hold.

    Definition A.5.2.1. Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. Let λ be a Haar measure on G.
Let {Uk }k≥0 be a sequence of λ-measurable subsets in G with e ∈ Uk for all k. We call {Uk }k≥0 a D-sequence
in G if {Uk }k≥0 satisfies the following conditions:
(1) (Integrability) For every integer k ≥ 0, λ(Uk ) is finite and nonzero.
(2) (Monotonicity) For every integer k ≥ 0, we have Uk+1 ⊂ Uk .
(3) (Doubling) There exists a positive real number C > 0 such that, for every integer k ≥ 0, we have:
(A.5.2.1)                                 0 < λ(Uk Uk−1 ) < C λ(Uk ).
We say a D-sequence {Uk }k≥0 is open, respectively symmetric, if and only if for each integer k ≥ 0, Uk is
open, respectively symmetric.
    We say a D-sequence {Uk }k≥0 is a D′ -sequence in G if and only if for every neighborhood V of the neutral
element in G, there exists an integer k ≥ 0 such that Uk ⊂ V .

     Remark A.5.2.2. The preceding definition can be pushed a bit further: a D′ -sequence {Uk }k≥0 is
called a D′′ -sequence in G if and only if it is a D′ -sequence and there exists a specified sequence {Vk }k≥0 of
λ-measurable subsets of G satisfying Vk Vk−1 ⊂ Uk for every integer k ≥ 0 and a positive real number C ′ > 0
such that, for every integer k ≥ 0, we have:
(A.5.2.2)                                      λ(Uk ) ≤ C ′ λ(Vk ).
One usually writes {Uk , Vk }k≥0 for the datum of a D′′ -sequence in G. We will not use this concept.

     Before we state and prove analogs of the Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Theorem and the Lebesgue Differen-
tiation Theorem, we discuss criteria for a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group to admit a D-sequence,
respectively a D′ -sequence.
570                     CHAPTER A. PREPARATIONS FROM ALGEBRAIC NUMBER THEORY


    Proposition A.5.2.3. Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, µG a choice of Haar measure
on G.
(1) If G is first countable and locally profinite, then it admits a D′′ -sequence of the form {Uk , Vk }k≥0 , with,
    for each integer k ≥ 0, Uk = Uk−1 , Vk = Uk2 , C ′ = 1, and Uk is a compact open subgroup of G.
(2) Let H ⊂ G be an open subgroup. Let {Uk }k≥0 be a sequence of subsets of H. Then {Uk }k≥0 is a
    D-sequence, respectively a D′ -sequence, for H if and only if it is so for G.
        It is open, respectively symmetric, for H if and only if it is so for G.
    Proof. (1) : By [DE, Thm. 4.1.6] and [DE, Prop. 4.1.5], G admits a unit-neighborhood base comprised
of compact open subgroups. We may assume such base to be countable. Indeed, for every countable unit-
neighborhood base B of e we may find for each U ∈ B an open, hence closed (hence compact open) subgroup
NU ⊂ U . The subset {NU : U ∈ B} is a countable unit-neighborhood base comprised of compact open
subgroups. We may extract a cofinal sequence {Uk }k≥0 from it.
    Since Uk is a subgroup for each integer k ≥ 0, we have Uk−1 = Uk and Uk Uk−1 ⊂ Uk . The sequence
{Uk }k≥0 is therefore an open symmetric D-sequence, with the choice C = 1.
    Since {Uk }k≥0 is cofinal in a neighborhood base of the neutral element in G, for any neighborhood V of
the neutral element in G there exists a large enough integer k ≥ 0 with Uk ⊂ V . The D-sequence {Uk }k≥0 is
therefore a D′ -sequence.
    (2) : Since µG |H is a Haar measure for H, for every µG -measurable subset A ⊂ G we see that A ∩ H is
µH -measurable and µH (A ∩ H) = µG (A ∩ H). In particular, if A ⊂ H then µH (A) = µG (A). This implies
that all the defining conditions on the D-sequence, respectively D′ -sequence {Uk }k≥0 for G hold for the same
sequence as a D-sequence, respectively D′ -sequence for H.                                                   □
    Remark A.5.2.4. Let G be a countable discrete abelian group. Then Uk := {e} for every integer k ≥ 0,
is an open, symmetric D-sequence, a D′ -sequence, and {Uk , Uk }k≥0 is a D′′ -sequence. Indeed, every Haar
measure λ on G is proportional to the counting measure by [DE, Prop.1.4.4], the constant of proportionality
given by c := λ({e}) ̸= 0.
    It follows that, under the above choices, λ(Uk ) = c for every k ≥ 0, and Uk+1 ⊂ Uk . The doubling
condition holds with C = 2. Since every unit-neighborhood of G contains e, {Uk }k≥0 is a D′ -sequence.
    Upon choosing Vk := Uk for every integer k ≥ 0, and C ′ = 1, then λ(Uk ) = λ(Vk ), and hence (A.5.2.2)
holds too, and {Uk , Vk }k≥0 is a D′′ -sequence.
    Lemma A.5.2.5. Let G1 , G2 be Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups, and let G := G1 × G2 be the
product topological group. Let µ1 , µ2 be Haar measures on G1 , respectively G2 . Let µ := µ1 ⊗ µ2 be the product
Haar measure on G. Let {Uk }k≥0 be a sequence of µ1 -measurable subsets in G1 , and {Uk′ }k≥0 a sequence of
µ2 -measurable subsets in G2 . If {Uk }k≥0 is a D-sequence, respectively a D′ -sequence, for G1 , and {Uk′ }k≥0 is a
D-sequence, respectively a D′ -sequence, for G2 , then {Uk × Uk′ }k≥0 is a D-sequence, respectively a D′ -sequence,
for G. For each integer k ≥ 0, if Uk and Uk′ are open, respectively symmetric, then so is Uk × Uk′ .
     Proof. Since, for any two measurable subsets B1 ⊂ G1 , B2 ⊂ G2 , we have µ(B1 × B2 ) = µ1 (B1 )µ2 (B2 ),
and since the property of being an open subset respectively a symmetric subset is stable under finite products,
all defining conditions for {Uk × Uk′ }k≥0 follow from those of {Uk }k≥0 , respectively {Uk′ }k≥0 .         □
     Proposition A.5.2.6. Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. Assume G is second-countable.
     Let H ⊂ G be a closed subgroup. Let µH be a choice of Haar measure on H, µG a choice of Haar measure
on G, and µG/H the unique Haar measure on G/H induced by the choices µG on G and µH on H as per
Theorem D.1.2.1. Assume H is discrete, and normalize µH so as to have µH ({1}) = 1. Let q : G → G/H be
the continuous quotient homomorphism.
     Assume that there exists a relatively compact Borel subset E ⊂ G whose interior is non-empty and contains
the neutral element, and such that the continuous map q|E : E → G/H is a bijection.

    Let {Uk }k≥0 be a sequence of Borel sets in G/H such that Uk+1 ⊂ Uk for every integer k ≥ 0. Then
{Uk }k≥0 is a D-sequence for G/H, respectively a D′ -sequence for G/H, if and only if

is a D-sequence, respectively a D′ -sequence, for G. If E is symmetric then {Uk }k≥0 is symmetric if and only

     Remark A.5.2.7. In light of Lemma A.5.2.10 below, if H is discrete then there exists a Borel section to
q : X → X/H. Discreteness of H is essential to ensure that such Borel section F ⊂ X (i.e. a Borel subset F
such that q|F is a continuous bijection) can be used to compute the µG/H -measure of measurable subsets A in
X/H, by computing the µG -measure of q −1 (A) ∩ F .
    Before proving the Proposition, we record here the following result from [Kech, Ch. II, §15, Thm. 15.1]
for which we need only an elementary special case:
    Theorem A.5.2.8 (Lusin-Souslin Theorem on Borel embeddings). Let X, Y be separable and completely
metrizable7 topological spaces, f : X → Y a continuous map.
    For B ⊂ X a Borel set, if f |B is injective then f (B) ⊂ Y is a Borel set.
    We only need this for the quotient map G → G/H with G a second-countable locally compact topological
abelian group and H a discrete subgroup. In such cases, we can pick a fundamental domain F ⊂ G with
µ(∂F ) = 0 (for a Haar measure µ on G) such that Int(F ) → G/H is a homeomorphism onto an open image
who complement in G/H has measure 0. In such cases. the conclusion of Theorem A.5.2.8 is clear when we
complete the σ-algebra of Borel sets (i.e., we regard all measure-0 sets as Borel sets).
     Remark A.5.2.9 (Spherical boundedness and second-countability). Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact
abelian group. As such, it is a completely regular topological space (see [Fol, Cor. 4.33]), i.e. for a point
x ∈ G and a closed subset A ⊂ G not containing x, there exists a continuous real-valued function f on G such
that f (x) = 1 and f (A) = {0}. In making this deduction, the group structure and continuity of the group
operations, is not being used.
     First countability is in fact a necessary and sufficient condition for a Hausdorff topological group to be
metrizable (i.e. the underlying topology, uniformizable in the sense of [Bou-GT, Ch. II, §4.1, Def. 1, p. 198],
see [Bou-GT, Ch. III, §3.1, Def. 1, p. 243], which is to mean that it is induced by a uniform structure, is in
fact metrizable, which is to mean it is induced by a metric); see [Birkhoff, Theorem, p. 428].
     The metric inducing the topology can be chosen to be left-invariant, and a direct construction is given in
[Struble, Lemma 1, p. 217].
     The second axiom of countability for Hausdorff locally compact topological groups G (not necessarily
abelian) is characterized by boundedness of the spheres with respect to a left-invariant metric inducing
the topology: this is [Struble, Theorem, p. 217]. Recall that a subset B ⊂ G is called bounded if for any
unit-neighborhood U , there exist finitely many g1 , . . . , gN such that g1 U ∪ . . . ∪ gN U contains B (i.e. B
is “totally bounded” with respect to the uniform structure on G; we refer the reader to [Bou-GT, Ch. II,
Exercises, §4,(7), p. 210]).
     If G is a Hausdorff locally compact second countable topological group, then there exists a family of
open subsets {Ur }r∈R>0 such that, for all real numbers r1 , r2 > 0, Ur is bounded and symmetric, and
                                                                               S
Ur1 Ur2 ⊂ Ur1 +r2 , and such that {Ur }r>0 is a unit-neighborhood base, and r>0 Ur = G. This is [Struble,
Lemma 2, p. 218].

    A.5.3. Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Theorem on Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups.
We now know that the Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups GL1 (AF ), GL1 (AF,S × O   b F,Σ −S ), GL1 (AF,S ),
                                                                                              F

their closed subgroups of norm-1 elements, their class groups CF , CF,S , JF,S , and their subgroups of norm-1
elements, admit symmetric open D′ -sequences.
    We will now show how to construct an analog, for Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups that admit
Borel D-sequences, and, at times, D′ -sequences as the need arises, of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function,
and we will be discussing analogs of the Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Theorem and Lebesgue’s Differentiation
Theorem.
    We begin with the following result from [HR-2, Ch. XI, §44]:
    Theorem A.5.3.1. Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, µG a Haar measure on G.
    Let {Uk }k≥0 be a D-sequence for G. We let F ⊂ P(G) be the collection of all subsets of G of the form
xUk , for x ∈ G and k ≥ 0 an integer. Let F′ ⊂ F be a subset.
    Let B ⊂ G be a µG -measurable subset such that:

    Remark A.5.3.2. The Theorem is [HR-2, Ch. XI, Thm. 44.11, p. 638], and it is a generalization of the
Vitali Covering Lemma (see [StSha-III, Ch. 3, §1, Lemma.1.2, p. 102]).
    We note that in [HR-2, Ch. XI, Thm.44.11, p. 638], the subset B ⊂ G, denoted by E, is not assumed to
be measurable. The notation λ(E) and λ(E · U1 ) is to mean λ∗ (E), λ∗ (E · U1 ), in the sense of [Bou-I, Ch. IV,
§1, No. 4, Def. 4, INT IV.10].
    We will now discuss some aspects of the proofs of the main results from [HR-2, Ch. XI, §44.50], resting
on [HR-2, Ch. XI, Thm. 44.13].
    We will be assuming the Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G under consideration is second countable,
which, in light of the following Lemma, leads to promoting identities and properties valid locally almost
everywhere (i.e almost everywhere within every compact subset), into assertions valid almost everywhere.
    We recall that, for a Hausdorff locally compact15 topological space X, and a measure µ on X, a subset
A ⊂ X is locally µ-negligible if and only if for every x ∈ X there exists a neighborhood U of x such that
A ∩ U is µ-negligible (see [Bou-I, Ch. IV, §5, No. 2, Def. 4, INT IV.61]).
   Lemma A.5.3.3. Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. Assume G is second countable. Let
µG be a choice of Haar measure on G.
   Let A ⊂ G be a subset. If A is locally µG -negligible, then A is µG measurable and µG -negligible.
    Proof. Let {Km }m≥0 be a countable exhaustion of G by compact subsets. Then A ∩ Km is µG -negligible
       S
and A = m≥0 (A ∩ Km ), which gives µG (A) = 0. In particular, A is µG -measurable.                    □

                                                       APPENDIX B


                      Preparations from Analytic Number Theory

     In this Appendix we collect some results from analytic number theory and cover them in the generality of
all Hecke L-functions of an arbitrary number field.
     We review classical facts on the growth of “finite” Hecke L-functions (i.e., without Γ-factors) over vertical
strips, classical zero-free regions1 for Hecke L-functions, and convergence of partial Euler products over the
1-line (i.e. the vertical line {Re(s) = 1}). We also discuss Weil’s own idelic formulation of the Explicit
Formulas, incorporating Connes’ observations on the local Fourier transform in relation to Weil’s principal
values.

                                      B.1. Convexity bound on Lf (s, χ)
       In this section we record classical facts about growth bounds for Hecke L-functions and their derivatives.

       B.1.1. Growth order of Lf (s, χ) over the critical strip. Recall that Lf (s, χ) is defined as
                                               Y
                                  Lf (s, χ) :=    (1 − χ(p)N (p)−s )−1
                                                  p⊂OF

for Re(s) > 1, where the product is indexed by the prime ideals of OF (noting that χ(p) := 0 if χ is ramified
at vp ). and is absolutely convergent for Re(s) > 1, uniformly on Re(s) ≥ 1 + ε for each ε > 0.
    The function Lf (s, χ) has a Dirichlet series expansion
                                                        X      χ(I)
                                           Lf (s, χ) =
                                                              N (I)s
                                                         0̸=I⊂OF

which is absolutely convergent for Re(s) > 1, uniformly on Re(s) ≥ 1 + ε for each ε > 0, where χ(I) := 0 if I
is not coprime to the conductor of χ.

    B.1.1.1. Phragmen-Lindelöf and convexity bound on Lf (σ + it, χ). In this subsection we record the
arguments to establish the classical polynomial growth bound on Lf (1/2 + it, χ) for arbitrary continuous
                                       B.1. CONVEXITY BOUND ON Lf (s, χ)                                      589


               cF (i.e. L(1/2 + it, χ) = Oε (|t|1/4+ε ) for every ε > 0), the bound
characters χ ∈ C
                                            Lf (1 + it, χ) = Oε (|t|ε )
for every ε > 0, and deduce the classical convexity bound Lf (s, χ) for s ∈ C[1/2,1] from the Phragmen-Lindelöf
Theorem.
     The results in this subsection can be sharpened and have been so in the existing literature (see, for
instance, [MVe, Thm. 5.1] for π = 1). We will be requiring them only in the form and strength discussed
below, which is classical and obtained by following the methods in [T2, Ch. V, §5.1].
     We recall from [T1, Ch. 9, §9.41] that for f (s) a meromorphic function on a half-plane C>a whose poles,
if any, are all contained within a horizontal vertically bounded strip within the complex s-plane, if f is of
finite order within C>a (see [T1, Ch. 9, §9.4]) then we may define the function µ(σ) for σ > a as the infimum
of the real numbers ξ ∈ R≥0 such that
                                              f (σ + it) = Oσ (|t|ξ )
as |t| → ∞. The function µ is continuous and convex downwards as a consequence of the Phragmen-Lindelöf
Theorem, as we’ll soon review. Its value is zero if f is bounded on Re(s) = σ.
     In particular, if f is an absolutely convergent Dirichlet series over C>b with b > a then µ(σ) = 0 for every
σ > b, and hence µ(b + ε) = 0 for every ε > 0 since any Dirichlet series which is absolutely convergent is also
bounded over closed half-planes of absolute convergence. It follows that we have µ(b) = 0 by continuity. We
refer the reader to [T1, Ch. 9, §9.41], where the continuity and downward convexity properties of µ(σ) are
deduced from the Phragmen-Lindelöf Theorem. Since in [T1, Ch. 9, §9.41] such properties are only proved in
the case f is holomorphic over C>0 , we include a discussion on the function µ and its properties below.

    Lemma B.1.1.1. Let a, b ∈ R be real numbers, a < b, f : C>a → C a meromorphic function. Assume:

(1) The poles of f are simple and finitely many.
(2) There exists a real number ξ > 0 such that
(B.1.1.1)                                       f (σ + it) ≪ |t|ξ
    as |t| → +∞, uniformly with respect to σ > a.

Then for every σ1 < σ2 ∈ (a, +∞) the function
(B.1.1.2)                  µ(σ) := inf{k ∈ R≥0 : f (σ + it) ≪ |t|k as |t| → ∞} < ∞
satisfies
(B.1.1.3)                                µ(σ) ≤ tµ(σ2 ) + (1 − t)µ(σ1 )
for every t ∈ [0, 1] and σ := tσ2 + (1 − t)σ1 ∈ [σ1 , σ2 ]. Moreover, µ is continuous as a function (a, +∞) → R≥0
and for all ε > 0 we have f (σ + it) = Oε,σ1 ,σ2 (|t|µ(σ)+ε ) as |t| → ∞ uniformly in σ ∈ [σ1 , σ2 ].

    Proof. Let s1 , . . . , sN be the poles of f . We consider the function
                                                      Y
(B.1.1.4)                                   g(s) :=        (s − sk )f (s)
                                                   1≤k≤N

that is a holomorphic function over C>a by assumption (1). We call µg the µ-function of g, which is defined
(and finite) by assumption (2).
    We have µg (σ) = µ(σ) + N for all σ > a. Indeed, we have µg (σ) ≤ µ(σ) + N by definition, and since
Q
  1≤k≤N (s − sk ) is nowhere vanishing for all ordinates of large enough absolute value, and bounded above
uniformly with respect to all such ordinates by a nonzero positive real number, the reverse inequality also
holds.

     B.2.1. Complements on the Mellin Transform. Recall the definition of the Hardy space H p (C<a )

     In this section we provide formulas similar to those above, when the holomorphic function Φ(s) is not in
the class H p (C<a ), but rather it satisfies certain decay properties towards infinity uniformly only on vertical
strips7 and not necessarily over the half-plane C<a . Such analogs will involve integrating over the vertical
lines bounding a fixed vertical strips.
     We will also be needing an asymptotic version of Cauchy’s Residue Theorem, valid under the same
assumptions on Φ(s) as above. The holomorphic functions Φ(s) we will be considering are Mellin transforms
of Schwartz functions on the real line whose support is contained within R>0 , which satisfy decay conditions
towards both ∞ and 0.

    B.2.1.1. Schwartz functions with exponential and semi-exponential decay. We recall that a function
ϕ : R → C is Schwartz if and only if ϕ ∈ C ∞ (R) and
                                       ||ϕ||m,N := sup (1 + |x|N ) |∂xm ϕ(x)| < ∞
                                                    x∈R

for all integers N, m ≥ 0.
       The space of all Schwartz functions on R is denoted by S(R), topologized by the family of seminorm
{|| · ||m,N }m,N ≥0 . The locally convex space S(R>0 ) of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on the real abelian Lie group

R>0 is isomorphic to S(R) under the exponential map exp : R → R>0 , with the topology generated by the
family of seminorms resulting from the exponential change of variables. Namely, for ϕ ∈ C ∞ (R>0 ) the rapid
decay condition is defined by
                                   ||ϕ||m,N := sup (1 + |log(t)|N ) |(t∂t )m ϕ(t)| < ∞
                                               t∈R>0

for all m, N ≥ 0.
     We now define a subspace of S(R>0 ) comprised of those functions that decay very rapidly towards both
∞ and 0.

    Definition B.2.1.1 (Schwartz-Bruhat functions on R>0 with (semi-)exponential decay). Let ϕ ∈ S(R>0 )
be a Schwartz-Bruhat function. Say ϕ has:
(1) forward semi-exponential decay if ϕ and its derivatives decay faster than any positive power of t−1 as
    t → +∞. We denote by SSE (R>0 ) the space of ϕ’s with foward semi-exponential decay.
        Likewise say ϕ has backward semi-exponential decay if ϕ and its derivatives decay faster than any
    positive power of t as t → 0+ . We denote by ŠSE (R>0 ) the space of ϕ’s with backward semi-exponential
    decay.
(2) exponential decay if ϕ and its derivatives decay faster than any positive power e−|log(t)| , as |log(t)| → +∞.
    We denote by SE (R>0 ) the C-linear space of Schwartz-Bruhat functions of exponential decay.

    Remark B.2.1.2. The role of applying ∂t in the preceding definition can be replaced by applying t∂t ;
the latter has the merit of being invariant and negating under inversion on t. It is elementary to check that
membership in SSE (R>0 ) is equivalent to the requirement ta ϕ ∈ S(R>0 ) for all a ≥ 0, and via the exponential
isomorphism R ≃ R>0 this corresponds to functions f ∈ S(R) such that f (j) ∈ O(e−x ) as x → +∞ for all
j ≥ 0.
    We will often abbreviate “forward exponential decay” into “exponential decay”, when no confusion is
expected to arise.8

    Remark B.2.1.3. The notion of “polynomial growth” over R>0 is defined via the usual concept for
functions on the real line upon performing the exponential change of variables t = ex : a function f : R>0 → C
has at most polynomial growth over R>0 if for every integer N ≥ 0 there exists a real number CN > 0 such
that |f (t)| ≤ CN |log(t)|N .

     Lemma B.2.1.4. Let ϕ ∈ S(R>0 ) be a Schwartz-Bruhat function. We define ϕ̌ the function on R>0
assigned by:
(B.2.1.1)                                              ϕ̌(t) := ϕ(1/t)
for t ∈ R>0 (so ϕ ∈ SE (R) if and only if ϕ̌ ∈ SE (R)),
(1) If ϕ ∈ ŠSE (R>0 ) then the extension of ϕ to R by zero for t ∈ (−∞, 0] is Schwartz over R.
(2) The involution ϕ 7→ ϕ̌ is a linear topological automorphism of S(R>0 ) respecting the linear subspace
    SE (R>0 ), and identifying SSE (R>0 ) with ŠSE (R>0 ).
(3) The extension by zero of any function in SE (R>0 ) to the real line is Schwartz.
(4) The operator t∂t on S(R>0 ) preserves SSE (R>0 ), ŠSE (R>0 ), and SE (R>0 ).

     Proof. (1) : We need to check smoothness at t = 0 of ∂tN ϕ for every integer N ≥ 0. We know that
∂tN ϕ exists and is smooth over R× . It is therefore enough to check that it is continuous at t = 0: that says
∂tN ϕ → 0 as t → 0+ for each N . For t = ex we have ∂t = e−x ∂x , so we are given that f (x) := ϕ(ex ) ∈ S(R)
and its derivatives all have decay more rapid than e−M |x| as x → −∞ for each M > 0 and we want to show

the desired decay as x → −∞ clearly holds.
     (2) and (3) follow from the definitions and from (1).
     (4) : If ϕ ∈ SSE (R>0 ) then for any real number A > 0, we have tA ϕ ∈ S(R>0 ). It follows that
(t∂t )(tA ϕ) ∈ S(R>0 ). But (t∂t )(tA ϕ) = AtA ϕ + tA (t∂t )ϕ ∈ S(R>0 ), which gives tA (t∂t )ϕ ∈ S(R>0 ). It follows
that (t∂t )ϕ has semi-exponential decay. The same assertion holds for backward semi-exponential decay (by
passing to 1/t) and exponential decay in place of semi-exponential decay.                                          □

      Corollary B.2.1.10. Let ϕ ∈ S(R>0 ) be a Schwartz-Bruhat function with exponential decay. Then:
(1) For every integer n ≥ 0, the functions M (ϕ)(n − s) and M (s + n) are entire and satisfy the inequality from
    (B.2.1.28) on each vertical strip C[a,b] . In particular, they are bounded on vertical strips of bounded width.
(2) Let f : C(a,b) → C, for a < b fixed real numbers, be a meromorphic function with finitely many poles
    contained in C(a,b) . Assume that there exist real numbers A, B > 0 such that for a < σ < b we have
(B.2.1.39)                                      |f (σ + iy)| ≤ A|y|B
      for all |y| ≫ 0 (largeness uniform in such σ). Then for every integer n ≥ 1, the meromorphic functions
      f (s)M (ϕ)(s + n) and f (s)M (ϕ)(−s + n) satisfy the inequality from (B.2.1.26) for all large enough |y| > 0.
    Proof. (1) : We have M (ϕ)(−s) = M (ϕ̌)(s), and since ϕ is Schwartz with exponential decay, so is ϕ̌.
Proposition B.2.1.9(1) and (2) therefore apply and gives (1) for n = 0.
    We have M (ϕ)(s + n) = M (tn ϕ)(s), and since ϕ is Schwartz with exponential decay, so is tn ϕ for every
integer n ∈ Z. We may therefore assume n = 0 and the foregoing applies.
    (2) : By (1) and (B.2.1.26), the inequality in (B.2.1.27) holds for f (s)Φ(s) so long as (B.2.1.39) does, and
hence both hold for all large enough |y| ≫ 0.                                                                   □
    B.2.2. Asymptotic Cauchy Integral Formula. We begin by studying the Cauchy Integral Formula
applied to the special case of holomorphic functions Φ over an open bounded vertical strip such that Φ(s)
decays rapidly as |s| → ∞ uniformly on the vertical strip.

    B.2.2.1. Cauchy Integrals. We introduce a class of holomorphic functions that comprises the Mellin
transforms of all Schwartz functions with exponential decay.
    Definition B.2.2.1. Let a < b be real numbers. Let Φ : C(a,b) → C be a holomorphic function. We say
that Φ is uniformly Schwartz over the vertical strip C(a,b) if and only if for every ε > 0 such that a + ε < b − ε,
and for every integer N ≥ 1, there exists a real number CN,ε > 0 such that for all sufficiently large |y|
uniformly over all a + ε ≤ σ ≤ b − ε we have
                                                              CN,ε
(B.2.2.1)                                     |Φ(σ + iy)| ≤
                                                               |y|N
(so in particular Φ is bounded on each C(a+ε,b−ε) ).
     If Φ is entire, we say it is Schwartz on vertical strips if and only if for every bounded open interval
(a, b) ⊂ R it is uniformly Schwartz over the vertical strip C(a,b) . If Φ : C<b → C is holomorphic, we say it is
Schwartz on the half-plane C<b if and only if for every ε > 0 and for every integer N ≥ 1, Φ(σ + iy) satisfies
condition (B.2.2.1) for all large enough |y| uniformly over all σ ≤ b − ε.
     The “justification” of this terminology is that by Lemma D.3.1.1 each of the derivatives ∂yj (Φ(σ + iy)
satisfy the same uniform decay estimates as |y| → ∞ when σ varies in a compact interval. In other words, the
Schwartz decay properties along each vertical line have uniform constants and uniform largeness conditions on
|y| as σ varies in a compact interval.
    Example B.2.2.2. If ϕ ∈ S(R>0 ) is a Schwartz-Bruhat with exponential decay, then Φ := M (ϕ) is
Schwartz on vertical strips by Proposition B.2.1.9(2). Indeed, for any non-empty vertical strip of the form
C(a,b) , we may any real number ε > 0 and let CN,ε := CN,a−ε,b+ε . By Proposition B.2.1.9(2), the condition in
(B.2.2.1) is satisfied by the restriction of Φ to C(a,b) .
                                   B.2. ASYMPTOTIC CAUCHY INTEGRAL FORMULA                                             601


   By Proposition B.2.1.5(1,2), Schwartz-Bruhat functions ϕ of exponential or semi-exponential decay over
R>0 provide examples of holomorphic functions Φ(s) := M (ϕ)(s) on either C, C>0 or C<0 that are uniformly
Schwartz over the open vertical strips of bounded width contained within such domains in C.

    We record here the following general estimate for the Mellin transform of smooth functions on R>0 that
are Schwartz-Bruhat, but neither exponentially nor semi-exponentially decaying. It is a uniform version of the
Riemann-Lebesgue Lemma, and provides examples of holomorphic functions over a vertical strip C(a,b) of
bounded width that are uniformly Schwartz on all open vertical sub-strips.

    The function f (u) = −∞ Φ(ix)e−ixu dx is Schwartz since Φ is Schwartz on vertical lines, and it is in

decay. The entire functions Φ such that (B.2.1.27) holds with a constant CN,a,b which does not depend on a, b,

Schwartz decay property across the entirety of the strips a + ε ≤ σ ≤ b − ε for all sufficiently small ε > 0. We
only need the uniform vertical Schwartz decay “near” the vertical edges σ = a, b and a sufficient supply of
horizontal segments arbitrarily high up and low down on which there is such decay:

                                    B.3. Asymptotic Residue Theorem
    In this section we discuss a consequence of Cauchy’s Residue Theorem under a Schwartz condition uniform
on upper and lower halves of a vertical strip, combined with a condition on the distribution of the poles of the
meromorphic function across the vertical strip.

     B.3.1. Slow growth near the poles. We discuss a growth condition for meromorphic functions on
vertical strips, near their poles, to identify a class of such functions that, when multiplied by an entire function
that is Schwartz on vertical strips, decays on bounded horizontal segments whose ordinate tends to ±∞.

    B.3.1.1. Polar locations and vertical growth. We introduce a condition on the location of the poles of a
meromorphic function f in a vertical strip that will combine correctly with the Schwartz condition uniformly
on vertical strips introduced in Definition B.2.2.1 for a holomorphic function Φ, leading to an asymptotic
version of Cauchy’s Residue Theorem for Φ(s)f (s).

    Definition B.3.1.1. Let a < b be real numbers. Let f : C(a,b) → C be a meromorphic function. We say
that f has slow growth near its poles if and only if:
(1) there exists a real number α > 0 such that for each integer k there exists a real number Tk , satisfying the
    following properties:
    (a) |T±(k+1) | ≥ |T±k |.
    (b) lim|k|→+∞ |Tk | = +∞.
    (c) Tk = O(|k|α ) as |k| → +∞.
    and f is holomorphic over a small enough horizontal strip containing the horizontal line R + iTk in its
    interior,
(2) there exists a real number β > 0 and a real number Aa,b,β > 0, neither depending on σ, such that for
    every integer k ∈ Z and a < σ < b,
(B.3.1.1)                                    |f (σ + iTk )| ≤ Aa,b |k|β ,
(3) there exist real numbers ε1 , ε2 > 0 such that 0 < ε1 < ε2 < (b − a)/2 and such that f (a + ε1 + it) and
    f (b − ε2 + it) are continuous functions of t ∈ R growing at most polynomially as |t| → +∞. In particular,
    no pole of f is contained within the vertical lines a + ε1 + iR and b − ε2 + iR.
We refer to the sequence {Tk }k∈Z as a sequence that witnesses the slow growth of f near its poles.

    We now show that if f : C(a,b) → C is meromorphic and with slow growth near its poles, and if
Φ : C(a−ε,b+ε) → C is holomorphic and uniformly Schwartz on the vertical strip C(a−ε,b+ε) for some ε > 0
then line integrals of Φ(s)f (s) over horizontal segments contained within C(a,b) vanish asymptotically along
the ordinates {Tk }k∈Z as |k| → ∞.

     Lemma B.3.1.2. Let a < b be real numbers, f : C(a,b) → C a meromorphic function with slow growth near
its poles within C(a,b) . Let ε > 0 be a real number and Φ : C(a−ε,b+ε) → C a holomorphic function, uniformly
Schwartz over the vertical strip C(a−ε,b+ε) . Then for {Tk }k∈Z,|k|≥2 ⊂ R witnessing the slow growth condition

    B.3.2. The Asymptotic Residue Theorem. We now discuss a consequence of Cauchy’s Residue

                                     B.4. Explicit Formulas for Hecke L-functions
    In this section we review for ease of access the explicit formulas for Hecke L-functions proved by Weil in
[Weil-b]. Barner’s generalization in [Bar, §2] has the advantage of identifying a class of functions on which
the functionals arising in the explicit formulas and corresponding to the Archimedean places attain a simpler
form.
    The main references for this section are Lang’s book [Lang-b, Ch. XVII], where the explicit formulas are
reproved under conditions that mildly generalize Barner’s in [Bar, §2].
    Occasional reference is also made to Lang’s book [Lang-a, Ch. X], an earlier edition to [Lang-b] (where
the arguments in Weil’s original article [Weil-b] are presented and, specifically, the continuity properties of
the functionals arising in the explicit formulas for Hecke L-functions are proved).

    B.4.1. Complements on Poisson Summation and Cauchy Integrals. In this subsection we will be
proving identities between values of Dirac combs on piece-wise smooth functions on the positive real half-line
with isolated jump singularities, by means of Poisson Summation and contour integration of their Mellin
transform.
                                B.4. EXPLICIT FORMULAS FOR HECKE L-FUNCTIONS                                        607




     B.4.1.1. Slow decay in the presence of isolated jump singularities. In this subsection we recall basic
properties of the Mellin transform of smooth functions supported over the positive reals and decaying rapidly
at zero and infinity, and we recall the Poisson Summation Formula over R>0 and its quotients by the discrete
subgroups θZ , for θ ∈ R>0 − {1}.
     Let θ ∈ R>0 − {1}. A continuous character χ : θZ → U(1) is of the form χ(θm ) = θimx for some x ∈ R.
The imaginary number ix is uniquely determined modulo the discrete group 2πiZ/log(θ). We will refer to a
choice of ix as log χ(θ), and all constructions and assertions made throughout this section involving log χ(θ)
will, a priori, depend on such choice.
     For a function ϕ : R → C, we say ϕ is piece-wise smooth if and only if there is a discrete subset Σ ⊂ R
such that ϕ is smooth on R − Σ and all ϕ(j) ’s have both one-sided limits at each x ∈ Σ. We refer the reader to
[Fol-2, Ch. 2, §2.2, p. 32] for more on piece-wise smooth functions on the real line. A function ϕ : R>0 → C is
called piece-wise smooth if and only if ϕ(ex ) is piece-wise smooth as a function of x ∈ R.
     We begin with the following:

    Lemma B.4.1.1 (Slow decay in the presence of isolated jump singularities). Let ϕ : R>0 → C be a function.

    B.4.1.2. Cauchy Integrals of Φ(s)L′v (χ, s)/Lv (χ, s) and weighted Dirac combs. We give preparations on
using the Asymptotic Residue Theorem to compute line integrals of Φ(s)L′v (χ, s)/Lv (χ, s) with v a finite
place of a number field F . In what follows we write Lf (s, χ) for the finite Hecke L-function of a continuous
(unitary) character χ ∈ CcF , and Φ for the entire Mellin transform of a choice of Schwartz function on R>0
with exponential decay (Definition B.2.1.1(2)).
    For F a number field, χ ∈ C cF a continuous character, and σ ∈ R a real number, the formal sum of Dirac
measures
                                               X
(B.4.1.18)                            Dχ,p :=       χ(pm )N (p)mσ δN (p)m
                                                        m>0

will be referred to as the local Dirac comb at the maximal ideal p ⊂ OF , assuming χ is unramified at p.
     The formal sum Dχ,p consists of terms in the topological dual space S(R)′ (called “tempered distributions”)
of the locally convex Schwartz space S(R), and it makes sense as an element of S(R)′ too: if f ∈ S(R) satisfies
                               B.4. EXPLICIT FORMULAS FOR HECKE L-FUNCTIONS                                    611


|f (x)| ≤ A|x|−(σ+2) for |x| ≥ 1 then
                             X                             X                  A
                                 N (p)mσ |f (N (p)m )| ≤ A   N (p)−2 =               ,
                              m>0
                                                                          N (p)2 − 1
                                                          m≥1
                                                   σ+2
so for any ε > 0 if we require |f (x)| ≤ B/(1 + |x| ) for all x ∈ R and sufficiently small B (depending on ε
and N (p)) then |Dχ,p (f )| < ε. The sum Dχ,p therefore converges for the weak topology σ(S(R)′ , S(R)) on
S(R)′ since it converges pointwise.

     Remark B.4.1.6. Although not needed for our purposes, the sum Dχ,p even converges for the strong-dual
topology of uniform convergence on bounded subsets of S(R) in the sense of topological vector spaces (not to
be confused with metric-boundedness; see §C.2.1–§C.2.2 for a discussion of topologies on topological duals of
Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces).
     To prove the convergence in the strong-dual topology S(R)′β , we first note that S(R) is complete and
barreled (as is any Fréchet space [Scha, Ch. II, 7.1]) and its closed bounded subsets (in the sense of topological
vector spaces) are compact by Lemma D.1.3.7(3). For any barreled Hausdorff locally convex topological vector
space E, a sequence {φn } in E ′ that is pointwise convergent (i.e., {φn (x)} is convergent in C for all x ∈ E) is
pointwise bounded, which is to say it is bounded for the weak topology σ(E ′ , E). Thus, by [Scha, Ch. IV, 4.6]
the pointwise limit φ : E → C belongs to E ′ and φn → φ uniformly on all precompact subsets of E. Since
bounded subsets have bounded closure [Scha, Ch. I, 5.1], if all closed bounded subsets of E are compact (such
as for E = S(R)) then φn → φ uniformly on bounded subsets; i.e., φn → φ in Eβ(E      ′
                                                                                        ′ ,E) .

    B.4.3. Fourier transform of log| · |v . Let F be a number field, v a fixed place of F .

                                  B.5. Recurrence and equidistribution
    In this section we record a proof of a uniform version of the Kronecker-Weyl Theorem, and prove, as an
application required in Chapter ?? of this work, the strong recurrence on vertical strips of the reciprocal Euler
factors of Hecke L-functions. We will be discussing the concept of recurrence for holomorphic functions on
vertical strips, and basic permanence properties as the need arises.

    B.5.1. Preparations. This section is devoted to reviewing the small amount of ergodic theory required,
providing some complements with a view towards the intended applications. Most of the results herein are
well-known or direct consequences of well-known mathematics, and can be found in the referred literature.
We include the arguments here for completeness, ease of access, and to discuss minor variations needed for
applicability.
    We will not be requiring the general Ergodic Theorem of Birkhoff-Khinchin (see, for instance, [CFSS,
Ch.1,§2,Thm.1]), nor theory and lexicon from ergodic theory. We will be very briefly pointing out to the
reader how the results discussed below fit within terminology and principles of ergodic theory. Each will be an
incarnation of the classical Kronecker-Weyl Theorem, expressing the unique ergodicity of certain linear flows
on tori.
    Main references for the results and respective preparations throughout this section are [HK, Part
1,Ch.4,§4.1,4.2] (focusing on the one and two-dimensional cases only), and the unpublished [Hu1, §4.3] and
[Hu2, Appendix A], for proofs of the finite-dimensional continuous and discrete versions, respectively, of the
classical Kronecker-Weyl Theorem.
    We denote by
                                                   T := R/Z
the additive compact Hausdorff topological group of the unit circle. For any integer N ≥ 1, we write [N ] for
the ordered subset

Theorem B.5.2.1. In this case, γ N is a one-parameter subgroup of the torus TN , and it induces a continuous
flow on TN by left-translation with dense image.


    B.5.2. Kronecker-Weyl. The following Theorem is the multi-dimensional version of [HK, Part 1,
Thm.4.1.15] and its method of proof is analogous to the argument [HK, Part 1, §4.1.6]. We will only be
requiring the case when (τ1 , . . . , τN ) ∈ RN has Q-independent coordinates. A full proof in the general case
when the vector (τ1 , . . . , τN ) ∈ RN in the statement has not necessarily Q-independent coordinates can be
found in the appendix of [Hu1, §4.3, Proof of Lemma 4.3], and we will be following it closely to establish the
case of continuous functions.

    B.5.2.1. The classical Kronecker-Weyl Theorem. For any integer N ≥ 1, we say a function u : TN → C is
Riemann-integrable if and only if the composition u ◦ θ : [0, 1)N → C is a function whose real and imaginary
parts are both Riemann-integrable on the half-open cube [0, 1)N in the standard sense of Riemann-integrability
on convex subsets within Euclidean spaces.
    We denote by µN the volume-1 Haar measure on TN , and recall that µN agrees under θN with the
measure induced by restriction to [0, 1)N of the Lebesgue measure λN on RN , i.e.
                                             µN = (θN )∗ (λN |[0,1)N )
since [0, 1)N is a fundamental domain for the continuous action by left-translations of the closed discrete
subgroup ZN ⊂ RN .

    Theorem B.5.2.1 (Kronecker-Weyl). Let τ := (τ1 , . . . , τN ) ∈ RN be a vector. Let 0 ≤ d ≤ N be the
dimension of the Q-linear subspace generated within R by the coordinates of τ .
    Then

    Proof of Theorem B.5.2.1. (1) : The case N = 1 is easy, so assume N > 1. We start off by discussing
the special case in which the coordinates of τ are Q-linearly independent.

                                                  (t − t′ ) · τ ∈ ZN
gives a Q-linear dependence relation among the N coordinates of τ since N > 1, a contradiction. Thus, γ is
injective.

such it is contained in the kernel a non-trivial character χ : TN → T if the dimension of G is less than N . But
                     Q a

dependence relation on the coordinates of τ , contradicting the assumption. We deduce that we have G = TN .
     In the general case, let G be the closure of the image of γ. This is a closed connected subgroup of TN ,

     B.5.3. Strong recurrence of non-Archimedean Euler factors. We begin by recalling basic concepts
on self-approximation properties of holomorphic and meromorphic functions on an open non-empty vertical
strip in C.

     We recall that the notion of (strong) “recurrence” for a holomorphic function on a vertical strip CI , for

§1.4] (respectively [Ba1, Ch. 2, §2.3]).

    B.5.3.3. Preparations on recurrence. We begin with a few permanence properties of strong recurrence for

    Lemma B.5.3.4. Let I ⊂ R be an open non-empty bounded interval, and f : CI → C a holomorphic
function.
(1) If f is strongly recurrent on the compact subset K ⊂ CI then it is strongly recurrent on any compact
    subset K ′ ⊂ K.
(2) If f is strongly recurrent on any closed disc contained within CI then it is strongly recurrent on any
    compact subset contained within CI .
    Proof. We prove (1). If, for every ε > 0, the set XK (ε) ⊂ R has positive upper-density, then so does
XK ′ (ε), since XK (ε) ⊂ XK ′ (ε). This proves (1).

K.                                                                                                           □

is itself analytic, and U is one of its level sets. Note that since ε > 0, U does not contain (tv )v∈S = 0, and
hence this function is analytic and nonzero, thus exhibiting U as an analytic subset of G.
     Since θS is itself analytic (i.e. its coordinate functions are complex-valued real-analytic functions) then
the pre-image of U in RS under θS is a real-analytic subset of RS , and its intersection with [0, 1)S therefore
has Lebesgue measure zero by [Mit, Prop. 1]. Its image under the smooth composition of θS followed by the
real-analytic diffeomorphism Td → G therefore has µG -measure zero.                                            □

                         B.6. Classical zero-free regions for Hecke L-functions
     In this section, we recall well known results on the existence of classical zero-free regions for general Hecke
L-functions of arbitrary number fields, and discuss estimates on the polynomial growth of the finite L-function,
its holomorphic derivatives of any order on vertical strips of bounded width, and of its reciprocal on the 1-line.


    B.6.1. Zero-free regions for Hecke L-functions and estimates on L′f (s, χ)/Lf (s, χ). We record
here analogs of the main results on zero-free regions for the Riemann ζ-function, and estimates for ζ ′ (s)/ζ(s)
on the 1-line, adapted to the case of finite Hecke L-functions.

   B.6.1.1. Classical zero-free region for Lf (s, χ). We recall the statement of the following well-known result,
whose proof goes back to the argument of Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin:

    Proposition B.6.1.1 (Classical zero-free region for Lf (s, χ)). Let F be a number field, χ ∈ C    cF a
continuous character. There exists an absolute constant A > 0, and a real number AF,χ > 0 depending only on
F and χ, such that Lf (s, χ) has no complex zeros in the region:
                                                             A
(B.6.1.1)                              σ ≥1−
                                                [F : Q]4 log(AF,χ (|t| + 3))
and if Lf (σ, χ) = 0 for some σ ∈ [1/2, 1] then χ is quadratic and σ is unique, simple, and satisfies σ < 1.

    The real number AF,χ can in fact be chosen to be |N (dF/Q )||NF/Q (fχ )| where fχ is the conductor of χ
[IK, Ch. 5, §5.1, (5.4)]. Proposition B.6.1.1 can be deduced from [IK, §5.4, Thm. 5.10, p. 106] upon setting
d = [F : Q], AF,χ := q(f, 0) in the notation of loc.cit. to denote the analytic conductor of the L-function (see
[IK, Ch. 5, (5.7), p. 95]), and noting that the Rankin-Selberg convolutions Lf (s, χ ⊗ χ) and Lf (s, χ ⊗ χ) both
exist with the former entire when χ ̸= χ (equivalently, when χ2 =   ̸ 1) since Lf (s, χ2 ) is entire when χ is not
quadratic, and the latter is ζF (s) (so it has a simple pole at s = 1).

                        B.7. Reciprocals and Partial Euler products on the 1-line
    Let F be a number field, χ ∈ C cF a continuous character. In this section we will be establishing a precise
estimate to the reciprocal partial Euler products for the finite Hecke L-function Lf (s, χ), on the vertical line
Re(s) = 1.

    B.7.1. The Dirichlet polynomials of L′f (s, χ)/Lf (s, χ) on the 1-line. Leading to the analysis of
partial Euler products and their reciprocals, for Lf (s, χ), we need to study the Dirichlet polynomials of the
Dirichlet series that sums to L′f (s, χ)/Lf (s, χ).

    Remark B.7.2.7. For χ ∈ C     cF of the form χ = | · |−it0 for t0 ∈ R, the reciprocal partial Euler products
                                                          F
Ef,x (s, χ) converge to 1/Lf (s, χ) pointwise over 1 + iR, and locally uniformly on 1 + i(R − {t0 }).
    The convergence over any interval containing t0 in its interior is not uniform. Indeed, the partial products
indexed by the integers x ≤ n ≤ N contributing in the limit to e−Gx (t) oscillate too much and can only be
kept bounded by a uniform constant when t is kept within (t0 − A, t0 + A) as A decreases towards zero at
least as fast as 1/log(N ).
