                             C.1. Locally convex topological vector spaces
    Throughout this first section we provide initial guidance through the vast literature on locally convex
topological vector spaces, highlighting the concepts and results that will be used throughout this work,
indicating where to find them, and introducing the conventions that will be regularly in force. Later
sections give an overview of more advanced notions, such as topologies on duals and tensor products,
nuclearity (of spaces and of linear maps), integration valued in locally convex spaces satisfying a completeness
condition (this goes far beyond the more familiar Banach case, and is a generality we require crucially), and
holomorphicity/meromorphicity for functions valued in suitable locally convex spaces.
    Fourier theory for tempered distributions on Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups G, and topological
properties of the Schwartz-Bruhat space S(G) as a locally convex topological vector space, will be a primary
focus (with a view towards the intended applications) in Appendix D building upon the present Appendix.
     C.1.1. References on basic concepts. A vector space E is a topological vector space if and only if it
is a topological space over a topological field, and the operations defining the linear structure are continuous.
The notation tvs is an abbreviation for topological vector space. The class of topological vector spaces we will
be working with is that of locally convex topological vector spaces over C.
     We recall the basic terminology below, in the form of a roadmap to the literature, to facilitate the reader’s
access to it. The references [Bou-TVS, Ch. I], [Scha, Ch. I], [Jar, Ch. 2], [Kothe-I, Ch. 3, §15], and [NB,
Ch. 4] provide basic general background on topological vector spaces over C. Similar and simpler concepts for
topological R-vector spaces can be found in [Bou-TVS, Ch. II], and indication of how to adapt the results
there to the case of C-vector spaces is given in [Bou-TVS, Ch. II, §8].
     Here are some basic concepts to keep in mind for a tvs E over C and a subset C ⊂ E:
(1) We say C is convex if for all x, y ∈ C, the line segment {t x + (1 − t)y : t ∈ [0, 1]} joining x and y is
    contained in C. See [Scha, Ch. II, §1] for basic stability properties of convex subsets.
         The intersection of all convex subsets of E containing a subset A ⊂ E is called the convex hull of A.
    We will denote it Ch(A). A direct description of Ch(A) is as the set of all finite R-linear combinations
    P                                                                                          P
       k≥1 λk xk of elements xk of A, subject to the constraint that λk ≥ 0 for every k and      k≥1 λk = 1.
(2) We say C is circled if λC ⊂ C for all λ in the closed unit disc D ⊂ C. The smallest circled subset of E
    containing a subset A ⊂ E is called the circled hull of A, denoted ch(A).
(3) We say C is absolutely convex if it is both convex and circled. This is a way to define the concept of a
    “disc” (or “ball”) in a C-vector space without having a normed structure: the absolutely convex subsets
    are regarded as the “discs” in E.
         The absolutely convex hull, also called the convex circled hull, of a subset A ⊂ E is the convex hull of
    the circled hull; it is denoted cch(A) (in [Scha, p. 39] and [Kothe-I, p. 173] it is denoted Γ(A)). We use
    the terminology “convex circled” rather than “absolutely convex”.
         We refer the reader to [NB, Def. 4.2.7, Thm. 4.2.8] for a simple criterion for C to be its own convex
    circled hull in E; see also [Jar, §6.1, Prop. 1] (for r = 1) and [NB, Thm. 4.2.11].
(4) We say C is absorbing if for every x ∈ E there exists ε > 0 such that for all λ ∈ C with |λ| ≤ ε, λx ∈ C.
    In other words, each point of E is carried into C (“absorbed” by C) by all sufficiently small scaling factors.
    Absorbing subsets are also called radial (see [Scha, p. 11] and [NB, Def.4.1.2(b)]).
    Remark C.1.1.1. In some references the concept of circled subset is referred to as “balanced” (e.g., see
[Tre, Def. 3.2] and [NB, Def. 4.1.2(a)]), and the term “circled” is sometimes reserved for those subsets C of a
topological C-vector space E such that λC ⊂ C for λ ∈ C with |λ| = 1 (i.e., C is preserved under “rotations”).
We will avoid this latter concept altogether; “circled” and “balanced” are synonymous for us.
    A topological vector space E is called locally convex if it has a neighborhood base at 0 consisting of convex
subsets. Due to the linear structure being continuous in a topological vector space, every point x of E then
658            CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


has a neighborhood base given by x-translates of convex circled subsets. We further refer the reader to [Scha,
Ch. I, §1 §6; Ch. II, §1, §4] for the basic generalities on the construction of linear topologies and locally convex
topologies.

    C.1.1.1. Basic constructions. For a subset A ⊂ E of a topological vector space, we can form closures of
the hulls discussed in the foregoing. These are:
(1) the closure Ch(A) of the convex hull of A, called the closed convex hull;
(2) the closure ch(A) of the circled hull of A, called the closed circled hull;
(3) the closure cch(A) of the convex circled hull of A, called the closed convex circled hull.
    Remark C.1.1.2. The closure of a circled hull and the circled hull of a closure are not interchangeable.
An example over R is the hyperbola A = {xy = 1} ⊂ R2 as noted just after the proof of [Jar, §2.2, Prop. 1]
(the circled hull ch(A) = ch(A) is the region {0 < xy ≤ 1} ∪ {(0, 0)}, and its closure is {0 ≤ xy ≤ 1}).
     C.1.2. On the topology of locally convex topological vector spaces. We recall some basic facts
about the topology of a topological C-vector space, then specializing to the locally convex case. Every
topological vector space E has a neighborhood base at 0 consisting of closed circled subsets, as well as open
circled subsets (since int(A) is circled when A is). Via convex hull, these can be taken to be convex too when E
is locally convex [Scha, Ch. I, Cor. to 1.3]. The convexity assumption on the members of a neighborhood base
of 0 is what distinguishes locally convex topological vector spaces from arbitrary topological vector spaces.
    Remark C.1.2.1. A useful structure with which any tvs is endowed (but we won’t need) is that of a
canonical uniformity. We refer to [Bou-GT, Ch. II, §1.1, Def. 1] for the definition of uniform structure and the
topology associated to such a structure, and [Scha, Ch. I, 1.4] for relating the topology on a topological vector
space to a unique translation-invariant uniform structure. We further refer the reader to [Kothe-I, Ch. 1, §5],
[Bou-TVS, Ch. I, §1.4] for more on uniform structures and the canonical uniformity of a topological vector
space. For our purposes, the concept of uniformity can be avoided since (as we shall discuss) completion for
Hausdorff topological vector spaces can be made using Cauchy nets rather than going through the theory of
completion for uniform spaces.
    C.1.2.1. Local convexity and fundamental families of continuous seminorms. An equivalent way to describe
the topology on locally convex topological vector spaces is through continuous seminorms (as developed in
[Scha, Ch. II, §1, §4], [Bou-TVS, Ch. II, §1, §4], [NB, Ch. 5]).
    The linear span of every absorbing convex circled subset A ⊂ E is equipped with a real-valued function
(C.1.2.1)                                    pA (x) :=      inf       λ
                                                         x∈λA,λ∈R>0

called its Minkowski functional (or gauge functional). Under the above assumptions on A, pA is a seminorm
[Scha, Ch. II, 1.4]. The Minkowski functional can be used to translate the datum of a neighborhood base at 0
of open, or closed, circled convex subsets into a family of seminorms, and conversely [Scha, Ch. II, 1.5-1.6, §4].
For instance, continuity of a seminorm p is equivalent to {p < 1} being a neighborhood of 0.
     Given a collection of seminorms {pi } on E, if we define
                                            Ui := {x ∈ E : pi (x) ≤ 1}
then the collection of subsets {n−1 U } as n varies over all the positive integers and U varies over all finite
intersections Ui1 ∩ · · · ∩ Uim is a neighborhood base at 0 for a unique locally convex topology, and every locally
convex topology on E arises in this way. The topology is Hausdorff exactly when the only x ∈ E such that
pi (x) = 0 for all i ∈ I is x = 0; we then say {pi }i∈I is separating.
    C.1.3. Convergence and completeness. A Hausdorff topological vector space E is metrizable if and
only if it has a countable base of 0-neighborhoods, in which case there is a translation-invariant metric [Scha,
                              C.1. LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES                                        659


Ch. I, 6.1] (this provides a pseudo-norm | · | : E → R≥0 such that the metric d(x, y) = |x − y| induces the
topology). However, examples of much importance in number theory and in this work are non-metrizable,
such as Schwartz spaces of non-archimedean local fields and Schwartz spaces of adele rings and of idele class
groups of number fields. Nonetheless, even in the absence of a metric, there are good notions of completion
and completeness as we shall now discuss.
    In [Bou-GT, Ch. II, §3.3, Def. 3], the notion of completeness (for uniform spaces) is defined through
the convergence of Cauchy filters. For the concept of filter and its use to define convergence in topological
spaces, we refer to [Bou-GT, Ch. I, 6, 7]. We will use nets instead of filters (to be discussed below). For the
correspondence between nets and filters (and their equivalent encoding of convergence) we refer the interested
reader to [Sm] and to [Cl, §6] (where the results of [Sm], building on work of Bartle in [Ba], are further
spelled out and the two convergence concepts are related in [Cl, §6. Thm. 6.4]), and to [NB, Ch. 1, §1.1.2],
with emphasis on [NB, Thms. 1.1.8, 1.1.9].

    Definition C.1.3.1. Let E be a topological vector space.
(1) A net in E is a map f : J → E from a directed set J (also denoted {fj }j∈J ).
(2) A net f : J → E converges in E if there exists x ∈ E such that for every 0-neighborhood U ⊂ E there
    exists j0 so that x − fj ∈ U for all j ≥ j0 (this x is unique when E is Hausdorff).
(3) A net {fj }j∈J in E is called Cauchy if and only if for every 0-neighborhood U ⊂ E there exists a j0 ∈ J
    such that for all j, j ′ ≥ j0 we have fj − fj ′ ∈ U . Two Cauchy nets {xj }j∈J and {yj ′ }j ′ ∈J ′ in E are
    equivalent if and only if the net {xj − yj ′ }(j,j ′ )∈J×J ′ converges to 0; equivalently, for every 0-neighborhood
    U ⊂ E there exist j0 ∈ J and j0′ ∈ J ′ such that xj − yj ′ ∈ U for all j ≥ j0 , j ′ ≥ j0′ (this is clearly an
    equivalence relation).
(4) A subset A ⊂ E is called complete when it is Hausdorff and every Cauchy net in E valued in A converges
    in A.
(5) The topological vector space E is called Fréchet when it is locally convex, complete, and metrizable.

     In the metrizable case, completeness in the classical sense of Cauchy sequences guarantees completeness
in the broader sense of nets because there is a countable base of 0-neighborhoods. Indeed, if {xj }j∈J is a
Cauchy net in a metrizable E, say with | · | : E → R≥0 a pseudo-norm for which the metric |x − y| induces
the topology [Scha, Ch. I, 6.1], then for all n ≥ 1 there exists jn ∈ J with |xj − xj ′ | < 1/n for all j, j ′ ≥ jn .
We can arrange that jn+1 ≥ jn for all n, so {yn := xjn } is a Cauchy sequence in E such that |xj − yn | < 1/n
for all j ≥ jn . Thus, if the limit ℓ := limn→∞ yn ∈ E exists then we see that xj → ℓ.
     For any Hausdorff topological vector space E, there is an initial object (E,
                                                                               b i) among complete Hausdorff
topological vector spaces equipped with a continuous linear map from E, with the canonical map i : E → E        ba
topological embedding (in particular, injective) and a base of closed 0-neighborhoods in E given by closures in
                                                                                           b
Eb of 0-neighborhoods in E. We call (E,    b i) the completion of E. The construction of completion for metric
spaces via equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences can be adapted to Cauchy nets to build (E, b i), as is done in
[?]. The universal mapping property, topological embedding property of i, and 0-neighborhood base description
in Eb are all seen from that construction.

     Remark C.1.3.2. The main technical difficulty in the construction (in contrast with the metric setting) is
that the directed set J can vary a lot (especially when it is uncountable); e.g., in the definition of Cauchy net
{fj }j∈J there is no constraint on the cardinality of J and so there is no “set of all nets valued in E”. But all
we need is a set of all equivalence classes of nets valued of E, and this does exist because we claim every net
f : J → E is equivalent to a net x : J ′ → E where J ′ has cardinality bounded in term of E.
     Such set-theoretic control is not addressed in [?], and it can be handled as follows. For each j ∈ J, let
Fj ⊂ E be the subset of points fi for all i ≥ j; this throws away the indexing information on points provided
by f : J → E. Each Fj is a non-empty subset of E and any two contain a third, so the set F of subsets
660            CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


Fj ⊂ E is directed by reverse inclusion; beware that a containment Fj ⊂ Fj ′ (and even an equality) does not
imply j, j ′ ∈ J are comparable (nor equal when Fj = Fj ′ ). The Cauchy hypothesis implies that for every
0-neighborhood U ⊂ E there exists F ∈ F so that any two points in F have difference contained in U . Thus,
if we define a net x : F → E by letting xF ∈ F be a choice of point for each F ∈ F then {xF }F ∈F is Cauchy
and equivalent to the given Cauchy net {fj }j∈J : for a choice of 0-neighborhood U ⊂ E there exists j0 ∈ J so
that fj − fj ′ ∈ U for all j, j ′ ≥ j0 , so if F0 := Fj0 then xF − fj ∈ U for all F ⊂ F0 and all j ≥ j0 . Since F
has cardinality bounded by that of the power set of E, we have the desired set-theoretic control.
     In most other references (e.g., [Tre, Ch. 5]), arguments based on Cauchy filters are used to construct E.
                                                                                                            b
The relation between completeness by Cauchy-net convergence and completeness by Cauchy-filter convergence
is discussed in [NB, Thm. 3.1.6] (in the wider setting of commutative topological groups). Another approach
is given in [NB, §3.7, §4.8], which uses a notion of completeness that makes sense for non-Hausdorff E (in
which case completions can fail to be unique even up to linear topological isomorphism [NB, Ex. 3.7.3]).
     Remark C.1.3.3. We have opted in favor of nets over filters because for our purposes arguments via
nets foster reasoning by analogy with sequential convergence in corresponding classical situations. Since the
topology of locally convex vector spaces is generated by a family of seminorms, nets are convenient for studying
the convergence of vector-valued integrals (often valued in non-normable complete locally convex topological
vector spaces) and other settings that shall arise in this work.
     The role of nets rather than just sequences is crucial, because many Hausdorff locally convex spaces of
importance in this work do not have a countable base of 0-neighborhoods (equivalently are not metrizable
[Scha, Ch. I, 6.1]). This happens for the Schwartz-Bruhat space S(G) where G is the adele ring AF and idele
class group CF of a number field F as well as a non-archimedean local field L (even though S(L) has countable
C-dimension); such spaces S(G) are studied in depth in Appendix D.
     To explain this non-metrizability, we first note that §C.1.5 will discuss a natural Hausdorff locally convex
topology on direct limits E = lim En where the En ’s are Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces and
                               −→
the continuous linear transition maps En → En+1 are topological embeddings (this is generally strictly coarser
than the “inductive limit topology” as in general topology: the continuous bijection from the topological
inductive limit to the locally convex inductive limit is usually not a homeomorphism). When the En ’s are all
complete then such E is complete [Scha, Ch. II, 6.6] but if the En ’s are all Fréchet and En = ̸ En+1 for all n
then E cannot be metrizable because otherwise it would be Fréchet (by completeness) and so Lemma C.1.5.4
below applied to the identity map E → lim En would force E = En for all sufficiently large n, a contradiction.
                                         −→
The topology on S(G) for the number-theoretic examples G mentioned above is always of such type lim En
                                                                                                           −→
that we have just seen is never metrizable.
     Remark C.1.3.4. Much as the quotient of a Banach space by a closed subspace is again Banach (using
an associated “residue norm”), the quotient E/M of a Fréchet space E modulo a closed subspace M is Fréchet:
it inherits local convexity from E, and by [Scha, Ch. I, 6.3] it is complete and metrizable. However, beyond
the metrizable setting the quotient of a complete Hausdorff locally convex E modulo a closed subspace can
fail to be complete; examples are given in [Scha, Exer. 11, p. 192].
     C.1.4. Boundedness and quasi-completeness. For a topological vector space E, a subset A ⊂ E is
called bounded if for every neighborhood U of 0 in E there exists λ ∈ C× such that λ A ⊂ U (equivalently,
A ⊂ µ U for some µ ∈ C). Observe that this notion is intrinsic to the topological vector space structure and is
generally not the same as metric-boundedness when E is metrizable (since one can always find a bounded
metric giving the same topology), but it is the same as norm-boundedness when E is normable. Boundedness
is an important notion in this work.
     In the absence of a norm it may seem difficult to verify boundedness in examples, so it is useful to have a
some criteria for boundedness. In a Hausdorff locally convex vector space E whose topology is generated by a
                                C.1. LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES                                            661


family of seminorms {pi }i∈I , a subset B ⊂ E is bounded if and only if either of the following (equivalent)
conditions holds:
(1) pi (B) ⊂ R is bounded for every i ∈ I (this restates the definition of boundedness since the pi ’s define the
    topology of E),
(2) for any sequence {bk }k≥1 ⊂ B and sequence {λk }k≥1 in C tending toward 0, λk bk → 0 [Scha, Ch. I, 5.3].
A useful alternative criteria from [Scha, Ch. IV, 3.3] identifies boundedness with “weak boundedness”:

    Proposition C.1.4.1. Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space. A subset B ⊂ E is
bounded if and only if the image ℓ(B) ⊂ C is bounded for every continuous linear functional ℓ : E → C.

     Definition C.1.4.2. A subset A of a Hausdorff topological vector space E is called relatively compact
if its closure in E is compact, and it called pre-compact if its closure in the completion E
                                                                                           b is compact (i.e.,
pre-compactness means relative compactness in E). b

     Relatively compact subsets of E are pre-compact since a compact subset of E is certainly also closed
in E. By [Tre, Prop. 6.9] (whose proof uses self-contained arguments with filters, ultrafilters, and Cauchy
    b
filters, the latter of which can be used to make Cauchy nets by picking a point in each member of the
filter), pre-compactness for a subset A ⊂ E is equivalent to total boundedness of A in E: A is covered by
finitely many translates of each 0-neighborhood V ⊂ E. Totally bounded subsets A ⊂ E are bounded (in
particular, pre-compact subsets of E are bounded), but the converse is false; e.g., the closed unit ball in any
infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is bounded but non-compact and so is not pre-compact, hence not totally
bounded.

    Remark C.1.4.3. We caution the reader that pre-compactness is defined differently in various references.
For example, total boundedness in E is taken as the definition of pre-compactness in [NB, Def. 3.3.1], in
which case the work shifts to proving total boundedness in E     b implies relative compactness. In [Scha, p. 8]
pre-compactness for a subset A ⊂ E is defined as compactness for the completion of A in the sense of uniform
structures, but it is noted in [Scha, p. 25] that this is equivalent to compactness of the closure in Eb and to
total boundedness (these equivalences are sufficient for all use of pre-compactness in [Scha]). For the purpose
of our literature citations related to pre-compactness, the equivalence of total boundedness of A ⊂ E and
compactness of the closure of A in E b [Tre, Prop. 6.9] is sufficient.

    Many locally convex topological vector spaces, some of interest to this work, are not complete. Here are
two related examples arising from any infinite-dimensional Hilbert space H.

     Example C.1.4.4. The locally convex weak topology σ(H, H ′ ) on H of convergence under continuous
functionals (i.e., a base of 0-neighborhoods is given by {|⟨·, x1 ⟩| < ε, . . . , |⟨·, xn ⟩| < ε} ⊂ H for x1 , . . . , xn ∈ H
and ε > 0) is not complete. Indeed, if ℓ ∈ H ∗ is a discontinuous linear functional on H then for each finite-
dimensional subspace V ⊂ H we can use the Hahn-Banach Theorem to build a continuous ℓV = ⟨·, xV ⟩ ∈ H ′ ≃
H extending ℓ|V [Scha, Ch. II, 4.2]. Ordering the set of such V ’s via inclusion, we see that {xV }V is a Cauchy
net in H (since for any y1 , . . . , yn ∈ H we have ⟨xV − xW , yi ⟩ = 0 when V, W contain all yi ’s), but {xV } has
no limit x ∈ H for the weak topology. Indeed, if xV → x weakly then ⟨y, x⟩ = lim⟨y, xV ⟩ = lim ℓV (y) = ℓ(y)
for all y ∈ H, which is to say ℓ = ⟨·, x⟩, contradicting that ℓ is discontinuous.

     Example C.1.4.5. Equip the space B(H) of bounded linear operators on H with the locally convex
strong operator topology of pointwise convergence (rather than the operator-norm topology). A discontinuous
linear functional on H can be used (similarly to Example C.1.4.4) to construct a Cauchy net in BSOT (H)
that is not bounded (in contrast with Cauchy sequences, which are bounded in any topological vector space);
this implies BSOT (H) is not complete. See Remark C.4.3.4 for details on the construction.
662             CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


     In both of the preceding examples, the failure of completeness has a salvage: those spaces are quasi-
complete: closed bounded subsets are complete (in the sense of convergence of Cauchy nets). Some references
call this bounded completeness. It is immediate from the definitions that any complete E is quasi-complete.
     Since all Cauchy nets in a compact subset of a Hausdorff topological vector space clearly converge, quasi-
completeness of Hσ(H,H ′ ) in Example C.1.4.4 is a consequence of two facts: (i) Proposition C.1.4.1 and (ii) all
bounded subsets of such a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space E are pre-compact relative to the
weak topology σ(E, E ′ ) (essentially Alaoglu’s theorem: [Scha, Ch. IV, Cor. 2 to 5.5]). Quasi-completeness of
BSOT (H) in Example C.1.4.5 is deduced from the Uniform Boundedness Principle for Banach spaces: see
Lemma C.2.1.7 (applied with E = F = H and S the set of finite subsets of H).
     Quasi-completeness is a consequential concept throughout this work, insofar as there is a good integration
theory for functions valued in quasi-complete Hausdorff locally convex topological complex vector spaces.
This goes far beyond the Banach-valued theory of Bochner that is inapplicable for our purposes (since
we need to work with infinite-dimensional nuclear Fréchet spaces, and those are never normable [Tre,
Cor. 2 to Prop. 50.2]). The key stability property of quasi-completeness that enables integration theory to take
off is [Scha, Ch. II, Cor. to 4.3]: the closed convex circled hull of a pre-compact subset of a quasi-complete
Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space is compact. More on quasi-completeness and its role
will be discussed in §C.4 on integration in the sense of Pettis and §C.5 on holomorphy and meromorphy for
vector-valued functions on a Riemann surface (such as the surface Ω(CF ) of quasi-characters of the idele class
group CF of a number field F ).

      Example C.1.4.6. Of main interest to this work are the following classes of locally convex spaces:
(1) separable Hilbert spaces: they are locally convex since their topology is even normed, and are complete
    (so quasi-complete).
(2) Banach spaces: specifically, the Banach space of bounded linear operators on a Hilbert space equipped
    with the operator-norm topology. By completeness, they are quasi-complete too.
(3) The spaces S(G) of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on second-countable locally compact abelian groups G,
    especially those G of arithmetic origin such as the adele ring of a number field, the idele class group of
    a number field, and their local analogs. As was discussed in Remark C.1.3.3, these have natural locally
    convex topologies that are often non-metrizable but complete.
         Much deeper is that such spaces S(G) are nuclear (a concept reviewed in §C.2.4) and Montel (this
    means compactness of closed bounded subsets and reflexivty in the sense that the continuous double-duality
    map E → (Eβ′ )′β for the strong-dual topologies [Scha, pp. 144-5] is a topological isomorphism). These
    further properties are established in Theorem D.1.5.7.
(4) LF-spaces: As will be discussed in §C.1.5, for any inductive system {Eα } of locally convex topological
    vector spaces there is a natural locally convex topology on lim Eα making it have the expected universal
                                                                   −→
    mapping property [Scha, Ch. II, p. 54]. By construction the natural continuous linear map ⊕Eα → lim Eα
                                                                                                           −→
    is a topological quotient map, so a base for the topology in such inductive limits is given by the image of
    a base for the topology in the corresponding locally convex direct sum ⊕Eα ; one such base for the latter
    is given in (C.1.5.1) below.
         The most important cases of interest are Hausdorff locally convex countable inductive limits E = lim En
                                                                                                           −→
    of Fréchet spaces En , which are called LF-spaces as in [Gro-f, Def. 4 p. 146]. We call such E a strict
    LF-space when we can choose the transition maps En → En+1 to be topological embeddings, in which
    case it is automatic (i.e., does not need to be imposed as an additional requirement) that E is Hausdorff
    and En → E is a topological embedding for all n [Scha, Ch. II, 6.4]. The strictness hypothesis is assumed
    for all work with inductive limits in [Scha] (after the initial construction) and in [Tre] (see [Tre, p. 126]).
         There is a powerful Open Mapping Theorem for LF-spaces without a strictness assumption (see
    Theorem C.1.5.5 below); its proof ultimately bootstraps from the more familiar Fréchet case. This result is
                              C.1. LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES                                        663


    often used in the present work to deduce that an LF-space not yet known to be strict is actually so. From
    the definitions one sees that any quotient of an LF-space is an LF-space, but beware that a quotient of a
    strict LF-space can fail to be strict. Indeed, since E = lim En is always a topological quotient of ⊕n≥1 En
                                                             −→
    that is itself strict (as lim FN for FN = ⊕1≤n≤N En with the evident transition maps), any non-strict
                              −→
    LF-space provides such an example and [SN, §2, Ex. 2] gives a class of such examples.

     Remark C.1.4.7. The vast majority of the Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces of interest
to this work are nuclear Montel LF-spaces. In fact, they will generally arise for us as a strict countable locally
convex inductive limit of nuclear Fréchet spaces (such inductive limits are always nuclear and Montel by
[Scha, Ch. II, 6.6, Cor. to 7.2; Ch. III, Cor. to 7.4] and [Tre, Cor. 3 to Prop. 50.2]), but sometimes the verification
of strictness rests on the Open Mapping Theorem for general LF-spaces. Good properties of strict inductive
limits are provided throughout [Scha], which is our main reference on the matter (but again, we emphasize
the power of Open Mapping Theorem for LF-spaces without a strictness hypothesis).

    We will provide guidance on where to find the required foundational results on locally convex topological
vector spaces as the need arises. Our main references are [Scha, Ch. I–IV] (especially for duality and some basic
aspects of nuclearity) and [Tre] (especially for topological tensor products and deeper aspects of nuclearity),
along with [Gro-b] for Grothendieck’s work on topological tensor products and nuclear spaces (particularly the
inductive tensor product topology that we need rather crucially and does not seem to be systematically treated
apart from [Gro-b]). Some other useful references are [Bou-TVS, Ch. II, IV], [Jar, Ch. 2, 6, 8], [Cnw-a,
Ch. IV], and [NB, Ch. 4, 5, 8],

     C.1.5. Inductive limits and detection of limit subspaces. In this subsection we discuss some
complements around inductive limits in the category of locally convex topological vector spaces (over C), with
a focus on the special case of a sequence {Ek }k≥0 of Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces
equipped with continuous injective linear maps fk : Ek → Ek+1 for each k ≥ 0.
     If {Eα , fαβ } is an inductive system of locally convex topological vector spaces over C, we can put a locally
convex topology on E := lim Eα having the desired universal property (namely, a linear map g : E → F to a
                             −→
locally convex topological vector space F is continuous if and only if the composite linear maps Eα → E → F
are all continuous) provided that this can be done for the direct sum ⊕Eα . Indeed, if direct sums can be
equipped with such a locally convex topology then the quotient topology on E from the direct sum via the
usual algebraic construction of E will do the job for E due to the universal property of the quotient topology
on V /W for any locally convex V and linear subspace W (since the topology on V /W is also locally convex).
     For an arbitrary algebraic direct sum E = ⊕Eα of locally convex Eα ’s, a locally convex topology on E
having the categorical mapping property for a direct sum is the one with a base of 0-neighborhoods given by

     Let us now focus on the special case that E is Hausdorff and is the locally convex inductive limit of a
countable inductive system {(Ek , fk )}k≥0 for which the transition maps fk : Ek → Ek+1 are injective. The
best-behaved situation is when each fk is moreover a topological embedding and the Ek ’s are all Hausdorff;
such cases are called strict. In the strict case (as we noted in Example C.1.4.6(4)), automatically such an
inductive limit E is Hausdorff and each Ek → E is a topological embedding. (Beware that in [Scha] the
terminology “locally convex topological vector space” includes a Hausdorff hypothesis but the terminology
“locally convex topology” does not). The following is given in [Gro-f, p. 146].

    Definition C.1.5.2. A locally convex topological vector space E is called an LF-space if it is Hausdorff
and E = lim Ek for a sequence of continuous linear maps fk : Ek → Ek+1 between Fréchet spaces.
        −→
     Letting ik : Ek → E be the natural continuous linear map, by the universal property of E we see that
for the formation of E it is harmless to replace each Ek with Ek / ker(ik ) (which is also Fréchet since ker(ik )
is closed due to continuity of ik and the Hausdorff hypothesis on E; see Remark C.1.3.4). In other words,
we lose no generality in Definition C.1.5.2 by assuming the fk ’s are injective. The following description of
boundedness in the strict case under a closedness hypothesis on the maps Ek → Ek+1 (as holds when all Ek ’s
are complete, for example) is [Scha, Ch. II, 6.5] and is very useful:

     Proposition C.1.5.3. If E = lim Ek is strict with each Ek → Ek+1 a closed embedding, a subset B ⊂ E
                                    −→
is bounded if and only if B is a bounded subset of some Ek .

    Remarkably, if E = lim Ek with each Ek → Ek+1 injective between Fréchet spaces and without assuming
                        −→
such maps are topological embeddings (or equivalently that each ik : Ek → E is a topological embedding), the
Open Mapping Theorem for Fréchet spaces yields a continuous factorization property through the Ek ’s:
                              C.1. LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES                                      665


     Lemma C.1.5.4. Let E be a Hausdorff topological vector space equipped with continuous linear injections
                                                                                             S
ik : Ek → E from Fréchet spaces for k ≥ 1 such that ik (Ek ) ⊂ ik+1 (Ek+1 ) for all k and E = k ik (Ek ). Any
continuous linear map u : F → E from a Fréchet space F factors continuously through some ik : Ek → E.

     Proof. This result is [Gro-f, Thm. 1, p. 147], and for the convenience of the reader we provide the proof.
Let Hk = {(x, y) ∈ F × Ek : u(x) = ik (y)}, a subspace of the Fréchet F × Ek that is closed since E is Hausdorff
(as the diagonal of E is then closed in E × E), so Hk is Fréchet. The linear projection pk : Hk → F to the
first factor is injective since ik is injective, with pk (Hk ) ⊂ pk+1 (Hk+1 ) for all k. By hypothesis F is the union
of the rising countable sequence of linear subspaces pk (Hk ) (since each u(x) ∈ E lies in some ik (Ek )), so the
Fréchet property of F implies via the Baire category theorem that one of the linear subspaces pk0 (Hk0 ) has
closure in F with non-empty interior, so that closure is equal to F . In other words, the continuous linear
injection pk0 : Hk0 → F has dense image for some k0 .
     We claim pk0 is surjective. Since Hk0 is a complete metric space, by [Gro-f, Lemma, p. 39] a sufficient
criterion for surjectivity is that the closure pk0 (U ) ⊂ F is a 0-neighborhood for every 0-neighborhood U ⊂ Hk0 .
Pick any 0-neighborhood U ⊂ Hk0 , and then choose a 0-neighborhood V ⊂ Hk0 so that V − V ⊂ U . Closures
in F are obtained via sequential limits since F is metrizable, so pk0 (V ) − pk0 (V ) ⊂ pk0 (V − V ) ⊂ pk0 (U ).
Thus, it suffices to show that differences among pk0 (V ) exhaust a 0-neighborhood in F .
            S
     Since n≥1 nV = Hk0 , the countable collection npk0 (V ) of subsets of F has union pk0 (Hk0 ) that is dense
in F . Thus, by the Baire category theorem some n0 pk0 (V ) has closure in F with non-empty interior. Hence,
pk0 (V ) has closure in F with non-empty interior. Differences among pairs from any non-empty open subset of
F exhaust a 0-neighborhood, so pk0 (V ) − pk0 (V ) is a 0-neighborhood in F as desired.
     By the Open Mapping Theorem for complete metrizable topological vector spaces (see [KG, pp. 53-54],
where the existence of a translation-invariant metric [Scha, Ch. I, Thm. 6.1(iv)] is used near the end of the
proof), the continuous linear bijection pk0 is a topological isomorphism and so its continuous inverse F → Hk0
followed by the continuous projection Hk0 → Ek0 defines a continuous linear map v : F → Ek0 such that
ik0 ◦ v = u.                                                                                                        □

    The preceding lemma is used in the proof of the Open Mapping Theorem for LF-spaces which does not
require strictness. One even gets a more general result:

    Theorem C.1.5.5 (Open Mapping Theorem). Let q : F → E be a surjective continuous linear map
between Hausdorff topological vector spaces with E an LF-space and F exhausted by a rising sequence of images
of continuous linear maps un : Fn → F with Fréchet Fn ’s (e.g., F also an LF-space). Then q is open, or
equivalently F/ ker(q) → E is a topological isomorphism.
    In particular, a continuous linear surjection between LF-spaces is open.

     Although there is no strictness hypothesis, it is assumed each of E and F is Hausdorff. This result is a
special case of [Gro-f, Thm. 2(1), p. 148], which works with a wider class of spaces E that Grothendieck called
“strictly bornological” [Gro-f, p. 148] (later called “ultrabornological”: see [NB, Def. 13.2.3(b), Ex. 13.2.8(d),
Thm. 13.2.11]). For the reader’s convenience, we give Grothendieck’s proof specialized to the context as stated
in Theorem C.1.5.5 that suffices for our needs.

     Proof. We write E = lim Ek for an inductive system {Ek } of Fréchet spaces, and since E is Hausdorff
                            −→

consideration of the universal property of lim Ek we see that the natural map lim Ek′ → E is an isomorphism.
                                           −→                                    −→

can likewise replace F by the Hausdorff F/ ker(q) (note that ker(q) is closed since E is Hausdorff), so q is now
a linear bijection, and we can then replace each Fn by Fn / ker(un ) so that each un is injective (beware that

   C.1.5.1. Acyclicity and limit subspaces of LF-spaces. A technically important but rather subtle aspect of
LF-spaces is centered around the following concept:

    Definition C.1.5.6. Let E be an LF-space, and let fk : Ek → Ek+1 be a sequence of injective linear maps
(not necessarily a topological embedding) between Fréchet spaces such that E ≃ lim Ek . A closed subspace
                                                                                −→
F ⊂ E is called a limit subspace if for Fk = F ∩ Ek equipped with with the subspace topology from Ek , the
continuous linear bijection lim Fk → F a topological isomorphism.
                            −→
     The preceding concept is independent of the choice of defining sequence {Ek } for E. Indeed, if {Ek′ } is a
second such defining sequence then Ek → E factors continuously through some Ek′ ′ → E by Lemma C.1.5.4
and likewise each Ek′ ′ → E factors continuously through some Ek → E. This ensures that for Fk = F ∩ Ek
and Fk′ ′ = F ∩ Ek′ ′ the natural linear bijection between the countable inductive limits lim Fk and lim Fk′ ′ (via
                                                                                          −→         −→
their identifications with F ) is a topological isomorphism.
     Closed subspaces F ⊂ E in LF-spaces are not generally limit subspaces, by they are under some favorable
conditions. We provide a sufficient criterion below, recorded here for ease of access. This rests on the concept
of acyclicity that was developed by Palamodov [Pa, §7, p. 38] (resting on homological techniques) and Retakh
[Ret], and further studied by Vogt (see [Vogt-1, §2], and specifically [Vogt-1, §2, Thm. 2.10, p. 67], where
Retakh’s characterization of acyclic LF-spaces is reproved avoiding homological methods).
     Strict LF-spaces are acyclic, as we will be discussing below, and we will see in Theorem C.1.5.11 that if
each of the members Ek of a defining countable strict inductive system is nuclear then any closed subspace
F ⊂ E for which q : E → E/F lifts bounded subsets (i.e., each bounded B ⊂ E/F has the form q(B ′ ) for
bounded B ′ ⊂ E) is a limit subspace and so is itself a strict LF-space. These conditions will always be fulfilled
for the applications discussed throughout this work.
     For the following example due to Grothendieck, we refer the reader to the discussion in the second half of
[Gro-e, §II.3, p. 98]. It provides an example of a closed subspace F of a strict locally convex inductive limit E
of an increasing sequence of Fréchet spaces Ek such that F is not an LF-space.

    Example C.1.5.7 (A closed subspace of a strict LF-space which is not a limit subspace). There exists
a countable locally convex direct sum E of Banach spaces and a closed subspace F ⊂ E such that F is not
an LF-space with respect to the subspace topology. In particular, F is not a limit subspace. This answers a
question of Dieudonné and Schwartz from 1954 [DS, §15, no. 2, p. 97].

below to recognize limit subspaces within strict locally convex countable inductive limits of nuclear Fréchet

     Definition C.1.5.9. For a continuous linear map f : E → F between Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector spaces, we say a bounded subset B ⊂ F can be f -lifted if and only if there exists a bounded subset
B ′ ⊂ E such that B ⊂ f (B ′ ) (it is clearly equivalent to require f (B ′ ) = B). If this condition holds for all
bounded subsets in F then we say f lifts bounded subsets or satisfies the bounded lifting property.
     A class of locally convex spaces E for which the bounded lifting property is satisfied by every quotient
map q : E → E/F modulo a closed subspace was identified by Grothendieck in [Gro-e, II.4, Thm. 12, p. 119]:
the Fréchet spaces E that are also Schwartz, a concept introduced in [Gro-e, II.4, Def. 5, p. 117]. (The result
is more precise: every bounded subset of E/F is contained in q(C) for a compact subset C ⊂ E.)
     One of the equivalent definitions of being Schwartz (for a locally convex topological vector space E) is that
for every closed convex circled 0-neighborhood U ⊂ E there exists a 0-neighborhood V ⊂ E with pre-compact

For our purposes, nuclear spaces are the key source of locally convex spaces that are Schwartz:
    Example C.1.5.10. If a locally convex topological vector space E is a nuclear then we claim it is Schwartz.
By [Scha, Ch. III, 7.2], for every convex circled 0-neighborhood U ⊂ E (in particular, such U that are closed)
there exists a convex circled 0-neighborhood V ⊂ U such that the natural map of Banach spaces T : E  cV → EcU
is nuclear. But any nuclear map between Banach spaces is a norm-topology limit of finite-rank operators
[Scha, p. 98] and hence is compact. Since V maps into the closed unit ball of E    cV , its image under T has
compact closure. Taking U to be closed, such V fulfills the requirement in the definition of E to be Schwartz.
    The examples of the bounded lifting property that arise throughout this work are quotient maps q : E ↠ G
where G is Hausdorff and E is a strict countable inductive limit of nuclear Fréchet spaces (it is not apparent yet
that all such q satisfy the bounded lifting property since such an E is generally not Fréchet, but in Corollary
C.1.5.13 we will see that they all do). Note that any such E is nuclear, hence Schwartz, and G = E/F for the
subspace F = ker(q) ⊂ E that is closed since G is Hausdorff. Such quotients arise in the following result.
     Theorem C.1.5.11 (Recognizing limit subspaces of strict LF-spaces). Let E be a strict countable inductive
limit of nuclear Fréchet spaces. For any closed subspace F ⊂ E, the following are equivalent:
(1) F is a limit subspace; i.e., for {Em }m≥0 a strict defining increasing sequence of nuclear Fréchet spaces,
    the subspace topology on F equals the locally convex inductive limit topology of the inductive system
    {F ∩ Em }m≥0 where each F ∩ Em is given the subspace topology from Em ;
(2) the quotient map q : E → E/F satisfies the bounded lifting property; i.e., for every bounded subset
    B ⊂ E/F , there exists a bounded subset B ′ ⊂ E such that B ⊂ q(B ′ ).
     The result is actually true more broadly, when F is merely assumed to be step-wise closed: F ∩ Em is
closed in Em for every integer m ≥ 0. This is wider generality because there are examples of non-closed linear
subspaces of strict LF-spaces that are step-wise closed: the discussion at the end of [Gro-e, §II.3, p. 98] gives a
strict LF-space E and a non-closed subspace F ⊂ E such that the intersection of F with each Fréchet subspace
E0 ⊂ E is closed in E0 . The equivalence in Theorem C.1.5.11 with F merely assumed to be step-wise closed
is [Wngr-2, §3, Cor. 3.4, p. 254], where each Fréchet Em is assumed merely to be Schwartz (which implies
nuclearity by Example C.1.5.10).
    Remark C.1.5.12. If E is a strict countable inductive limit of nuclear Fréchet spaces Em as in Theorem
                                                   ′                        ′                          ′
C.1.5.11(1) then every strict defining sequence {Em  } for E has all terms Em  nuclear since (i) each Em  → E is
a topological embedding by strictness, (ii) nuclearity is inherited by both strict countable inductive limits (so
                                          ′
E is nuclear) and subspaces (such as Em     ⊂ E) by [Scha, Ch. III, 7.4].
    Corollary C.1.5.13. Let E be a strict countable inductive limit of nuclear Fréchet spaces, and F ⊂ E
a closed subspace. Assume E/F (with the quotient topology) is also a strict countable inductive limit of a
countable sequence of nuclear Fréchet spaces.
    The quotient map q : E → E/F lifts bounded subsets, so the closed subspace ker(q) ⊂ E is a limit subspace
and hence ker(q) is a strict countable inductive limit of nuclear Fréchet spaces.
      The proof of [FlM, §5.5, Corollary, p. 110] inspires the argument given below.
    Proof. Once it is shown that q satisfies the bounded lifting property, the rest follows from Theorem
C.1.5.11. By hypothesis, the Hausdorff quotient E/F is the locally convex inductive limit of an increasing
sequence of nuclear Fréchet subspaces {Qm }m≥0 , and E is the locally convex inductive limit of an increasing
sequence of nuclear Fréchet spaces {Em }m≥0 . Define Pm := Em /(ker(q) ∩ Em ) equipped with the quotient
topology inherited from Em .
                             C.1. LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES                                      669


     We do not (yet) know if the continuous linear injections Pm → Pm+1 are topological embeddings, and
in the absence of such strictness for {Pm } we don’t (yet) know the locally convex topological vector space
P := lim Pm is Hausdorff (a property that is required in the definition of “LF-space”). But we can directly
      −→
verify the Hausdorff property: the natural linear bijection f : P → E/F is continuous and has Hausdorff
target, so f −1 (0) = {0} is closed in P , ensuring the topological group P is Hausdorff. Thus, P is an LF-space,
so the Open Mapping Theorem for LF-spaces (namely Theorem C.1.5.5) can be applied to conclude that f is a
topological isomorphism. Hence, for each k ≥ 0 we can apply Grothendieck’s Factorization Theorem (namely
Lemma C.1.5.4) to Qk ,→ E/F ≃ P to conclude that it factors continuously through Pm(k) → P ≃ E/F for
some m(k) ≥ 0.
     Let B ⊂ E/F be a bounded subset. Since E/F is the strict inductive limit of the complete Qk ’s (with each
topological embedding Qk → Qk+1 closed due to completeness of the Fréchet spaces Qk ), for sufficiently large k
we have B ⊂ Qk with B is bounded in Qk [Scha, Ch. II, 6.5]. The image of B under the continuous Qk → Pm(k)
(which we also denote as B) is therefore bounded in Pm(k) . Since nuclear spaces are Schwartz (Example
C.1.5.10), such as the Fréchet Em ’s, by [Gro-e, II.4, Thm. 12, p. 119] for any closed subspace M ⊂ Em(k) the
quotient map Em(k) → Em(k) /M lifts bounded subsets. Applying this to M = ker(q) ∩ Em(k) = F ∩ Em(k)
(closed in Em(k) since F → E is a closed embedding and each Em → E is a topological embedding by strictness
of {Em }), there exists a bounded subset B ′ ⊂ Em(k) whose image in Em(k) /M = Pm(k) contains B. The
image of B ′ under the continuous map Em(k) → E is bounded, and that bounded subset of E clearly has
image in E/F containing the bounded B ⊂ E/F , so we are done.                                                  □

    topology of simple (or pointwise) convergence.
(2) Lγ (E, F ) if S is the collection of all pre-compact subsets of E. The S-topology on Lγ (E, F ) is called
    the topology of pre-compact convergence.
(3) Lβ (E, F ) if S is the collection of all bounded subsets of E. The S-topology on Lβ (E, F ) is called the
    topology of bounded convergence.

    Case (2) is relevant to traces for nuclear operators between Hausdorff locally convex spaces, as discussed
in §C.2.4.5.

    An important property of S-topologies is that a subset of L (E, F ) that is bounded with respect to
the topology of pointwise convergence is bounded with respect to any S-topology on L (E, F ) so long as
E is quasi-complete and S is a cofiltered collection of bounded subsets of E whose union is E (i.e. not
merely linearly generating a dense subspace): see [Scha, Ch.III, Cor. to 3.4]. The following result (see [Scha,
Ch.III, Cor. to 4.4]) is important for later use.6

   Lemma C.2.1.7 (Quasi-completeness of mapping spaces). Let E, F be Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector spaces. Assume:
(1) E is barreled.
(2) F is quasi-complete.
(3) S is a cofiltered collection of bounded subsets of E whose union is E.
Then LS (E, F ) is quasi-complete.

    Remark C.2.1.8. If E = F = H is a Hilbert space and S is the collection of all finite subsets of H
respectively the collection of all bounded subsets of H then Lemma C.2.1.7 implies quasi-completeness of
BSOT (H) respectively BNT (H) (operator-norm topology). Indeed, every Hilbert space (and even every Fréchet
space) is barrelled [Scha, Ch.II, Cor. to 7.1]) and complete. Of course, as is well-known, BNT (H) is even
complete.

     Let E, F be two Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces. On L (E, F ), the topology of
uniform convergence on the bounded subsets of E will be of particular importance, because it is a flexible
topology to define distributions. Specifically, E will be chosen to be a “familiar” locally convex topological
linear space (of functions), and F will be chosen to be an operator algebra with topologies of varying degrees
of strength; Lβ (E, F ) will be a space of “F -valued distributions”.
     In order to study continuous linear mapping spaces topologized with a suitable S-topology, we need two
topologies on tensor products of Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces. In order to discuss
the first, we now recall some terminology on equicontinuity. A subset H ⊂ L (E, F ) is called equicontinuous
if and only if for every 0-neighborhood V ⊂ F there exists a 0-neighborhood U ⊂ E such that f (U ) ⊂ V
for every f ∈ H. We refer the reader to [Scha, Ch. III, §4] for more on equicontinuity and the Uniform
Boundedness Principle. Important properties of equicontinuous subsets in L (E, F ) are the following (see
[Scha, Ch. III, Cor. to 4.1, 4.5]):

    Lemma C.2.1.9. Let E, F be Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces, H ⊂ L (E, F ) an
equicontinuous subset.
(1) H is bounded in LS (E, F ) for S any collection of bounded subsets of E whose union linearly generates a
    dense subspace of E.
(2) The subspace topologies on H inherited from either Lσ (E, F ) or Lγ (E, F ) are the same.

    C.2.2. Topologies of a duality and the equicontinuous compactology. We will say a few words
on bornologies and on topologies associated to certain bilinear pairings (in effect, convergence conditions via
linear functionals), explaining the role that the main results on them serve throughout our work.

    C.2.2.1. Generation of polar topologies: bornologies and topologies of a duality. Let E be a Hausdorff
locally convex topological C-vector space. A bornology on E is a non-empty collection of subsets of E, cofiltered
by upward-inclusion, such that each of its members is bounded with respect to the σ(E, E ′ )-topology. Note
that boundedness in the given topology on E and in the σ(E, E ′ )-topology are the same [Scha, Ch. IV, 3.3].
The defining condition of a bornology on E is that for each B ∈ S and λ ∈ C× there exists C ∈ S such that
λB ⊂ C. All the S-topologies defined in Definition C.2.1.5 are induced by bornologies.
    As in [Scha, Ch. IV, §1], we now consider a bi-linear pairing
(C.2.2.1)                                       ⟨·, ·⟩ : E × F → C
with E, F two Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces. We assume that the pairing ⟨·, ·⟩ is
separating: if x ∈ E and ⟨x, ·⟩ = 0 as a linear functional on F then x = 0, and similarly for ⟨·, y⟩ as a linear
functional on E. The notation ⟨E, F ⟩ refers to the datum (E, F, ⟨·, ·⟩).
    The datum of a separating bi-linear pairing g : E × F → C leads to the definition of the weak topology
σ(E, F ) on E and the weak topology σ(F, E) on F , respectively defined as the topology of pointwise convergence
with respect to the family of linear maps {g(·, y) : y ∈ F } on E and {g(x, ·) : x ∈ E} on F respectively. This
leads to the concepts of weak boundedness and weak compactness in E, F , which underlie other topologies
associated to ⟨E, F ⟩ via the following construction.
    For A ⊂ F a subset, we define its polar set in E with respect to the duality ⟨E, F ⟩ to be
(C.2.2.2)                      A◦ := {x ∈ E : |⟨x, y⟩E,F | ≤ 1, for all y ∈ A} ⊂ E
(this is called the absolute polar of A in [Scha, Ch. IV, p. 125], where polar is defined using Re(⟨x, y⟩) as is also
done in [Bou-TVS, Ch. II, §8, No. 4, Def. 1, p. II.64]; the two concepts agree when A is circled), and similarly
for any subset A ⊂ E we define its polar set in F with respect to the duality ⟨E, F ⟩ to be
(C.2.2.3)                      A◦ := {y ∈ F : |⟨x, y⟩E,F | ≤ 1, for all x ∈ A} ⊂ F.
    Polars provide a general recipe to produce 0-neighborhoods in either one of the two linear spaces
E, F in a duality ⟨E, F ⟩. Note that if V ⊂ E a vector subspace, the subset V ◦ ⊂ F is the orthogonal
(annihilator) V ⊥ = annF (V ). The reader may want to compare the construction and use of polars with that
of orthogonals/annihilators from the structure theory of Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups, which is
used in Appendix D to construct and study Schwartz-Bruhat spaces of functions on Hausdorff locally compact
abelian groups. When taking F to be the algebraic dual E ∗ of E we denote by A• the polar sets in either
direction with respect to the pairing ⟨·, ·⟩E,E ∗ .
    We can use polars in E ∗ of 0-neighborhoods of E to identify the continuous dual of E within E ∗ :
                                                    [
(C.2.2.4)                                     E′ =      U • ⊂ E∗

where U0 (E) is a 0-neighborhood base in E. The meaning of (C.2.2.4) is that a linear functional on E is
continuous if and only if it is bounded on a 0-neighborhood in E.
    The datum of a duality ⟨E, F ⟩ leads to an axiomatization of the robust theory of Banach spaces and their
duals, with generalization of the main concepts (such as reflexivity) to the case of general Hausdorff locally
convex topological C-vector spaces. A key basic result is:
    Theorem C.2.2.1 (Bi-polar Theorem). Let ⟨E, F ⟩ be a duality. Let A ⊂ E be a subset. Then:
(C.2.2.5)                                      (A◦ )◦ = cch(A ∪ {0})
674            CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


where the right side of (C.2.2.5) is the σ(E, F )-closure of the convex circled hull of A in E.

     Our convention has been to define polar of A ⊂ E to be {y ∈ F : |⟨x, y⟩| ≤ 1 for all x ∈ A} which some
references call the absolute polar, in contrast with real polar {y ∈ F : Re |⟨x, y⟩ ≤ 1 for all x ∈ A}. Since the
absolute polar A◦ agrees with the real polar of the circled Ab = D · A for D ⊂ C the closed unit disk, Theorem
C.2.2.1 for real polars as in [Scha, Ch. IV, 1.5] yields the result for absolute polars as stated above.
     An efficient account of the basic properties of polars is given in [Scha, Ch. IV, §1] and [NB, Thms. 8.3.6,
8.3.7]. From the definition one sees that the polar set A◦ ⊂ F of a subset A ⊂ E is always convex, circled
and σ(F, E)-closed, and is absorbing (i.e. radial) if and only if A is σ(E, F )-bounded. This paves the way to
defining 0-neighborhood bases within E respectively F via polars of subsets of F respectively E, and then
using the Bi-polar Theorem as a dictionary to establish basic properties of such “polar” topologies.
     To a directed collection of σ(F, E)-bounded subsets of F , we assign the corresponding collection of polars
in E. The idea is to think of a σ(F, E)-bounded subset B ⊂ F as a replacement for the unit ball in the normed
dual of a normed space, and define the function:
                                            pB (x) := sup |⟨x, y⟩E,F |
                                                      y∈B

a seminorm on E. The “unit ball” with respect to pB is exactly the polar set U := B ◦ , and so long as the
chosen class of σ(F, E)-bounded subsets of F satisfies basic stability properties, this construction leads to a
0-neighborhood base of a linear topology on E, with the polar sets B ◦ playing the role of unit-balls. Polar
topologies are therefore defined by using polarity to indicate which subsets are supposed to serve as unit-balls.
This is the origin of the concept of bornology, whose definition we recalled at the beginning of this subsection.

     C.2.2.2. Consistent topologies. We conclude this account of the main elements of the construction of
polar topologies by highlighting a great advantage of the local convexity assumption on linear topologies of
topological vector spaces. It affords flexibility on the concepts of boundedness, closure, and denseness in terms
of refining the polar topology on E induced by a duality ⟨E, F ⟩.
     Specifically, certain properties of subsets of E defined in terms of a polar topology using F are independent
of the choice of such topology so long as the polar topology is consistent with ⟨E, F ⟩ in the sense that the
space of continuous linear functionals on E with respect to that topology is exactly F . For example, the weak
topology σ(E, F ) on E is always consistent with a given separating duality g : E × F → C (as is a given
Hausdorff locally convex topology on E when F = E ′ is the topological dual and g is the evaluation pairing).
     A first important example of this phenomenon is the equivalence of boundedness and weak boundedness,
as well as formation of closure, respectively weakly closure for convex sets in any Hausdorff locally convex
topological C-vector space: see [Scha, Ch. IV, 3.1, 3.3].
     Although consistency is defined on all linear topologies on E, for Hausdorff locally convex topologies the
extremes of such consistent topologies are known. This is the content of the Mackey-Arens Theorem [Scha,
Ch. IV, 3.2-3.3]. It rests crucially on the local convexity assumption and ultimately on separations theorems
[Scha, Ch. II, §9] relying upon the Hahn-Banach Theorem. The statement of the result is that such topologies
are precisely those which are finer than σ(E, F ) and coarser than the Mackey topology τ (E, F ) that is the
S-topology on E for the collection S of all subsets of F that are convex, circled and σ(F, E)-compact. (In
[Jar], this topology is denoted using the letter µ rather than τ .)
     In the absence of local convexity, control on polar topologies is lost: we refer the reader to the example of
ℓp (N) for 0 < p < 1 (see [Voigt, Ch. 5, Ex. 5.5(a), p. 38]). Most notable among the polar topologies that are
not necessarily consistent is the strong topology β(E, F ) that is always stronger than the Mackey topology.
By [Scha, Ch. IV, 5.2], the condition under which the strong-dual topology β(E ′ , E) agrees with the Mackey
topology τ (E ′ , E) is barreledness of E [Scha, Ch. II, §7]: this means that the barrels of E (closed, convex,
circled and absorbing subsets, examples of which are provided by the polars of weakly bounded subsets) are
        C.2. COMPLEMENTS ON MAPPING SPACES, TOPOLOGICAL TENSOR PRODUCTS, AND NUCLEARITY                         675


0-neighborhoods in E. Under such an additional condition, a tighter relation between equicontinuous and
bounded subsets is attained in the form of a general version of the Uniform Boundedness Principle (see [Scha,
Ch. III, 4.2-4.3]).
    Further classes of Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces will be discussed as the need arises.

    C.2.2.3. Uniform convergence on the weakly closed convex and circled equicontinuous subsets of E ′ . With
an eye towards the discussion of ε-tensor products, and the proofs of several “kernel theorems” in Appendix D,
we record the following result for which we refer the reader to [Scha, Ch. IV, Cor. 3 to 1.5] for a proof.

    Lemma C.2.2.2 (Topology of uniform convergence on the equicontinuous subsets of E ′ ). Let E be a
Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space, and E the collection of all equicontinuous subsets of E ′ that
are convex, circled, and closed with respect to the σ(E ′ , E)-topology on E ′ . Then the family of subsets of E
(C.2.2.6)                                      U := {U ◦ : U ∈ E}
(where U ◦ is the polar of U in E with respect to the duality ⟨E, E ′ ⟩) is a 0-neighborhood base for the given
topology on E.

     The collection E from Lemma C.2.2.2 is usually referred to as the equicontinuous compactology on E ′ . The
weak-closedness and convexity assumptions on U considered in (C.2.2.6) are harmless because every subset
U ⊂ E satisfies U ◦ = U ◦◦◦ by [Scha, Ch. IV, Cor. 1 to 1.5] with U ◦◦ weakly closed and convex as described by
the Bi-Polar Theorem.
     The collection E will underlie the definition of the injective tensor product topology ⊗ε in §C.2.3.1 but
via Lemma C.2.2.2 it also leads to a tool underpinning proofs of “kernel theorems” in use throughout this
work (these are results which say that certain function spaces on X × Y coincide with a suitably completed
tensor product of corresponding function spaces on X and on Y ) and comparisons among multiple topologies
on tensor products. In the presence of favorable conditions (such as nuclearity of at least one of the tensor
factors) this includes criteria under which there is equality between the injective tensor product topology
⊗ε and the projective tensor product topology ⊗π (see §C.2.3.1 and §C.2.3.2). Such equality is a powerful
feature because the injective topology is well-behaved for topological embeddings and the projective topology
is well-behaved for quotient maps.
     A prototypical such application occurs in the proof of the kernel theorem for the Schwartz space of
Euclidean spaces: that the continuous linear map S(Rn ) ⊗π S(Rm ) → S(Rn × Rm ) extends to a linear
topological isomorphism S(Rn ) ⊗  b π S(Rm ) → S(Rn × Rm ). Nuclearity of the Schwartz spaces identifies
injective and projective topologies on the tensor product, and then Lemma C.2.2.2 is the additional ingredient
used to show that a net in S(Rn ) ⊗π S(Rm ) converges in S(Rn × Rm ) only if it converges in S(Rn ) ⊗π S(Rm ).
     Among the advantages of the local convexity condition (most of which rest on the separation theorems
which constitute forms of the Hahn-Banach Theorem) is the stability of important concepts and properties of
subsets of Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces with respect to change of topology compatibly
with a duality in the presence of local convexity (the bounds on such topologies being described by the
Mackey-Arens Theorem). Another is the description of locally convex topologies by means of fundamental
families of seminorms (see the discussion in §C.1.2), and the characterization of the given topology as the
topology of uniform convergence on the closed convex circled equicontinuous subsets of the continuous dual.

    C.2.3. Topological tensor products. Throughout this subsection, we provide an overview about three
Hausdorff locally convex topologies on E ⊗ F for any two Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces
E and F . These are the injective tensor product (also called the “ε-tensor product”), the projective tensor
product (also called the “π-tensor product”), and the inductive tensor product. When E ⊗ F is equipped
with such topologies, we denote the resulting locally convex topological vector space as E ⊗ε F , E ⊗π F , and
676             CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


E ⊗ι F respectively. The corresponding completions are denoted E ⊗    b εF , E⊗
                                                                              b π F , and E⊗F respectively. The
inductive tensor product is the least-encountered in the published literature, but it serves an important role in
our work.

     C.2.3.1. Injective tensor products by bi-equicontinuous convergence. We start with the ε-topology, also
called the “injective tensor product” because it interacts well with subspace inclusions [Tre, Prop. 43.7] (as
we shall discuss). For Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces E1 and E2 , we write B(E1 , E2 ) for
the space of continuous bilinear forms E1 × E2 → C and B(E1 , E2 ) for the space of separately continuous
bilinear forms E1 × E2 → C (i.e., continuous in each entry when the other is fixed). By [Tre, Prop. 42.4], the
canonical linear map
(C.2.3.1)                                      ρ : E ⊗ F → B(Eσ′ , Fσ′ )

     Let E ′ = L (E, C) denote the topological dual of a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space E, on

subsets of E.

     Remark C.2.3.1. The Mackey topology on E ′ can be described in another way in an important class of
examples. If E has the Heine-Borel property that all closed bounded subsets are compact (conversely, compact
subsets in any Hausdorff topological vector space are always closed and bounded) then Eτ′ clearly agrees with
the topology Eγ′ of pre-compact convergence. The most interesting class of E with the Heine-Borel property
are Montel spaces [Scha, Ch. IV, p. 147], which (as is explained in Appendix D) includes many function spaces
of interest to us, such as Schwartz spaces on the adelic ring and idele class group of a number field. All barreled
quasi-complete nuclear spaces are Montel (by [Tre, Cor. 1 to Prop. 50.4] and [Scha, Ch. IV, 5.6]; nuclearity
will be reviewed in §C.2.4).

     C.2.3.2. Projective tensor products. Another topology on tensor products of Hausdorff locally convex
topological C-vector spaces we need is the projective tensor product topology, also called the π-topology. For
E, F two Hausdorff locally convex complex vector spaces, there exists on the algebraic tensor product E ⊗ F
a unique locally convex topology such that for any locally convex complex vector space G, continuous linear
maps E ⊗ F → G correspond bijectively to continuous (i.e. not merely separately continuous) bilinear maps
E × F → G. This topology is referred to as the projective tensor product topology on E ⊗ F , and when E ⊗ F
is equipped with this topology it is denoted
(C.2.3.14)                                                  E ⊗π F.
The space of B(E, F ) of continuous bilinear forms on E × F is linearly identified with the continuous dual of
E ⊗π F .
    By [Tre, Ch. 43] (or [Scha, Ch. III, pp. 93-94]), a fundamental system of neighborhoods of 0 for this
topology on E ⊗ F is given by the convex circled hulls of the sets of the form
(C.2.3.15)                                 Ui ⊗ Vj = {ui ⊗ vj : ui ∈ Ui , vj ∈ Vj }
where Ui and Vj vary through fundamental systems of neighborhoods of 0 in E, respectively F . This description
of a base of 0-neighborhoods clearly implies the associativity of the π-topology for tensor products of finitely
many Hausdorff locally convex spaces.
     The projective tensor product of two Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces is Hausdorff
[Tre, Prop. 43.3]. The completion of E ⊗ F with respect to the projective topology is denoted E ⊗     b π F . Its
formation is compatible with completion of the factors by [Tre, Prop. 43.9] and the universal property of
completion.
     The analog of Lemma C.2.3.5 for projective tensor products holds by [Jar, §15.4, Thm. 1, p. 332]).10
     By [Scha, Ch. III, 6.4], in the special case when the tensor factors E, F of the projective tensor product
E⊗ b π F are Fréchet spaces, the general element of E ⊗ b π F can be written in the form
                                                  X
(C.2.3.16)                                           λk xk ⊗ yk
                                                        k≥1

where {λk } is an absolutely summable sequence in C and {xk }k≥1 , {yk }k≥1 are sequences in E, F respectively
that converge to 0 (it is readily checked that conversely all such infinite series converge within E ⊗
                                                                                                     b π F ). This
result due to Grothendieck is extremely useful when carrying out calculations, as we shall see (for example) in
Appendix D.
     Of great importance is the good behavior of ⊗π with respect to quotient maps. If T1 : E1 → F1 and
T2 : E2 → F2 are quotient maps between Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces then T1 ⊗π T2 is
clearly a quotient map by (C.2.3.15), but the analogue for the completions is more subtle [Tre, Prop. 43.9]:
    Proposition C.2.3.7. If T1 : E1 → F1 and T2 : E2 → F2 are quotient maps between Hausdorff locally
convex topological vector spaces then T1 ⊗
                                         b π T2 is a quotient map onto its image (given the subspace topology),
and it is surjective when E1 and E2 are metrizable.
     The surjectivity of T1 ⊗

The projective tensor product topology is finer than the injective tensor product topology: the identity map
ρ : E ⊗π F → E ⊗ε F on E ⊗ F is continuous [Tre, Prop. 43.5]. When one of E or F is nuclear (a topic to be
discussed in §C.2.4) then the linear bijection ρ : E ⊗π F → E ⊗ε F is a homeomorphism, so in such cases
E⊗ b π F inherits the good properties of E ⊗ b ε F with respect to subspace inclusions in F .
    Remark C.2.3.8 (On the equicontinuous subsets of (E ⊗ε F )′ ). We now record a useful observation from
the paragraph following [Tre, Def. 49.1, p.500] that provides a description of equicontinuous subsets of the

topological dual of E ⊗ε F for Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces E and F . By definition, a
0-neighborhood base of E ⊗ε F is given by polars (A′ ⊗ B ′ )◦ for A′ ⊗ B ′ := {a′ ⊗ b′ : a′ ∈ A′ , b′ ∈ B ′ } with

     This description of the equicontinuous subsets of (E ⊗ε F )′ will be used when proving “kernel theorems”
in Appendix D. (By Lemma C.2.2.2, the given topology on a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
space is the same as the topology of uniform convergence on the weakly closed convex circled equicontinuous
subsets of the topological dual. When applied to E ⊗ε F that gives us nothing new via the preceding bipolar
description since M ◦◦◦ = M ◦ for any subset M of a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space [Scha,
Ch IV, Cor. 1 to 1.5].)

resting on the preceding description. It is particularly useful when E or F is nuclear because the resulting
topological equality E ⊗π F = E ⊗ε F in such cases (as noted above, and to be discussed further in §C.2.4)
then relates the projective tensor product topology to a function space on a product.

     C.2.3.3. Metrizability, and separately continuous and continuous bi-linear forms. We next record a criterion
to determine when a separately sequentially continuous bilinear map E × F → G between Hausdorff locally
convex topological C-vector spaces E, F, G is sequentially continuous. When sequences are sufficient to probe
the topologies of E and F , this will provide a mechanism for sometimes verifying that a given separately
continuous bilinear mapping is continuous. For example, sometimes this can be used to show continuity of
linear maps from projective tensor products, in view of the universal mapping property of projective tensor
products. We refer the reader to the proof of [Bou-TVS, Ch. III, §5, no. 2, Prop. 2, p. III.29; Cor. 1, p. III.30]
for similar arguments resting on the Uniform Boundedness Principle.
    Proposition C.2.3.11 (Sequential continuity of separately sequentially continuous bi-linear mappings).
Let E, F, G be Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces. Let:
(C.2.3.21)                                              A:E×F →G
11Why is this result recorded, since it is never cited anywhere? Is it implicit somewhere else?
682             CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


be a separately sequentially continuous bi-linear mapping. If E is Fréchet then A is sequentially continuous.

    Proof. Let {um }m≥0 ⊂ E be a null-sequence in E (i.e., converging to 0), and {vm }m≥0 ⊂ F a convergent
sequence in F . It suffices to show A(um , vm ) → 0. By separate sequential continuity of A and E being a
metric space, the linear operators A(·, vm ) : E → G are continuous. Moreover, for every u ∈ E, the subset
{A(u, vm )}m≥0 ⊂ G is bounded since A(u, ·) : F → G is continuous.
    Thus, the sequence {A(·, vm )}m≥0 ⊂ L (E, G) is pointwise bouinded, so since E is Baire (as it is Fréchet),
we see by [Scha, Ch. III, 4.2] that {A(·, vm )}m≥0 ⊂ L (E, G) is equicontinuous. Let U ⊂ G be any 0-
neighborhood. There therefore exists a 0-neighborhood U0 ⊂ E such that A(U0 , vm ) ⊂ U for every integer
m ≥ 0. Being {um }m≥0 a null-sequence, there exists m0 ≥ 0 such that for every integer m ≥ m0 , we have
um ∈ U0 . It follows that for every m ≥ m0 , A(um , vm ) ∈ U , and hence limm→+∞ A(um , vm ) = 0.           □


    C.2.3.4. Inductive tensor products. One more locally convex topology on algebraic tensor products of
Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces features throughout this work: the inductive tensor
product topology. As literature references, we mention [Scha, Ch. III, p. 96] and [Gro-b, Ch. I, §3, No. 1,
Def. 3, p. 74].
    For E, F two Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces, we define on E ⊗ F the locally convex
topology that is finest among those such that for any Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space G,
the bilinear maps
                                                E×F →G
that are separately continuous make the corresponding linear map E ⊗ F → G be continuous. That such
a Hausdorff locally convex topology on E ⊗ F indeed does exist is the content of [Gro-b, Ch. I, §3, No. 1,
Prop. 13, p. 73].12 We denote by
(C.2.3.22)                                              E ⊗ι F
the algebraic tensor product topologized in this manner, and refer to it as the inductive tensor product of E
and F .
    We claim E ⊗ι F is Hausdorff. It suffices to show 0 is a closed point. The identity map on E ⊗ F is
continuous as a bijective map of topological groups E ⊗ι F → E ⊗π F because the continuous bilinear pairing
E × F → E ⊗π F is separately continuous. Thus, the Hausdorff property of E ⊗π F gives the desired closedness
of {0} in E ⊗ι F . With the Hausdorff property established, there is a good notion of completion for E ⊗ι F ,
which we denote as
(C.2.3.23)                                              E ⊗ F.
    As a consequence of Proposition C.2.3.11 and universal mapping properties of the inductive and projective
tensor product topologies, we have the following:

      Corollary C.2.3.12. Let E, F be two Fréchet spaces. Then the canonical continuous linear map
(C.2.3.24)                                        E ⊗ι F → E ⊗π F
is a linear topological isomorphism. In particular, the induced continuous linear map E ⊗ F → E ⊗
                                                                                                b π F between
completions is a topological isomorphism.
