    C.2.4. Nuclear spaces. The two topological tensor products ⊗π and ⊗ε of Hausdorff locally convex
topological C-vector spaces E, F are related: the projective topology ⊗π on E ⊗ F is finer than the injective
topology ⊗ε , which is to say the identity map
(C.2.4.1)                                      E ⊗π F → E ⊗ε F
is continuous. This is deduced from their respective universal properties (see [Tre, Prop. 43.5]).
     We are interested in two aspects relating to these two locally convex topologies on E ⊗ F :
(1) to discuss when (C.2.4.1) is a topological isomorphism;
(2) to illustrate when the natural map E ′ ⊗ F → LS (E, F ) has dense image with respect to suitable
    S-topologies, and which such topologies qualify.
These questions were the subject of a significant portion of Grothendieck’s doctoral dissertation, and we refer
the reader particularly to [Gro-b, Ch. I, §5; Ch. II, §3].

    C.2.4.1. Characterizations of nuclearity. The first of the two questions at hand, namely when the
continuous linear bijection E ⊗π F → E ⊗ε F is a homeomorphism for Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector spaces E, F , is best phrased as asking when for a fixed Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
space E the natural transformation E ⊗π (·) → E ⊗ε (·) of functors from Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector spaces to Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces is an isomorphism; i.e., when is
(C.2.4.1) a topological isomorphism for all F ?
    The second part of Grothendieck’s doctoral dissertation is devoted to answering and studying this question,
leading to the definition of nuclear spaces. The following is [Gro-b, Ch. II ,§2.1, Def. 4].

     Definition C.2.4.1 (Nuclear Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces). Let E be a Hausdorff
locally convex topological C-vector space. We say E is nuclear if and only if the identity map E ⊗π F → E ⊗ε F
is a linear topological isomorphism for every Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space F .

     It is equivalent to work with the completed tensor products in this definition, since the uncompleted
versions are Hausdorff (and so topologically embed into their completions). There is a different definition of
nuclearity given in [Scha, Ch. III, p. 100], but this is equivalent to the above definition by combining [Scha,
Ch. III, 7.2] with a long list of equivalents to Definition C.2.4.1 given in [Tre, Thm. 50.1].
     As simple as Definition C.2.4.1 appears, the theory of nuclearity cannot take off the ground without
concrete and usable characterizations. These all rest on the concept of nuclear operator between Banach
spaces, which we will be recalling throughout §C.3. We briefly recall for now a concrete characterization
(which however is not the definition) (see [Scha, Ch. III, Rem. to 7.1]): for E, F Banach spaces, a continuous
linear operator T : E → F is nuclear if and only if there exists an absolutely summable sequence {λk }k≥0 in C,
686            CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


a sequence {fk }k≥0 ⊂ E ′ converging to 0 (in the usual Banach-dual topology), and {xk }k≥0 ⊂ F converging
to 0 such that
                                               X
(C.2.4.2)                                 T =      λk (⟨·, fk ⟩E,E ′ )xk
                                                k≥0

where any such sum always converges pointwise on E. In particular, finite-rank linear maps are nuclear.
    With this concept in mind, nuclearity of a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E is
characterized as follows (see [Scha, Ch. III, 7.2(b)⇔(c)] and [Tre, Thm.50.1] for the proof):

   Theorem C.2.4.2 (Characterizations of nuclearity - I). Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector space. The following conditions are equivalent:
(1) E is nuclear.
(2) For any convex circled 0-neighborhood U ⊂ E, there exists a convex circled 0-neighborhood V ⊂ U such
    that the canonical continuous linear map E  bV → E bU is nuclear, where E  bU is the completion of E for the
    gauge semi-norm pU associated to U as in (C.1.2.1) and likewise for V .
(3) For any Banach space F , the canonical continuous linear map E ⊗     b πF → E ⊗ b ε F is a topological isomor-
    phism.
(4) For any Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space F , the canonical continuous linear map E ⊗ b πF →
    E⊗ b ε F is topological isomorphism.

    Upon defining the general concept of nuclear maps (not only for continuous linear maps between Banach
spaces), nuclearity for E as in the preceding theorem is further characterized by the following property of
E: for any Banach space F , any continuous linear map E → F is nuclear. For more characterizations of
nuclearity of spaces, see [Tre, Thm. 50.1].

     C.2.4.2. Continuous dual of E ⊗ε F . The proof of equivalences of the many characterizations of nuclearity
in [Tre, Thm.50.1] rests on a description of the continuous dual of E ⊗ε F (the uncompleted injective tensor
product of two Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces) provided in the fundamental [Tre,
Prop.49.1] in terms of integral bilinear forms on E × F that we now review.
     Integral bilinear forms and their use in describing the continuous dual of E ⊗ε F also underlie further
characterizations of nuclearity we will not need, such as combinatorial control over the equicontinuous subsets
of the continuous dual of a nuclear space resting on integration over compact (or weakly compact) Choquet
simplices, which turns out to characterize nuclearity and for which we refer the reader to [Jar, §21.4, Thm. 3,
p. 490].
     The description of the continuous dual of E ⊗ε F , which we will be recalling from [Tre, Prop.49.1] shortly
rests on the following construction that we wish to further explain before referring the reader to [Tre, Ch. 49,
p. 501] and the discussion contained therein. Recall that for any Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
space E and any convex circled and absorbing subset U (not necessarily a 0-neighborhood), we topologize the

local Banach space of E at U . By [Scha, Ch. II, 1.5], EbU only depends on the closure of U .

    We will be using below the following observation: by Lemma C.2.1.7, if E is barrelled then Eσ′ is quasi-
complete, and hence the (weakly-)closed convex circled hull of a weakly compact subset of Eσ′ is weakly
compact. This is a consequence of the preservation of pre-compactness (i.e., compactness of closure in the
completion) under formation of the convex circled hull in any Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
space [Scha, Ch. II, 4.3]. Indeed, in a quasi-complete Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space F any
pre-compact subset C ⊂ F is bounded in Fb (as compactness implies boundedness) and hence is bounded in F .
Thus, the closure C ⊂ F is bounded [Scha, Ch. I, 5.1] and thus is complete in F (as F is quasi-complete), so
C is also closed in F . By pre-compactness of C in Fb, this gives the compactness of C as desired.
    Remark C.2.4.5. The barreledness of E above as a sufficient condition for quasi-completeness of Eσ′
cannot be entirely dropped: there are examples of Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces E for
which Eσ′ is not quasi-complete.
    We refer the reader to [Gro-e, II, §1, p. 88] for an example of a Fréchet space F whose strong dual
E := Fβ′ is not bornological (equivalently, not barrelled; see [Scha, Ch. IV, 6.6]) and whose weak dual Eσ′ is
not quasi-complete. To see this example is not quasi-complete, we assume to the contrary that the nuclear
space Eσ′ is quasi-complete and seek a contradiction. 15

    C.2.4.4. Permanence properties. Nuclearity satisfies the following permanence properties, contained within
[Scha, Ch. III, 7.4, 7.5].
    Lemma C.2.4.10 (Permanence properties). Nuclearity of Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
spaces is stable under passage to:
(1) linear topological subspaces, Hausdorff quotients by linear subspaces;
(2) linear topological products indexed by an arbitrary set, countable topological direct sums;
(3) binary projective tensor products (i.e. if two Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces E, F are
    nuclear then E ⊗π F is nuclear).
    We further recall the following nuclearity criterion from [Tre, Prop. 50.6]:17
     Lemma C.2.4.11 (Duality and nuclearity for Fréchet spaces). Let E be a Fréchet space. Then E is nuclear
if and only if so is Eβ′ .
    We will use the following permanence properties that follow from Lemma C.2.4.10(1, 2):
   Lemma C.2.4.12 (Nuclearity of inductive and projective limits). A Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector space E is nuclear if any of the following conditions hold:
(1) E is the locally convex inductive limit of a sequence of nuclear Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
    spaces.
(2) E is a projective limit, indexed by an arbitrary co-filtered set, of nuclear Hausdorff locally convex topological
    C-vector spaces.
    Remark C.2.4.13. The Hausdorff assumption on E is also assumed18 in [Gro-b, Ch. II, §2, no. 2, Cor. 1]
insofar as it is necessary to deduce nuclearity from presenting the locally convex inductive limit as a separated
quotient of a nuclear locally convex topological direct sum. The assumption is needed since separatedness
is not generally inherited by locally convex inductive limits. We have specialized part (1) to the case the
inductive system of nuclear spaces is comprised of Hausdorff spaces too.
     Remark C.2.4.14. We further refer the reader to [Scha, Ch.III, §7] for a discussion of the above results
from the second part of Grothendieck’s dissertation, noting that the Hausdorff property is part of the definition
of “locally convex topological vector space” in [Scha, Ch. II, p. 47].

     The next lemma records two properties of main interest for us about nuclear spaces beyond their defining
condition from Definition C.2.4.1. The first of the two properties stated in the lemma will be used systematically
throughout this work to infer that certain Fréchet spaces, or strict inductive limits of Fréchet spaces, are
reflexive by deducing that they are Montel via [Tre, Cor. 3 to Prop. 50.2], which asserts that any nuclear
Hausdorff locally convex C-vector space that is also barreled and quasi-complete is Montel (all Fréchet spaces
are barreled [Scha, Ch. II, Cor. to 7.1]). The second will be used to infer that in the presence of the equivalent
conditions from Lemma C.2.4.15, the traces of nuclear operators (to be discussed in §C.3) can be computed as
matrix traces relative to a Schauder basis if one exists.

topological C-vector space. Assume E is nuclear.
(1) Every bounded subset of E is pre-compact. In particular, for any Hausdorff locally convex topological
    C-vector space F , Lγ (E, F ) = Lβ (E, F ).
(2) The image of E ′ ⊗ E under λ from (C.2.4.6) is dense in Lγ (E, E) (so all four properties in Lemma
    (C.2.4.15) hold).
      Proof. Part (1) is [Scha, Ch. III, Cor. 2 to 7.2], and part (2) is [Scha, Ch. III, Cor. 2 to 9.1].        □

are dense) where the target has the topology of convergence on the bounded subsets of E.

    C.2.5. Complements on the finest locally convex topology. Finite-dimensional C-vector spaces
have a unique Hausdorff topological vector space structure [Scha, Ch. I, 3.2]. Building on that, as a piece of
algebra, there is the notion of finest locally convex topology on a C-vector space E. This can be described
in two ways (which must therefore coincide): it is defined by the family of all seminorms on E, and it is
the locally convex inductive limit of the collection of finite-dimensional subspaces. This will be used only in
countable-dimensional cases, so such spaces are then even strict LF-spaces.
    One example is the Schwartz-Bruhat function space S(Fv ) = Cc∞ (Fv ) for F a number field and v a finite
place of F . Another such example is S( v∈S Fv ) for S a finite set of finite places of F , as are S(AfF ) (for AfF
                                          Q

the finite adeles of F ) and S( b v∈S
                                   / (Fv , OFv )) for S any finite set of places of F containing the Archimedean
                               Q

places of F . In this subsection we record some basic facts about this topology, most of which are elementary.
     Proposition C.2.5.1 (Properties of the finest locally convex topology). Let E be a C-vector space, τ its
finest locally convex topology.
(1) The topology τ is defined by the family of all seminorms on E, and is the locally convex inductive limit of
    all finite-dimensional subspaces of E.
(2) For any Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space M , any linear map T : E → M is continuous.
    In particular, the inclusion (E, τ )′ ⊂ E ∗ is an equality of vector spaces.
(3) Every C-linear subspace of E is τ -closed and topologically complemented, so τ is inherited by all C-linear
    subspaces and quotients of E. Moreover, (E, τ ) is complete.
19This result is [Tre, Prop. 50.5] without needing any of the extra generalities above, none of which are therefore ever cited, so
why include any of the stuff above?
692            CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


(4) A subset B ⊂ E is τ -bounded if and only if it is contained in a finite-dimensional subspace of E and
    bounded with respect to the Euclidean topology on such a subspace.
(5) A subset C ⊂ E is τ -sequentially closed if and only if its intersection with each finite-dimensional C-linear
    subspace of E is closed.
(6) If E is has countable dimension then (E, τ ) is a nuclear strict LF-space. In particular, with respect to τ
    any such E is complete, nuclear and Montel, and its strong dual Eβ′ is a nuclear Fréchet space.

     Proof. We discussed (1) already (namely both descriptions are finest among all locally convex topologies,
so they must coincide). The assertion in (2) is immediate from the description as a locally convex inductive
limit. To see (3), if E0 ⊂ E is a C-linear subspace and E1 ⊂ E is a linear complement then for the respective
finest locally convex topologies τj on Ej we see that E0 ⊕ E1 → E is a topological isomorphism since every
finite-dimensional subspace of E is contained in F0 ⊕ F1 for finite-dimensional subspaces Fj ⊂ Ej .
     The completeness of (E, τ ) is immediate from yet another description of τ as a locally convex direct
sum of lines, since completeness is inherited by arbitrary locally convex direct sums [Scha, Ch. II, 6.2]. This
description via a direct sum of lines yields the assertion in (4) from a general property of bounded subsets of
locally convex direct sums [Scha, Ch. II, 6.3]. Since convergent sequences in a Hausdorff topological vector
space are bounded, the sufficiency in (5) is immediate from (4). The necessity in (5) is clear.
     Finally, in the countable-dimensional case we can express E as a strict countable inductive limit of
finite-dimensional spaces, so E is a nuclear strict LF-space since finite-dimensional spaces are certainly nuclear
and strict countable inductive limits preserve nuclearity [Scha, Ch. III, Cor. to 7.4]. Likewise the Montel
property is preserved by such inductive limits [Scha, p. 147], so E is Montel. Nuclearity of Eβ′ is inherited
from that of E because E is a nuclear Fréchet space [Tre, Prop. 50.6]. Completeness of Eβ′ is a consequence
of the bornological property of E [Scha, Ch. IV, 6.1], where the bornological property is inherited through
inductive limits from the finite-dimensional case [Scha, Ch. II, Cor. 1 to 8.2].
     It remains to show in (6) that Eβ′ is metrizable. Since E is a locally convex countable direct sum of lines,
which in turn can be viewed as the strict locally convex direct limit of finite direct sums among such lines,
Lemma C.1.6.1(2) yields that the strong dual is the locally convex countable product of (the duals of such)
lines. The topology on such a product is the product topology, so the metrizability is immediate from the
countability of the product.                                                                                    □

    One final permanence property of the finest locally convex topology concerns stability under tensor
products in the countable-dimensional case:

     Lemma C.2.5.2. Let E1 , E2 be two Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces. Assume E1 , E2
are countably C-linearly generated, and carry the finest locally convex topology. Then so do E1 ⊗π E2 , E1 ⊗ε E2
and E1 ⊗ι E2 , so all three topologies on E1 ⊗ E2 coincide and are complete.

    Proof. The completeness of the finest locally convex topology on any C-vector space is part of Proposition
C.2.5.1(3). Since E1 , E2 are nuclear, the continuous linear map E1 ⊗ε E2 → E1 ⊗π E2 given by the identity
on E1 ⊗ E2 is a topological isomorphism by Theorem C.2.4.2(4) (this gives isomorphism after passing to
completions, but both topological tensor products topologically embed into their completions and so we get
the assertion without passing to completions). Thus, it suffices to analyze the projective topology and the
inductive topology on E1 ⊗ E2 .
    By (C.2.3.26), E1 ⊗ι E2 carries the finest locally convex topology on E1 ⊗ E2 . Since E1 and E2 are
each topologically a locally convex direct sum of lines (with their unique Hausdorff topological vector space
structure), and lines are normable, by Proposition C.2.3.9(1) it follows that E1 ⊗π E2 is also a locally convex
direct sum of countably many lines; i.e., this projective tensor product topology is the finest locally convex
topology on E1 ⊗ E2 .                                                                                        □
                                          C.3. NUCLEAR OPERATORS                                            693


                                          C.3. Nuclear operators
    In this section we collect results on nuclear operators. We will be first discussing a few complements
on nuclear operators on general Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces, with emphasis on
a factorization principle enabling the computation of nuclear traces of nuclear operators equipped with a
factorization through a continuous injective linear map between Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
spaces. This has appeared before in [Me1, §4, Cor. 4.7, p. 28], and we discuss it here in detail for ease of
access.
    We will then focus on the case of nuclear operators on Hilbert spaces, and methods to compute their traces.
We will first discuss some complements on the strong operator topology (i.e., pointwise convergence) on the
C-algebra of continuous endomorphisms on a Hilbert space, then recall the basic properties of Hilbert-Schmidt
and nuclear operators on a Hilbert space and several convergence results of compositions with sequences of
orthogonal projectors and more general self-adjoint operators. We include proofs of some of these results for
ease of access.
    We will then briefly discuss the Schatten-von Neumann classes of index p = 1, 2 for operators between two
(possibly distinct) Hilbert spaces. We conclude this section on nuclear operators with a discussion of a special
class of nuclear operators: those associated to a measurable integral kernel on Hilbert spaces of the special
form L2 (X, µ), for X a Hausdorff locally compact topological space and µ a Radon measure on X. We will
discuss how to “smoothen” their integral kernel along the diagonal, and use that smoothening to compute
nuclear traces.

    C.3.1. Preparations. Let E, F be Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces. For Banach E,
the strong dual Eβ′ for E Banach has its topology defined by the dual norm ||φ|| = sup||x||≤1 |φ(x)|. In general
there is a canonical continuous linear map
(C.3.1.1)                                   Eβ′ ⊗π F → Lβ (E, F ).
The target has the topology of uniform convergence on bounded sets, so for Banach E and F it is the
operator-norm topology and so in such cases the target is complete. Thus, for Banach E and F , (C.3.1.1)
uniquely extends by continuity to a continuous linear map
(C.3.1.2)                                       b π F → Lβ (E, F ).
                                            Eβ′ ⊗
For Banach E and F , nuclear maps in Lβ (E, F ) are defined to be those in the range of (C.3.1.2); these have
an explicit description as in (C.2.4.2).

    Remark C.3.1.1. Beyond the Banach setting there is another class of sufficient conditions for completeness
of the target of (C.3.1.1), with a stronger conclusion: if E and F are complete, E is barreled, and Eβ′ is
nuclear and complete (these hold when E and F are Banach with E nuclear; see [Tre, Prop. 50.6] for the
nuclearity of Eβ′ when E is nuclear Fréchet), [Tre, Prop. 50.5] gives that the target of (C.3.1.1) is complete
and the resulting continuous linear extension in (C.3.1.2) is a topological isomorphism.

    To extend the concept of nuclearity for continuous linear maps T : E → F beyond the Banach setting,
consider a convex circled absorbing subset U ⊂ E (e.g., a convex circled 0-neighborhood). By the absorbing
property, U spans E linearly. The separated completion of the seminormed space (E, pU ), with pU : E → R≥0
the Minkowski functional of U from (C.1.2.1), is denoted E    bU and is a Banach space.
    Given instead a bounded convex circled subset B ⊂ E, the linear span EB = ∪m≥1 mB of B in E equipped
with its Minkowski functional pB : EB → R≥0 is also a normed space (i.e. its semi-normed topology is already
separated). If (EB , pB ) is a Banach space already before completion, we refer to B as a Banach disc.
    For E, F two locally convex topological C-vector spaces, a continuous linear operator T : E → F is termed
nuclear if and only if there exists a convex circled 0-neighborhood U ⊂ E and a Banach disc B in F , such that
694           CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


T (U ) ⊂ B, and the induced linear map T : E   bU → FB is nuclear within L (E bU , FB ) between Banach spaces;
i.e., it is of the form recalled in (C.2.4.2).
      Every nuclear operator between two Banach spaces E, F is in particular a limit in the topology of bounded
convergence (and so in any coarser S-topology) of finite-rank operators since (C.3.1.1) is continuous. This
holds more generally for nuclear maps between Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces, with the
explicit description (C.2.4.2) in the Banach case replaced by a mildly generalized description as follows (see
[Scha, Ch. III, 7.1, Remark] for a proof):

     C.3.3. Topologies on the endomorphism algebra of a Hilbert space. We recall that a Hausdorff
locally convex topological complex vector space E is complete if and only if it is complete as a uniform space
(every topological vector space has a canonical uniform structure, and it is with respect to this structure that
completeness is defined in [Scha, Ch. I, pp. 6-10]), equivalently if and only if every Cauchy net converges to an
element of E. We further refer the reader to [NB, §3.1] for more on completeness, and to [NB, Thm. 3.1.6]
for the dictionary between Cauchy nets and Cauchy filter-bases.
     Completeness for a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space E that is already quasi-complete is a
genuinely stronger condition than quasi-completeness. The key issue is that completeness entails every Cauchy
net converging to an element of E, while quasi-completeness is the condition that any bounded Cauchy net is
convergent. Cauchy sequences are bounded, but generally not Cauchy nets.
     For example, for a Fréchet space E (so it is barreled [Scha, Ch. II, Cor. to 7.1]), the weak topology Eσ′
on E ′ is quasi-complete by Lemma C.2.1.7 but the topological embedding Eσ(E      ′            ∗
                                                                                     ′ ,E) ,→ Eσ(E ∗ ,E) is identified

with the completion (see Lemma C.4.1.2 for a self-contained argument via some literature references). The
algebraic dual E ∗ strictly contains E ′ when E is infinite-dimensional, so in such cases Eσ′ is quasi-complete
but not complete. In metrizable locally convex topological vector spaces, it was explained after Definition
C.1.3.1 that the concepts of completeness and metric (equivalently sequential) completeness coincide, and
these both agree with quasi-completeness because Cauchy sequences in a Hausdorff topological vector space
are always bounded.
     For H a complex Hilbert space, we denote by B(H) the C-vector space of all bounded linear operators
on H. Recall that the strong operator topology, denoted “SOT”, on B(H) is the topology of pointwise
convergence, generated by the family of seminorms
(C.3.3.1)                                    qu (T ) := ||T (u)||H , u ∈ H
                                           C.3. NUCLEAR OPERATORS                                              697


where || · ||H is the norm on H. The operator-norm of a bounded linear operator T : H → H is defined as
(C.3.3.2)                                  ||T || :=       sup         ||T (u)||
                                                       u∈H,||u||H ≤1

and promotes B(H) to a Banach space. We denote it by BSOT (H) when endowed with the strong operator
topology, and BNT (H) when endowed with the operator-norm topology.

    Lemma C.3.3.1 (Properties of the strong-operator topology). Let H be a complex Hilbert space.
(1) If H is separable then every bounded subset in BSOT (H) is metrizable.
(2) BSOT (H) is Hausdorff locally convex and quasi-complete.

    Proof. (1) : This is [Cnw-a, Ch. IX, Prop. 1.3(e)], where “bounded” is meant for the norm topology on
B(H), which is the same as boundedness in BSOT (H) by [Scha, Ch. III, 3.4].
    (2) : The locally convex strong operator topology on B(H) is clearly Hausdorff. Let {Ti }i∈I be a bounded
Cauchy net in BSOT (H), with I a directed set. Since the evaluation maps eϕ : B(H) → H sending T to
eϕ := T (ϕ) for every ϕ ∈ H are continuous with respect to the strong operator topology, the net {Ti (ϕ)}i∈I
is Cauchy and hence it converges in H since H is complete. We call T (ϕ) the limit in H. By the Uniform
Boundedness Principle [Scha, Ch. III, Cor. to 4.2], supi∈I ||Ti || is finite. Thus, T is a bounded linear operator
on H and Ti converges to T in the strong operator topology by design. This proves that every bounded
Cauchy net of BSOT (H) converges in BSOT (H).                                                                   □

    We further refer the reader to Remark 4.3.1.6, for more on the topology of BSOT (H) specifically, and
on topological properties of the topological group of unitary operators on a Hilbert space in the special case
H = L2 (G, µ) for a second-countable Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G and a choice of Haar measure
µ on G.

     C.3.4. Trace-class operators on Hilbert spaces. Hilbert spaces have the approximation property by
[Scha, Ch. III, Cor. 1 to 9.2]. Nuclear endomorphisms of a Hilbert space are exactly the trace-class operators
(see [Kub, Thm.6.1]), and serve as a familiar example.

    C.3.4.1. Trace-class operators: definitions and basic properties. In the special case of Hilbert spaces, we
favor the notation BNT (H) over Lβ (H), and BSOT (H) over Lσ (H), the former being endowed with the
norm topology, the latter with the strong operator topology.

    Lemma C.3.4.1. Let H be a Hilbert space. Let Σ be an orthonormal basis of H. If T ∈ BNT (H) is nuclear
(equivalently, trace-class) then:
                      P
(1) the infinite sum ϕ∈Σ |⟨T (ϕ), ϕ⟩H | converges;’ i.e., ⟨T (ϕ), ϕ⟩H vanishes for all but countably many ϕ, and
    the sum of the countably many nonzero ones is absolutely convergent.
                            P
(2) The value of the sum ϕ∈Σ |⟨T (ϕ), ϕ⟩H | is independent of the choice of Σ.
                                                P
(3) The value of the absolutely convergent sum ϕ∈Σ ⟨T (ϕ), ϕ⟩H is independent of the choice of Σ.

    We refer the reader to [Cnw-c, Ch. 3, Prop. 18.9] for the proof of Lemma C.3.4.1. The following is [Cnw-c,
Ch. 3, Def. 18.10]:

    Lemma C.3.4.3. Let H be a Hilbert space, A a compact operator on H, Q ∈ B(H). Let {Qm }m≥0 be a
sequence of bounded operators on H such that Qm → Q in BSOT (H). Then Qm A → QA with respect to the
operator-norm topology, i.e. in BNT (H).
     Proof. By [Cnw-a, Ch. II, Thm. 4.4(c)], there exists a sequence {Ak }k≥0 of operators on H of finite
rank, such that ||Ak − A|| → 0 as k → +∞. Let ε > 0 and choose k0 ≥ 0 so large that we have ||Ak − A|| < ε/2
for all k ≥ k0 .
    We have ||Qm (Ak − A)|| ≤ ||Qm || ||Ak − A||, which is bounded above by 2ε ||Qm || for all k ≥ k0 . Since
{Qm }m≥0 ⊂ BSOT (H) is a convergent Cauchy sequence, hence bounded, by the Uniform Boundedness
Principle there exists a positive real number L > 0 such that supm≥0 ||Qm || < L. It follows that we have, for
every k ≥ k0 and every integer m ≥ 0:

(C.3.4.1)                                   ||Qm (Ak − A)|| ≤    .
                                                              2

(C.3.4.2) ||(Qm − Qm′ )A|| ≤ ||(Qm − Qm′ )A − (Qm − Qm′ )Ak )|| + ||(Qm − Qm′ )Ak || ≤ Lε + ||(Qm − Qm′ )Ak ||.

      Since A is therefore a finite sum of rank-1 operators, we may and do assume A is an operator of rank 1;

      Lemma C.3.4.4. Let H be a Hilbert space. Then:

    normed space.

(C.3.4.3)                               ||AT ||Tr = ||T A||Tr ≤ ||A|| ||T ||Tr .

    || · ||Tr -topology.
(4) N(H) contains the range of H ′ ⊗π H → BNT (H) as a dense linear subspace. In particular, N(H) is
    separable as a normed space if H is separable as a Hilbert space.
(5) Let {Pi }i∈I ⊂ B(H) be a net of bounded operators strongly converging to zero. Let F ∈ B(H) be a
    finite-rank operator. Then {Pi F }i∈I converges to zero in N(H), i.e. with respect to the trace-norm
    topology.
    Proof. Since the concepts of nuclear operator and of trace-class operator are equivalent for endomorphisms
of a Hilbert space (see [Kub, Thm.6.1]), we use the theory of trace-class operators.
    (1) : This is [Cnw-c, Ch. 3, Thm. 18.11(a)].
    (2) : This is [Cnw-c, Ch. 3, Thm. 18.11(g, e)].

     (5) : Let m be the rank of F , and let {αi,1 , . . . , αi,ki } be (without multiplicity) the eigenvalues of |Pi F |,
which is a positive, compact, self-adjoint operator. Note that since Pi F is of finite rank, so is (Pi F )∗ · (Pi F ),
and hence so is its square-root |Pi F |. The ranks of each are bounded above by m, and hence ki ≤ m, and each
αi,n is a nonnegative real number. We may order the αi,n increasingly, and assume αi,ki is their maximum.
Since F is finite-rank and Pi → 0 in BSOT (H), then Pi F → 0 in norm. The norm of each Pi F is αi,ki , and
hence the net {αi,ki } tends to zero.
               P
      The sum 1≤n≤ki αi,n is the trace-norm of Pi F for each i ∈ I, and since ki ≤ m for each i ∈ I, we have
||Pi F ||Tr ≤ mαi,ki → 0, and so Pi F → 0 in N(H).                                                                    □

    C.3.6. Schatten-von Neumann classes of index p = 1, 2. In this subsection we continue to discuss

    C.3.7. Integral kernels. We further recall here a result describing a class of examples of nuclear
operators, and how to compute their trace. For X a Hausdorff locally compact second-countable topological
space, and µ a Radon measure on X, we consider the Hilbert space L2 (X, µ) of µ-measurable square µ-integrable
functions on X, topologized with the L2 -norm topology.
    A nuclear operator A on E := L2 (X, µ) is, in particular, Hilbert-Schmidt (see [Cnw-c, Prop.18.8(c)]); i.e.,
A ∈ Sp (E) for p = 1, 2, and it therefore corresponds to a unique element of E ′ ⊗
                                                                                 b σ E (see Proposition C.3.6.4)
               ′ b                      2
which, since E ⊗ σ E is isometric to L (X × X, µ ⊗ µ), corresponds to a unique (µ ⊗ µ)-measurable function
k(x, y) ∈ L2 (X × X, µ ⊗ µ) such that the effect of A on ϕ ∈ L2 (X, µ) is by convolution, i.e. we have
                                                   Z
                                         (Aϕ)(x) =     k(x, y)ϕ(y) dµ(y)
                                                      X
as µ-measurable and square µ-integrable functions on X.
    Characterizing nuclearity of A in terms of the integral kernel k is a non-trivial task. In the special case A
is positive, this is indeed possible. Using an analog of the Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Theorem and an analog
of Lebesgue’s Differentiation Theorem (for which we refer the reader to the discussion in §A.5.1 and §A.5.2,
§A.5.3 and §A.5.4 of Appendix A.5 in the special case X = G is a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group
equipped with a D′ -sequence, which serves the same purpose of the open balls in Euclidean spaces through
the proof of the inequalities of the Maximal Theorem, and their application to the Differentiation Theorem),
which the reader will find discussed in an axiomatized manner using martingales in [Bris-a, §2, pp. 231-2],
and in [Bris-b, §2, p. 1182] in the case of Euclidean spaces (and more general subsets of Euclidean spaces), we
can “smoothen” the kernel function k(x, y) along the diagonal in X × X (which is a (µ ⊗ µ)-null set, on whose
points the kernel function may be undefined), to define a new µ-measurable function e     k(x, x) out of k(x, y). It
turns out (see [Bris-a, Thm. 4.2, p. 238]) that A is nuclear if and only if k(x, x) is absolutely µ-integrable as a
                                                                            e
µ-measurable function of x ∈ X defined µ-almost everywhere.
    Beyond the case of positive operators this characterization breaks down, as illustrated by means of an
example (see [Bris-b, Example 3.2, p. 1186] for the well known example of the Volterra operator on L2 ([0, 1], λ),
with λ the normalized Lebesgue measure on R, which is a Hilbert-Schmidt operator whose kernel has an
absolutely integrable smoothening along the diagonal).
    It is always possible to factorize a nuclear operator on a Hilbert space as the composition of two Hilbert-
Schmidt operators, and it turns out that the convolution of their own Hilbert-Schmidt kernels makes sense
along the diagonal (i.e., away from a subset of the diagonal of µ-measure zero, it agrees with the smoothening
708            CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


of the kernel function associated to the nuclear operator itself, viewed as a Hilbert-Schmidt operator; see
[Bris-a, Thm. 3.3, p. 238]).
    This observation is used, for example, in [Arthur, §3,Lemma 3.8,p.353] (where the kernels H ′ and H ′′ are
Hilbert-Schmidt kernels, whose convolution is the kernel H whose associated operator is nuclear and whose
trace is being computed in the Lemma) in the process of proving instances of the classical Arthur-Selberg
trace formula.
    If the operator A is assumed to be nuclear, then the smoothening of its Hilbert-Schmidt kernel along the
diagonal (in whichever way it is computed, whether through Lebesgue’s Differentiation or by convolution of
two factor Hilbert-Schmidt kernels) can be used to compute its nuclear trace. This is an important result,
which generalizes a classical Theorem of Mercer (see [Bris-b, Prop. 1.2, p. 1182]) asserting that when the
Hilbert-Schmidt kernel of the nuclear operator A is continuous as a function of (x, y) ∈ X × X then its integral
along the diagonal as a function of (x, x) and with respect to the Radon measure µ on X equals the nuclear
trace of A.

    Theorem C.3.7.1 (Trace formula for integral nuclear operators). Let X be a Hausdorff locally compact

          and

                                                         X

                                 C.4. Integration in the sense of Pettis
     One essential tool to analyze holomorphic scalar-valued functions is contour integration. We now discuss
its counterpart for vector-valued functions, with a view towards the applications of interest, with values in a
locally convex space that is generally not Banach. We have selected the integral in the sense of Pettis, and
we will be collecting the necessary foundations throughout this section. The material in this section will be
used for integration of certain linear operators varying continuously over a Hausdorff locally compact abelian
topological group.
     All locally convex topological vector spaces throughout this section will be Hausdorff and over the complex
numbers.
                                     C.4. INTEGRATION IN THE SENSE OF PETTIS                                         709


    C.4.1. Weak completion. We begin by recalling a few facts about the relation of a Hausdorff locally
convex topological C-vector space E, and the algebraic dual (E ′ )∗ of its continuous dual E ′ .
    The algebraic dual of a complex vector space V is simply the complex vector space V ∗ of all C-linear
forms on it. If V and W are two such spaces equipped with a bilinear pairing
                                                  ⟨·, ·⟩ : V × W → C
yielding linear injections V ,→ W ∗ and W ,→ V ∗ then we say “V and W are in duality” and write ⟨V, W ⟩ to
denoted this data (as in [Scha, Ch. IV, §1]).
     We recall that on a Hausdorff locally convex topological complex vector space E, we find the locally
convex weak topology σ(E, E ′ ) generated by the family of seminorms
                                                       qφ : E → R≥0
defined by qφ (u) := |φ(u)| as φ varies over E ′ . By the Hahn-Banach Theorem, σ(E, E ′ ) is Hausdorff. We
sometimes refer to the given topology on E as the initial topology, as in [Bou-TVS, p. IV.4] (where σ(E, E ′ )
is referred to as the weakened topology on E).
     Among the Hausdorff locally convex topologies T on E, a special class are those for which E ′ is the
subspace of E ∗ consisting of T -continuous linear functionals; these are called polar topologies, or consistent
with the pairing between E and E ′ . The weak topology is polar, as is the Mackey topology τ (E, E ′ ) defined as
the topology of uniform convergence in E on the weakly-compact convex circled subsets in E ′ . Among the
topologies such that the continuous dual of E remains E ′ , σ(E, E ′ ) is the coarsest and τ (E, E ′ ) the finest
(and the initial topology sits between them); see [Scha, Ch. IV, §3-§4] for more on such topologies. We will
now look into σ(E, E ′ ) more closely.
     Given a locally convex topological complex vector space E, there exists a canonical C-linear map
(C.4.1.1)                                           ιE : E → (E ′ )∗
sending u ∈ E to the C-linear form ιE (u) on (E ′ )∗ taking a continuous linear form φ ∈ E ′ to φ(u). This is
injective by the Hahn-Banach Theorem [Scha, Ch. III, Cor. 1 to 4.2].
    The map ιE enjoys the following naturality property:

    Lemma C.4.1.1. Let E, E1 , E2 be Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces. Then ιE from
(C.4.1.1) is injective and the σ((E ′ )∗ , E ′ )-topology on (E ′ )∗ induces the σ(E, E ′ )-topology on E as the subspace
topology. Moreover:
(1) The C-linear injection ιE : E → (E ′ )∗ is continuous with respect to the initial topology on the source and
    the σ((E ′ )∗ , E ′ )-topology on the target.
(2) For any continuous C-linear operator T : E1 → E2 , the algebraic dual map T ∗ : E2∗ → E1∗ restricts to a
    C-linear map T ′ : E2′ → E1′ and this is continuous with respect to the σ(E2′ , E2 )-topology on the source and
    the σ(E1′ , E1 )-topology on the target. Moreover, the algebraic dual (T ′ )∗ : (E1′ )∗ → (E2′ )∗ of the topological
    dual T ′ is continuous with respect to σ((E1′ )∗ , E1′ ) and σ((E2′ )∗ , E2′ ), and the following diagram

(C.4.1.2)                                           E1
                                                              T         / E2
                                                 ιE1                           ιE2
                                                                          
                                                  (E1′ )∗             / (E2′ )∗
                                                            (T ′ )∗

    commutes.

   Proof. Assertion (1) is a matter of unraveling definitions (continuity even holds using σ(E, E ′ ) on E).
Then (2) is also definition-chasing.                                                                      □

    C.4.2. Vector-valued measurable and integrable functions. We recall that for a complex Borel
measure µ on a locally compact Hausdorff space X, µ is a Radon measure if and only if the total variation |µ|
of µ is a Radon measure (see [Fol, Thm. 7.16]). Moreover, ||µ|| := |µ|(X) is a norm on the complex vector
space of complex bounded Radon measures on X. For X that is also second-countable, every complex Borel
measure finite on compact subsets is Radon by [Fol, Thm. 7.8].
    Definition C.4.2.1. Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff space and µ a Radon measure on X. Let E

(1) f is weakly measurable if and only if for every φ ∈ E ′ , the function φ ◦ f : X → C is µ-measurable.

    Remark C.4.2.2. When E is a Banach space, there is Bochner’s theory of E-valued integration that can
be developed in a style similar to scalar-valued integration, as is done for example in [Lang-d, Ch. VI]. Any
f : X → E that is integrable in the sense of Bochner is also integrable in the sense of Pettis with the same
         R
value for X f dµ ∈ E, since the formation of the Bochner integral commutes with continuous linear mappings
E → F (such as a continuous linear functional E → C).
    The relation between the two theories is often not needed in this work because (as was noted §C.1.4)
the Banach-valued theory is often not applicable due to infinite-dimensional nuclear spaces E never being
normable [Tre, Cor. 2 to Prop. 50.2]. Nonetheless, the Bochner integral often agrees with the integral in the
                                   C.4. INTEGRATION IN THE SENSE OF PETTIS                                      711


sense of Pettis when E is a Banach space. Specifically, we may deduce (from [Za, Ch. 6, §31, p. 222,(e)], for
instance) as a consequence of Pettis’ Separable Measurability Theorem (see [DU, Ch. II, §1, Thm. 2]) that the
two integrals coincide when the function is continuous and weakly integrable on a locally compact Hausdorff
Radon space and valued in a separable Banach space. For all the intended purposes of this work, the two
theories of integration will coincide when both are available.
    C.4.3. Integrability criteria and permanence properties. We recall that C(X), the C-vector space
of continuous complex-valued functions on the topological space X, is a Banach space with respect to the
uniform norm if X is a compact Hausdorff topological space. The C-linear space M (X) of complex Radon
measures on X is its continuous dual [Fol, Thm. 7.1, Cor. 7.18], with ||µ|| as the dual norm on M (X). In
particular, for such compact Hausdorff X, by Agaoglu’s Theorem [Scha, Ch. III, Cor. to 4.3; Ch. IV, 3.1]
the subset M ≤1 (X) of such measures µ with ||µ|| ≤ 1 is weakly-compact (i.e., compact with respect to
σ(M (X), C(X))). We refer to the weak topology on M (X) (i.e., the σ(M (X), C(X))-topology) as the vague
topology as in [Fol, p. 223].

    Remark C.4.3.3. In the proof of Theorem C.4.3.2, we used properties of the σ(M (X), C(X))-topology
for X a compact Hausdorff topological space.
    Vague continuity on the cone of positive Radon measures can be thought of as a generalization of an
analog of the Monotone Convergence Theorem, while continuity on weakly bounded subsets of M (X) can be
thought as being in a similar vein as the Dominated Convergence Theorem.
     We are going to be routinely making two assumptions on E throughout our work, aside from E being
locally convex: that E be Hausdorff, and quasi-complete. In our situations of interest, these will always be
satisfied. This and Lemma C.4.3.1 provide an integrability criterion for continuous compactly supported
functions (see Theorem C.4.3.5 below).
     A priori, the linear form X f dµ is only contained in the weak completion (E ′ )∗ of E (see the start of
                               R

Lemma C.4.3.1). For the purposes of this work, there will be two avenues to decide when a weakly integrable
function f : X → E is integrable (in the sense of Definition C.4.2.1(3)). Quasi-completeness of E is one of
them. The definition of quasi-completeness is that every bounded closed subset of E is complete. (Here we are
using boundedness in the sense of locally convex topological vector spaces.) This is equivalent to saying that
every bounded Cauchy net in E converges in E. It is therefore also referred to as bounded completeness. We
refer the reader to [Scha, Ch. I, 5.6; Ch. II, Cor. to 4.3] for some properties of quasi-complete Hausdorff locally
convex topological vector spaces.
    Remark C.4.3.4 (Cautionary remark on boundedness and net-convergence). For the purposes of checking
convergence or continuity in a Hausdorff topological vector space with nets, we are allowed to test such
                                  C.4. INTEGRATION IN THE SENSE OF PETTIS                                      713


conditions upon replacing an I-indexed net {xi }i∈I with the resulting I0 -indexed net obtained by restriction
to I0 ⊂ I, with I0 := {i ∈ I : i ≥ i0 }, for some fixed arbitrary i0 ∈ I; we refer to {xi }i≥i0 as a tail of the
original net. It is elementary that every Cauchy sequence in a topological C-vector space E is bounded (in
the sense of topological vector spaces), but in metrizable locally convex topological C-vector spaces even a
convergent net can fail to be “eventually bounded” (i.e., no tail {xi }i≥i0 is bounded).
      To make examples, we begin with the simpler construction of an unbounded convergent net. Let I = R>0
equipped with its natural ordering. Define za := a−1 ∈ C for each a ∈ I. The net of complex numbers
{za }a∈I is convergent to 0 ∈ C, but the net is not bounded in C. However, this net is eventually bounded;
e.g., {za }a≥1 is bounded.
      To make a net converging to 0 in the meterizable case such that the net is not eventually bounded, consider
an infinite-dimensional nuclear metrizable locally convex space F (such as the Schwartz space S(R)) and pick
a decreasing base of convex 0-neighborhoods U1 ⊃ U2 ⊃ · · · (this exists by metrizability). For each nonzero
x ∈ U1 , define n(x) to be the largest positive integer N such that x ∈ UN , and let J be the set U1 − {0} with
the partial ordering x ≥ y precisely when n(x) ≥ n(y). Defining xj = j ∈ U1 , the net {xj }j∈J converges to 0
and we claim no tail {xj }j≥j0 is bounded. Suppose to the contrary that some such tail is bounded, so the
convex 0-neighborhood Un(xj0 ) is bounded. Then F is normable [Scha, Ch. II„ 2.1], but a nuclear normable
locally convex space is finite-dimensional [Tre, Cor. 2 to Prop. 50.2], a contradiction.
      In the non-metrizable locally convex case, to make a Cauchy set that is not eventually bounded (as will
also help to make examples that are quasi-complete but not complete, a distinction that does not arise in
the metrizable setting), let H be an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space and E := BSOT (H) be the
C-vector space of bounded endomorphisms of H equipped with the strong operator topology (i.e., pointwise
convergence). By Lemma C.3.3.1, this E is Hausdorff, locally convex, and quasi-complete. We will construct a
Cauchy net in E that has no limit (so E is not complete) so by quasi-completeness of E such a Cauchy net
cannot be eventually bounded (as otherwise it would have a limit, by quasi-completeness). This also shows E
is not metrizable, since quasi-completeness implies completeness in the metrizable case.
      To make the desired Cauchy net, let φ ∈ H ∗ − H ′ be a discontinuous linear functional on H (as exists
since H is infinite-dimensional). Then by extending the restriction of φ on each finite-dimensional subspace to
a continuous linear functional on H using the Hahn-Banach Theorem (in the form given in [Scha, Ch. II, 4.2])
and partially ordering the set I of finite-dimensional subspaces of H by inclusion, we obtain a net {φi }i∈I ⊂ H ′
of continuous linear functionals converging to φ “pointwise”: for every h ∈ H, we have φi (h) → φ(h) as a net
of complex numbers.
      Upon fixing h ∈ H nonzero, we obtain a net {Ai }i∈I ⊂ E by defining Ai (u) := φi (u) · h for each u ∈ H,
and Ai → A pointwise on H for A(u) := φ(u) · h but A is not a bounded operator on H. Explicitly, we have
||Ai (u) − A(u)||H = |φi (u) − φ(u)| ||h||H → 0. In particular, {Ai }i∈I ⊂ E is a Cauchy net. But this net has no
limit in E, since a limit (if one exists) would have to agree pointwise with the discontinuous A.


     C.4.3.2. Stability properties of vector-valued integrals and integrability criteria. Quasi-completeness of a
Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space E is a useful criterion for integrability in favorable cases: if
f is continuous and compactly supported, then it is integrable in the E-valued sense.

     Theorem C.4.3.5 (Pettis’ Integrability Criterion). Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff space and µ
a finite complex Radon measure on X. Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space and
f : X → E a compactly supported continuous function. If E is quasi-complete then f is µ-integrable.

     This is [Gro-a, Lemme 2], where the assumptions of the Lemma are met because convex hulls interact
well with pre-compactness in the quasi-complete case: in a Hausdorff quasi-complete locally convex topological
C-vector space, the convex circled hull of any pre-compact subset is pre-compact [Scha, Ch. II, Cor. to 4.3].
714            CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


    Proof. For closed Z ⊂ X with supp(f ) ⊂ Z, we have Z f dµ = X f dµ in E ′ by the respective

    Lemma C.4.3.11. Let E be a complex Hilbert space, and B(E) the vector space of continuous C-linear

     C.4.3.3. Continuity criterion. For X a locally compact Hausdorff space and E a Hausdorff locally
convex topological C-vector space, a net {fi }i∈I of continuous functions on X valued in E converges to
f : X → E uniformly on compact subsets, or locally uniformly, if for every compact subset K ⊂ X, the net
{fi |K }i∈I converges to f |K uniformly. In turn, by this we mean that for every continuous seminorm ν on E,
limi∈I supx∈K ν(fi − f ) = 0. In other words, the terminology for uniform and locally uniform convergence of
nets of continuous scalar-valued functions retains the same meaning for continuous E-valued functions. Such
convergence can be equivalently tested on a generating family of continuous seminorms on E.
    Lemma C.4.3.12. Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space, and (X, µ) a locally
compact Hausdorff topological space with µ a finite complex Radon measure. Let I be a directed set, and {fi }i∈I
a net of continuous, µ-integrable functions fi : X → E converging uniformly to the continuous µ-integrable
function f : X → E. Then
                                                Z           Z
(C.4.3.15)                                  lim     fi dµ =    f dµ.
                                            i∈I X            X
                           R

    Remark C.4.3.13. We will specialize the concepts and results in this subsection to two classes of E: they
are Hilbert spaces, and the C-vector space of bounded linear endomorphism of a Hilbert space equipped with
the locally convex strong operator topology, on the one hand, and with the operator-norm topology (which
makes it into a Banach space), on the other. Hilbert spaces, as complete metric spaces, are quasi-complete
as a consequence of the definition. As for E := BSOT (H), the space of bounded linear endomorphisms of a
Hilbert space H endowed with the strong operator topology, E is indeed quasi-complete, as a consequence of
the Uniform Boundedness Principle: see Lemma C.3.3.1.

   We have now discussed all the required preparations on integration of functions defined on locally compact

               C.5. Meromorphic functions valued in a quasi-complete locally convex tvs
     We begin by recalling the classical concept of holomorphy for functions valued in a locally convex topological
complex vector space. Our main reference for the concept and basic characterizations of holomorphy for
functions valued in a locally convex topological vector space is [Gro-a]. We will occasionally use [Gro-b,
Ch. II, §3] to characterize certain spaces of holomorphic and meromorphic functions as projective tensor
products, under favorable conditions that we will find to be met in our situations of interest.
     The literature on holomorphic and meromorphic functions valued in locally convex complex vector spaces
is extensive. Sources of input for the material in this subsection and the next are [Kruse, §3,7], [Jor-a,
§3], and [BJM]. The latter two in particular further build from work of Grosse-Erdmann in [GE] on the
topologies on spaces of scalar-valued meromorphic functions on complex domains, an analog of which we will
be requiring.
     The main difference between the existing literature and the material discussed in this section is that we
will be allowing Riemann surfaces as domains of definition for meromorphic vector-valued functions, which
entails some, while limited, non-trivial amount of additional work.
720            CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


    C.5.1. Vector-valued continuous and differentiable functions. For a Hausdorff locally compact
space X, we denote by X its one-point compactification, with ∞ the point at infinity, i.e. {∞} = X − X.
The space X is compact Hausdorff, and X ⊂ X is an open subset whose subspace topology is the intrinsic
topology on X.
    We say a continuous complex-valued function f on X tends to zero at infinity if and only if it is bounded
on X and its (hence existing) continuous extension F : X → C satisfies limx→+∞ F (x) = 0. This limit is in
the sense of convergence in general topological spaces, defined by means of Cauchy filter-base or Cauchy net
convergence.
    We further recall that on Cb (X), the C-vector space of complex valued bounded continuous functions on
X, we may define the uniform norm
(C.5.1.1)                                      ||f ||u := sup |f (x)|
                                                        x∈X

which promotes Cb (X) to a complex Banach space. We call the norm-topology on Cb (X) the topology of
uniform convergence.
    Within Cb (X) we further find the C-vector subspace Cc (X) of continuous complex-valued compactly
supported functions. This is, algebraically, the filtered colimit of the C-linear subspaces C(X, K) of continuous
functions on X whose support is contained within the compact subset K ⊂ X. We denote by KX the set of all
compact subsets of X. An inclusion of compact subsets K ′ ⊂ K induces a C-linear extension-by-zero operator
                                             C(X, K ′ ) → C(X, K)
realizing Cc (X) as Cc (X) = colim C(X, K) as a C-linear subspace of Cb (X). The uniform norm on Cb (X)
                              K∈KX
endows each C(X, K) with the structure of a complete normed space, since it is a closed subspace of C(K),
this latter equipped with the topology of uniform convergence.
     We may endow Cc (X) with two topologies: one is the topology of uniform convergence inherited from Cb (X).
This is a Hausdorff norm-topology and as such locally convex. We note that the subspace Cc (X) ⊂ Cb (X)
equipped with the topology of uniform convergence is not complete. Its completion is denoted C0 (X), and it
is the subspace of Cb (X) of those bounded continuous functions that vanish at ∞.
     The other topology on Cc (X) is the locally convex inductive limit topology, upon endowing each C(X, K)
with its norm-topology induced by the uniform norm. With this topology, Cc (X) is a locally convex topological
C-vector space, and it is Hausdorff because this topology is finer than the topology of uniform convergence,
which is Hausdorff. We refer to the locally convex inductive limit topology on Cc (X) as the inductive limit
topology on Cc (X). Assuming X is second-countable, so there is a countable cofinal system of K’s with respect
to inclusion, the subspace topology on C(X, K) from the inductive limit topology on Cc (X), is its original the
topology of uniform convergence by [Scha, Ch. II, 6.4] (this uses that the inclusions C(X, K) → C(X, K ′ ) for
K ⊂ K ′ are not only topological embeddings with respect to the uniform norm but are also closed embeddings
since C(X, K) is complete).
     When the continuous functions on X are valued in a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space
E, similar notions exist and properties hold. Our main reference for the extension of these concepts to the
case of E-valued functions is [Bou-I, Ch. III, §1].
     We fix a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E. The C-vector space C(X, E) of continuous
E-valued functions is endowed with the topology generated by the collection of seminorms
(C.5.1.2)                                   qK,ν (f ) := sup ν(f (x))
                                                         x∈K

as ν varies over the set S(E) of all continuous seminorms on E (ν ◦ f is continuous on K, hence bounded)
and K varies over the set KX of all compact subsets of X.
             C.5. MEROMORPHIC FUNCTIONS VALUED IN A QUASI-COMPLETE LOCALLY CONVEX TVS                        721


     The family {qK,ν }(K,ν)∈KX ×S(E) is separating because if qK,ν (f ) = 0 for all (K, ν) ∈ KX × S(E) then
f (x) = 0 for all x ∈ K and all K ∈ KX , and hence f = 0. In particular, endowed with this topology, C(X, E)
is Hausdorff. We refer to this locally convex topology on C(X, E) as the topology of uniform convergence on
compact subsets.

   C.5.1.1. Properties of the spaces of continuous compactly supported E-valued functions. The following is
[Bou-I, Ch. III, §1.1, Def. 1].
    Definition C.5.1.1. Let X be a Hausdorff locally compact space and E a Hausdorff locally convex
topological C-vector space. Let f : X → E be a continuous E-valued function. We define the support of f as
the closure of the open subset
(C.5.1.3)                                     Xf := X − f −1 (0)
and denote it by supp(f ). We say f is compactly supported if and only if supp(f ) is a compact subset of X.
We denote by Cc (X, E) the C-vector space of all compactly supported E-valued continuous functions on X,
and for any compact subset K ⊂ X, by C(X, K; E) the linear subspace of Cc (X, E) of all those compactly
supported E-valued functions whose support is contained in K. We topologize Cc (X, E) with the locally
convex inductive limit of the topologies on C(X, K; E), each induced by the family of seminorms {qK,ν }ν∈S(E)
from (C.5.1.2).
    Remark C.5.1.2. On Definition C.5.1.1, we make the following observations.
(1) The subspace topology on Cc (X, E) inherited from the topology on C(X, E) of uniform convergence on
    compact subsets is locally convex .Its inductive limit topology (see [Scha, Ch. II, §6, pp. 56-60]) is also
    locally convex. These two topologies are generally not the same; we refer the reader to Example C.5.1.5.
    The former is coarser than the latter (i.e., the bijection limK C(X, K; E) → Cc (X, E) is continuous when
                                                               −→
    the target has the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets). When considering Cc (X, E)
    as a locally convex topological C-vector space, we will always be assuming that the topology it is being
    endowed with is the locally convex inductive limit topology.
   Lemma C.5.1.3. Let X be a Hausdorff locally compact space, E a Hausdorff locally convex C-vector space.
Then
(1) The locally convex topological C-vector space Cc (X, E) of continuous E-valued compactly supported functions
    on X is Hausdorff. For any compact subset K ⊂ X, the topology induced on C(X, K; E) by Cc (X, E) is
    the topology of uniform convergence, and each of the linear subspaces C(X, K; E) of Cc (X, E) is closed.
(2) If X is the topological disjoint union of an I-indexed family of locally compact Hausdorff spaces {Xi }i∈I
    then the canonical C-linear map

(C.5.1.4)                                  Cc (X, E) →       Cc (Xi , E)

    is a linear topological isomorphism.
(3) If X is paracompact and E is quasi-complete then Cc (X, E) is quasi-complete.
(4) If X is paracompact then for every bounded subset B ⊂ Cc (X, E) there exists a compact subset K ⊂ X
    such that B ⊂ C(X, K; E) (so it is bounded in C(X, K; E) by (1)).
(5) Cc (X, E) ⊂ C(X, E) is a dense subspace with respect to the topology of uniform convergence on compact
    subsets.
(6) If E is quasi-complete, C(X, E) is locally convex, Hausdorff and quasi-complete with respect to the topology
    of uniform convergence on compact subsets.

where {νi }i∈I is a generating family for the locally convex topology on E. Since E is Hausdorff, {νi }i∈I is
separating. It follows that qK,i (f ) = 0 for all i ∈ I implies f (x) = 0 for all x ∈ K, for any compact subset
K ⊂ X. This gives f = 0, so C(X, E) is Hausdorff.
    Let K ⊂ X be a compact subset. Then the restriction maps
                                           ρK : C(X, E) → C(K, E)
form a projective system, The topology on each C(K, E) is generated the family of seminorms {qK,i }i∈I
from (C.5.1.5), for K fixed. The topology on C(X, E) is clearly the projective limit of the topologies on
C(K, E). By [Scha, Ch. II, 5.3], we are thereby reduced to the case X is compact Hausdorff. In particular,
C(X, E) = Cc (X, E) and hence is quasi-complete by (3).                                                 □

    Remark C.5.1.4. By part (2), we see that part (4) is a special case of [Scha, Ch. II, 6.3, 6.5], a theorem
of Dieudonné and Schwartz.

     Example C.5.1.5 (Distinctness of the two topologies on Cc (X, E)). Assume X is a Hausdorff, locally
compact, paracompact space, and E is a Fréchet space. By Lemma C.5.1.3, Cc (X, E) is a strict locally convex
inductive limit of the closed topological linear subspaces C(X, K; E) (see [Scha, Ch. II, p. 57]). Every Cauchy
sequence in Cc (X, E) is bounded and hence contained within C(X, K; E) for some compact subset K ⊂ X
and bounded there. The locally convex topological C-vector space C(X, K; E) is a Fréchet space, and as such,
any Cauchy sequence in C(X, K; E) converges in C(X, K; E).
     Assume that, for a locally compact Hausdorff abelian group G, X carries a continuous free proper action
of G. Let K ⊂ X be a non-empty compact subset, and f ∈ Cc (X, K; E) a fixed function. The action of G by
left translation provides a family of functions fg := Lg (f ), where (Lg (f ))(x) = f (g −1 x) for all x ∈ X and
each g ∈ G.
     We now specialize to the case X = R and G = Z acting on X by additive translation, and E = C. Let K
be the unit interval in R and pick f ̸= 0. Then the sequence fn := Ln (f ) in Cc (R) does not converge in Cc (R).
Indeed, if it did then it would have to be contained and converge in some C(K ′ , C) for some compact subset
K ′ ⊂ R, which cannot be since supp(fn ) ∩ K ′ = ∅ for all integers n ∈ Z with |n| ≫ 0, and hence {fn }n≥1 , a
sequence of functions whose supports are non-empty in R, cannot be contained in a single C(K ′ , C). On the
other hand, the sequence {fn }n≥1 tends to the constant function 0 in C(R), and so it is a null sequence in the
linear space Cc (R) endowed with the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets.
     For E an arbitrary nonzero Fréchet space, choose a nonzero vector e ∈ E. The sequence {ϕn }n≥0 ⊂
Cc (R, E) defined by ϕn := fn ⊗ e, viewed as a sequence in Cc (R, E) under the injective linear map
                                            Cc (R) ⊗ E → Cc (R, E)
is also a sequence which does not converge to 0 with respect to the locally convex inductive limit topology but
is a null sequence in Cc (R, E) endowed with the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets.
              C.5. MEROMORPHIC FUNCTIONS VALUED IN A QUASI-COMPLETE LOCALLY CONVEX TVS                                 723


    A similar example can be made with R replaced by any Hausdorff locally compact space containing a
non-empty open subset which is a topological manifold.
    We will be henceforth assuming, unless otherwise stated, that Cc (X, E) is endowed with the locally convex
inductive limit topology of the topologies of uniform convergence on each C(X, K; E) as in Definition C.5.1.1.
We will be assuming that C(X, E) is endowed, instead, with the topology of uniform convergence on compact
subsets (so Cc (X, E) → C(X, E) is .continuous but generally not a topological embedding).

    C.5.1.2. Vector-valued differentiability. We let k be either one of the Archimedean topological fields
k = R, C, and E a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space. We will be closely following [Kruse,
Def. 3.1] in defining three concepts of differentiability for E-valued functions on an open subset Ω ⊂ k d for an
integer d ≥ 0.
    The Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces throughout this subsection will still be assumed to
be complex topological vector spaces even when k = R, in which case for E = C the differentiable vector-valued
functions discussed herein will recover the classical notion of differentiable complex-valued functions on a
Euclidean space over the reals. In other words, the topological field k is not the scalar field of the topological
vector spaces occurring throughout this subsection: such field is always assumed to be C.
    We denote by | · | the Euclidean norm on k, whether real or complex. We further denote by | · | again, the
Euclidean norm on k d for any d ≥ 0.
    Throughout this subsection, occasional references are made to the basic results on the integral in the
sense of Pettis from §C.4.3: the Mean-Value Theorem (Theorem C.4.3.1; see also Theorem C.4.3.2), and the
Integrability Criterion of Theorem C.4.3.5.
     Definition C.5.1.6 (Weak differentiability). Let d ≥ 0 be an integer, and Ω ⊂ k d an open subset. Let
E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space, and f : Ω → E a function. We say f is weakly
differentiable over Ω if and only if for every φ ∈ E ′ , the function ⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ : Ω → C defined by
(C.5.1.6)                                           ξ 7→ ⟨f (ξ), φ⟩E,E ′
is once-differentiable in the ordinary sense (i.e. real-differentiable if k = R, and differentiable in the complex
sense if k = C; see Remark C.5.1.7).
     For f weakly differentiable over Ω, we define the function Df : Ω × k d → (E ′ )∗ by requiring that
(C.5.1.7)                             ⟨Df, φ⟩E,E ′ := D⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ : Ω × k d → C
be the function of (ξ1 , ξ2 ) ∈ Ω × k d given by (ξ1 , ξ2 ) 7→ Dξ1 ⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ (ξ2 ), with Dξ1 ⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ the differential
of the C-valued function ⟨f (ξ), φ⟩E,E ′ of ξ ∈ Ω at ξ1 ∈ Ω.
    We refer to Df as the weak differential of f . If Df : Ω × k d → (E ′ )∗ is continuous we say f is weakly
continuously differentiable.
    Remark C.5.1.7. For a scalar-valued function f : Ω → C, Ω ⊂ k d an open subset, to be differentiable “in
the ordinary sense”, we mean that there exists a (clearly unique) k-linear map Jξ0 : k d → C such that
                                                  f (ξ0 + ξ) − f (ξ0 ) − Jξ0 (ξ)
(C.5.1.8)                                   lim

exists and vanishes. Specifically, we are not assuming that Jξ0 (ξ) ∈ C is continuous in (ξ0 , ξ); i.e., continuous
as a map Ω × k d → C. Differentiable “in the ordinary sense” does not mean “continuously differentiable”. In
(C.5.1.8), Jξ0 (ξ) refers to the effect of the k-linear functional Jξ0 on the vector ξ ∈ k d . If k = C, and f is
complex-differentiable, then in particular we have Jξ0 (ξ) = f ′ (ξ0 )ξ.
    Much as for the integral in the sense of Pettis in §??, we now discuss differentiability for vector-valued
functions in the weak sense first and then see when such a condition is equivalent to a stronger one.

    Remark C.5.1.10. We note that if k = R and d = 2, then upon identifying R2 with the complex plane,
Gateaux-differentiability of a function f : C → C (choosing E = C) does not imply differentiability in the
complex sense, i.e. upon rethinking f as a function k d → C with k = C and d = 1. For k = C and d = 1,
Gateaux-differentiability amounts to differentiability in the complex sense, which we shall be discussing in
§C.5.2.1.

    Remark C.5.1.11. We note that there is no continuity assumption on f in any of the conditions assigned
in Definition C.5.1.8.

    Lemma C.5.1.15 (On weak differentiability). Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
space, d ≥ 1 an integer, k either one of the Archimedean topological fields k = R, C, endowed with their
Euclidean topology. Let Ω ⊂ k d be an open subset, and f : Ω → E a function. Then the following conditions
are equivalent:
(1) f is weakly differentiable over Ω, and the weak differential Df is a continuous function Ω × k d → (E ′ )∗
    with respect to the product topology on the source and the σ((E ′ )∗ , E ′ )-topology on the target.
(2) f satisfies the following conditions:
    (a) f is weakly differentiable in the ei -direction over Ω, for every 1 ≤ i ≤ d.
    (b) Di f : Ω → (E ′ )∗ is continuous with respect to the Euclidean topology on the source and the σ((E ′ )∗ , E ′ )-
        topology on the target, for every 1 ≤ i ≤ d.

    Proof. (1) ⇒ (2) : By assumption, the weak differential Df : Ω × k d → (E ′ )∗ is continuous with respect
to the product topology on the source and the σ((E ′ )∗ , E ′ )-topology on the target. It then follows that
(Df )(·, ei ) is an (E ′ )∗ -valued ei -direction weak derivative on Ω, and by hypothesis in (1) this is continuous
with respect to the topology on Ω and the σ((E ′ )∗ , E ′ )-topology on (E ′ )∗ . This proves that (2.a) and (2.b)
hold.
    (2)⇒ (1) : If f is weakly differentiable in the ei -direction for all i with continuous derivatives with respect to
the topology on Ω and the σ((E ′ )∗ , E ′ )-topology on (E ′ )∗ then for every φ ∈ E ′ the function ξ 7→ ⟨f (ξ), φ⟩E,E ′
admits partial derivatives at all points of Ω, and they are each continuous. It is therefore differentiable on Ω.
Since φ ∈ E ′ arbitrary, f is weakly differentiable with ei -direction weak derivative (Df )(·, ei ). Thus, for every
ξ2 = 1≤i≤d ci (ξ2 )ei ∈ k d for ci (ξ2 ) ∈ k,
      P

(C.5.1.29)                                    Df (ξ1 , ξ2 ) =   ci (ξ2 )Di f (ξ1 )
                                                        1≤i≤d

    We collect here for later use two important permanence properties of directional derivatives for functions
valued in a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space:

    Lemma C.5.1.17 (Permanence properties of vector-valued differentiability). Let E be a Hausdorff locally
convex topological C-vector space, k either one of the fields k = R, C, endowed with their Euclidean topology.
Let Ω1 , Ω2 ⊂ k d be open subsets, and f : Ω2 → E a function. Let ϕ : Ω1 → Ω2 be a differentiable function.
Then:
(1) If f is weakly differentiable over Ω2 , so is f ◦ ϕ over Ω1 .
(2) If f is differentiable over Ω2 then so is f ◦ ϕ and we have
(C.5.1.35)                             D(f ◦ ϕ) = (Df )(ϕ, Dϕ) : Ω1 × k d → E

      over Ω1 × k d )

    Remark C.5.1.18. When writing (ϕ, Dϕ) : Ω1 × k d → Ω2 × k d , it is understood that the dependency on Ω1
of ϕ and Dϕ is, for both, through the same copy of Ω1 . That is to say that, as a function Ω1 × k d → Ω2 × k d ,
we write (ϕ, Dϕ) to mean (ξ1 , ξ2 ) 7→ (ϕ(ξ1 ), (Dϕ)(ξ1 , xi2 ).

     Proof. (1) : If f is weakly differentiable over Ω2 then for any φ ∈ E ′ the function ⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ : Ω → k
is differentiable and hence so is the composition ⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ ◦ ϕ = ⟨f ◦ ϕ, φ⟩E,E ′ . Since φ is arbitrary, f ◦ ϕ is
weakly differentiable.
    (2) : By (1), f ◦ ϕ is weakly differentiable. The weak differential Df is therefore defined. Let φ ∈ E ′ be
the arbitrary continuous linear form on E. We compute, for every (ξ1 , ξ2 ) ∈ Ω1 × k d :
                            ⟨D(f ◦ ϕ)(ξ1 , ξ2 ), φ⟩E,E ′ = Dξ1 ⟨f ◦ ϕ, φ⟩E,E ′ (ξ2 )

    C.5.1.4. Vector-valued differentiability criterion. We will now discuss a differentiability criterion, extending
Lemma C.5.1.13 to higher order directional derivatives. Such a criterion will hold under the additional
assumption on the Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E being quasi-complete. The following
Lemma is the key ingredient upon which the differentiability criterion of Theorem C.5.1.24 below rests.
    We record here the following consequence of Lemma C.5.1.12, Lemma C.5.1.13, Lemma C.5.1.15 and
Lemma C.5.1.16:
     Theorem C.5.1.21 (Strong vector-valued differentiability). Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector space, d ≥ 1 an integer, k either one of the Archimedean topological fields k = R, C, endowed with
their Euclidean topology. Let Ω ⊂ k d be an open subset, f : Ω → E a function. The following conditions are
equivalent:
732              CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


(1) f is continuously differentiable over Ω.
(2) f is weakly differentiable, the weak differential Df : Ω × k d → (E ′ )∗ is valued in E and continuous with
    respect to the product topology on the source and the initial topology on the target E.
(3) f is weakly differentiable in the ei -direction for each 1 ≤ i ≤ d, and each of the directional derivatives Di f
    is valued in E and continuous with respect to the Euclidean topology on Ω and the initial topology on E.
(4) f is Gateaux-differentiable within (E ′ )∗ , and the limit
                                                      f (ξ1 + hξ2 ) − f (ξ1 )
(C.5.1.38)                                    lim
                                            h→0,h∈W             h
      (with W ⊂ k the subset W := {h ∈ k : h ̸= 0, ξ1 + hξ2 ∈ Ω}) is, as a function of (ξ1 , ξ2 ) ∈ Ω × k d , valued
      in E and continuous with respect to the product topology on the source and the given topology on E.

     Proof. If (1) holds then f is weakly differentiable by Lemma C.5.1.12((2) ⇒ (1)) and the weak differential
Df agrees with the differential in (1), which implies the continuity assertion on Df as a function Ω × k d → E.
Thus, (1) implies (2).
     If (2) holds then f is weakly differentiable in the ei -direction by Lemma C.5.1.15, and by (C.5.1.14) each
Di f is valued in E and continuous with respect to the Euclidean topology on Ω and the initial topology on E.
This implies that (3) holds.
     If (3) holds, then since Df = 1≤i≤d ci Di f , for ci ∈ (k d )∗ the i-th coordinate projection linear form, i.e.
                                     P

for each (ξ1 , ξ2 ) ∈ Ω × k d we have:
                                                         X

                                                        1≤i≤d

and each ci is continuous, we deduce from (3) that Df is valued in E and continuous with respect to the product
topology on Ω × k d and the given topology on E. We deduce that f is weakly continuously differentiable and
by Lemma C.5.1.13(2) is continuously differentiable over Ω, so (1) holds.
    If (4) holds then by Lemma C.5.1.16(3) so does (1). If (1) holds then by Lemma C.5.1.13(2) we get (4). □

     We will now be discussing an important differentiability criterion in the special case E is quasi-complete,
due to Grothendieck (see [Gro-a, §2 ,Footnote 4, p. 39]) and whose proof is recorded in more detail by
Schwartz in [Sch-b, Appendice, Lemma II, p. 146]. We’ll give a somewhat different proof below. Before we do
so, we include below a result on removable singularities for vector-valued functions, smooth away from an
isolated point, adapting an argument from [Ga-2, §15.1].

     Definition C.5.1.23 (Order-m differentiability). Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
space, k either one of the fields k = R, C, endowed with their Euclidean topology. Let Ω ⊂ k d be an open
subset, and f : Ω → E a function. Let m ≥ 1 be an integer. If m = 0, we say that f is continuously
differentiable 0 times if and only if f is Lipschitz-continuous, i.e. for any ξ, ξ ′ ∈ Ω, ξ ̸= ξ ′ , such that |ξ ′ − ξ| ≤ 1,
the ratio:
                                                      f (ξ ′ ) − f (ξ)
(C.5.1.43)
                                                         |ξ ′ − ξ|
is contained in a bounded subset of E.
     If m ≥ 1, we say that f is continuously differentiable m times if and only if:
(1) f is weakly differentiable in the ei -direction for 1 ≤ i ≤ d.
(2) For every 1 ≤ i ≤ d, the directional derivatives Di f is valued in E and continuous with respect to the
    Euclidean topology on Ω and the initial topology on E.
734             CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


(3) For every 1 ≤ i ≤ d, the directional derivatives Di f is continuously differentiable m − 1 times.
We say f is infinitely differentiable, or smooth, if and only if for every integer m ≥ 0, f is continuously
differentiable m times.
     We denote by C m (Ω, E) the C-vector space of E-valued functions continuously differentiable m times,
and by C ∞ (Ω, E), equivalently E(Ω, E), the C-vector space of infinitely differentiable E-valued functions.
