C.5.1.16(3) applies to give f is C 1 with values in E.
     We have shown that for each integer 1 ≤ i ≤ d, Di f is valued in E and continuous with respect to the
Euclidean topology on Ω and the initial topology on E. Note that for each integer 1 ≤ i ≤ d, the function Di f
is E-valued, continuous, and weakly continuously differentiable m − 1 times. By inductive hypothesis, it is
continuously differentiable m − 2 times. We have therefore shown that f is continuously differentiable m − 1
times.                                                                                                               □
     Corollary C.5.1.25 (On the agreement of the concepts of E-valued smoothness). Let E be a Hausdorff
locally convex topological C-vector space. Let d ≥ 1 be an integer, k either one of the two Archimedean
topological field k = R, C, endowed with their Euclidean topology.
     Let Ω ⊂ k d be an open subset, f : Ω → E a function. Assume E is quasi-complete. Then, the following
conditions are equivalent:
(1) f is infinitely differentiable.
(2) For every φ ∈ E ′ , the C-valued function ⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ on Ω is infinitely differentiable, i.e. an element of
    C ∞ (Ω).
    Note that for d = 1 and k = C, this implies that the weakly infinitely differentiable E-valued functions on
Ω are exactly the holomorphic E-valued functions (see Definition C.5.2.1(4)).
    The concept of vector-valued infinite differentiability defined in [Tre, Def. 40.1] is the same as the one
in Definition C.5.1.23. The one in force throughout [Sch-b] is the “weak” notion in Corollary C.5.1.25(2),
             C.5. MEROMORPHIC FUNCTIONS VALUED IN A QUASI-COMPLETE LOCALLY CONVEX TVS                         735


so for E quasi-complete the two notions are equivalent by Corollary C.5.1.25. We may define a concept of
infinite differentiability in the sense of Gateaux, building on Lemma C.5.1.16 (requiring directional derivatives
to be E-valued and weakly continuous on Ω), and Corollary C.5.1.25 implies that for E quasi-complete it is
equivalent to infinite differentiability as defined in Definition C.5.1.23.
     For the purposes of this work, E will always be quasi-complete. Thus, there will be no ambiguity as to
the meaning of “smooth E-valued function”.

    C.5.1.5. Spaces of smooth vector-valued functions. In this subsection we record a few facts about spaces of
smooth vector-valued functions with values in a Hausdorff locally convex quasi-complete topological C-vector
space E.
    Recall that we write T for the 1-dimensional compact real torus R/Z, which is smoothly isomorphic to
U(1) under the exponential function t 7→ exp(2πit).

    Definition C.5.1.26 (Vector-valued smooth function spaces). Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex
topological C-vector space, d ≥ 0 an integer. Assume E is quasi-complete. We define:
(1) S(Td , E) to be the linear subspace of C ∞ (Rd , E) of those E-valued smooth functions that are invariant
    under the continuous left-translation action of the discrete co-compact closed subgroup Zd ⊂ Rd .
         We topologize S(Td , E) with the unique Hausdorff topological vector space structure for which a net
    {fi }i∈I ⊂ S(Td , E) converges to 0 in S(Td , E) if and only if for every φ ∈ E ′ , the net of smooth complex-
    valued functions {⟨fi , φ⟩E,E ′ }i∈I converges to 0 with respect to the topology of uniform convergence over
    Td , uniformly as φ varies over each equicontinuous subset of E ′ .
(2) S(Rd , E) to be the linear subspace of those f ∈ C ∞ (Rd , E) such that for any complex-valued polynomial
    function p on Rd , and every integral multi-index α ∈ Nd , p · Dα f takes values in a bounded subset of E,
    where Dα := 1≤i≤d Dα
                  Q           i
                             i (the boundedness can be checked weakly, by [Scha, Ch. IV, 3.3]).
         We topologize S(Rd , E) with the unique Hausdorff topological vector space structure for which a net
    {fi }i∈I ⊂ S(Rd , E) converges to 0 in S(Rd , E) if and only if for every φ ∈ E ′ , the net of smooth complex-
    valued functions {⟨fi , φ⟩E,E ′ }i∈I converges to 0 with respect to the topology of uniform convergence over
    Rd , uniformly as φ varies over each equicontinuous subset of E ′ .

    Remark C.5.1.27. Definition C.5.1.26 makes sense for an arbitrary Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector space E (no quasi-completeness hypothesis) by defining smooth E-valued functions as those that are
weakly infinitely differentiable and by defining the two respective function spaces S(Td , E) and S(Rd , E) as
the linear subspaces of C ∞ (Rn , E) of those smooth E-valued functions f : Rd → E such that for any φ ∈ E ′ ,
the complex-valued smooth function ⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ is Zd -invariant over Rd , respectively Schwartz over Rd .
    This latter way to define S(Td , E) and S(Rd , E) is denoted in [Sch-b, §1,p.102] by H e d (E) for H either
S(T ) or S(R ). By [Sch-b, Prop. 8, p. 104], for E quasi-complete this definition and Definition C.5.1.26 are
    d         d

equivalent; see also Corollary C.5.1.25, and [Sch-b, Prop. 4, p. 97].

    Remark C.5.1.29. Definition C.5.1.26 makes sense for the arbitrary Hausdorff locally convex topological C-

    Most of the following properties of S(Rd , E) are due to Schwartz, and we further refer the reader to
[Sch-b, §1,p.93].

     Theorem C.5.1.30 (Main properties of the function spaces S(Td , E) and S(Rd , E)). Let E be a Hausdorff
locally convex topological C-vector space, d ≥ 1 an integer. Assume E is quasi-complete.
(1) The spaces S(Td , E) and S(Rd , E) are quasi-complete.
(2) If E is complete then S(Td , E) and S(Rd , E) are complete.
(3) If E is a Fréchet space then so are S(Td , E) and S(Rd , E).
                                                         ′    ′
(4) For d, d′ ≥ 1 two integers, and X = Td , Rd , Y = Td , Rd respectively, the injective linear map
(C.5.1.47)                                C ∞ (X × Y ) → C ∞ (X, C ∞ (Y ))
      defined by sending a smooth complex-valued function f (x, y) on X × Y to the smooth C ∞ (Y )-valued
      function x 7→ f (x, ·) is bijective and it is compatible with the linear subspaces S(X × Y ) and S(X, S(Y )),
      inducing a linear topological isomorphism
(C.5.1.48)                                   S(X × Y ) → S(X, S(Y )).

    Proof. (1) and (2) : Let {fi }i∈I ⊂ S(Rd , E) be a bounded Cauchy net. Since S(Rd ) is complete, it
converges weakly; i.e., with respect to the σ(S(Rd , E), S(Rd , E)′ )-topology on S(Rd , E).
    Since it is bounded by assumption, for each x ∈ Rd Remark C.5.1.28 gives that {fi (x)}i∈I is a bounded
Cauchy net in E, which therefore converges for each x ∈ Rd since E is quasi-complete. We denote by
f : Rd → E the limit function. For any φ ∈ E ′ , ⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ is the pointwise limit of ⟨fi , φ⟩, yet ⟨fi , φ⟩ is Cauchy
in the complete S(Rd ) and so has a limit in S(Rd ). Hence, ⟨f, φ⟩ is that limit, so it is Schwartz.
    By Corollary C.5.1.25, f is smooth as an E-valued function. For any polynomial function p on Rd and
every multi-index α ∈ Nd , p · Dα f takes values in a weakly bounded subset of E since each ⟨f, φ⟩ is Schwartz,
so p · Dα f takes values in a bounded subset of E by [Scha, Ch. IV, 3.3]. We deduce that f ∈ S(Rd , E). It
remains to show that fi → f in S(Rd , E). If φ ∈ E ′ varies over an arbitrary equicontinuous subset A of E ′
then by equicontinuity we have ⟨fi , φ⟩E,E ′ → ⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ uniformly with respect to φ ∈ A. We deduce that
fi → f in S(Rd , E), by definition of the locally convex topology on S(Rd , E).
    The same argument works if {fi }i∈I is an arbitrary (not necessarily bounded) Cauchy net in S(Rd , E)
and E is complete rather than just quasi-complete.
    The case of S(Td , E) is seen by means of the same argument: we have only used completeness of S(Rd )
and quasi-completeness, respectively completeness, of E.
    (3) : If E is a Fréchet space, then since S(Td ) and S(Rd ) are both metrizable, the description of the
topology on S(Td , E) and S(Rd , E) by means of the fundamental families of continuous seminorms from
(C.5.1.45) and (C.5.1.46) shows that we may choose the index sets I to be countable, which proves that
S(Td , E) and S(Rd , E) are complete, by (2), and metrizable, hence Fréchet spaces.
             C.5. MEROMORPHIC FUNCTIONS VALUED IN A QUASI-COMPLETE LOCALLY CONVEX TVS                            737


    (4) : Using the formula

    C.5.2. Holomorphic vector-valued functions. We start by defining basic concepts of continuity and
holomorphy for vector-valued functions on open subsets of C.

     C.5.2.1. Grothendieck’s criterion for holomorphy. For a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector
space E, we will be identifying E as a linear subspace of (E ′ )∗ (although not topologically) under the linear
map ιE : E → (E ′ )∗ from (C.4.1.1) and studied in Lemma C.4.1.1, when saying that certain linear forms on
E ′ are “elements of E”, or are “contained in E”. These will ordinarily be integrals in the sense of Pettis, which,
recall, are defined for general E as elements of (E ′ )∗ . The concept of integrability was defined in Definition
C.4.2.1(3) via such integrals being contained in E.
     Recall that we call Ω ⊂ C a domain, or a complex domain, if Ω ⊂ C is non-empty open and connected.
   Definition C.5.2.1. Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space, and Ω ⊂ C a
domain. We say a function f : Ω → E is:
(1) weakly continuous if and only if for every continuous linear functional φ ∈ E ′ , the function ⟨f (ξ), φ⟩E,E ′ is
    continuous as a function of ξ ∈ Ω (equivalently, f is continuous when E is given the σ(E, E ′ )-topology).
(2) weakly continuously differentiable k times, for an integer k ≥ 1, if and only if for every continuous linear
    functional φ ∈ E ′ , the function ⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ on Ω is an element of C k (Ω).
(3) Weakly holomorphic if and only if for every continuous linear functional φ ∈ E ′ , the function ⟨f, φ⟩E,E ′ on
    Ω is holomorphic in the sense of complex analysis.
(4) Complex-differentiable, or holomorphic, if and only if for every ξ0 ∈ Ω
(C.5.2.1)                                  lim (ξ − ξ0 )−1 (f (ξ) − f (ξ0 ))
                                           ξ→ξ0

    exists in E as ξ → ξ0 in the complex sense (in particular, f : Ω → E is continuous).
    Remark C.5.2.2. Reprising the terminology from Definition C.5.1.8, holomorphy of the E-valued function
f on Ω ⊂ C is equivalent to differentiability, upon choosing k = C, d = 1.
    In [Gro-a, Thm.1], Grothendieck established the equivalence of the concept of weak holomorphy in
Definition C.5.2.1(3) with seemingly stronger notions of holomorphy, showing that analogs of the Cauchy
integral formula and familiar results from complex analysis, adapt to the case of E-valued functions with
minor changes, as long as vector-valued integrals are contained in E.
738               CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


    Remark C.5.2.3. In [Gro-a, Thm.1(4)], complex-differentiable functions are termed “strongly differen-
tiable”.

    We record Grothendieck’s Theorem (see [Gro-a, Thm.1]) below. Throughout this work an arc Γ ⊂ Ω,
for Ω a complex domain, will always refer to a continuous and piecewise-C 1 map γ : [a, b] → Ω, for a, b ∈ R,
a < b, such that Γ = γ([a, b]).

    C.5.4. Vector-valued Residue Theorem. We recall that by a cycle Γ on Ω, we mean a formal sum

therefore the analog of Cauchy’s Residue Theorem, for E-valued holomorphic functions on Ω.

   We see from Theorem C.5.4.1 how it is natural to constrain E so as to ensure that f be integrable in the

Theorem C.4.3.5.
   The following is an analog of Riemann’s Theorem on removable singularities. We refer the reader to
[Kruse, Thm. 7.4].

C-vector space, Ω ⊂ C a domain, Z ⊂ Ω a discrete subset and f : Ω − Z → E a holomorphic function. If
for every ξ0 ∈ Ω there exists a disc B ⊂ Ω containing ξ0 , such that f is bounded on B − Z, then f uniquely
extends to a holomorphic function f : Ω → E.

    Here too quasi-completeness is being used to know holomorphic is equivalent to weakly holomorphic.
Finer analytic continuation results are available (see [Jor-b, Thms.6,8]) again under a local completeness
assumption.
    We will, throughout this work, always be able to assume quasi-completeness of the Hausdorff locally convex
topological C-vector space of values of the holomorphic and meromorphic functions of interest since these
spaces will always be the strong dual of a quotient of the Schwartz-Bruhat space of the global, respectively
S-local, adeles of a number field F , for F a finite set of places containing all the Archimedean places. Such
duals are quasi-complete, and even complete.

   C.5.4.1. Vector-valued Identity Theorem. We record here below the following analog of the Identity
Theorem from classical complex analysis:

    Lemma C.5.4.3. Let E be a Hausdorff quasi-complete locally convex topological C-vector space, Ω ⊂ C
a domain, (f1 , D1 ) and (f2 , D2 ) two meromorphic E-valued functions on Ω. Let B ⊂ Ω − (D1 ∪ D2 ) be a
non-empty open disc such that
(C.5.4.2)                                          f1 |B = f2 |B .
Then f1 and f2 agree as holomorphic functions on Ω − (D1 ∪ D2 ).

     Proof. For φ ∈ E ′ , the classical Identity Theorem applies to ⟨f1 , φ⟩ and ⟨f2 , φ⟩, so ⟨f1 , φ⟩ = ⟨f2 , φ⟩ for
all φ. Thus, f1 = f2 .                                                                                             □

    For a Hausdorff quasi-complete locally convex topological C-vector space E, the complex vector spaces
                                               H (Ω, E), M (Ω, E)
can be topologized (the former with the topology of locally uniform convergence, the latter with a certain
locally convex inductive limit topology) and are well-behaved. Their respective Hausdorff locally convex
742           CHAPTER C. PREPARATIONS ON LOCALLY CONVEX TOPOLOGICAL VECTOR SPACES


topologies are themselves quasi-complete, and promote the residue operators to continuous linear maps. They
have been studied, for example, in [Jor-a, BJM], in analogy with [GE] on the case of M (Ω, E) for E = C.
    We will not require a study of the complex vector spaces H (Ω, E) and M (Ω, E) for quasi-complete E:
rather, we will be studying, throughout Appendix D and the main text, smaller linear subspaces of holomorphic
and meromorphic vector-valued functions satisfying decay conditions uniformly over vertical strips of bounded
width, topologized with stronger topologies of uniform convergence over vertical strips of bounded width.

             D.1. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT SPACE OF A HAUSDORFF LOCALLY COMPACT ABELIAN GROUP                            745


            D.1. Schwartz-Bruhat space of a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group
    In this section we describe, for any Hausdorff locally compact abelian topological group G, the C-vector
space of Schwartz functions S(G) and its locally convex topology. Important examples of such G for our
purposes are not only the adele ring AF and its factor fields Fv for the places v of F , but also the multiplicative
analogues GL1 (AF ) and Fv× as well as the idele class group CF and its S-local analogue CF,S . (Beware that
for non-archimedean v, S(Fv× ) is much larger than the more widely-seen space Cc∞ (Fv× ) of locally constant
functions with compact support away from 0; it includes functions f (x) with sufficiently rapid decay as
|x| → 0, ∞.)
    We will then recall properties of the Fourier transform on S(G) and discuss some examples of interest, as
well as define the concept of vector-valued tempered distribution on G. The latter is needed to prove “kernel
theorems” that express function spaces on a product as suitably completed tensor products of function spaces
on the factors; such results are a crucial tool to built operators for a product group from operators associated
to the factor groups.
    To succinctly state the main result of this Appendix, let us first recall some terminology for Hausdorff
locally convex topological vector spaces that is reviewed in much more detail in Appendix C.1. We say such
a space E is bornological if any seminorm on E that is bounded on bounded subsets is continuous (this is
equivalent to another definition given without the language of seminorms in [Scha, Ch. II, p. 61], via the
relation to seminorms to circled convex subsets in [Scha, Ch. II, 1.5, 1.6]). We say E is barrelled if every
barrel (i.e., closed convex circle absorbing subset) is a neighborhood of 0; see [Scha, Ch. II, §7] for more on
barrelledness. For instance, Fréchet spaces are barrelled [Scha, Ch. II, Cor. to 7.1].
    Finally, we say E is Montel if it is reflexive (i.e., the natural map to the strong double dual is a topological
isomorphism) and has the Heine-Borel property: closed bounded subsets are compact. It is equivalent (by
[Scha, Ch. IV, 3.1, 5.6]) for E to be barrelled and have the Heine-Borel property. Every barrelled quasi-
complete nuclear space is Montel [Tre, Cor. 3 to Prop. 50.2], so for example every nuclear Fréchet space is
Montel. The latter applies to S(RN ), but not to inductive limits such as S(Qp ) or S(AF ) that are complete
[Scha, Ch. II, 6.6] but non-metrizable (they don’t have a countable base of 0-neighborhoods).
    The main result we aim to prove in this Appendix is that if G is second countable (i.e., has a countable
base for the topology) then S(G) is a complete bornological Montel space whose strong dual S(G)′β is nuclear
(the strong dual is then also complete and Montel, as holds for the strong dual of any bornological Montel
space [Scha, Ch. IV, 5.9, 6.1]). Nuclearity is always inherited by the strong dual for nuclear Fréchet spaces
[Tre, Prop. 50.6], but we need cases such as G = AF and G = CF for which S(G) is not Fréchet, so the
nuclearity of the strong dual of S(G) is a genuinely additional property for E = S(G) in general.
    The same assertion for Cc∞ (G) in place of S(G) is proved as [Bru, §8, Cor. 2 to Prop. 10], and [Bru,
§9, Prop. 11] states that this holds for S(G) by similar arguments, but no details are provided. (In [Bru]
the topological hypothesis on G is “separable”, which is defined therein to mean “metrizable and covered
by countably many compact subsets”; for Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups this is equivalent to
being second countable by Remark A.5.2.9, so it matches the topological hypothesis we shall use but we
won’t need that.). Since S(G) is much larger than Cc∞ (G), and studying it entails much greater attention
to decay estimates than for Cc∞ (G), a complete treatment of the matter is provided herein. The arguments
presented here follow closely those in the early sections of [Bru]. We briefly indicate what happens beyond
the second-countable case in Remark D.1.5.8, and primarily focus on second countable G since it is the sole
case of relevance for us.
    We will be relying on basic duality theory for Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups, for which the
reader is referred to [DE, Ch. 3]. We will be referring to [Ru, Ch. 1, 2] and [DE, Ch. 3, 4] for foundational
material on the structure of Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups, Pontryagin duality and Fourier Theory,
and we will give some references to [Bru] and [Wa, §2] connected to the definition of the Schwartz space S(G).
746                               CHAPTER D. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT FUNCTIONS


Toward the end of this section we define distributions on G valued in a Hausdorff locally convex topological
C-vector space E due to its role in the proof of “kernel theorems” as noted above; this includes studying
required properties of differential operators and the Fourier transform.

We denote by S(G) the C-vector space of all smooth functions on G that decay rapidly towards infinity. We

      Remark D.1.3.2. The locally convex topological vector space S(G) is Hausdorff, by setting α, β, γ, δ = 0.
    Beware that the specific seminorms on C ∞ (G) defined above depend very much on the choice of coordinates
on G. But the topology is independent of such a choice thanks to:
    Lemma D.1.3.3. Let G = Rm × Tn × Zr × F for a finite abelian group F and integers m, n, r ≥ 0. For
every continuous automorphisms ϕ of G and f ∈ S(G), the pullback f ◦ ϕ : G → C belongs to S(G) and
f 7→ f ◦ ϕ is a topological automorphism of S(G).
    Proof. We will describe a general ϕ as a composition of finitely many types of automorphisms that can
be analyzed directly. Since the unique maximal compact subgroup of G is Tn × F and its identity component
is Tn , Since all automorphisms of Rm and of Zr are linear and of Tn arise from an element of GLn (Z), it is
clear that an automorphism arising from ones of the factors Rm , Tn , Zr , and F has the desired properties.
Thus, for a general ϕ we readily reduce to the case when ϕ is the identity on the factor group Tn and its
restriction to each of the four factor groups yields the identity when projected back onto that factor.
    By connectedness considerations, the effect of such a ϕ on Rm is given by x 7→ (x, f (x), 0, 0) for a
continuous homomorphism f : Rm → Tn . Automorphisms of the form (x, z, a, b) 7→ (x, f (x)z, a, b) are readily
seen to preserve the Schwartz decay property because f (x) = (f1 (x), . . . , fn (x)) for fj : Rm → T given by
x 7→ e2πi⟨x,cj ⟩ for some c1 , . . . , cn ∈ Rm . Thus, we can further reduce to the case that ϕ is the identity on the
factor group Rm . ϕ(x, z, a, b) = (x + L1 (a), zL2 (a)L3 (b), a, b + L4 (a)) for homomorphisms
                            L1 : Zr → Rm , L2 : Zr → Tn , L4 : Zr → F, L3 : F → Tn .
                D.1. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT SPACE OF A HAUSDORFF LOCALLY COMPACT ABELIAN GROUP                                            751


Hence, we can focus on the cases in which all but one of these homomorphisms is trivial. The family of
seminorms (D.1.3.10) defining the Schwartz topology allows us to handle the L1 -cases and the L2 -cases (since
we can explicitly describe the possibilities for such L1 and L2 via “linear” formulas). The L4 -cases are easily
handled since in such cases ϕ commutes with every ∂xα and ∂zβ . The L3 -cases are handled by again using the
family of seminorms (D.1.3.10).                                                                               □

     Proof. The proof of (1) is standard, similarly to any locally convex topology defined by a countable

     For (2), we first verify completeness by consider a Cauchy net {fi }i∈I in S(G) for the locally convex
topology induced by the family of seminorms || · ||(α,β,γ,δ) from (D.1.3.6), with I a directed set. The uniform
limit of {fi }i∈I in C0 (G) exists, since C0 (G) equipped with the uniform norm is a Banach space. We denote
such limit by f . The restriction to every fibre over the projection G → Zr × F is a uniform limit of smooth
functions with uniformity in each of its derivatives too. Formation of the derivatives ∂xα ∂zβ f , which exist
fibre-wise over Zr × F , is continuous over G by uniformity of the convergence and so f is smooth over G.
     We now show fi → f in the topology of S(G) by using the family of seminorms P1 in (D.1.3.8) to carry
over the classical argument for the completeness of S(Rm ). We have, for every ε > 0 and uniformly with
respect to (x, z, a, b) ∈ G, the net {fi }i∈I being Cauchy in S(G) and since the locally convex topology on S(G)
is, by Lemma D.1.3.4, equivalently generated by the family of seminorms P1 :

relations to be shown. It is in the proof of the reverse one that we use the ε-topology, and Lemma C.2.2.2 is

form (A′ ⊗ B ′ )◦◦ (bipolar), for A′ ⊂ E ′ and B ′ ⊂ F ′ equicontinuous.

the subspace topology.

     (3) : By Lemma D.1.3.5, S(G) is Hausdorff and complete. By (2), S(G) is isomorphic to the completed
projective tensor product of S(Rm ), S(Tn ), sr = S(Zr ) and CF . Each is nuclear (see [Tre, Cor. to Thm. 51.5]
for S(Rm ) and [Tre, Thms. 51.3, 51.5] for S(Tn ) and sr ), so S(G) is nuclear by [Scha, Ch. III, 7,5]. Since
S(G) is a Fréchet space by Lemma D.1.3.5, its strong dual S(G)′β is complete (as for any metrizable locally
convex space) by [Scha, Ch. II, 8.1; Ch. IV, 6.1]. Likewise nuclearity of the strong dual is inherited from that
of the Fréchet S(G) by [Tre, Prop. 50.6]. The Montel property for S(G) (in particular, reflexivity) holds as for
all nuclear Fréchet spaces [Tre, Cor. 3 to Prop. 50.2], and the strong dual thereby inherits the Montel property
(in particular, reflexivity) by [Scha, Ch. IV, 5.9]. Reflexive spaces are barrelled by [Scha, Ch. IV, p. 144], so
S(G) and S(G)′β are barrelled.                                                                                 □
    D.1.4. Structure theory of Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups. In this section, we recall

    D.1.5. Schwartz-Bruhat space of a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. The scope of this
subsection is to define the Schwartz-Bruhat space of an arbitrary Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G,
and fill in the arguments for [Bru, §9, Prop. 11] in the special case when G is second countable. We will only
briefly indicate how the results extend beyond the second-countable case.

      D.1.5.1. Good subgroups and structural pairs. Here is terminology and notation following [Bru, §9]:
    Definition D.1.5.1 (Structural pairs of G). Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group.
(1) A closed subgroup k ⊂ G is called good if and only if its annihilator k ⊥ ⊂ G
                                                                                b is both open (equivalent to
    compactness of k) and compactly generated.
(2) A pair (Γ, k) of subgroups of G is called structural if and only if Γ ⊂ G is an open compactly generated
    subgroup of G, k ⊂ G is a good subgroup of G, and k ⊂ Γ.
We define F the set of structural pairs (Γ, k) of G.
     Note that if k1 , k2 ⊂ G are good subgroups then so is k1 ∩ k2 . To see this, it suffices to show that the
evident inclusion k1⊥ k2⊥ ⊂ (k1 ∩ k2 )⊥ is an equality. This amounts to surjectivity of k1⊥ × k2⊥ → (k1 ∩ k2 )⊥ , so
it suffices to check that the injective dual map G/(k1 ∩ k2 ) → (G/k1 ) × (G/k2 ) has closed image. But this
image is that of the closed diagonal in G × G under the quotient map G × G → (G/k1 ) × (G/k2 ) which is
proper since the ki ’s are compact.
     Lemma D.1.5.2 (Properties of structural pairs). Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. Then

   Definition D.1.5.3 (Schwartz-Bruhat functions on Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups). Let G be
a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, f : G → C a function.
(1) Let p ≥ 0 be an integer. We say f is p-times differentiable if and only if there exists a good subgroup
    k ⊂ G such that f is k-invariant, and for every structural pair (k, Γ) of G the restriction f |Γ is such that
    the unique function f0 : Γ/k → C satisfying f |Γ = f0 ◦ r(k,Γ) is C p on the Lie group Γ/k (for its unique
    smooth structure respecting the group structure). We denote by C p (G) the C-vector space of p-times
    differentiable functions on G. We say f is smooth if and only if it is p-times differentiable on G for every
    integer p ≥ 0. We denote by C ∞ (G) the C-vector space of smooth functions on G.
(2) We say f is a Schwartz-Bruhat function on G if and only if:
    (1) There exists a structural pair (k, Γ) of G such that f is supported in Γ and k-invariant.
    (2) The unique f0 ∈ C ∞ (Γ/k) such that f = r(k,Γ) ◦ f0 satisfies the following condition: for a choice of
         isomorphism
(D.1.5.3)                                ϕ0 : Γ/k → Rm × Tn × Zr × F
           for unique integers m, n, r ≥ 0 and a finite abelian group F , the smooth function f0 ◦ ϕ−1
                                                                                                    0 is of rapid
           decay at infinity on Γ/k in the sense of Definition D.1.3.1(2).
      We denote by S(k, Γ) the C-vector space of smooth functions on G supported in Γ and k-invariant, such
      that the unique C-valued smooth function induced on the quotient Γ/k has rapid decay at infinity on Γ/k.
      We topologize S(k, Γ) with the Hausdorff locally convex topology of S(Rm × Tn × Zr × F ) by transport
      of structure along the isomorphism ϕ0 of Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups provided by (D.1.5.3);
      this is well-defined by Lemma D.1.3.3.

     Lemma D.1.5.4. Pullback along the proper map Γ1 /k2 ↠ Γ1 /k1 carries S(Γ1 /k1 ) to functions on the open
subgroup Γ1 /k2 ⊂ Γ2 /k2 whose extension by 0 to Γ2 /k2 lies in S(Γ2 /k2 ) (where each Γi /ki is an elementary
abelian Lie group, so the open subgroup Γ1 /k2 ⊂ Γ2 /k2 is also an elementary abelian Lie group). The resulting
inclusion S(Γ1 /k1 ) → S(Γ2 /k2 ) is a topological embedding (hence closed, by completeness of S(Γ1 /k1 )).

    Proof. We just have to check that for an elementary abelian Lie group A, compact subgroup k ⊂ A,
and open subgroup A′ ⊂ A:
        (i) pullback along A ↠ A/k carries S(A/k) into S(A) via a topological embedding onto the subspace of
            k-invariant elements.
       (ii) Extension by zero carries S(A′ ) into S(A) via a topological embedding.
   First we settle (i). By consideration of the maximal compact subgroup of A and the structure of connected
compact abelian Lie groups, we can choose an isomorphism
                                            A ≃ Rm × Tn × Zr × F
so that k is the product of some of the T-factors and a subgroup F ′ ⊂ F inside A. Thus, we get compatible
descriptions of S(A) and S(k), so also S(A/k), as completed tensor products in (D.1.3.20). This reduces us to
the separate cases A = Rm , Tn , Zr , F . The cases of Rm and Zr are obvious (k = 0), the case of F is clear.
For A = Tn we know k 0 is a torus that arises as a direct factor of A, so it suffices to separately treat the case
k = k 0 and k finite. Since S(Tn ) = C ∞ (Tn ) with the topology of uniform convergence in all derivatives, the
case of finite k is clear while for the case of k a torus we have S(A) = S(A′ )⊗b π S(k), from which the desired
properties are immediate.
    Turning to (ii), if we fix an isomorphism A = Rm × Tn × Zr × F (so F is the torsion subgroup of the
component group of A) then the clopen A′ contains the identity component Rm × Tn and so is determined by
             D.1. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT SPACE OF A HAUSDORFF LOCALLY COMPACT ABELIAN GROUP                            763


its component group π0 (A′ ) as a subgroup of π0 (A). Letting F ′ = π0 (A′ )tor , we have A′ ⊂ Rm × Tn × Zr × F ′
inside A. The special case A′ = Rm × Tn × Zr × F ′ is immediate from (D.1.3.20) applied to A and A′ , so
we may now assume F ′ = F . More precisely, now F ⊂ A′ inside A. Thus, A′ is determined by the maximal
torsion-free quotient M of π0 (A′ ) as a subgroup of the corresponding quotient Zr for A.
     The “elementary divisor” description of M ⊂ Zr allows us to harness the infinite divisibility of A0 = Rm ×Tn
to possibly change the identification of A with Rm × Tn × Zr × F (adapted to a preliminary choice of analogous
decomposition for A′ ) so that we have A′ = Rm × Tn × M × F inside A with M ⊂ Zr equal to ⊕ri=1 (ni Z) for
some integers ni ≥ 0. The family of seminorms (D.1.3.9) applied to A and A′ then yields the result.             □

    We conclude that the directed system of S(k, Γ)’s is strict in the sense that its transition maps are
topological embeddings. Thus, the collection of all Schwartz-Bruhat functions on G is a C-vector space that
we call the Schwartz-Bruhat space of G and is made into a locally convex topological vector space via the
locally convex inductive limit topology induced by the canonical linear isomorphism
(D.1.5.4)                                     S(G) = colim S(k, Γ)
                                                      (k,Γ)∈F

whose injective transition maps are topological embeddings.
    From the construction it is clear that left translation of G on itself carries S(G) onto itself, but it is less
evident (in such generality) that the action map G × S(G) → S(G) is continuous. Such continuity is proved in
Proposition D.1.9.2.

    Remark D.1.5.5. For any Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G, define C ∞ (G) to be the colimit of
the spaces C ∞ (Γ/k) of smooth functions (similarly to the colimit that defines S(G)). Clearly S(G) ⊂ C ∞ (G).
    Also, every χ ∈ Gb has smooth restriction to Γ as a function χ : G → C× ⊂ C. Indeed, we can pick an
open compactly generated subgroup U ⊂ G     b containing χ, so its annihilator k in G is compact by Lemma
D.1.4.6(4), hence a good subgroup of G, and by design χ(k) = 1. We may and do replace k with k ∩ Γ so that
k ⊂ Γ. Then χ|Γ descends to a continuous character of the elementary abelian Lie group Γ/k. The latter
character is smooth, so χ|Γ ∈ C ∞ (Γ).


    D.1.5.3. Main Structure Theorems on Schwartz-Bruhat spaces.

     Lemma D.1.5.6 (Strictness of the inductive system {S(k, Γ)}(k,Γ) ). Let G be a second-countable Hausdorff
locally compact abelian group, and B ⊂ S(G) a bounded subset.
(1) The topology on S(G) is Hausdorff and for any structural pair (k, Γ) of G the locally convex topology
    induced on S(k, Γ) by S(G) is the intrinsic locally convex topology of S(k, Γ) = S(Γ/k).
(2) There exists a structural pair (k, Γ) of G such that B is the image of a bounded subset of S(k, Γ) into S(G).

    This result holds without second-countability for G, but the proof is then more technical (e.g., (2) is
proved by building a projector via integration over compact subgroups k ⊂ G) and we do not need it.

    Proof. Since G is second-countable, there is a countable cofinal system of structural pairs (kn , Γn ) and so
S(G) is a “strict inductive limit” of a sequence of Hausdorff locally convex spaces S(kn , Γn ). But such inductive
limits E = colimEn always satisfy the two asserted properties: E is Hausdorff with En → E a topological
embedding [Scha, Ch. II, 6.4], and every bounded subset of E arises from a bounded subset of some En [Scha,
Ch. II, 6.5].                                                                                                    □

    The following is the main result of this subsection, and a special case of [Bru, §9, Prop. 11]:

   Theorem D.1.5.7 (Main Structure Theorem on Schwartz-Bruhat spaces). Let G be a second-countable
Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. The Hausdorff locally convex S(G) is barrelled and bornological,
764                               CHAPTER D. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT FUNCTIONS


Moreover, both S(G) and its strong dual S(G)′β are complete, nuclear, and Montel (hence reflexive). In
particular, S(G)′β is barrelled.

     Proof. Since each S(k, Γ) = S(Γ/k) is a Fréchet space by Lemma D.1.3.7, hence each of them is both
barrelled and bornological [Scha, Ch. II, Cor. to 7.2, Cor. 1 to 8.2], the countable strict inductive limit S(G) is
also barrelled and bornological by [Scha, Ch. II, Cor. to 7.1, 8.1].
     Each S(k, Γ) = S(Γ/k) is complete, nuclear, and Montel by Lemma D.1.3.7(3). These properties then
hold for S(G) since each is inherited under countable strict inductive limits E = colimEn of Hausdorff locally
convex topological vector spaces: [Scha, Ch. II, 6.6] for completeness, [Scha, Ch. III, Cor. to 7.4] for nuclearity,
and [Scha, Ch. IV, 5.8] for the Montel property (to be precise, the latter reference is for inheriting reflexivity,
but for the Heine-Borel property of E = colimEn we simply observe that a closed bounded subset K ⊂ E
arises from a bounded subset of some En that in turn must be closed in En since En → E is a topological
embedding, so the Heine-Borel property of En makes K compact in En , thus also in E).
     Turning to the strong dual S(G)′β , it inherits the Montel property from that of S(G) because the strong
dual of a Montel space is always Montel [Scha, Ch. IV, 6.1]. For completeness, the strong dual Eβ′ of any
bornological (Hausdorff locally convex) E is complete by [Scha, Ch. IV, 5.9]. For nuclearity for S(G)′β , we
first note that since S(G) is nuclear and complete, the strong dual topology on S(G)′ coincides with the
Mackey topology τ (S(G)′ , S(G)) (as for any complete nuclear E [Tre, top of p. 522]). This is useful because
the Mackey topology on the topological dual of a countable strict inductive limit E = colimEn coincides
                             ′
with the inverse limit lim En,τ  of the topological duals equipped with their Mackey topologies τn′ = τ (En′ , En )
[Scha, Ch. IV, Rem. to 4.5]. But with En = S(Γn /kn ) we likewise have En,τ   ′       ′
                                                                                ′ = En,β , so the known nuclearity
                                                                                n
of S(A)β for elementary abelian Lie groups A gives nuclearity for S(G)β since nuclearity is inherited under
        ′                                                                    ′

inverse limits of Hausdorff locally convex topological vector spaces by [Scha, Ch. III, Cor. to 7.4]. Barrelledness
for S(G)′β holds as a general property of reflexive spaces (see [Scha, Ch. IV p. 144]).                          □

    Remark D.1.5.8. We note that if G is not second-countable then (see [Bru, §9, Prop. 11] S(G) is still
bornological, complete, and Montel but it is never nuclear: see the discussion in [Bru, top of p. 54], where
the absence of second-countability causes the existence of an uncountable topological direct sum of copies
of C to split off from S(G) linearly and topologically. That obstructs nuclearity because topological direct
summands inherit nuclearity by [Scha, Ch.III, 7.2] but an uncountable direct sum of copies of C (with its
locally convex inductive limit topology) is never nuclear, by [Tre, Thm. 51.2]. The proof of completeness of
S(G) beyond the second-countable case requires some additional work when adapting the proof of completeness
of Cc∞ (G) in [Bru, §4, Thm. 1], ultimately resting on Grothendieck’s characterization of completeness [Scha,
Ch. IV, Cor. 2 to Thm. 6.2].

    We record below an important property of the Schwartz-Bruhat space S(G) of a second-countable Hausdorff
locally compact abelian group called acyclicity (for which we refer the reader to §C.1.5). This is useful when
inductive tensor products of nuclear Fréchet spaces carry linear topological embeddings to linear topological
embeddings. This will be used throughout the proof of Theorem D.3.3.7(1).

    Proposition D.1.5.9 (Acyclicity of S(G) - I). Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. Assume
G is second-countable. Then S(G) is acyclic.

    Proof. The space S(G) is a countable strict locally convex inductive limit of nuclear Fréchet spaces,
hence complete by [Scha, Ch. II, 6.6]/ But acyclicity and completeness are equivalent for such inductive limits
by [Wngr-2, §3, Thm. 3.3, p. 253], which applies because nuclear Fréchet space are always Montel (by [Scha,
Ch. IV, 5.6] and [Tre, Cor. 1 to Prop. 50.2]).                                                               □

     D.1.6. Differential operators on Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups. For G a (real or
complex) Lie group, we have the notion of its Lie algebra g, which, as a linear space is the tangent space at
the neutral element of G, the Lie group being a differentiable manifold. The Lie algebra can be defined purely
topologically. For an arbitrary Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, a Lie “algebra” can be defined as
follows:

      Definition D.1.6.1. Let G be a topological group. We define the topological Lie algebra of G to be the
set
(D.1.6.1)                                   L(G) := Homcont (R, G)
of one-parameter subgroups of G, i.e. of all continuous homomorphisms R → G, topologized with the compact
open topology.

    Remark D.1.6.2. The space L(G) makes sense for non-commutative G too, and is defined in Definition
D.1.6.1 for arbitrary topological groups. In special cases, it carries finer structures that approximate the
defining elements of the Lie algebra of a Lie group. In general, we may write
(D.1.6.2)                                      expG : L(G) → G
for the continuous map
(D.1.6.3)                                 expG (a) := a(1), a ∈ L(G)
766                                CHAPTER D. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT FUNCTIONS


and refer to it as the exponential map of G. In favorable situations, it is possible to identify on L(G) the
structure of a Lie algebra and construct on G the structure of a Lie group. For instance, if G admits a
continuous faithful finite dimensional complex representation, then G is a Lie group.

    Remark D.1.6.3. For G a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, L(G) is a Hausdorff locally convex
topological R-vector space. We will never need this, but let us briefly indicate where this topology comes from.
A canonical R-vector space structure is defined by pointwise addition and pre-composition with R-scaling
on itself. By Pontryagin duality, G is isomorphic as a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group to its own
Pontryagin bidual, and so by Lemma D.1.4.7 it admits a neighborhood base at the neutral element comprised of
quasi-convex subsets: subsets U ⊂ G such that for every g ∈ G outside U there exists χ ∈ G    b with Re(χ(u)) ≥ 0
for every u ∈ U and Re(χ(g)) < 0 (such χ is an element of the analog of the polar set of U as defined for
subsets of locally convex topological C-vector spaces). Thus, by [Au, Prop. 1.2(ii), (iii)], L(G) with its R-linear
structure is a Hausdorff locally convex R-vector space.

   The following description of L(G) for G a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group is a consequence of

     D.1.6.1. Degree-1 differential operators and differential characterization of smoothness. We now character-

topological Lie algebra L(G) of a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, we can define differential operators
on G. We will then use them to provide a characterization of smoothness, and check that the definition
recovers the familiar one when G is of the form G = Rm × Tn × Zr × F , for integers m, n, r ≥ 0 and a finite
group F , the definition of which was initiated in Definition 2.1.1.4.

    Lemma D.1.6.6. Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, and f ∈ C 1 (G). Then ∂a f is a
continuous function on G. Moreover, ∂a preserves the C-linear subspace C ∞ (G) ⊂ C 1 (G) and satisfies

    We call the operators ∂a : C ∞ (G) → C ∞ (G) first-order differential operators.

    Proof. Fix f ∈ C 1 (G) and a structural pair (k, Γ) of G such that f is supported on Γ and is k-invariant.
Then the unique function f0 ∈ C(Γ/k) such that f0 ◦ r(k,Γ) = f , for r(k,Γ) : Γ → Γ/k the continuous quotient
homomorphism from (D.1.5.2), is C 1 on the elementary abelian Lie group Γ/k in the sense of Definition
D.1.5.3(1). The one-parameter group a : R → G has homomorphic image contained in a path-connected
subgroup of G. In particular, it is contained in every open compactly generated subgroup, hence it lands in Γ.
    Thus, we have a one-parameter subgroup a0 : R → Γ/k by composition with the continuous quotient
homomorphism r(k,Γ) , and by k-invariance of f we have f (ga(t)) = f0 (ga0 (t)) where g := r(k,Γ) (g). Since

This reduces the claims in the lemma to the case when G is an elementary abelian Lie group, say say isomorphic

within Rm × Tn × {0} × {0}. Since R and Rm × Tn are Lie groups, a is smooth and ∂a f is the directional
derivative of f along the smooth curve a. Now all of the assertions can be seen by inspection.              □

    Lemma D.1.6.7 (Invariance and commutation of degree-one differential operators). Let a, b : R ⇒ G be
one-parameter subgroups; i.e., a, b ∈ L(G). Then:
(1) ∂a is a G-invariant C-linear operator on C ∞ (G) that depends R-linearly on a, and it restricts to a
    continuous endomorphism of S(G).
(2) As C-linear operators on C ∞ (G), we have [∂a , ∂b ] = 0; i.e., ∂a ∂b = ∂b ∂a .

     Proof. Pick f ∈ C ∞ (G), so f ∈ C ∞ (Γ/k) ffor some compact subgroup k ⊂ G with open compactly
generated orthogonal k ⊥ and an open compactly generated subgroup Γ ⊂ G containing k. In particular, f is
k-invariant and Γ contains the support of f .
     Since U := a(R) · Γ ∪ b(R) · Γ is an open subset of G that is a symmetric neighborhood of the neutral
element, it generates an open subgroup of G that is also compactly generated (since both R and Γ are so).
We may replace Γ with this open subgroup so that a, b are valued in Γ. The direct limit definitions of C ∞ (G)
and S(G) as well as of the topology on the latter thereby allows us to rename Γ as G to arrange that G is
compactly generated. Since a and b take values in the identity component of G, we can also assume without
loss of generality that G is connected.
     It follows that G/k is an abelian Lie group, and by design f arises by pullback from some f0 ∈ C ∞ (G/k).
Thus, ∂a f is the pullback of the output of the differential operator ∂a on f0 ∈ C ∞ (G/k) where a is the
composition of a with the quotient homomorphism G → G/k. The same holds for ∂b f using the composition b
of b with the quotient homomorphism G → G/k. To check (1) and (2) it now suffices to do so with G replaced
                                                                                        ⊥
by G/k ′ for each compact subgroup k ′ ⊂ G with compactly generated orthogonal k ′ . In other words, we
may rename G/k as G to assume that G is a connected abelian Lie group. In this case the assertions are
standard.                                                                                                   □

     D.1.8. Support of tempered distributions on Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups. Let
G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. Recall that S(G) is endowed with a natural Hausdorff locally
convex topology, propagated from the special case G is an elementary abelian Lie group (see §D.1.5, and [DE,
Ch. 3, 4]) using the structure theory of Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups. In Theorem D.1.5.7 (which
is [Bru, §10, Prop. 11]) the main properties of the Hausdorff locally convex topology on S(G) and its strong
dual S(G)′β were recorded when G is second-countable.
     We refer to S(G)′β (the continuous dual of S(G), equipped with the Hausdorff locally convex “strong dual”
topology of uniform convergence on the bounded subsets of S(G)) as the space of tempered distributions on G.
When G is an elementary abelian Lie group, say G ≃ Rm × Tn × Zr × F , the description of S(G) as a completed
tensor product in (D.1.3.20) implies density of the image of the continuous injection D(G) := Cc∞ (G) → S(G)
by reduction to the classical case of Rm [KG, Thm. 30, p. 74] (where the proof for m = 1 easily adapts to
general m) and the straightforward case of Zr , so passage to direct limit with subspaces S(k, Γ) then gives the
same density result for general G. In particular, the induced map on topological linear duals S(G)′ → D(G)′
is injective for general G. In this way we view the space of tempered distributions as a special subspace of the
space of all distributions (continuous linear functionals on compactly supported smooth functions), equipped
with a finer strong dual topology.

    D.1.8.1. Kernel Theorems. We let (m, k, r) ∈ N3 be a triple of non-negative integers, F a finite abelian
group, and consider the elementary abelian Lie group:
                                          G := Rm × Tk × Zr × F.
Describing tempered distributions on G amounts to describing tempered distributions on Rm , Tk , Zr and F ,
respectively, in light of the following:

     D.1.8.2. Supports. We recall that a tempered distribution T on G = Tn is simply a distribution, since
S(Tn ) = D(Tn ) (:= Cc∞ (Tn )). In particular, the support of T is (by definition) the smallest closed subset
K of Tn such that ⟨T, f ⟩S(Tn )′ ,S(Tn ) = 0 for any f ∈ S(Tk ) supported in Tn − K. Since the support of any
f ∈ S(Tn ) is compact, using a smooth partition of unity it is equivalent to say that the support of T is the
closed subset K ⊂ Tn whose complement is the union of those open U ⊂ Tn such that ⟨T, f ⟩S(Tn )′ ,S(Tn ) = 0
for every Schwartz function f on Tn supported in U .
     The notion of support of a tempered distribution on Rm is defined by adapting the notion of support of
distributions on Rm as in [Horm, Ch. II, §2.2, Def. 2.2.2]: it is the closed subset K ⊂ Rm whose complement
is the union of those open U ⊂ Rm such that ⟨T, f ⟩S(Rm )′ ,S(Rm ) = 0 for every Schwartz function f on Rm
supported over U .

    Definition D.1.8.2. Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. Let T ∈ S(G)′ be a tempered
distribution on G.
(1) The vanishing locus of T is defined to be the union of all open subsets U ⊂ G such that ⟨T, f ⟩S(G)′ ,S(G) = 0
    for every f ∈ S(G) supported in U .
(2) The support of T , denoted supp(T ) ⊂ G, is defined to be the complement of V (T ) in G.

     Lemma D.1.8.4. Let G be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, T ∈ S(G)′ a tempered distribution.
For each structural pair (k, Γ) for G (i.e., Γ ⊂ G an open compactly generated subgroup, k ⊂ G a compact
subgroup with open compactly generated orthogonal k ⊥ , and k ⊂ Γ; see Definition D.1.5.1), let T(k,Γ) ∈ S(Γ/k)′
denote composition of T with the continuous map S(Γ/k) ≃ S(k, Γ) ,→ S(G) (see Definition D.1.5.3).
     The open subset V (T ) = G − supp(T ) ⊂ G is contained in the union of the open preimages under Γ → Γ/k
of V (T(k,Γ) ) ⊂ Γ/k as (k, Γ) varies over the directed set of all structural pairs of G.

    Proof. A point g ∈ Γ/k belongs to V (T(k,Γ) ) if and only if there exists an open neighborhood U ⊂ Γ/k
of g such that ⟨T(k,Γ) , f ⟩ = 0 for every f ∈ S(Γ/k) supported in U . This vanishing condition says
                                                ⟨T, fe⟩S(G)′ ,S(G) = 0
for fe the extension by zero from Γ to G of the composition of f with the quotient homomorphism Γ → Γ/k.
Such f ’s are exactly the k-invariant Schwartz-Bruhat functions supported in the open preimage U of U in Γ.
     Now consider a point g ∈ V (T ). There exists an open and compactly generated subgroup Γ ⊂ G containing
g and a compact subgroup k ⊂ G contained in Γ and with compactly generated orthogonal k ⊥ ⊂ G.        b Note
that Γ is necessarily also closed in G. By definition of V (T ), there exists an open neighborhood U ⊂ G of g
such that ⟨T, f ⟩S(G)′ ,S(G) = 0 for every f ∈ S(G) whose support is contained in U . We can shrink U around
g so that U ⊂ Γ. By Lemma D.1.4.7, we can shrink k so that kg ⊂ U ⊂ Γ, and then find an open V ⊂ U
around g so that kV ⊂ U . Thus, we can replace U with kV to arrange that U is the preimage in Γ of an open
subset U ⊂ Γ/k containing g := g mod k. This implies U ⊂ V (T(k,Γ) ), so since the initial arbitrary choice of
g ∈ V (T ) belongs to U , we have shown V (T ) is contained in the desired union.                           □

    D.1.9. Continuity of translation on Schwartz-Bruhat spaces. With the aim to make Lemma 4.3.3.1
and its corollaries applicable, we discuss continuity properties of the left-translation action of a Hausdorff
locally compact abelian group G on its Schwartz-Bruhat space S(G). Since both G and S(G) are generally
studied via direct limits from the case of elementary abelian Lie groups, we begin with a basic lemma on
inheritance of continuity through locally convex inductive limits.

    Lemma D.1.9.1. Let H be a Hausdorff locally compact topological group that is the union of an increasing
sequence of open subgroups {Hn }n≥1 . Let {En } be a strict inductive system of Hausdorff locally convex
topological vector spaces such that every En is barrelled, and let E = lim En .
                                                                       −→
    If an action of H on E makes Hn act continuously on En for every n then theaction map H × E → E is
continuous.

     Proof. The space E is barrelled by [Scha, Ch. II, Cor. 1 to 7.2]. Each h ∈ H lies in some Hn0 , so the
h-action on E carries En into itself for all n ≥ n0 with h : En → En a topological isomorphism for such n
(since Hn acts continuously on En ). Thus, h : E → E is a topological isomorphism, so the H-action on E is
encoded in a group homomorphism ρ : H → L(E) into the vector space of continuous linear endomorphisms of
E. Since H is locally compact, continuity for its action on E is equivalent to the conjunction of two properties:
             D.1. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT SPACE OF A HAUSDORFF LOCALLY COMPACT ABELIAN GROUP                            781


(i) equicontinuity at 0 ∈ E for the subset ρ(K) ⊂ L(E) for every compact subset K ⊂ H, (ii) for each x ∈ E
and 0-neighborhood U ⊂ E the existence of an e-neighborhood Ω ⊂ H such that Ω.x ⊂ x + U .
     First we verify (i). The barrelledness of E ensures (by [Scha, Ch. III, 4.2]) that equicontinuity holds if the
subset K.x ⊂ E is weakly bounded for every x ∈ E: that is, {ℓ(k.x)}k∈K is bounded in C for each continuous
linear functional ℓ ∈ E ′ . Thus, it suffices that K.x is compact for each x ∈ E. The open cover {Hn ∩ K} of K
has a finite subcover, so K ⊂ Hn for sufficiently large n. By taking n big enough, also x ∈ En . Since Hn acts
continuously on En , we see that K.x is compact inside En and so the boundedness of ℓ(K.x) follows.
     To verify (ii), pick n for which x ∈ En . Since Hn acts continuously on En , there is an e-neighborhood
Ω ⊂ Hn such that Ω.x ⊂ x + (U ∩ En ) ⊂ x + U . Since Hn is open in H, we are done.                               □

    Proposition D.1.9.2. Let G be a second-countable Hausdorff locally compact abelian group. The left-
translation action ρ : G × S(G) → S(G) is continuous. In particular, for any compact subset K ⊂ G the map
K × S(G) → S(G) is uniformly continuous over K in the sense that for any 0-neighborhood U ⊂ S(G) there is
a 0-neighborhood V ⊂ S(G) such that K.V ⊂ U .

     Proof. If the G-action is continuous then the uniform continuity property for compact subsets K ⊂ G is
immediate from the fact that k.0 = 0 for all k ∈ K. To prove the continuity of the G-action we first reduce
to the case that G is an elementary abelian Lie group. Since G is second-countable, there is a countable
directed system of structural pairs (kn , Γn ) (see Definition D.1.5.1) such that colim S(kn , Γn ) → S(G) is a
linear topological isomorphism with each injection S(Γn /kn ) = S(kn , Γn ) → S(G) a topological embedding.
We apply Lemma D.1.9.1 to H = G with Hn = Γn and En = S(kn , Γn ) ≃ S(Γn /kn ) (so E = S(G)). Note that
the barrelledness of such En ’s follows from S(A) being a Fréchet space for elementary abelian Lie groups A,
since every Fréchet space is barrelled [Scha, Ch. II, Cor. to 7.1]. This reduces the continuity task to the case of
the groups Γn /kn that are elementary abelian Lie groups.
     We can write G = Rm × Tn × Zr × F for integers m, n, r ≥ 0 and a finite abelian group F . By (D.1.3.20),
S(G) is the completed projective tensor product of S(Rm ), S(Tn ), S(Zr ), and S(F ) = CF . The left G-action
on S(G) preserves the subspace given by the “uncompleted” projective tensor product. To reduce the continuity
verification to the action of G on the uncompleted projective tensor product, we apply:

     Lemma D.1.9.3. Let E be a Hausdorff topological vector space and H a topological group equipped with
                                b preserving the subspace E. If each h ∈ H acts continuously on E

uj ∈ Uj for a base of convex circled 0-neighborhoods Uj ⊂ Ej . For a choice of U1 and U2 , pick convex circled

    We are reduced to treating the separate cases G = Rm , Tn , Zr , F . The case G = F a finite abelian group

     D.1.10. Examples: global and S-local idele classes. As per the general definition of the C-linear
space of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group G, upon calling G either
CF or CF,S , then S(G) is the locally convex inductive limit of a system of Fréchet spaces S(Γ/k) where Γ ⊂ G
is open and compactly generated, k ⊂ Γ is compact with (open and) compactly generated annihilator k ⊥ in G. b
In particular, if G is second-countable then S(G) is a strict LF-space.

                        D.2. Schwartz-Bruhat functions on modulated groups
     In this section we introduce modulated groups, a special case of Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups
G, unifying examples of interest to this work, such as global and S-local idele class groups. This section
will enable systematic use of linear and topological properties of the Mellin transform for G equipped with a
proper continuous surjective homomorphism | · |G : G → R>0 ; such a G is called R>0 -modulated.

    D.2.1. Preparations on modulated groups. The compact Hausdorff abelian group CF1 acts on S(CF )
by continuous left-translation: (g.f )(x) = f (g −1 x) (for the continuity property more broadly. See Proposition
D.1.9.2). The same holds for the compact Hausdorff abelian groups CF,S          1
                                                                                    acting on S(CF,S ), and JF,S
                                                                                                              1

acting on S(JF,S ). The Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups CF , CF,S and JF,S are three examples of
“modulated” groups. This concept was discussed by Weil in [Weil-e, §3, p. 6] with the aim of treating certain
representation-theoretic preparations towards the explicit formulas for Artin L-functions in a unified manner,
encompassing Weil groups.

    D.2.1.1. Modulated groups: definition and canonical measure. Let G be a second-countable Hausdorff
locally compact abelian group equipped with a continuous proper homomorphism
                                                  | · |G : G → R>0

(so G1 := ker(| · |G ) is compact). For a choice of continuous character ω ∈ G
the subspace of Schwartz-Bruhat functions f on G that are ω-homogenous in the sense that g.f = ω(g)f for
all g ∈ G1 ; this is a closed subspace since the G-action on S(G) is continuous.
     Recall from Theorem D.1.5.7 that the Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space S(G) is complete,
and by Proposition D.1.9.2 every compact subset K ⊂ G acts uniformly continuously on S(G); in particular,
the G1 -action on S(G) is uniformly continuous. This allows us to build averaging operators over G1 valued in
S(G) via Pettis integration, as follows.

    Definition D.2.1.1 (Modulated groups). Let G be a second-countable Hausdorff locally compact abelian
group. We say G is modulated if there is given a non-trivial continuous proper homomorphism
(D.2.1.3)                                           | · |G : G → R>0 .
We call | · |G the module of G, and denote by Γ the closed image of | · |G in R>0 . We define:
(1) G1 := ker(| · |G ), a the compact subgroup of G;
(2) the canonical Haar measure µcan on G to be the unique Haar measure on G such that for every real
    number Λ > 1, upon denoting by G[1/Λ,Λ] the compact subset of G defined as the pre-image of the compact
    interval [1/Λ, Λ] ⊂ R>0 under the proper homomorphism | · |G , we have
(D.2.1.4)                                  µcan (G[1/Λ,Λ] ) = 2 log(Λ) + O(1)
    as Λ → +∞ (such a measure exists because | · |G is non-trivial).

     The condition (D.2.1.4) uniquely determines µcan , but to see the existence of µcan it is useful first to show
(as one sees directly in all cases of interest) that | · |G admits continuous homomorphic sections:

     Remark D.2.1.2. The closed subgroup Γ ⊂ R>0 is either of the form tZ for a unique t ∈ R>1 or is R>0
(the case | · |G is surjective), and in all cases we claim | · |G admits continuous homomorphic sections τ : Γ → G
(each thereby inducing an isomorphism G ≃ G1 × Γ depending on the choice of τ ). This is clear when Γ is
infinite cyclic. When | · |G is surjective, the existence of τ follows from the proper |·G : G → R>0 being a
quotient map and G necessarily having an open subgroup of the form K × RN for some compact group K
and integer N ≥ 1 [Ru, Thm. 1.2.4].
     Modulated groups are discussed by Weil in his paper on the explicit formulas for Artin L-functions of
number fields; we refer the reader to [Weil-e, §3, pp. 5-6]. Many non-compact Hausdorff locally compact
groups of arithmetic integer, abelian and non-abelian, are modulated. The examples throughout this work
will be (CF , | · |F ), (CF,S , | · |F ◦ iF,S ), and (JF,S , | · |F,S ), with iF,S : CF,S → CF the continuous open injective
homomorphism induced by the inclusion GL1 (AF,S × O                   b Σ −S ) → GL1 (AF ).

    Remark D.2.1.3 (Canonical measure on modulated groups). For G a Hausdorff locally compact modulated
abelian group and τ : Γ → G a continuous homomorphic section to the module | · |G (which defines an
isomorphism G1 × Γ ≃ G), to build µcan we use
                                                   µcan = µ1,can × µΓ
where µ1,can is the volume-1 Haar measure on G1 and µΓ is a Haar measure on Γ ⊂ R>0 satisfying
(D.2.1.5)                                 µΓ ([1/Λ, Λ] ∩ Γ) = 2 log(Λ) + O(1)
as Λ → +∞.
     To see such a µΓ exists, we separately treat the cases Γ = R>0 and Γ = tZ for some t > 1. In the case
Γ = R>0 we use µΓ = dt/t (in this case the O(1)-term in (D.2.1.5) vanishes). In the case Γ = tZ with t > 1,
take µΓ to be counting measure multiplied by log(t); this satisfies (D.2.1.5) because the difference between
2 log(Λ) and
                                      #{m ∈ Z : 1/Λ ≤ tm ≤ Λ}log(t)
is bounded (by log(t)) as Λ → +∞.

    D.2.2. Complements on the G1 -isotypes of S(G) for modulated groups G. By Lemma 4.3.3.1(2)
(applied to the G1 -action on E = S(G) defined by f 7→ ω(g) g.f for g ∈ G1 ), ΦG,ω induces a linear topological
isomorphism
(D.2.2.1)                                ΦG,ω : S(G)(ω) → H0 (ω, S(G))
where S(G)(ω) is the linear quotient S(G)/ ker(ΦG,ω ) equipped with the quotient topology. The kernel of
ΦG,ω is the closure in S(G) of the subspace of differences {f − ω(g) g.f : f ∈ S(G), g ∈ G1 } by Lemma
4.3.3.1(3), so S(G)(ω) is the maximal Hausdorff quotient of the space of G1 -coinvariants of S(G) under the
action f 7→ ω(g) g.f (g ∈ G1 ). For this reason, S(G)(ω) is also denoted H0,cont (ω, S(G)).
     For a Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space E equipped with a left action ρG of G by linear
topological automorphisms, we say ρG is uniformly continuous on a subset Σ ⊂ G if and only if for every
0-neighorhood U ⊂ E there exists 0-neighborhood V ⊂ E so that ρG (σ, x) ∈ U for all σ ∈ Σ. Equivalently,
this says that for every net {xi }i∈I ⊂ E converging to x ∈ E and every 0-neighborhood U ⊂ E there exists i0
so that ρG (σ, xi ) − ρG (σ, x) = ρG (g, xi − x) ∈ U for all i ≥ i0 and all σ ∈ Σ. For example, Proposition D.1.9.2
the G-action on S(G) is uniformly continuous on any compact subset K ⊂ G.

    Proof. Assertion (1) is a special case of Lemma D.1.8.1(1). For assertion (2), we first treat the case
E = S(G) with i the identity. We have S(Γ) = H0 (G1 , S(G)) (functions independent of the second component

     Now we turn to the general case of (2). The assumed continuity of Mχ with respect to the topology
on S(G) by E under i allows us to conclude by using Lemma D.2.2.1(4) with T = Mχ 10 provided that the
Hausdorff quotient E(ω) of E inherits completness from E and the continuous linear map Mχ (S(Γ)) → E(ω)
is a topological embedding with dense image. Let us now verify these two properties.
     The completeness of E(ω) holds because the natural map H0 (ω, E) → E(ω) is a topological isomorphism
(see (4.3.3.2)) and H0 (ω, E) inherits completeness due to its closedness inside E. The map Mχ (S(Γ)) → E(ω)
(where S(Γ)) is given the subspace topology from E) is topologically identified with the map H0 (ω, S(G)) →
H0 (ω, E) ≃ E(ω) that is a topological embedding when S(G) is given the subspace topology from E. The
image of this map is also dense because the map is linearly identified with S(G)(ω) → E(ω) whose image is
dense since S(G) is dense in E.                                                                           □

                       D.3. Schwartz-Bruhat functions with I-exponential decay
    We now relate spaces of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on the positive real line with exponential or semi-
exponential decay to spaces of holomorphic functions on the complex plane or half-planes, with rapid decay
uniformly over vertical strips of bounded width.

   D.3.1. Schwartz-Bergman spaces. We begin with the following application of the Asymptotic Residue
Theorem (see Theorem B.3.2.1).

   The following Lemma is reminiscent of properties of Bergman Spaces and their completeness (see [HKZ,

    Lemma D.3.1.2 (Uniform Schwartz topology and Lp -convergence on vertical lines). Let I ⊂ R be a

   Definition D.3.1.3 (Schwartz-Bergman spaces). Fix 1 < p < ∞ and I ⊂ R a non-empty open interval.
We define the Schwartz-Bergman space AS(CI ) to be the C-linear space S(CI ) of holomorphic functions on
CI that are Schwartz uniformly on the vertical strips of bounded width within CI , topologized with the
                       D.3. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT FUNCTIONS WITH I-EXPONENTIAL DECAY                                  801


Hausdorff locally convex topology generated by the countable family of seminorms {pm,N }m,N ≥0 defined as:
                            pm,N (ϕ) := ||(am + ix)N ϕ(am + ix)||Lp (R,dx) , m, N ≥ 0
with {am }m≥0 ⊂ I a choice of sequence of positive rational numbers as in Lemma D.3.1.2.

    Remark D.3.1.4. Lemma D.3.1.2 shows that AS(CI ) is a separable Fréchet space, and its topology does
not depend on the choice of {am }m≥0 , nor on the choice of p > 1.

    D.3.2. Fourier-Mellin transform on SI (R>0 ). We now relate the spaces of Schwartz-Bruhat functions
SE (R>0 ), SSE (R>0 ) and ŠSE (R>0 ) with the Schwartz-Bergman spaces AS(CI ) for I = R, I = R>0 and
I = (−∞, 0) by means of the Mellin transform. We begin with a definition.

    Definition D.3.2.1 (Schwartz-Bruhat functions on R>0 with I-exponential decay). Let I ⊂ R be a
non-empty interval. We define SI (R>0 ) ⊂ C ∞ (R>0 ) to be the linear subspace of those smooth functions ϕ on
R>0 satisfying the following condition: ta ϕ(t) ∈ S(R>0 ) for all a ∈ I.
    We call SI (R>0 ) the C-linear space of Schwartz-Bruhat functions of I-exponential decay. We topologize
SI (R>0 ) with the (visibly Hausdorff) projective topology [Scha, Ch. II, §5] induced by the ta -multipliiers
(D.3.2.1)                                     Ta : SI (R>0 ) → S(R>0 )
for every a ∈ I (i.e., Ta (ϕ) = ta ϕ). In other words, the topology on SI (R>0 ) is the subspace topology arising
from the linear injection T = a∈I Ta : SI (R>0 ) → a∈I S(R>0 ), Equivalently, a net {ϕα } in SI (R>0 )
                                   Q                        Q

converges to ϕ ∈ SI (R>0 ) if and only if Ta (ϕα ) → Ta (ϕ) in S(R>0 ) for all a ∈ I.

      Remark D.3.2.2. Each operator Ta intertwines with the left-translation action by R>0 up to a controlled
scalar multiplication: Ta (c.ϕ) = ca (c.(Ta (ϕ))) for c ∈ R>0 . Thus, SI (R>0 ) has a natural R>0 -action via
(c.f )(t) = f (c−1 t) that is moreover continuous, and uniformly so for the action of compact subsets of R>0
(thanks to the known case of S(R>0 ) ≃ S(R)).


    D.3.2.1. Basic properties of SI (R>0 ).

    Lemma D.3.2.3. Let I ⊂ R be a non-empty interval. The following hold:
(1) The Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector space SI (R>0 ) is Fréchet and nuclear (hence Montel).
(2) The Hausdorff strong dual SI (R>0 )′β is complete, nuclear, and Montel.
(3) If 0 ∈ I, then SI (R>0 ) is naturally a linear subspace of S(R>0 ) and the resulting injective linear inclusion
                                                SI (R>0 ) ⊂ S(R>0 )
    is continuous.
(4) If I = [0, +∞) then SI (R>0 ) = SSE (R>0 ), as C-linear subspaces of S(R>0 ).
(5) If I = (−∞, 0] then SI (R>0 ) = ŠSE (R>0 ), as C-linear subspaces of S(R>0 ).
(6) If I = R then SI (R>0 ) = SE (R>0 ) as C-linear subspaces of S(R>0 ).

     The implication “nuclear Fréchet ⇒ Montel” noted in (1) is a special case of [Tre, Cor. 3 to Prop. 50.2]
(since all Fréchet spaces are barrelled [Scha, Ch. II, Cor. to 7.1]).

     Proof. (1) : Since the topology on SI (R>0 ) is the subspace topology inherited from the product topology
on a∈I S(R>0 ) via a linear injection T = a∈I Ta : SI (R>0 ) → a∈I S(R>0 ), SI (R>0 ) is nuclear because
    Q                                          Q                    Q

arbitrary products and subspaces of nuclear spaces are nuclear [Scha, Ch. III, Thm. 7.4].
     Since {a} ⊂ I for every a ∈ I, we have a linear inclusion Sa : SI (R>0 ) ⊂ S{a} (R>0 ), and Sa is clearly
continuous. Letting Ra : S{b} (R>0 ) ≃ S{b+a} (R>0 ) be the linear homeomorphism given by t−a -multiplication
for all a, b ∈ R, the linear image of SI (R>0 ) within the product a∈I S{a} (R>0 ) under the continuous linear
                                                                  Q
802                                    CHAPTER D. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT FUNCTIONS


map a∈I Sa is the closed linear subspace of those elements {ϕa : a ∈ I} satisfying (Rb−1 ◦ Ra )(ϕa ) = ϕb for
      Q

all a, b ∈ I. Hence, SI (R>0 ) is complete since a∈I Sa is a linear topological embedding and each S{a} (R>0 )
                                                    Q

is complete (being isomorphic to S{0} (R>0 ) = S(R>0 )).
     We may write I as the countable union of closed intervals [a, b] ⊂ R, and by a similar argument SI (R>0 )
is therefore realized as a topological subspace (hence as a locally convex topological C-linear subspace) of
the countable product of the S[a,b] (R>0 )’s, the linear topological embedding being induced by the natural
continuous linear maps SI (R>0 ) → S[a,b] (R>0 ).
     We further claim that S[a,b] (R>0 ) is carried onto a closed subspace of the product S{a} (R>0 ) × S{b} (R>0 )
via the “diagonal” map f 7→ (f, f ). To see this, via the change of variables ex = tb−a we reduce to showing (i)
if f ∈ S(R) satisfies ex f ∈ S(R) then ecx f ∈ S(R) for all 0 < c < 1, (ii) the space of pairs (f1 , f2 ) ∈ S(R) with
f2 = ex f1 is closed. Since ecx f = e(c−1)x (ex f ) with c − 1 < 0, by separately treating x < 0 and x > 0 we get
(i). The closedness in (ii) follows from consideration of convergent sequences (as S(R) is metrizable). Finally,
the continuous linear bijection S[a,b] (R>0 ) → S{a} (R>0 ) × S{b} (R>0 ) onto a closed subspace is a topological
embedding because the same calculations show that convergence in S{c} (R>0 ) for a < c < b is controlled by
simultaneous convergence in both S{a} (R>0 ) and S{b} (R>0 ).
     It follows that S[a,b] (R>0 ), and hence SI (R>0 ), is a Fréchet space (as a countable product of complete
metric spaces is a complete metric space). Being nuclear and Fréchet, we are done.
     (2) : By [Scha, Ch. II, 8.1; Ch. IV, 6.1], SI (R>0 )′β is complete. By [Tre, Prop. 50.6], SI (R>0 )′β is nuclear.
Finally, by [Scha, Ch. IV, 5.9], SI (R>0 )′β is Montel.
     (3) : If 0 ∈ I then the inclusion of intervals {0} ⊂ I induces an injective continuous linear operator
SI (R>0 ) → S{0} (R>0 ). We conclude by observing that we have S{0} (R>0 ) = S(R>0 ) by definition.
     Assertions (4), (5) and (6) are a consequence of the definitions (see Definition B.2.1.1).12                  □
    Remark D.3.2.4 (On nuclearity of SI (R>0 )). Let I ⊂ R be a non-empty interval. The definition of
SI (R>0 ) realizes it, through the proof of Lemma D.3.2.3(1), as a subspace of sN where s = S(Z) is the nuclear
Fréchet space of rapidly decreasing Z-indexed sequences. The relation of such Schwartz functions to s is
explained in the proof of [Tre, Cor. to Thm. 51.5] via Fourier series, and the inheritance of nuclearity under
passage to subspaces and arbitrary products is [Tre, (50.3), (50.5) in Prop. 50.1] (or see [Scha, Ch. III, 7.4]).

    Definition D.3.3.1 (Schwartz-Bruhat functions with I-exponential decay on R>0 -modulated groups).
Let (G, | · |G ) be an R>0 -modulated group. Let I ⊂ R be a non-empty interval. We define SI (G) to be the
C-vector space of those continuous functions ϕ on G satisfying | · |aG ϕ ∈ S(G) for all a ∈ I. We refer to SI (G)
as the C-vector space of Schwartz-Bruhat functions on G with I-exponential decay. Similarly to Example
D.3.2.2, SI (G) has a left G-action via (g.ϕ)(x) = ϕ(g −1 x).
(1) For I = [0, +∞), we write SSE (G) := SI (G) and refer to its elements as Schwartz-Bruhat functions on G
    with forward semi-exponential decay.
(2) For I = (−∞, 0], we write ŠSE (G) := SI (G) and refer to its elements as Schwartz-Bruhat functions on G
    with backward semi-exponential decay.
(3) For I = R, we write SE (G) := SI (G) and refer to its elements as Schwartz-Bruhat functions on G with
    exponential decay.

    For G = R>0 this definition of SI (G) coincides with Definition D.3.2.1. In that special case, we saw in
the proof of the Fréchet property for SI (R>0 ) in Lemma D.3.2.3(1) that membership in S[a,b] (R>0 ) amounts
to membership in S{a} (R>0 ) and S{b} (R>0 ). The same holds in general:

       Lemma D.3.3.2. For an R>0 -modulated group G and real numbers a < c < b, if ϕ : G → C satisfies
| · |aG ϕ, | · |bG ϕ ∈ S(G) then | · |cG ϕ ∈ S(G).

      Proof. By renaming | · |aG ϕ as ϕ and replacing the modulus with | · |b−a      G , we have to show that if
ϕ, | · |G ϕ ∈ S(G) then | · |cG ϕ ∈ S(G) for all 0 < c < 1. By definition of S(G), there exists a compact subgroup
k ⊂ G with k ⊥ compactly generated such that ϕ is k-invariant. Since | · |G is trivial on k, we can pass to
G/k = R>0 × (G1 /k) so that G1 is an elementary abelian Lie group.
      Using R ≃ R>0 via ex , we can arrange that G = Rm × Tn × Zr × F for integers m ≥ 1, n ≥ 0, r ≥ 0, and
a finite abelian group F with the modulus given by |(x, z, a, b)| = ex1 . We are given ϕ(x, z, a, b) ∈ S(G) such
                          D.3. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT FUNCTIONS WITH I-EXPONENTIAL DECAY                              805


that ex1 ϕ(x, z, a, b) ∈ S(G) and want to show that if 0 < c < 1 then ecx1 f (x, z, a, b) ∈ S(G). The calculation
used to treat the case G = R in the proof of Lemma D.3.2.3(1) carries over essentially without change to
the present more general setting using the seminorms (D.1.3.8)). One difference from the case G = R is that

    We fix an R>0 -modulated group G and now topologize SI (G) by following the same approach used to

    Definition D.3.3.3 (Topology on SI (G)). Let G be an R>0 -modulated group, k ⊂ G a compact subgroup
with compactly generated orthogonal k ⊥ ⊂ G.
                                           b We define

(D.3.3.1)                                            SI (k, G) ⊂ SI (G)
to be the linear subspace of k-invariant Schwartz-Bruhat functions with I-exponential decay. We topologize

(D.3.3.2)                                  Ta : SI (k, G) → S(k, G) = S(G/k)
assigned by Ta (ϕ) := | · |aG ϕ.
     We topologize SI (G) as the locally convex inductive limit of the family {SI (k, G)}k of linear subspaces of
SI (G) as k ⊂ G varies over the compact subgroups with finitely generated orthogonal, partially ordered by
downward inclusion. (The inductive limit is SI (G) as a vector space since whether or not a given function
f : G → C is k-invariant is the same as for | · |aG f for a ∈ R because | · |G is trivial on k.) We refer to this
topology on SI (G) as the inductive topology on SI (G).
    Example D.3.3.4. When the preceding topology on SI (G) is applied to the modulated group G = R>0
with | · |G : G → R>0 the identity map, it recovers the topology in Definition D.3.2.1 since R>0 has no
non-trivial compact subgroups.
     Example D.3.3.5. For any a ∈ R, multiplication by | · |aG carries S{a} (G) linearly and topologically iso-
morphically onto S(G) (as functions on G, S{a} (G) = | · |−aG S(G)). For a, b ∈ R, correspondingly multiplication
by | · |a−b
        G   carries S{a} (G) linearly and  topologically isomorphically onto S{b} (G).
     For I = [a, b], the space SI (k, G) is identified via f 7→ (f, f ) linearly and topologically with a closed
subspace of S{a} (k, G) × S{b} (k, G). To prove this, by passing to G/k = R>0 × (G1 /k) as in the proof of
Lemma D.3.3.2 we can carry over the same considerations with ecx for 0 ≤ c ≤ 1 as in the proof of the
closed embedding property for the case G = R>0 that arose in the proof of the Fréchet condition in Lemma
D.3.2.3(1).
     A general non-empty interval I ⊂ R is exhausted by countably many compact intervals, so we can
similarly conclude that SI (k, G) is a closed subspace of a countable direct product of copies of the space
S(k, G) = S(G/k) that is nuclear Fréchet, so SI (k, G) is nuclear [Scha, Ch. III, 7.4] and Fréchet. It likewise
follows that SI (k, G) is separable (i.e., has a countable dense subset) since every subset of a separable metric
space is separable and each metric space S(G/k) is separable by (D.1.3.20) (ultimately because the spaces
S(Z) ≃ S(T) and S(R) are separable).14
     Since the transition maps S(k, G) → S(k ′ , G) for k ′ ⊂ k are topological embeddings, the same holds for

inductive limit. Continuing to assume G is second-countable, since each SI (k, G) is topologized as a projective
limit of copies of the Hausdorff locally convex space S(k, G) = S(G/k) that is nuclear and complete (see
Lemma D.1.3.7(3) applied to the elementary abelian Lie group G/k) it follows that each of the spaces SI (k, G)

and then their countable strict inductive limit SI (G), is both nuclear and complete [Scha, Ch. III, Cor. to 7.4;

    Remark D.3.3.6. Let G be an R>0 -modulated group and I ⊂ R a non-empty interval. For every a ∈ R,
the linear operation ϕ 7→ | · |aG · ϕ carries each ϕ ∈ SI (G) to a smooth function on G and so this operation
takes value within S−a+I (G). By design of the topology on SI (G) and S−a+I (G) from Definition D.3.3.1, this
operator is a linear topological isomorphism Ma : SI (G) → S−a+I (G). In particular, SE (G) is stable under
multiplication by continuous quasi-characters of arbitrary exponent, and multiplication by any of them is a
linear topological automorphism.


       D.3.3.1. The main Structure Theorem on Schwartz-Bruhat functions with I-exponential decay. The
topological space of Ω(G) of continuous quasi-characters of any modulated group (G, | · |G ) is endowed with a
natural structure of Riemann surface, namely the open subsets {| · |sG χ0 } for χ0 ∈ G c1 (these are the connected
components) have the topology of either infinite cylinders (when the image of | · |G is discrete) or C (in the
R>0 -modulated case). In the latter case, the connected components are the fibers of the continuous surjective
restriction map Ω(G) → Ω(G1 ) = G       c1 .
       In the R>0 -modulated case, using unitary base points χ0 yields a well-defined function Re : Ω(G) → R via
| · |sG χ0 7→ Re(s) (this is the usual “real part” on copies of C whose base point has an ambiguity corresponding
to vertical translation). For any non-empty interval I ⊂ R we then denote by Ω(G)I the subset of points in
Ω(G) whose “real part” belongs to I (this is a copy of CI ⊂ C for each connected component of Ω(G)). We
endow the interior of Ω(G)I inside Ω(G), if non-empty, with the structure of Riemann surface inherited from
the ambient Ω(G).
