     Remark D.3.3.9 (On the role of acyclicity of Schwartz-Bruhat spacess). In §C.1.5, we discussed inductive
limits of Hausdorff locally convex topological C-vector spaces, and the concept of acyclicity, one of whose
applications is to provide a criterion to detect limit subspaces of LF-spaces (i.e. closed subspaces whose
subspace topology is itself the LF-topology induced from the ambient): see Corollary C.1.5.13.
     In Proposition D.1.5.9, we proved that for any Hausdorff locally compact second countable abelian group,
the Schwartz-Bruhat space S(G) is acyclic, because it is a countable strict inductive limit of Fréchet spaces
(strictness is the key point).
     Acyclicity of the Schwartz-Bruhat space of G1 will be used in proving part (4) of Theorem D.3.3.7 by
realizing SI (G) as a limit subspace of a strict LF-space, hence itself an LF-space. This will enable us to
apply the Open Mapping Theorem (see [Gro-f, Ch. 4, §5, Thm. 2(1)]) to the continuous linear bijection from
(D.3.3.3) with SI (G) re-topologized as in part (4).

     Before we prove Theorem D.3.3.7, we discuss the following aspect on SI (G). We defined on SI (G) the
inductive topology. There is another natural topology on SI (G), whose nature is projective. One part of the
following result is that (at least for second-countable G) both topologies have the same bounded subsets.16

     Define E := SI (R>0 ). Let p be a continuous norm (not just seminorm) on E; e.g., pullback along

for the strong-dual topology. (Although references may differ on whether the “polar” is taken in a real or
complex sense [NB, Def. 8.3.1, Rem. 8.3.2], since U is circled the meanings of U ◦ and U ◦◦ are the same for
both notions.) By the Hahn-Banach Theorem, it is the same to show that a continuous linear functional on
Eβ′ vanishing on W (equivalently on U ◦ ) must be 0. By semi-reflexivity of E, the continuous linear functionals
on Eβ′ are the same as on Eσ′ [Scha, Ch. IV, 5.5]. Thus, it is the same to show W is dense in E ′ for the weak

annihilates W (or equivalently U ◦ ) then x = 0.
     For any such x, the line Rx lies inside the bipolar U ◦◦ . Since U is convex and closed for the given topology
of E, it is also closed for the weak topology σ(E, E ′ ) [Scha, Ch. IV, 3.1]. Thus, by the Bipolar Theorem (see
[Scha, Ch. IV, 1.5] for the real case, and [NB, Thm. 8.3.8] for the complex case) we have U ◦◦ = U . The
condition Rx ⊂ U then forces x = 0 since U is the closed unit ball for a norm on E. This completes the proof
that U ◦ has dense span in Eβ′ . Each topologically embedded subspace S(k, G1 ) ⊂ S(G1 ) is complete and hence
closed, so to show that a continuous T : Eβ′ → S(G1 ) has image contained in some S(k, G1 ) it suffices by our
density conclusion to show T (U ◦ ) is contained in some S(k, G1 ).
     Since T is continuous, it carries bounded sets onto bounded sets. Every bounded subset of S(G1 ) is
contained in some S(k, G1 ) by [Scha, Ch. ,II, 6.5], so it suffices to show that the polar U ◦ of the closed unit

barrelled, and bornological, as all of these properties are inherited under countable strict inductive limits (see

    D.3.4. Uniform Riemann-Lebesgue Lemma on R>0 -modulated groups. We include here an
analog for second-countable R>0 -modulated groups of the Uniform Riemann-Lebesgue Lemma from Proposition
B.2.2.3. We refer the reader to §D.1.6 for differential operators on Hausdorff locally compact abelian groups
and their interaction with the Fourier transform on Schwartz-Bruhat functions (see Lemma D.1.6.19).
    We recall for ease of access that for G an R>0 -modulated Hausdorff locally compact abelian group, Ω(G)

write Ω(G)I for the domain

it is therefore uniquely associated to c. The function σ : Ω(G) → R is continuous and surjective. The next
result is a generalization of Proposition B.2.2.3(2), but first we need to record a useful observation:

     Remark D.3.4.1. Let I be a non-empty interval. We claim any invariant differential operator D on C ∞ (G)
preserves the subspace SI (G) ⊂ C ∞ (G). It suffices to treat the case D = ∂b for a 1-parameter subgroup
b : R → G. For a ∈ I and ϕ ∈ SI (G) we want to show that | · |aG D(ϕ) ∈ S(G). By hypothesis | · |aG ϕ ∈ S(G),
so D(| · |aG ϕ) ∈ S(G). The product rule for D = ∂b gives
                                        D(| · |aG ϕ) = r| |aG ϕ + | · |aG D(ϕ)
where |b(t)|G = ert for some r ∈ R. Since r| · |aG ϕ ∈ S(G) by the definition of SI (G), and we have noted that
D(| · |aG ϕ) ∈ S(G), it follows that | · |aG D(ϕ) ∈ S(G) as desired.

    D.3.6. Approximation by smooth compactly supported functions. The following approximation
result will be useful for us:
    Lemma D.3.6.1 (Approximation by smooth compactly supported functions). Let (G, | · |G ) be a second-
countable locally compact Hausdorff R>0 -modulated abelian group. Let I ⊂ R be a non-empty interval. Then
D(G) := Cc∞ (G) is a dense subspace of SI (G) with continuous inclusion.
    We equip D(G) with the usual countable strict inductive limit topology (via any choice of countable
exhaustion of G by compact subsets).
    Proof. Each ϕ ∈ D(G) certainly satisfies | · |aG ϕ ∈ S(G) for every a ∈ R, so D(G) ⊂ SI (G).
    For every a ∈ R, multiplication by the smooth function | · |aG is continuous and continuously invertible
on D(G). Thus, the composition of Ta : SI (G) → S(G) with the injective linear inclusion D(G) ⊂ SI (G) is
continuous for every a ∈ R. By design of the projective topology on SI (G), the inclusion
                                                  jG : D(G) → SI (G)
is therefore continuous.
     Upon choosing a continuous homomorphic section τ to | · |G , by Theorem D.3.3.7(1) (which uses second-
countability of G) we have a linear topological isomorphism SI (G) ≃ S(G1 ) ⊗ SI (R>0 ) = D(G1 ) ⊗ SI (R>0 )
(the final equality using that G1 is compact). We similarly have a linear topological isomorphism D(G) ≃
D(G1 ) ⊗ D(R>0 ) by [Bru, §5, Thm.3(a), p. 55]. The continuous inclusion D(G) → SI (G) is thereby identified
with the natural continuous map
(D.3.6.1)                      idD(G1 ) ⊗ jR>0 : D(G1 ) ⊗ D(R>0 ) → D(G1 ) ⊗ SI (R>0 )
since by continuity is suffices to check on the dense subspace D(G1 ) ⊗ D(R>0 ) (and so by linearity it suffices
to check on elementary tensors).
    To prove (D.3.6.1) has dense image, we claim it suffices to treat the case G = R>0 . In other words, if the

image. By the Hahn-Banach Theorem, it suffices to show that the induced map between continuous linear
820                              CHAPTER D. SCHWARTZ-BRUHAT FUNCTIONS


duals is injective. The continuous dual is insensitive to passage to completion, so it is the same as showing
that the natural map

    The continuous linear dual of an inductive tensor product E ⊗ι F (for Hausdorff locally convex E and F ) is
the space of “separately continuous” bilinear forms B : E × F → C (i.e., B(x, ·) : F → C and B(·, y) : E → C
are continuous for all x ∈ E and y ∈ F ). In other words, if B : D(G1 ) × SI (R>0 ) → C is a separately
continuous bilinear map that vanishes on D(G1 ) × D(R>0 ) then we want to show B = 0 if D(R>0 ) is dense
in SI (R>0 ). But such vanishing for B is immediate from such density due to continuity of B in the second
variable for each fixed entry in the first variable.

    In this appendix we review the theory of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces. Our intent is to
present a comprehensive treatment in a uniform and detailed manner, also carefully handling set-theoretic
aspects and including comprehensive references to the literature to build the geometric foundations required
to make sense of “periodic quotient stacks” associated to primes. This provides insight into the main trace
calculation upon which Refined Explicit Formulas rest. It also makes the connection of our work to Deninger’s
work, though strictly speaking this is not logically needed for our main trace work (but it guided how we
discovered our trace formula results).
    We settle on some notation and terminology.
      Notation E.0.0.1. We write:
(1) Sets for the large category whose objects are sets, and morphisms are functions between sets.
(2) Spaces for the large category whose objects are topological spaces, and morphisms are continuous
    functions between topological spaces.
(3) For a topological space X, X set for the set underlying X.
(4) For topological spaces X, Y , C(X, Y ) for the set of all continuous functions f : X → Y .
      Terminology E.0.0.1. We call:
(1) A space any object of Spaces, i.e. any topological space. We will use this abbreviation whenever an
    adjective is to precede “topological space”. For instance, “compactly generated topological space” will be
    abbreviated to “compactly generated space”.
(2) A map, or continuous map, f : X → Y between spaces X and Y any continuous function f : X → Y . We
    include the word continuous when there is potential for ambiguity.
(3) A set-function f : X → Y between sets X and Y is any function f : X → Y . We denote by Map(X, Y )
    the set of all set-functions X → Y .
(4) A set-function f : X → Y between spaces X and Y is any set-function f : X set → Y set , not necessarily
    underlying a continuous function. For a continuous map f : X → Y , we write f set for its underlying
    set-function. We write (·)set for the resulting forgetful functor Spaces → Sets.
(5) A compact space is a topological space such that every open cover of K has a finite refinement.
(6) A locally compact space is a topological space such that every point has a fundamental system of compact
    neighborhoods.
     Our main references for general topology throughout this appendix are [Du], [Bou-GT], [Ke], and
[SP]. In particular, we refer to [Bou-GT, Ch. I ,§1, §5], [Du, Ch. III], and [SP, Tags 004O, 0405] for
background material on point-set topology, to [Bou-GT, Ch. I, §8], [Du, Ch. VII, §1-3], and [SP, Tag 08ZD]
for background material on separation axioms, [Bou-GT, Ch. I, §9], [Du, Ch. X, §1,6,9], [Ke, Ch. 5], and [SP,
Tags 0059, 08ZQ] for background material around compactness, and [Du, Ch. XII, §1-3], and [Ke, Ch. 7] for
background material on function spaces. We will further refer to [SP, Tag 005M] on proper maps, and [SP,
Tags 08ZW, 0908] on profinite spaces and Stone-Čech compactifications.
     We caution the reader about diverging terminologies within the above sources. Specifically, our use
of the word compact follows [Du, Ke] but not [Bou-GT, SP], where the same adjective is replaced by
quasi-compact. We further caution the reader that several sources within the literature that will be occasionally
referred to throughout this work use the word compact to mean compact and Hausdorff (see, for example,
[LGL, Rezk, Ste]). Throughout this work, we shall always clarify when a separation assumption is being
made.
     We further settle on the following:
      Terminology E.0.0.2. We let X, Y be topological spaces, and f : X → Y a continuous map.
(1) The quotient topology on f (X) is the finest topology on f (X) making the induced map f : X → f (X)
    continuous (i.e., U ⊂ f (X) is open if and only if f −1 (U ) is open in X). This may not be the subspace
                                     E.1. COMPACTLY GENERATED SPACES                                          825


    topology on f (X). We call a map f for which it agrees with the subspace topology a strict map (see part
    (1) of [SP, Tag 0406]).
(2) The image of X under f , denoted f (X) or Im(f ), is the subset f (X) of Y endowed with the quotient
    topology induced from the topology on X.
(3) The pre-image of a subspace Z ⊂ Y along the continuous map f : X → Y is the subset f −1 (Z) ⊂ X
    endowed with the subspace topology induced from the topology on X.
(4) We say f is an immersion if and only if it is injective and strict.
(5) We say f is submersive if and only if it is surjective and strict (see part (2) of [SP, Tag 0406]).
(6) We say f is étale if and only if it is a local homeomorphism.
We further clarify that when considering more than one topology on the same underlying set of a fixed
topological space X, we shall use the terminology intrinsic topology on X to refer to the topology that X is
equipped with from the outset of the discussion.
     We caution the reader on differing nomenclature choices for (4) and (5) between this work and some of
the sources we shall be referring to throughout. The class of morphisms we call immersions is referred to as
“inclusions” in [Rezk, Str]. Other terms used to refer to submersive maps within the literature that we shall
refer to throughout are identification maps (see, for example, [Br4, Ch. 4]), quotient maps (see [Str, Def. 2.18])
or proclusive maps/proclusions (see, for example, [Rezk, §9.1] and [Ste, Def. 2.5]). We shall make use of the
preceding “Terminology” section occasionally also to make local clarifications later throughout this appendix
as the need arises, so as to remove all terminological ambiguities.


                                    E.1. Compactly generated spaces
     This section is devoted to collecting background material on compactly generated spaces. Its purpose is
to pave the way for a discussion in §E.2 of the theory of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces, whose
category serves as an ambient category within which we shall construct a small site of topological spaces.
When arguments are not given here, they are referenced into other sources.
     The class of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological spaces, abbreviated “CGWH”, was in-
troduced with the intent of constructing a large category of topological spaces that, while containing most
examples of spaces of interest, such as locally compact Hausdorff topological spaces and CW complexes, also
has good categorical properties, with particular emphasis on a cartesian closed monoidal category structure.
     Compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces have so far had a prominent role to play within the
literature around homotopy theory; see for example [BG, Ch.8] for an account and complements on [Ste],
with basic applications to homotopy theory in [BG, Ch. 9]. We refer the reader to [LMS] for an example of
the foundational use of compactly generated spaces in stable homotopy theory, starting with [LMS, Ch. I, §1]
on the equivariant stable category, and to J.P. May’s work [May] on iterated loop spaces. We further refer the
reader to L.G. Lewis’ Ph.D. thesis [LGL] and its appendix [LGL, Appendix A] containing a comprehensive
account of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces, which will also serve as one of our main sources for
this section and the next.
     The terminology often used to refer to such a category of topological spaces is “convenient”, and the idea
was axiomatized and studied systematically in the early 1960’s. We refer the reader to R. Brown’s D.Phil.
thesis [Br1], with particular emphasis on [Br1, Ch. I, Thm. 2.36, Thm. 2.37] and the preceding discussion in
[Br1, Ch. I, §2] on k-spaces where, preceding the introduction of the concept of closed monoidal categories by
a few years, the author discusses exponential spaces in a manner that is a precursor to Steenrod’s article [Ste]
where a candidate convenient category of topological spaces was introduced and studied, and its monoidal
structure and cartesian closure discussed. To the best of the author’s knowledge, Brown’s papers [Br2] and
[Br3], both following Brown’s thesis and pre-dating Steenrod’s 1967 article, are the foothold of the search for
826                                    CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


convenient categories of spaces and for the identification of their desired properties, whose development then
gained traction after [Ste] and [Vogt].
     The concept of “k-space”, where the letter k is understood to refer to the german word “kompakt”, predates
Brown’s thesis and the very idea of a convenient category. It appears to go back to Princeton lectures by
Hurewicz from the late 1940’s, and was first introduced in the literature in [Ga, Definition, p. 303]. It can
be found in Kelley’s book on general topology (see [Ke, Ch. 7, p. 130]) from 1955. It was after [Br1] and
particularly in [Br2] that the importance of k-spaces, in their definition from [Ke, Ch. 7, p. 130] was observed.
We refer the reader to [Br2], where the author advertised the category of k-spaces as a possible candidate for
a convenient category, before an axiomatization of “convenience” was made in the literature (see [Br2], and
[Vogt] for discussions of convenient categories and their properties). The reader is further referred to [nLab1,
§6] for further historical information on the inception and development of these themes.

      The defining properties of a convenient category C of topological spaces are usually assumed to be:
(1) C is a subcategory of Spaces that is full and replete (i.e., any object of Spaces isomorphic to an object
    of C is an object of C),
(2) C contains all CW complexes and most examples of spaces of practical interest (see the beginning of [Ste,
    §1]),
(3) C is closed under small limits and colimits (see [Vogt, §2, Thm. 2.1]),
(4) for every object X in C, closed subspaces of X are objects in C (see [Vogt, §2, Axiom 1]); it is sometimes
    required that open subspaces also satisfy this property (see [Vogt, §2, Axiom 1∗ ]).
(5) C is cartesian closed (see [Vogt, §2, Axiom 2] for axioms in this direction, and [Br3, §1] on the exponential
    law; see also [Ste, §1, (1),(2)]) with respect to its cartesian monoidal structure (see [MacL, Ch. VII,
    §7-8]).
     The reader is especially referred to [ELS], particularly to [ELS, §3, §5], and to [ELS, Thm. 5.15], where
a comprehensive treatment of convenient categories, their stability with respect to internal exponentiation,
and their general construction, alongside a uniform proof of cartesian closedness, is given. We further refer
the reader to [nLab1, Def. 2.1] and the discussion in [nLab1, §2] for an overview around the concept of
“convenient category” of topological spaces.
     We will use [ELS] to highlight the relation between some of the differing definitions of convenient categories
based on compactly generated spaces.
     The notion of compactly generated spaces we adopt here is the one introduced in [McC, §2, p. 275]
under the term “k-spaces”, and in [LGL, Appendix A, §1, p. 148], which is also the notion in [Str, Def. 1.1]
and [Rezk, §3.1] (in the latter, also under the term “k-spaces”), the only differences being with respect to
terminology. The notion of k-space in [Ke, Ch. 7, p. 230] is defined using the immersions of compact subspaces
as test continuous maps for closure of subsets and does not incorporate a Hausdorff condition on the test
compact subspaces. It is therefore different from ours (see §E.2.4 and especially Lemma E.2.4.11 for an
example illustrating the difference).
     We further refer the reader to [LM, §1], where compact generation is also defined in terms of intersections
with compact, possibly non-Hausdorff, subspaces (see the end of [LM, p. 1]), as in [Ke]. A definition is given
in [Vogt, §5,(iii)] after an axiomatic development leading to a general method to construct large categories
of topological spaces stable under certain categorical operations, and it is equivalent to the one adopted
throughout this work. Another is introduced in [Vogt, §5, (iv)] which is related to the one in [Ke, Ch. 7,
p. 230] via Lemma E.2.4.2. In Steenrod’s paper (see [Ste, p.2]), a Hausdorff condition is built into the very
definition of compact generation, to arrange for all compact subspaces of compactly generated spaces to
be closed. In a similar vein, we shall eventually incorporate a weak Hausdorff condition, as in [McC, §2],
[LGL, p. 148], and throughout loc.cit., which is sufficient to ensure that all compact subspaces of compactly
                                       E.1. COMPACTLY GENERATED SPACES                                            827


generated (weakly Hausdorff) spaces are closed. Weakening the Hausdorff condition in [Ste, §2] rendered itself
necessary to arrange for better stability properties of the resulting convenient category, especially in regard to
computation in Spaces of certain classes of colimits.
     Other features of the category of (weakly Hausdorff) compactly generated spaces are the availability of a
simple classification of important classes of maps (such as regular monomorphisms, which are shown to be the
closed immersions, and regular epimorphisms, which are shown to be the submersive maps; see Definition
E.2.3.14 for these notions of regularity), together with stability of submersive maps under arbitrary base
change. Such stability leads to a transparent description of the canonical topology on small full subcategories
of the category of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces closed under pullbacks, contributing to
rendering them a suitable choice (for our intended purposes) to underlie small sites.
     The weak Hausdorff condition can be found in [McC, §2,p.275], where it is attributed to J.C. Moore.
This appears to be the first source within the literature recording the concept. We refer the reader to the
beginning of [McC, §2] for further motivation for the weakening of the Hausdorff condition from [Ste].
     We may summarize the differences between the various concepts of compact generation for topological
spaces as being mostly in regard to whether or not the test spaces for openness, equivalently closedness, of
subsets is assumed to satisfy a non-trivial separation condition or just be compactness.
     The main divergences between the theories are discernible from a number of features, such as the fact
that the notion of compact generation adopted throughout this appendix is stable under passage to arbitrary
open subspaces, which does not hold in other theories and especially without a separation condition on the
compact test spaces (see §E.2.4 and especially Lemma E.2.4.12 for an example of this discrepancy). Stability
of compact generation under passage to open subspaces of a space X may not hold when the compact test
spaces are assumed to be compact subspaces of X, even under a Hausdorff assumption, as is done in [Ste]. It
does hold for regular open subspaces (see [Ste, 2.4]).
     The approach we adopt throughout this work is the approach of [LGL, Appendix A], [McC, §2], [Str, §1,
§2], and [Rezk, §3.1] (we recall for the sake of clarity that in this latter reference, “compact spaces” is equivalent
to “compact Hausdorff spaces” here, insofar as “quasi-compactness” is used in loc.cit. to refer to compact
spaces in this work). The notion of compactly generated space in [McC, §2] and [Rezk, §5] is equivalent to
our notion of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff space. Weakly Hausdorff spaces throughout this appendix,
and “k-Hausdorff” spaces in [Rezk, §4] are different concepts, but they are equivalent conditions on compactly
generated spaces (see [Rezk, Prop.11.4]) and so most results in loc.cit. can be referred to throughout this
appendix with only minor terminological caveats for the reader, which will be stated as the need arises.
     The advantages of using the category of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces are several. As
an instance, the fact that the categories of compactly generated spaces and of compactly generated weakly
Hausdorff spaces are cartesian-closed monoidal categories implies that product functors have right-adjoints,
and as such commute with all small colimits (see [LGL, Cor. 5.6]). This implies, in particular, compatibility
of submersive maps with finite products (see [LGL, Prop. 5.8]), which does not hold in the category of all
topological spaces (see Example E.1.2.18). We establish this here with and without separation assumptions,
as a consequence of cartesian closure (Lemma E.2.2.10, respectively Lemma E.1.2.13), combined with the
characterization of submersive maps as the effective epimorphisms in each category (Lemma E.2.3.8, respectively
Lemma E.1.2.14); see Definition E.2.3.14 for this notion of effectivity. Within such categories, CW complexes
are examples of objects, and products of CW complexes are again CW complexes.
     The properties we are most interested in arranging for a convenient category of topological spaces are:

(1) stability of all objects under passage to closed subspaces,
(2) stability of all objects under passage to open subspaces,
(3) existence of finite limits and finite colimits,
(4) stability of submersive maps under arbitrary pull-backs,
828                                         CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


(5) computability in Spaces of certain push-outs.
     Arranging all of the above properties requires a delicate balancing act, which leads to the combination
of compact generation with the weak Hausdorff separation condition in a natural manner. We will show by
example how compact generation is sufficient to arrange for (1), (2), (3) and (5) to hold (see Lemma E.1.2.25
for (1) and (2), Lemma E.1.2.2 for (3) and (5)), but not for (4) (see Example E.1.2.16).
     Imposing a Hausdorff condition on all objects, in combination with compact generation, as is done in
[Ste], is sufficient to arrange for (1), (3), and (4) to hold (see [Ste, §2,2.4] for (1), see Lemma E.2.2.5 combined
with the fact that finite limits and finite colimits of Hausdorff spaces are Hausdorff for (3), and see Lemma
E.2.3.6 combined with (3) for (4)), but not for (2) (although see [Ste, §2,2.4]) and most importantly not for
(5) (see Example E.2.3.12).
     Combining compact generation with the weak Hausdorff separation condition arranges for all five properties
to hold, and upon arriving at the category of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces, in §E.3 we shall
be selecting small full subcategories with enough closure properties to serve as small sites.
     Our main sources throughout this section concerning compactly generated spaces are [LGL, §4, §5],
[McC, §2], [Str, §2], [Rezk, §8, §11], and occasionally [ELS, §3, §5]. As mentioned in the incipit of [Str],
the unpublished Ph.D. thesis of J. McClure contains an account of the theory of CGWH spaces as well.

      E.1.1. Preparations on compactly generated spaces. We begin with a definition:

      Definition E.1.1.1. Let X be a topological space.
(1) Let Z ⊂ X be a subspace. We say Z is k-closed if and only if for every2 compact Hausdorff topological
    space K and continuous map g : K → X, g −1 (Z) is a closed subspace of K.
(2) We denote by k(X) the topological space whose underlying set is X set and whose topology is the coarsest
    topology such that all the k-closed subsets of X are closed in k(X). We call the topology on k(X) the
    compactly generated topology, or k-topology, on X.

      Remark E.1.1.2. On Definition E.1.1.1, we make the following observations.
(1) We note that the identity set-function k(X) → X is always continuous, which is to say that the topology
    of k(X) is finer than the topology of X. Indeed, for any Z ⊂ X closed, any compact Hausdorff space K,
    and any continuous map g : K → X, the subspace g −1 (Z) ⊂ K is closed. The closed subspaces of X are
    therefore closed in k(X) as well.
(2) We note that, as a direct consequence of part (2) of Definition E.1.1.1, a subspace Z ⊂ X is k-closed if
    and only if Z ⊂ k(X) is closed.

      Our definition of “compactly generated” space will rest on:

      Lemma E.1.1.3. Let X be a topological space. The following four conditions are equivalent:
(1) For all topological spaces Y and any set-function f : X → Y , the following conditions are equivalent:
    (a) f is continuous.
    (b) For every compact Hausdorff space K and every continuous map g : K → X, the composition f ◦ g is
        continuous.
(2) There exists a set SX of compact Hausdorff spaces such that for all topological spaces Y and any set-function
    f : X → Y , the following conditions are equivalent:
    (a) f is continuous.
    (b) For every element K ∈ SX , and every continuous function g : K → X, the composition f ◦ g is
        continuous.

2Need to address, maybe with cross-reference, why no set-theoretic issues with this definition being over “all” pairs (K, g).

(3) A subspace U ⊂ X is open if and only if for every compact Hausdorff space K and every continuous
    function g : K → X, the pre-image g −1 (U ) is open in K.

(4) There exists a set I, a compact Hausdorff space Ki for each i ∈ I, and for Y := i∈I Ki the I-indexed
    co-product a submersive map q : Y → X.

    Before we can prove Lemma E.1.1.3, we need the following preparation:

    Lemma E.1.1.4 (On bouquets of traits and discrete two-point sets). Let X be a topological space.
(1) Assume that there exist x, y ∈ X, with x ̸= y, such that for every subset A ⊂ X containing x, respectively
    y, A is closed. Then X is discrete and satisfies all four conditions in Lemma E.1.1.3.
(2) Assume that there exists a unique point x ∈ X such that every subset A ⊂ X containing x is closed in X.
    (a) The subspace X − {x} ⊂ X is open and has the discrete topology.
    (b) Let Z ⊂ X be the connected component of x, and V the closure of X − Z in X. Then:
          (i) the natural continuous surjective map
                                                     a
(E.1.1.1)                                      f :Z     V →X
               is submersive (i.e., topologically a surjective quotient map);
          (ii) for any compact Hausdorff space K and continuous map g : K → V , the image g(K) ⊂ V is
               compact Hausdorff and closed in V , with K → g(K) submersive;
         (iii) there exists a compact Hausdorff space K and a submersive map K → Z.
    (c) If X satisfies condition (1) in Lemma E.1.1.3 then it also satisfies condition (2).

     Proof. (1) : Note that U := X − {x} is open in X since {x} is closed. We first show U is discrete, by
proving all subsets of U are closed in U . Let B be any subset of U and C be its closure in X. Since B ∪ {x}
is closed (as it contains x), either C = B or C = B ∪ {x}. Either way, this closure meets U in B, so B is
closed in U . It follows that X − {x} is discrete. The same holds for X − {y}, and since x ̸= y we have that X
is covered by the open subsets X − {x} and X − {y} each of which has all points open, so all points of X are
open; i.e., X is discrete. Discrete spaces are easily seen to satisfy all four conditions in Lemma E.1.1.3 (since
any continuous map to such a space from a compact Hausdorff space has finite image and clopen fibers, and
all maps from a discrete space are continuous).
     (2.a) is a consequence of the proof of (1). We prove (2.b). Let Z be the connected component of X
containing x. Then Z is closed in X, and since Z and V are two closed subsets of X which cover X clearly (i)
holds. Before we prove (ii) and (iii), we make a couple of observations about Z and V .
     Firstly, we claim the only open subset U ⊂ Z that is open in Z and contains x is Z itself. Indeed, any
such U is closed in X (as all subsets of X containing x are closed by hypothesis) and so closed in Z, so U is
clopen in the connected Z and non-empty (as it contains x), forcing U = Z as desired.
     Next consider the closure V of X − Z. Similarly to the argument in (1), since (X − Z) ∪ {x} is closed
in X we see that either V = X − Z (in which case the closed Z is also open and f from (E.1.1.1) is a
homeomorphism) or V = (X − Z) ∪ {x}. In particular, V meets X − {x} in exactly X − Z.
     (ii): We denote by K0 the (quasi-)compact continuous image of K in V . We claim this image is closed in
V . If K0 contains x then K0 is closed in X, hence in V . If not then K0 is compact within V − {x} which is
discrete by (2.a). It follows that K0 is finite, and since every point of V is closed in V it follows again that
K0 is closed in V (and even finite discrete). This says V is weakly Hausdorff: for every compact Hausdorff
space K and continuous map g : K → V , the image g(K) is closed in V (see Definition E.2.1.1). We now
make two (non-circular) forward references to §E.2: by Remark E.2.1.2 the subspace K0 ⊂ V is then also
weakly Hausdorff, and by Lemma E.2.1.4 it is Hausdorff since it is a continuous image of a compact Hausdorff
space. In particular, K0 is compact Hausdorff. Since g : K → K0 is a continuous surjection between compact
Hausdorff spaces, it is submersive.
830                                    CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


    (iii): We let S 1 be the unit circle, and 0 ∈ S 1 a marked point (which we assume, upon parametrizing S 1
as R/Z under the exponential submersion exp(2πit) : R → S 1 , to correspond to the image of t = 0). We
consider the quotient of the set-theoretic coproduct i∈I Si1 , where Si1 is S 1 and I is the index set Z − {x}, by
                                                       `

the equivalence relation identifying all the marked points of the Si1 ’s. We call 0 the image of each, equivalently
any, of the marked points 0i ∈ Si1 in the quotient.
     We call HI the resulting quotient set, which we topologize as follows. For a subset U ⊂ HI containing 0,
we say it is open if and only if it is the union of all but finitely many of the images in HI of the Si1 ’s along
with open subsets Ui ⊂ Si1 containing 0i for the remaining finitely many i ∈ I. We say that a subset U ⊂ HI
which does not contain 0 is open if and only if it is a union of the images of open subsets Ui ⊂ Si1 for every
i ∈ I (the notation HI intends to refer to the Hawaiian earring, which is the special case I = N).
     Then HI is compact Hausdorff. The map g sending 0 to x and Si − {0i } to i ∈ Z − {x} is surjective
and we claim it is continuous. Let U ⊂ Z be an open subset. We want to show g −1 (U ) is open in HI . If U
contains x then U = Z (recall from the proof of (2.a) that Z has no proper open subset containing x), so we
may focus on U not containing x. But then g −1 (U ) inside HI is the union of the punctured circles Si − {0i }
for i ∈ U , and that is also open in HI .
     To show g is submersive, let C ⊂ Z be a subset whose pre-image g −1 (C) is closed in HI . We want to
show C is closed in Z, or equivalently in X. If C ⊂ {x} then C is closed. If not, C meets the complement
Z − {x} of x. In particular, g −1 (C) contains the image of Si1 − {0i } for some i ∈ I. But g −1 (C) is closed so it
contains the closure in HI of that ith punctured circle, hence it contains 0. It follows that C = g(g −1 (C))
contains g(0) = x, and hence C is closed in X (as is every subset of X containing x, by hypothesis).
    (2.c) : For the purposes of proving that (1) implies (2) in Lemma E.1.1.3, by (2.i) and closedness of Z
and V in X it is enough to separately treat Z and V in place of X. The implication holds for V by (2.ii) (by
using the set of closed compact Hausdorff subspaces of V ), and for Z by (2.iii).                                 □
    Remark E.1.1.5. Let W be a trait: the finite topological space {0, 1} with 0 closed and 1 a generalization
of 0 (equivalently, W is the spectrum of a discrete valuation ring). The proof of (2.iii) from Lemma E.1.1.4
shows that Z is homeomorphic to the glueing along x ∈ Z of copies of W indexed by the set Z − {x}. It is a
bouquet of traits bundled at x, indexed by Z − {x}.
     Proof of Lemma E.1.1.3. We assume (1) and will deduce (4) holds. First we show that naturally
X = k(X). Let Y be the topological space Y := k(X); i.e., the set X set endowed with the k-topology on X.
By (1) applied to this choice of Y and to f = id : X → Y the identity set-function on the shared underlying
set, f is continuou by design of the topology on Y . On the other hand, the topology of Y is finer than that of
X by part (1) of Remark E.1.1.2. It follows that f −1 (also the identity as a set-function) is continuous, and
hence the identity set-function is a homeomorphism; i.e., the two topologies on the set underlying X are the
same.
     If X is discrete, then the four conditions in Lemma E.1.1.3 all hold for X. By Lemma E.1.1.4, it is enough
to treat the cases in which either X contains exactly one point x ∈ X such that any subset A ⊂ X containing
x is closed, or contains no such point. In the former case, by Lemma E.1.1.4(2.c) all four conditions in Lemma
E.1.1.3 hold for X. We therefore may and do now assume without loss of generality that for any point x ∈ X,
there exists a non-closed subset A ⊂ X such that x ∈ A holds.
     We now call Σ ⊂ 2X × X the set of pairs (A, x) such that A is a non-closed subspace of X, x ∈ A is a

map g : K → X, such that g −1 (A) is not closed in K, and g −1 ({x}) ̸= ∅. Indeed, as A is not closed in X,
there exists K compact Hausdorff and g : K → X a continuous map, such that g −1 (A) is not closed in K
since X has the k-topology. If g −1 ({x}) is non-empty we are done, and otherwise define K ′ := K {x}, also

     Remark E.1.1.6. Construction (6.4) from [Jech, Part I, §6] can be found on p. 65 of loc.cit. after [Jech,
Part I, §6, Lemma 6.3] upon which it rests, and it is credited to Dana Scott and often referred to as “Scott’s
trick”. It rests on the Axiom of Regularity. In particular, the construction of the set SX in the proof of Lemma
E.1.1.3 does not use any stronger version of the Axiom of Choice, and is therefore valid within ZFC, which is
what this Remark is aimed at highlighting (in fact, it does not use the Axiom of Choice either).

      Definition E.1.1.7. We define:
(1) a topological space X to be a compactly generated space if and only if it satisfies the equivalent conditions
    of Lemma E.1.1.3.
(2) the category CG whose objects are compactly generated spaces, and morphisms are continuous maps of
    topological spaces. We shall refer to CG as the category of compactly generated spaces.

     Remark E.1.1.8. On the construction of k(X) from Definition E.1.1.1 we observe that we can use the
terminology introduced in Definition E.1.1.1 to rephrase Definition E.1.1.7. Specifically, a topological space X
is compactly generated if and only if k(X) = X. Since k(X) and X share the same underlying set, it makes
sense to compare their topologies.

      The following example exhibits compact generation as a non-vacuous condition on topological spaces.

     Example E.1.1.9. Let X be an uncountable set equipped with the co-countable topology (i.e., the open
subsets are ∅ and complements of countable subsets, so the closed subsets are X and the countable subsets).
We claim X is not compactly generated. Indeed, we claim that k(X) is discrete.
     To see this, let Z be any subset of X and K any compact Hausdorff space, with g : K → X an arbitrary
continuous map, so g(K) is a compact subspace of X and inherits the co-countable topology from X. It is
therefore finite discrete, and Z ∩ g(K) is open in g(K). As such, its pre-image in K, which agrees with g −1 (Z),
is also open. This proves that any subset of X is k-open in X, and hence k(X) is discrete.
                                       E.1. COMPACTLY GENERATED SPACES                                          833


    If X was compactly generated then it would have to be discrete. As X is uncountable, the co-countable
topology on it is not discrete. Any non-closed subspace Z ⊂ X is therefore a k-closed non-closed subspace.
For further discussion of examples for the co-countable topology, we refer to [StSe, Part II, 29, 21].

    We refer to §E.2.4 for an example-driven illustration of the relations between the various definitions of
compact generation present within the literature. This is located after §E.2.3 so as to facilitate the construction
of examples resting on results discussed up to and including §E.2.3.

     E.1.2. Categorical and topological stabilities of compactly generated spaces. Before moving
forward, we recall several facts about the large category CG of compactly generated spaces and some important
closure properties it enjoys. Our main sources for the materials collected in this subsection are [LGL, §2, §3,
§5], [McC, §2], [Str, §1, §2], [Rezk, §8]. We shall refer to [ELS, §5] as well, concerning arguments towards
the cartesian closure of CG as a cartesian monoidal category.
     We first recall the relation between the large categories CG and Spaces. This latter, recall, is the category
whose objects are topological spaces, and morphisms are continuous maps between topological spaces (see
part (2) of Notation E.0.0.1). The forgetful functor
(E.1.2.1)                                     ucg : CG → Spaces
sends a compactly generated space to itself as a topological space, and continuous maps to continuous maps.

    Lemma E.1.2.1. The assignment X ⇝ k(X) is a functor
(E.1.2.2)                                      k : Spaces → CG
that satisfies the following properties:
(1) k is right-adjoint to the forgetful functor ucg : CG → Spaces. Explicitly, any continuous f : X → Y with
    k-closed X uniquely factors continuously through the natural continuous bijection k(Y ) → Y .
(2) The unit η : id → k ◦ ucg of the adjunction (ucg , k) is a natural isomorphism of functors; this is the inverse
    X → k(X) to the natural homeomorphism k(X) → X for k-closed X.

     Proof. We check functoriality of the formation of k(·), from which the rest is clear (as k(X) → X via idX
is a homeomorphism for k-closed X). We have to show that if f : X → Y is a continuous map of topological
spaces then any k-closed subset Z of Y has k-closed pre-image in X. For any continuous map g : K → X
from a compact Hausdorff space K, the pre-image g −1 (f −1 (Z)) of f −1 (Z) in K agrees with the pre-image
(f ◦ g)−1 (Z) of Z to K under the composition with f , and it is therefore closed in K by continuity of the
composition f ◦ g. It follows f −1 (Z) is k-closed.                                                          □

of small limits and small colimits:

    An important property of CG is that it has an internal Hom-space bifunctor endowing CG with a
cartesian-closed monoidal structure (we refer the reader to [Kel, §1.5], and [MacL, Ch. VII, §7, §8], for
                                      E.1. COMPACTLY GENERATED SPACES                                           835


foundational material on monoidal categories; the term “cartesian” refers to the ⊗ bifunctor, denoted □ in
[MacL, Ch. VII, §7, §8], being the cartesian product). We briefly discuss this aspect and some consequences
of direct use for this appendix, with a view towards the next section on compactly generated weakly Hausdorff
spaces, where the weak Hausdorff condition on objects will strengthen consequences of cartesian closure.
     Our standard references for closed symmetric monoidal categories are [MacL, Ch. VII, §1] for monoidal
categories in general, [MacL, Ch. VII, §7] and [EK, Ch. III] for closed categories and closed symmetric
monoidal categories, and [MacL, Ch. VII, §8] for the category of compactly generated Hausdorff spaces. We
do not incorporate any separation condition into the definition of the objects of CG, and we will impose only
a weakening of the Hausdorff separation condition when we introduce the full subcategory of weakly Hausdorff
compactly generated spaces, but the proof we give for cartesian closedness of CG follows the same general
pattern of [Ste, §5] and [MacL, Ch. VII, §8].
     A reference pinpointing the general structures underlying cartesian closedness of convenient categories
of spaces is [ELS, §5]. We further refer the reader to Mac Lane’s paper [MacL2] where associativity and
commutativity coherences in monoidal categories are derived from the basic defining axioms of coherence
within a monoidal category (see diagrams (3), (4), (7) in [MacL, Ch. VII, §1]). The theme of how to
derive general coherences from (3),(4) and (7) of [MacL, Ch. VII, §1] is reprised in [MacL, Ch. VII, §2] and
developed in [MacL2], with particular emphasis on [MacL2, Thm. 4.2], where coherence of the associativity
and commutativity natural isomorphisms of a monoidal category are reduced to the pentagonal [MacL2,
§3, 3.5] and hexagonal [MacL2, §4, 4.5] axioms. We discuss the closed monoidal category structure on CG
so as to include self-contained arguments for CG, compatibly with the definition of compact generation in
Definition E.1.1.7. Our main references for results on function spaces within CG and the resulting closed
monoidal category structure on CG (and later CGWH) are [LGL, §5], [ELS, §5], [Str, §2], and [Rezk, §8].
    Definition E.1.2.6. Let X and Y be compactly generated spaces.
(1) For any compact Hausdorff space K, continuous map g : K → X, and open subspace U ⊂ Y , let N (g, K, U )
    denote the subset of C(X, Y ) consisting of continuous maps f : X → Y such that (f ◦ g)(K) ⊆ U :
(E.1.2.4)                         N (g, K, U ) = C(X, Y ) ×g∗ ,C(K,Y ),j∗ C(K, U )
            ∗
    where g : C(X, Y ) → C(K, Y ) is f 7→ f ◦ g and j∗ : C(K, U ) → C(K, Y ) is f 7→ j ◦ f for j : U → Y the
    open immersion. (Note that N (g, ∅, ∅) = C(X, Y ) for the unique j : ∅ → X.)
         We denote by B the set of subsets N ⊂ C(X, Y ) of the form N = N (g, K, U ) for some compact
    Hausdorff space K, continuous map g : K → X, and open subspace U ⊂ Y .
(2) The compact-open topology on C(X, Y ) is the unique topology on C(X, Y ) admitting B as a sub-base (see
    [SP, Tag 08ZI] and [SP, Tag 08ZJ], as well as [Du, Ch. III, Thm. 3.1] and the discussion after [Ke, Ch. 1,
    Thm. 12, p. 48]). In other words, finite intersection among members of B are a base for the topology. We
    call the sub-base B the standard sub-base for the compact-open topology on C(X, Y ). (In Lemma E.1.2.8
    we give a set-theoretic consistency check, showing that the compact-open topology can be defined using a
    set of triples (g, K, U ) rather than just a class.)
     Remark E.1.2.7. We note that the compact-open topology referred to above is not the usual notion of
topology on function spaces under the same name. Indeed, for topological spaces X and Y , one usually defines
the compact-open topology on C(X, Y ) as the topology having as sub-base the collection of subsets N (g, K, U )
for g : K → X an immersion of a compact space K. Throughout this appendix, the terminology “compact-open
topology” will solely be referring to the topology introduced in Definition E.1.2.6(2), generating a finer topology.
The topology defined in Definition E.1.2.6 is a topology on C(X, Y ), for compactly generated X and Y , such
that k(C(X, Y )) defines an internal mapping functor promoting CG to a closed monoidal category with respect
to the cartesian monoidal structure (we refer the reader to [MacL, Ch. VII] for background on cartesian
monoidal categories, and to [MacL, Ch. III, §1, Prop. 5] for the construction of a canonical monoidal structure
836                                   CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


on categories with finite products and a final object). Proving this fact is the purpose of the next results (see
Lemma E.1.2.12 and Proposition E.1.2.13).
     The reader may wonder whether the k-topology on the compact-open topology on C(X, Y ) is the only
topology promoting the set-valued bifunctor of continuous maps between compactly generated spaces to an
internal Hom-functor promoting CG to a cartesian closed monoidal category. We refer the reader to [ELS,
§5] for a discussion pertaining uniqueness aspects of the k-topology associated to the compact-open topology
being considered (see especially [ELS, §5, Thm. 5.15]). We follow [LGL, §5] throughout the discussion on
function spaces of compactly generated spaces, and later on compactly generated spaces incorporating a
separation condition (see Proposition E.2.2.10).

     Remark E.1.2.11. We highlight here how the approaches to compactly generated function spaces in the
above sources relate to one another. Throughout this work, we proceed as in [LGL, §5], and, specifically, we
define the compact-open topology on function spaces in the sense of Definition E.1.2.6, following [LGL, §5,
p. 160]. This is the approach adopted in [Str, §2] as well. We caution the reader that the topology defined
on function spaces in [Rezk, §8, 8.1] is not generally equivalent to the compact-open topology as defined in
[LGL, §5, p. 160] and [Str, Def. 2.8], and throughout this appendix. It is in fact finer (see [Rezk, Lemma
8.4]). However, applying k removes this discrepancy: by [ELS, Thm. 5.15], the compactly generated function
spaces associated to either topology are the same. Equivalently, the functor k(·) identifies the topology defined
in [Rezk, §8, 8.1] on function spaces with the k-topology on the compact-open topology defined in [LGL, §5,
p. 160], [Str, Def. 2.8], and this appendix.

     For any x ∈ X, ψ ′ (h)(x) = h(x, ·) = h ◦ ix as a set-function Y → Z for the visibly continuous x-insertion

is continuous as a map

(E.1.2.23)                                     h∗∗ : C(X, W1 ) → C(X, W2 )

     We recall, as a consequence of [MacL, Ch.I II, §1, Prop. 5], that the internal product in CG, alongside the
final object of CG (a point endowed with the discrete topology), determine a canonical (cartesian) symmetric
monoidal structure on CG, whose structure morphisms are provided by the cited Proposition. We refer to it
via the succint notation (CG, ×, ∗), where ∗ denotes the final object of CG, expecting no confusion to arise.
    Proposition E.1.2.13. The bifunctor:
                                            C ontk : CGopp × CG → CG
endows the symmetric monoidal category (CG, ×, ∗) with the structure of a cartesian closed symmetric
monoidal category enriched over itself.
    The Proposition is proved in [Str, Prop. 2.12], resting on [Str, Prop. 2.11] which is in turn a consequence
of the Tube Lemma (recalled in [Str, Lemma 2.5]) that was used in the proof of Lemma E.1.2.12 (for the
continuity of i).
    Proof. By Lemma E.1.2.12 there exists a natural homeomorphism
                               θX,Y,Z : C ontk (X × Y, Z) → C ontk (X, C ontk (Y, Z)).
By the very definition of closed monoidal category (see [MacL, Ch. VII, §1] and [EK, Ch. III]), the cartesian
(symmetric) monoidal structure (×, ∗) uniquely determined on CG by [MacL, Ch. III, §1, Prop. 5] is therefore
closed, the internal-Hom bifunctor being given by C ontk (·, ·).                                            □
    As a direct application of Proposition E.1.2.13, we now prove that products in CG of submersive maps
are submersive. We begin with a characterization of submersive maps in CG, and further refer the reader to
[LGL, §5, Lemma 5.7] and its proof:
     Lemma E.1.2.14. Let X, Y be compactly generated spaces, and f : X → Y a continuous map. The
following conditions are equivalent:
(1) There exists a compactly generated space R, two maps s, t : R ⇒ X, and a homeomorphism c : coeq(s, t) →
    Y , such that the canonical map p : X → coeq(s, t) satisfies c ◦ p = f .
(2) f is the co-equalizer in CG of the diagram p1 , p2 : X ×f,Y,f X ⇒ X, where p1 , p2 are the two projections.
(3) f is a submersive map.
     Proof. We have (1) ⇒ (3) since p is submersive in (1). We now assume that (3) holds, and prove that (2)
holds. We choose R := X ×f,X,f X, with the two maps to X defined to be the two projections p1 , p2 : R ⇒ X.
We check that if f is submersive then f : X → Y is the co-equalizer of p1 , p2 in CG. By Lemma E.1.2.2(2),
we may compute the co-equalizer of the two projections p1 , p2 in Spaces. We call X ′ := ucg (X) and
Y ′ = ucg (Y ), and retain the notation f for the continuous map ucg (f ), and R′ the topological fibre product
R′ := (f, f )−1 (∆X (X)). Its topology is the subspace topology of the product topology on X ×0 X. We denote
the two projections by p′1 , p′2 : R′ ⇒ X ′ . The quotient X ′ /R′ is the topological co-equalizer of p′1 , p′2 . Part (2)
of Lemma E.1.2.2 implies that we have X ′ /R′ = k(X ′ /R′ ) = coeq(p1 , p2 ), where p1 := k(p′1 ) and p2 := k(p′2 ).
This latter co-equalizer is the co-equalizer in CG. The evident map c′ : X ′ /R′ → Y ′ is a homeomorphism by
design of R′ since f is submersive. Since X ×f,Y,f X = k(X ′ ×0f,Y ′ ,f X ′ ) = k(R′ ) by Lemma E.1.2.2(1), then
c := k(c′ ) is a homeomorphism coeq(p1 , p2 ) → Y such that c ◦ k(φ) = f for the natural map φ : X ′ → X ′ /R′ ,
and so (2) is proved. If (2) holds, then we may set R := X ×f,Y,f X, and (s, t) = (p1 , p2 ), with p1 , p2 : R ⇒ X
the two projections, to deduce that (1) holds.                                                                          □
    Remark E.1.2.15. We have shown in Lemma E.1.2.14 that submersive maps are exactly the regular
epimorphisms in CG, and the effective epimorphisms in CG. We caution the reader that, despite the Lemma,
CG is not a regular category. We refer the reader to [Bor2, Ch. 2] for the foundational material on regular
categories, and specifically for [Bor2, Ch. 2, Def. 2.1.1]. Stability of regular epimorphisms under arbitrary
842                                   CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


pull-backs is a defining requirement of regularity. For regularity to hold for CG, regular epimorphisms should
therefore be stable under arbitrary base change internally in CG. This does not hold, as Example E.1.2.16
below shows. To obtain a regular large category of topological spaces we will be incorporating a separation
condition on objects in the next section, §E.2. Nonetheless, Lemma E.1.2.17 on preservation of submersiveness
under direct products in CG holds with no separation conditions (see also [LGL, §5, Prop. 5.8]).
   The following example is [Bor2, Counterexample 2.4.5], as a counterexample to regularity for the category
Spaces. It can be adapted as below to serve the same purpose for CG:
     Example E.1.2.16. Let X := {1, 2, 3, 4} endowed with the topology τX := {∅, {1, 2}, X}, Y := {a, b, c}
endowed with the topology τY := {∅, Y }, and Z := {α, β, γ} endowed with the topology τZ := {∅, {α, β}, Z}.
We define f : X → Y to be f (1) = a, f (2) = b = f (3), f (4) = c, and g : Z → Y to be g(α) = a,
g(β) = c = g(γ). We have P := X ×0f,Y,g Z = {(1, α), (4, β), (4, γ)} endowed with the topology τ :=
{∅, {(1, α)}, {(1, α), (4, β)}, P }. The map f is submersive, whereas the first projection fZ : P → Z is not,
since fZ−1 ({α}) = {(1, α)} is open, while {α} is not. Since X, Y, Z and P are finite topological spaces, they
are all compactly generated (for example by [Str, Prop. 1.6], and the topological fibre product P is therefore
a fibre product in CG by Lemma E.1.2.2(1). This is an example of a submersive map in CG which is not
stable under arbitrary base change internally in CG.
      Here is the promised result on stability of submersive maps under products in CG:
   Lemma E.1.2.17. Let X, Y, X ′ , Y ′ be compactly generated spaces, and f : X → X ′ , g : Y → Y ′ submersive
maps. Then:
                                          (f, g) : X × Y → X ′ × Y ′
is a submersive map.
     Proof. We may factor (f, g) as (f, id) : X × Y → X ′ × Y , followed by (id, g) : X ′ × Y → X ′ × Y ′ . It
is therefore enough to treat the case Y = Y ′ and g = id. By Lemma E.1.2.14, X ′ is the co-equalizer of
the two projections X ×f,X ′ ,f X ⇒ X in CG. Lemma E.1.2.12 implies that the product functor (·) × Y
is a left-adjoint, and hence commutes with representable colimits. As co-equalizers are small colimits, all
representable by Lemma E.1.2.2(2), we conclude.                                                             □
    The above Lemma E.1.2.17 does not hold in Spaces, as the following example shows. The existence of
examples in Spaces such as Example E.1.2.18 is one of the reasons why we shall be relying on the category
of compactly generated spaces (and its variant incorporating a weak Hausdorff condition on objects, to be
discussed in §E.2) to select better categories of topological spaces to serve as a small site.
     Example E.1.2.18. We let X := Q be endowed with the subspace topology inherited from the Euclidean
topology on R, and we let X ′ be the quotient of X obtained by identifying the subset of integers Z ⊂ Q
to {0}. The continuous map f : X → X ′ is submersive by construction. On the other hand, the map
(f, id) : X ×0 X → X ′ ×0 X of topological products is not submersive (see [Br4, Ch. 4, Example 4] for a proof
of this assertion).


     E.1.2.1. Examples and permanence properties of compactly generated spaces. Building on the previous
section and especially on Lemma E.1.2.1, Lemma E.1.2.2, Lemma E.1.2.10 and Proposition E.1.2.13, we
collect here results that exhibit familiar classes of topological spaces to be compactly generated, and will
establish when formation of products and, on occasion, passage to subspaces, preserves compact generation by
preserving some stronger property of topological spaces. In particular, we will collect sufficient conditions for
constructions in CG to be computable in Spaces, for special classes of compactly generated spaces. This
includes all topological spaces of interest for using this appendix to study periodic orbits in our main work.
                                         E.1. COMPACTLY GENERATED SPACES                                        843


    Proposition E.1.2.19. We have:
(1) all locally compact Hausdorff spaces are compactly generated,
(2) the product in Spaces of a compactly generated space and a locally compact Hausdorff space is compactly
    generated (so it computes the product in CG).
    We refer the reader to [Str, Prop. 2.6].
     Proof. We call I the set of all compact Hausdorff subspaces of X, and for i ∈ I let Ki be the compact
Hausdorff subspace i ⊂ X. Since X is locally compact Hausdorff, the interiors of the Ki cover X. Upon
calling gi : Ki → X the immersion, we have gi−1 (Z) = Z ∩ Ki for every subspace Z ⊂ X. It follows from the
local nature of closedness that a subspace Z such that gi−1 (Z) is closed in Ki for every i ∈ I is itself closed in
X. We now consider the continuous map:
                                                a       a
(E.1.2.29)                                 q :=    gi :    Ki → X
                                                      i∈I     i∈I

We have shown that every subspace Z of X such that q −1 (Z) is closed in i∈I Ki , is closed in X. This proves
                                                                        `

(1). To prove (2), we use a related method along with Lemma E.1.1.3(3) to reduce to checking the product
against a compact Hausdorff space is compactly generated.4 Hence, (E.1.2.29) is submersive and so X is
compactly generated.                                                                                       □
     Remark E.1.2.20. On the above Lemma E.1.2.19, we observe that the Hausdorff assumption in both
part (1) and part (2) of the Lemma cannot be dropped altogether. We refer the reader to Lemma E.2.4.9,
for a counter-example, given by the one-point compactification of the rationals endowed with their subspace
topology inherited from the Euclidean topology on R. We refer the reader to [StSe, Part II, 35]. This is
an example of a compact topological space (in fact, even weakly Hausdorff, as will be discussed in Lemma
E.2.4.9; we refer the reader to Definition E.2.1.1 for the weak Hausdorff separation condition and to §E.2 for
the related material) such that its compact topological self-product is not compactly generated.
      Another class of topological spaces that can be seen to be compactly generated, is that of sequential
spaces. We recall that a topological space X is sequential if and only if any sequentially closed subset Z ⊂ X
(i.e. such that for any sequence {zn }n≥0 ⊂ Z converging to a point x ∈ X, we have x ∈ Z) is closed in Z (see
[Fr, Prop. 1.1] and the definition on [Fr, §1, p. 109] before [Fr, Prop. 1.2]). Examples of sequential spaces
are all topological spaces satisfying the first axiom of countability. In fact, any sequential space receives a
submersive map from a first-countable topological space (see [Fr, Cor. 1.14]).
      We have the following:
    Proposition E.1.2.21. We have:
(1) all sequential topological spaces are compactly generated,
(2) the product in Spaces of two first-countable topological spaces is compactly generated and computes the
    product in CG.
     Proof. We prove (1). We let X be a sequential space, and Z ⊂ X a k-closed subset . We are to show
that Z is sequentially closed, hence closed, in X. Let {zn }n≥0 ⊂ Z be a sequence converging to a point x ∈ X.
We endow N with the discrete topology, and call K the one-point compactification of N. This K is compact
Hausdorff, and we may define the set-function g : K → X by assigning g(n) := zn for all integers n ≥ 0, and
g(∞) := x. Since the sequence {zn }n≥0 is convergent to x, g is continuous. It follows that g −1 (Z) is closed in
K. Since {zn }≥0 is contained in Z, we deduce the containment N ⊂ g −1 (Z). As N ⊂ K is dense and g −1 (Z)
is closed in K, we deduce that we have K = g −1 (Z), and hence ∞ ∈ g −1 (Z). It follows x ∈ Z, and Z is
sequentially closed, hence closed in X. By part (3) of Lemma E.1.1.3, X is compactly generated, proving (1).
4The compact generatedness has to be justified; was not explained.
844                                    CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


     Part (2) follows from the fact that, for first-countable spaces X, Y , and any (x, y) ∈ X ×0 Y , the set of
open subspaces U ×0 V as U ranges over the elements of a countable base at x, and V ranges over the elements
of a countable local base at y, is a countable base at (x, y), therefore proving that X ×0 Y is first-countable.
As first-countable topological spaces are sequential (see part (2) of [Fr, Cor. 1.14]), part (1) applies and implies
that X ×0 Y is compactly generated. It follows that we have k(X ×0 Y ) = X ×0 Y , and hence X ×0 Y
computes in Spaces the product X × Y in CG by part (1) of Lemma E.1.2.2.                                          □

    Remark E.1.2.22. Another way to see that a sequential space X is compactly generated is to directly
exhibit a submersive map from a locally compact Hausdorff space. To do this, we consider the set I of all
convergent sequences in X. For i ∈ I, we denote by x(i) the associated sequence x(i) = {xn (i), n ≥ 0} ⊂ X.
We call K the one-point compactification of N (with N endowed with the discrete topology), we define
Ki := K for every i ∈ I, and we define:         a
                                             q:    Ki → X
                                                     i∈I
by sending any non-negative integer n ∈ Ki , to xn (i) and ∞ ∈ Ki to a choice of limit limn→∞ xn (i) in X. As
every point of X is the limit of a constant sequence in X, q is surjective. The argument at the beginning of
the proof of Proposition E.1.2.21 shows that a subspace Z ⊂ X is closed if and only if q −1 (Z) is, and hence q
is submersive.

    Remark E.1.2.23. We note that the topological product of two sequential spaces may not be sequential.
We refer the reader to Example E.1.2.24 below for an example. Another example exhibiting this phenomenon
can be found in [ABM, §2] (see, specifically, [ABM, §2, Property IV]). This is the reason for the stronger
assumption in part (2) of Proposition E.1.2.21.

    Example E.1.2.24. As in Example E.1.2.18, we let X := Q be endowed with the subspace topology
inherited from the Euclidean topology on R, and we let X ′ be the quotient of X obtained by identifying the
subset of all integers Z ⊂ Q to {0}. The product space X ′ ×0 X is an example of:
(1) a product of compactly generated spaces which is not compactly generated,
(2) a product of sequential spaces which is not sequential (see [Fr, §1, p. 109] before [Fr, Prop. 1.2]).
Indeed, we note that X ×0 X is compactly generated by Lemma E.1.2.21. Moreover, Lemma E.1.2.17 implies
that X ′ ×0 X is not compactly generated: if it were then the topological product map (f, id) would be
submersive by the Lemma, contradicting Example E.1.2.18.

    We prove the following basic permanence properties for the condition of compact generation for topological
spaces.

     Lemma E.1.2.25. Let X be a compactly generated topological space, and T ⊂ X be a subspace. Assume
that one of the following conditions holds:
(1) T is closed in X with respect to the subspace topology.
(2) T is open in X with respect to the subspace topology.
(3) T is locally closed in X with respect to the subspace topology.
Then T is compactly generated.

      The Lemma is also proved in [Str, Lemma 2.26].

    Proof. By Lemma E.1.1.3, there exists a set I, compact Hausdorff topological spaces Ki for every i ∈ I,
and a submersive map:                          a
                                            q:     Ki → X.
                                                    i∈I
                                      E.1. COMPACTLY GENERATED SPACES                                       845


If T is closed, then q ′ : q −1 (T ) → T is a submersive map. As q −1 (T ) is a closed subspace of i∈I Ki , it
                                                                                                     `
                  `
is of the form i∈I Ci for closed subspaces Ci ⊆ Ki . As each Ki is compact Hausdorff, so is each Ci , so
T is compactly generated, proving (1). If T is open in X, then q ′ : q −1 (U ) → U is also a submersive map
and since q −1 (U ) ⊆ i∈I Ki is open, it is locally compact Hausdorff. As every locally compact Hausdorff
                          `

topological space is compactly generated by Proposition E.1.2.19, proving part (2) is now accomplished as

                                                                   `

for q ′ = q|q−1 (U ) : q −1 (U ) → U , Lemma E.1.1.3 implies that U is compactly generated, as desired. Part (3)

    We complement the above result with a stability result for closed immersions under products, which we
can now prove upon combining Lemma E.1.2.17 and the above Lemma E.1.2.25:
   Lemma E.1.2.26. Let X, Y, X ′ , Y ′ be compactly generated spaces, and f : X → X ′ , g : Y → Y ′ closed
immersions. Then:
                                         (f, g) : X × Y → X ′ × Y ′
is a closed immersion.
    Proof. We may factor (f, g) as (f, id) : X × Y → X ′ × Y , followed by (id, g) : X ′ × Y → X ′ × Y ′ . It is
therefore enough to treat the case Y = Y ′ and g = id. Thus, we are reduced to the case f is the inclusion of
a closed subspace of X ′ . The subspace X ×0 Y ⊂ X ′ ×0 Y is closed with respect to the subspace topology.
By part (2) of Remark E.1.1.8, X ×0 Y is closed with respect to the subspace topology of the k-topology on
k(X ′ ×0 Y ) = X ′ × Y as well, and by part (2) of Lemma E.1.2.25, X ×0 Y is compactly generated and hence
computes X × Y , exhibiting X × Y as a closed subspace of X ′ × Y , as desired.                               □
      Here is a criterion to detect immersions of compactly generated spaces, for later use:
     Lemma E.1.2.27. Let X, Y be compactly generated topological spaces, and f : X → Y a continuous
injective map. The following are equivalent:
(1) f is an immersion.
(2) For any compactly generated topological space T and any set-function g : T → X, g is continuous if and
    only if the composition f ◦ g is continuous.
     Proof. That (1) ⇒ (2) is obvious. Conversely, suppose for all continuous g : T → X that f ◦ g is
continuous. We will deduce (1). Let i : X → f (X) be the continuous bijective map induced by f , with f (X)
being endowed with the subspace topology from the topology of Y . We call i′ : f (X) → Y the immersion, and
we have i′ ◦ i = f and f ◦ i−1 = i′ . By the foregoing (especially (2)), both i and i−1 are continuous. Hence f
is an immersion.                                                                                             □
    As an application of Lemma E.1.2.27, we conclude this subsection by determining when the continuous
push-forward between function spaces along an immersion is an immersion.
      Lemma E.1.2.28. Let X, Y be compactly generated spaces, i : Z → Y an immersion. Then the induced
map
                                        i∗ : C ontk (X, Z) → C ontk (X, Y )
is an immersion. If i is a closed immersion then i∗ is a closed immersion.
    Proof. Let g : T → C ontk (X, Z) be an arbitrary set-function from a compactly generated topological
space T such that i∗ ◦g is continuous. By Lemma E.1.2.12, the associated set-map h : T ×X → Y is continuous,
and the associated set-map corresponding to g satisfies i ◦ h′ = h. As i is an immersion, g is continuous. By
Lemma E.1.2.27, we deduce that i∗ is an immersion.
846                                    CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


    We now assume that i is a closed immersion. We may assume Z = i(Z). We now observe that in this case
we have:                                  \
                         C ontk (X, Z) =     (C ontk (X, Y ) − N (ix , {x}, Y − Z))
                                            x∈X
with ix : {x} → X the inclusion in X of the point x, which is an infinite intersection of closed subspaces,
hence closed in C ontk (X, Y ). As the image of i∗ is, therefore, closed, i∗ is a closed immersion.     □

                         E.2. Compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces
    In this section we introduce a weakening of the Hausdorff separation condition, and discuss its effects on
compactly generated spaces. Specifically, we shall establish improved closure properties for the resulting full
subcategory of CG. Sources for this section are [LGL, §3], [McC, §2], [Rezk, §4] and [Str, §1].
    E.2.1. Preparations on compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces. We begin with a definition,
introducing the weak Hausdorff separation condition:
    Definition E.2.1.1. A topological space X is weakly Hausdorff if and only if for every compact Hausdorff
topological space K and continuous map f : K → X, f (K) is a closed subspace of X.
      Remark E.2.1.2. Clearly subspaces of weakly Hausdorff spaces are weakly Hausdorff.
    Remark E.2.1.3. We recall that if X is Hausdorff then any compact subspace is closed. In particular,
Hausdorff spaces are weakly Hausdorff. For an example of a weakly Hausdorff (compact) topological space
that is not Hausdorff, we refer the reader to Lemma E.2.4.9.
   Lemma E.2.1.4. Let K be a compact weakly Hausdorff topological space. Assume that there exists a
compact Hausdorff topological space K ′ and a surjective continuous map q : K ′ → K. Then K is Hausdorff.
     Proof. Since K is weakly Hausdorff, every point of K is closed and so q has compact fibers over K.
Indeed, for every x ∈ K, q −1 ({x}) is closed in K ′ , and this latter is a compact Hausdorff topological space. It
follows q −1 ({x}) is compact. It is moreover Hausdorff. For any C ⊂ K ′ closed, C is compact Hausdorff in
K ′ and so q(C) is compact in K, and closed since K is weakly Hausdorff by assumption. We deduce that q
is a closed map, and so q is submersive. Let x, x′ ∈ K be distinct points. Since K is weakly Hausdorff, its
points are closed. As K ′ is normal and q −1 ({x}) and q −1 ({x′ }) are closed, there exist disjoint open subspaces
U, U ′ ⊂ K ′ such that q −1 ({x}) ⊂ U and q −1 ({x′ }) ⊂ U ′ . The subspaces of K ′ given by K ′ − U and K ′ − U ′
are closed, and as q is a closed map, then C := q(K ′ − U ) and C ′ := q(K ′ − U ′ ) are closed. It follows that
K − C and K − C ′ are disjoint open subspaces of K containing x and x′ respectively. We deduce that K is
Hausdorff.                                                                                                       □
      Lemma E.2.1.5. If X is a weakly Hausdorff topological space then so is k(X).
    Proof. Let K be a compact Hausdorff topological space, and g ′ : K → k(X) a continuous map. Compose
with the continuous bijection k(X) → K to define a continuous g : K → X. Since X is weakly Hausdorff,
g(K) is closed in X. By continuity of k(X) → X, it follows that g ′ (K) is closed in k(X). We deduce k(X) is
weakly Hausdorff.                                                                                         □
      Lemma E.2.1.6. Let X be a topological space. We consider the following conditions:
(1) X is weakly Hausdorff,
(2) the image ∆ ⊂ X ×0 X of the diagonal morphism ∆X : X → X ×0 X, is k-closed,
(3) for every compact Hausdorff space K and every continuous map g : K → X, the topological fibre product
    K ×0g,X,g K is closed in K ×0 K.
Then (1) ⇒ (2) and (2) ⇔ (3). Moreover, if X is compactly generated then (1) ⇔ (2).
                           E.2. COMPACTLY GENERATED WEAKLY HAUSDORFF SPACES                                    847


    We refer the reader to [Str, Prop. 2.14] and to [Rezk, Prop. 4.2]. We further refer the reader to Lemma
E.2.4.9, exhibiting an example of a weakly Hausdorff and compactly generated space X whose topological
diagonal subspace is not closed.

    Proof. Suppose X is weakly Hausdorff. For any compact Hausdorff topological space K and continuous
map g : K → X ×0 X, we call g1 , g2 : K ⇒ X the composition of g with the first and second projection,
respectively. We claim that
(E.2.1.1)                              g −1 (∆) = {x ∈ K | g1 (x) = g2 (x)}

C := g1 (K) ∪ g2 (K) is therefore closed in X, and g(K) is contained in C ×0 C ⊂ X ×0 X. We call D the
image of the topological diagonal ∆C : C → C ×0 C. Clearly
(E.2.1.2)                                      g −1 (D) = g −1 (∆)
                             `                                               `
as subspaces of K. Since K K is compact and Hausdorff, defining h : K K → C to be g1 on the first
copy of K and g2 on the second makes h a continuous surjection from a compact Hausdorff space. By Lemma
E.2.1.4, C is compact Hausdorff. Thus, D is a closed subspace of C, so by (E.2.1.2) the subspace g −1 (∆) of K
from (E.2.1.1) is a closed subspace of K since g is continuous. This proves the claim, which in turn proves
that ∆ is k-closed in X ×0 X, establishing (2) from (1).
    We now assume that (2) holds, and prove (3). Let K be a compact Hausdorff space, g : K → X a
continuous map. Then we have:
(E.2.1.3)                            K ×0g,X,g K = (g, g)−1 (∆) ⊂ K ×0 K

K ′ is compact and Hausdorff. Then by (3) we have K ′ ×0h,X,h K ′ is closed in K ′ ×0 K ′ . Clearly K ×0g1 ,X,g2 K

We have:
                                        (g1 , g2 )−1 (∆) = K ×0g1 ,X,g2 K
as subspaces of K ×0 K, and so indeed (g1 , g2 )−1 (∆) is closed in K ×0 K.

continuous map,
                                        (g ′ )−1 (g(K)) = p2 ((g, g ′ )−1 (∆))
as subspaces of K ′ where p2 : K ×0 K ′ → K ′ is the second projection. As ∆ is k-closed by (2), (g, g ′ )−1 (∆) ⊂
K ×0 K ′ is closed, and its image in K ′ under p2 is closed, as p2 is a closed map by [SP, Tag 005P]. This
proves that g(K) is k-closed in X. As X is compactly generated, g(K) is closed by Remark E.1.1.8.                □

   Remark E.2.1.7. We note that part (2) of Lemma E.2.1.6 suggests a weakening of the notion of weakly
Hausdorff space. Spaces whose diagonal subspace is k-closed are called k-Hausdorff. Weakly Hausdorff and
k-Hausdorff are not equivalent concepts (see Example E.2.1.10). However, they are for compactly generated
848                                     CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


spaces, which is the content of the last assertion in Lemma E.2.1.6. We refer the reader to [Rezk, §4] for
background material on k-Hausdorff spaces and how it relates to compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces.
Throughout this appendix, we limit ourselves to the weak Hausdorff property, as it is equivalent to the correct
separation condition to impose on compactly generated spaces (namely, the k-Hausdorff separation condition)
to obtain the desired improvements to the category CG, and because it can be directly compared to other
separation axioms. It is stronger than T1 (see Example E.2.1.8) and weaker than T2 (see Example E.2.1.9
below, which can be arranged to be compactly generated: see Lemma E.2.4.5). As a separation axiom, it is
sometimes referred to as t2 .
   Example E.2.1.8. Let X be an infinite set endowed with the co-finite topology. Then X is T1 , but not
weakly Hausdorff (it violates Lemma E.2.1.6(2)).
    Example E.2.1.9. Let Y be any Hausdorff space that is not locally compact. Then the one-point
compactification X := Y + is an example of a weakly Hausdorff topological space that is not Hausdorff.
Examples are [StSe, Part II, 35], which is also Example E.2.4.4, or a product of an uncountable number of
copies of R, respectively of [0, 1]. Another example is [StSe, Part II, 99].
     Example E.2.1.10. We let X be the one-point compactification of the Arens-Fort space (see [StSe, Part
II, 26]). Then X is not weakly Hausdorff. Indeed, we let (0, 0) be the origin in the Arens-Fort space, the
unique non-isolated point in the Arens-Fort space. Then X − {(0, 0)} is homeomorphic to the one-point
compactification of a discrete space (see [StSe, Part II, 26,(8)]) and it is compact Hausdorff. It is, however,
non-closed in X. The space X is, nonetheless, k-Hausdorff. This is [PB, Space S000165].
      The following lemma concludes the preparations:
     Lemma E.2.1.11. Let X be a compactly generated space, and R ⊂ X × X an equivalence relation. Then
the following conditions are equivalent:
(1) the quotient space X/R is weakly Hausdorff,
(2) R is a closed subspace of X × X.
      We refer the reader to [Str, Prop. 2.17, Prop. 2.20], and [Str, Cor. 2.21].
     Proof. We call ∆ the diagonal subspace in (X/R) ×0 (X/R). Since X/R inherits compact generatedness
from X, the map q : X × X → (X/R) × (X/R) is a submersive map by Lemma E.1.2.17 applied to X = Y ,
X ′ = Y ′ = X/R, and f = g chosen to be the quotient map X → X/R. As q −1 (∆) = R ⊂ X × X, we see that
(2) is equivalent to the statement that ∆ is closed in (X/R) × (X/R), since q is a submersive map. This latter
assertion is in turn equivalent to ∆ being k-closed in (X/R) ×0 (X/R). By the equivalence of part (1) and
part (2) of Lemma E.2.1.6, which holds since X is compactly generated, we conclude.                         □
    Example E.2.1.12. As a simple example of a non-closed R ⊂ X × X resulting in a non-weakly Hausdorff
(compactly generated) quotient, we take X to be the real line R endowed with its Euclidean topology, and R
to be the subset of R ×0 R of those elements (x, y) such that x = 0 if and only if y = 0, and if y =
                                                                                                   ̸ 0 then
x/y ∈ Q× . Then R is not closed in the compactly generated Hausdorff R ×0 R. We note that R ×0 R = R × R
(Proposition E.1.2.19(2)). The quotient X/R is homeomorphic to the quotient of R by the left-multiplication
action by Q× , with Q× being endowed with the subspace topology inherited from the Euclidean topology on
R. This quotient is then not weakly Hausdorff.
