     In light of Proposition E.2.1.13, we see that compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces are closely
related to locally compact Hausdorff spaces. As for general compactly generated spaces, they are quotients of
locally compact Hausdorff spaces, and the Proposition shows that the weak Hausdorff condition on an object
X means that we may choose, as the set SX from Lemma E.1.1.3 of those compact Hausdorff spaces that
compactly generate X, the set of compact Hausdorff subspaces. We can further characterize those objects of
CGWH that are locally compact Hausdorff by rephrasing the locally compact condition on X as a stronger
smallness condition on SX .
     We need the following:

      Lemma E.2.1.15. Let {Xn }n≥0 be a directed sequence of topological spaces. Assume:
(1) for every integer n ≥ 0, Xn is a T1 -space;
(2) for X = colimn≥0 Xn in Spaces, the canonical maps fn : Xn → X have finite fibres.
Then for every compact subspace K ⊂ X, there exists an integer n ≥ 0 such that K is contained in the image
of Xn .

      We also refer the reader to [VLH, Lemma 2.4].

     Proof. 5 We let K ⊂ X be a compact subspace. For every integer n ≥ 1 such that (fn (Xn ) −
fn−1 (Xn−1 )) ∩ K ̸= ∅, we choose xn in the intersection. The sequence F := {xn }n≥0 is such that for every
subset E ⊂ F , E ∩ fn (Xn ) is a finite6 set for every n ≥ 0. As f : Xn → fn (Xn ) has finite fibres, fn−1 (E) is a
finite set, hence closed in Xn since Xn is T1 . By design of the topology on X, E is closed as a subspace of X.
Since E was an arbitrary subset of F , we deduce that the subspace topology on F inherited from the topology
of X is the discrete topology. As K is a subspace of X and F is contained in K, F is discrete as a subspace of
K. Since K is compact, F is finite7 and therefore entirely contained in fN (XN ) for large enough N ≥ 0. In
particular, we have (X − fN (XN )) ∩ K = ∅, and hence K ⊂ fN (XN ), as desired.                                  □

     We recall that a topological space is hemicompact if the set of all of its compact subspaces has a countable
co-final subset.

      Lemma E.2.1.16. Let X be a topological space. Assume:
(1) X is hemicompact.
(2) X is first-countable.
Then X is locally compact.

     Proof. We let {Kn }n≥0 be a sequence of compact subspaces such that every compact subspace K ⊂ X
is contained in Kn for some integer n ≥ 0. Let x ∈ X be a point, and {Um }m≥0 a countable local base at
x. We may and do assume that Um+1 ⊆ Um holds for every m ≥ 0. Suppose that for every integer n ≥ 0,
(X − Kn ) ∩ Un ̸= ∅. We choose xn in the intersection and consider the union of the sequence and its limit
point F := {xn }n≥0 ∪ {x}. Then F ⊂ X is compact, and hence contained in KN , for some integer N ≥ 0.
However, since xN ∈ F is an element of UN , it cannot be an element of KN , a contradiction. It follows that
there exists an integer n ≥ 0 such that Un is contained in Kn , and hence Kn is a compact neighborhood of x
in X. As x ∈ X is arbitrary, X is locally compact.                                                        □

    E.2.2. Categorical and topological stabilities of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces.
We now define the category of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces, as a full subcategory of CG, the
category of compactly generated spaces.

    Definition E.2.2.1. We call CGWH the category whose objects are compactly generated weakly
Hausdorff topological spaces, and morphisms are continuous maps of topological spaces. We refer to CGWH
as the category of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces.

    Our aim is to now collect results that show that the full subcategory CGWH of CG retains many of
the good properties of CG, such as closure under small limits and small colimits, and the cartesian-closed
monoidal structure, and has additional features that will become convenient later. One disadvantage of
CGWH is that small colimits in CGWH cannot be computed in Spaces. In other words, the forgetful
functor to Spaces does not reflect small colimits. However, all the small colimits of interest for the purposes
of this appendix will indeed be reflected by the forgetful functor, and can be computed by their topological
counterpart. One important advantage of CGWH is that submersive maps will turn out to be exactly the
universally effective epimorphisms of CGWH, therefore providing a direct and concrete description of the
canonical topology on CGWH, and rendering the development of a theory of stacks in groupoids over a site
of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces efficient.
    In this subsection, we study analogs for CGWH of the closure properties of CG. We begin by comparing
the two categories. We consider the forgetful functor:
(E.2.2.1)                                   uwh : CGWH → CG
sending a compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological space to itself as a compactly generated space,
and sending continuous maps to continuous maps. We further define:
(E.2.2.2)                                ucgwh : CGWH → Spaces
to be the forgetful functor sending a compactly generated weakly Hausdorff space to itself as an ordinary
topological space, and sending continuous maps to continuous maps. Since ucg ◦ uwh = ucgwh , the notation
being used should be un-ambiguous.
    We now discuss the existence of a left-adjoint
                                             h : CG → CGWH
to the forgetful functor. In other words, h(X) ∈ CGWH is an initial object receiving a continuous map from
X ∈ CG. Its construction and properties are briefly recalled below. (We refer the reader to [Str, Prop. 2.22].)

    Definition E.2.2.2. Let X be a compactly generated space. We define:
(E.2.2.3)                                       RX ⊂ X × X
to be the intersection of all closed equivalence relations on X (for the k-topology on X × X). We define the
topological space:
(E.2.2.4)                                      h(X) := X/RX
endowed with the quotient topology. We call:
(E.2.2.5)                                      qX : X → h(X)
the quotient map.
852                                    CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


    Remark E.2.2.3. For X a compactly generated space, since the equivalence relation RX ⊂ X × X from
(E.2.2.3) is closed, the quotient space h(X) is compactly generated weakly Hausdorff by Lemma E.2.1.11.

      We now check that formation of RX from (E.2.2.3) is natural in X, and therefore h(X) defines a functor:
(E.2.2.6)                                      h : CG → CGWH.

which means that f factors through qX . We further observe that both q and ψ are unique: q by universality of

of the map f ′ of (E.2.2.10). We have shown that for any compactly generated spaces X, Y with Y weakly
Hausdorff, and any continuous map f : X → Y , f factors uniquely through qX : X → h(X) from (E.2.2.5).
This proves functoriality of h(·) and part (2). Part (3) is clear from the universal property, and (4) is part of
the formalism of adjunction.                                                                                   □

    The following remark is the analog for CGWH of Remark E.1.2.3.
    Remark E.2.2.6. On the construction and properties of h(X), we observe:
(1) the functor h(·), by its very design, generally does not preserve underlying sets, contrary to the functor
    k(·) that only modifies the topology on spaces,
(2) small limits in CGWH can be computed in CG by Lemma E.2.2.5(1), and by Lemma E.1.2.2(1) their
    underlying set is the limit of the underlying sets of the objects within the diagram in CGWH,
(3) if P : I → CGWH is a diagram such that the limit of the induced diagram ucg ◦ uwh ◦ P = ucgwh ◦ P in
    Spaces is compactly generated weakly Hausdorff then limI (ucg ◦ uwh ◦ P ) = limI (ucgwh ◦ P ) computes
    limI P in CGWH,
(4) contrary to the case of colimits in CG, the underlying set of a small colimit in CGWH is not the colimit
    of the underlying sets of the objects within the diagram in CGWH unless the colimit computed in CG
    is already weakly Hausdorff; see Example E.2.2.7 below.
     Example E.2.2.7. The following is an example of a small (filtered) colimit in CGWH of a small diagram
P : I → CGWH, such that the set-theoretic colimit colimi∈I P (i)set is not the set underlying colimI P . We
let I := N>0 be the positive integers with their natural order, defining MapI (i, j) to be the singleton set if
i ≤ j, and the empty set otherwise. We define P (i) := S 1 , the unit circle, and for any morphism i → j in I,
we set P (i → j) to be the the map raising z ∈ S 1 to the 2j−i -th power. Then the colimit in Spaces of the
resulting diagram of underlying topological spaces is not T1 , even though each P (i) is compact Hausdorff.
In particular, the colimit colimI P in CGWH will have as its underlying set a non-trivial quotient of the
set-theoretic colimit of the underlying sets of the P (i)’s. The reader is referred to [Du, Appendix 2, Example
2, p. 422].

    E.2.3. Permanence properties of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces. Examples of
compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological spaces are all locally compact Hausdorff topological spaces
by (1) in the next lemma.

    Proposition E.2.3.1. We have:
(1) all locally compact Hausdorff topological spaces X are compactly generated weakly Hausdorff,
(2) the product in Spaces of a compactly generated weakly Hausdorff space and a locally compact Hausdorff
    space is compactly generated weakly Hausdorff and computes the product in CGWH.

    Proof. By Lemma E.1.2.19(1), X is compactly generated; it is weakly Hausdorff since it is Hausdorff.
By Lemma E.1.2.19(2), X ×0 Y is compactly generated and the product X × Y in CG can be computed
in Spaces. By Lemma E.2.2.5(1), the product X × Y in CG computes the product in CGWH, and the
Proposition is proved.                                                                               □

    Remark E.2.3.2. On the above Lemma E.2.3.1, we make the following observations:
(1) it will allow us to compute internal products of the locally compact Hausdorff topological spaces intervening
    in our constructions of topological stacks of interest by working within Spaces, therefore leaving no
    ambiguity as to where products are being formed and allowing access to product topologies of the spaces
    involved.
(2) The Hausdorff assumption in part (2) of the Lemma cannot be dropped altogether. We refer the reader to
    Lemma E.2.4.9, for a counter-example.

    We conclude this subsection by reviewing a number of permanence properties enjoyed by CGWH, and
with a result providing a concrete description of the (regular) monomorphisms and (regular) epimorphisms in
CGWH. We first prove the following analog of Lemma E.1.2.27, now characterizing immersions in CGWH
rather than in CG:

     Lemma E.2.3.3. Let X, Y be compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces and f : X → Y a continuous
injective map. The following are equivalent:
(1) f is an immersion.
(2) For any compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological space T and any set-function g : T → X, g is
    continuous if and only if f ◦ g is continuous.

    For the proof of this result, also see [Str, Cor. 2.29].

     Proof. By Lemma E.1.2.27, f is an immersion if and only if for any compactly generated space T and
any set-function g : T → X, f ◦ g is continuous if and only if g is. We claim that it is enough to verify this
condition when T is, in addition, weakly Hausdorff. Indeed, let T be any compactly generated space and
g : T → X any set-function. If g is continuous, it factors through the continuous quotient map T → h(T ) by
Lemma E.2.2.4(2), as X is weakly Hausdorff. If f ◦ g is continuous, then f ◦ g factors through h(T ) by Lemma
E.2.2.4(2), as Y is weakly Hausdorff. In this latter case, g itself factors through h(T ), as f is continuous and
injective. Either way, we may replace T with h(T ) and assume that T is weakly Hausdorff.                       □

    Lemma E.2.3.4. Let g : X → Y be a continuous map of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological
spaces. If f is a continuous section to g, then f is a closed immersion and g is a submersive map.

     Proof. Since g is a continuous surjection, the existence of f clearly implies that g is a quotient map,
hence submersive, and f is an immersion. We now observe that we have f (Y ) = {x ∈ X | f (g(x)) = x}. It
follows that we have:
                                      f (Y ) = (f ◦ g, id)−1 (∆X (X)),
856                                    CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


and as ∆X (X) ⊂ X ×0 X is k-closed in X ×0 X by part (2) of Lemma E.2.1.6, f (Y ) is also k-closed in X,
hence closed, as X is compactly generated. It follows that f is a closed immersion.                   □

      We now prove permanence properties for (closed) immersions under composition.

   Lemma E.2.3.5. Let f : X → Y and g : Y → Z be continuous maps of compactly generated weakly
Hausdorff topological spaces.
(1) If g ◦ f is an immersion then so is f .
(2) If g ◦ f is a closed immersion then so is f .
(3) If g ◦ f is an open immersion then f is a locally closed immersion.

    Proof. Assertion (1) holds with general topological spaces (for each open U ⊂ X and an open V ⊂ Z
such that (g ◦ f )−1 (V ) = U , we have f −1 (W ) = U for the open W = g −1 (V ) ⊂ Y ). For (2) and (3), we can
replace Z with the subspace (g ◦ f )(X) ⊂ Z to reduce to the case that Z = X; i.e., f is a section to g. Then
we are done by Lemma E.2.3.4.                                                                                 □

    We now survey a number of permanence properties of certain classes of morphisms in CGWH. For the
proof of the following lemma, we refer the reader to [Str, Prop. 2.32].

     Lemma E.2.3.6. The following classes of morphisms in CGWH are stable under finite compositions and
arbitrary base-change, and are local on the target:
(1) Injective maps.
(2) Surjective maps.
(3) Immersions.
(4) Closed immersions.
(5) Open immersions.
(6) Submersive maps.

    We note that by Example E.1.2.16, part (6) of the Lemma does not hold if we drop the weak Hausdorff
assumption. Stability of submersive maps under arbitrary base change is an advantage of the category CGWH
over the category CG.

    Proof. As fibre products in CGWH can be computed in CG by part (1) of Lemma E.2.2.5, and since
the forgetful functor CG → Sets preserves fibre products by Lemma E.1.2.2(1), checking (1) and (2) is
reduced to showing that injective, respectively surjective, set-functions remain injective, respectively surjective,
after arbitrary set-theoretic fibre product, and are stable under finite compositions, which is indeed the case.
    Obviously immersions, closed immersions, open immersions, and submersions are stable under finite
compositions. Being an injective, respectively surjective, continuous map is local on the target, and being
an immersion is also local on the target. Closed, respectively open, immersions are also local on the target
because closed, respectively open maps are. Submersiveness is also local on the target. We are now to check
that immersions, closed immersions, open immersions and submersive maps are stable under arbitrary base
change in the category CGWH. To this end, we consider the following cartesian diagram in CGWH:

base-change in CGWH.

   We discuss properties of submersive maps within the category CGWH. Here is an analog in CGWH of

   Lemma E.2.3.8. Let X, Y be compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces, and f : X → Y a continuous

    projections.
(3) f is a submersive map.

from (E.2.2.5), we have

    Example E.2.3.11. We let P := [−1, 1] − {0} endowed with the subspace topology inherited from the

note that the push-out of p is not only not an immersion, but not even injective. In other words, Lemma
E.2.3.10 does not hold if one drops the assumption on p being a closed immersion.

    We refer the reader to Example E.2.2.7 (which is [Du, Appendix 2, Example 2, p. 422]) for an example
of a colimit in Spaces of a small directed system of compactly generated and Hausdorff spaces that is not
weakly Hausdorff and therefore does not compute the colimit internal to CGWH.
    The following example illustrates the advantage of working within the category CGWH as opposed to
the category of compactly generated Hausdorff spaces considered in [Ste]:

     Example E.2.3.12. We let Z be a compactly generated non-regular Hausdorff topological space (for an
explicit example of a non-regular Hausdorff topological space that is compactly generated, we refer the reader
to [StSe, Part II, 78]), and p : P → Z the closed immersion of a closed subspace witnessing the non-regularity
of Z. We let X be a point, and q : P → X the quotient map collapsing P to a single point. While Lemma
                                                            `
E.2.3.10 does still ensure that in Spaces the push-out X q,P,p Z is compactly generated weakly Hausdorff
                                 `
and computes the push-out X q,P,p Z in CGWH, the topological push-out is non-Hausdorff, even though
X, P, Z are compactly generated and Hausdorff and p is a closed immersion. Indeed, such push-out is Z/P ,
and any point z ∈ Z that cannot be separated from the closed subspace P , has image in Z/P that cannot be
separated from the point induced as the image of P in the quotient.
     This clarifies the advantage of weakening the Hausdorff condition considered in [Ste] to a weak Hausdorff
separation condition. Namely, while arbitrary topological colimits of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff
spaces may not compute the internal colimit in CGWH, as illustrated by Example E.2.3.11, push-outs in
CGWH along closed immersions can indeed be computed in Spaces. Within the category of compactly
generated Hausdorff spaces of [Ste], not even these can be computed in Spaces.
                                                                                 `0
     Remark E.2.3.13. We observe that the submersive map f : Z → Y := X q,P,p Z in Spaces obtained
as the push-out in Spaces of the submersive map q in Example E.2.3.12, is not open.9 This illustrates
the additional degree of flexibility of incorporating the weak Hausdorff separation assumption on compactly
generated spaces, as opposed to the Hausdorff condition. Indeed, quotients of compactly generated weakly
Hausdorff spaces by closed equivalence relations are compactly generated weakly Hausdorff by Lemma E.2.1.11,
while the analogous result does not hold upon replacing the weak Hausdorff condition with the Hausdorff
condition. It only holds if, in addition,10 the quotient map is open.

    We conclude this section by discussing a result that provides a concrete characterization of several
important classes of morphisms in CGWH. In light of Example E.1.2.16, this is, in turn, an advantage of the
category CGWH over the category CG. First we recall a definition:

 862                                   CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


     Definition E.2.3.14. In a category C, an epimorphism is called regular if and only if it is the co-equalizer
 of a pair of morphisms, and a monomorphism is called regular if and only if it is the equalizer of a pair of
 morphisms.
     If C contains all small limits and colimits, an epimorphism in C is called effective if and only if it is the
 co-equalizer of its own kernel pair, and is called universally effective if this property holds after arbitrary
 pull-back. A monomorphism X → Y is called effective if and only if X → Y ×Q Y is an isomorphism, for the
 pushout Q of the two copies X ⇒ Y of the given monomorphism.11 We say C is regular if every pull-back of a
 regular epimorphism is a regular epimorphism (see [Bor2, Def. 2.1.1]).

       Proposition E.2.3.15. We have:
 (1) The monomorphisms in CGWH are the injective continuous maps.
 (2) The epimorphisms in CGWH are the continuous maps with dense image.
 (3) The regular monomorphisms in CGWH are the closed immersions.
 (4) The regular epimorphisms in CGWH are the submersive maps.
 (5) The effective monomorphisms in CGWH are the closed immersions.
 (6) The effective epimorphisms in CGWH are the submersive maps.
 (7) The universally effective epimorphisms in CGWH are the submersive maps.
 (8) The isomorphisms in CGWH are the homeomorphisms.
 (9) Monomorphisms in CGWH are stable under products, co-products and compositions.
(10) Regular monomorphisms in CGWH are stable under products, co-products and compositions.
(11) Epimorphisms in CGWH are stable under finite products, co-products and compositions.
(12) Regular epimorphisms in CGWH are stable under finite products, co-products and compositions.
(13) Every morphism in CGWH is universally the composition of a regular epimorphism followed by a
     monomorphism.
(14) CGWH is a regular category.

     Within CGWH, it is our convention to refer to a pull-back as a base-change. Regularity for CGWH
implies several structural properties for continuous maps between compactly generated weakly Hausdorff
spaces that will not hold for general topological spaces, following from [Bor2, Ch.2,Thm.2.1.3]. In particular,
within CGWH any continuous map factors as a submersive map followed by a continuous injective map, and
the factorization is unique up to homeomorphism, which implies that it is preserved by base-change. While we
will not rely on regularity of CGWH, but only indirectly and with no necessity to appeal to the general theory
around the concept, we will use stability of submersive maps under arbitrary base change systematically.
     Lemma E.2.3.8 identifies the regular epimorphisms in CGWH as exactly the submersive maps, since
Lemma E.2.3.6(6) proves stability of submersive maps under arbitrary base change, and such stability implies
regularity of CGWH, so we are implicitly using regularity of CGWH. This should further motivate the
choice of CGWH as the category of “convenient” topological spaces of reference.
     The assertion analogous to Proposition E.2.3.15(7) does not hold for CG (and hence for Spaces) as
illustrated by Example E.1.2.16, which exhibits an example of a submersive map whose base change in CG is
not submersive.
     We further mention that, in fact, CGWH is also a co-regular category: see [Str, §3, Thm. 3.1] for a
discussion on the co-regularity of CGWH, which ultimately amounts to combining [Bou-GT, §3,3.5] with
Lemma E.2.3.10 and Lemma E.2.2.5.
     Before we prove Proposition E.2.3.15, we introduce the following auxiliary construction, to be used in the
argument.

    E.2.4. Counter-examples on compact generation and separation conditions. In this subsection
we collect a number of examples illustrating the necessity of assumptions being made throughout the previous
sections. We also highlight key differences between the definition of compact generation for spaces adopted
throughout this work, and other definitions present within the literature. We focus specifically on the following
two, apart from the one adopted throughout this appendix (see Definition E.1.1.7):

     Definition E.2.4.1. Let X be a topological space. We say:
(1) X is a Kelley compactly generated space if and only if for any subspace U ⊂ X, U is open if and only if
    for any compact subspace K ⊂ X, U ∩ K is open in K.
(2) X is a Steenrod compactly generated space if and only if for any subspace U ⊂ X, U is open if and only if
    for any compact Hausdorff subspace K ⊂ X, U ∩ K is open in K.

    We have the following simpler analog for Kelley compact generation of Lemma E.1.1.3, which we record
here to aid in the construction of examples:

     Lemma E.2.4.2. Let X be a topological space. Then the following conditions are equivalent:
(1) X is Kelley compactly generated.
(2) For any topological space Y and set-function f : X → Y , the following conditions are equivalent:
    (a) f is continuous.
    (b) For any compact subspace K ⊂ X immersed through i : K → X, the composition f ◦ i is continuous.
(3) A subspace U ⊂ X is open if and only if for any compact topological space K and any continuous map
    g : K → X, g −1 (U ) is open in K.
                                                                                      `
(4) There exists a set I, a compact topological space Ki for each i ∈ I, and for Y := i∈I Ki the I-indexed
    co-product topological space, a submersive map q : Y → X.

      Proof. We prove that (1) and (2) are equivalent. For any topological space Y and set-function f : X → Y ,
if f is continuous then part (b) of (2) also holds. Conversely, if part (b) of (2) holds for all (K, i) then for
any open subspace V ⊂ Y , by writing U := f −1 (V ), for any compact subspace K ⊂ X immersed through
i : K → X we see that (f ◦ i)−1 (V ) is open in K by continuity of f ◦ i and we have U ∩ K = (f ◦ i)−1 (V ).
By (1), U is open in X, forcing f to be continuous. This proves (2) assuming (1). Conversely, if (2) holds,
then we choose Y to be the topological space whose underlying set is X set , and whose topology is the coarsest
topology such that every subset Z for which K ∩ Z is closed in K is itself closed in Y . We let f be the identity
set-function. By (2), f is continuous. Since the topology of Y on X set is finer than that of X, f −1 is also
continuous, and hence f is a homeomorphism. This shows (2) implies (1).
      Since (3) implies (1) as a consequence of the definitions, we prove the converse. If (1) holds, we let K be an
arbitrary compact topological space and g : K → X an arbitrary continuous map. Then g factors as g = i ◦ g ′
where i is the immersion of the image K ′ := g(K) ⊂ X, and g ′ : K → K ′ is continuous and surjective. Clearly
K ′ is a compact subspace of X. If the intersection of U with any compact subspace K ′ ⊂ X is open, then
g −1 (U ) = (g ′ )−1 (U ∩ K ′ ) is open in K and hence U is open. Thus, (1) and (3) are therefore equivalent.
     We now assume (2). We let I be the set of all compact subspaces of X. For i ∈ I, we denote Ki the
                                                                                                       `
corresponding compact subspace of X, and gi : Ki → X the immersion. Upon writing Y := i∈I Ki and
       `
q := i∈I gi , the map q : Y → X is continuous and surjective. Moreover, for any topological space Z and any
set-function f : X → Z, by part (2) the map f is continuous if and only if f ◦ q is continuous. By [Bou-GT,
Ch. I, §4, Prop. 6], q is submersive, and (4) is proved. Conversely, we assume that (4) holds. We let U ⊂ X be

14why citing for verifying a definition?
866                                   CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


a subspace such that for any compact subspace K ⊂ X, U ∩ K is open in K. Then, U ∩ q(Ki ) is open in the
compact subspace q(Ki ) for every i ∈ I, which forces q −1 (U ) to be open in Y . As q is submersive, U is open
in X, hence X is Kelley compactly generated.                                                                 □
    We will now show by example that the two concepts of compact generation introduced in Definition E.2.4.1
are not equivalent to one another, nor are they equivalent to compact generation as defined in Definition
E.1.1.7 and throughout this appendix. We first establish a result in the affirmative:

      Lemma E.2.4.3. Let X be a topological space. We have:
(1) If X is Steenrod compactly generated, then it is compactly generated.
(2) If X is compactly generated, then it is Kelley compactly generated.

     Proof. Assume that X is Steenrod compactly generated, and let U ⊂ X be a subspace. We assume that
for any compact Hausdorff space K and any continuous map g : K → X, g −1 (U ) is open in K. In particular,
this holds as (K, g) range over all compact Hausdorff subspaces of X, g being the immersion of such subspace.
As X is Steenrod compactly generated, U is open, proving that X is compactly generated in the sense of
Definition E.1.1.7, and (1) follows. If X is compactly generated, then by part (4) of Lemma E.1.1.3 there
                                                                                           `
exists a set I and for every i ∈ I a compact Hausdorff space Ki , with a submersive map q : i∈I Ki → X. By
the equivalence of parts (4) and (1) of Lemma E.2.4.2 above, X is Kelley compactly generated.             □
      We now examine the following example:

    Example E.2.4.4. We let Y := Q be the rational numbers equipped with the subspace topology induced
by the inclusion Q ⊂ R, the reals being endowed with their Euclidean topology. We define X := Y + to be the
one-point compactification of Y . Since every neighborhood of the point X − Y has non-empty intersection with
every non-empty open subspace of X, X is non-Hausdorff. It is, however, weakly Hausdorff, as any compact
subspace of X is closed. We refer the reader to [StSe, Part II, 35] for a discussion of further properties of this
example.

    The following Lemma illustrates how the assumption in Lemma E.2.1.4 concerning the existence of a
continuous surjection from a compact Hausdorff space, cannot be dropped. It also illustrates how the weak
Hausdorff separation condition is genuinely weaker than the Hausdorff separation condition.

    Lemma E.2.4.5. There exists an example of a compact, compactly generated, weakly Hausdorff space that
is not Hausdorff.

     Proof. We let X be the topological space from Example E.2.4.4. Then X is compact and weakly
Hausdorff. It is also compactly generated by Lemma E.1.2.21, since it is sequential (see [StSe, Part II, 35]).
It is, however, non-Hausdorff.                                                                             □
      We consider the following:

   Example E.2.4.6. The Sierpiński space S is the topological space whose underlying set is {0, 1} and
whose topology τ is the collection of subsets of S:
                                                  {∅, {1}, S}.

      Lemma E.2.4.7. There exists a compactly generated space that is not Steenrod compactly generated.

    Proof. The space S from Example E.2.4.6 is compactly generated by Lemma E.1.2.21, as every finite
space is sequential. On the other hand, it is not Steenrod compactly generated, as the only compact Hausdorff
subspaces K of S are the one-element sets {0} and {1}, and any subset Z ⊂ S satisfies Z ∩ K is closed in K.
As the topology on S is not discrete, S is not Steenrod compactly generated.                              □
                           E.2. COMPACTLY GENERATED WEAKLY HAUSDORFF SPACES                                     867

the various notions of compact generation reviewed here, and hence no potential for ambiguity as to which
one is being referred to:

(1) X is Kelley compactly generated.
(2) X is compactly generated.
(3) X is Steenrod compactly generated.

     The following lemma illustrates how, upon dropping the Hausdorff assumption in Lemma E.2.1.4, topolog-
ical products of a compact weakly Hausdorff space and a compactly generated (weakly) Hausdorff space may
not be compactly generated.

    Lemma E.2.4.9. There exists an example of a topological space X such that:
(1) X is compact, compactly generated weakly Hausdorff (and not Hausdorff),
(2) X ×0 X is not compactly generated.

    Proof. We let Y be the rational numbers endowed with the subspace topology inherited from the
Euclidean topology on R, and X := Y + the one-point compactification as in Example E.2.4.4. Then X is
weakly Hausdorff and compact. It is also compactly generated, as it is sequential (see [StSe, Part II, 35]). If
X ×0 X was compactly generated then X × X = k(X ×0 X) would coincide with X ×0 X (i.e., k-closed is the
same as closed in X ×0 X). Since X is weakly Hausdorff, the diagonal subspace ∆X (X) would then be closed
in X ×0 X (see Lemma E.2.1.6), so X would be Hausdorff, a contradiction.                                     □

    We consider the following:

    Example E.2.4.10. We let Y be a topological space such that:
(1) Y is T1 .
(2) Every compact subspace of Y is finite and discrete.
(3) Y is non-discrete.
Then the one-point compactification X := Y + is an example of a compact non-discrete space equipped with
an open subspace all of whose compact subspaces are finite. Examples of spaces such as Y can be found in
[StSe, Part II, 25, 26].
868                                      CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


    Lemma E.2.4.11. There exists an example of a Kelley compactly generated space that is not compactly
generated.

     Proof. Indeed, the space X is Example E.2.4.10 is an example of a Kelley compactly generated space
(since Y is T1 and X − Y is a closed point) and we claim it is not compactly generated. If it was compactly
generated then by Lemma E.1.2.25(2) every open subspace of X would have to be compactly generated,
whereas Y is not (since k(Y ) is discrete but Y is not discrete).                                        □

      Lemma E.2.4.12. There exists an example of a topological space X and an open subspace U ⊂ X such that
(1) X is Kelley compactly generated.
(2) U is not Kelley compactly generated.

    Proof. Let X be the topological space from Example E.2.4.10. Then X is Kelley compactly generated
as noted in the proof of Lemma E.2.4.11. On the other hand, upon choosing U := Y as in the Example, Y is
not compactly generated (also seen in the proof of Lemma E.2.4.11).15                                 □

    Compact generation is inherited by open subspaces by Lemma E.1.2.25, whereas by Lemma E.2.4.12
Kelley compact generation is not.

     We recall the construction of the Von Neumann universes, following [Kunen, Ch. 3, §2] and [Jech, Part I,

    The discussion in the present section is aimed at constructing a small subcategory of CGWH stable under
enough categorical operations to serve the purpose of underlying a site, over which we shall be considering
stacks in groupoids. We will be, in the process, arranging for the closure of such a category under enough
many small limits and colimits to ensure our concrete constructions of interest will involve spaces always
contained within it.
    For any ordinal α, we construct the set Vα as follows, proceeding recursively. We define:
                                               V0 := ∅, Vα+1 := 2Vα ,
with, recall, 2Vα denoting the power-set of Vα , and for a limit ordinal α we further set:
                                                        [
                                                 Vα :=      Vβ ,
                                                            β<α

determining Vα by transfinite recursion. We refer the reader to [Kunen, Ch. III, Def. 2.1] and the discussion
in loc.cit. following it, for further background on the sets Vα . We further refer the reader to the discussion
before [Jech, Lemma 6.3]. We refer the reader to [SP, Tag 000B] and the subsequent section as well, where
the Vα ’s are referred to as partial universes. We refer to the sets Vα as the Von Neumann’s universe of level α.
They satisfy the following properties, seen by transfinite induction (see [Kunen, Ch. III, Lemma 2.3]):
(1) each Vα is a transitive set,
(2) if α ≤ α′ then Vα ⊂ Vα′ .
(3) α ⊂ Vα .
The union WF of all the Vα as α varies across all limit ordinals is a proper class, called the class of well-founded
sets. By [Kunen, Ch. III, Lemma 2.14], ultimately resting on the Axiom Schema of Regularity and the Axiom
of Choice, every set in the class of all sets, and likewise every topological space in the class of all topological
spaces, is an element of WF.
     Before moving forward, we establish two preparatory results. The following lemma assumes the Axiom of
Choice.
   Lemma E.3.1.2. Let κ be a cardinal, and Sets≤κ the class of all sets J whose cardinality satisfies |J| ≤ κ.
Then there exists a sub-class Sets≤κ ⊂ Sets≤κ such that:
(1) Sets≤κ is a set.
(2) For any J ∈ Sets≤κ there exists J ′ ∈ Sets≤κ and a bijective set-function f : J ′ → J.
    Proof. Let λ be a cardinal satisfying λ ≤ κ. By the Axiom of Choice, there exists an ordinal α such
that |α| = λ. We denote αλ := inf{α | |α| = λ}, the initial ordinal associated to λ. As αλ ⊂ Vαλ and, for all
cardinals λ, λ′ satisfying λ ≤ λ′ ≤ κ, we have16 αλ ≤ αλ′ ≤ ακ , we deduce the containments Vαλ ⊂ Vαλ′ ⊂ Vακ
by [Kunen, Ch. III, Lemma 2.3]. We set Sets≤κ := Vακ +1 . For any element J of Sets≤κ , there exists a least
ordinal α|J| with |J| = |α|J| |, and we have α|J| ⊂ Vα|J| ⊂ Vακ , implying α|J| ∈ Vακ +1 = Sets≤κ . In other
words, there exists an element J ′ ∈ Sets≤κ , itself a set, and a bijection f : J ′ → J.                   □
    Definition E.3.1.3. For a cardinal ν, a ν-small category is any small category I whose underlying set of
objects satisfies |I| ≤ ν and for every pair of objects i, i′ ∈ I we have |MapI (i, i′ )| ≤ ν.
     Building on Lemma E.3.1.2 we now prove an analog for small index categories17. Namely, we prove that
there exists a set of small categories whose sets of objects and morphisms have cardinality bounded above by
a fixed arbitrary cardinal ν, and such that any such small category is isomorphic to a category that is an
element of such a set.

                                                    |C(K)| ≤ κ.

      E.3.2. α-small compactly generated and weakly Hausdorff spaces. We assign the following:
      Definition E.3.2.1. Let α be an ordinal, and ν be a cardinal.
(1) The category CGWHα has as its objects the compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological spaces
    whose underlying sets are elements of Vα , and its morphisms are continuous maps of topological spaces.
    We call α-small the compactly generated and weakly Hausdorff spaces that are the objects of CGWHα .
                       E.3. SMALL COMPACTLY GENERATED WEAKLY HAUSDORFF SPACES                                 873


(2) For C a category, I a ν-small category, and P : I → C a diagram, we call P a ν-small diagram and denote
    by limI P respectively colimI P its ν-small limit respectively ν-small colimit if representable in C.
(3) We say that a category C contains all ν-small limits respectively contains all ν-small colimits (or that
    ν-small limits, respectively ν-small colimits, are representable in C) if and only if for any ν-small diagram
    P : I → C the object limI P respectively colimI P exists in C.

    Remark E.3.2.2. On Definition E.3.2.1, we make the following observation. Every topological space is
homeomorphic to one whose underlying set is in the class WF. This is [Kunen, Lemma 2.14], and justifies the
approach taken throughout to bound the size of the topological spaces in our sought-for small subcategory of
the category CGWH of all compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological spaces. We refer the reader to
[Jech, Lemma 6.3] that establishes that every set is in some Vα , as a consequence of the Axiom of Regularity
in ZF− . In particular, this makes no use of the Axiom of Choice.

    The following result is an analog of [SP, Tag 000J]. We keep the notation similar so as to enable the
reader familiar with loc.cit. to closely follow the analogous steps within the arguments.

     Lemma E.3.2.3. Let S0 be a set of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological spaces and ν an
arbitrary infinite cardinal. Then there exists a limit ordinal α, depending on S0 and ν, such that:
(1) S0 is contained in Vα .
(2) For any α-small space X and any compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological space Y with
                                          size(Y ) ≤ Bound(size(X))
    (see (E.3.1.1)) there exists an α-small space X ′ and a homeomorphism X ′ → Y .
(3) ν-small limits and colimits are representable in CGWHα and the forgetful functor to CGWH preserves
    them.

    The following argument is an adaptation to the context of this work of the argument of [SP, Tag 000J],
with minor adjustments and complements.

   Proof. We define a function f on ordinals as follows. We set f (0) = 0. Suppose f (α) is already defined.

      E.3.3. Size-bound criteria. We have the following Lemma, in analogy with [SP, Tag 000P].

      Lemma E.3.3.1. Let X be a compact Hausdorff topological space. Then:
                                              size(X) ≤ max{ℵ0 , 2|C(X)| }.

ideal of f vanishing on X), and the number of such ideals is at most 2|C(X)| .                          □

    E.3.4. Closure properties of CGWHα . We collect here the properties that the category CGWHα
enjoys.

     Proposition E.3.4.1. For S0 a set of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological spaces, ν an
infinite cardinal, and α a limit ordinal as provided by Lemma E.3.2.3, the category CGWHα satisfies the
following properties:
(1) ν-small limits and colimits are representable in CGWHα and the forgetful functor to CGWH commutes
    with them.
(2) Fibre products exist in CGWHα and the forgetful functor to CGWH commutes with them.
(3) Countable coproducts exist in CGWHα and the forgetful functor to CGWH commutes with them.
(4) For any object X in CGWHα and any immersion Z → X with Z compactly generated weakly Hausdorff,
    there exists an object Z ′ in CGWHα and a homeomorphism Z ′ → Z.
(5) For any object X in CGWHα and any open, respectively closed, respectively locally closed, immersion
    Z → X (so Z is compactly generated weakly Hausdorff by Lemma E.1.2.25), there exists an object Z ′ in
    CGWHα and a homeomorphism Z ′ → Z.

     Proof. By Lemma E.3.2.3(3), part (1) holds. Parts (2) and (3) are a consequence of part (1) since
ν is infinite. We prove parts (4) and (5). In both cases, the cardinality of the set I of compact Hausdorff
subspaces of Z is bounded above by size(X). Likewise, for any compact Hausdorff subspace K of Z, we have
size(K) ≤ size(X), as ΣK ,→ ΣX because the image of K under the immersion Z → X is a compact Hausdorff
                                                                                S
subspace of X as well. We now observe that the set I defined above is such that K∈I K is Z by Proposition
E.2.1.13. By Lemma E.3.3.4, we deduce that Z is homeomorphic to an object of CGWHα . This proves (4)
and (5).                                                                                                 □

    Remark E.3.4.2. We do not address whether the function space C ont(X, Y ), for α-small compactly
generated topological spaces X and Y , is homeomorphic to an object of CGWHα , as this would be of
no use for the purposes of this appendix. Such objects would not endow CGWHα with the structure of
a cartesian closed symmetric monoidal category. Indeed, the obstruction to CGWHα being a cartesian
closed symmetric monoidal category such that the forgetful functor to CGWH is a strict closed functor; i.e.,
it preserves internal Hom-bifunctors, is that the category CGWHα is not replete. This is because it is a
small category by design, whereas CGWH is large. If CGWHα was cartesian closed, and if the forgetful
functor (which, in light of Proposition E.3.4.1(1) is product-preserving and hence automatically a “strong
 878                                   CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


 closed functor” between symmetric monoidal categories) were a strict closed functor then CGWHα would
 have to contain all function spaces of all pairs of its objects. This cannot be, as Example E.3.4.3 below
 shows. Proposition E.3.4.1 shows, however, that despite not being cartesian closed, the category CGWHα
 does still enjoy important consequences of cartesian-closedness of CGWH that we have collected in the
 previous sections. Most importantly, formation of products in CGWHα commutes with representable colimits.
 Proposition E.3.4.1 also ensures that ν-small colimits (and ν-small limits) are representable.
     Example E.3.4.3. We let X0 := ∅, equipped with the empty topology. We note that X is compactly
 generated and weakly Hausdorff (by definition, or, for instance, by Remark E.2.1.2). We further let Y := {0, 1}
 endowed with the discrete topology, so Y is also compactly generated and weakly Hausdorff. For any ordinal
 β, we call:
                                            Xβ+1 := C ont(Xβ , Y )
therefore assigning Xβ by transfinite recursion. All the Xβ are compactly generated and weakly Hausdorff by
Proposition E.2.2.10. However, the size of the underlying set of Xβ+1 is ℶβ (see [Kunen, Ch. I, §10, Def. 10.44])
which, for large enough β, exceeds the size of the von Neumann universe Vα (see [Kunen, Ch. III, §3, Lemma
2.13]) that contains all of the objects of CGWHα . We let γ := inf{β | Xβ ∈   / Vα }, so Xγ is an example of an
object of CGWHα such that C ont(Xγ , Y ) is not an object of CGWHα but only is homeomorphic to such
an object.
       We denote by:
(E.3.4.1)                                 uα : CGWHα → CGWH
 the forgetful functor. The functor uα is fully faithful by design, and it commutes with ν-small limits and
 ν-small colimits by Proposition E.3.4.1. In particular, it commutes with finite limits and finite colimits.
     We conclude this subsection with a description of important classes of morphisms within CGWHα , in
 the spirit of Proposition E.2.3.15.
       Proposition E.3.4.4. We have:
 (1) The monomorphisms in CGWHα are the injective continuous maps.
 (2) The epimorphisms in CGWHα are the continuous maps with dense image.
 (3) The regular monomorphisms in CGWHα are the closed immersions.
 (4) The regular epimorphisms in CGWHα are the submersive maps.
 (5) The effective monomorphisms in CGWHα are the closed immersions.
 (6) The effective epimorphisms in CGWHα are the submersive maps.
 (7) The universally effective epimorphisms in CGWHα are the submersive maps.
 (8) The isomorphisms in CGWHα are the homeomorphisms.
 (9) Monomorphisms in CGWHα are stable under products, coproducts and compositions.
(10) Regular monomorphisms in CGWHα are stable under products, coproducts and compositions.
(11) Epimorphisms in CGWHα are stable under finite products, coproducts and compositions.
(12) Regular epimorphisms in CGWHα are stable under finite products, coproducts and compositions.
(13) Every morphism in CGWHα is universally the composition of a regular epimorphism followed by a
     monomorphism.
(14) CGWHα is a regular category.
     We recall the notion of regular category (see [vO, Def.4.1]): a category is regular when it contains finite
 limits, the kernel pair of any morphism has a co-equalizer, and regular epimorphisms are stable under arbitrary
 base change.
     Proof. As the forgetful functor uα is faithful, it reflects monomorphisms, proving (1), and epimorphisms,
 proving (2). As uα is fully faithful, it is conservative, i.e. it reflects isomorphisms. We now prove (3) and
                       E.3. SMALL COMPACTLY GENERATED WEAKLY HAUSDORFF SPACES                               879


(5). By Lemma E.3.4.1(1), CGWHα contains equalizers and co-kernel pairs, and the forgetful functor uα to
CGWH commutes with them. It follows that uα reflects effective monomorphisms, and that a monomorphism
in CGWHα is regular if and only if it is effective. Suppose f : X → Y is a closed immersion of objects of
CGWHα . Then uα (f ) is a closed immersion in CGWH, hence an effective monomorphism in CGWH by
Proposition E.2.3.15. It follows f that is an effective monomorphism in CGWHα . Conversely, if f is an
effective monomorphism in CGWHα , then uα (f ) is an effective monomorphism in CGWH, hence a closed
immersion by Proposition E.2.3.15(5) and therefore f is a closed immersion.
     We now prove (4) and (6). By part (1) of Lemma E.3.4.1, the category CGWHα contains co-equalizers
and kernel pairs. It follows that epimorphisms are regular if and only if they are effective. Moreover, as
uα is fully faithful and commutes with finite limits and colimits by part (1) of Lemma E.3.4.1, uα reflects
effective epimorphisms. Suppose f : X → Y is a submersive map of objects in CGWHα . Then uα (f ) is a
submersive map in CGWH, hence an effective epimorphism in CGWH by part (4) of Proposition E.2.3.15.
As uα reflects effective epimorphisms, it follows that f is an effective epimorphism in CGWHα , equivalently
a regular epimorphism. Conversely, assume f is an effective epimorphism. As uα commutes with co-equalizers
by part (1) of Lemma E.3.4.1, uα (f ) is a regular epimorphism, hence a submersive map, implying that f is a
submersive map. This proves (4) and (6).
     We now prove part (7). Since CGWHα contains fibre products, and uα commutes with them, submersive
maps between objects of CGWHα remain submersive under base change along an arbitrary morphism in
CGWHα , since the same is true in CGWH by part (4) of Lemma E.2.3.6. By part (6), submersive maps
are universally effective epimorphisms. Conversely, since universally effective epimorphisms are, in particular,
effective epimorphisms, they are submersive maps by (6). Part (8) follows, for instance, from parts (2) and
(3). For parts (9) and (11), we observe that since uα reflects monomorphisms and epimorphisms, then part
(9) and part (11) follow from part (9) and Proposition E.2.3.15(11). As uα reflects effective monomorphisms
and effective epimorphisms, then by (3) and (4), parts (10) and (12) follow from Proposition E.2.3.15(10, 12).
Part (13) is a formal consequence of the fact that CGWHα is closed under finite limits and finite colimits by
Lemma E.3.4.1(1), and regular epimorphisms are stable under arbitrary base change by (4) and (7). These
three conditions say that CGWHα is a regular category (see [vO, Def. 4.1]) and by [vO, Prop. 4.2], which
proves (14).                                                                                                 □

    The above Proposition E.3.4.4 is saying that even though CGWHα is not cartesian closed as a cartesian
symmetric monoidal subcategory of CGWH (i.e. a cartesian symmetric monoidal category such that the
forgetful functor uα is a strict closed functor), it inherits the good properties of CGWH collected in this
appendix, many of which are a consequence of cartesian closure of CGWH.

    E.3.5. The site of small compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces. We let:
(1) S0 be an arbitrary set of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces.
(2) ν an arbitrary infinite cardinal.
We shall refer to the datum (S0 , ν) as basic setup. By Lemma E.3.2.3 there exists a limit ordinal α and a
small category CGWHα with the following properties:
(1) S0 is contained in the objects of CGWHα .
(2) I-indexed limits and colimits exist in CGWHα and are preserved by the forgetful functor to CGWH, as
    long as the cardinality of I is at most ν.
    When paired with Proposition E.3.4.1 on closure properties of CGWHα , we obtained Proposition E.3.4.4
that gives a topological description of key classes of morphisms in CGWHα . We are allowed to choose a
basic setup (S0 , ν) that fits our requirements.
    We are now going to use Proposition E.3.4.4 to construct a site. The topology of our choosing will be
the canonical topology itself. Proposition E.3.4.4 enables a concrete description for it (see Lemma E.3.5.7).
880                                    CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


The methods in use within this subsection follow [SP, Tag 00VH], and [KS, Ch. 16-17], and particularly [KS,
Ch. 16, §16.1] and [KS, Ch. 17, §17.1-17.2].
    We begin with the following construction:

    Construction E.3.5.1. We let S0′ be the smallest set of compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological
spaces, satisfying the following properties:
(1) S0′ contains the following topological groups:
    (a) Q, Q× with the discrete topology.
    (b) Z and all its finite abelian quotients, all with the discrete topology.
    (c) Z× p , Zp with the p-adic topology.
    (d) R, R× , C, C× , all with the Euclidean topology.
    (e) AQ with the adelic topology.
    (f) A×  Q with the idelic topology.
    (g) The closed subgroups of all of the above.
(2) S0′ contains CP1 .
(3) S0′ is closed under countable products and coproducts in CGWH.
(4) For any X ∈ S0′ , all closed equivalence relations R ⊂ X × X are contained in S0 , and the quotients X/R
    are contained in S0′ .
We let ν := Bound(supX∈S0′ {size(X)}) (see (E.3.1.1) from Definition E.3.1.1 for the definition of the “size” of
a compactly generated weakly Hausdorff space, alongside the Bound(·) function on cardinals) and call S0′′ the
set CH≤ν provided by Lemma E.3.1.6. For S0 := S0′ ∪ S0′′ . the pair (S0 , ν) is our choice of basic setup. We let
α be the limit ordinal provided by Lemma E.3.2.3 associated to this choice of S0 and ν.

     We refer the reader to §E.3.1 for the construction of CH≤ν , and likewise for the construction of Sets≤ν
and Cat≤ν . These are sets, the first a set of representatives for the homeomorphism classes of all compact
Hausdorff spaces of size bounded above by ν, the second a set of representatives for all sets of cardinality
bounded above by ν, the third a set of representatives for the isomorphism classes of small categories, whose
sets of objects and morphisms has cardinality bounded above by ν. Constructing the three sets was carried
out in Lemma E.3.1.2, Lemma E.3.1.4, and Lemma E.3.1.6.
     We now construct three classes of coverings on CGWHα , for α the limit ordinal constructed in Construction
E.3.5.1, depending on the basic setup (S0 , ν) chosen in Construction E.3.5.1.

      Definition E.3.5.2. We define:
(1) The class Cov0 (CGWHα ) whose elements are families of closed immersions {fi : Ti → T }i∈I for
    I ∈ Sets≤ν and T ∈ S0 , for (S0 , ν) the basic setup constructed in Construction E.3.5.1, and Ti a compact

    We proceed as in [SP, Tag 000W] to obtain a site in the sense of [SP, Tag 00VH], and [KS, Ch. 16-17].
   Construction E.3.5.4. By [SP, Tag 000W], we pick out a set of coverings in Cov1 (CGWHα ) and

(4) For every {fi : Ti → T }i∈I ∈ Covi (CGWHα )κ,β , for i = 1, 2, the defining axioms for coverings (see [SP,

(5) every element in Cov1 (CGWHα ), respectively Cov2 (CGWHα ), is combinatorially equivalent to (infor-

    That large enough κ and β as in Construction E.3.5.4 exist is the content of [SP, Tag 000W].
    Definition E.3.5.5. We define:
(1) J1 the topology on CGWHα generated by Cov1 (CGWHα )κ,β . We refer to J1 as the submersive-covering
    topology on CGWHα .
(2) J2 the topology on CGWHα generated by Cov2 (CGWHα )κ,β . We refer to J2 as the open-covering
    topology on CGWHα .
    Remark E.3.5.6. On Definition E.3.5.5, we make the following observations.
(1) The pairs (CGWHα , Covi (CGWHα )κ,β ) are sites in the sense of [SP, Tag 00VH], and in the sense of
    [KS, Ch. 17, Def. 17.2.1]. We further refer the reader to [KS, Ch. 16, Def. 16.1.2], [KS, Ch. 16, Def. 16.1.5],
    and [SP, Tag 00YW] on how to relate the two approaches to the construction of categories of sheaves
    of sets on sites whose underlying categories are small, through the concept of topology generated by a
    set of coverings (see [KS, Ch. 16, Def. 16.1.5] and the discussion from [KS, Ch. 16, p. 392] following the
    Definition, and [SP, Tags 00YZ, 00Z1]). In particular, the pairs (CGWHα , J1 ) and (CGWHα , J2 ) are
    sites in the sense of [KS, Ch. 17, Def. 17.2.1].
882                                    CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


(2) We recall that the topology (in the sense of [SP, Tag 00Z4], which is also [KS, Ch. 16, Def. 16.1.2])
    on the small category (pre-site, in the terminology of [KS, Ch. 17, Def. 17.1.1]) CGWHα generated
    by Covi (CGWHα )κ,β for i = 1, 2 respectively is the assignment T ⇝ Ji (T ), for every object T ∈
    Ob(CGWHα ), where Ji (T ) is the set of sieves S ⊂ hT of the form SU = S({fj : Tj → T }j∈I ), for some
    element U = {fj : Tj → T }j∈I ∈ Covi (CGWHα )κ,α , where SU is the unique smallest sieve S such that
    each fj belongs to S(Tj ). Such SU indeed exists by part (4) of [SP, Tag 00YZ] (see also the discussion on
    [KS, Ch. 16, §1, p. 392] after [KS, Ch. 16, Def. 16.1.5]).
(3) We note that the topology J1 is finer than the topology J2 (see [SP, Tag 00Z6]), which is to say that for
    every object T of CGWHα , J2 (T ) ⊂ J1 (T ). Indeed, for any open covering {fi : Ti → T }i∈I , the map:
                                              a       a
                                                 fi :     Ti → T
                                               i∈I     i∈I

    is open and surjective, and hence submersive by [SP, Tag 02YB]. The element {fi : Ti → T }i∈I of
    Cov2 (CGWHα )κ,β is therefore an element of Cov1 (CGWHα )κ,β and the sieve it generates is a covering
    sieve for J1 , i.e. it is contained in J1 (T ). This shows the containment J2 (T ) ⊂ J1 (T ). In particular, to
    show that J2 is sub-canonical, it is enough to show that J1 is.
(4) We note that the ordinal β and the cardinal κ in the definition of Covi (CGWHα )κ,β provided by
    [SP, Tag 000X] for i = 1, 2 respectively are a priori distinct, and should be denoted β1 , κ1 and β2 , κ2 .
    Upon inspection of the proof of [SP, Tag 000X], one can replace each βi , respectively κi , with some
    β ≥ max{β1 , β2 }, respectively κ ≥ max{κ1 , κ2 }, and arrange for the same β and the same κ to ensure the
    existence of Covi (CGWHα )κ,β , for i = 1, 2, satisfying the desired properties.
(5) We note that the dependency of the topologies J1 , J2 on CGWHα on β and κ, while a priori stringent,
    is mitigated by [SP, Tag 00VY], from which we deduce that we may replace Covi (CGWHα )κ,β , for
    i = 1, 2, respectively, with any other set of coverings of the same class Covi (CGWHα ) respectively (see
    parts (2) and (3) of Definition E.3.5.2) such that every element U ∈ Covi (CGWHα ) is combinatorially
    equivalent to an element of the set, without changing the topos of sheaves of sets with respect to the
    resulting topology. In other words, the dependency of the topoi Shv(CGWHα , Ji ) for i = 1, 2 on β and κ
    is not too stringent.

    We conclude this section with one final consideration on the topologies J1 and J2 . It is that J1 is
sub-canonical (and hence so is J2 by part (3) of Remark E.3.5.6). In fact, we shall show that J1 is the canonical
topology itself on CGWHα (which is, recall, the coarsest topology with respect to which all representable
pre-sheaves are sheaves; see [SP, Tag 00ZA], and also [SP, Tags 00Z8,00Z9] applied to the collection of all
pre-sheaves of sets).

      Lemma E.3.5.7. The topology J1 on CGWHα is the canonical topology.

    Proof. This is a direct consequence of Proposition E.3.4.4(7), which implies that the covering sieves of
J1 are exactly those generated by jointly surjective families of universal effective epimorphisms. By [SGA3,
Exp .IV, Prop. 2.3], J1 is the canonical topology on CGWHα .                                              □

     Remark E.3.5.8. We point out to the reader [Les, Prop. 4.7], where a characterization of the canonical
topology on CGWH is provided. This can be used to deduce Lemma E.3.5.7. We caution the reader that
we have endeavoured to only define topologies on “pre-sites” in the sense of [KS, Ch. 17, Def. 17.1.1], hence
without allowing large categories. One can, however, define the concept of a Grothendieck topology on any
category, as in [SGA4, Exp. II, §1], and hence define the canonical topology as in [SGA4, Exp. II, §2, Def. 2.5].
We further point out that, in this sense, one can define the canonical topology on the large category Spaces.
It turns out that it is defined by those covering sieves generated by families of maps that are jointly surjective
and jointly universally submersive, where a continuous map is universally submersive if and only if it remains
                                            E.4. TOPOLOGICAL GROUPOIDS                                         883


submersive under arbitrary topological base change. It is a feature of CGWH that submersive maps are
stable under arbitrary base change internally in CGWH (see Lemma E.2.3.6(6)), and one that does not hold
not only in Spaces but also in CG, the category of compactly generated spaces (see Example E.1.2.16). This
is one of the reasons for adopting CGWH as ambient category for the relevant site.
    We conclude by introducing some terminology, to be used throughout the remainder of this appendix.
    Definition E.3.5.9. For the choice of limit ordinal α made in Construction E.3.5.1, and for the choices
of cardinal κ and limit ordinal β made in Construction E.3.5.4, we denote by:
(1) CGWHα,τ the site (CGWHα , J1 ).
(2) CGWHα,σ the site (CGWHα , J2 ).
We refer to CGWHα,τ as the topological τ -site, and to CGWHα,σ as the topological σ-site.
    We will be mostly using the topological τ -site throughout the remainder of this appendix, with only
occasional reference to the σ-site. In other words, the “open-covering” topology will play a very limited role.

                                            E.4. Topological groupoids
     The stacks of interest for the purposes of this appendix will always be fibered in groupoids. In fact they
will always be quotient stacks associated to explicit topological groupoids. The aim of this section is to collect
here what is needed on the subject of topological groupoids for our later use with 2-categorical constructions
in §E.5-§E.6.
    E.4.1. Groupoids in sets and internal groupoids. There exist several sources within the literature
covering some of the material of this section. We will be occasionally following [Hig], [CdSW, Part VI]
and [N, §3.2]. In terms of notation, we follow the notational choices of [SP, Tag 022L] closely, in analogy
with [SP, Tag 0437] for “groupoids in schemes” and “groupoids in spaces”, so as to facilitate the reader who
wishes to skip this section and the next on a first reading and rely on their own familiarity with the algebraic
counterparts of the topics discussed within them.
    We first recall the following:
    Definition E.4.1.1. A groupoid in sets is the datum (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) of:

(vi) a set-function i : R → R called the inversion,
satisfying the following axioms:
(1) Associativity:
