We define the category Groupoids whose objects are the class of all groupoids in sets and morphisms are
morphisms of groupoids.

      Notation E.4.1.1. We abbreviate the notation (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) to R ⇒ X, or (X, R, s, t, c), when no
confusion is expected to arise. Moreover, for a morphism between groupoids assigned by a pair of set-functions
(f1 , f2 ) as in (E.4.1.7), we often write f for both f1 and f2 , so as to simplify the notation. Source and target
of each f are expected to leave no ambiguity as to whether an f is a set-function on objects or on morphisms.

     Remark E.4.1.2. On Definition E.4.1.1, we make the following observations:
(1) We note that the datum of a groupoid in sets is equivalent to the datum of an (effective) small category
    (see Definition E.5.1.15) all of whose morphisms are isomorphisms. Indeed, given a groupoid in sets
    (X, R, s, t, c, e, i), we may construct the category CR whose set of objects is defined to be Ob(CR ) := X,
    and whose morphisms are defined as follows. For any pair of objects x, y ∈ Ob(CR ), HomCR (x, y) :=
    s−1 (x) ∩ t−1 (y). The axioms from Definition E.4.1.1 ensure that the above assignment indeed is a (small)
    category. We will occasionally use this perspective, especially throughout the development and use of the
    desired theory of stacks in groupoids on a suitable site on topological spaces. For g ∈ R with s(g) = x and
    t(g) = y, we may write g : x → y to view g as a morphism x → y in CR .
(2) In (E.4.1.8) for the definition of morphisms of groupoids, concerning compatibility with the composition
    laws we note that by (E.4.1.9) on compatibility with source and target morphisms the set-function (f2 , f2 ) :
    R × R → R′ × R′ restricted to R ×s,X,t R ⊂ R × R factors through a set-function R ×s,X,t R → Rs′ ′ ,X ′ ,t′ R′ ;
    it is this set-function that is being referred to in Axiom (2) on compatibility with composition laws. We
    denote this set-function by (f2 , f2 ) again, as it is uniquely determined by (f2 , f2 ) : R × R → R′ × R′ ,
    expecting no confusion to arise.

    We now prove a first lemma that reduces the task of verifying the defining compatibilities of a morphism
of groupoids:
                            (f1 , f2 ) : (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) → (X ′ , R′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ , i′ )
to the task of verifying compatibility of f1 and f2 with (s, t, c) and (s′ , t′ , c′ ) only.

    Lemma E.4.1.3. Let (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) and (X ′ , R′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ , i′ ) be two groupoids in sets. Let f1 : X → X ′
and f2 : R → R′ be set-functions. The following conditions are equivalent:
(1) (f1 , f2 ) is a morphism of groupoids.
(2) f1 and f2 satisfy the following compatibilities:
    (a) s′ ◦ f2 = f1 ◦ s.
    (b) t′ ◦ f2 = f1 ◦ t.
    (c) f2 ◦ c(·, ·) = c′ (f2 (·), f2 (·)).

    Proof. In terms of the associated small categories CR and CR′ , condition (2) says (f1 , f2 ) defines
a covariant functor F : CR → CR′ . Since any covariant functor respects identity maps and inverses of
isomorphisms, we are done.                                                                             □

     The following result is also a direct consequence of the axioms, and will be used later.

     Lemma E.4.1.4. Let (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) be a groupoid in sets, and x, y, z, w ∈ R such that:
(1) (x, y), (z, w) are elements of R ×s,X,t R.
(2) c(x, y) = c(z, w).
Then:
                                    c(c(i(y), i(x)), c(z, w)) = (e ◦ s)(y) = (e ◦ s)(w).
886                                     CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


      Proof. In terms of the associated small category CR , we’re given a commutative diagram of isomorphisms
                                                             y
                                                         a       /b
                                                     w                  x
                                                        
                                                       b′        / c
                                                             z

and the assertion is y −1 x−1 (zw) = ida , which is clear.                                                        □

    E.4.2. Groupoids internal to CGWH. We now assign the notion of groupoid internal to any category.
While it will be useful to have the general concept within this appendix, we shall not need it beyond this
appendix apart from the notion of groupoids internal to the category CGWH, the large category of topological
spaces constructed in Definition E.2.2.1.

     Definition E.4.2.1. Let A be a category, and assume fibre products are representable in A . An
A -groupoid is the datum (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) with X, R objects of A , and s, t : R ⇒ X, c : R ×s,X,t R → R,
i : R → R, e : X → R morphisms in A such that the diagrams as in Definition E.4.1.1 commute. We denote
the category of A -groupoids by A -Grpd.
     A map of groupoids (X, R) → (X ′ , R′ ) is a pair of morphisms f1 : X → X ′ and f2 : R → R′ such that the
analogues of (E.4.1.8)–(E.4.1.11) commute.

    Remark E.4.2.2. We define PShv(A ) the functor category Functors(A opp , Sets) and refer to it as the
category of pre-sheaves of sets on A , following [SGA4, Exp. I, §1, Def. 1.3] and [SP, Tag 00V1]. We denote
by:
                                              h : A → PShv(A )
the functor-of-points functor (see [SP, Tag 001O]), defined by the assignment, for every object X of A :
                                           T ⇝ hX (T ) := HomA (T, X),
and we write h(f ) for the effect of h on morphisms f in A , as opposed to hf . In particular, we shall denote
by h(f )(T ) the value at the object T of A of the morphism of pre-sheaves of sets h(f ) : hX → hY , for a
morphism f : X → Y in A . We may then assign the notion of groupoid-object in A by means of analogy with
Definition E.4.1.1: a groupoid-object in A is the datum of objects X, R of A , and morphisms:
                           s, t : R ⇒ X, c : R ×s,X,t R → R, e : X → R, i : R → R
such that for every object T in A , the datum:
                           (hX (T ), hR (T ), h(s)(T ), h(t)(T ), h(c)(T ), h(e)(T ), h(i)(T ))
is a groupoid in sets in the sense of Definition E.4.1.1. Morphisms of internal A -groupoids are likewise pairs
of morphisms (f1 , f2 ) : (X, R) → (X ′ , R′ ) in A such that (h(f1 )(T ), h(f2 )(T )) is a morphism of groupoids in
sets in the sense of Definition E.4.1.1 for every object T of A .

    Definition E.4.2.3. We define the category of topological groupoids to be the category CGWH-Grpd
of Definition E.4.2.1. We shall be referring to the objects of CGWH-Grpd as topological groupoids.

    The above definition means that we are assuming that both sets of objects and morphisms of the groupoid
are compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological spaces, and that all the structure morphisms are
continuous maps. Note that CGWH does contain all fibre products, by Lemma E.2.2.5(1).

   Remark E.4.2.4. We observe that for an arbitrary subspace T ⊂ X, the subspaces s−1 (T ) and t−1 (T ) of
R may not be compactly generated. When T = {x} is a point, however, they both are, since s, t are continuous
maps between compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces, and weakly Hausdorff spaces are T1 -spaces (every
                                          E.4. TOPOLOGICAL GROUPOIDS                                             887


point is the continuous image of {∗} and thus is closed), hence T is closed, and so are s−1 (T ) and t−1 (T ).
By Lemma E.1.2.25, these subspaces are compactly generated, and they are weakly Hausdorff (as are all
subspaces). This is, more generally, the case when T is open, or locally closed, again by Lemma E.1.2.25.

    We have the following:

    Lemma E.4.2.5. Let (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) be a topological groupoid. Then:
(1) the unit map e is a closed immersion.
(2) The source and target maps s, t : R ⇒ X are submersive.

    Proof. The assertions follow from Lemma E.2.3.4, as e is a continuous section to both s, t and all
topological spaces are objects of CGWH.                                                             □

    Lemma E.4.2.6. Let (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) be a topological groupoid. Then the fibre product R ×0s,X,t R is closed
as a subspace of R × R and so belongs to CGWH coinciding with R ×s,X,t R.

    Proof. This is a special case of Lemma E.2.2.5(1), but we review the proof in this case for the reader’s
convenience. Indeed, we have, as subspaces of R ×0 R:
                                         R ×0s,X,t R = (s, t)−1 (∆X (X)).
Since X is compactly generated weakly Hausdorff, by Lemma E.2.1.6 the diagonal subspace ∆X (X) ⊂ X ×0 X
is k-closed. As (s, t) : R ×0 R → X ×0 X is continuous, the subspace R ×0s,X,t R ⊂ R ×0 R is also k-closed.
It follows that R ×0s,X,t R is a closed subspace of R × R, and as such it is compactly generated by Lemma
E.1.2.25(2), and weakly Hausdorff (as are all subspaces of R × R). In particular, R ×0s,X,t R = R ×s,X,t R, as
desired.                                                                                                    □

    Lemma E.4.2.7. Let (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) be a topological groupoid. For any x ∈ X, the subspace of R:
(E.4.2.1)                                     Rx := s−1 (x) ∩ t−1 (x)
is a compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological group, closed as a subspace of R.

    Proof. As compactly generated weakly Hausdorff spaces are T1 -spaces, Rx is T1 as a subspace of R, and
as such it is compactly generated by Lemma E.1.2.25 and weakly Hausdorff (as are all subspaces of R). Since
the group law, and the inversion homomorphisms are induced by c and i on R, they are continuous, making
Rx into a topological group.                                                                             □

    There’s an evident formal analogy between the datum of a groupoid in sets and that of an equivalence
relation on a set. We make this analogy precise:

    Remark E.4.2.8. We make the following observations:
(1) Let (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) be a groupoid in sets. Then the image of the set-function:
                                                (t, s) : R → X × X
    is an equivalence relation on X. Note the order of source and target morphisms being exchanged in the
    definition of (t, s). Conversely, given an equivalence relation R ⊂ X × X, there exists, up to isomorphism
    of groupoids in sets, a unique groupoid:
                                                 (X, R′ , s, t, c, e, i)
    such that:
    (1) j : R′ → X × X is injective.
    (2) R = j(R′ ) ⊂ X × X.
888                                     CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


    Indeed, we may set R′ := R, and s, t the compositions of the inclusion R ⊂ X × X with the two projections
    p2 , p1 : X × X → X, respectively, where p1 is the left projection, and p2 is the right projection.
(2) If (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) is a topological groupoid, then the image of (t, s) endowed with the subspace topology
    is a topological equivalence relation on X × X, and the above construction provides a method to construct
    a topological groupoid from a topological equivalence relation. We caution the reader that such relation
    may not be closed, as is typically the case when the groupoid is an action groupoid associated to the
    continuous, non-proper action of a (compactly generated weakly Hausdorff) topological group.
          Beware that the topology on the image of (t, s) is, by convention, the quotient topology and this
    may not be the subspace topology inherited from X × X; i.e., (t, s) may not be a strict map (see part
    (3) of Terminology E.0.0.2). Topological groupoids therefore generalize the assignment of topological
    equivalence relations, allowing more flexibility beyond the case of immersed equivalence relations in X × X.
    The resulting quotients therefore necessitate a more robust geometric theory than that of topological
    quotients, which leads us to the necessity of an appropriate theory of stacks, to supply the otherwise
    missing geometric objects serving as the quotients.


    E.4.2.1. Constant groupoids. The following construction and the subsequent Lemma explain how one can
view a space X as a “constant” topological groupoid.
      Construction E.4.2.9. Let X be an object in CGWH. We denote by ConstX the datum:
(E.4.2.2)                        (X, ∆(X), s = id, t = id, e = id, c = id, i = id)
where ∆(X) is the diagonal subspace within X × X. Then ConstX is a topological groupoid.
    Definition E.4.2.10. For X a compactly generated weakly Hausdorff space, we refer to ConstX as the
constant groupoid on X.
   Lemma E.4.2.11. The assignment Const defined as X ⇝ ConstX on objects of CGWH and as (f, f ) :
ConstX → ConstY on morphisms f : X → Y in CGWH, is a fully faithful functor:
(E.4.2.3)                              Const : CGWH → CGWH-Grpd.
      Proof. The set HomCGWH (X, Y ) is sent under Const onto the subset of
                                       HomCGWH-Grpd (ConstX , ConstY )
given by the pairs of maps f = (f1 : X → Y, f2 : ∆(X) → ∆(Y )) where f1 = f2 . The spaces of morphisms of
ConstX , ConstY contain the identities only, and so this subset is the entire Hom-set in CGWH-Grpd, since
the only morphisms (f, f ′ ) : ConstX → ConstY of topological groupoids must, for every x ∈ X, preserve the
identities; i.e., f ′ (e(x)) = e′ (f (x)). This forces f = f ′ , which is what we needed to show.        □


   E.4.2.2. Action groupoids. We show how to assign a topological groupoid to the datum of an action of a
compactly generated weakly Hausdorff topological group G on a compactly generated weakly Hausdorff space
X. For such G and X, we assume that G acts on X continuously via a morphism in CGWH:
(E.4.2.4)                                        a : G × X → X.
    Construction E.4.2.12. We denote by G × X ⇒ X the topological groupoid assigned by the datum
(X, R, s, t, c, e, i), where
(E.4.2.5)                                          R := G × X
and
(E.4.2.6)              s, t : R ⇒ X,    (g, x) ⇝ s(g, x) := x, (g, x) 7→ t(g, x) := a(g, x),
                                      E.5. 2-CATEGORICAL PREPARATIONS                                         889


with a : G × X → X the action map from (E.4.2.4). We further define:
(E.4.2.7)            c : R ×s,X,t R → R,    ((g, x), (g ′ , x′ )) 7→ c((x, g), (x′ , g ′ )) := (gg ′ , x′ )
and:
(E.4.2.8)                               e : X → R,       x 7→ e(x) := (1, x)

(E.4.2.9)                        i : R → R (g, x) 7→ i(g, x) := (g −1 , a(g, x)).
The datum G × X ⇒ X indeed assigns a topological groupoid in the sense of Definition E.4.2.3.


                                      E.5. 2-categorical preparations
     In this subsection we collect background material on 2-categories, up to and including the concept of
2-fibre products. We will then include some examples of interest, and explain how the category of A -groupoids
is a 2-category in a natural manner.
     2-categories were first introduced, in their “strict” form by J. Bénabou in [Be, Example (5)] and J.-M.
Maranda in [Mar, Def. 1], building in some measure on Ehresmann’s work on double categories and structured
categories ([Ehr1] and [Ehr2]). Our main references will be [Bor1, Ch. 7], [GR, Ch. 2], M. Hakim’s Ph.D.
thesis [Ha, Ch. 1], alongside [SP, Tag 003G] and [SP, Tag 003O]. Our aim is to give a self-contained treatment
of a special case of the theory of 2-categories, encompassing only basic terminology and constructions, and
including a concrete discussion of 2-fibre products in (strict) (2, 1)-categories. These will suffice for all
intended applications, insofar the category of stacks in groupoids on the topological site CGWHα,τ that was
constructed in §E.3.5 will be one example of such a (strict) (2, 1)-category, and all constructions of interest to
this appendix will be performed intrinsically within it.
     The concept of a 2-category serves the purpose of keeping track of morphisms between morphisms, a
notion that often arises when studying moduli spaces of structures equipped with non-trivial symmetries.
     We begin by describing the structures that are present within the category of all small categories, for
later axiomatizing them into the concept of a 2-category. This example will serve as guidance and will justify
the terminology that we shall be introducing accordingly afterwards. It will also enable us to construct more
examples and, most importantly, once we formally endow the category of all small categories with the structure
of a 2-category it will contain, in the appropriate 2-categorical sense, all examples of 2-categories of main
focus within this appendix. The various operations and constructions that will be discussed explicitly for it
will thereby encompass all cases of interest. In this section, functors are understood to be covariant.


    E.5.1. The category of all small categories. Main sources for the material discussed in this section
are [SP, Tag 003D] and [Bor1, Ch. 7, §7.1].
    E.5.1.1. The categories Cat and Cat∗ . We begin with a Definition:

    Definition E.5.1.1. We call Cat the category whose objects are small categories, and whose morphisms
are functors between small categories.

     The category Cat is endowed with more structure than that of an ordinary category. Namely, for any
pair of small categories A, B, and any two functors F, F ′ : A ⇒ B, we also have all natural transformations
of functors, denoted F ⇒ F ′ , and it is the purpose of this section to recall how to record such additional
structure within Cat in a robust manner.
     Before axiomatizing it into the notion of a 2-category, of which Cat will turn out to be a first example,
we describe some operations on objects, morphisms and natural transformations of functors within Cat.
890                                    CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


    E.5.1.2. Structures on the category of all small categories. For a triple of small categories A, B, C, and
functors F : A → B and G : B → C, we may compose functors to obtain the functor:
(E.5.1.1)                                        G ◦ F : A → C.
For a triple of functors between a fixed pair of small categories F, F ′ , F ′′ : A ⇒ B, we may consider natural
transformations t : F ⇒ F ′ and t′ : F ′ ⇒ F ′′ , and compose them to obtain a natural transformation which we
denote:
(E.5.1.2)                                       t′ ⊙ t : F ⇒ F ′′ .
We call ⊙ from (E.5.1.2) the vertical composition of natural transformations of functors.

      Notation E.5.1.1. We let A, B be small categories and F : A → B a functor.
       (1) We denote by 1F the identity natural transformation 1F : F ⇒ F .
       (2) We denote, for A = B, by idA the identity functor F : A → A, sending every object and morphism
           of A to itself.
In particular, for any small category A, 1idA denotes the identity natural transformation of the identity functor
on A.

    Lemma E.5.1.2. Let A, B be small categories, F, F ′ : A ⇒ B functors and t : F ⇒ F ′ a natural
transformation of functors. Then we have:
(E.5.1.3)                                     1F ⊙ t = t ⊙ 1F = t
making 1F a unit for the vertical composition ⊙ of natural transformations. Moreover, ⊙ is associative.

      Proof. For an arbitrary object a of A, we have:
                             (1F ⊙ t)a = idF (a) ◦ ta = ta = ta ◦ idF (a) = (t ⊙ 1F )a
where the innermost compositions are as morphisms in B. Associativity of ⊙ is a direct consequence of
associativity of composition of morphisms in any category.                                         □

   As a direct consequence of the definition in (E.5.1.2) and Lemma E.5.1.2, for small categories A, B we
may define:
(E.5.1.4)                                        HomCat (A, B)
to be the category of functors A → B, whose morphisms are natural transformations of functors, and whose
composition law is ⊙.

    Situation E.5.1.3. We fix a triple of small categories A, B, C and two pairs of functors F, F ′ : A ⇒ B
and G, G′ : B ⇒ C, we consider natural transformations t : F ⇒ F ′ and s : G ⇒ G′ .

      We can compose t and s from Situation E.5.1.3 as well, to obtain a natural transformation:
(E.5.1.5)                                    s ⋆ t : G ◦ F ⇒ G′ ◦ F ′ .
We shall call it horizontal composition of natural transformations of functors. Constructing s ⋆ t (mainly that
two possible definitions agree) and proving its properties is one of the main purposes of this subsection.

    Remark E.5.1.4. We recall for the reader, in the hope of motivating this endeavor, that all examples of
2-categories of interest throughout this work will be encompassed by Cat in the appropriate sense. Vertical
and horizontal compositions of natural transformations of functors will, in particular, be taking place, or at
least be computable, within Cat. The constructions contained within this subsection will therefore cover all
cases of interest.
                                       E.5. 2-CATEGORICAL PREPARATIONS                                         891


    We start with the case G = G′ and s = 1G .

    Construction E.5.1.5. Let A, B, C be a triple of small categories, and F, F ′ : A ⇒ B a pair of functors.
Let G : B → C be a functor, and t : F ⇒ F ′ a natural transformation as in Situation E.5.1.3. We call 1G ⋆ t
the natural transformation:
(E.5.1.6)                                    1G ⋆ t : G ◦ F ⇒ G ◦ F ′
defined as follows. For any object a ∈ A, we assign:
(E.5.1.7)                         (1G ⋆ t)a := G(ta ) : (G ◦ F )(a) → (G ◦ F ′ )(a)
where ta is the morphism F (a) → F ′ (a) in B induced by the natural transformation t : F ⇒ F ′ evaluated
at the object a ∈ Ob(A). One checks that 1G ⋆ t indeed is a natural transformation since for any morphism
f : a → a′ in A, the following diagram in B commutes

(E.5.1.8)                                        F (a)
                                                            ta
                                                                 / F ′ (a)

                                              F (f )                    F (f )
                                                                       
                                                F (a′ )          / F ′ (a′ )
                                                           ta′

and upon evaluating G on the (E.5.1.8), we obtain a morphism
(E.5.1.9)                             (G ◦ F )(f ) : (G ◦ F )(a) → (G ◦ F )(a′ )
exhibiting naturality of G(ta ) as a consequence of naturality of ta with respect to morphisms in A. Compatibility
with compositions of morphisms in A is a consequence of both naturality of t and functoriality of F and G.

    The following is straightforward.

   Lemma E.5.1.6. Let A, B, C be a triple of small categories, and F, F ′ , F ′ a triple of functors from A to
B. Let G : B → C be a functor, and t : F ⇒ F ′ , t′ : F ′ ⇒ F ′′ natural transformations. We have:
(E.5.1.10)                   1G ⋆ 1F = 1G◦F , (1G ⋆ t′ ) ⊙ (1G ⋆ t) = 1G ⋆ (t′ ⊙ t)
and:
(E.5.1.11)                                             1idA ⋆ t = t
In particular, the assignment:
                                 G∗ := G ◦ (·) : HomCat (A, B) → HomCat (A, C)
is a functor.

   Within Situation E.5.1.3, we now construct horizontal compositions of natural transformations in the case
F = F ′ , t = 1F and s is an arbitrary natural transformation s : G ⇒ G′ .

    Construction E.5.1.7. Let A, B, C be a triple of small categories, and F : A → B a functor. Let
G, G′ : B ⇒ C be a pair of functors, and s : G ⇒ G′ a natural transformation. We call s ⋆ 1F the natural
transformation:
(E.5.1.12)                                   s ⋆ 1F : G ◦ F ⇒ G′ ◦ F
defined as follows. For any object a ∈ A, we assign:
(E.5.1.13)                        (s ⋆ 1F )a := sF (a) : (G ◦ F )(a) → (G ◦ F ′ )(a)
892                                     CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


where sF (a) is the morphism (G ◦ F )(a) → (G′ ◦ F )(a) in C induced by the natural transformation s : G ⇒ G′ .
To check that s ⋆ 1F indeed is a natural transformation, we observe that sF (a) is natural with respect to
morphisms on a by functoriality of F and naturality of s.
     Lemma E.5.1.8. Let A, B, C be a triple of small categories, and F : A → B a functor. Let G, G′ , G′′ a
triple of functors from B to C, and s : G ⇒ G′ , s′ : G′ ⇒ G′′ natural transformations. We have:
(E.5.1.14)                              (s′ ⋆ 1F ) ⊙ (s ⋆ 1F ) = (s′ ⊙ s) ⋆ 1F
and:
(E.5.1.15)                                          s ⋆ 1idB = s
In particular, the assignment:
                                 F ∗ := (·) ◦ F : HomCat (B, C) → HomCat (A, C)
is a functor.
    Proof. To check all the identities, it is enough to evaluate them on an arbitrary object a of A, respectively
an arbitrary object b of B, as the reader may carry out.                                                       □
      We further note that these constructions are compatible with one another in the following sense:
      Lemma E.5.1.9. We have:
(E.5.1.16)                                  1G1 ⋆ (1G2 ⋆ t) = 1G1 ◦G2 ⋆ t
for any natural transformation of functors t : F ⇒ F ′ : A → B, and functors G2 : B → C and G1 : C → D.
We further have:
(E.5.1.17)                                  (s ⋆ 1F1 ) ⋆ 1F2 = s ⋆ 1F1 ◦F2
for any natural transformation of functors s : G ⇒ G′ : C → D and functors F2 : A → B and F1 : B → C.
Moreover, for any natural transformation of functors s : G ⇒ G′ : B → C, and any functors F : A → B and
H : C → D, we have:
(E.5.1.18)                                1H ⋆ (s ⋆ 1F ) = (1H ⋆ s) ⋆ 1F .
    Proof. The result is obtained analogously to Lemma E.5.1.6 and Lemma E.5.1.8, by evaluating all
natural transformations on objects and deducing the desired identities from the definitions alone, using
functoriality of the component functors and naturality of the component natural transformations.       □
      We have the following:
     Lemma E.5.1.10. We let F, F ′ : A ⇒ B and G, G′ : B ⇒ C be functors between small categories, and let
t : F ⇒ F ′ and s : G ⇒ G′ be natural transformations of functors. Then the following identity of natural
transformations of functors A → C holds:
(E.5.1.19)                          (1G′ ⋆ t) ⊙ (s ⋆ 1F ) = (s ⋆ 1F ′ ) ⊙ (1G ⋆ t).
    This result is obtained analogously to Lemma E.5.1.6 and Lemma E.5.1.8, by evaluating all natural
transformations on objects and deducing the desired identities from the definitions alone, using functoriality
of the component functors and naturality of the component natural transformations. We further refer the
reader to [SP, Tag 003D].
    Definition E.5.1.11. For t : F ⇒ F ′ and s : G ⇒ G′ two natural transformations of the functors
F, F ′ : A ⇒ B and G, G′ : B ⇒ C, define
(E.5.1.20)                        s ⋆ t := (1G′ ⋆ t) ⊙ (s ⋆ 1F ) : G ◦ F ⇒ G′ ◦ F ′ .
                                          E.5. 2-CATEGORICAL PREPARATIONS                                                893


   In light of Lemma E.5.1.10, the construction of s ⋆ t is well-posed. This is the alternate notion of
composition for natural transformations of functors promised in (E.5.1.5), which we shall refer to as horizontal
composition.
   We now establish properties of the two composition laws ⋆ and ⊙ on natural transformations.

    Lemma E.5.1.12. The composition ⋆ is associative, and for every small category A, the identity natural
transformation 1idA of the identity functor is a unit for both ⊙ and ⋆.

    Proof. We let A, B, C, D be four small categories, and F, F ′ : A ⇒ B, G, G′ : B ⇒ C, H, H ′ : C ⇒ D
three pairs of functors. We let t : F ⇒ F ′ , s : G ⇒ G′ and r : H ⇒ H ′ be three natural transformations of
functors. For an arbitrary object a of A, we have:
                           ((r ⋆ s) ⋆ t)a = ((1H ′ ◦G′ ⋆ t) ⊙ ((r ⋆ s) ⋆ 1F ))a
                                         = ((1H ′ ◦G′ ⋆ t) ⊙ (((1H ′ ⋆ s) ⊙ (r ⋆ 1G )) ⋆ 1F ))a
                                         = (1H ′ ◦G′ ⋆ t)a ◦ ((1H ′ ⋆ s) ⊙ (r ⋆ 1G ))F (a)
                                         = H ′ (G′ (ta )) ◦ H ′ (sF (a) ) ◦ rG(F (a)) .
We also have:
                                 (r ⋆ (s ⋆ t))a = ((1H ′ ⋆ (s ⋆ t)) ⊙ (r ⋆ 1G◦F ))a
                                               = H ′ ((s ⋆ t)a ) ◦ rG(F (a))
                                               = H ′ ((1G′ ⋆ t)a ◦ (s ⋆ 1F )a ) ◦ rG(F (a))
                                               = H ′ (G′ (ta )) ◦ H ′ (sF (a) ) ◦ rG(F (a)) .
We deduce that (r ⋆ s) ⋆ t = r ⋆ (s ⋆ t). For every small category A, the identity natural transformation of the
identity functor 1idA is a unit for both ⊙ by Lemma E.5.1.2 applied to F = 1idA , and for ⋆ by (E.5.1.11) from
Lemma E.5.1.6 and (E.5.1.15) from Lemma E.5.1.8.                                                              □

    Lemma E.5.1.13. Let A, B, C be three small categories, and consider triples of functors F, F ′ , F ′′ from A
to B and G, G′ , G′′ from B to C equipped with natural transformations t : F ⇒ F ′ , t′ : F ′ ⇒ F ′′ , s : G ⇒ G′ ,
and s′ : G′ ⇒ G′′ . Then we have:
(E.5.1.21)                               (s′ ⊙ s) ⋆ (t′ ⊙ t) = (s′ ⋆ t′ ) ⊙ (s ⋆ t).

    Proof. For any object a of A, we have:
             ((1G′′ ⋆ (t′ ⊙ t)) ⊙ ((s′ ⊙ s) ⋆ 1F ))a = (1G′′ ⋆ (t′ ⊙ t))a ◦ ((s′ ⊙ s) ⋆ 1F )a
                                                     = G′′ (t′a ◦ ta ) ◦ (s′F (a) ◦ sF (a) )
                                                     = G′′ (t′a ) ◦ G′′ (ta ) ◦ s′F (a) ◦ sF (a)
                                                     = ((1G′′ ⋆ t′ ) ⊙ (1G′′ ⋆ t) ⊙ (s′ ⋆ 1F ) ⊙ (s ⋆ 1F ))a
                                                     = ((1G′′ ⋆ t′ ) ⊙ ((s′ ⋆ 1F ′ ) ⊙ (1G′ ⋆ t)) ⊙ (s ⋆ 1F ))a
and by Lemma E.5.1.2 on associativity of ⊙, we deduce:
       (1G′′ ⋆ t′ ) ⊙ ((s′ ⋆ 1F ′ ) ⊙ (1G′ ⋆ t)) ⊙ (s ⋆ 1F ) = ((1G′′ ⋆ t′ )) ⊙ (s′ ⋆ 1F ′ ) ⊙ ((1G′ ⋆ t) ⊙ (s ⋆ 1F ))
                                                             = (s′ ⋆ t′ ) ⊙ (s ⋆ t).
                                                                                                                          □

    Lemma E.5.1.14. Let A, B, C be small categories. Then the assignment:
(E.5.1.22)              cA,B,C (·, ·) := (◦, ⋆) : HomCat (A, B) × HomCat (B, C) → HomCat (A, C)
894                                           CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


defined as the composition of functors from (E.5.1.1) on objects, and the horizontal composition of natural
transformations from (E.5.1.20) on morphisms, is a functor. Moreover, we have the following identities:
       (1) For small categories A, B, functors F, F ′ : A ⇒ B, and a natural transformation t : F ⇒ F ′ , we
           have:
            (a) cA,A,B (idA , F ) = cA,B,B (F, idB ) = F .
            (b) cA,A,B (1idA , t) = cA,B,B (t, 1idB ) = t.
       (2) For small categories A, B, C, D, functors F, F ′ : A ⇒ B, G, G′ : B ⇒ C, H, H ′ : C ⇒ D, and
           natural transformations t : F ⇒ F ′ , s : G ⇒ G′ , r : H ⇒ H ′ , we have:
            (a) cA,B,D (cA,B,C (F, G), H) = cA,B,D (F, cB,C,D (G, H)).
            (b) cA,B,C (cA,B,C (t, s), r) = cA,B,D (t, cB,C,D (s, r)).
   We recall that the product HomCat (A, B) × HomCat (B, C) is the product of two small categories (see
[SP, Tag 001K]). We further refer the reader to [SP, Tag 003F].
   Proof. This is a direct consequence of Lemma E.5.1.12, which can be applied by Lemma E.5.1.13.
Explicitly, we let (F, G), (F ′ , G′ ) and (F ′′ , G′′ ) be three objects in the product category:
                                               HomCat (A, B) × HomCat (B, C)
and t : F ⇒ F ′ , s : G ⇒ G′ , t′ : F ′ ⇒ F ′′ , s′ : G′ ⇒ G′′ natural transformations of functors defining
morphisms (t, s) and (t′ , s′ ) in the product category. Then
                     (◦, ⋆)(F, G) = G ◦ F, (◦, ⋆)(F ′ , G′ ) = G′ ◦ F ′ , (◦, ⋆)(F ′′ , G′′ ) = G′′ ◦ F ′′
on objects, and
                                           (◦, ⋆)(t, s) = s ⋆ t, (◦, ⋆)(t′ , s′ ) = s′ ⋆ t′
on morphisms.
   We are to check, upon denoting by □ the composition of morphisms in the product category:
                                    (◦, ⋆)((t′ , s′ )□(t, s)) = ((◦, ⋆)(t′ , s′ )) ⋆ ((◦, ⋆)(t, s)).
Since we have (t′ , s′ )□(t, s) = (t′ ⊙ t, s′ ⊙ s), we deduce the identity of morphisms in HomCat (A, C):
                                       ((◦, ⋆)(t′ , s′ )) ⋆ ((◦, ⋆)(t, s)) = (s′ ⋆ t′ ) ⊙ (s ⋆ t)
and we have (s′ ⊙ s) ⋆ (t′ ⊙ t) = (s′ ⋆ t′ ) ⊙ (s ⋆ t) from Lemma E.5.1.13, which is what we needed to show. The
desired identities are a reformulation of (E.5.1.11) from Lemma E.5.1.6 and of (E.5.1.15) from Lemma E.5.1.8,
for part (b) of (1), and of Lemma E.5.1.12 for part (b) of (2). Parts (a) of (1) and of (2) is a consequence of
the fact that on objects, c•,•,• is defined via composition of functors between small categories.             □
     E.5.1.3. Effective small categories. We now revisit the category Cat under a different perspective, which
will be of use throughout and will give us the opportunity to make examples. We begin with a definition:
     Definition E.5.1.15. Call Cat∗ the category whose objects are 6-tuples (X, A, s, t, c, e) as for groupoids
in sets in Definition E.4.1.1 but without the inversion axioms (this is why we write “A” instead of “R”), and
likewise for morphisms.18 A functor between objects in Cat∗ is a map between such 6-tuples as in (E.4.1.7)
but without the inversion aspect.
    Objects in Cat∗ are called effective small categories. There is an evident analogy between Cat∗ and the
category Cat from §E.5.1.1. We define the analog of natural transformations of functors:
      Definition E.5.1.16. Let (X, A, s, t, c, e) and (X ′ , A′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ ) be in Cat∗ and
                           F := (f, g), F ′ := (f ′ , g ′ ) : (X, A, s, t, c, e) → (X ′ , A′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ )
18Previously had not included compatibility with e’s, which was surely an oversight.
                                                    E.5. 2-CATEGORICAL PREPARATIONS                                                           895


two functors.
    We define a natural transformation t : F ⇒ F ′ to be a set-function:
(E.5.1.23)                                                            T : X → A′
such that for all x ∈ X we have T (x) : f (x) → f (x′ ) and for every a : x → y the diagram
                                                                            g(a)
(E.5.1.24)                                                        f (x)              / f (y)

                                                              T (x)                        T (y)
                                                                                           
                                                                 f ′ (x)             / f ′ (y)
                                                                           g ′ (a)

commutes.

     As for the category Cat, we highlight here additional structures that the category Cat∗ is equipped with.

     Construction E.5.1.17. Let (X, A, s, t, c, e), (X ′ , A′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ ) and (X ′′ , A′′ , s′′ , t′′ , c′′ , e′′ ) be three
effective small categories.

      Remark E.5.1.20. On the categories Cat and Cat∗ , we make the following remarks.
       (1) Both Cat and Cat∗ have a final object. It is given, for Cat, by the small category with only one
           object, which we denote •, whose only morphism is the identity, which we denote e• , and for Cat∗
           by the datum (X, A, s, t, c, e) with X = {1}, A = X, s = t = id, c : A ×s,X,t A = A the unique
           morphism, e : X → A the identity. In both cases, we denote the final object by 1.
       (2) Throughout the next section we shall use the two examples of Cat and Cat∗ as the archetypal
           example of a 2-category. We shall be proving that, according to the appropriate notion of equivalence
           of 2-categories, they are equivalent (in fact, isomorphic) as 2-categories, and they may therefore be
           thought of as the same, for all practical purposes. This will provide us with a rigorous dictionary to
           turn results on groupoids and topological groupoids into assertions about small categories, functors
           and natural transformations, while at the same time enabling us to construct more examples.
               Most importantly, all 2-categories of interest throughout this appendix will be contained as
           sub 2-categories of Cat, whether directly in its category of small categories incarnation, or as sub
           2-categories of Cat∗ . In particular, the reader may think of the operations occurring denoted ◦, ⊙, ⋆
           occurring throughout this appendix as being exactly those constructed explicitly in this subsection.

     E.5.2. 2-categories. We discuss here the basic definitions. We refer the reader to [Bor1, Ch.7], [GR,
Ch.2], [Ha, Ch.I,§1], and [SP, Tag 003H], for the corresponding subjects within the sources. We will closely
follow the former two, while for the most part adopting the notation in use in the latter two. The main
difference between this subsection and the referred sources is that we allow the objects of our 2-categories
to be elements of proper classes. We reserve the terminology small 2-category to refer to those 2-categories
whose objects form a set. Our envisioned examples are: groupoids internal to the large category CGWH,
the 2-category Groupoids of all groupoids in sets introduced in Definition E.4.1.1 (see part (3) of [SP, Tag
003J]) and the 2-category of stacks in groupoids on a site. Large categories will have a limited role throughout,
but we shall need the language to speak of 2-functors and 2-fibre products within some.
     E.5.2.1. Basic notions on 2-categories.

      Definition E.5.2.1. A 2-category C is the datum of:
       (1) A class of objects Ob(C).
       (2) For each pair of objects (A, B) ∈ Ob(C) × Ob(C), a small category HomC (A, B).
                                             E.5. 2-CATEGORICAL PREPARATIONS                                          899


           (a) We call 1-morphisms the objects of HomC (A, B), denoted f : A → B.
          (b) We call 2-morphisms the morphisms of HomC (A, B), denoted α : f ⇒ g, for two objects
               f, g : A ⇒ B.
           (c) For two 2-morphisms α : f ⇒ g and β : g ⇒ h, we write β ⊙ α for their composition. We call
               vertical composition the operation ⊙.
      (3) For each triple of objects A, B, C ∈ Ob(C), a composition bifunctor:
                              cA,B,C : HomC (A, B) × HomC (B, C) → HomC (A, C).
          Given 1-morphisms f : A → B and g : B → C, and 2-morphisms α : f ⇒ g and β : g ⇒ h, we write:
           (a) g ◦ f for cA,B,C (f, g) : A → C.
          (b) β ⋆ α for cA,B,C (α, β) : f ⇒ h.
      (4) For every object A ∈ Ob(C), a unit functor:19
                                                   uA : 1 → HomC (A, A)
            where 1 denotes the final object of Cat (see Remark E.5.1.20).
The bifunctors cA,B,C and the functor uA are assumed to satisfy the following axioms:
      (1) (Unit Axiom) The following diagram is commutative:
(E.5.2.1)
           1 × HomC (A, B) o                  HomC (A, B)                                     / HomC (A, B) × 1

              (uA ,id)                                                                                    (id,uA )
                                                                                                     
     HomC (A, A) × HomC (A, B)                         / HomC (A, B) o                   HomC (A, B) × HomC (B, B)
                                              cA,A,B                          cA,B,B

          where the top horizontal arrows are equivalences of categories, and where id denotes, within (E.5.2.1),
          the identity functor.
      (2) (Associativity of Compositions Axiom) The following diagram is commutative:
                                                                         (id,cB,C,D )
(E.5.2.2)       HomC (A, B) × HomC (B, C) × HomC (C, D)                                 / HomC (A, B) × HomC (B, D)

                              (cA,B,C ,id)                                                               cA,B,D
                                                                                                    
                         HomC (A, C) × HomC (C, D)                                             / HomC (A, D)
                                                                            cA,C,D

where id denotes, within (E.5.2.2), the identity functor. We say a 2-category is small if the class Ob(C) is a
set.

    Remark E.5.2.2. We make the following observations:
      (1) The functors HomC (A, B) → HomC (A, B) × 1 on the top row of (E.5.2.1) are defined by sending
          an object f ∈ Ob(HomC (A, B)) to (f, •) ∈ HomC (A, B) × 1, and likewise sending a morphism
          α : f ⇒ g to (α, e• ).
      (2) The functor uA is equivalent to the datum of a distinguished object •A ∈ Ob(HomC (A, A)), together
          with its identity, which we denote eA : •A → •A . See also [GR, Ch. 2, §2.1, p. 71].
      (3) In light of (1) above, we may rephrase the Unit Axiom in the above Definition E.5.2.1 as follows.
          For each triple of objects A, B, C ∈ Ob(C), we have, for any 1-morphisms f, f ′ ∈ Ob(HomC (A, B))
          and every 2-morphism α : f ⇒ f ′ :
                                             cA,A,B (•A , f ) = cA,B,B (f, •B ) = f

19Do we need to axiomatize that u (·) : A → A is an isomorphism, or is this automatic?
                                 A
900                                      CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


           and:
                                        cA,A,B (eA , α) = cA,B,B (α, eB ) = α.
           We note that we are not assuming •A and •B to be the identity functors of A and B respectively,
           although this will be the case in all situations of interest throughout this work (since this is indeed
           the case for Cat and Cat∗ ).
       (4) In light of (1) above, we may rephrase the Associativity of Compositions Axiom in the above
           Definition E.5.2.1 as follows. For every quadruple of objects A, B, C, D ∈ Ob(C), and every f, f ′ ∈
           Ob(HomC (A, B)), g, g ′ ∈ Ob(HomC (B, C)) and h, h′ ∈ Ob(HomC (C, D)), we have:
                                 cA,B,D (cA,B,C (f, g), h) = cA,B,D (f, cB,C,D (g, h))
           and for every 2-morphisms α : f ⇒ f ′ , β : g ⇒ and γ : h ⇒ h′ , we have:
                                cA,B,D (cA,B,C (α, β), γ) = cA,B,D (α, cB,C,D (β, γ)).
       (5) Definition E.5.2.1 above is [Bor1, Ch. 7,Def. 7.1.1]. It is also the Definition introduced in [GR, Ch. 2,
           §2.1], with one difference. We are allowing Ob(C) to be a proper class, as opposed to a set. None
           of the arguments in loc.cit. for the results that we require are affected by this additional amount
           of generality. We shall in any event recall the required arguments here, exhibiting explicitly that
           this is indeed the case. We shall follow [GR, Ch.2§2.1] to treat pseudo-functors, and we shall then
           specialize to the case of strict (2, 1)-categories only, with the aim of constructing two types of 2-fibre
           products in strict (2, 1)-categories.
       (6) In light of parts (1), (2), and (3) of this Remark, small 2-categories in the sense of Definition E.5.2.1
           agree with 2-categories as defined in [Ha, Ch. I, §1].
       (7) For a pair of objects A, B ∈ Ob(C), we think of the objects of HomC (A, B) as arrows f : A → B,
           and are occasionally also referred to as 1-cells in the literature, such as in [Bor1, Ch.7] and [GR,
           Ch.2]. For two 1-morphisms f, g ∈ Ob(HomC (A, B)), morphisms f ⇒ g are also referred to as 2-cells
           in the literature, as done in [Bor1, Ch. 7] and [GR, Ch. 2]. Our preferred choice of terminology
           follows [Ha, Ch. I, §1, (1.3)], where it is referred back to Bénabou’s paper [Be], and it is also the
           terminology from [SP, Tags 003G, 003O, 02XG] and [SP, Tags 02XP, 02XQ].

     E.5.2.2. Basic notions on 1-morphisms. Throughout this subsection, we fix a 2-category C.
     We now define when two objects of a 2-category are “equivalent”, respectively “isomorphic”, and what it
means for 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms to be “invertible”. The definition below is [Bor1, Def.7.1.2], and it
is directly analogous to the concept defined right after [Ha, Ch.I,(1.3.3)], [SP, Tag 003L], and [GR, Ch.2,
Def.2.1.3].

      Definition E.5.2.3. Let C be a 2-category, and A, B ∈ Ob(C) be objects, and f : A → B a 1-morphism.
       (1) We say that f is an equivalence, or essentially invertible, if and only if there exist two 1-morphisms
           g, h : B ⇒ A, and two 2-isomorphisms:
                                          α : •A ⇒ g ◦ f, β : f ◦ h ⇒ •B .
       (2) We say that f is an isomorphism if and only if there exist two 1-morphisms g, h : B ⇒ A such that
           the elements •A and g ◦ f of the set Ob(HomC (A, A)) are the same element, and the elements •B
           and f ◦ h of the set Ob(HomC (B, B)) are the same element. In this case, we define α and β to be
           the identities.
       (3) We say that a 1-morphism g : B → A is right-adjoint to f : A → B if and only if there exists
           2-morphisms ϵ : f ◦ g ⇒ •B and η : •A ⇒ g ◦ f such that the following triangular identities hold:
                                (1g ⋆ ϵ) ⊙ (η ⋆ 1g ) = 1g ,   (ϵ ⋆ 1f ) ⊙ (1f ⋆ η) = 1f .
                                     E.5. 2-CATEGORICAL PREPARATIONS                                         901


         We also say that f is left-adjoint to g, and call ϵ the unit and η the co-unit of the adjunction (f, g).
     (4) For a 1-morphism g : A → B, a 2-morphism α : f ⇒ g is invertible if and only if it is an isomorphism
         in the category HomC (A, B). We call an invertible 2-morphism a 2-isomorphism.

     We now introduce terminology to define what it means for a diagram to commute in C, or commute up to
2-isomorphisms.

     Definition E.5.2.4. Let A, B, C, D ∈ Ob(C) be objects, and f : A → B, g : B → C, h : A → D,
k : D → C, 1-morphisms. We consider the following (possibly non-commutative) diagram:
                                                          f
(E.5.2.3)                                         A                /B

                                                 h                       g
                                                                    
                                                  D                /C
                                                          k

(1) For objects A, B ∈ Ob(C), 1-morphisms f, f ′ : A ⇒ B, and a 2-morphism α : f ⇒ f ′ , we write:
                                                          f

                                                  A        α8B

    to denote the cumulative datum of ((A, B), (f, f ′ ), α).
(2) We say that (E.5.2.3) is oriented if and only if there exists a 2-morphism α : g ◦ f ⇒ k ◦ h. In this case,
    we say that the diagram (E.5.2.3) is oriented by α. We also call α the orientation of the diagram.
(3) We say that (E.5.2.3) is commutative if and only if g ◦ f = k ◦ h as objects of HomC (A, C). As a
    consequence, commutative diagrams are oriented (by the identity on g ◦ f = k ◦ h).
(4) We say (E.5.2.3) is 2-commutative if and only if it is oriented by a 2-morphism α : g ◦ f ⇒ k ◦ h, and α is

    Remark E.5.2.5. We note that [GR, Ch. 2, Rem. 2.1.4] applies to our Definition E.5.2.3 as well, despite
our assumption that the objects of C be allowed to be a class, as opposed to a set. In particular, we have:
     (1) If a 1-morphism f : A → B in C is an equivalence in the sense of part (1) of Definition E.5.2.3, then
         we can choose g = h in part (1) of Definition E.5.2.3. The argument to see this is identical to [GR,
         Ch.2,Rem.2.1.4,(i)], because the objects A, B are fixed, and HomC (A, B) is a small category.
     (2) For f : A → B and g : B → C equivalences in C, the composition g ◦ f : A → C is also an equivalence.
         The argument to see this is identical to [GR, Ch.2,Rem.2.1.4(ii)].
     (3) Let f, g : A ⇒ B be 1-morphisms, and α : f ⇒ g a 2-isomorphism. Then f is an equivalence if and
         only if g is. In other words, the notion of equivalence introduced on 1-morphisms of C in part (3) of
         Definition E.5.2.3 propagates along 2-isomorphisms between 1-morphisms. The argument to see this
         is identical to [GR, Ch.2,Rem.2.1.4,(iii)].
     (4) Suppose (f, g) is an adjunction, with f : A → B and g : B → A two 1-morphisms. Let g ′ : B → A
         be another right-adjoint for f . Then g and g ′ are 2-isomorphic, i.e. there exists a 2-isomorphism
         α : g ⇒ g ′ . The argument to see this is identical to the argument in [GR, Ch.2,Rem.2.1.4(v)].
902                                    CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


      (5) Suppose (f, g) is an adjunction, with f : A → B and g : B → A two 1-morphisms. Let α : f ⇒ f ′
          and β : g ⇒ g ′ be 2-isomorphisms. Then (f ′ , g ′ ) is also an adjunction. The argument to see this is
          identical to that in [GR, Ch. 2, Rem. 2.1.4(iv)].

    E.5.2.3. 2-categories and ordinary categories. We first describe a construction to associate an ordinary
category to a 2-category:

    Construction E.5.2.6. We let C be a 2-category. We define Cat(C) to be the locally small category
whose objects are the objects of C, Ob(C), and whose morphisms are the 1-morphisms of C. Composition of
morphisms in Cat(C) is defined to be the composition of 1-morphisms of C via the functor c•,•,• of part (3) of
Definition E.5.2.1.

    We now discuss a construction to associate a 2-category to an ordinary category. This will enable us
to “view” ordinary categories as a special instance of 2-categories, and will give us access to the concept of
pre-sheaves on an ordinary category, valued in a 2-category.

    Construction E.5.2.7. We let C be a locally small category. We define 2-Cat(C) to be the 2-category
assigned as follows.
      (1) We define:
(E.5.2.4)                                    Ob(2-Cat(C)) := Ob(C)
          which is to say that the objects of 2-Cat(C) are the objects of C.
      (2) For any pair of objects A, B ∈ Ob(2-Cat(C)), we define the category Hom2-Cat(C) (A, B) as follows:
           (a) we define:
(E.5.2.5)                           Ob(Hom2-Cat(C) (A, B)) := HomC (A, B)
               which is to say that the objects of Hom2-Cat(C) (A, B) are the elements of the Hom-set
               HomC (A, B) of C.
           (b) We define, for any f, g ∈ Ob(Hom2-Cat(C) (A, B)) the set HomHom2-Cat(C) (f, g) to be the single-
               ton set if f = g as elements of HomC (A, B), and the empty set otherwise. We denote by 1f the
               only element of HomHom2-Cat(C) (f, f ).
          This is to say that the objects of 2-Cat(C) are defined to be exactly the objects of C, the 1-morphisms
          of 2-Cat(C) are defined to be the morphisms of C, and the 2-morphisms of 2-Cat(C) are defined to
          be all and only the identities on the 1-morphisms.
      (3) We define, for any triple of objects A, B, C ∈ Ob(2-Cat(C)):
(E.5.2.6)           cA,B,C : Hom2-Cat(C) (A, B) × Hom2-Cat(C) (B, C) → Hom2-Cat(C) (A, C)
            as follows:

(E.5.2.7)                                     cA,B,C (f, g) := g ◦ f
               where g ◦ f is the composition of f and g as morphisms of C.

               we define cA,B,C (α, β) to be cA,B,C (α, β) := 1g◦f if f = f ′ and g = g ′ .
          To see that the assignment in part (b) of (3) is well-defined, we observe that for f ̸= f ′ or g ̸= g ′ ,
          cA,B,C is not defined since either there is no 2-morphism f ⇒ f ′ or there is no 2-morphism g ⇒ g ′ .
      (4) For every object A ∈ Ob(2-Cat(C)), we set:
                                          uA : 1 → Hom2-Cat(C) (A, A)

            by defining, having Ob(1) = {•} and Hom1 (•, •) = {e• } (see part (1) of Remark E.5.1.20 and part
            (2) of Remark E.5.2.2), uA (•) := idA , the identity map on the object A of C, and uA (e• ) := 1idA :
            idA → idA , the identity on idA .

We now check that the above assignments indeed satisfy the axioms from Definition E.5.2.1. For the Unit
Axiom (Axiom (1) from Definition E.5.2.1), we have, for every triple of objects A, B, C ∈ Ob(2-Cat(C)) and
f ∈ Ob(Hom2-Cat(C) (A, B)):
                                 cA,A,B (1idA , f ) = f = cA,B,B (f, 1idB )
and the same axiom on 2-morphisms is indeed satisfied as the relevant Hom-sets are either empty, in which
case the assertion is vacuously true, or contain only the identity endomorphism 1idA . Finally, the Associativity
Axiom (Axiom (2) from Definition E.5.2.1) is satisfied as composition of morphisms in C is associative, as C is
a category. We deduce that 2-Cat(C) is a 2-category in the sense of Definition E.5.2.1.


     E.5.3. Pseudo-functors. The purpose of this subsection is that of providing the language that is
necessary to define sub 2-categories and their properties relative to an “ambient” 2-category. All the examples
of 2-categories throughout this appendix will be constructed as sub 2-categories of the 2-category Cat of
all small categories (see §E.5.1). We will be returning to the examples of Cat and its variant Cat∗ from
Definition E.5.1.15 after we collect the basic concepts around functors between 2-categories.

    We illustrate the meaning of the two axioms from Definition E.5.3.1 above. Let f : A → B and g : B → C
be two 1-morphisms. Then we may evaluate FA,B and FB,C on each, and then compose. We obtain:
                              cF (A),F (B),F (C) (FA,B (f ), FB,C (g)) = FB,C (g) ◦ FA,B (f )
according to the notation introduced in Terminology E.5.2.4. We may also first compose to obtain cA,B,C (f, g),
and then evaluate FA,C on the result, to get FA,C (g ◦ f ). γA,B,C (f, g) is a 2-isomorphism between the two
1-morphisms FB,C (g) ◦ FA,B (f ) and FA,C (g ◦ f ). Specifically, we have the 2-isomorphism:
                                    γA,B,C (f, g) : FB,C (g) ◦ FA,B (f ) ⇒ FA,C (g ◦ f )
naturally in f, g.

    Example E.5.3.2. In the case of Construction E.5.2.6, to a pseudo-functor between 2-categories F : C → C′ ,
we associate the functor Cat(F ) : Cat(C) → Cat(C′ ) given by the class function Ob(C) → Ob(C′ ) induced by F
on objects, and by the effect of F on 1-morphisms prescribed by part (2) of Definition E.5.3.1, on morphisms
of Cat(C) and Cat(C′ ), respectively.

    Example E.5.3.3. In the special case of Construction E.5.2.7, we have an ordinary (locally small) category
C, and its associated 2-category 2-Cat(C). Let F : C → D be a functor between ordinary (locally small)
categories. We may associate to it the datum (F, F•,• , γ•,•,• , δ• ) of a pseudo-functor 2-Cat(C) → 2-Cat(D)
as per Definition E.5.3.1, by defining the class function F on objects to be the same class function from the
objects of C to the objects of D, and for any pair of objects A, B ∈ Ob(2-Cat(C)):
                             FA,B : Hom2-Cat(C) (A, B) → Hom2-Cat(D) (F (A), F (B))
                                           E.5. 2-CATEGORICAL PREPARATIONS                                            905


is defined on objects to be the effect of F on morphisms of C, and on morphisms to be the unique assignment
sending the identities to the identities. In this case, γA,B,C and δA are the identity for all A, B, C objects of
2-Cat(C).
     The Unit Axiom from Definition E.5.3.1 encodes the correct behavior of the datum (F, F•,• , γ•,•,• , δ• )
with respect to passage from 1F (A) to FA,A (1A ). Namely, we are not assuming that pseudo-functors preserve
the identities, i.e. 1F (A) and FA,A (1A ) may not be equal as elements of the set of objects of the category
HomC (F (A), F (A)), but they are isomorphic, and the axiom defines a notion of naturality for this isomorphism,
codifying the compatibility of a pseudo-functor with it.
     We first note that the composition of the leftmost vertical arrow followed by the bottom horizontal arrow
in (E.5.3.3) is always a 2-isomorphism. This is due to the fact that in light of the Unit Axiom in the very
definition of a 2-category, i.e. Axiom (1) from Definition E.5.2.1.20
     Specifically, for any 1-morphism f : A → B, the composition FA,B (f ) ◦ 1F (A) is FA,B (f ), which in turn can
be written as FA,B (f ◦ 1A ). “Writing FA,B (f ) as FA,B (f ◦ 1A )”, and likewise “writing 1B ◦ FA,B (f ) as FA,B (f )”,
involves passage from one to the other via the composition bifunctor, which by Axiom (2) from Definition
E.5.2.1 satisfies cF (A),F (A),F (B) (1F (A) , FA,B (f )) = FA,B (f ), and hence FA,B (cA,A,B (1A , f )) = FA,B (f ). This
is the reason why we write 1FA,B (f ) for the canonical 2-(iso)morphisms placed as the leftmost vertical arrow
and the bottom horizontal arrow in (E.5.3.3) and (E.5.3.4).
     Axiom (1) in Definition E.5.3.1 compares the canonical 2-isomorphism FA,B ◦ 1F (A) ⇒ FA,B (f ◦ 1A )
obtained by composition of the two 1FA,B (f ) as discussed above, to the 2-morphism obtained instead by using
(δA )∗ : 1F (A) ⇒ FA,A (1A ) to replace 1F (A) in FA,B (f ) ◦ 1F (A) with FA,A (1A ), for then passing to FA,B (f ◦ 1A )
using γA,A,B (1A , f ). The first operation is a 2-isomorphism FA,B (f ) ◦ 1F (A) ⇒ FA,B (f ) ◦ FA,A (1A ), given
by 1FA,B (f ) ⋆ (δA )∗ . The content of the axiom is that the two compositions, namely FA,B (f ) ◦ 1F (A) and
FA,B (f ◦ 1A ), are 2-isomorphic.
     As for the Axiom on Associativity of Compositions, it similarly encodes that the two possible results of
grouping compositions together in a triple composition are 2-isomorphic.
    Notation E.5.3.1. We introduce the following notation:
      (1) We denote, for any (f, g) ∈ Ob(HomC (A, B)) × Ob(HomC (B, C)), the “(f, g)-section” γA,B,C (f, g)

          by γf,g , omitting A, B, C from the notation when no confusion is expected to arise.
      (2) We denote, for any 1-morphism f : A → B, by F (f ) the 1-morphism FA,B (f ) : F (A) → F (B).
     Remark E.5.3.4. We make the following observations on Definition E.5.3.1. In the special case when

    Remark E.5.3.5. We let I be a locally small category, and now describe the pseudo-functors from 2-Cat(I),

                                                1F (f ) ⋆ δx = γf,1x

    If we rename γ•,•  as α•,• and ⊙ as ◦ (and we therefore reverse the order of all compositions), we recover

      E.5.3.2. Degrees of faithfulness. We introduce the following:

      Definition E.5.3.6. Let C and C′ be 2-categories, and F : C → C′ a pseudo-functor. We say:
       (1) F is weakly faithful if and only if for any pair of objects A, B ∈ Ob(C), the functor:
                                   FA,B : HomC (A, B) → HomC (F (A), F (B))
           is faithful.
       (2) F is faithful if and only if for any pair of objects A, B ∈ Ob(C), the functor:
                                   FA,B : HomC (A, B) → HomC (F (A), F (B))
           is fully faithful.
       (3) F is strongly faithful if and only if for any pair of objects A, B ∈ Ob(C), the functor
                                   FA,B : HomC (A, B) → HomC (F (A), F (B))
           is fully faithful and the set-function induced on objects is injective.
       (4) F is fully faithful if and only if for any pair of objects A, B ∈ Ob(C), the functor:
                                  FA,B : HomC (A, B) → HomC′ (F (A), F (B))
           is an equivalence of categories.
       (5) F is strongly fully faithful if and only if for any pair of objects A, B ∈ Ob(C), the functor:
                                  FA,B : HomC (A, B) → HomC′ (F (A), F (B))
           is an isomorphism of categories.
                                             E.5. 2-CATEGORICAL PREPARATIONS                                               907


      (6) F is a 2-equivalence if and only if it is fully faithful and for every object B ∈ Ob(C′ ) there exists an
          object A ∈ Ob(C) and an equivalence F (A) → B in C.
      (7) F is a strong 2-equivalence if and only if it is fully faithful and for every object B ∈ Ob(C′ ) there
          exists an object A ∈ Ob(C) and an isomorphism F (A) → B in C.
      (8) F is an isomorphism if and only if it is strongly fully faithful and a strong 2-equivalence.
      (9) F is strict if and only if the structure natural transformations γ•,•,• and δ• in the coherence constraint
            F
          (γ•,•,• , δ•F ) for F are the identity.

    We can now define the concept of a sub 2-category of a 2-category:

    Definition E.5.3.7. Let C be a 2-category. We say:
      (1) C′ is a sub 2-category of C if and only if:
           (a) C′ is a 2-category.
           (b) The class of the objects of C′ is a sub-class of the class of the objects of C.
           (c) The inclusion class function F : Ob(C′ ) → Ob(C) is part of the datum of a pseudo-functor
               (F, F•,• , γ•,•,• , δ• ) : C′ → C. We call F the inclusion functor.
           (d) The inclusion functor F is weakly faithful.
      (2) C′ is a strict sub 2-category of C if and only if is is a sub 2-category and the inclusion functor is strict.
      (3) C′ is a full sub 2-category of C if and only if C′ is a sub 2-category and the inclusion functor is fully
          faithful.
      (4) C′ is a strong sub 2-category of C if and only if C′ is a sub 2-category and the inclusion functor is
          strongly faithful.

    E.5.4. Comparing Cat∗ and Cat. We consider the following assignment.

    Construction E.5.4.1. For any effective small category (X, A, s, t, c, e) (see Definition E.5.1.15), we
associate the category C(X,A) such that:
      (1) Ob(C(X,A) ) := X.
      (2) For any two objects x, y ∈ Ob(C(X,A) ), we define HomC(X,A) (x, y) := s−1 (x) ∩ t−1 (y).
      (3) For any two morphisms f ∈ HomC(X,A) (x, y) and g ∈ HomC(X,A) (y, z), we define g ◦ f := c(f, g).
    For any functor F = (f1 , f2 ) : (X, A, s, t, c, e) → (X ′ , A′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ ):
      (1) for any object x ∈ C(X,A) , we define ϕF (x) := f1 (x).
      (2) For any morphism f ∈ HomC(X,A) (x, y), we define ϕF (f ) := f2 (f ).
    We call ϕF : C(X,A) → C(X ′ ,A′ ) the assignment defined above on objects and morphisms.

    We have the following consistency checks:

    Lemma E.5.4.2. For any effective small category (X, A, s, t, c, e), the datum C(X,A) is a small category.
The assignment:
(E.5.4.1)                                           (X, A, s, t, c, e) ⇝ C(X,A)
is functorial, the functoriality being defined by ϕ constructed in Construction E.5.4.1.

    Proof. The very definition of ϕ ensures compatibility with composition of morphisms on source and
target, since, for any functor F = (f1 , f2 ) : (X, A, s, t, c, e) → (X ′ , A′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ ), ϕF is defined to be f2 on
morphisms, and (f1 , f2 ) is a morphism of effective small categories. In particular, f2 is compatible with
the composition laws c, c′ , which translates into ϕF being compatible with composition of morphisms, as
desired.                                                                                                                      □
    We have the following:
908                                          CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


      Lemma E.5.4.3. The assignment:
(E.5.4.2)                                                ϕ : Cat∗ → Cat
defined in Construction E.5.4.1 is an isomorphism of locally small categories.

    Proof. Indeed, for any two effective small categories (X, A, s, t, c, e) and (X ′ , A′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ ), the functor
ϕ induces an injective set-function:
                  ϕ : HomCat∗ ((X, A, s, t, c, e), (X ′ , A′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ )) → HomCat (C(X,A) , C(X ′ ,A′ ) ).
To see this, we observe that by design of ϕ, for any functor F = (f1 , f2 ) : (X, A, s, t, c, e) → (X ′ , A′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ ),
f2 is uniquely determined by ϕF . As for f1 , one recovers it by computing the effect of ϕF on objects of C(X,A) ,
which are, by definition, the set X. We now prove surjectivity of the map that ϕ induces on Hom-sets. Let
F : C(X,A) → C(X ′ ,A′ ) be a functor. We may define f1 : X → X to be f1 (x) := F (x), as X = Ob(C(X,A) ) by
definition of C(X,A) . We can reconstruct A as:
                                                  a
                                 A=                              HomC(X,A) (x, y)
                                           (x,y)∈Ob(C(X,A) )×Ob(C(X,A) )

and so f2 (a) := F (a) defines a pair of set-functions (f1 , f2 ) : (X, A) → (X ′ , A′ ).
     Compatibility with s, t, c, e follows from the definition of C(X,A) and the composition of morphisms in C(X,A) .
This proves that ϕ is fully faithful. For C a small category, we call X := Ob(C), A := (x,y)∈X×X HomC (x, y),
                                                                                           `

and define s, t : A ⇒ X as follows. For any a ∈ A, there exists a unique pair (x, y) ∈ X × X such
that a ∈ HomC (x, y). We define s(a) := x and t(a) := t. For a, a′ ∈ A such that s(a) = t(a′ ), we have
a ∈ HomC (x, y) and a′ ∈ HomC (z, x), and so the composition a ◦ a′ makes sense. We denote it by c(a′ , a), and
this provides a set-function A ×s,X,t A → A. Finally, we define e : X → A by e(x) := idx . We therefore obtain
a 6-tuple (X, A, s, t, c, e) from C, and the axioms (??), (??), (??) and (??) from Definition E.5.1.15 are seen
to be satisfied by (s, t, c, e) upon inspection of the defining axioms of a category. This shows that C = C(X,A) ,
i.e. C is isomorphic as a category to a category of the form C(X,A) . This shows that ϕ : Cat∗ → Cat from
(E.5.4.2) is an isomorphism of categories.                                                                       □

      We can promote ϕ to a pseudo-functor as follows:

       Construction E.5.4.4. For any natural transformation T : F ⇒ F ′ between functors F = (f1 , f2 ), F ′ =
(f1′ , f2′ ) : (X, A, s, t, c, e) ⇒ (X ′ , A′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ ), we define ϕ(T ) to be the natural transformation of functors
ϕF ⇒ ϕF ′ characterized by the following property: for any object x in C(X,A) , the datum of ϕ(T )x is the
morphism f1 (x) → f1′ (x) in C(X ′ ,A′ ) given by T (x) ∈ (s′ )−1 (f1 (x)) ∩ (t′ )−1 (f1′ (x)) = HomC(X ′ ,A′ ) (f1 (x), f1′ (x)).
Naturality of ϕ(T )x with respect to x is a consequence of (E.5.1.24) from Definition E.5.1.16. See also Remark
??.

    Lemma E.5.4.5. The locally small categories Cat and Cat∗ are, in a canonical way, 2-categories, whose
composition bifunctors are the bifunctors c•,•,• constructed in Lemma E.5.1.14 and Lemma E.5.1.19. The
functor ϕ : Cat∗ → Cat is a strict isomorphism of 2-categories.

     Proof. Indeed, since the composition of morphisms in C(X,A) for (X, A, s, t, c, e) an effective small
category, is defined by means of the composition law c, and ϕ is defined in terms of the component set-functions
of functors between effective small categories (see Definition E.5.1.15 and Construction E.5.4.4), ϕ is compatible
with composition of 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms on the nose, forcing γ•,•,• and δ• to be the identity, so ϕ
is a strict pseudo-functor. By Lemma E.5.4.3 it induces an essentially surjective functor on Hom-categories.
Such functor is also fully faithful because, given a natural transformation of functors T : F ⇒ F ′ between
effective small categories F = (f1 , f2 ), F ′ = (f1′ , f2′ ) : (X, A) ⇒ (X ′ , A′ ), T is a set-function T : X → A′ ,
                                          E.5. 2-CATEGORICAL PREPARATIONS                                                909


and knowledge of the associated natural transformation is knowledge of a coherent family of set-functions
f1 (x) → f1′ (x) for every x ∈ X.
     To reconstruct T , one defines T (x) to be the element a′ ∈ A′ corresponding to the morphism f1 (x) → f1′ (x)
under ϕ, and seeing that indeed this construction recovers T is a simple consequence of the definitions. More
generally, any natural transformation T : F ⇒ F ′ between functors of small categories C → C′ produces, by
means of the above construction, a set-function T : Ob(C) → Arrows(C′ ) satisfying the defining axioms (see
Definition E.5.1.16), and hence the functor induced by ϕ on Hom-categories is an isomorphism of categories,
so ϕ is strongly fully faithful. Upon combining strong full faithfulness with Lemma E.5.4.3 and with the
strictness of ϕ proved in the foregoing, we deduce ϕ is a strict isomorphism of 2-categories, as desired.       □

    Remark E.5.4.6. In light of Lemma E.5.4.5, we can now give meaning to the sentence “we view the datum
of (X, A, s, t, c, e) as a small category”, which is commonly done when discussing, for instance, groupoids and
stacks in groupoids on a site. Conversely, we may “view a small category as the datum of (X, A, s, t, c, e)”, for
appropriate structure morphisms (s, t, c, e), and this sentence now has an un-ambiguous meaning provided by
Lemma E.5.4.5, insofar it refers to the functor ϕ : Cat∗ → Cat being a strict isomorphism of 2-categories.

    We have the following simple but useful Lemma:

    Lemma E.5.4.7. Let A and B be small categories. If all the morphisms of A′ are isomorphisms, then for
any pair of functors F, F ′ : A ⇒ B, any natural transformation t : F ⇒ F ′ is an isomorphism of functors.

     Proof. For every object a of A, ta : F (a) → F ′ (a) is a morphism in A′ . By assumption, every morphism
in A′ is an isomorphism, and hence for every object a of A, there exists a necessarily unique inverse t−1
                                                                                                        a to
ta in A′ . This gives a natural transformation t−1 : F ′ ⇒ F . That t−1 is the inverse of t follows from the
               a for every object a of A.
definition of t−1                                                                                           □

    We now consider the inclusion of the category Groupoids into the category Cat∗ , assigned by sending
the datum of a groupoid in sets (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) (see Definition E.4.1.1) to the effective small category
(X, R, s, t, c, e) (“forget i”). We call:
(E.5.4.3)                                     ugpd : Groupoids → Cat∗
the fully faithful inclusion functor of ordinary categories.

    Lemma E.5.4.8. The category Groupoids is a 2-category upon endowing it with the composition bifunctor
constructed on effective small categories in Lemma E.5.1.14. The functor ugpd : Groupoids → Cat∗ from
(E.5.4.3) extends to a strongly fully faithful strict pseudo-functor.

     Proof. All we need to check is that for any two groupoids (X, R, s, t, c, e, i) and (X ′ , R′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ , i′ )
and any functor F = (f1 , f2 ) : (X, R) → (X ′ , R′ ), any natural transformation T : X → R′ is invertible. This
is indeed the case, as we may define T −1 to be i′ ◦ T , and verify it is indeed inverse to T upon proceeding
similarly to Lemma E.5.4.7.                                                                                              □

    Remark E.5.4.9. The pseudo-functor ϕ : Groupoids → Cat induces a strict isomorphism of 2-categories
between the 2-category Groupoids and the sub 2-category of all small categories whose morphisms are all
isomorphisms. We may therefore view any such category in its effective-small-category incarnation, and
we shall do so without mentioning ϕ, knowing that interchanging between the two perspectives amounts to
appealing to ϕ being a strict isomorphism of 2-categories. We will call Groupoids both the category defined
in Definition E.4.1.1, and the image of ϕ, and we shall be identifying their 2-category structures.

    We have the following example of a pseudo-functor that is not strongly fully faithful (nor fully faithful)
but is strongly faithful.
910                                     CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


    Lemma E.5.4.10. The category of topological groupoids CGWH-Grpd is a 2-category. Moreover, the
forgetful functor u : CGWH-Grpd → Groupoids is a strict faithful pseudo-functor.

    Proof. The forgetful functor induces injective set-functions on objects of the Hom-categories by faithful-
ness of the forgetful functor CGWH → Sets. For any two objects of CGWH-Grpd, the induced functor
between Hom-categories is faithful for the same reason. Strictness of u follows from the fact that morphisms
between topological groupoids are defined analogously to morphisms of groupoids in sets (see Definition
E.4.1.1) and hence the structure maps of the coherence constraint of u are the identity.                   □

    E.5.6. 2-final objects in Diagrams(f, g). We will now define the concept of 2-fibre products, and
we shall then discuss a series of examples of 2-categories of interest that contain 2-fibre products. First, we
introduce the concept of final objects in a 2-category. One way to assign conditions on objects of a 2-category
C is to assign such conditions on the ordinary category Cat(C) associated to C (see Construction E.5.2.6).
We recall that an object x in a locally small category D is weakly terminal if and only if for every object
y ∈ Ob(D), there exists a morphism y → x in D (see [Ka, §2], especially the discussion after [Ka, Thm. 2.1]).

     Definition E.5.6.1. Let C be a 2-category. An object A of C is final in C if and only if:
       (1) As an object of Cat(C), A is weakly terminal.
       (2) For any object B of C and any two 1-morphisms f, g : B ⇒ A, there exists a unique 2-isomorphism
           α : f ⇒ g in C.

     Several ambiguities arise around the concept of final objects in a 2-category, and one has to start
distinguishing among varying degrees of strength of the notions of final objects. We refer the reader to [GR,
Ch. 2, §2.5] for a discussion of 2-limits and 2-colimits and related (non-)uniqueness aspects, and especially the
discussion between [GR, Ch. 2, §2, Def. 2.5.14] and [GR, Ch. 2, §2, Prop. 2.5.15], for a useful special situation
when final objects can be defined.
     The definition of final objects provided in Definition E.5.6.1 is sufficient for all our purposes. In particular,
by introducing a suitable diagram 2-category Diagrams(f, g) as provided by Lemma E.5.5.4, we can define
the notion of 2-fibre products that will be used to assign conditions on 1-morphisms of stacks in groupoids.
Such notion can be introduced in wider generality, and we refer the interested reader to [GR, Ch. 2, §2,
Rem. 2.5.2,(v)].
     We can now assign the following:

   Definition E.5.6.2. Let C be a 2-category, A, B, C ∈ Ob(C), f : B → A and g : C → A two 1-morphisms.
We define a 2-fibre product for (f, g) in C to be any final object of the 2-category Diagrams(f, g).

     The above Definition E.5.6.2 in particular means that a 2-fibre product of f, g is the datum of an object
P of C, equipped with 1-morphisms a : P → B, b : P → C and a 2-isomorphism ϕ : f ◦ a ⇒ g ◦ b making the
following diagram 2-commute:
                                                      b /
                                                 P        ;C C
                                                           a                  g
                                                              {       ϕ     
                                                            B               /A
                                                                    f

such that every other object of Diagrams(f, g) has a 1-morphism to (P, a, b, ϕ), and for any two 1-morphisms
p = (k, α, β) : (D, a′ , b′ , ϕ′ ) → (P, a, b, ϕ) and q = (k ′ , α′ , β ′ ) : (D′′ , a′′ , b′′ , ϕ′′ ) → (P, a, b, ϕ), there exists a
unique 2-isomorphism γ : p ⇒ q in Diagrams(f, g), i.e. a unique 2-isomorphism:
                                                               γ : k ⇒ k′
