    E.5.7. 2-fibre products and 1-fibre products. We have collected basic examples of 2-categories and of
pseudo-functors. We will now briefly focus on those 2-categories all of whose 2-morphisms are 2-isomorphisms.
These will be the only 2-categories of interest throughout the development of the sought-for theory of stacks
in groupoids on a suitable site of topological spaces.
    In this section, we shall recall results concerning the existence of 2-fibre products in 2-categories of interest.
Our main source within the literature will be [SP, Tags 003O, 02XG, 02XJ, 003S], to which we shall refer the
reader for the relevant arguments, with occasional exceptions. This will conclude the 2-categorical preparations
needed later in this appendix.
    We begin with a definition:
   Definition E.5.7.1. Let C be a 2-category. We say that C is a strict (2, 1)-category if and only if every
2-morphism in C is a 2-isomorphism.
     The notion of strict (2, 1)-category is also known, in the literature, under the terminology of groupoid-
enriched category (see [FM, §1]). For every pair of objects A, B ∈ Ob(C) of a strict (2, 1)-category C, the
category HomC (A, B) is a groupoid (see [SP, Tag 003I]) whose set of objects is the set of 1-morphisms
f : A → B, and whose set of morphisms is the set of 2-morphisms f ⇒ f ′ , all isomorphisms.
     E.5.7.1. Strict (2, 1)-categories of interest. We will now discuss four examples of strict (2, 1)-categories,
ultimately focusing on the example of stacks in groupoids over a site, for which we will discuss existence of
2-fibre products.
      Example E.5.7.2. We recall that upon fixing a small category D, we may consider the following datum:
       (1) the class of all pairs (S, p) where S is a small category and p : S → D is a functor.
       (2) For any two pairs (S, p) and (S′ , p′ ), the category Hom((S, p), (S′ , p′ )) whose:
            (a) objects are functors F : S → S′ such that p′ ◦ F = p.
            (b) Morphisms t : F ⇒ F ′ for F, F ′ : (S, p) → (S′ , p′ ) are natural transformations of functors such
                that p′ (tA ) = 1p(A) for every object A ∈ Ob(S).
We note that for any two pairs (S, p) and (S′ , p′ ), there is a faithful forgetful functor:
                                           Hom((S, p), (S′ , p′ )) → HomCat (S, S′ )
given by sending a functor F : S → S′ to itself forgetting its compatibility with p and p′ , and sending a
natural transformation t : F ⇒ F ′ to itself. The bifunctor (◦, ⋆) constructed in §E.5.1 (see Definition E.5.1.11)
restricts to a bifunctor:
           c(S,p),(S′ ,p′ ),(S′′ ,p′′ ) : Hom((S, p), (S′ , p′ )) × Hom((S′ , p′ ), (S′′ , p′′ )) → Hom((S, p), (S′′ , p′′ ))
which satisfies the Axioms from Definition E.5.2.1 by Lemma E.5.1.14. We denote the resulting 2-category by
Cat/D. We refer to it as the 2-category of categories over D. The compositions within Cat/D are inherited
from those on Cat, and hence the worked example of Cat (see Definition E.5.1.20 and Lemma E.5.1.14) can
be used to compute compositions within Cat/D.
     We note that the 2-category described in Example E.5.7.2 is not a strict (2, 1)-category. However, we can
associate to any 2-category a strict (2, 1)-category by re-defining the sets of 2-morphisms to be comprised only
of those 2-morphisms that are isomorphisms (see [SP, Tag 02X8], and specifically [SP, Tag 003K]).
     Within the strict (2, 1)-category (Cat/D)strict associated to Cat/D from Example E.5.7.2, we make the
following Construction.
                                        E.5. 2-CATEGORICAL PREPARATIONS                                       915


    Construction E.5.7.3. We let F : (X, pX ) → (S, pS ) and G : (Y, pY ) → (S, pS ) be morphisms of categories
over D. We define X ×F,S,G Y to be the small category whose:
     (1) objects are 4-tuples (A, x, y, ϕ) with A ∈ Ob(D), x ∈ Ob(XA ), y ∈ Ob(YA ), ϕ : F (x) → G(y) is an
         isomorphism in S.
     (2) Morphisms (A, x, y, ϕ) → (A′ , x′ , y ′ , ϕ′ ) are given by pairs (a, b) with a : x → x′ a morphism in X,
         b : y → y ′ a morphism in Y, satisfying the following properties:
          (a) pX (a) = pY (b) as morphisms of D.
          (b) As morphisms of S, we have the identity:
                                              ϕ′ ◦ F (a) = G(b) ◦ ϕ.
We further define the functors p1 : X ×2F,S,G Y → X and p2 : X ×2F,S,G Y → Y to be the forgetful functors. We
note that X ×2F,S,G Y can be made into an object of (Cat/D)strict by equipping it with the projection to D
given by the composition π := pX ◦ p1 = pY ◦ p2 . We call ψ : F ◦ pX → G ◦ pY the natural transformation of
functors assigned on the arbitrary object ξ := (A, x, y, ϕ) by:
                                 ψξ := ϕ : F (pX (ξ)) = F (x) → G(y) = G(pY (ξ)).
We denote by:
(E.5.7.1)                                          X ×2F,S,G Y
the datum (X ×2F,S,G Y, p1 , p2 , ψ).
    For the strict (2, 1)-category associated to Cat/D, we have the following:
     Lemma E.5.7.4. Let D be a small category. Let F : X → S and G : Y → S be 1-morphisms of categories
over D. A 2-fibre product in the strict (2, 1)-category (Cat/D)strict of all small categories over D for (F, G)
exists, and it is equivalent to X ×2S Y from Construction E.5.7.3.
    Proof. This is [SP, Tag 0040]. We further refer to the reader to [Ac, Ch. I, Lemma 1.2.1].                 □
    We recall here for the reader’s convenience the following definition (see [SP, Tag 02XK]):
    Definition E.5.7.5. Let D be a small category, p : S → D a small category over D. For any pair of
objects A, B ∈ Ob(S), a strongly D-cartesian morphism f : A → B is a morphism in S such that for every
object C ∈ Ob(C) the map:
                        HomS (C, A) → HomS (C, B) ×HomD (p(C),p(B)) HomD (p(C), p(A))
assigned by sending g : C → B to (f ◦ g, p(g)), is a bijection.
    We observe that for any object A of S with p(A) = D in D, and any morphism ϕ : D′ → D in D, if a
strongly cartesian morphism f : A′ → A exists such that p(f ) = ϕ, then the pair (A′ , f ) is unique up to unique
isomorphism in S by Yoneda’s Lemma. We may therefore denote refer to the pair (A′ , f ) via the notation
ϕ∗ A → A. Strongly cartesian morphisms satisfy the following basic permanence properties:
    Lemma E.5.7.6. Let D be a small category, p : S → D a small category over D.
     (1) Strongly cartesian morphisms in S are stable under finite compositions.
     (2) For any pair of objects A, B ∈ Ob(S), if f : A → B is an isomorphism, then f is strongly cartesian.
     (3) Let f : A → B be a strongly cartesian morphism between objects of S. If p(f ) is an isomorphism in
         D, then f is an isomorphism.
    Proof. We refer the reader to [SP, Tag 02XL] and [Ac, Ch. I, Lemma 1.3.1].                                 □
    Following [SP, Tag 02XM], we recall the following:
916                                        CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


     Definition E.5.7.7. Let D be a small category and p : S → D a small category over D. We say p : S → D
is a fibered category if and only if for every object A ∈ Ob(S), and any morphism ϕ : D → p(A) in D, there
exists a strongly cartesian morphism f : ϕ∗ A → A with p(f ) = ϕ.
    Example E.5.7.8. (The 2-category of fibered categories over a fixed category) We let D be a small
category. We define Fib/D to be the sub 2-category of the 2-category Cat/D assigned as follows:
       (1) The objects of Fib/D are small fibered categories p : S → D.
       (2) The 1-morphisms F : (S, p) → (S′ , p′ ) are 1-morphisms in Cat/D that, in addition, satisfy the
           property of preserving strongly cartesian morphisms.
       (3) The 2-morphisms of Fib/D are those natural transformations of functors t : F ⇒ F ′ , for 1-morphisms
           F, F ′ : (S, p) → (S′ , p′ ), such that t is a 2-morphism in Cat/D.
We define the composition bifunctor:
        c(•, •) : HomFib/D ((S, p), (S′ , p′ )) × HomFib/D ((S′ , p′ ), (S′′ , p′′ )) → HomFib/D ((S, p), (S′′ , p′′ ))
to be the restriction of the composition bifunctor on Cat/D, which is in turn the restriction of the composition
bifunctor (◦, ⋆) from §E.5.1. The above datum is a 2-category, denoted Fib/D. We shall refer to it as the
2-category of categories fibered over D.
     The above example is [SP, Tag 02XP], and as noted in loc.cit., Fib/D is a genuine 2-category. In order
to state the next Lemma, we therefore pass to its associated strict (2, 1)-category, (Fib/D)strict . The following
Lemma is [SP, Tag 02XQ]:
     Lemma E.5.7.9. Let D be a small category. Then the strict (2, 1)-category associated to Fib/D contains
2-fibre products, and they are computed by the 2-fibre products in (Cat/D)strict from Lemma E.5.7.4. Moreover,
for any object T of D, and any 1-morphisms f : X → S and g : Y → S of categories fibered over D, we have a
canonical isomorphism of fibre categories:
                                            (X ×2f,S,g Y)T = XT ×2fT ,SU ,gT YT
where the 2-fibre product XU ×2fU ,SU ,gU YU is formed in Cat.
     Proof. This is [SP, Tag 02XQ] and [SP, Tag 02XI]. We further refer the reader to [Ac, Ch.I,Lemma
1.3.6] and to [Ac, Ch.I,Lemma 1.2.2].                                                               □
     Example E.5.7.10. We may now consider the full sub 2-category Groupoids/D of Fib/D of those
fibered categories p : S → D whose fibre categories over D are all groupoids. Then Groupoids/D is a strict
(2, 1)-category with 2-fibre products.
    Lemma E.5.7.11. Let D be a small category. Then the strict (2, 1)-category Groupoids/D of small
categories fibered in groupoids over D has 2-fibre products, and they are computed by the 2-fibre products in
(Cat/D)strict .
      Proof. This is [SP, Tag 0041]. We further refer the reader to [Ac, Ch.I,Lemma 1.5.3].                               □
   Remark E.5.7.12. In Lemma E.5.7.11, we may choose D = 1, the final object in Cat (see part (1) of

implies the existence of 2-fibre products of groupoids in sets, described by Construction E.5.7.3.
      Finally, the last example is the one of our interest.

    Proof. This is [SP, Tag 02ZL].                                                                               □
     E.5.7.2. 1-fibre products. We want a notion of fibre products for stacks in groupoids on a site that is
rarely used within the literature. It will enable us to compute the stack-theoretic intersection of certain “graph”
and “diagonal” sub-stacks of a topological stack of key interest to our work. We review the construction here
concerning such an alternate version of fibre products for categories over a fixed small category D, and we
will recall criteria for its existence which, contrary to 2-fibre products and as illustrated in Lemma E.5.7.4 ,
does not always hold within the strict (2, 1)-category of stacks in groupoids on a site. Our main source within
the literature for the material within this subsection is [Ac, Ch.I-II], with particular emphasis on [Ac, Ch. I,
Lemma 1.2.3, Prop. 1.3.1,Thm. 1,Thm. 2] and [Ac, Ch. II, Thm. 4].
    Definition E.5.7.14. Let C be a 2-category, A, B, C ∈ Ob(C), f : B → A, g : C → A two 1-morphisms
in C. We define the 1-fibre product for (f, g) in C, denoted B ×1f,A,g C, to be the fibre product of (f, g) in the
ordinary locally small category Cat(C) of Construction E.5.2.6.
    Lemma E.5.7.15. The 2-category Cat contains 1-fibre products.
    Proof. Let A, B, C ∈ Ob(C), f : B → A, g : C → A two 1-morphisms in Cat. We define B ×1f,A,g C to
be the category whose class of objects is:
                                   Ob(B ×1f,A,g C) := Ob(B) ×f,Ob(A),g Ob(C)
and for any two objects (x, y), (x′ , y ′ ), we define the set of morphisms to be:
                        Hom((x, y), (x′ , y ′ )) := HomB (x, x′ ) ×f,HomA (z,z′ ),g HomC (y, y ′ )
where z := f (x) = g(y) and z ′ := f (x′ ) = g(y ′ ). Composition of morphisms in B ×1f,A,g C is defined
component-wise. The forgetful functors p1 : B ×1f,A,g C → B and p2 : B ×1f,A,g C → C satisfy f ◦ p1 = g ◦ p2
as 1-morphisms in Cat. For the proof that (B ×1f,A,g C, p1 , p2 ) verifies the universal property of fibre products
in Cat(Cat), we refer the reader to [Ac, Ch.I,Lemma 1.2.3], applied to C = 1, the final object in Cat (see
part (1) of Remark E.5.1.20).                                                                                    □
    In the 2-category of all small categories over a fixed small category D, 1-fibre products exist. This is the
content of the following:
    Lemma E.5.7.16. Let D be a small category. The 2-category Cat/D contains 1-fibre products.
    Proof. To see this, it is enough to check that 1-fibre products in Cat are contained in the sub 2-category
Cat/D. Equivalently, that given objects (A, pA : A → D),(B, pB : B → D), (C, pC : C → D) of Cat/D, and
1-morphisms f : B → A and g : C → A in Cat/D, the 1-fibre product B ×1f,A,g C formed in Cat is itself a
category over D. This is seen by defining p : B ×1f,A,g C → D as the composition pA ◦ f ◦ p1 = pA ◦ g ◦ p2 , and
then checking that the resulting object of Cat/D indeed satisfies the universal property of fibre products in
Cat(Cat/D). We refer the reader to the proof of [Ac, Ch.I,Lemma 1.2.3] for this verification.                  □
     It is not always the case that 1-fibre products exist in Fib/D, the 2-category of all small categories fibered
over the fixed small category D. For a discussion on 1-fibre products in fibered categories we refer the reader
to [Ac, Ch.I,p.31-33], with emphasis on [Ac, Ch. I, Examples 4, 5]. The obstruction to the existence of 1-fibre
products of fibered categories is the fact that it is not generally true that, given 1-morphisms f : B → A,
g : C → A, for all objects U of D we have (d∗ x, d∗ y) ∈ Ob(B ×1f,A,g C) for all (x, y) ∈ Ob(B ×1f,A,g C) and
d : U ′ → U a morphism in D. This is also the only obstruction. We have the following definition, which is
[Ac, Ch. I, Def. 1.3.5]:
   Definition E.5.7.17. Let (A, pA ), (B, pB ), (C, pC ) be three small categories fibered over D, and f :
B → A, g : C → A be two 1-morphisms of small categories fibered over D. The 1-fibre product in Cat/D,
918                                    CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


B ×1f,A,g C, has enough component-wise pullbacks if and only if for all (x, y) ∈ Ob(B ×1f,A,g C) and d : U ′ → U
any morphism in D, we have:
       (1) (d∗ x, d∗ y) is an object of B ×1f,A,g C.
       (2) (d∗ x → x, d∗ y → y) is a morphism of B ×1f,A,g C.
    Terminology E.5.7.1. We note that the terminology being adopted here of “1-fibre products” corresponds
to the terminology “fibre products” of [Ac, Ch.I], and that the condition of having “enough component-wise
pullbacks” corresponds to having “componentwise pullbacks”, as defined in [Ac, Ch. I, Def. 1.3.5].
     Lemma E.5.7.18. Let D be a small category, and (A, pA ), (B, pB ), (C, pC ) be three small categories fibered
over D. Let f : B → A, g : C → A be two 1-morphisms of small categories fibered over D, such that the 1-fibre
product in Cat/D, B ×1f,A,g C, has enough component-wise pullbacks. Then a 1-fibre product for (f, g) exists
in the 2-category Fib/D, and it is computed by the 1-fibre product B ×1f,A,g C for (f, g) in Cat/D.
     Proof. We refer the reader to [Ac, Ch.I,Thm.1] for the proof of the first assertion in the Lemma. To
verify that B ×1f,A,g C satisfies the universal property, it is enough to observe: as soon as B ×1f,A,g C is
an object of Fib/D it induces an object in Cat(Fib/D), the forgetful functor Cat(Fib/D) → Cat(Cat/D)
induced by the forgetful pseudo-functor Fib/D → Cat/D is conservative, and conservative functors reflect
representable limits.                                                                                     □
    Remark E.5.7.19. In Lemma E.5.7.18, we may choose D = 1, the final object in Cat (see part (1) of
Remark E.5.1.20). In this case, Fib/D = Cat as 2-categories. The Lemma implies the existence of 1-fibre
products of small categories, defined in Definition E.5.7.14.
      Within Cat/D, 1-fibre products and 2-fibre products are related according to the following:
   Lemma E.5.7.20. Let (A, pA ), (B, pB ), (C, pC ) be three categories over D, and f : B → A, g : C → A two
1-morphisms of categories over D. There exists a canonical 1-morphism of categories over D:
(E.5.7.2)                                 p : B ×1f,A,g C → B ×2f,A,g C
such that:
       (1) p is a fully faithful functor of small categories.
       (2) If (A, pA ), (B, pB ), (C, pC ) are fibered categories over D, and B ×1f,A,g C in Cat/D has enough
           component-wise pullbacks, then p is a 1-morphism of fibered categories over D.
      Proof. We refer the reader to [Ac, Ch. I, Prop. 1.3.1] for the proof of the Lemma.                         □
    We note that the functor p from (E.5.7.2) in Lemma E.5.7.20 above may not be essentially surjective (see
[Ac, Ch. I, Example 7] for an explicit example).
     Lemma E.5.7.21. Let D be a small category. Let (A, pA ), (B, pB ), (C, pC ) be three small categories fibered
in groupoids over D, and f : B → A, g : C → A two 1-morphisms of categories fibered in groupoids over
D. Then a 1-fibre product for (f, g) exists in the 2-category Groupoids/D of all small categories fibered in
groupoids over D if and only if a 1-fibre product for (f, g) exists in the 2-category Fib/D of all small categories
fibered over D.
     Proof. The inclusion functor Groupoids/D → Fib/D is strict and strongly fully faithful, and hence
the induced ordinary functor Cat(Groupoids/D) → Cat(Fib/D) is fully faithful. As fully faithful functors
reflect representable limits, a 1-fibre product for (f, g) exists in Groupoids/D if and only if B ×1f,A,g C,
formed in Cat/D, has enough component-wise pullbacks. Indeed, if so then B ×1f,A,g C is fibered over D
by Lemma E.5.7.18, and fibered in groupoids, hence an object of Groupoids/D. As the forgetful inclusion
functor Cat(Groupoids/D) → Cat(Fib/D) is fully faithful and hence reflects representable limits, B ×1f,A,g C
                                           E.5. 2-CATEGORICAL PREPARATIONS                                                   919


is a fibre product in Cat(Groupoids/D) if and only if it is a fibre product in Cat(Fib/D). Conversely, if a
1-fibre product for (f, g) exists in Groupoids/D, then its image under the forgetful functor to Fib/D is also
a 1-fibre product for (f, g), in the 2-category Fib/D. This is so because Cat(Groupoids/D) → Cat(Fib/D)
preserves representable fibre products. It follows B ×1f,A,g C has enough component-wise pullbacks.        □
    Remark E.5.7.22. In Lemma E.5.7.21, we may choose D = 1, the final object in Cat (see part (1) of
Remark E.5.1.20). In this case, Groupoids/D = Groupoids as strict (2, 1)-categories. The Lemma implies
the existence of 1-fibre products of groupoids in sets, since they exist in Fib/D = Cat by Remark E.5.7.19.
    We will need a criterion for the existence of 1-fibre products in Fib/D. First, we recall a key construction:
    Construction E.5.7.23. We let D be a small category, and F : Dopp → Groupoids a functor. We

     Such fibered categories (E.5.7.6) are called split. We’ll be interested in the case D = CGWHα and F
the “functor of points” oof a fixed groupoid in CGWHα . The category over D assigned by (SF , pF ) is a

(E.5.7.7)                                       SF ×1t,SH ,s SG → SF ×t,H,s G
In particular, SF ×1t,SH ,s SG has enough component-wise pullbacks, and is the 1-fibre product of t, s in

    We now assume the fixed small category D is endowed with the structure of a site, so stackification of

     We will be applying Lemma E.5.7.24 and Lemma E.5.7.25 to show21 that the stackification of the split
fibered category SF for
                                F := Hom(·, (X1 , R1 ) ×(Y,R) (X2 , R2 ))
(given (Xi , Ri ) → (Y, R) in CGWHα ) is a 1-fibre product [X1 /R1 ] ×1[Y /R] [X2 /R2 ] of (quotient) stacks in

     We conclude this section by discussing an example of a situation where 1-fibre products of stacks in
groupoids over a site indeed exist not only as a category over the base site, but as a stack in groupoids.

    Lemma E.5.7.26. Let A, B, C be three categories fibered in groupoids over a small category D, and let
f : B → A and g : C → A two 1-morphisms. If A is fibered in sets then the 1-fibre product B ×1f,A,g C as a
category over D is fibered in groupoids and isomorphic to the 2-fibre product B ×2f,A,g C.

     Proof. For any object U of D, the objects of (B ×2f,A,g C)U = BU ×2fU ,AU ,gU CU are triples (x, y, ϕ)
with x ∈ Ob(BU ), y ∈ Ob(CU ), and α an isomorphism α : fU (x) → gU (y). Since A is fibered in sets, AU is
a discrete category, forcing fU (x) = gU (x). It follows that the very construction of 2-fibre products agrees,
in this case, with that of 1-fibre products. In particular, the functor p of Lemma E.5.7.20, which is fully
faithful by the Lemma, is surjective on objects, and hence an isomorphism of categories over D. In particular,
B ×1f,A,g C contains enough component-wise pullbacks, and hence it is a fibered category over D by Lemma
E.5.7.18.                                                                                                   □

    Lemma E.6.1.2. Let:
                                           F : 2-Cat(CGWHopp
                                                         α,τ ) → Cat
be a strict pseudo-functor between 2-categories. The datum SF is a small category, the assignment pF : SF →
CGWHα,τ is a functor, and the pair (SF , pF ) is a fibered category. Moreover, if:
(1) F factors as a functor through the inclusion pseudo-functor Groupoids → Cat, then (SF , pF ) is fibered
    in groupoids.
(2) F factors as a functor through the inclusion pseudo-functor Sets → Cat (sending a set to the discrete
    category over it, then (SF , pF ) is fibered in sets).
     Proof. A verification of the assertion on SF being a category can be found in [Ac, Ch.I,§1.4,p.40,41].
Since Ob(SF ) constructed in Construction E.6.1.1 is a set by design, SF is a small category. A verification
of the assertion that pF : SF → CGWHα,τ is a functor is a direct consequence of the definition of the
composition of morphisms of SF in (E.6.1.3) of Construction E.6.1.1. A verification of the assertion on
pF : SF → CGWHα,τ being a fibered category can be found in [Ac, Ch.I,§1.4,p.41,42,43]. That pF is a
fibration in discrete categories is seen by forming, for any object U of CGWHα,τ , the fibre category (SF )U
and observing that
                                               Ob((SF )U ) = F (U )
and for any two objects x, x′ ∈ (SF )U ,
                                         Hom(SF )U (x′ , x) = HomF (U ) (x′ , x)
and hence (SF )U = F (U ). The Lemma therefore follows from [SP, Tag 003V] and [SP, Tag 02Y2].                         □
    Remark E.6.1.3. We make the following observations on the preceding lemma.
  (i) In part (1), the pseudo-functor F “factoring through” the inclusion pseudo-functor Groupoids → Cat
      means that F is the composition of a pseudo-functor F ′ : 2-Cat(CGWHopp     α,τ ) → Groupoids followed by
      the inclusion pseudo-functor Groupoids → Cat. Likewise, in part (2), the pseudo-functor F “factoring
      through” the inclusion pseudo-functor Sets → Cat means that F is the composition of a pseudo-functor
      F ′ : 2-Cat(CGWHopp  α,τ ) → Sets followed by the inclusion pseudo-functor Sets → Cat.
 (ii) The fibered category (SF , pF ) constructed in Construction E.6.1.1 and Lemma E.6.1.2 is an example
      of a split fibered category. The general notion of split fibered category is rendered invariant under
      isomorphism of fibered categories by declaring (see [SP, Tag 02XW]) that split fibered categories are
      precisely those fibered categories over a fixed small category that are isomorphic in the 2-category Fib/D
      (see part (2) of Definition E.5.2.3) to a fibered category of the form (SF , pF ). To assign this concept
      using equivalences in Fib/D as opposed to isomorphisms would render it unimportant, insofar every
      fibered category is equivalent to a split one (see [SP, Tag 004A]).
    A reference for background around the following definition is [GR, Def.3.4.10(i)].
   Definition E.6.1.4. For a small category (X, p) fibered in groupoids over CGWHα,τ , and for any α-small
compactly generated weakly Hausdorff space T , a covering sieve F ∈ J1 (T ) is called of effective descent if and

      We are now ready to assign the notion of stacks in groupoids on topological spaces:

  Definition E.6.1.6. A stack in groupoids on CGWHα,τ is the datum of a small category p : X →

groupoids.

     E.6.3. Inertia stack and coarse space. Inertia stacks are designed to keep track of automorphisms of
objects of a stack that lift the identity on the base in a suitable sense, depending on the situation.
     The general construction for fibered categories is in [SP, Tag 04Z2], and we refer to [SP, Tag 034I,(2)]
for the definition of the absolute inertia fibered category. We now recall the definition in [SP, Tag 034I,(2)],
spelled out within the intended framework of this appendix.

    Definition E.6.3.1. Let p : X → CGWHα be a stack in topological groupoids over CGWHα,τ . The
inertia stack IX of X is the category IX fibered over CGWHα whose:
(1) objects are pairs (x, f ) with x an object of X and f : x → x an automorphism with p(f ) = id.
(2) Morphisms (x, f ) → (y, g) are given by morphisms ϕ : x → y in X making the following diagram commute:
                                                               ϕ
                                                          x        /y
                                                      f                   g
                                                                  / y
                                                          x
                                                               ϕ

The category IX is equipped with a functor q : IX → CGWHα defined on objects as (x, f ) 7→ p(x).

    Before discussing inertia groups, their meaning, and how they can be viewed as being classified by IX , we
recall the following basic result which is [SP, Tag 034H].

     Lemma E.6.3.2. Let X be a stack in topological groupoids over CGWHα,τ . Then there is an equivalence
in the (2, 1)-category of categories over CGWHα :
                                           IX → X ×∆,(X×CGWHα X),∆ ×X
and q : IX → CGWHα makes IX into a fibered category.
                                                     E.6. STACKS ON CGWHα,τ                                     925


    Remark E.6.3.3. We further recall (see [SP, Tag 042H] and [SP, Tag 04Z3]) that for a stack in topological
groupoids X, there is always a canonical 1-morphism:
                                                              ι : IX → X
defined on objects as (x, f ) 7→ x and on morphisms as (ϕ : (x, f ) → (y, g)) 7→ ϕ, with the last ϕ : x → y
regarded as a morphism in X. There moreover exists a section
                                                              ε : X → IX
defined on objects as x 7→ (x, idx ) and on morphisms by sending ϕ : x → y to ϕ : (x, idx ) → (y, idy ) viewed as
a morphism in IX .

    Terminology E.6.3.1. For a stack X in topological groupoids, we say the inertia stack is trivial if the
canonical 1-morphism:
                                            ι : IX → X
is an equivalence. We shall see how this means that all the inertia groups of X at all points of X are trivial.

   We will only ever be interested in the inertia stacks and groups of quotient stacks in topological groupoids.
We therefore describe the inertia stack of such a stack in topological groupoids here below. First, a definition.

    Definition E.6.3.4. Let (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) be a topological groupoid. Its inertia group I[G⇒X] is defined
as the fibre product in CGWHα :
                                        I[G⇒X] := X ×∆,X×X,(s,t) G.
This is made into a relative topological group over X by the continuous multiplication law over X induced by
the composition law c on [G ⇒ X].

     Lemma E.6.3.5. Let (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) be a topological groupoid. Then I[G⇒X] is closed in G with respect to
the topology induced by the second projection:
                                                I[G⇒X] = X ×∆,X×X,(s,t) G → G.
Moreover, if X is Hausdorff then I[G⇒X] can be computed in Spaces.
                                                       S
     Proof. Set-theoretically, I[G⇒X] is the union x∈X Ix , and so I[G⇒X] is the set-theoretic equalizer of s, t.
It is also the topological equalizer, since the forgetful functor CGWHα → Sets is faithful and commutes with
small limits. Thus I[G⇒X] is closed in G by Lemma E.2.3.9 as long as ∆ : X → X × X is a closed immersion in
Spaces, which it is by Lemma E.2.1.6 since all objects in CGWHα are weakly Hausdorff. If X is Hausdorff
then by Lemma E.2.3.1 I[G⇒X] can be computed in Spaces because X × X can, and X ×∆,X×X,(s,t) G is a
fibre product in Spaces by Lemma E.2.3.9.                                                                    □

   We have the following description of the inertia stack of the quotient stack [X/G] in terms of the chart
G ⇒ X for [X/G]:

     Lemma E.6.3.6. Let (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) be a topological groupoid. We set G′ := G ×s,X I[G⇒X] , and further
define:
(1) s′ : G′ → I[G⇒X] , by s′ (r, g) := g.
(2) t′ : G′ → I[G⇒X] , by t′ (r, g) := c(r, c(g, i(r))).
(3) c′ : G′ ×s′ ,I[G⇒X],t′ G′ → G′ , by c′ ((r, g), (r′ , g ′ )) := (c(r, r′ ), g).
Then (I[G⇒X] , G′ , s′ , t′ , c′ ) together with the uniquely determined unit section e′ and inverse map i′ , is a
topological groupoid. Moreover, we have a canonical equivalence of stacks in topological groupoids:
                                                        I[X/G] = [I[G⇒X] /G′ ].
926                                       CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


    Proof. The proof proceeds in a manner that is identical to the case of groupoids in schemes, and we
record it here to provide more details and to remind the reader of the construction of the morphism:
                                           I[X/G]prestack → [I[G⇒X] /G′ ]prestack .
We refer the reader to [SP, Tag 06PB] for the direct analog for groupoids in schemes. By [SP, Tag 06NS], it
is enough to prove this on the level of pre-stacks.
     We need to show that there is an equivalence of fibered categories:
                                           I[X/G]prestack → [I[G⇒X] /G′ ]prestack .
For T in CGWHα , a T -object in the inertia fibred category I[X/G]prestack is the datum of an object x in the
fibre category over T and an automorphism g of x. We may interpret x as a morphism x : T → X, and g as a
morphism g : T → G, such that s ◦ g = t ◦ g = x. This means that g factors through I[G⇒X] . A morphism in
the inertia fibred category (x, g) → (y, h) over the space T is the datum of a morphism r : T → G such that
s ◦ r = x and t ◦ r = y, and the diagram:
                                                       r /
                                                   x       y
                                                        g                   h
                                                                    / y
                                                            x    r

commutes. This is by [SP, Tag 034H], and means the identity:
                                                     c(r, g) = c(h, r)
using the composition law c. Incorporating the effect of the inverse map i, we can also write:
                                            c(c(r, g), i ◦ r) = c(r, c(g, i ◦ r))
which means “r ◦ (g ◦ r ) = h” and “(r ◦ g) ◦ r−1 = h”, respectively. Once again this gives a unique element
                           −1

of G′ acting as a morphism between objects, i.e. elements in I[G⇒X] . Not only this constructs a morphism
of fibred categories I[X/G]prestack → [I[G⇒X] /G′ ]prestack , but it proves it is both fully faithful and essentially
surjective.                                                                                                        □

    We have the following simple criterion for the triviality of the inertia stack of the quotient stack associated
to a topological groupoid:

   Lemma E.6.3.7. Let (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) be a topological groupoid. Assume (s, t) : G → X × X is injective.
Then the canonical 1-morphism:
                                               ι : I[X/G] → [X/G]
is an equivalence.

      Proof. The section ε to ι discussed in Remark E.6.3.3 shows that the functor
                                                      I[X/G] → [X/G]
is essentially surjective. If (s, t) : G → X × X is injective then the morphism I[G⇒X] → X given by the first
projection in the construction of I[G⇒X] 22 is also injective, hence surjective by the existence of a section to ι.
This forces ι to be faithful. Moreover, it also forces G′ → G to be an isomorphism, and therefore ι is fully
faithful, hence an equivalence.                                                                                 □

      We further have the following representability criterion:23
22Clarify here with a reference
23There seems to be no actual discussion of coarse spaces anywhere here, complementing this result, yet coarse spaces are the
entire purpose of all of this effort. Must address it.
                                           E.6. STACKS ON CGWHα,τ                                              927


    Proposition E.6.3.8. Let [G ⇒ X] be a topological groupoid. Assume:
(1) (s, t) : G → X × X is a closed immersion,
(2) the continuous map X → X/G is a quotient map.
Then [X/G] is representable, and the representing object of CGWHα is the quotient topological space X/G.
Equivalently, there is a canonical equivalence:
                                                 [X/G] ≃ X/G.
    The condition on the map X → X/G being a quotient map is typically easy to arrange. The usual
obstruction to representability is the discrepancy between the intrinsic topology on G and the induced topology
on G from X × X, with the latter product being in Spaces. If X is Hausdorff this is indeed the case. More
generally, this can fail and then one can get a quotient stack in topological groupoids which is not representable
despite having trivial inertia stack.
     Proof of Proposition E.6.3.8. Under the assumptions of the Proposition, X/G is compactly generated
and weakly Hausdorff. By Lemma E.6.3.7, the inertia stack of [X/G] is trivial. This implies that not only X/G
is an object of CGWHα (it is α-small since X is), but that the morphism [X/G] → X/G is representable,
and so [X/G] is itself representable. Let T be the representing object. By Yoneda’s Lemma, the morphism
[X/G] → X/G is therefore induced by a unique continuous map T → X/G. Moreover, the morphism X → [X/G]
is always representable by quotient maps, which forces X → T to be itself a quotient map. One checks, by
assumption (1) and Lemma E.6.3.7, that the induced equivalence relation R := X ×T X on X yields a trivial
inertia stack I[R⇒X] , which forces the map R → G to be surjective. By the final assertion in Lemma E.2.3.5,
the map R → G is therefore a closed immersion and hence a homeomorphism, and T receives a homeomorphic
quotient map from X/G which is a section to the map T → X/G, so the Proposition is proved.                  □
   We now recall foundational material about inertia groups, highlighting how to view them as fibers of the
morphism ι : IX → X.
    Lemma E.6.3.9. Let (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) be a topological groupoid. For a point x ∈ X, let Ix = {y ∈ G :
s(y) = x = t(y)}. Then Ix equipped with the topology induced by G is a topological group.
    Proof. A quick way to see this is by observing that the first projection I[G⇒X] → X makes I[G⇒X] into
a relative topological group over X, whose multiplication X-morphism is induced by the composition law on
G of [G ⇒ X]. The fiber of I[G⇒X] → X over x is exactly Ix with the induced topology from the topology on
G.                                                                                                      □
    Lemma E.6.3.10. Let (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group. Then all the
topological groups Ix are locally compact Hausdorff.
    Proof. Closed subspaces of locally compact Hausdorff topological spaces are locally compact Hausdorff,
and Ix is closed in G since x ∈ X is closed (as X is weakly Hausdorff).                                □
    For x : T → X, define a sheaf Ix:T →X of groups on CGWHα,τ whose sections interpolate the topological
groups Iy . For any object T ′ of CGWHα , let

denote the set of pairs (f, ϕ) with f : T ′ → T a morphism and ϕ an automorphism of f ∗ (x) as an object of
X(T ′ ). The map
                                                 Ix:T →X → hT
sending a T ′ -section (f, ϕ) to f ∈ hT (T ′ ) makes Ix:T →X into a sheaf of groups over T .
     For the canonical map x : X → X := [X/G], Ix:X→X is nothing but I[G⇒X] from Definition E.6.3.4, with
its own map to X.

                               (f, ϕ) 7→ ((f ∗ (x), f ∗ (x)), ϕ) ∈ (X ×∆,X×X,∆ X)(T ′ ).
The right vertical map ι sends an element (a, ϕ) of IX (T ′ ) (with a ∈ X(T ′ ) and ϕ ∈ G(T ′ ) an automorphism
of a such that ∆X (a) = (s, t)(ϕ) in X × X) to a ∈ X(T ′ ) viewed as an object of X(T ′ ).
    We have:
                          X(T ′ ) = [G(T ′ ) ⇒ X(T ′ )], IX (T ′ ) = [G′ ⇒ I[G(T ′ )⇒X(T ′ )] ]
where G′ refers to the notation from Lemma E.6.3.6. The groupoid-theoretic fibre product thereby recovers
the description of Ix:T →X (T ′ ) as in the construction of Ix:T →X .                                  □

    Remark E.6.3.12. In the special case T = X and x is the quotient X → [X/G], Ix:T →X = I[G⇒X] and for
any point y ∈ X the induced morphism y : {y} → X → X fits into the assertion of the Lemma with T = {y}
and gives:
                            Iy:{y}→X = {y} ×y,X,ι IX = {y} ×y,X I[G⇒X] = Iy .
In other words, the inertia stack interpolates the inertia groups of all points of X.

     E.6.4. Equivalences. In this subsection we focus on stacks in topological groupoids that are equipped
with a chart, introduce related some concepts and establish some consistency checks.
     We have associated a stack in topological groupoids to a topological groupoid in a functorial manner. We
will now compare the two notions to study how far this functorial assignment is from being fully faithful.

      Lemma E.6.4.1. Let (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) and (X ′ , G′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ , i′ ) be two topological groupoids, and:
                                                   f : [G ⇒ X] → [G′ ⇒ X ′ ]
a morphism of topological groupoids. We write f = (f1 , f2 ) to denote the map f1 : X → X ′ on Ob-sets and the
map f2 : G → G′ on Mor-sets. Let f also denote the induced morphism:
                                                      f : [X/G] → [X ′ /G′ ]
of quotient stacks. The following are equivalent:
(1) f is fully faithful.
                                                E.6. STACKS ON CGWHα,τ                                                     929


(2) The natural map:
                                                 G → (X × X) ×X ′ ×X ′ G′
    is an isomorphism.
    Proof. The argument is identical to that in the proof of [SP, Tag 046S], noting that one has to use the
topology on CGWHα,τ to work locally and pick local sections, and that the analog of [SP, Tag 044V] still
holds for topological groupoids and their quotient stacks, with an identical proof.                      □
    Lemma E.6.4.2. Let (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) and (X ′ , G′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ , i′ ) be two topological groupoids, and:
                                                 f : [G ⇒ X] → [G′ ⇒ X ′ ]
a morphism of topological groupoids. We write f = (f1 , f2 ) to denote the map f1 : X → X ′ on Ob-sets and the
map f2 : G → G′ on Mor-sets. Let f also denote the induced morphism:
                                                    f : [X/G] → [X ′ /G′ ]
of quotient stacks. The following are equivalent:
(1) f is an equivalence.
(2) f satisfies the following two conditions:
    (a) the natural map
                                           G → (X × X) ×X ′ ×X ′ G′
        is an isomorphism,
    (b) the composition
                                                                pr      s′
                                                X ×f1 ,X ′ ,t′ G →2 G′ → X ′
        is a submersion.
    Proof. Just as for the analog of the result for groupoids on algebraic spaces (see [SP, Tag 046T]), one
uses [SP, Tag 046N] which characterizes equivalences between stacks on a site. The argument to check that
the assumptions of [SP, Tag 046N] are satisfied, using full faithfulness of f which is a consequence of Lemma
E.6.4.1, is identical to the argument in [SP, Tag 046T] upon replacing all objects in the site with objects in
CGWHα and replacing the fppf topology on algebraic spaces with the topology on CGWHα,τ .                    □
    Definition E.6.4.3. Let (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) and (X ′ , G′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ , i′ ) be two topological groupoids, and:
                                                 f : [G ⇒ X] → [G′ ⇒ X ′ ]
a morphism of topological groupoids. We write f = (f1 , f2 ) to denote the map f1 : X → X ′ on Ob-sets and
the map f2 : G → G′ on Mor-sets. Let f also denote the induced morphism:
                                                    f : [X/G] → [X ′ /G′ ]
of quotient stacks. We say f is a standard Morita equivalence if and only if:
(1) f1 : X → X ′ is a submersion,
(2) the induced map G′ → (X × X) ×(f1 ,f1 ),X ′ ×X ′ ,(s′ ,t′ ) G′ is an isomorphism.
    We have the following:
    Lemma E.6.4.4. Suppose (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) and (X ′ , G′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ , i′ ) are two topological groupoids, and:
                                                 f : [G ⇒ X] → [G′ ⇒ X ′ ]
is a morphism of topological groupoids. If f is a standard Morita equivalence then the induced morphism of
quotient stacks:
                                             f : [X/G] → [X ′ /G′ ]
930                                          CHAPTER E. TOPOLOGICAL STACKS


is an equivalence.

    Proof. Indeed, submersiveness of f1 implies submersiveness of X ×f1 ,X ′ ,t′ G′ → G′ (by Lemma E.2.3.6(6)),
and since G′ → X ′ is submersive (as it has a continuous section) we get the result by Lemma E.6.4.2.       □

      A partial converse holds:

      Lemma E.6.4.5. Suppose (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) and (X ′ , G′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ , i′ ) are two topological groupoids, and
                                                   f : [G ⇒ X] → [G′ ⇒ X ′ ]
is a morphism of topological groupoids. Suppose that the induced morphism between quotient stacks
                                                      f : [X/G] → [X ′ /G′ ]
is an equivalence. Then there exists a topological groupoid (X ′′ , G′′ , s′′ , t′′ , c′′ , e′′ , i′′ ) and morphisms of topological
groupoids
                            g : [G′′ ⇒ X ′′ ] → [G ⇒ X], h : [G′′ ⇒ X ′′ ] → [G′ ⇒ X ′ ]
such that g and h are standard Morita equivalences, and f ◦ g = h.

    Not all equivalences of quotient stacks are induced by a morphism of topological groupoids. However,
they are up to standard Morita equivalence.

    Lemma E.6.4.6. Suppose (X, G, s, t, c, e, i) and (X ′ , G′ , s′ , t′ , c′ , e′ , i′ ) are two topological groupoids, and we
are given a morphism between quotient stacks
                                                     f : [X/G] → [X ′ /G′ ].
Then there exists a topological groupoid (X ′′ , G′′ , s′′ , t′′ , c′′ , e′′ , i′′ ), a standard Morita equivalence
                                                  g : [G′′ ⇒ X ′′ ] → [G ⇒ X]
and a morphism of topological groupoids
                                                 h : [G′′ ⇒ X ′′ ] → [G′ ⇒ X ′ ]
such that f ◦ g = h.

      Proof. The idea is to form the 2-fiber product:
                                           X := [X/G] ×[X ′ /G′ ] X ′             / X′


                                                                                     
                                                      [X/G]                    / [X ′ /G′ ]

and observe that there exists an induced epimorphism:
                                                       X ×[X/G] X ′ → X
with X ×[X/G] X ′ representable. Let X ′′ be the representing object, so there are evident maps X ′′ ⇒
X, X ′ . Then one checks that upon calling G′′ := X ′′ ×[X/G] X ′′ , and upon defining the structure maps
to make a topological groupoid [G′′ ⇒ X ′′ ] accordingly, the resulting morphism of topological groupoids
g : [G′′ ⇒ X ′′ ] → [G ⇒ X] (using G′′ → X ×[X/G] X = G) is a standard Morita equivalence. One then uses
G′ → X ′ ×[X ′ /G′ ] X ′ = G′ (resting on f : [X/G] → [X ′ /G′ ]) to define
                                                 h : [G′′ ⇒ X ′′ ] → [G′ ⇒ X ′ ],
and this works.                                                                                                                  □

    Remark E.6.4.7. Standard Morita equivalences in CGWHα,τ -Grpd satisfy the right-Ore conditions.

equivalent, as a 2-category, to the 2-category of stacks in topological groupoids X → CGWHα,τ equipped
with a representable epimorphism X → X from an object of CGWHα .
